notes.explains: After gaining a kingside space advantage, White opens files on the queenside to give the major pieces access to the seventh and eighth ranks, where checkmate threats become decisive. The queen and rooks coordinate to attack the weak pawns and the king.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage on one side, use it to create threats on the other side by opening files for your heavy pieces. Combine mating threats with material gains.
notes.plans: Continue with b5 to open the queenside, then bring the rook to the second rank and the queen to f7 to create threats against the king and the a-pawn.

notes.explains: In this position, white's pieces are coordinating well, with threats like queen f7 and rook to b1 creating both tactical and mating ideas. Black's position is difficult because any attempt to address one threat allows another.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are well-coordinated, look for moves that create multiple threats, especially those that combine material gains with checkmating threats. This forces the opponent to defend against everything at once.
notes.plans: Continue to press with the initiative, looking for breakthroughs that exploit the opponent's lack of coordination.

notes.explains: Black's idea of knight d7 to prepare g5 was too slow. Once white successfully parried it, white's lead in development on the queenside became decisive, allowing white to convert the advantage.
notes.teaches: In the Exchange Slav, both sides must be urgent with their queenside play. A slow plan can allow the opponent to seize the initiative and create a favorable imbalance.
notes.plans: If you are white, aim to maintain the initiative and exploit any slow moves by black. If you are black, look for more active and faster setups.

notes.explains: The Exchange Slav is not a boring, passive opening. It requires urgent play from both sides, as white's queenside pressure can become overwhelming if black is too slow.
notes.teaches: Do not underestimate the Exchange Slav. It can lead to sharp, tactical battles where every tempo matters. Both sides need to actively fight for the initiative.
notes.plans: Study typical plans and move orders in the Exchange Slav to be prepared for the urgent nature of the position.

notes.explains: In the game, black's queen e8 was a critical mistake, allowing white to build up a winning attack. The move bishop g5 would have kept black in the game by challenging white's setup.
notes.teaches: In the Exchange Slav, be wary of passive moves like queen e8. Look for active defensive moves that contest key squares and maintain piece activity.
notes.plans: If you are black, consider bishop g5 to challenge white's plans and keep the position balanced.

notes.explains: The upcoming endgame class will cover important rook endgames, starting with basic ones and moving to more complex but crucial positions.
notes.teaches: Rook endgames are fundamental and often appear in practical play. Understanding key principles and patterns is essential for converting wins and saving draws.
notes.plans: Study basic rook endgames first, then progress to more complex ones, focusing on active rook play and king involvement.

notes.explains: In this Ruy Lopez, both players choose solid, non-risky setups. White avoids the Marshall Attack by playing d3 instead of rook e1, postponing the rook move and keeping the game in a more controlled, strategic channel.
notes.teaches: When facing a well-prepared opponent, you can sidestep sharp theoretical lines by choosing a quieter move order that still maintains central pressure.
notes.plans: White will later play c3 and d4 to challenge the center, while black consolidates the e5 pawn and prepares queenside play.

notes.explains: Black plays b5 and d6, typical Spanish moves that consolidate the e5 pawn and prepare to challenge the bishop. White responds with c3 and d3, creating a flexible setup where the bishop can retreat to c2 if needed.
notes.teaches: In the Ruy Lopez, the c3-d3 setup is a flexible way to support the center and keep the bishop active, while also preparing to meet ...Na5 with b4 or Bc2.
notes.plans: White aims to play d4 at the right moment, while black looks to play ...Na5 and ...c5 in Chigorin style.

notes.explains: White plays a4 to undermine the b5 pawn, and black responds with ...Bd7. Black's main plan is to play ...Na5 and ...c5, but white prevents this by playing Bc2, so that if ...Na5, white can play b4 and chase the knight away.
notes.teaches: When your opponent threatens a typical maneuver, you can often prevent it by repositioning a piece to a square that allows a pawn push to expel the knight.
notes.plans: White will continue with rook e1 and then the knight maneuver to g3, preparing the central break d4.

notes.explains: White is not yet ready to play d4 because of tactical issues like ...exd4 and ...Bg4, so he embarks on the classical Spanish maneuver of bringing the knight from b1 to g3 via d2-f1, improving the knight's prospects and supporting the center.
notes.teaches: In the Ruy Lopez, when the immediate central break is not available, a standard plan is to reroute the queen's knight to g3, where it supports the center and eyes f5.
notes.plans: White will play Nf1-g3, and if black takes on e4, white can recapture, though the position remains balanced.

notes.explains: Black plays ...d5, threatening to take on e4. White chooses to take on d5, giving up the center pawn but gaining compensation through black's queenside weaknesses and the target e5 pawn.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is worth giving up a center pawn to create long-term weaknesses in the opponent's camp, as long as you have sufficient compensation.
notes.plans: White will develop the bishop to d2 and continue to pressure the e5 pawn and the queenside weaknesses.

notes.explains: White has given up the center pawn, leaving black with an extra pawn in the middle, but white gains compensation through black's queenside weaknesses and the target on the e5 pawn.
notes.teaches: In such double-edged positions, material imbalance can be offset by dynamic factors like weak pawns and active piece play.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit the e5 pawn and queenside weaknesses, while black should consolidate and maintain the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's b4 push leaves the b-pawn isolated and unsupported, creating a classical weakness on the queenside. White can fix the a-pawn with a5 and target the b4 pawn.
notes.teaches: When an opponent advances a pawn without support, it can become a permanent target. Fixing pawns on the same color as your bishop can create long-term pressure.
notes.plans: White should play a5 to fix the a-pawn and then pressure the b4 pawn with pieces like the bishop on a4.

notes.explains: White's d4 break exploits the momentary disconnect in black's camp: the knight on a7 is offside, and the rook on b8 is inactive. This central push creates tactical threats.
notes.teaches: When enemy pieces are temporarily misplaced, a central pawn break can create immediate threats and unbalance the position.
notes.plans: White should follow up with d4, and if black captures, recapture with the rook to damage black's structure.

notes.explains: Black has reorganized well, achieving firm control of d5 and compensating for the weakened e6 and a6 pawns. White's knight on g3 is the inactive piece.
notes.teaches: After a dynamic sequence, it's crucial to identify which of your pieces is underperforming and find a route to activate it.
notes.plans: White should bring the knight to e4, where it hits the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6, forcing favorable exchanges.

notes.explains: In this position, the bishop defends the a-pawn and the knight controls key central squares like d4. The knight on g3 is out of play, and the move Nf5 is prevented by the rook on b5. The trade on e4 is favorable because it removes the misplaced knight and weakens Black's control over f6.
notes.teaches: When a piece is out of play, look for trades that activate your position and remove your opponent's defenders. Central control is often worth more than material.
notes.plans: After the trade, White can target the weak pawns on a5 and e4, while Black must reorganize.

notes.explains: The move Bxh6 is a speculative piece sacrifice. It's not objectively correct, but it creates practical winning chances by exposing the black king and disrupting Black's coordination. This type of move is typical of players who are willing to take risks for a win.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a dubious sacrifice can be a practical tool, especially when the opponent is under pressure and must find precise moves over the board.
notes.plans: After Bxh6, Black must capture, and White gets a dangerous attack with queen checks and threats.

notes.explains: Black faces a difficult choice after the sacrifice. The natural move Kh8 is actually less accurate than the counterintuitive Ke7, which runs into the attack but is objectively better. This illustrates the psychological difficulty of choosing moves that look dangerous but are correct.
notes.teaches: In critical positions, the most logical-looking move may not be the best. Players must rely on calculation and trust their analysis, even when the move appears risky.
notes.plans: If Black plays Kh8, White can continue the attack; if Ke7, Black can consolidate.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, White's attack is strong because Black's pieces are poorly coordinated, especially the king on h8 is exposed. White can target the a-pawn and create threats against the black king, while Black's minor pieces struggle to defend effectively.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are uncoordinated, even a material deficit can be compensated by attacking chances. Coordination is often more important than material count.
notes.plans: White should aim to take the a-pawn and continue the attack; Black must try to coordinate pieces and defend.

notes.explains: In this position, the black king on h8 is exposed, and the black light pieces are not coordinating well. White's rook(s) can be more effective than the two minor pieces if they don't cooperate.
notes.teaches: When evaluating material imbalances, consider piece coordination and king safety. Two minor pieces are usually better than a rook, but if they are uncoordinated and the king is vulnerable, the rook can be superior.
notes.plans: White should focus on attacking the exposed king, using the rook and pawns to create threats, while black must try to coordinate pieces and defend.

notes.explains: White chose to continue the attack with queen and rook rather than trade pieces, exploiting the exposed black king. The black king has little cover, and white's material investment (three pawns for a piece) is justified by the ongoing attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, prioritize attack over material trades. A material deficit can be acceptable if the attack is decisive.
notes.plans: White should continue to bring pieces to the attack, using checks and threats to force the king into a mating net.

notes.explains: Black made a decisive mistake by playing knight takes d4, allowing white to win the knight and deliver a mating attack. After that, black's defenses crumbled.
notes.teaches: In a difficult defensive position, avoid moves that open lines or remove key defenders. Look for ways to consolidate and reduce the attacker's initiative.
notes.plans: White executes the finishing combination, forcing checkmate.

notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez, after the Open Variation (knight takes e4), black can introduce a spicy twist with d4 and bishop e7, an idea previously played by Jeroen Piket. White must be prepared for such novelties, especially against a known opponent.
notes.teaches: In the Open Ruy Lopez, black has various move orders and ideas to create imbalance. Both sides should be familiar with the main lines and typical tactical motifs.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the initiative and exploit any inaccuracies, while black seeks to prove the soundness of the new idea.

notes.explains: After the sequence with rook takes c4 and d5, black can win the piece back, but white ends up with two pieces versus a rook. Here, white's pieces have more activity and coordination than in the earlier example, making white better.
notes.teaches: When comparing two pieces versus a rook, the activity and coordination of the pieces are crucial. If the pieces are well-placed and the rook is passive, the two pieces can be superior.
notes.plans: White should use the active pieces to create threats and exploit the rook's lack of activity.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, Black can play d5, attacking the bishop and rook simultaneously. After the tactical sequence, White must recapture on e5 to avoid hanging the knight, and White ends up with two pieces versus a rook, which is favorable because the pieces have more activity.
notes.teaches: When material is uneven, activity and coordination matter more than raw count. Two active pieces can outweigh a rook if the rook's side lacks coordination.
notes.plans: White should aim to keep the initiative and use the piece activity to create threats, while Black must try to consolidate and find counterplay.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2 to pressure the bishop and prevent Black from castling easily, then follows with f4, aggressively challenging Black's setup and keeping the king in the center. Black responds with g6 to defend key squares, and White plays Nc3 attacking the a-pawn.
notes.teaches: In the opening, preventing the opponent from castling and keeping their king in the center can be a key strategic goal, even at the cost of pawn structure.
notes.plans: White continues to develop and maintain pressure, while Black must decide whether to capture the a-pawn or push the b-pawn, weighing the weakness of the a-pawn against the health of the pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black has a choice between taking on a3 or pushing the b-pawn. Taking on a3 often yields little because those extra pawns cannot advance and do not cover important squares. White instead plays b3, preferring a healthy pawn structure and treating the a-pawn as a long-term weakness.
notes.teaches: Not all extra pawns are equal; a pawn that is weak and cannot advance may be more of a liability than an asset. Maintaining a sound pawn structure is often more important than grabbing material.
notes.plans: White aims to exploit the weakness of the a-pawn in the long run, while Black must find a way to activate the pieces and create counterplay.

notes.explains: After a series of centralizing moves, the position features a 'big meeting' in the center, with pieces clustered around the central squares. White's pieces are better placed, and Black's bishop on d6 is not effectively defending the king or attacking, as the pawn on e5 is well protected.
notes.teaches: Centralizing pieces is a fundamental principle that rarely goes wrong, even without deep theory. A piece that is not defending or attacking effectively is a liability.
notes.plans: White has threats of bringing the knight to g5 and f6, while Black's pieces are scattered. White must still play precisely to avoid giving Black counterchances.

notes.explains: Black plays a series of defensive moves, including Bb7, to block entry squares and seemingly reach an equal position. However, the position is actually very delicate, and Black has only one single move to survive, which is the counterintuitive Bh4, aiming to put pressure on White's position.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, there may be only one precise move to hold the balance. Finding such moves requires both memory and a deep feel for the position, and it is understandable to miss them without prior study.
notes.plans: Black must find the only move to survive, while White continues to press with threats against the weakened king side.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, Black has only one precise defensive resource to survive. The move Bh4 looks illogical but serves two purposes: it pressures the knight and bishop while also controlling the g3 square, preventing the knight from using it.
notes.teaches: When defending a difficult position, look for moves that serve multiple defensive purposes, even if they look unnatural. A single move can both create threats and restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Black intends to follow up with Qe7 to increase pressure, while White should seek active counterplay, such as Rf1 to prepare rook lifts or centralization.

notes.explains: After White's best response Rf1, the line continues with Qc8, Nf6+, and a sequence leading to an endgame where Black sacrifices a rook but gains enough counterplay with the rook and queen against White's exposed king.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up material is the only way to survive; the resulting activity and counterplay can compensate for the deficit. These 'strange' moves are hard to find without prior knowledge.
notes.plans: Black should aim to create threats against the white king, especially on the dark squares, while White must consolidate and convert the material advantage carefully.

notes.explains: When Black errs with Qc8 instead of the precise defense, White becomes clinical. By keeping pieces on the board with Bh3 and Qd3, White ensures that the rook and bishop tandem will outperform Black's rooks.
notes.teaches: When you have a material or positional advantage, avoid unnecessary trades that could let the opponent off the hook. Keep the pieces that give you the best winning chances.
notes.plans: White will aim to improve piece activity, possibly with Rf1-h1, and prepare to transition into a favorable endgame while maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: In the resulting endgame, White's d-pawn becomes a protected passed pawn, and the bishop is poised to support it. Black's rooks are helpless against the pawn's advance, especially once the bishop reaches a strong diagonal.
notes.teaches: A protected passed pawn in the endgame is a decisive advantage. Use the king and bishop to support its advance, and restrict the opponent's rook activity by controlling key squares.
notes.plans: White will push the d-pawn, use the bishop to defend it, and aim to create additional passed pawns on the queenside with a3-b4. Black must try to generate counterplay, but the pawns are unstoppable.

notes.explains: As the endgame progresses, White's connected passed pawns on the queenside, supported by the bishop, prove decisive. Black's attempts to create counterplay are insufficient, and White's king can also join the attack.
notes.teaches: Connected passed pawns are extremely powerful, especially when supported by a bishop. In rook endgames, keep the rooks on the board to maintain winning chances, but be ready to trade if it leads to a winning pawn endgame.
notes.plans: White will advance the a- and b-pawns, use the bishop to control key squares, and bring the king to support the pawns. Black's only hope is to create perpetual check, but White's king can escape.

notes.explains: The king walks around the back door to support the passed pawn, while the bishop and rook coordinate to create threats. The defender has no way to stop the check and the pawn promotion.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the king is a powerful attacking piece. Use it to escort passed pawns and create mating threats, while the minor pieces control key squares.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawn, use the king to support it, and keep the opponent's king cut off.

notes.explains: The defender resigned when the a-pawn was running and there was no way to stop the promotion. The game was effectively over.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the position is lost and avoid prolonging a hopeless defense. In winning endgames, convert efficiently by advancing passed pawns and using all pieces.
notes.plans: Continue the promotion plan and force resignation.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, white is up a pawn but the win is not trivial. The rook on b4 is ideally placed: it attacks the weak a-pawn, defends the b-pawn, and covers the kingside. However, a naive plan of bringing the king to the queenside fails because black can activate the rook and create counterplay with passed pawns, likely drawing.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the activity of the rook and the king's ability to support pawns are crucial. Simply having an extra pawn is not enough if the opponent can generate active counterplay.
notes.plans: White should seek a plan that improves the position without allowing black's rook to become active. The move g4 is a counterintuitive but strong idea, as it prepares to undermine black's kingside pawns while keeping the rook on b4.

notes.explains: Black's rook to c1 is a defensive resource, aiming to attack the b-pawn from behind with Rb1. If black just passes, white's rook can go to b4, so black prepares to challenge the b-pawn.
notes.teaches: When defending an endgame, it's important to find active defensive setups that create threats against the opponent's weaknesses, even if you are a pawn down.
notes.plans: Black plans Rb1 to attack the b-pawn, forcing white to decide how to handle the pressure.

notes.explains: The move g4 is counterintuitive because it seems to weaken the kingside, but it actually serves to create a passed pawn and deflect the black rook from its defensive duties. It also prepares to undermine black's pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, pawn breaks can be used to create passed pawns and activate the rook, even if they appear to weaken your own pawns. The key is to calculate the resulting rook activity and pawn races.
notes.plans: White plays g4, aiming to create a passed pawn on the kingside and force black's rook to deal with it, while the white rook remains active on b4.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, White's rook on b4 is well placed: it defends the kingside weaknesses, attacks the a4 pawn, and ties Black's rook to the b-file. The g3 pawn is a weakness that the rook cannot defend, so advancing it to g4 moves the weakness to a square the rook can guard, while also restricting the black king and creating a new weakness on f5 if Black trades.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, it is often worth advancing a pawn to eliminate a weakness and place it on a square where the rook can defend it, even if it allows pawn trades. The attacking side should seek to create a passed pawn majority on the side where they have more pawns, while keeping the opponent's king passive.
notes.plans: White aims to create connected passed pawns on the queenside, using the rook on b4 to pressure a4 and force Black's rook to stay passive. If Black's rook leaves the b-file, White can capture a4 and create a decisive 2-vs-0 pawn majority.

notes.explains: After g4, Black can play f5, trading pawns, but this gives White a new weakness to attack on f5 and leaves Black's king passive on g7. If Black declines the trade, White can advance the king up the board to support the pawns.
notes.teaches: When advancing a pawn to improve your structure, be prepared for the opponent to trade, but evaluate whether the resulting position still favors you. A passive king and a new weakness can outweigh the loss of a pawn.
notes.plans: White will continue to improve the king's position, aiming to support the queenside pawns and eventually win the a4 pawn, while keeping Black's king out of play.

notes.explains: White's rook on b4 is ideally placed: it defends the kingside, attacks a4, and prevents Black's rook from becoming active. If Black plays Rh1, White can trade the h-pawn for the g-pawn, and then either win with a check or advance the connected passed pawns.
notes.teaches: A rook on a file that both defends and attacks can neutralize the opponent's rook and create winning threats. Trading pawns to create connected passed pawns is often decisive, especially when the opponent's king is far away.
notes.plans: White will aim to trade the h-pawn for the g-pawn, then advance the connected passed pawns, using the king to support them. If Black's rook leaves the b-file, White can capture a4 and create a winning majority.

notes.explains: After the sequence g4, f5, gxf5, gxf5, White plays Ke3, preparing to advance the king. Black responds with Kh5, and White has several plans: bring the king to d2-c2 to force the rook off b1 and win a4, or play Kf4 to support the kingside pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the king's activity is crucial. Choosing the right square for the king can decide between winning and drawing. It's important to consider multiple plans and pick the one that maximizes your chances.
notes.plans: White can choose between advancing the king to the queenside to win the a4 pawn, or to the kingside to support the pawns. The best plan depends on Black's defensive setup.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, White has a choice among several plans. One plan is to bring the king to f4, sacrificing the h4 pawn to capture the f5 pawn, creating a strong passed e-pawn. Another is to bring the king to c2, force the rook off b1, and capture the a4 pawn. A third is to capture on a4 immediately, giving up the b2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When choosing a plan in a rook endgame, consider the activity of the king and the resulting pawn structure. A king that can join the attack and create a passed pawn is often more valuable than winning a pawn passively.
notes.plans: If the king goes to f4, the plan is to take on h4, then f5 with check, and then advance the e-pawn, using the rook to block checks. If the king goes to d2, the plan is to reach c2, force the rook off b1, and capture a4.

notes.explains: The king to f4 plan is winning, but it requires a precise move: rook g4 check. This rook placement blocks checks and allows the e-pawn to advance more easily, while the black king is either too far away or in the way of its own pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the rook can be used not only to cut off the enemy king but also to shield your own king from checks while advancing a passed pawn. This is a common technique to facilitate pawn promotion.
notes.plans: After rook g4 check, White advances the e-pawn, using the rook to block checks and the king to support the pawn. The black king is either too far away or blocks its own pawn's advance.

notes.explains: The king to d2 plan is less convincing. After capturing a4, the position is much closer to a draw because the black king is more active, and black has a passed pawn on f5 and the potential for another on h4. The white king is passively placed on c3, and the queenside pawns are less significant.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a rook endgame, consider the activity of both kings and the presence of passed pawns. A passive king and multiple black passed pawns can offset a material advantage.
notes.plans: If White goes for the d2 plan, they must be careful to keep an eye on black's passed pawns and avoid allowing black to activate their king. The position may be holdable for black with accurate defense.

notes.explains: The plan of getting the king to f4 is best because it gives an active king and proximity to the h-pawn. The key idea is to play rook g4 check before pushing e4, placing the rook on an active square.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, coordinate your rook and king to maximize activity. Use checks to improve rook placement before advancing pawns.
notes.plans: White should aim for king f4, with the rook on g4 to support the e-pawn advance, while keeping threats on the queenside.

notes.explains: Taking on a4 immediately relieves tension on b2, which is less effective than keeping the threat. Similarly, playing king d2 or c2 is passive. It's better to maintain threats on the queenside.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, keep tension and threats rather than resolving them prematurely. This forces the opponent to defend and gives you flexibility.
notes.plans: White should keep the a4 pawn as a threat, only taking it later if needed, while focusing on king activity.

notes.explains: After black plays rook b2, white responds rook b4, and black gets behind the a4 pawn with rook a2. Black then plays h6, placing the pawn where the king can defend it. White eventually plays king f4 anyway, but now the rook is tied down.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, pawn placement matters. Putting pawns on squares where the king can defend them frees the rook for other duties.
notes.plans: White should aim to activate the king while keeping the rook active, but must be careful not to get tied down.

notes.explains: Black cannot capture on e2 because white will simply capture on f5, and the black king on h5 is poorly placed, leading to a winning endgame for white. Black's king is too far from the action.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, king position is paramount. A poorly placed king can turn a seemingly good capture into a losing move.
notes.plans: Black should avoid taking on e2 and instead look for ways to improve king activity or create counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's inventive move rook c2 sets up stalemate tricks. If white captures on f5, rook c4 is strong, forcing the white rook to leave, and black can take on a4, leading to a draw.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, look for tactical resources like stalemate tricks and counterplay. Sometimes a counterintuitive move can save a lost position.
notes.plans: Black should consider rook c2 to create threats and force white to avoid taking on f5. White must find the precise move e4 to maintain winning chances.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, black can save the game by sacrificing the rook for the pawn and promoting his own pawn, leading to a drawn tablebase position. The key is to find a move like rook c2 that sets up this defensive resource.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a defender can sometimes draw by sacrificing the rook for the pawn when the resulting position is a theoretical draw, especially if the defender has a pawn of his own to promote.
notes.plans: Black should aim to force the exchange of rooks and promote his own pawn, while white must avoid allowing this simplification if he wants to win.

notes.explains: White has a winning endgame if he can keep the a-pawn on the board and advance it, but if the a-pawn is traded off, the resulting endgame is often drawn. The rook is best placed actively, such as on a6, to support the pawn's advance.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames with a passed pawn, the stronger side should keep the pawn on the board and use the rook to support its advance, while avoiding trades that lead to drawn positions.
notes.plans: White should push the a-pawn forward step by step, using the rook to protect it, and bring the king to the queenside to support promotion.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame with multiple pawns, choosing which pawn to capture first can be critical. Taking the f5 pawn first eliminates the opponent's main counterplay, while leaving it for later allows the opponent to create threats. The resulting passed e-pawn and potential queenside passer give winning chances.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice of captures, prioritize eliminating the opponent's most active pawn or counterplay, even if it means dealing with other pawns later.
notes.plans: Capture the f5 pawn first, then use the passed e-pawn and queenside majority to press for a win.

notes.explains: In queen endgames, king safety is the first priority. Here both kings are relatively safe, though black's extra c-pawn gives slightly more shelter. The next factor is piece activity: white's knight can jump to f5, but black has a strong square on d4 for its knight, which can also prevent white's jump.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, evaluate king safety first, then piece activity and pawn structure. A well-placed knight can compensate for an opponent's active piece.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play ...Nd4 to control key squares and neutralize white's knight, while white should seek to activate the knight and create pawn breaks.

notes.explains: When evaluating an endgame, check for passed pawns first. Here neither side has a passed pawn or immediate potential to create one, which contributes to the position being equal. Despite that, one side may still be preferable due to minor advantages like piece placement or pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a passed pawn is a major advantage; if neither side has one, look for other imbalances such as better piece activity or safer king to decide which side to prefer.
notes.plans: Both sides should aim to create a passed pawn or improve piece activity to tip the balance.

notes.explains: In this queen endgame, neither side has a passed pawn nor immediate potential to create one, making the position objectively equal. However, black has more dynamic options, such as invading on the dark squares or advancing the h-pawn, while white's only active plan is c3 and d4, which carries risks.
notes.teaches: In equal endgames, prefer the side with more active possibilities and safer king. Even if the position is objectively drawn, practical chances matter.
notes.plans: Black can aim for queen activity on the dark squares and h-pawn advances; white should consider c3 and d4 but be wary of weakening king safety.

notes.explains: White's move g4 is a serious mistake because it allows black to create a passed h-pawn. In queen endgames, a passed pawn is a decisive advantage. After g4, black can play Nxf5, and if white recaptures with the e-pawn, black's h-pawn becomes a dangerous passer.
notes.teaches: Avoid creating weaknesses that allow your opponent to generate a passed pawn, especially in queen endgames where such pawns are extremely powerful.
notes.plans: White should have avoided g4; if forced, white must recapture with the e-pawn to keep the h-pawn blocked, but black still retains an edge.

notes.explains: After white's c3 and d4, black's king is safer than white's. White's pawn advances have opened lines and weakened the king's position, allowing black to generate threats like Qe2+ and pick up queenside pawns. Even if white can create passed pawns, black's safer king is more valuable.
notes.teaches: When choosing between sides in an endgame, prioritize king safety over pawn structure. A safer king often outweighs the potential for passed pawns.
notes.plans: Black should exploit the weakened white king by activating the queen and targeting pawns; white must be cautious about further pawn pushes.

notes.explains: Black's h4 is a critical move, offering the h-pawn to activate the queen. If white captures, black recaptures on d4, leading to active queen play. Keeping the pawn on the board also carries risks, as white might generate counterplay with moves like Qh2 and e5.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, sacrificing a passed pawn can be a valid way to activate your pieces and create winning chances, but you must weigh the risks of allowing counterplay.
notes.plans: Black can choose between pushing the h-pawn to create threats or sacrificing it for activity; white must decide whether to capture or allow the pawn to advance.

notes.explains: In this queen endgame, black's pawn structure, though not classically better, is excellent for king safety, which is paramount. White's pawns may look better, but black's king is safe, and that lasting advantage is decisive.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, prioritize king safety over pawn structure. A safe king prevents perpetual checks and allows your own queen to be active.
notes.plans: Black should use the safe king to support the passed pawn, while white must seek active counterplay or perpetual check.

notes.explains: When defending a pawn-down queen endgame, it's crucial to eliminate pawns to increase drawing chances. Here, the defender plays a5 to trade off queenside pawns, reducing the attacker's material advantage.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, the defending side should actively seek to trade pawns, especially on the side where the opponent has a majority, to minimize the deficit.
notes.plans: The defender should aim to trade pawns and rooks, simplifying towards a drawn queen endgame or a queenless endgame.

notes.explains: In a rook and bishop endgame where the defender is down a pawn, the defender's priority is to trade off pawns, especially on the side where they are weak. Playing a pawn like a5 aims to liquidate the queenside pawns, reducing the attacker's winning chances.
notes.teaches: When defending a pawn-down endgame, actively seek to exchange pawns to simplify toward a theoretical draw. Even if the pawn advance looks passive, it can force favorable trades.
notes.plans: The defender should continue to look for pawn trades, while the attacker should avoid unnecessary pawn advances that create weaknesses.

notes.explains: The defending side in such endgames is often best served by passive but solid defense: placing pieces on good squares, restricting the opponent's pieces, and waiting for the attacker to commit. Active pawn advances by the defender can create weaknesses and expose the king.
notes.teaches: In a difficult endgame, the defender should prioritize solidity over activity. Let the opponent try to break through while you maintain a flexible, defensive setup.
notes.plans: The defender should keep pieces on flexible squares, avoid pawn moves that create weaknesses, and be ready to meet any invasion.

notes.explains: For the side with the extra pawn, the key to winning with bishops on the board is to create a passed pawn, especially on the e-file, and to use the bishops to create threats against the enemy king. Advancing pawns is part of the plan, but the real winning try is often to combine pawn advances with king attacks.
notes.teaches: In rook and bishop endgames, the presence of bishops allows you to attack the king, which can be more effective than simply grinding with pawns. Creating a passed pawn is a major goal, but it must be supported by piece activity.
notes.plans: The stronger side should advance pawns to create a passed pawn, while keeping bishops active to target the enemy king and restrict the defender's pieces.

notes.explains: In rook and bishop endgames, creating a passed e-pawn can be winning for white, but if black can neutralize it, the position often becomes a draw. The immediate moves are about restricting pieces and maneuvering.
notes.teaches: Assess whether a passed pawn can be supported and advanced; if not, the endgame may be drawn despite material or pawn structure advantages.
notes.plans: White should try to create and push the passed pawn; black should aim to block or trade it off.

notes.explains: White plays g4 to create attacking chances against the black king, even at the cost of trading h-pawns. The idea is to follow up with g5 to pressure the king, but this only works if the dark-squared bishops remain on the board.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's worth giving up pawns to open lines or create weaknesses around the enemy king, but you must ensure the attacking pieces (like bishops) stay on the board to make it effective.
notes.plans: White wants to play g5 and use the g-pawn to drive the king; black should seek to trade off the dark-squared bishops to defuse the attack.

notes.explains: Black's bishop to d4 forces the trade of dark-squared bishops, which is crucial because without them, white's attacking potential drops significantly. The resulting position becomes fortress-like for black.
notes.teaches: In positions where the opponent is trying to attack, trading off key defensive or attacking pieces can neutralize the threat and lead to a draw or a solid defense.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade dark-squared bishops and then consolidate, creating a fortress; white must avoid such trades if they want to keep winning chances.

notes.explains: In the rook and pawn endgame that arises, black can hold a draw by getting the king to g7 to defend the f6 pawn, effectively nullifying white's pawns. The only way for white to win is to zugzwang the black king or trap the bishop.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, a king in front of the pawns can often hold a draw, especially if it can defend key squares. Zugzwang is a common resource when the defender's pieces are tied down.
notes.plans: Black should aim for king to f8 and then g7 to defend f6; white must try to create zugzwang or trap the bishop to make progress.

notes.explains: In this pawn endgame, Black's king on f8 can reach g7, where it defends the f6 pawn and effectively neutralizes both white pawns. White cannot attack the dark squares to dislodge the king, so the position is drawn.
notes.teaches: A king placed in front of pawns can defend key squares and blockade them, making the position drawn even if material is unequal. Recognize when a king's central defensive posture nullifies an opponent's pawn majority.
notes.plans: If you are the defender, aim to get your king to a square where it defends the critical pawn and cannot be driven away. If you are the attacker, look for ways to create a second weakness or zugzwang to force the king away.

notes.explains: The idea of the defender's king defending a pawn from the side is similar to opposite-colored bishop endgames, where the defender can often hold a draw by placing pieces on squares the opponent cannot attack.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for defensive setups where your pieces cover the key squares and cannot be challenged by the opponent's pieces. This can turn a seemingly lost position into a draw.
notes.plans: When defending, seek to place your king and pieces on squares that are inaccessible to the opponent's pieces, creating a fortress-like structure.

notes.explains: White has no way to attack the dark squares, so the black king on g7 cannot be forced away. The only winning attempt would be to trap the bishop, but on an open board that is impossible.
notes.teaches: In endgames, if the opponent's pieces are on squares you cannot attack, you may not be able to make progress. Recognize when a position is drawn because the opponent's pieces are untouchable.
notes.plans: If you are the attacker, try to create weaknesses on the color complex you can attack. If you are the defender, keep your pieces on squares of the color the opponent cannot influence.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame study, the usual 'build a bridge' technique fails because the defending rook can harass the pawn from the side. The key is a tactical rook sacrifice to deflect the king and allow the pawn to promote.
notes.teaches: Sometimes in endgames, a tactical resource like a rook sacrifice is necessary to win, rather than relying on standard techniques.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, the king walks out to support the pawn, and the extra b-pawn prevents the defender's rook from stopping the promotion.

notes.explains: The presence of an extra b-pawn is crucial in this study because it shields the b7 pawn from the enemy rook's attacks on the b-file, making the promotion possible.
notes.teaches: In pawn races and endgames, extra pawns can serve as shields or blockers, not just as material.

notes.explains: When facing theoretical endgames, it's important to consider practical tries, especially in time trouble, by envisioning pawn exchanges that could give winning chances.
notes.teaches: In endgames, always look for the best practical try, not just the theoretical evaluation, because your opponent may err under time pressure.
notes.plans: Identify pawn pushes (like f5 or h5) that create passed pawns or improve your position, and choose the one that maximizes winning chances.

notes.explains: In this rook and pawn endgame, the key resource is creating a passed pawn. A protected passed pawn is even stronger, as it ties down the opponent's pieces and is a decisive advantage. The choice between pushing the f-pawn or the h-pawn is critical: pushing h5 would eliminate the potential of creating a passed pawn on the h-file, while f4-f5 aims to create a passer on the h-file after a trade.
notes.teaches: Always evaluate which pawn majority can produce a protected passed pawn. Avoid moves that destroy your own potential passers, as they also create targets for the opponent.
notes.plans: White should proceed with f4-f5, aiming to create a protected passed pawn on the h-file, while keeping the king active and the rook flexible.

notes.explains: After f5, Black captures, and White recaptures with the rook, creating a passed pawn on the f-file. Then White plays h5, creating a protected passed pawn (the f-pawn is protected by the h-pawn). This is a significant achievement, but the game is not yet won; the defender still has drawing resources.
notes.teaches: A protected passed pawn is a powerful asset, but the defender can still hold if they can blockade it or create counterplay. The attacker must use the king and rook actively to support the pawn's advance.
notes.plans: White should aim to advance the king to support the passed pawn, while the rook protects it from behind and cuts off the enemy king.

notes.explains: Black's defensive idea is to stop the advance of the f-pawn with f6, which also prevents the white king from penetrating via h4-g5. If White plays h6, the position is a draw because the black king gets in front of the pawn. White must avoid that and find a way to improve the king's position.
notes.teaches: The defender should aim to blockade the passed pawn and keep the enemy king out. The attacker must avoid moves that allow the defender to set up a blockade, and instead find ways to bring the king into the action.
notes.plans: White plays Rook d5 to clear the way for the king to approach f5, while also preparing to give checks. Black must choose the correct king retreat to avoid being trapped.

notes.explains: When faced with a checking rook, the defender must choose the king's square carefully. Going to h6 would trap the king, allowing the rook to check and force the king back, losing the pawn. The correct move is to go to g8, keeping the king cut off but safe, as rook and pawn alone cannot win if the king is cut off.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, king safety is paramount. Avoid moving to squares where the rook can harass the king and win pawns. Sometimes it's better to stay cut off than to step into a mating net or lose material.
notes.plans: White continues to probe with checks and tries to bring the king to f5, while Black must remain solid and avoid fatal king moves.

notes.explains: In a rook and pawn endgame, the defending king must choose a safe square. Some squares look safe but are illegal or lead to self-trapping; the correct square keeps the king cut off but avoids immediate loss.
notes.teaches: When your king is checked, choose the square that avoids further harassment and keeps the position tenable, even if it means staying cut off.
notes.plans: Place the king on the safest available square, accepting the cut-off but avoiding immediate pawn loss.

notes.explains: In a rook and pawn versus rook and bishop endgame, the attacking king must be brought in front of the pawn to support its advance. The defender's bishop may guard key squares, so the rook is used to harass the enemy king from the side, forcing it to give way.
notes.teaches: Use your rook to check the enemy king from the side, driving it away from the pawn's path, while your own king supports the pawn's advance. This is a standard technique in rook endgames.
notes.plans: Push the pawn forward, using checks from the side to force the enemy king away, and be ready to trade pieces if the defender captures the pawn, leading to a winning king and rook versus king endgame.

notes.explains: With an extra pawn, any rook exchange favors the side with the pawn. Using the rook as a shield to bring the king forward is a standard winning technique.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, if you are up a pawn, aim to exchange rooks to reach a winning king and pawn endgame.
notes.plans: Use the rook to shield the king from checks while advancing it to a dominant square.

notes.explains: The defender has multiple ways to hold: aggressive checking or passive defense. Passive defense can be less effort and safer, especially near time control.
notes.teaches: Choose the defensive method that requires the least calculation and is most reliable, especially when time is short.
notes.plans: Place the rook on the seventh rank and bring the king to g7 to create a solid fortress.

notes.explains: The attacker must anticipate checks and preempt them. A grandmaster move stops the check before it happens, rather than walking into it.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, when advancing your king, first neutralize the enemy rook's checking squares.
notes.plans: Play a rook check to force the enemy king to a less active square, then continue the king march.

notes.explains: After setting up a trap, the attacker must still find the most accurate continuation. A simple move like g5 can decisively win by cutting off the king and avoiding counterplay.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, look for the move that restricts the enemy king's activity and eliminates counterplay, even if it is not the most forcing.
notes.plans: Play g5 to secure the win, ensuring the enemy king cannot interfere with the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the defender's rook is poorly placed and the king is exposed to checks. The winning idea is to cut off the defender's rook with a pawn move, ensuring that the promotion square is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: A single inaccurate move in a drawn endgame can turn it into a loss. Always check for tactical resources like pawn breaks that restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to g5 to prevent the defender's rook from giving checks, then promote the h-pawn.

notes.explains: When defending a worse position, passive defense often fails. Active counterplay, even at the cost of material, can create practical chances and force the opponent to be precise.
notes.teaches: In difficult positions, look for aggressive moves that create threats against the opponent's king or weaknesses, rather than just waiting.
notes.plans: Seek counterplay with moves like knight e4, aiming for tricks against the king, and avoid entering lost endgames.

notes.explains: In a king and pawn endgame, the defender found a stalemate resource with a knight sacrifice. The knight on g4 cannot be captured because it would stalemate the defender, and the resulting position is drawn due to the weak pawn.
notes.teaches: Even in seemingly lost endgames, look for stalemate tricks and perpetual check ideas. A knight can be sacrificed to force a draw if the opponent cannot avoid the stalemate.
notes.plans: Use the knight to create a perpetual check or stalemate threat, and if possible, pick off a pawn to simplify to a drawn king and knight vs king.

notes.explains: In a knight endgame with few pawns, the knight's placement and the king's activity are critical. A move like knight f2 can allow the enemy king to escape, so it's often too adventurous. The knight should aim to control key squares and support pawn advances.
notes.teaches: In knight endgames, prioritize king activity and knight outposts over grabbing pawns if it lets the opponent's king become active. Sometimes the knight must go backward to come forward, using typical knight maneuvers.
notes.plans: Use the knight to harass the enemy pawns while keeping the king centralized. If the opponent repeats moves, find a new plan to improve the position.

notes.explains: Tactics are crucial even in endgames. A knight can force a draw by perpetual check or by winning a pawn, as seen with knight g7 forcing f6 and then knight t8 check, losing the f-pawn.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical resources in endgames, such as forks, checks, and pins, even when material is low. A draw can be secured by perpetual check or by winning the opponent's last pawn.
notes.plans: If you are defending, seek tactical tricks to hold the draw. If you are attacking, use tactics to convert your advantage.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame with four pawns versus three, the side with the extra pawn must create a passed pawn to have winning chances. Playing g4 fixes the h7 pawn, making it a potential target, and prepares to create a passer from the e and f pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames with a pawn majority, the key is to create a passed pawn. Fix your opponent's pawns to make them targets, and use your rook to support the pawn break.
notes.plans: Play h5 to exchange a pair of pawns and create a passer from the e and f pawns. Use the rook to cut off the enemy king and support the pawns' advance.

notes.explains: When defending a rook endgame, it's important to keep the rook active and find precise moves. Missing a move like rook e4 can give the opponent winning chances. The defender should look for ways to create counterplay, such as sacrificing a pawn to reach a drawn two-versus-one or creating a nuisance pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the defender must be precise. Look for active rook moves that create threats or force favorable pawn structures. Even in difficult positions, there may be drawing resources.
notes.plans: If defending, seek active rook play and pawn breaks to hold the draw. If attacking, keep the pressure and avoid allowing counterplay.

notes.explains: With connected passed pawns on e5 and f5, the rook supports them from behind. The immediate threats of f6 and e6 create decisive breakthroughs, forcing the defender to react or lose.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, place your rook behind passed pawns and advance them together. The threat of one pawn pushing while the other supports it can create unstoppable passed pawns.
notes.plans: Push the e- and f-pawns to the fifth rank, then use the rook to shield checks while the king advances to support the pawns.

notes.explains: When the defender checks repeatedly, the king can use the rook as a shield to advance toward the pawns, while the pawns continue to threaten promotion.
notes.teaches: In king-and-pawn endgames, the king must be active. Use checks as a way to improve your king's position, not just to avoid them.
notes.plans: March the king toward the passed pawns, using the rook to block checks, and only push the pawns when the king is close enough to support them.

notes.explains: The extra h-pawn is fixed and not a factor, so the focus remains on the e- and f-pawns. The defender's rook is passive, and the attacking king can triangulate to improve its position.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a fixed pawn on the side can be ignored if it doesn't create counterplay. Use triangulation to gain the opposition or improve your king's position.
notes.plans: Continue to bring the king closer, using the rook to cut off the defender's king, and prepare the final push e6 or f6.

notes.explains: The final breakthrough comes with e6, creating a protected passed pawn. The defender has no more checks, and the pawns roll forward to force promotion or win the rook.
notes.teaches: A protected passed pawn is a decisive advantage. When the defender runs out of checks, the pawns can advance to promote, often without needing to take the rook.
notes.plans: Push the protected pawn, and if the rook tries to stop it, use the other pawn to support or promote.

notes.explains: This endgame illustrates that a single trap or tactical idea can decide the game, but it requires the king to be activated throughout.
notes.teaches: Always activate your king in endgames. A well-timed pawn breakthrough can win, but only if the king is in position to support it.

notes.explains: In this English Opening line, after White plays Nxf6, Black's main recapture should be with the pawn, even though it looks scary because of aggressive lines like d5 or e4. The engine may show equality, but practically it's hard for Black to navigate without precise knowledge.
notes.teaches: When a recapture with a pawn looks dangerous but is theoretically sound, it's often the right practical choice if you know the key defensive ideas; otherwise, you may end up with a long-term structural disadvantage.
notes.plans: If Black recaptures with the queen instead, White can proceed with development and aim to exploit Black's weakened pawn structure.

notes.explains: After Black recaptures with the queen on f6, Black's pawns are separated into two islands, with doubled f-pawns and an isolated h-pawn. This makes pawn endgames very likely lost for Black, as the king must stay near the h-pawn to defend it.
notes.teaches: Pawn structure is a long-term factor; doubled and isolated pawns can be a decisive disadvantage in endgames, so it's worth accepting a temporary development deficit to avoid such a structure.
notes.plans: White should continue developing (e.g., a4, Bb2) while keeping the pawn structure in mind, aiming for a favorable endgame or middlegame attack.

notes.explains: When Black plays a5, White should not capture on a5 because that would create a weak a3-pawn and give Black counterplay with the bishop returning to a5. Defending the b4-pawn with Bc3 is also bad because it loses a pawn after a tactical sequence.
notes.teaches: When your pawn is attacked, consider all options: capturing, defending, or advancing. Sometimes advancing (b5) is the only way to maintain the pawn structure and avoid weaknesses.
notes.plans: After b5, White can proceed with d4 to challenge the center, as Black's f6-pawn is tied to defending e5.

notes.explains: After White plays d4, the f6-pawn is pinned to the defense of e5, so Black cannot easily play f5 or f4. If Black plays e4 to solidify the center, White can reroute the knight to an outpost like f4 or g3 to pressure the e4-pawn.
notes.teaches: A central pawn break (d4) can restrict the opponent's pawn moves and create outposts for your pieces. When the opponent's pawn is tied to defense, they lose flexibility.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and prepare to exploit the outposts or the pressure on e5.

notes.explains: The f6 pawn is fixed because it must defend e5, so black's f5 pawn is a permanent target. Black's e4 push would solidify the pawn structure but is a critical decision that may not yield immediate benefits.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is tied to defending a key central pawn, it becomes a fixed weakness that can be targeted. Consider rerouting a knight to outposts like f4 or g3 to pressure the opponent's structure.
notes.plans: Reroute the knight to f4 or g3 to pressure e4 and the f5 pawn.

notes.explains: Despite being behind in development, the position is comfortable because the queens are off the board, reducing king safety concerns, and the pieces have space. The opponent cannot easily punish the lag in development.
notes.teaches: Being behind in development is not always critical if the opponent lacks concrete threats, especially with queens off and no space disadvantage. Prioritize catching up in development while maintaining a sound structure.
notes.plans: Castle long to hide the king and bring the rook into play, then develop the bishop.

notes.explains: If black captures on d4, it opens the position but creates three pawn islands, separating the f-pawns from the queenside. This weakens black's structure and makes the f-pawns difficult to defend or advance.
notes.teaches: When considering a capture that opens the position, evaluate the resulting pawn structure. Creating multiple pawn islands can be a long-term weakness, especially if the opponent can blockade them.
notes.plans: If black takes on d4, recapture with the knight to keep the e-file closed and maintain pressure on the f-pawns.

notes.explains: Black's a4 move aims to bring the bishop to a5, but since the king will castle long, the rook doesn't need e1. The e-file remains closed after a recapture on d4, so the rook is better placed on g1 for a potential g-file attack.
notes.teaches: When choosing a rook's placement, consider the likely pawn structure and open files. A rook on a file that may open (like the g-file) can be more valuable than a conventional central file if the center is closed.
notes.plans: Castle long, then consider placing the rook on g1 to prepare a g-file attack, possibly trading off the f6 pawn to open the file.

notes.explains: The h4 push is not attractive because black can respond with h5, stopping the pawn's advance. The g-file plan offers more long-term prospects.
notes.teaches: Pawn storms on the flank require careful timing; if the opponent can easily block the pawn with a same-side pawn move, the attack may fizzle. Look for alternative plans that create lasting pressure.
notes.plans: Focus on the g-file plan rather than h4, aiming to open the file and attack black's king.

notes.explains: In this position, the plan of trading off the weak f6 pawn is considered, but it also opens the g-file for the opponent. The alternative of pushing h4 is less effective because black can respond with h5, limiting the pawn's advance.
notes.teaches: When considering pawn breaks, weigh the benefit of removing weaknesses against the potential opening of lines for the opponent. A pawn push that can be easily stopped by a symmetrical response may not be worth it.
notes.plans: Consider long castling to safety, but be aware that black might try to open the position with c6 or c5 to create counterplay.

notes.explains: After black plays c5, white can capture on e5 instead of c5, leading to a swap where black ends up with doubled c-pawns instead of doubled f-pawns. This is a favorable transformation for white.
notes.teaches: When your opponent creates doubled pawns, consider whether you can force a recapture that leaves them with a different set of doubled pawns, possibly less harmful to your structure.
notes.plans: Play Bc4 regardless of black's response, aiming to develop actively and keep the king safe. If black plays Be6, white can recapture on b5 with the bishop, maintaining safety.

notes.explains: In a variation where black tries to open the position with c6, white can respond tactically. If black captures on b5, white recaptures with the bishop, and the position remains safe for white. The engine confirms white is better, though not overwhelmingly.
notes.teaches: Tactical approaches in positions where you appear weaker on one side can be justified if calculation shows the tactics favor you. Always calculate before rejecting a move based on superficial safety.
notes.plans: If black plays c6, be ready to capture on e5 and then develop the bishop to c4, maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: In the endgame with two light pieces for a rook, the rook can be more agile due to open files, making the position tricky. White must be precise to convert the advantage.
notes.teaches: In piece-for-rook endgames, the side with the rook often has counterplay on open files, so the side with pieces must coordinate them well and avoid allowing the rook to become active.
notes.plans: Use the knight and bishop to target weaknesses and restrict the rook, while advancing pawns to create passed pawns.

notes.explains: In this position, the knight on c4 is less effective than the obvious knight to d7, which would be a natural and strong square. The speaker regrets not playing the straightforward move.
notes.teaches: Always consider the most natural, obvious moves first; they are often the strongest. Don't overlook simple development in favor of flashy alternatives.

notes.explains: The opponent played c5, closing the position to reduce the impact of his own weaknesses (king safety, doubled pawns). However, this move essentially kills his bishop, making it a serious positional concession.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has weaknesses, they may try to close the position to limit your attacking chances. Recognize that closing the position can also create new weaknesses, like a bad bishop.
notes.plans: Exploit the closed position by maneuvering pieces to target the weak pawns, especially the f6 pawn, and consider breaks to open lines when advantageous.

notes.explains: The speaker considered a tactical sequence with rook d6, but it fails because black can trap the rook on f6. The opponent had set a trap, but the speaker wisely avoids tactical complications and instead focuses on exploiting the structural weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Don't be lured into tactical battles if you have a clear positional advantage. Sometimes the best move is to decline a sacrifice or tactic and continue improving your position.
notes.plans: Target the weak pawn on f6 and consider plans like g4-g5 to undermine the pawn chain, but also look for more direct ways to exploit the weaknesses.

notes.explains: The plan of g4-g5 to attack the f6 pawn is possible, but the speaker realizes it might allow black to relieve the doubled pawns. Instead, he finds a more effective way: taking on e5 and then transferring the knight to e4, where it pressures f6 and can go to d6.
notes.teaches: When attacking a weakness, look for the most efficient method. Sometimes a slow plan is good, but if you can take immediate advantage, do so. Piece placement is key: a knight on e4 can be very powerful.
notes.plans: Play knight d2 to e4, from where it pressures f6 and can potentially go to d6, increasing pressure on black's position.

notes.explains: In this position, White has already created weaknesses in Black's camp and can now play actively instead of slowly. The knight transfer to e4 is strong because from there it can go to d6, pressuring the f6 pawn and supporting central breaks.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has weaknesses, switch from slow maneuvering to concrete action. Centralize your pieces on strong outposts like e4 to maximize pressure.
notes.plans: Play knight e4, then consider f4 to open the position, followed by rook f1 to exploit Black's passive pieces.

notes.explains: Black's pieces are poorly placed: the rook on a8 is out of play, and the bishop on c8 is stuck because b7 is hanging. White's pieces are better prepared for pawn trades in the center.
notes.teaches: Compare piece activity when considering pawn trades. If your pieces are more active, opening the position favors you.
notes.plans: Continue with f4, trade on e5, and use the rook on f1 to target f5.

notes.explains: By making quiet moves like bishop e2, White asks Black to find a plan, which can lead to mistakes. Black's attempt with f5 is likely to backfire in the long run.
notes.teaches: Use 'waiting moves' to put the burden on your opponent. Giving them rope often leads to errors, especially when they are already under pressure.
notes.plans: Keep applying pressure and be ready to exploit any inaccuracies.

notes.explains: After Black plays g4, White can use the pin on the g-file to win the light-squared bishop. Black's h5 move opens the g-file for White without the need to trade off the doubled pawns.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pawn moves help you achieve your strategic goals, it's a win-win. Recognize when their 'active' moves actually worsen their position.
notes.plans: Continue exploiting the open g-file and the weak bishop, converting the material advantage.

notes.explains: A strategy of trading down into a favorable endgame works when you have superior understanding or a comfortable position, not necessarily a higher rating. It is about being in a position of knowledge and steering the game to where you are most at ease.
notes.teaches: Choose plans that lead to positions you understand deeply, even against stronger opponents. Comfort and knowledge can outweigh raw rating.

notes.explains: Black's move c5 was a mistake because it left the dark-squared bishop passive and allowed White's pieces to occupy ideal squares, such as a knight on e4 pressuring f6 and d6.
notes.teaches: Avoid pawn moves that permanently trap your own bishop or give your opponent free rein to place their pieces on strong outposts.
notes.plans: Use the knight on e4 to increase pressure on f6 and d6, and prepare to exploit the weakened dark squares.

notes.explains: After black's bishop went to f5, White used pawns (g4, h4) to chase it, eventually trapping it on h7. Even if black defends the pawn, the bishop remains dead, effectively playing down a piece.
notes.teaches: When you can immobilize an opponent's piece with pawns, do so. A dead piece is often more valuable than winning a pawn, because it removes counterplay.
notes.plans: Continue to restrict the trapped bishop and use the extra material and active pieces to convert the advantage.

notes.explains: Even when objectively winning, if the opponent's pieces can come back to life, mistakes can happen. The goal is to keep their pieces dead and unable to move.
notes.teaches: Prioritize keeping the opponent's pieces passive over grabbing material. A position where the opponent has no counterplay is safer and easier to convert.

notes.explains: When you are already up material and your opponent keeps making passive moves that lose more material without generating counterplay, the game is effectively decided. The side with the advantage should simply continue improving and capturing.
notes.teaches: If your opponent is not creating threats, you should not rush; just keep taking what is offered and improve your pieces. Material advantages convert more easily when the opponent has no active play.
notes.plans: Continue to develop the bishop to the long diagonal, target weak pawns like b7, and prepare pawn breaks such as f4 to open lines for the bishop.

notes.explains: A knight on g5 may appear active, but it is vulnerable to being kicked away or to tactics involving the bishop on c2. The knight's threats (like Nxe6 or Ne4) are not real because the opponent can respond with strong moves that exploit the knight's position.
notes.teaches: Before placing a piece on an aggressive square, check if the opponent has a simple developing move that also attacks your piece or creates a bigger threat. A piece that can be driven back with tempo often wastes time.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays a move like Ng5, consider responses that either kick the knight (like h3) or exploit the diagonal with moves like Bc2, which may be stronger than immediate queen moves.

notes.explains: Queen moves like Qh6 or Qg6 can be one-move threats that are easily parried. For example, Qh6 threatens Qxh2, but if the opponent simply plays h3, the queen is misplaced and may be vulnerable to discoveries.
notes.teaches: Avoid placing the queen on squares where it can be attacked or where it becomes a target for discoveries. A queen should not be used for a one-move threat if the opponent can defend and gain a tempo.
notes.plans: Instead of speculative queen moves, look for moves that improve your position or create lasting pressure, such as Bc2, which may be more effective.

notes.explains: In this position, the queen on h6 or g6 looks tempting, but the opponent has a resource like Bc2 that refutes those ideas. The real issue is that the knight on g5 is not actually threatening anything concrete, so the pressure it seems to create is illusory.
notes.teaches: Before committing to a move, check if your opponent's apparent threats are real. If a piece like a knight on g5 has no clear follow-up, it may be misplaced, and you can ignore it or ask it to explain itself.
notes.plans: Consider developing the rook to e8 with the f8 rook, keeping the a8 rook active, and be ready to meet knight e4 with queen g6, which prevents the knight from taking on d6.

notes.explains: The knight on g5 is not threatening e6 or e4 because those moves fail tactically. For example, if the knight goes to e6, capturing on a6 loses, and if it goes to e4, there is a tactic involving Bxh2, Qh4, and a double attack on the king and bishop.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a knight outpost or a forward move, always check the tactical consequences. A move that looks aggressive can be refuted by a sequence that wins material or exposes the king.
notes.plans: If the knight goes to e4, be ready to play Bxh2, then after Qh4, Nxd6, Bxh4, and Kxh4, Qh4+ wins the bishop on e4. This leaves white with a bishop pair but down a pawn, which is still defensible.

notes.explains: The opponent's knight h3 was a positional mistake because the knight had no good square. The best practical chance for white was knight e4, even though it leads to a tactical sequence that loses a pawn but preserves the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is the one that gives you practical chances, even if it costs a pawn, because the bishop pair can create long-term compensation. Avoid making a move that leaves a piece passively placed without a plan.
notes.plans: If white plays knight e4, black should follow the forcing sequence to win a pawn, but then must be careful because white's bishop pair can generate sneaky threats. White should aim to survive and use the bishops actively.

notes.explains: The move c5 is interesting, but after dxc5, the queen can take on c3, creating threats. White can respond with Be3, connecting the rooks and preparing to recapture on c5 with whichever piece is appropriate.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn break like c5, be ready to recapture with the right piece. Connecting rooks and centralizing pieces can simplify the position and reduce tactical risks.
notes.plans: After c5, if black recaptures with the bishop, white can take on d7; if the knight recaptures, white can take with the other piece. White should aim to keep the position solid and avoid complications.

notes.explains: Playing f3 (or f6 for Black) is often a weakening move because it creates weaknesses around the king and opens diagonals for the opponent's bishops. It is only useful if it serves a concrete purpose, like bringing a knight back into play.
notes.teaches: Avoid pawn moves like f3/f6 unless they are necessary for a specific plan. Such moves can be a long-term weakness, so only play them when they are justified.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays f3, look for ways to exploit the weakened diagonal and the squares around their king. Consider opening the center or attacking on that side.

notes.explains: In this position, the knight on h3 is stuck and cannot easily return. The move Qh4 is strong because it prevents the opponent from playing f3 to free the knight, and it also supports an attack on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, look for moves that simultaneously restrict the opponent's pieces and improve your own. A move that does both is often the best.
notes.plans: Continue to restrict the knight and build up an attack. Use your pieces to target the weakened squares around the opponent's king, and be ready to switch to other plans if the opponent tries to free the knight.

notes.explains: If the opponent tries to bring the knight back with f4, that pawn move can become a target. The knight is still not free because f4 is hanging, and you can proceed with your own plans, like Nf6, with ideas of Ng4 or c5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a weakening pawn move to free a piece, do not panic. Often the pawn becomes a weakness that you can attack, and the piece is still not fully active.
notes.plans: Continue to develop your pieces and put pressure on the weak pawn. Look for ways to increase the pressure, such as attacking the pawn with pieces or opening lines.

notes.explains: The opponent's attempt to bring the knight back with Nf2 is impossible because it would allow a tactic: Bxa4, and if the queen takes, then Qg2 and Bf3 wins the queen. This shows that the knight is still trapped.
notes.teaches: Before allowing the opponent to free a piece, check for tactical resources that keep it trapped. Sometimes the opponent's attempt to improve a piece creates new weaknesses that you can exploit.
notes.plans: If the opponent tries to free the knight, be ready to punish it with tactics. Keep your pieces coordinated to create threats that prevent the opponent from improving their position.

notes.explains: When the opponent's knight is misplaced on h3 and the dark-squared bishop is active, the move f3 is often tempting but insufficient because it doesn't address the immediate threat to h2. The correct way to free the knight is to play f4, which blocks the bishop's diagonal and gives the knight a retreat square.
notes.teaches: When your piece is attacked or trapped, look for a pawn move that both blocks the opponent's attacking line and provides a retreat square, rather than a move that only superficially addresses the issue.
notes.plans: If you have a knight on h3 and your king is exposed, consider playing f4 to block the bishop and allow the knight to retreat to f2 or g1, while also preparing to challenge the center.

notes.explains: In a position with opposite-colored bishops and an exposed king, material is not the only factor. Even if the opponent can win a pawn, the resulting attack on the king can be decisive. Here, the bishop on b7 and the queen can coordinate to create threats that outweigh the material deficit.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and the opponent's king is exposed, consider sacrificing material to open lines and launch a direct attack. The initiative and attacking chances can be worth more than a pawn.
notes.plans: If the opponent captures a piece, respond by activating your pieces to target the enemy king, using checks and threats to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: When choosing between two candidate moves, the one that seems to have no immediate follow-up may be better if it creates long-term weaknesses in the opponent's position. Here, bishop g2 leaves the white king on g2 exposed, which is a permanent weakness that can be exploited later.
notes.teaches: Evaluate moves based on the resulting king safety and long-term weaknesses, not just immediate tactical threats. A move that exposes the enemy king can be more valuable than one that wins material but allows the king to escape.
notes.plans: After exposing the enemy king, bring your pieces to bear on the weakened squares, using threats to force the opponent to defend and eventually break through.

notes.explains: In a position with an exposed king, even a small material deficit is irrelevant if you can generate a mating attack. With three pieces attacking, you can often force checkmate without needing to regain the material.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is exposed, prioritize bringing all available pieces to the attack. A coordinated attack with three pieces can be decisive even if you are down material.
notes.plans: Use forcing moves like checks and threats to drive the king into a mating net, and do not be distracted by material gains that slow down the attack.

notes.explains: The opponent's reluctance to create weaknesses (like playing f4) allowed the knight on h3 to remain passive, but also left the king vulnerable. The player with the initiative should keep the pressure on, even if there is no immediate win.
notes.teaches: Do not avoid all pawn moves that create weaknesses if they are necessary to improve your piece activity or defend against threats. Conversely, if your opponent refuses to create weaknesses, you can use that to maintain pressure and slowly improve your position.
notes.plans: Continue to improve your pieces and create threats, forcing the opponent to make difficult decisions. If the opponent leaves a piece passively placed, exploit that by increasing the pressure on other parts of the board.

notes.explains: The player considered a knight move to g4 but rejected it because it would allow f4, defending the h2 square, and because the knight might be needed for tactics involving the e4 square.
