notes.plans: Black aims to complete development, castle kingside, and then challenge the center with moves like ...d6 and ...Re8.

notes.explains: The Morphy Defense (…a6) is a common way for Black to force White's bishop to retreat. This move gains time because White must move the bishop again, and it also prepares ...b5 to gain space on the queenside.
notes.teaches: Every move in the opening should have a purpose. Moves like ...a6 can gain time by attacking a piece and also create useful pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Black continues with ...Nf6, developing a piece and attacking the e4 pawn, while White castles to safety.

notes.explains: Black's move ...Be7 is a defensive move that blocks the e-file, preventing White's rook from attacking the king along that file. It also protects the f6 knight, anticipating a potential pin by White's bishop to g5.
notes.teaches: In the opening, it's crucial to anticipate your opponent's threats and make moves that address them. Understanding the purpose behind each move is more important than memorizing sequences.
notes.plans: Black is ready to castle, and White will continue with Re1, preparing to challenge the center.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on e7 prepares to win the e4 pawn by Nxe4, and if the knight is recaptured, the knight can go to c5 to attack the bishop on a4. If white takes the pawn, black can castle because the rook on e1 is not yet there to give check.
notes.teaches: Understanding the reasons behind opening moves is more important than memorizing them. Knowing why a move is played helps you find the right continuation when the memorized line ends.
notes.plans: White should protect the e4 pawn, but with the intention of playing for more than equality.

notes.explains: White protects the e4 pawn with Re1 rather than d3 or Nc3 because he wants to advance d2-d4, creating a strong pawn center. He first plays c3 to support the advance, so that if black takes on d4, he can recapture with the c-pawn and maintain two central pawns.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prefer moves that support your long-term plans over merely adequate ones. A strong pawn center can be a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: White will play c3 and then d4, aiming to establish a dominant pawn duo in the center.

notes.explains: After Re1, white threatens to win the e5 pawn by Bxc6, gxc6, Nxe5, and if the queen attacks the knight, it can retreat to f3, attacking the queen and protecting e4. Black must respond with b5 to drive the bishop back, which is why black played a6 earlier.
notes.teaches: Every move should have a purpose. The early a6 move was prophylactic, preparing to kick the bishop with b5 when needed.
notes.plans: Black will play b5, forcing the bishop to retreat, and then strengthen his pawn chain with ...d6 and ...c7.

notes.explains: Black castles to get the king to safety before white plays d4. White would like to play d4 immediately, but black could then play Bg4, pinning the knight and creating tactical threats against the d4 pawn. White must first prevent Bg4 with h3.
notes.teaches: Before executing a central pawn break, ensure that your opponent cannot create a pin or other tactical resource that would undermine it. Prophylactic moves like h3 can be necessary to secure the position.
notes.plans: White will play h3 to prevent Bg4, then proceed with d4.

notes.explains: After White plays d4, White has the aggressive center pawns on e4 and d4, putting pressure on Black's e5 pawn, which is attacked by the knight and the d4 pawn but only defended by the pawn. Black's Breyer maneuver redevelops the knight to d7, where it defends e5 and also supports the knight on f6, improving Black's central and kingside defense compared to the Chigorin.
notes.teaches: In the Ruy Lopez, Black's knight often goes to d7 to reinforce the e5 pawn and maintain a solid defensive structure, rather than being misplaced on the side.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Be7, ...Rf8-e8, ...g6, and ...Bf8-g7, completing a flexible setup.

notes.explains: White should not develop the c1-bishop prematurely: placing it on e3 would block the queen's defense of e4, and on g5 it would be ineffective because the f6 knight is well defended and Black could gain a tempo with ...h6. Instead, White develops the queen's knight to d2, intending a typical Ruy Lopez maneuver: Nb1-d2-f1-g3, where it protects e4 and eyes f5 without blocking the bishop.
notes.teaches: In the Ruy Lopez, White often uses the knight maneuver to f1-g3 to reinforce the center and prepare a kingside attack, while delaying the development of the c1-bishop until a better square becomes available.
notes.plans: White will play Nd2-f1-g3, then later develop the bishop to a more active diagonal.

notes.explains: Black develops the c8-bishop to b7, attacking the e4 pawn. Since the pawn is defended twice and attacked twice, White cannot proceed with the knight maneuver until he adds another defender. White voluntarily retreats the bishop from b3 to c2, protecting e4. This is similar to the Chigorin, but in the Breyer Black's knights are better placed, so the retreat is less of a concession.
notes.teaches: When a key pawn is under attack, it may be necessary to add a defender before executing a planned maneuver, even if it means retreating a piece to a less active square.
notes.plans: White will continue with Nd2-f1-g3, while Black prepares ...Re8, ...g6, and ...Bg7.

notes.explains: Black executes a redeployment: rook to e8, bishop from e7 to f8, then g6 and Bg7. This creates a fianchettoed bishop on g7, and the g6 pawn controls the f5 square, preventing White's knight from landing there. Black's setup is solid but defensive, while White has a space advantage with his center pawns and better piece activity.
notes.teaches: In the Breyer, Black often fianchettoes the king's bishop to create a robust kingside structure, while White aims to maintain central pressure and piece activity.
notes.plans: Black will castle kingside and aim for ...c5 to challenge White's center, while White will complete his knight maneuver and seek active play.

notes.explains: White's knight on g3 defends the pawn, and White's overall setup is sound: knights are well placed, the bishop is still to develop, and the pawn structure is aggressive. Black's position is not bad but is more defensive.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a position, compare the activity of pieces and the nature of pawn structures: an aggressive pawn structure with well-placed knights can outweigh a material threat that is easily parried.
notes.plans: White should continue developing the bishop and look to exploit the space advantage; Black should seek counterplay by completing development and challenging the center.

notes.explains: Black plays g6 to take away the f5 square from White's knights and prepares to fianchetto the bishop to g7, where it will exert pressure along the long diagonal. This is a typical plan in the Breyer to improve the bishop's scope.
notes.teaches: A pawn move like g6 can serve a dual purpose: it restricts enemy knight outposts and prepares a fianchetto, which is a common way to develop a bishop to a strong diagonal.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Bg7, completing kingside development, while White may expand in the center with d5 to gain space.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, challenging White's d4 pawn, and later c4, which takes squares away from White's bishop and opens a square for Black's knight to centralize. This is part of Black's plan to fight for central control and improve piece activity.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves can be used to restrict enemy pieces and create outposts for your own. A pawn advance like c4 can be a multi-purpose move that improves your position while limiting your opponent's options.
notes.plans: Black aims to centralize the knight and maintain a strong pawn chain; White should respond by developing pieces and challenging Black's central pawns.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to g5, pinning Black's knight. Black correctly responds with h6 to force the bishop to retreat before White can play Qd2, which would reinforce the pin and prevent h6.
notes.teaches: When a bishop pins a knight, the defender should often challenge the pin immediately with a pawn move like h6, especially if the opponent can strengthen the pin with a queen move.
notes.plans: After the bishop retreats, Black can proceed with his plan of centralizing the knight and completing development.

notes.explains: White plays d5, gaining space and cramping Black, but Black's solid pawn structure and well-developed pieces mean the space disadvantage is not critical. Later, White captures on f6, giving Black doubled pawns, but Black obtains two bishops and a defensible position.
notes.teaches: A space advantage is valuable, but it can be neutralized by a solid pawn structure and active pieces. Doubled pawns are a weakness, but they can be offset by the bishop pair, especially when the position is closed.
notes.plans: White should try to exploit the doubled pawns and the space advantage, while Black should use the bishops to defend and seek counterplay on the open lines.

notes.explains: White plays Qe3, attacking the c5 pawn, forcing Black to defend with Qc7. This prevents Black from playing Bg7 immediately because the pawn is under attack. The position is approximately even, with a slight edge for White.
notes.teaches: Attacking a pawn can force the opponent to make a defensive move that disrupts their planned development. This is a common way to gain a tempo or restrict the opponent's options.
notes.plans: White continues to pressure Black's queenside, while Black must defend the pawn and eventually find a way to develop the bishop.

notes.explains: White retreats the knight to f1, which seems odd but prepares a future g4 pawn advance to attack Black's kingside and open lines against the king. The knight on f1 also unblocks the f-pawn, allowing this plan.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece retreat is a strategic maneuver to prepare a pawn storm. A knight on the back rank can be repositioned to support a kingside attack.
notes.plans: White will aim for g4 to undermine Black's pawn structure and create attacking chances against the black king.

notes.explains: Black plays Rb8, placing the rook on the b-file to pressure White's b-pawn and potentially open lines with cxd4. However, this move has a drawback: it abandons the defense of the e-pawn, leaving the queen to defend it alone, which ties the queen down.
notes.teaches: Rook moves to semi-open files can create counterplay, but they can also leave other weaknesses. Always consider what a piece was defending before moving it.
notes.plans: Black is looking for counterplay on the queenside, but must be careful not to leave the kingside too weak. White may try to exploit the queen's limited mobility.

notes.explains: White makes a minor inaccuracy by moving the knight to d2, which is not a serious mistake but gives Black some chances. The position remains roughly balanced.
notes.teaches: Even small inaccuracies can matter in a balanced position. Always look for the most active square for your pieces, even when retreating.
notes.plans: Both sides should continue to improve their pieces and look for the best squares to activate them.

notes.explains: When the rook leaves the defense of a pawn, the queen becomes overloaded, tied to protecting that pawn. This creates a double-edged situation: the rook is more actively placed, but the queen's mobility is restricted.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a piece move leaves another piece overburdened. The opponent's queen being tied to defense can be a long-term weakness to exploit.
notes.plans: Consider moves that increase pressure on the pawn the queen must defend, forcing the queen to remain passive.

notes.explains: In this position, White missed a stronger move: queen to g5, which would attack the black king side and the temporarily undefended knight on f6. Instead, a quieter move allowed Black to equalize.
notes.teaches: When a piece is temporarily undefended, look for aggressive moves that exploit it, even if the move seems surprising. A 'minor mistake' can be missing a chance to create concrete threats.
notes.plans: If the queen goes to g5, Black must defend the knight, and White can then reposition the queen to h4, anticipating a knight retreat that would otherwise gain a tempo.

notes.explains: The queen on h4 is a strong square: it supports a pawn advance to g4, prepares to open lines, and avoids losing a tempo to a knight jump to h7. It also sets up a future pawn break and rook infiltration.
notes.teaches: Place pieces on squares where they support pawn advances and avoid being harassed by enemy pieces. A queen that is both safe and supportive of a pawn storm is very effective.
notes.plans: White plans to advance the g-pawn, open the rook file, and bring the rook and queen into the attack on the king.

notes.explains: White later played a passive bishop retreat, missing the aggressive g4 break that would attack Black's pawn chain. The computer recommends g4 as an exclamation move, breaking up Black's kingside structure.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a pawn break like g4 can be the key to opening lines and creating attacking chances. Passive moves allow the opponent to consolidate.
notes.plans: After g4, if Black captures, White recaptures and the queen goes to c8 to defend a pawn, while the knight moves to h4 to support the g-pawn.

notes.explains: Black can achieve equality with the move f5, which attacks White's pawn chain, creates a threat against the queen, and blocks the queen's defense of a pawn. This leads to complications.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn chain, look for breaks that undermine it and create tactical threats. A move like f5 can simultaneously attack multiple targets and disrupt the opponent's coordination.
notes.plans: Black plays f5, and after the dust settles, the position becomes complex with chances for both sides.

notes.explains: In this position, Black can achieve equality by breaking up White's pawn chain with f5, which attacks a pawn and creates tactical threats involving the queen and pawns.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong pawn center, look for pawn breaks like f5 to undermine it and create tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Play f5, and if White captures, recapture to open lines and generate threats.

notes.explains: After exchanges, Black should take central pawns when possible, as this brings the bishop to the center where it defends the kingside and can operate on key diagonals.
notes.teaches: Centralizing pieces, especially bishops, increases their activity and defensive potential.
notes.plans: Capture the d5 pawn with the bishop, then reposition it to support the kingside.

notes.explains: White made a passive move, allowing Black easier equality. White should have played g4 to maintain a slight edge, but instead allowed Black to redeploy the rook to e8.
notes.teaches: In balanced positions, proactive moves like g4 can preserve an advantage, while passive moves give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: White should seek active moves to maintain pressure, but if not, the game may simplify to a draw.

notes.explains: White chose to liquidate rooks and head for a draw, despite having a slight advantage. The computer suggested h4 to allow a knight to g5 and block Black's pawns, but White preferred simplification.
notes.teaches: When you have a small advantage, it's often better to keep pieces on the board and create pressure rather than trade down to a draw.
notes.plans: If playing for a win, consider h4 to improve piece activity and restrict Black's pawns.

notes.explains: White's h4 was a minor mistake because it opened a diagonal for Black's bishop. The pawn was better placed to restrict the bishop's activity.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves can create weaknesses; consider how they affect piece placement and diagonals.
notes.plans: Black should bring the bishop to the open diagonal to increase pressure.

notes.explains: White made a subtle mistake by moving the knight, leaving the back rank vulnerable. Better was to drop the queen back to defend the back rank and maintain the draw.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of back-rank weaknesses and ensure your pieces defend against tactical shots.
notes.plans: White should retreat the queen to defend the back rank, while Black can try to exploit the knight's misplacement.

notes.explains: Black started a good maneuver with Bh6, attacking the queen and knight, but missed the best continuation. The bishop on h6 creates threats because the knight is unprotected and the queen is not defending properly.
notes.teaches: When pieces are unprotected, look for tactical blows like bishop moves that attack multiple targets.
notes.plans: Black should continue with Bh6, and if White blocks with f4, there may be a pin and combinative ideas.

notes.explains: In this position, the queen on the back rank is better than dropping to a square where the bishop can capture the knight, because the queen would recapture and leave the pawn unprotected, allowing a knight fork that wins the ending.
notes.teaches: When evaluating queen moves, consider whether they leave pieces undefended or allow tactical shots like forks. Sometimes retreating the queen to a safer square is more important than immediate activity.
notes.plans: White should block the bishop's line with f4 to prevent the tactical sequence, but must be aware of the resulting pin and the potential for Black to exploit it with a combinative idea.

notes.explains: Black has a pin on the f4 pawn, and after pawn takes pawn, the bishop can take the pawn, winning material. The best move is to retreat the knight to a square that protects the key square and maintains the threat, rather than playing a queen move that looks active but is not best.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin, look for ways to reinforce the pressure rather than going for superficial queen activity. The best move often improves the position of a piece while maintaining the threat.
notes.plans: Black should move the knight back to protect the square and then execute the pawn-break sequence to win a pawn. White must defend the pawn, for example with Ng2.

notes.explains: The winning move for Black is a knight jump to a strong outpost square, anchored by a pawn, where it attacks the queen and also attacks an undefended pawn. White cannot defend both, and once that pawn falls, Black gets a passed pawn with a winning pawn majority.
notes.teaches: Knights on strong outposts can create double attacks that overload the defense. When calculating, look for quiet knight moves that hit multiple targets and are difficult to meet.
notes.plans: Black should play the knight to the outpost square, winning the pawn, and then convert the passed pawn. White has no adequate defense.

notes.explains: Even top players miss such moves in calculation. In the game, Black missed the knight move and instead repeated moves, likely due to time trouble, leading to a draw. Later, Black missed another winning idea involving a knight retreat that protects a pawn and blocks checks, freeing the queen to push the pawn and win the knight.
notes.teaches: Time trouble often causes even strong players to miss tactical resources. Always look for defensive moves that simultaneously create threats, such as a knight move that protects a pawn and blocks a check.
notes.plans: In the final position, Black should have played the knight back to a square that protects the pawn and blocks the queen's check, then push the pawn to win the knight. White's best defense is to block the passed pawn rather than take the pawn with check.

notes.explains: In the Breyer variation of the Ruy Lopez, Black plays a6 to prevent the bishop from pinning the knight, then retreats the knight to d7, a characteristic maneuver. In the Fischer-Spassky game, Fischer chose a different plan against Spassky's setup.
notes.teaches: The Breyer maneuver aims to reposition the knight to d7, supporting the center and preparing to challenge White's center. Understanding the typical plans in this variation is essential for playing it effectively.
notes.plans: In the game, Spassky played Bf8, and Fischer took a different approach. The lesson is to be flexible in the opening and choose plans based on the opponent's setup.

notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6, White can choose to retreat the bishop rather than pin the knight. Black's Breyer maneuver involves retreating the knight from c6 to b8 and then to d7, preparing to support the e5 pawn and reorganize the pieces.
notes.teaches: The Breyer is a solid and flexible setup for Black in the Ruy Lopez, aiming for a sound but passive position that can be equalized with accurate play.
notes.plans: Black typically develops the knight to d7, plays ...g6, ...Bg7, and ...f5 or ...d6, aiming for a slow buildup and counterplay on the kingside or center.

notes.explains: In the Breyer, Black has a choice between the traditional ...Bf8 and the more active ...a5. The computer suggests ...a5 is the best way to equalize, as it prepares to liquidate White's queenside pawns and reach an even game.
notes.teaches: When facing a space disadvantage, look for pawn breaks that can trade off weaknesses and simplify the position to achieve equality.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...a5, White may respond with b4, but Black can then play ...axb4 and ...bxa4, trading off the queenside pawns and easing the defense.

notes.explains: In the game, Spassky chose the traditional ...Bf8, which still allows equality but is not the most precise. The main line continues with White playing b3, Bb2, and Nbd2, fighting for control of key squares. Black must be careful to defend the e5 pawn and find active counterplay.
notes.teaches: Even in a solid opening, precise move orders matter; missing the most active continuation can give White more freedom, though the position remains defensible.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play ...c5 to challenge the center and trade off pawns, or use the queen to support the e5 pawn and prepare ...c5.

notes.explains: In the resulting middlegame, White has won a pawn but Black has compensation: two bishops, open lines, a strong passed pawn, and rooks on open files. The computer evaluates the position as even or only slightly better for White, with Black able to hold a draw.
notes.teaches: Material is not the only factor in a position; dynamic compensation such as piece activity, pawn structure, and open files can offset a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: Black should activate the bishops and rooks, use the passed pawn as a distraction, and aim to trade down to a drawn endgame if necessary.

notes.explains: In this study, black's king is boxed in by his own bishop and pawns, and the winning idea is to force zugzwang so that black must make a weakening move. The key is to restrict the black king's escape squares, especially a3, before committing to captures.
notes.teaches: When facing a king trapped by its own pieces, look for moves that further restrict its mobility rather than immediately grabbing material. Zugzwang often decides such positions.
notes.plans: Play a move like bishop d6 to control the a3 square, then respond to black's attempts to free the king by maintaining the net and only capturing when it doesn't let the king out.

notes.explains: If white prematurely plays bishop d5, black can promote the pawn, and after white captures, the black king escapes because the bishop no longer controls the key escape squares. The resulting material (two bishops vs one bishop) is only a draw, so the win is missed.
notes.teaches: In endgames and studies, do not rush to win pawns if it allows the enemy king to escape. Evaluate the resulting position for winning chances before trading off your advantage.
notes.plans: Avoid bishop d5; instead, use the bishop to maintain the king's confinement, then proceed with the zugzwang plan.

notes.explains: After the correct first move, black may try pawn moves like b5 or king moves like king a2. If black plays b5, white must be careful not to allow b3, which would give the king an escape square. White can respond with bishop f4 to keep control.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create luft for their king, you must anticipate and prevent pawn breaks that open escape squares. Keep your pieces on squares that control the critical points.
notes.plans: After bishop d6, if black plays b5, consider bishop f4 to stop b3, and then continue the zugzwang by forcing black to move the king or bishop.

notes.explains: In this endgame, White has a material advantage but must be precise because Black's king and pawns can create counterplay. The immediate threat is Black pushing the b-pawn to b3, which would allow the king to escape and complicate the win.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning endgame, identify and prevent the opponent's freeing moves before executing your own plan. Blockading a dangerous passed pawn is often more important than grabbing material.
notes.plans: White should first blockade the b-pawn (e.g., with a bishop on b4 or d6) to prevent it from advancing, then use checking moves and zugzwang to force the black king into a mating net.

notes.explains: The winning method involves forcing the black king to a2, where it is nearly stalemated, then using waiting moves to force Black to move the pawn, allowing a checkmate.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, stalemate-like positions can be used to your advantage by making waiting moves that force the opponent to weaken their position.
notes.plans: After the black king is on a2, play a waiting move with the bishop (e.g., bishop b3), and when Black captures, play king d1, and if the pawn pushes to a2, deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: In the next position, White has a passed f-pawn, but Black is trying to build a fortress. The key is to promote the pawn while preventing Black's knight from reaching e6 to block it.
notes.teaches: When promoting a pawn, you must anticipate the defender's piece placement and choose king moves that avoid allowing the defender to set up a blockade.
notes.plans: White should play f6, and after Black's knight check, choose the correct king square (not c7, which allows knight d4 and later e6) to keep the pawn's promotion path clear.

notes.explains: If White mistakenly plays Kc7, Black can play Nd4, aiming for e6 to block the f-pawn. White's attempts to dislodge the knight fail because the bishop is placed to restrict White's knight, and Black can sacrifice the bishop for the pawn if needed, leaving a drawn knight versus knight endgame.
notes.teaches: A fortress can arise when the defender's pieces restrict the attacker's pieces, even at material cost. Recognize when a blockade is unbreakable and avoid allowing it.
notes.plans: If Black achieves the blockade, White should seek to trade pieces or find a way to break the fortress, but in this case it is drawn.

notes.explains: Another defensive idea for Black is to allow the pawn to promote but then set up a fortress with a knight and bishop versus queen. If the knight reaches e4, it controls key squares around the black king, and the king can shuffle, making it impossible for White's king to approach.
notes.teaches: Even a queen can be held to a draw by a well-placed knight and bishop if they create a fortress. In endgames with material disadvantage, look for ways to restrict the opponent's king and pieces.
notes.plans: If Black can set up the knight on e4 and keep the king safe, the game is drawn despite the queen.

notes.explains: With the correct king move Kc8, Black's attempts to repeat the blockade fail. If Black tries Nd4, White can use checks and maneuvers to drive the knight away, eventually trading it off and winning. The difference is the king's position allows White to support the pawn and coordinate the pieces.
notes.teaches: The correct king placement can be the difference between a win and a draw. Always consider how your king supports your pawns and restricts the defender's pieces.
notes.plans: White should proceed with f7, using checks to deflect Black's knight, then bring the king to support the pawn and force the trade of knights.

notes.explains: In this endgame, the placement of the black bishop prevents White's knight from trading on h7, so the usual defensive resource is unavailable. White must find a precise sequence to break through Black's fortress.
notes.teaches: When a fortress seems solid, look for a deflection or a check that forces the defender's pieces away from key squares. Every piece's placement matters in determining whether a position is drawn or winning.
notes.plans: White should play Bf2+ to force the king to f2, then push f7 to promote with check, restricting Black's ability to set up a fortress. After promotion, use checks to pin the enemy knight and bring the king closer.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a b-pawn close to promotion, but Black has a knight and bishop that can create mating threats. The key is to use the promotion threat as a deflection to break Black's coordination.
notes.teaches: Double deflection: a pawn push that threatens promotion can force the defender to abandon a mating net or lose material. Always consider the promotion square as a powerful resource.
notes.plans: White should push b7, threatening promotion. If Black tries to set up a mate, White can respond with a move like Be2, threatening Nc3# and forcing Black to deal with the promotion threat.

notes.explains: Black's knight and bishop are coordinating to drive the white king to a corner of the same color as the bishop, where mate is possible. However, White's b-pawn can be pushed to create counterplay.
notes.teaches: In knight and bishop vs. king endings, the stronger side aims to force the king to the corner matching the bishop's color. But a passed pawn can change the evaluation, so always check for promotion tricks.
notes.plans: Black should try to maintain the mating net while dealing with the b-pawn. If White pushes b7, Black must find a way to stop promotion without losing the mating pattern.

notes.explains: White's attempt to stop the mating pattern with a move like Nf7 fails because Black can respond with Kc2, controlling the promotion square and keeping the attack. The b-pawn push is the only way to create real threats.
notes.teaches: When defending against a mating net, a pawn promotion threat can be the most effective resource. Moves that merely block the attack often fail because they don't address the root cause.
notes.plans: White should push b7 immediately, forcing Black to react. If Black plays a natural move like Bd6, White can continue with the promotion threat and eventually win material.

notes.explains: In this endgame, White is pushing a pawn to promote, and Black's most natural defensive try is to place the bishop on d6 to block the pawn. However, this also removes the bishop from participating in a mating net, so Black must weigh the trade-off between stopping the pawn and keeping mating chances.
notes.teaches: When defending against a passed pawn, the defender often has to commit a piece to block it, which can weaken other defensive or counterplay ideas. Always consider what the blocking piece gives up.
notes.plans: White should continue pushing the pawns, using the king to support them, while Black must decide between blocking the pawn or pursuing a mating attack.

notes.explains: Black tries to stop the pawns with the bishop, but the pawns are on separate diagonals, so the bishop cannot control both. This is unlike opposite-colored bishop endgames where one bishop can often stop multiple pawns on the same diagonal.
notes.teaches: Two passed pawns on different diagonals are much harder to stop with a single bishop than pawns on the same diagonal. The defender's task becomes nearly impossible if the pawns are far apart.
notes.plans: White should aim to advance both pawns, forcing the bishop to choose which one to block, and then use the other pawn to win.

notes.explains: After a knight check, White must choose the correct king square. Moving to b2 or a2 allows Black's knight to join the defense and restrict the white king, leading to a draw. The correct move is Kb1, which avoids the knight's harassment and keeps winning chances.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, the king's placement is critical. Avoid squares where the enemy knight can check or restrict your king, and look for the square that gives your king the most freedom while supporting your pawns.
notes.plans: White plays Kb1, then continues advancing the f-pawn, using the king to support it and avoiding the knight's checks.

notes.explains: Black tries to stop the pawns with knight and bishop, but White finds a beautiful resource: a knight sacrifice (or deflection) that forces the bishop away from the pawn's path, allowing a promotion. After the bishop is deflected, the king can capture it, and the pawns cannot be stopped.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied to stopping your passed pawns, look for tactical deflections or sacrifices to remove the key defender. Even in seemingly drawn positions, a precise tactic can create a win.
notes.plans: White plays the deflection move, then promotes one pawn, and the other pawn follows, securing the win.

notes.explains: In this endgame, both sides have clear goals: one side tries to promote pawns while the other tries to stop them. The bishop is tied to stopping the pawns, but it can be deflected, allowing a promotion.
notes.teaches: When defending against passed pawns, a piece can become overloaded if it must stop multiple threats. Look for deflection tactics to remove the defender and promote.
notes.plans: If the defender is deflected, push the pawn that promotes first, then use the newly promoted piece to win the other pawn.

notes.explains: A knight sacrifice on a key square forces the bishop to capture, deflecting it from stopping the pawns. After the bishop is gone, the pawns cannot be stopped.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a piece to deflect a defender is a common motif in pawn races. Even if the sacrifice is not immediately recaptured, the threat of promotion can force the defender to move.
notes.plans: If the bishop captures the knight, push the pawn that promotes first, then use the queen to win the other pawn.

notes.explains: In a position with two advanced pawns, the defending bishop can be restricted but still active. The attacking side can use the bishop's restricted mobility to create a winning plan.
notes.teaches: Even if a defender is tied to stopping pawns, it may still have defensive resources. Look for ways to exploit its restricted mobility or force it to abandon its post.
notes.plans: Use the king to support the pawns and force the bishop to choose between stopping one pawn or the other.

notes.explains: When pushing a pawn to promote, beware of checks that can deflect the king and allow the defender to capture the pawn. Sometimes a preparatory move is needed to avoid these checks.
notes.teaches: Before pushing a pawn, calculate all checks from the defender. If checks allow the pawn to be captured, consider a preparatory move that neutralizes those checks.
notes.plans: If a direct push fails due to checks, look for a move that either blocks the checks or forces the defender to abandon them.

notes.explains: In a position with a rook against two advanced pawns, the rook alone cannot stop the pawns if the king supports them. The defender must use the rook actively to prevent the pawns from advancing.
notes.teaches: Rooks are poor at stopping advanced passed pawns without king support. The defending side should place the rook behind the pawns or use it to cut off the king.
notes.plans: If defending, keep the rook active to prevent the pawns from advancing, and do not rush to capture a pawn if it allows the other to promote.

notes.explains: With two advanced passed pawns supported by the king, a lone rook cannot stop them. The defender must find precise moves to blockade and avoid rushing to grab a pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook versus pawns endgames, the defender should prioritize stopping the pawns over material gain, often using the rook to restrain and the king to assist.
notes.plans: For the defender: place the rook to attack the pawns from behind or side, use checks to drive the king away, and aim for a draw. For the attacker: advance the pawns with king support, restrict the rook, and look for tactical resources like underpromotion.

notes.explains: In a critical position, the attacker must not rush to push a pawn if it allows the defender to capture it and leave the pawn hanging. Instead, improving the king's position can create decisive threats.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a threat, first neutralize it, then find a way to win. Sometimes a quiet king move is stronger than an immediate pawn push.
notes.plans: For the attacker: move the king to support the pawns, create zugzwang, and force the defender into a losing position.

notes.explains: In a promotion race, promoting to a queen or rook may lead to stalemate, so underpromotion to a knight is necessary to deliver checkmate or avoid stalemate.
notes.teaches: Always consider underpromotion when a queen or rook would stalemate the opponent. A knight can give checks and create mating nets that other pieces cannot.
notes.plans: For the attacker: promote to a knight, use it to give checks, and drive the enemy king into a mating net or zugzwang.

notes.explains: In a position with an extra rook but vulnerable pawns, the attacker must find a move that creates a decisive threat, such as a bishop sacrifice to deflect the defender's pieces.
notes.teaches: When material advantage is not enough due to counterplay, look for tactical shots that eliminate the opponent's threats and create your own unstoppable promotion.
notes.plans: For the attacker: use a piece sacrifice to deflect the defender's rook or king, then promote a pawn. For the defender: try to create counterplay with passed pawns and checks.

notes.explains: In this study, White's rook and bishop are fighting against Black's advanced passed pawns. The immediate threat is Black promoting, so White must find a way to neutralize the pawns while supporting his own h-pawn's promotion.
notes.teaches: When facing a dangerous passed pawn, look for forcing moves that deflect the defender or bring your king closer to the action. A sacrifice can be the key to stopping promotion.
notes.plans: White should aim to eliminate Black's pawns or restrict them, while advancing the h-pawn with the support of the king.

notes.explains: The move bishop d5 is a check that forces Black to capture, removing a defender and clearing the path for White's pawn. This is a critical resource to prevent Black from promoting.
notes.teaches: A checking sacrifice can force the opponent's piece to a worse square or remove it entirely, often creating a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: After the bishop is captured, White's h-pawn can advance, and the rook can be used to stop Black's promotion attempts.

notes.explains: The move long castle (0-0-0) is a surprising resource that brings the king to the queenside to help stop Black's pawns from promoting. It also gives check, gaining time.
notes.teaches: Castling can be a defensive and offensive tool in the endgame, especially when it brings the king closer to the action and gives check.
notes.plans: With the king on c1, White can support the h-pawn's promotion while keeping Black's pawns under control.

notes.explains: In studies, it is standard that White moves first. The position features two pieces and pawns against a queen, but the goal is to trap the queen and promote a pawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a material disadvantage, look for tactical resources to trap the opponent's queen or create a passed pawn that cannot be stopped.
notes.plans: White should try to use the king's restricted position to create threats against the queen and advance the pawn.

notes.explains: In this study, White is a piece down and must be precise. The first instinct is to grab material, but that allows Black perpetual check and a draw. The black king is confined, so White can aim for mate threats with the queen on key squares like d1, e2, or f3.
notes.teaches: When material down, look for ways to restrict the enemy king and create mating threats rather than rushing to win back material. Sometimes the best move is a quiet one that maintains the bind.
notes.plans: Consider moves that keep the black king boxed in and prepare a decisive queen invasion, avoiding captures that release the pressure.

notes.explains: White has a passed pawn and a knight that restricts the black queen's checking squares. The idea is to advance the pawn while using the knight to cover key squares, even if it means sacrificing the pawn temporarily.
notes.teaches: A knight can be a great defender against enemy queen checks. Sometimes sacrificing a pawn is justified if it leads to a forced promotion or a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to promotion, using the knight to control checking squares and the king to escape any checks.

notes.explains: Black tries to force stalemate by sacrificing the queen, but White must avoid taking it. Instead, White sidesteps with the king, maintaining the mating net and keeping the pawn rolling.
notes.teaches: In endgames, be alert to stalemate tricks. When the opponent offers a queen sacrifice, evaluate whether taking leads to stalemate; sometimes you must decline and continue the plan.
notes.plans: Keep the king safe, avoid captures that stalemate, and continue supporting the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: In positions with queens on the board, the queen's activity is paramount. A passive queen can be dominated, while an active queen creates constant threats and limits the opponent's options.
notes.teaches: Centralize your queen in queen endgames; a centralized queen controls many squares and restricts the opponent's king and pieces.
notes.plans: Look for moves that improve your queen's activity while maintaining pressure on key targets.

notes.explains: When the opponent's king is exposed, mating threats can force the opponent to respond, giving you time to improve your position. Here, the queen's checks and threats create a net that the king cannot escape.
notes.teaches: Use checks and mating threats to drive the opponent's king into a worse position, even if the immediate mate is not possible.
notes.plans: Continue checking and threatening mate to force the king to a square where you can deliver a decisive blow.

notes.explains: A pawn move like g4 can be a powerful resource in queen endgames, creating threats and exploiting the opponent's pinned pieces or lack of coordination.
notes.teaches: Look for pawn breaks that create threats against the opponent's king or pieces, especially when the opponent's pieces are tied down.
notes.plans: After the pawn move, follow up with checks and threats to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: Pins are crucial in queen endgames. A pinned piece cannot move, allowing you to make captures or threats that would otherwise be impossible.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of pins; they can make a capture safe or force the opponent to leave a piece hanging.
notes.plans: Use the pin to win material or to force the opponent's king into a mating net.

notes.explains: In this study, the defender's queen is overloaded: it must both stop a promotion and guard against checks. The attacker exploits this by giving checks that force the king to a worse square, after which the queen cannot defend both threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is tied to multiple duties, look for forcing checks that drive the king to a square where the queen's defensive tasks become impossible to fulfill simultaneously.
notes.plans: Continue the forcing sequence of checks until the king is cornered, then deliver the mate that the queen can no longer prevent.

notes.explains: Endgame studies often feature themes like promotions, stalemates, zugzwang, and mates. While many studies end in a win or a draw via stalemate or repetition, some also showcase a direct mate, which is rare and instructive.
notes.teaches: Study compositions to see unusual combinations of themes (promotion, stalemate, zugzwang, mate) that sharpen tactical and endgame vision beyond typical play.

notes.explains: A pin is a tactic where one piece attacks a second piece, and if the second piece moves, a more valuable piece behind it is exposed to attack. Tactics are short-term, immediate advantages, unlike strategies which are long-term plans.
notes.teaches: Recognize pins as tactical opportunities that can yield immediate material or positional gains.

notes.explains: There are two types of pins: absolute and relative. An absolute pin occurs when the pinned piece is shielding the king, so moving it is illegal. A relative pin occurs when the pinned piece shields a non-king piece (like a queen), so moving it is legal but costly.
notes.teaches: Distinguish between absolute and relative pins to understand the legal and practical constraints on the pinned piece.

notes.explains: In the Trompowsky Attack (d4 Nf6 Bg5), the bishop pins the knight to the queen (relative pin). In the example with ...Bb4, the bishop pins the knight to the king (absolute pin). The pinned knight is 'petrified'—it cannot or should not move.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, it is effectively immobilized; you can attack it with pawns or other pieces to gain material.
notes.plans: In the position with a pawn on e5 attacking the pinned knight, the attacker should proceed to win the pinned piece, as the defender cannot move it away.

notes.explains: In the example from the Trompowsky, after e5 attacks the pinned knight, Black tries a counterattack with h6, but White can maintain the pin and eventually deliver checkmate with Qg4 and Qg7#. This shows that ignoring a pin can lead to severe consequences.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a pin, do not ignore it; address it or face tactical punishment. Conversely, exploit pins by building pressure on the pinned piece.
notes.plans: If the opponent fails to break the pin, look for mating patterns or material gains by increasing pressure on the pinned piece.

notes.explains: In the Budapest Gambit, Black sacrifices a pawn for rapid development and active piece play. The move ...Bb4+ is a check that also pins the knight, and it is played before ...Qe7 to avoid trapping the bishop.
notes.teaches: In openings, use pins to create tactical threats and maintain piece activity. Order your moves to keep pieces flexible and avoid self-trapping.
notes.plans: Continue developing while maintaining the pin and pressure on White's position.

notes.explains: In the Budapest Gambit, Black gives up a pawn to lure White into overextending, then develops pieces actively to regain it and create tactical threats.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn for rapid development and attacking chances can be a sound opening strategy if you have a concrete plan to recover the material or gain compensation.
notes.plans: Develop pieces to active squares, target the weak pawn, and look for tactical motifs like pins and forks.

notes.explains: When White plays Bf4 to defend the pawn, Black brings out a second knight to attack it again, and after White defends with Nf3, Black can choose between Qe7 or Bb4 check. Playing Bb4 first is better because it develops with tempo and avoids trapping the bishop.
notes.teaches: Prioritize developing pieces with tempo and avoid moves that trap your own pieces. Keeping pieces active is more important than rushing to regain material.
notes.plans: Play Bb4 check, then Qe7 to pile up on the pinned knight.

notes.explains: After Bb4, White may avoid Nc3 due to doubled pawns, but Nc3 is actually fine. If White plays Nd2, Black has created an absolute pin on the knight, which cannot move because it would expose the king.
notes.teaches: An absolute pin immobilizes a piece because moving it would leave the king in check. Recognizing pins is crucial for exploiting weaknesses.
notes.plans: Use the pin to pile up on the pinned piece and win material.

notes.explains: In this position, Black can sacrifice the bishop on f7 to exploit the pin. If White recaptures, Black delivers a smothered mate with the knight, because the queen pins the pawn to the king and the king is trapped.
notes.teaches: Pins can enable spectacular sacrifices and checkmate patterns. Even if the opponent doesn't fall for the trap, the threat can win material.
notes.plans: Sacrifice the bishop on f7, and if the pawn recaptures, deliver smothered mate with the knight.

notes.explains: Pinned pieces are 'petrified' and cannot move, but they also lose their defensive and attacking capabilities. A pinned knight that normally protects a pawn cannot do so, allowing tactics like capturing the pawn.
notes.teaches: Remember that pinned pieces don't protect. When a piece is pinned, it exerts no influence on the squares it would normally cover, so you can capture pieces it appears to defend.
notes.plans: Look for captures on squares that a pinned piece seems to defend but actually doesn't.

notes.explains: When a piece is pinned, adding more attackers to it (piling up) is often decisive because the pinned piece cannot escape. This principle applies in many positions.
notes.teaches: Pressure pinned pieces by attacking them with multiple pieces. Since they can't move, extra attackers usually win material.
notes.plans: Identify pinned pieces and bring additional attackers to bear on them.

notes.explains: In the Scotch Gambit, White sacrifices two pawns for development and then uses pins to win back material, such as playing Re1 to pin a knight to the king.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be justified if you have a plan to regain material through pins or other tactics. Development and initiative can compensate for material deficits.
notes.plans: Use pins to regain the sacrificed pawns and maintain pressure.

notes.explains: In a position with an unusual material imbalance (White has rook and bishop vs queen, plus extra pawns), the pinned knight is a key weakness. Simply capturing it would be an even trade, but pressuring it with a move like Nd5 exploits the pin to gain material or force concessions.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, you should pile on pressure rather than capture it immediately, because the pinned piece cannot move away or defend properly. This often leads to winning more material or a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, attacking the pinned knight. If Black defends, they risk losing their queen for insufficient compensation; otherwise, White will capture the knight and emerge with a material advantage.

notes.explains: In another position with a pinned knight, a pawn move like e5 attacks the pinned piece, increasing the pressure. Since the knight cannot move, it is effectively trapped, and the attack will yield an advantage.
notes.teaches: Using pawns to attack pinned pieces is a simple and effective way to increase pressure, as the pinned piece cannot escape.
notes.plans: Play e5, attacking the pinned knight. The knight cannot move, so White will win material or gain a significant positional edge.

notes.explains: In a Pirc Defense setup, Black aims for a fortified defensive structure with a safe king, while White uses the queen and bishop to pressure the kingside. Even strong players can miscalculate involving pins, showing that pin tactics are relevant at all levels.
notes.teaches: Pins are a fundamental tactical motif that can decide games at any level. Recognizing and exploiting pins is crucial in both attack and defense.
notes.plans: White should continue to build pressure on the kingside, using the bishop and queen to create threats, while Black must carefully defend and avoid falling into pin-related tactics.

notes.explains: In the Pirc Defense, Black aims for a solid, fortified setup with a safe king, while White typically uses the queen and bishop to pressure the kingside and potentially launch pawns. The early f4 in the 'Brit' opening can expose the king, so Black's setup is designed to counter that.
notes.teaches: Understand the typical plans in the Pirc Defense: Black builds a fortress, White attacks on the kingside. Recognize that early pawn breaks like e5 can be premature if the king is not castled and the position is not ready.
notes.plans: For White, continue developing and preparing kingside pressure, possibly with pawn advances. For Black, prioritize castling and completing development before striking in the center.

notes.explains: After Black plays e5 prematurely, White can exploit the pin on the knight. By trading pawns on e5 and then queens, White creates an absolute pin on the knight, making it immobile and vulnerable. This leads to a decisive advantage because Black cannot easily defend against the multiple threats.
notes.teaches: A pin can be a powerful tactical weapon, especially when it immobilizes a piece and allows you to build pressure. Look for ways to convert a relative pin into an absolute pin by trading off the piece in front of the pinned piece.
notes.plans: White should continue to pile pressure on the pinned knight, possibly with moves like Nd5, Rd1, or O-O, setting up double attacks. Black must find a way to break the pin, but many attempts fail due to tactical refutations.

notes.explains: Black's attempts to defend against the pin, such as Nd7, h6, or c6, all fail because White has stronger tactical resources. For example, if Black plays h6 to attack the bishop, White can capture on f6, winning a piece. If Black plays c6, White can capture on d7 and then fork the king and rook.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is pinned, they often try to break the pin with pawn moves or piece moves. Always check if those moves are actually playable by calculating the tactical consequences. Sometimes the pin is so strong that any defense loses material.
notes.plans: White should continue to exploit the pin with concrete tactics, aiming to win material or force a decisive advantage. Black must look for ways to neutralize the pin, but in this position, it seems impossible.

notes.explains: This position illustrates how a single natural-looking move like e5 can turn a balanced position into a losing one because it allows a pin that leads to a decisive attack. The computer evaluation jumps from 0.0 to +8 after e5, showing the severity of the mistake.
notes.teaches: Always consider whether your intended move allows your opponent to create a pin or other tactical motif. A move that looks normal can be a blunder if it exposes your pieces to tactical exploitation. Evaluate the safety of your king and the mobility of your pieces before making pawn breaks.
notes.plans: In similar positions, before playing a central pawn break, ensure your king is safe (castled) and that your pieces are not vulnerable to pins. If you are the one with the pin, look for ways to maximize its effect.

notes.explains: Pins are a fundamental tactical motif where a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it. This immobilizes the pinned piece, reducing its defensive and offensive capabilities.
notes.teaches: Remember the three principles of pins: pinned pieces are petrified (cannot move), pinned pieces do not protect (they lose their defensive influence), and you should put pressure on pinned pieces by adding attackers.
notes.plans: When you spot a pin, look for ways to add more attackers to the pinned piece, since it cannot escape.

notes.explains: In endgames with a queen and king versus a lone king, checkmate is possible but requires precise play. However, if you can win material via a pin, the task becomes much simpler.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical shortcuts like pins to convert a technically winning but difficult endgame into an easy one.
notes.plans: If you have a material advantage, simplify by winning more material through pins or other tactics.

notes.explains: A pin can be used not only to win material but also to force a draw when you are otherwise losing. In a position with a rook and bishop versus a knight, a pin can neutralize the extra piece.
notes.teaches: Pins are not always about winning; they can also be defensive resources to hold a difficult position.
notes.plans: When down material, look for pins that immobilize the opponent's pieces and prevent them from making progress.

notes.explains: Pins can also be used to win a rook or other major pieces. By pinning a knight to a rook, you can force the opponent to lose material because the knight cannot move.
notes.teaches: Always look for pins that target pieces lined up on the same file, rank, or diagonal.
notes.plans: If you can pin a minor piece to a major piece, add pressure to win the pinned piece or the major piece.

notes.explains: When you have a pin, you must be aware that the pinned piece can sometimes move if it can defend the piece behind it. In such cases, a trade may be acceptable.
notes.teaches: Pins are not absolute; if the pinned piece can move and defend, the pin may not be as strong. Evaluate whether a trade is favorable.
notes.plans: When considering a pin, check if the pinned piece can move to defend the attacked piece; if so, the pin may not yield an advantage.

notes.explains: Pinned pieces do not protect other pieces. This means that a move that would normally be a good capture may be illegal or bad because the pinned piece cannot recapture.
notes.teaches: Remember that a pinned piece loses its defensive capabilities, so you can often capture pieces that are defended only by the pinned piece.
notes.plans: When your opponent has a pinned piece, look for captures that exploit its lack of protection.

notes.explains: In some positions, you must be careful not to move your queen too aggressively because it might allow a checkmate on your own king. This is a common tactical motif where a pin or a discovered attack can be deadly.
notes.teaches: Always consider your own king's safety before moving pieces, especially the queen, as it can leave your king vulnerable to tactics.
notes.plans: When you have a material advantage, avoid unnecessary risks; consolidate your position and ensure your king is safe.

notes.explains: A pinned piece cannot protect other pieces, even though it may appear to defend them. This means attacks on pieces that are only defended by a pinned piece are often winning.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, it loses its defensive capabilities. Look for captures on pieces that are only defended by pinned pieces.

notes.explains: In positions with a pin, moving the queen too aggressively can expose the king to back-rank or diagonal threats, especially if the queen is not defended. Here, a dramatic queen move allows the bishop and queen to checkmate on g2.
notes.teaches: When exploiting a pin, be aware of your own king's safety and the safety of your queen. Avoid moves that create weaknesses or leave your queen hanging.
notes.plans: Choose a move that maintains the pin while keeping the king safe and the queen defended.

notes.explains: In a double pin, both the knight and bishop are pinned to the queen, so the opponent cannot defend both. A move like queen to d5 creates two threats simultaneously, and the opponent can only answer one.
notes.teaches: Pins can be used to create multiple threats. When two pieces are pinned, the opponent is overloaded and cannot defend both.
notes.plans: Look for moves that create two threats at once, especially when the opponent's pieces are pinned.

notes.explains: When a rook is pinned to the king, the knight cannot move without exposing the king. The pinned rook is stuck, and we can pile on pressure to win material.
notes.teaches: A pinned piece is a target. Add pressure to it with additional attackers to win it.
notes.plans: Play bishop to f4 to attack the pinned knight, and prepare to capture it.

notes.explains: In a pin, attacking the pinned piece with a queen can win material. Even if the opponent tries tricky checks, the pin holds and the piece is lost.
notes.teaches: Use your queen to attack a pinned piece. Be aware of defensive tricks, but the pin often ensures you win material.
notes.plans: Play queen to b2 to attack the rook, and if the opponent tries rook to c2 check, simply capture it.

notes.explains: When a piece is pinned, you can pile on pressure by adding more attackers. Even if the opponent tries to defend, the pinned piece is often lost.
notes.teaches: To win a pinned piece, bring more attackers to bear on it. The opponent cannot easily defend because the pinned piece is immobile.
notes.plans: Play rook to c1 to add pressure to the pinned piece.

notes.explains: When capturing a pinned piece, it may be safe to capture with either piece, as long as you maintain safety. Here, capturing with the rook defends the queen, and capturing with the queen gets out of harm's way.
notes.teaches: When recapturing a pinned piece, choose the capture that best maintains your position, whether it's defending your queen or moving it to safety.

notes.explains: In this game, after e4 e6 d4 c5, the position resembles a Sicilian Defense. Black's setup with ...c5 aims to provoke white into capturing, allowing black to recapture with the bishop and develop, possibly with ...Qb6 to attack f2. However, this plan leaves the d5 pawn weak and backward.
notes.teaches: Recognize when an opponent's development plan creates a structural weakness. Here, black's desire to develop quickly with ...c5 and ...Bxc5 leaves the d5 pawn vulnerable, which white can target.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit the backward d5 pawn by advancing d4-d5, gaining space and fixing the weakness.

notes.explains: White plays Bb5+ at a moment when black's c5 pawn and traded bishop make it strong. Normally this check is not effective because black can trade or push a pawn, but here the knight is forced to block, pinning itself against the king.
notes.teaches: A check can be used to force a piece to a passive square, creating a pin. The value of such moves depends on the surrounding pawn structure and piece placement.
notes.plans: After ...Nd7, white can continue developing with Nc3, preparing to create further pins and pressure.

notes.explains: With Bg5, white creates a double pin: both black knights are pinned by bishops. Although the knights appear to defend each other, they are actually immobile and just cramp black's position, preventing the queen from moving to useful squares.
notes.teaches: Pins can restrict the opponent's pieces even when they seem to defend each other. A pinned piece is often worse than a defended one because it cannot move without exposing a more valuable target.
notes.plans: White should look for a way to exploit the congestion, perhaps by attacking the pinned knights or increasing pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: In the position after ...Be7, white has several good moves like castling or doubling rooks, but there is a more crushing idea. The key is to find a move that breaks the coordination of black's pieces, often by capturing a pinned piece or delivering a decisive tactic.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied up, look for a forcing move that exploits the overloaded or pinned pieces. Sometimes the best move is not the most obvious development but a tactical strike.
notes.plans: White should consider moves that increase pressure on the pinned knights or open lines against the king, aiming for a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: The position features a knight pinned by a bishop, and the defender of the pin is also pinned. This creates a double pin that restricts the opponent's pieces and makes defensive moves like bishop e7 or h6 too slow.
notes.teaches: Pins can be used to restrict the opponent's pieces and create tactical opportunities. When a piece is pinned, it cannot move legally, so you can target it with additional pressure.
notes.plans: Continue to pile pressure on the pinned piece, using threats to win material or force a favorable trade. Look for ways to remove the defender of the pinned piece.

notes.explains: The move d6 is not just a pawn sacrifice; it opens lines for the bishop and prepares a knight jump to d5, which creates threats and exploits the pins.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn move that appears to lose material can be a tactical resource if it activates pieces and creates threats. Always consider the resulting position after the sacrifice.
notes.plans: After d6, if the pawn is taken, use the open lines to launch an attack, possibly with a knight to d5, targeting the pinned pieces.

notes.explains: When the opponent tries to break the pin with a move like h6, you can simply trade bishops, and the pin remains because the knight cannot recapture. This leaves the opponent with a weak pawn structure and hanging pieces.
notes.teaches: To exploit a pin, you often need to remove the defender of the pinned piece. Trading off the defender can leave the pinned piece helpless and the opponent's position compromised.
notes.plans: If the opponent tries to break the pin, trade pieces to maintain the pin and then target the resulting weaknesses, such as doubled pawns or exposed king.

notes.explains: In the given position, white has a winning advantage because the pins are so strong that every defensive try fails. Moves like bishop e7 or h6 are too slow, and white can win material in all variations.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong pin, you should look for ways to make it decisive. If the opponent's defenses are all insufficient, you can confidently proceed with your plan.
notes.plans: Continue to increase pressure, possibly by castling and bringing the rook to an open file, then use the pin to win material or force a decisive attack.

notes.explains: Pins are powerful but not always perfect. There are cases where a pin can be broken or backfire, so you must be cautious when relying on pins.
notes.teaches: Always check if the pinned piece can be defended or if the pin can be broken by a tactical resource. Pins are most effective when the pinned piece is valuable and cannot be easily defended.

notes.explains: In the Smith-Morra Gambit, White sacrifices two pawns for rapid development and activity. Black's bishop to g4 pins the knight to the queen, but this pin is flawed because the bishop is undefended.
notes.teaches: A pin is only effective if the pinned piece cannot move without losing material of greater value. If the pinning piece is undefended, it can become the target of a discovered attack.
notes.plans: White can exploit the undefended bishop with moves like bishop takes f7, winning the bishop back after the king recaptures, or with a knight move that creates a double attack.

notes.explains: In the Philidor Defense, Black's bishop to g4 pins the knight, but White can use an intermediate move (in-between move) to break the pin.
notes.teaches: An 'in-between' move (Zwischenzug) can disrupt a pin by removing the target of the pin or forcing a response that frees the pinned piece.
notes.plans: In this position, White can play d4 and then, after Black captures, use the intermediate move to remove the pin and win a pawn.

notes.explains: The Elephant Trap is a tactical idea in the opening where Black can set a trap for White.
notes.teaches: Be aware of tactical traps in common openings; they often rely on undefended pieces or overloading.
notes.plans: If White falls into the trap, Black can win material or gain a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: In the Philidor Defense, after the opponent captures a knight, the correct response is to recapture with the queen, winning the pawn back and restoring material equality.
notes.teaches: When you can recapture with the queen and regain the pawn, it's often the simplest way to maintain balance.
notes.plans: Recapture the pawn and continue developing normally.

notes.explains: In the Queen's Gambit, if Black accepts the gambit by taking the c-pawn, White typically wins it back by advancing the e-pawn and then having the bishop recapture. It's usually not worth Black trying to hold onto the extra pawn.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, the side offering the pawn often has a clear way to regain it, so accepting can lead to a simple trade.
notes.plans: White recaptures the pawn and develops; Black should not overextend to keep the pawn.

notes.explains: In the Queen's Gambit Declined, after d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5, Black's knight on f6 is pinned. A tricky move is Nd7, which looks like a blunder because it seems to lose a pawn and blocks the queen's defense. However, it sets a trap: if White takes the pawn, Black can play Nxd5, sacrificing the queen but delivering a nearly mating attack. White's best defense is to return the queen, leading to a position where Black has won a knight for a pawn and has a material advantage.
notes.teaches: Pins can be exploited by the pinned side if the pinning piece is overextended. A move that looks like a blunder may be a deep trap, so be cautious when your opponent allows a pin.
notes.plans: Black executes the trap to win material; White must find the only defensive move to avoid mate.

notes.explains: In a Smith-Morra Gambit position, after White plays Bxf7+, Black might respond with Kd7. White can simply move the bishop back, having won a pawn for nothing, and Black's king is exposed on d7. The pin on the knight remains, and White is happy with the material gain.
notes.teaches: When you can win a pawn and force the enemy king to move, it's often a good deal even if the piece retreats. Exposing the king can create long-term weaknesses.
notes.plans: White retreats the bishop, keeps the extra pawn, and later may exploit the king's position with moves like Ne5 if the pin allows.

notes.explains: In the Légal Trap, White creates a pin on the knight and then sacrifices the queen with Nxe5. If Black takes the queen, the king is checkmated because all escape squares are covered. If Black declines, White wins a pawn and has a good position.
notes.teaches: A pin can be a double-edged sword: the pinned piece may become a target for tactical motifs like discovered attacks or mating nets. Always check if the pin can be turned against you.
notes.plans: White executes the sacrifice to win material or mate; Black must avoid taking the queen and instead find a way to minimize losses.

notes.explains: When you have won a pawn and the opponent tries to hold onto everything, they often create weaknesses. Taking a knight with a pawn can create doubled pawns, and taking a bishop can weaken the opponent's pawn structure further. Even if your bishop is hanging, the opponent may have a tactical resource like a queen fork to win back material.
notes.teaches: If you are already winning a pawn, don't overcomplicate. Simple recaptures that maintain your material advantage are often best. Be aware of tactical resources like forks that can win back material for the opponent.
notes.plans: Continue to consolidate your extra pawn, especially if it is a center pawn, by developing pieces and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: In an Italian Game with an aggressive d4, if the opponent declines the gambit and plays a developing move like Be7, White can regain the pawn with Nxd4. Black may then push f4 to support a center pawn and prepare e5, while also looking to develop the bishop to b6 to pressure the king.
notes.teaches: Familiarity with gambit lines helps you know when to accept or decline. If the opponent declines, you can often regain the pawn and still have a good position. Be aware of pawn pushes that support central control and piece development.
notes.plans: After regaining the pawn, continue development and watch for threats like Bc5 pinning the queen to the king. Consider moves that create counterplay, such as Bb5+ to stall and create tactical opportunities.

notes.explains: In a position with a double pin, the opponent's queen is attacked and also pinned to the king, so it cannot move without losing the king. This can lead to checkmate or winning the queen.
notes.teaches: Double pins are extremely powerful because they restrict the opponent's pieces in multiple ways. Look for opportunities to create pins that limit the mobility of the opponent's most valuable pieces.
notes.plans: If you have a double pin, consider sacrificing material to deliver checkmate or to win the pinned piece. Keep the pressure on and avoid giving the opponent counterplay.

notes.explains: When down a piece, a pawn break like c4 can force the opponent's knight to move, allowing your rook to pin the bishop to the king. This can create a passed pawn and drawing chances.
notes.teaches: In endgames, pawn breaks can create tactical opportunities even when material is down. Pins can restrict the opponent's pieces and allow your pawns to advance. Use active rook play to create counterplay.
notes.plans: Push the c-pawn to force the knight away, then use the pin on the bishop to march the pawn forward. Aim to create a passed pawn and use the rook to support it.

notes.explains: In a materially worse position, down a piece, the only drawing move is a pawn advance that forces the enemy knight to move, after which the rook pins the bishop to the king. The pin prevents the opponent from capturing the pawn, allowing us to win back the piece.
notes.teaches: When you are losing, look for tactical resources like pins and pawn pushes that can force the opponent's pieces to awkward squares and create counterplay.
notes.plans: Push the c-pawn to c4, forcing the knight to move, then use the rook to pin the bishop to the king, and eventually win back the piece to reach a drawn endgame.

notes.explains: In another losing position, the only drawing move is a bishop capture on e5. The opponent cannot recapture with the pawn because that would lose the queen, so they must recapture with the queen, after which we recapture with the pawn, and the rook remains to win back the piece.
notes.teaches: Precise move order is crucial in tactical sequences; a different order may allow the opponent to escape with the material.
notes.plans: Execute the sequence in the exact order: bishop takes e5, if queen recaptures, pawn takes queen, then use the rook to win back the piece.

notes.explains: Even when objectively losing, there may be a hidden drawing tactic. The key is to stay alert and search for forcing moves that create threats and force the opponent to react.
notes.teaches: Never give up in a lost position; look for tactical chances that can turn the game around or salvage a draw.

notes.explains: The romantic era of chess, often dismissed as crude and unscientific, actually featured players with deep understanding and modern ideas. Their games are rich in concepts still used by top players today.
notes.teaches: Study classic games from the 19th century to see the origins of modern attacking and positional ideas. These players were not just sacrificers; they had profound strategic insight.

notes.explains: Players like Anderssen and Morphy were not only brilliant tacticians but also had exceptional technique and positional understanding. Morphy, in particular, was considered a chess genius by many, including Bobby Fischer.
notes.teaches: Recognize that historical players can be as strong as modern ones in their understanding, and their games offer valuable lessons in initiative, development, and attack.

notes.explains: In the Italian Game, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5, the move Ng5 is a principled try. This line was later used successfully by Capablanca, who scored three wins with it.
notes.teaches: The Italian Game offers sharp attacking possibilities, and Ng5 is a critical test of Black's setup. Studying such lines helps understand typical tactical motifs.
notes.plans: After Ng5, White aims to exploit the f7 weakness and create immediate threats, while Black must respond accurately to maintain equality.

notes.explains: In a game between Anderssen and Steinitz, Anderssen played an unusual sequence of rook moves, moving the same rook seven times in the opening. This was excessive, but it demonstrates the creative and imaginative play of the era.
notes.teaches: While such rook maneuvers are often too slow, they show the importance of flexibility and the willingness to explore unconventional ideas. However, in modern chess, such play is rarely justified.

notes.explains: In this game, White played many rook moves early, which is unusual and may be excessive, but it demonstrates creative thinking. The resulting position gave White a good opening, though perhaps not perfect.
notes.teaches: Even if an idea is overdone, the imagination behind it can be valuable. In chess, creative play can lead to interesting positions, but one must balance it with sound principles.

notes.explains: After White played Bishop e3, allowing doubled pawns, the square e5 became a permanent weakness. The doubled pawns not only are weak themselves but also create weak squares in front of them, which can become outposts for enemy pieces. Additionally, the communication between White's pieces is damaged, making it harder to coordinate.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not just a static weakness; they also create weak squares that can be occupied by enemy pieces. When a square like e5 is weak, it becomes an eternal outpost for a knight, and if that knight is exchanged, another piece can take its place. This also disrupts piece communication, making it harder to transfer pieces across the board.
notes.plans: Black should aim to occupy the weak square e5 with a knight, and if that knight is exchanged, bring another piece to that square. White must try to challenge the blockade and improve piece coordination.

notes.explains: In this game, Morphy demonstrated an exceptional feel for dynamics. Instead of playing solidly, he chose an aggressive plan, using the pawn hook on h3 to launch an attack on the White king. The doubled pawns and lack of communication among White's pieces made it difficult for White to defend.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has doubled pawns and poor piece communication, you can use pawn hooks to open lines against their king. The weak squares and lack of coordination can be exploited by dynamic play, even if the opponent has more space.
notes.plans: Black should continue the attack on the kingside, using the pawn hook on h3 to open lines. White must try to exchange the knight on e5 and improve piece coordination to defend.

notes.explains: The plan of playing King h8, Rook g8, and then g7-g5 (or similar) to attack the enemy king, using a pawn hook, was later used by many top players, including Fischer and Kramnik, in similar pawn structures. This shows the lasting value of Morphy's ideas.
notes.teaches: Classic games can contain plans that are ahead of their time. Studying them can reveal ideas that become standard in modern chess, such as using a pawn hook to launch a kingside attack in hedgehog-like structures.

notes.explains: The opponent's h3 pawn becomes a hook for attacking the white king. The white pieces suffer from a lack of communication, especially the rook on the third rank, and some squares are hard for white to access.
notes.teaches: A pawn move like h3 can be a double-edged sword: it may create a hook for the opponent's attack, and it can also leave weaknesses or reduce piece coordination.
notes.plans: Black should aim to use the h3 hook to open lines against the white king, while white must try to improve piece coordination and find counterplay.
