notes.explains: The speaker chose a different move (Bc3) instead of the objectively best Bb4, because they were attached to attacking the king. After Bc3, the knight is freed and can join the attack, but the position is less forcing.
notes.teaches: Avoid being attached to a single plan like checkmating. Always reassess the position and be willing to choose the objectively best move, even if it is less flashy.
notes.plans: If the opponent sacrifices the exchange on f6, take it and rely on the strong bishop pair and the weak king to maintain a lasting advantage.

notes.explains: In this Najdorf structure, White's bishop is better than Black's and Black has a weakness, while White can use the g-file. Even if a move like Bb4 is objectively best, a direct attacking plan can still be justified if it leads to a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a lasting positional edge, you can still choose a concrete attacking plan if it is objectively strong; don't automatically reject attacking ideas just because a quieter move is also good.
notes.plans: Use the g-file to pile pressure on the king, while keeping the bishop pair and exploiting Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black plays h5 to reach a familiar setup, and White repeats the same line. White's setup is comfortable, and Black's king is a target. White plays g3 and f5 to make Black's bishop bad and dreams of a knight landing on e4, but this is one-dimensional thinking.
notes.teaches: Avoid one-dimensional attacking plans that ignore the opponent's resources. Even when you have a strong attack, you must respect the opponent's counterplay and keep your pieces harmoniously placed.
notes.plans: White should combine the attack with improving pieces, such as placing a knight on e4, while being ready to meet Black's counterplay.

notes.explains: In this position, White's most dangerous piece is the queen, so Black tries to exchange queens. Black plays Qc7 and Qc4 to offer a trade, and if White avoids it, Black can put a bishop on h4 with the queen defending it, which is annoying.
notes.teaches: When facing an attack, exchanging queens can be a key defensive resource. Also, a queen can support a bishop on an outpost like h4, making it hard to dislodge.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade queens to reduce White's attacking potential, while White should avoid the exchange and keep the pressure.

notes.explains: After a queen trade, the game reaches a playable endgame where both sides have chances. White's knight is strong, but Black has enough counterplay if played accurately. Black's careless play, like taking with the queen instead of the rook, leads to a quick collapse.
notes.teaches: In endgames, precise piece placement and avoiding careless captures are crucial. Even a small inaccuracy can turn a playable position into a losing one.
notes.plans: White should keep the knight centralized and use the g-file to create threats, while Black must defend accurately and avoid weakening moves.

notes.explains: When you have a winning position, there are often many tempting continuations, but you must choose the one that actually works. Careless calculation can turn a win into a draw or loss.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, take time to verify the most forcing and safe line rather than assuming any move wins.
notes.plans: Calculate the key variations, such as Bxg6 and Qh5, to ensure the attack is decisive.

notes.explains: In the Najdorf structure, the placement of the kings matters. When Black has castled kingside, White's pawn storm gains tempo because the pawns attack pieces, whereas in the other position (king still in the center) the pawn pushes are not tempo moves and give Black time for counterplay.
notes.teaches: Pawn storms are more effective when they come with tempo, hitting pieces and forcing reactions. Compare the two castling situations to decide whether to push pawns.
notes.plans: Start the attack with f5 to prevent Black's bishop from taking on g4, then follow with g4-g5 to push back the knights.

notes.explains: After f5, White's plan is to push g4-g5 and then f6, driving back Black's pieces. Black's g7 pawn becomes a major weakness, and White's pieces can invade quickly.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pawn structure has a fixed weakness (like g7), you can sacrifice material to keep the initiative and prevent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Rg1 to prepare g4, and if Black takes on g3, recapture with the rook to maintain pressure on the g-file.

notes.explains: In this sharp attacking position, White's initiative is built on the weakness of the g7-pawn and the rapid coordination of pieces. Black's defensive task is difficult because White's pieces are entering quickly, and the g7-pawn is a permanent target.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's king is exposed and a key pawn is weak, prioritize the speed of your attack over material gains. Every tempo matters, so calculate carefully before committing to a piece sacrifice or a deep maneuver.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain the attack by keeping the dark-squared bishop active, threatening moves like Rg3, doubling rooks, and Qh6, while ensuring the black king cannot escape.

notes.explains: After a capture on g3, White has several reasons to prefer recapturing with the pawn: it opens the c-file, stops Black's queen from entering c4, and keeps the queen on a useful diagonal for potential trades or a jump to h6. Additionally, the pawn on g3 controls key squares and supports the attack.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider not just the immediate material but also the resulting pawn structure and open files. A pawn recapture can create long-term advantages like open files and control of central squares.
notes.plans: White will use the open c-file and the queen's diagonal to continue the attack, possibly trading bishops to expose the king or jumping the knight to an outpost.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on h4 is a mistake because it allows White to take the g3 pawn, which is the key to Black's defense. If Black can hold onto that pawn, the g-file is closed and the attack is stifled, but if White captures it, the attack becomes overwhelming.
notes.teaches: In defense, holding onto a key pawn can be more important than material or activity. Recognize which pawns are the pillars of your defense and avoid moves that allow them to be captured.
notes.plans: White will capture the g3 pawn, opening the g-file and intensifying the attack. Black must find a way to create counterplay, but White's pieces are too active.

notes.explains: White's position is almost winning because Black is completely paralyzed: the queen, bishop, and knight have no good squares, and Black has no active moves. This gives White the luxury of improving the worst-placed piece, the knight, by rerouting it to e4 via d2.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is tied down and has no counterplay, you should not rush the attack. Instead, take time to improve your worst piece and strengthen your position, as the threat of the attack remains.
notes.plans: White plays Nd2, intending Ne4 with tempo, after which Black is even more restricted. White can then decide whether to continue the attack or convert the advantage.

notes.explains: The position changes constantly, and the same ideas may no longer be relevant. In the game, White had to adapt to the changing circumstances and not cling to an earlier plan that was no longer effective.
notes.teaches: Always re-evaluate the position after each move, asking yourself what has changed and how it affects your plan. Be willing to abandon an idea that is no longer sound, even if you are attached to it.

notes.explains: In the Ragozin Defense, after d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Nc3 Bb4 Bg5 h6, White can retreat the bishop to d2 instead of the usual Bxf6 or Bh4. This retreat is a flexible move that keeps the bishop and prepares a possible kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays a move like h6, it creates a hook on the kingside. Retreating the bishop to d2 can be a way to maintain tension while keeping the option of a later g4-g5 attack.
notes.plans: White aims to provoke ...h6, then retreat the bishop to d2, and if Black castles kingside, launch a pawn storm with g4 and g5, using the hook on h6 to open lines.

notes.explains: In the position after Bg5 h6 Bd2, Black's natural moves include c5, Nbd7, or O-O. The move Ne4 is not good because the knight on c3 is no longer pinned, so White can simply take it with Nxe4, and the knight on d2 defends the bishop.
notes.teaches: A pin can make moves like Ne4 strong, but when the pin is broken, such moves often fail tactically. Always check if the tactical resource is still available after the opponent's last move.
notes.plans: Black should choose a solid developing move like c5 or O-O, but must be aware that castling kingside may invite a pawn storm.

notes.explains: White's g4 push is justified here because Black has castled kingside, White has not castled (so the king is safe on e1 or can move to the queenside), and Black's h6 pawn provides a hook for g5, which would open lines against the black king.
notes.teaches: A kingside pawn storm with g4-g5 is playable when the opponent has castled kingside, your own king is not on that side, and you have a hook (like h6) to open files. Without these conditions, such a move is often too weakening.
notes.plans: White will play g4, then g5, and if Black allows, capture on h6 to open the h-file and attack the black king.

notes.explains: The g4 push is playable when Black has castled kingside and included h6, while White has not yet castled. This specific setup makes the pawn thrust a real threat because it can open lines against the black king.
notes.teaches: Recognize the pattern: if Black has h6 and White can play g4, the timing may be right to start a kingside attack, even if it is not objectively crushing.
notes.plans: If the position allows, consider g4 to open files against the enemy king, especially when the opponent has weakened their kingside with h6.

notes.explains: After g4, Black has several reasonable replies, such as capturing on c3, developing normally with Nbd7, playing Re8, or counterattacking with c5. The move Nxg4 is risky because White can respond with Rg1, creating strong threats.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn storm, avoid grabbing the pawn if it allows the attacker to open lines with tempo. Instead, consider solid development or counterplay in the center.
notes.plans: If Black captures on c3 and White recaptures with the bishop, Black can aim to plant a knight on e4 to block the attack and gain counterplay.

notes.explains: White delayed h4 in favor of Qc2, which prepares queenside castling and places the queen on an active diagonal. This move also sets up the possibility of playing g5 first, which gains a tempo compared to h4 immediately.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is better to delay an obvious attacking move to first improve your position or prepare a more forcing breakthrough. Here, g5 first forces ...hxg5, then h4 opens the h-file without giving Black time to address the center.
notes.plans: White intends to play g5, then h4, opening the h-file and launching a direct attack on the black king, while Black is distracted by queenside pressure.

notes.explains: When attacking with a g-pawn, the order of pawn moves matters. Playing g5 before h4 can gain a tempo because if the opponent captures on g5, recapturing with the h-pawn opens the h-file immediately, denying the opponent time to address their own counterplay.
notes.teaches: In pawn-storm attacks, consider the most forcing move order. Sometimes playing the more aggressive pawn push first (g5) and following with the support pawn (h4) creates threats faster than the reverse order.
notes.plans: If the opponent allows it, recapture on g5 with the h-pawn to open the h-file and continue the attack with maximum tempo.

notes.explains: The downside of playing g5 before h4 is that if the opponent does not capture, the g-pawn remains on g5, which can be a weakness. In the game, the opponent instead played g4, allowing the knight to use the h-pawn to land on g5, giving the attacker strong piece activity.
notes.teaches: When choosing between pushing the g-pawn or the h-pawn, weigh the benefit of opening lines against the potential weakness of an advanced pawn. Sometimes keeping the pawn on g5 can block your own pieces, so consider whether you want the pawn to remain there.
notes.plans: If the opponent allows, use the h-pawn to support a knight landing on g5, creating a powerful attacking piece.

notes.explains: A better defensive try for the opponent would have been to play h5, keeping the g-pawn on g5 and files closed. This would limit the attacker's piece activity and force them to deal with the pawn, rather than allowing a knight to occupy g5.
notes.teaches: When defending against a pawn storm, consider moves that keep the position closed and restrict the opponent's pieces. Sometimes allowing a pawn to remain on a square like g5 is less dangerous than opening lines for the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays h5, the attacker can recapture on b6 and continue with normal development, maintaining pressure without being down material.

notes.explains: In the actual game, the opponent captured the g5 knight, which was fatal. After the recapture, the attacker had overwhelming threats. A better try would have been to develop with knight c6, even if it allows the attacker to win material, because it keeps the position more solid.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong attack, sometimes it is better to give up material to keep the position closed and avoid opening lines for the opponent's pieces. Capturing an attacking piece can open critical files and lead to a decisive attack.
notes.plans: If the opponent avoids the capture, the attacker can continue with natural moves like e3 or castle queenside, maintaining the initiative and pressure.

notes.explains: In this position, White's attack is overwhelming because Black's king is exposed and White has multiple threats converging on d5. Black's defensive tries like knight d7 or knight c6 fail to cover all the threats, and even moves like d6 or queen c6 are winning for White.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is weak and your pieces are actively placed, look for ways to create multiple threats that cannot all be parried. A single defensive move often cannot address all the attacking ideas.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by exploiting the weak king, possibly with a decisive tactic or a mating net.

notes.explains: The game reached a position where White has a forced checkmate with a sequence involving rook checks and a queen sacrifice, exploiting the pin on Black's queen. The key is the pin that prevents the queen from defending the mating square.
notes.teaches: Recognize mating patterns that involve pins and sacrifices. Even if a mate is missed in the game, the pattern is important to remember for future positions.
notes.plans: If the opportunity arises, execute the mating sequence; otherwise, maintain the pressure and convert the advantage.

notes.explains: In the first game, the move g4 was justified because Black had castled kingside, committed to h6, and White's position remained flexible. These conditions made the pawn thrust effective as an attacking move.
notes.teaches: A pawn storm like g4 is appropriate when the opponent has weakened their kingside and your own king is safe. Flexibility in your own setup is key to launching such an attack.
notes.plans: Proceed with the pawn storm, opening lines against the enemy king.

notes.explains: In the Kramnik–Aronian game, White played h3 prematurely, committing to a kingside move while Black still had the option to castle queenside. This allowed Black to launch a successful attack because Black's position remained flexible.
notes.teaches: Avoid committing to pawn moves that weaken your own king or waste time when the opponent's plans are still unclear. Keep flexibility to respond to the opponent's setup.
notes.plans: If the opponent commits too early, exploit the flexibility to choose the best side to attack and proceed with a pawn storm.

notes.explains: In a kingside attack, every tempo matters. Delaying the attack to address the center or to make preparatory moves like h6 can allow the defender to consolidate and blunt the assault.
notes.teaches: When launching a kingside attack, prioritize speed over material or central activity. Avoid unnecessary preparatory moves that give the opponent time to organize a defense.
notes.plans: If you have a lead in development and the opponent's king is exposed, seek the fastest way to open lines and bring pieces to the attack, even if it means sacrificing material.

notes.explains: In the position discussed, Black's attack is best initiated with Rg8 rather than h6. Rg8 prepares g5 while also bringing the rook to the g-file, and it saves a tempo because the h-pawn can later go directly to h5 in one move.
notes.teaches: When preparing a pawn storm, choose moves that serve multiple purposes. A rook lift to the g-file can support the pawn break and also create immediate threats, saving time compared to a single-purpose pawn move.
notes.plans: Play Rg8, then follow up with g5 and h5, using the rook to pressure the g-file and the pawns to open lines against the king.

notes.explains: After White plays Kh1 to avoid tactics on the g-file, Black continues with Nh5, bringing the knight to an attacking square and supporting the g5 break without wasting a tempo on h6.
notes.teaches: In an attack, use pieces to support pawn breaks rather than spending time on pawn moves that can be made later. A knight on h5 can both attack and support the g5 push.
notes.plans: Play Nh5, then g5, aiming to open the g-file and create threats against the enemy king.

notes.explains: When White plays c3, Black must decide whether to capture on e5 or continue the attack. Taking on e5 with the queen is too slow because White can then capture the knight on h5, and the attack stalls.
notes.teaches: In a kingside attack, avoid deviating to win material if it gives the opponent time to consolidate. Keep the attack flowing even if it means ignoring a central pawn.
notes.plans: Instead of taking on e5, play g4 immediately, continuing the pawn storm and maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: After White plays d4 and g3 to close the kingside, Black must find a way to continue the attack. Simply bringing pieces without a plan is ineffective; you need concrete ideas like undermining the pawn structure or exploiting weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When the opponent closes the position, look for ways to break through, such as sacrificing a piece to open lines or using the pawns to create weaknesses. Patience and creativity are needed to maintain the attack.
notes.plans: Consider moves like ...Nxg3 if it leads to a concrete breakthrough, or reposition pieces to target the weakened squares around the king.

notes.explains: When the opponent has weakened the light squares with pawn advances on the kingside, the defender's pieces should target those squares rather than trying to break through the closed pawn structure directly.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, look for weaknesses created by pawn moves and aim your pieces at those squares, often with a thematic pawn break like f5.
notes.plans: Develop pieces with the idea of playing f5, but first ensure the king is safe and the queen is displaced from its active post.

notes.explains: The move c5 is a useful way to displace an active enemy queen, forcing it to a less effective square and gaining time for development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is causing threats, a pawn move that attacks it can both gain tempo and improve your own piece coordination.
notes.plans: After the queen retreats, continue developing with tempo (e.g., bishop b6) and then execute the planned f5 break.

notes.explains: When the opponent plays bishop g5, capturing it with the h-pawn opens the h-file, giving more attacking avenues against the king. This is often the correct response even if it creates a weakness.
notes.teaches: In an attack, opening lines (especially files) toward the enemy king is often worth giving up a bishop, as it increases the attacking potential.
notes.plans: After hxg5, continue with f4 to break through on g3, then bring the rook to d3 and the other rook to d1 to pile up on the king.

notes.explains: The final combination involves a bishop sacrifice on d5, followed by a pawn storm on g3 and a mating net with queen and rooks. Even a pinned queen can be part of the attack if the king is trapped.
notes.teaches: When the king is surrounded by enemy pieces, a sacrifice can open the final lines, and even a pinned piece can participate if the mate is unavoidable.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, use the open g-file and the queen to deliver checkmate, as the king has no escape squares.

notes.explains: The early pawn move h3 by White creates a hook for Black to play g5, starting a kingside attack. This is a common idea in many openings, and even if you don't use it yourself, you must be aware of it.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves like h3 can be a target for a pawn storm (g5-g4) to open lines against the king. Recognize such hooks and consider attacking them.
notes.plans: If your opponent plays h3, consider preparing g5 to undermine the kingside, but ensure your own king is safe first.

notes.explains: In this position, white has castled and played h3, while black has not yet castled and is aiming for a kingside pawn storm with g5-g4. White's queenside is undeveloped and there is no immediate central counterplay, making black's attack especially potent.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has castled and you have not, and they start pushing kingside pawns, you must consider whether their attack will simply crush you before you can organize counterplay. Recognizing this danger is crucial even if you don't play such attacks yourself.
notes.plans: If you are the defender, look for ways to create counterplay in the center or on the queenside to distract from the kingside attack. If you are the attacker, ensure your pieces are well-placed to support the pawn storm.

notes.explains: The g5-g4 idea is not always good; its success depends on factors like whether the opponent has castled, whether they have committed to h6, and whether your pieces are positioned to support the attack. In this game, white's lack of development and central presence makes it a strong choice.
notes.teaches: Before launching a kingside pawn attack, evaluate the opponent's development and central control. If they are behind in development and lack central counterplay, the attack is more likely to succeed.
notes.plans: If you are considering g5-g4, check that your pieces are active and that the opponent cannot easily strike back in the center. If you are facing it, try to keep your pieces flexible and avoid weakening your kingside prematurely.

notes.explains: In the Nimzo-Indian, a move like c6 can be a useful idea: it sacrifices a pawn that is 'dead' anyway to force black to recapture with a pawn rather than a piece, altering the pawn structure and potentially gaining time.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up a pawn that has no future can be a good way to force a favorable recapture or to open lines for development. Look for such 'dead' pawns in your own positions.
notes.plans: After c6 and dxc6, white can develop pieces naturally, gaining tempo on black's pieces, and then continue with queenside play or central expansion.

notes.explains: In the Nimzo-Indian, even after black castles early, white can still consider aggressive moves like g4. This is a typical attacking idea in many openings, but it must be timed correctly.
notes.teaches: Kingside pawn storms can appear even in classical openings like the Nimzo-Indian. Be alert for such ideas and know when they are justified.
notes.plans: If playing g4, ensure your king is safe and your pieces support the advance. If facing it, consider central breaks to counter.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian line, White's c6 pawn break gains time on the knight and opens the d-file, which becomes a factor against Black's uncastled king. The central queen on e5 and active pieces give White a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: A pawn break like c6 can be used to gain tempo and create long-term pressure along an open file, especially when the opponent's king is still in the center.
notes.plans: White should continue with natural development and consider an immediate g4 to start a kingside attack, exploiting the awkward placement of Black's knights.

notes.explains: White's g4 is strong here because Black has not played h6, so the threat of g5 is not only to the knight on f6 but also to the h-pawn. This dual threat makes it hard for Black to defend both.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn storm like g4-g5, look for double threats: the pawn advance can attack a piece and a pawn simultaneously, overwhelming the defense.
notes.plans: White should aim to play g5, forcing Black to deal with the knight threat and the h-pawn, while maintaining the central pressure with the queen on e5.

notes.explains: Black's knights are poorly placed, and attempts to regroup fail tactically: for example, ...Nd6 allows Rd1, and ...Qd6 runs into g5 followed by Bg2. Black's position collapses quickly.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are awkwardly placed, look for tactical blows that exploit the lack of coordination, often with a pawn advance or a rook lift.
notes.plans: White should continue with g5 and then collect the knight on f6, winning material, as in the game continuation.

notes.explains: The move c6 was a key part of White's opening prep, leading to a crushing advantage. Modern practice prefers bxc6 to support the center with d5, avoiding the loose structure that allows White's attack.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, recapturing with the b-pawn to maintain a strong center is often more solid than taking with the d-pawn, which can leave weaknesses and open lines for the opponent.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the initiative with active piece play and the g4 break, while Black should seek to consolidate the center to neutralize White's attack.

notes.explains: In the second game (Queen's Gambit Declined), after c4 e6 Nc3 d5 d4 Be7 Nf3 Nf6 Bg5 h6 Bh4 O-O, White considered g4 but it is premature because g5 is not a serious threat: Black can meet it with Ne4, creating an awkward pin on the bishop.
notes.teaches: Before playing a committal pawn push like g4, ensure that the follow-up (g5) actually threatens something concrete; if the opponent can ignore it or create counterplay, the pawn move may just weaken your position.
notes.plans: Instead of g4, White should play a solid developing move like e3, keeping the option of a later pawn storm while maintaining flexibility.

notes.explains: The move Rg1 also fails to prepare g4 effectively because Black can simply play a useful move like b5 or c5, and if White plays g5, Black's Ne4 is still strong. The bishop on h4 is awkwardly placed, which is the root of the problem.
notes.teaches: When considering a flank attack, check if your own pieces are well-placed to support it; an awkwardly placed piece (like a bishop on h4 that can be pinned) can undermine the entire plan.
notes.plans: White should avoid overextending on the kingside and instead focus on central control and completing development; a later g4 might be possible after improving the bishop's position.

notes.explains: When the opponent plays a slow move like c6 instead of challenging the center with c5, the g4 pawn storm gains time. The bishop on h4 is awkward and doesn't support the attack well, whereas a better-placed bishop and a solid center make g4 more effective.
notes.teaches: The viability of a kingside pawn storm depends on the opponent's center play and piece placement. If the opponent is slow to develop or challenge the center, g4 can be a powerful attacking idea.
notes.plans: If the opponent plays passively, prepare g4 with moves like h4 and g5, aiming to open lines against the king.

notes.explains: In the game, after e3, Nxe7, Rxe7, and c6, g4 was a strong move. The follow-up h4 (rather than immediate g5) was correct because g5 would allow the knight to escape to g5 with no threats. After h4, e5, and exchanges, g5 gave White a significant advantage, with a thorn pawn on g5 and a weakened d5 pawn for Black.
notes.teaches: When launching a pawn storm, timing is crucial. Sometimes you need to prepare with h4 before g5 to prevent the opponent's pieces from escaping or counterattacking.
notes.plans: Continue to press on the kingside, using the g5 pawn as a hook to open lines, and target the weakened d5 pawn in the endgame.

notes.explains: When Black has played c6, the center is temporarily stable, so White can spend a few moves on the kingside with h4 and g5 to open lines before Black's central play gets going.
notes.teaches: The timing of a flank pawn push like g4 depends on the opponent's ability to counter in the center; if their central play is slow, you have time to expand on the flank.
notes.plans: Play h4 and g5 to open the kingside, creating attacking chances before Black can organize in the center.

notes.explains: The g4 idea is uncommon but playable in many positions, and even top players use it, so it's not just a gimmick.
notes.teaches: Unusual but sound ideas can be effective because opponents are often unprepared for them; it's worth both trying them yourself and knowing how to meet them.

notes.explains: If you face g4 as Black, you need to know how to respond; otherwise you can be caught off guard.
notes.teaches: Study common flank attacks from the defender's perspective so you aren't surprised by moves like g4.
notes.plans: Learn typical defensive setups against early g4, such as central counterplay or piece placement to blunt the attack.

notes.explains: In the Rapport-Jobava system, White plays d4, Nc3, and Bf4, effectively reaching a Chigorin Defense with an extra tempo compared to the standard line where Black plays d5 and Nc6. This extra tempo can be significant because it allows White to create immediate tactical threats.
notes.teaches: The value of a tempo in the opening can be decisive; even a single extra move can transform a solid defense into a dangerous attacking system.
notes.plans: White aims to exploit the early bishop on f4, which controls c7, and the absence of the c-pawn to create threats against Black's position.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 Bf4, if Black plays …c5 and White responds e3, then after …cxd4 exd4, Black's natural developing move …Nc6 is actually losing due to the tactical shot Nb5. The bishop on f4 covers c7, and the knight on b5 cannot be captured because the bishop defends it, leading to a fork on c7.
notes.teaches: In the opening, a seemingly natural developing move can be punished by a concrete tactic. Always check for tactical resources before making a routine move.
notes.plans: White's plan is to jump the knight to b5, threatening Nc7+ forking the king and rook, and if Black tries to avoid it with ...e5, White can capture on c5 and win a pawn.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...a6 to prevent Nb5, the center becomes static and the play can become dry. However, White can still create dynamic play by treating the position like a sharp Sicilian, using pawn advances like h3 and g4 to gain space and attack.
notes.teaches: Even in a quiet-looking position, you can create imbalances and attacking chances by using pawn storms and piece pressure, especially when the opponent's pieces are passively placed.
notes.plans: White can play h3 to ask the bishop on g4 where it wants to go, and if it retreats to h5, then g4 and Ne5 can follow, gaining time and space. If Black plays ...e6, then h4 can be powerful to ruin Black's structure.

notes.explains: In the resulting position after Black takes on f3 and plays ...Nc6, White's aggressive style is shown by long castling, heading for the jugular. White is willing to expose the king to attack in order to launch a direct assault on Black's king.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must take risks and castle on the opposite side to generate attacking chances. Aggressive play can be justified if you can create threats faster than your opponent.
notes.plans: White will continue with pawn advances like g4 and h4 to open lines against the black king, while using pieces to control key squares and defend against counterplay.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...Bb4 and ...Ne4, it looks dangerous for White's king, but White can calmly defend with a move like a3 (or similar) to overprotect the queenside pawns and neutralize the threats. The position remains under control for White.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, it's important to remain calm and find defensive resources that maintain the balance. Overprotecting key pawns can defuse an opponent's attack.
notes.plans: White can consolidate the position, aiming to use the extra space and piece activity to convert the advantage in the middlegame or endgame.

notes.explains: A knight on c1 (similar to a defensive knight on f8) can be a key defensive resource, making it very hard for the opponent to deliver checkmate. Even if the knight is captured, it can be recaptured, and the defensive structure remains solid.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece placed on an unusual square can provide crucial defense. Look for such defensive resources to neutralize an enemy attack.
notes.plans: Use the knight on c1 to cover key squares and prevent mating threats, then continue with your own plans.

notes.explains: In this closed position, White has a space advantage on the kingside with a pawn on g4. The long-term plan is to launch a pawn storm on the kingside, using the extra space to push g5 and h4.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage on one side, that is usually the side where you should attack. Pawn storms are most effective when you have more pawns and space.
notes.plans: Prepare the kingside pawn storm by connecting rooks and developing pieces to support the advance, while keeping an eye on the opponent's counterplay.

notes.explains: Black castled into the attack, but when the opponent has pawns ready to advance (g5 and h4), castling into that wing can be dangerous. White's rook on g1 is ready to support the pawn storm.
notes.teaches: Before castling, consider whether the opponent's pawns are poised to attack that side. Sometimes it's better to keep the king in the center or castle to the other side.
notes.plans: Continue the kingside attack, using the rook and pawns to open lines against the enemy king.

notes.explains: White sacrifices a bishop on g7 to expose the king, relying on the coordination of rooks and queen to continue the attack. The compensation is not material but positional: the king is exposed, and there are loose pieces to pick up.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be justified by initiative and attacking chances, even if material compensation is not immediate. Look for ways to expose the enemy king and coordinate your pieces to exploit it.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with queen and rooks, targeting the exposed king and loose pieces, while maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: Black's natural move knight e7 fails tactically because White has a forced sequence: queen e6 check, then after rook takes and king takes, a bishop move eliminates the knight defending f6, allowing queen f6 checkmate. This shows that even natural defensive moves can be refuted by precise calculation.
notes.teaches: When considering a move, always check for forcing sequences that might exploit the weakening of key squares. A move that seems to defend can often create new tactical vulnerabilities.
notes.plans: Black must find a different way to defend, perhaps by hiding the king or creating counterplay, but the immediate threat is decisive.

notes.explains: White plays rook takes g7, a move that aims to disrupt Black's coordination. If Black recaptures with the king, White has a similar tactical idea with bishop takes c4. But when Black recaptures with the queen, White can play queen takes d5, hitting multiple targets: the knight on c6, and x-raying to a8 and e4. This creates a 'jackpot' of threats.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for moves that create multiple threats simultaneously, especially those that exploit the opponent's lack of coordination. A single move can overload the defense.
notes.plans: White continues to press, winning material and maintaining the initiative, while Black struggles to coordinate.

notes.explains: After a series of forcing moves, White emerges with two extra pawns by move 25, a winning advantage against a strong grandmaster. The key was combining material gains with relentless pressure, not allowing Black to stabilize.
notes.teaches: Converting an advantage requires maintaining pressure and avoiding unnecessary complications. Even when winning, continue to follow basic principles: activate pieces, centralize, and keep the king safe.
notes.plans: White should consolidate the extra pawns, activate all pieces, and prepare to convert the advantage in the endgame or by continuing the attack.

notes.explains: In the later phase, White's pieces are all centralized and mutually defending, while Black's king is stuck in the corner. White's d-pawn advances, becoming a dangerous passed pawn, and White is happy to exchange queens to promote.
notes.teaches: Even with a winning position, keep applying basic principles: centralize pieces, ensure they defend each other, and advance passed pawns. A centralized army is both strong defensively and offensively.
notes.plans: White pushes the d-pawn toward promotion, using the active pieces to support it, and is willing to trade queens to simplify into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: In the Rapport-Jobava System, the move Nb5 attacks the c7 pawn, forcing Black to play ...Na6 to defend. This leaves the knight on a6 poorly placed, while White's knight on c3, though not ideal, is better than Black's misplaced knight.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is forced to make a move that misplaces a piece, you can be satisfied with a slightly awkward piece of your own, as the long-term positional gain is in your favor.
notes.plans: White should continue developing, aiming to control key central squares like e5, and later exploit the poor placement of Black's knight on a6.

notes.explains: In the slower setup of the Jobava System, White plays a3 to prevent Bb4+ after c4, which could lead to uncomfortable complications. This allows White to maintain a solid pawn structure and avoid early checks.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's important to make a prophylactic move to prevent your opponent's active ideas, even if it seems slow. This can be crucial for maintaining a safe king and avoiding tactical tricks.
notes.plans: White should continue with natural development, aiming for a Queen's Gambit Declined type of position, with control over e5 and pressure on Black's position.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...Bxf4, White recaptures with the bishop, but this gives away the important e5 square. White then places a knight on e5, supported by two pawns, creating a powerful outpost that restricts Black's pieces, especially the c8 bishop.
notes.teaches: A knight on a strong outpost, supported by pawns, can be a decisive advantage. It restricts the opponent's pieces and provides a base for further attacks.
notes.plans: White should use the knight on e5 to pressure Black's position, possibly with moves like Qf3 to increase the pressure, while Black struggles to activate the c8 bishop.

notes.explains: In a position where White has a strong knight on e5, Black tries to exchange pieces and activate the c8 bishop with ...b6 and ...c5. White responds with Qf3, and then chooses a concrete move like Nb5, which is aggressive but not necessarily best, yet it creates practical problems for Black.
notes.teaches: Concrete players often prefer moves that create immediate threats and practical difficulties for the opponent, even if they are not objectively best. This can be a valid strategy, especially in complex positions.
notes.plans: White should continue to create threats and maintain pressure, while being aware of potential weaknesses in their own position. The knight on e5 remains a key asset.

notes.explains: In this system, Black's light-squared bishop on c8 is often a long-term problem because it takes many moves to develop actively. White's setup can exploit this by keeping pressure and forcing Black to spend time on defensive moves.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a poorly placed piece, try to maintain tension and avoid premature captures; provoke weaknesses or time-wasting moves instead.
notes.plans: Continue developing and centralizing, while keeping the c8 bishop restricted.

notes.explains: White chose an aggressive move (knight to b5) rather than a quieter developing move, aiming to create practical problems for Black, especially since Black's king is still in the center. This is a common approach for concrete players who prioritize active play over theoretical soundness.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a move that is not objectively best can be excellent in practice because it forces your opponent to solve difficult problems, especially when their king is uncastled.
notes.plans: Keep the initiative and look for ways to exploit the central king.

notes.explains: Black avoided wasting time on a6, correctly recognizing that such a move would be a success for White, who could then open the queenside and attack the d5 pawn. Instead, Black traded pieces and kept the position balanced.
notes.teaches: Do not make pawn moves that are not necessary; if your opponent is trying to provoke you, it is often better to ignore the threat and continue with your own plans.
notes.plans: Maintain the balance and look for counterplay.

notes.explains: White played f5, a strong central break that creates threats and forces Black to react. If Black captures, White recaptures and gets a powerful passed pawn on the d-file, which is ideal for an endgame. This move is aggressive and prevents Black from rolling forward.
notes.teaches: In positions that appear slow, you must be alert to central breaks that can give you a lasting advantage, especially if they lead to a favorable endgame with a passed pawn.
notes.plans: After f5, if Black captures, recapture and aim for a winning endgame with the passed pawn.

notes.explains: White played rook e1, a simple developing move that brings the rook into play. This follows basic principles and improves the position without needing flashy tactics. Later, White centralized the rook on d4, showing the power of centralization.
notes.teaches: You don't always need spectacular moves; simple moves that improve your pieces and follow principles can be very effective. Centralize your rooks on open or semi-open files.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece activity and centralize.

notes.explains: Black tried to set up e5, but White prevented it with rook e5, maintaining pressure. White then identified a long-term plan: if Black does nothing, White can push g4-g5, starting a kingside attack that could lead to mate once the f-pawn advances.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a solid but passive position, look for pawn storms on the side where you have space and can create mating threats.
notes.plans: Push g4-g5 to start a kingside attack, aiming for f6 and mate.

notes.explains: After exchanges, White reached an endgame with an extra pawn on the queenside and a king that is much closer to the passed pawns than Black's king on g8. This is a typical winning scenario: the king supports the passed pawns while the opponent's king is far away.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the king's activity is crucial. A king that is closer to the passed pawns often decides the game.
notes.plans: Bring the king to support the queenside pawns, and use the rook to harass Black's pawns.

notes.explains: White has an extra queenside pawn and a king that is much closer to the potential passed pawns than Black's king on g8. This makes the endgame favorable for White, so White wants to exchange queens and reach that endgame.
notes.teaches: When you have a lasting structural advantage, aim to simplify into the endgame where your advantage can be converted.
notes.plans: White should try to trade queens and then push the queenside pawns with the support of the king.

notes.explains: Black declines the queen exchange because White's king is strong in the endgame, but Black still has counterplay in the middlegame, including threats against White's king and pawns.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you should avoid simplifying if your opponent's endgame is better, and instead seek active counterplay in the middlegame.
notes.plans: Black should keep queens on and create threats against White's king and kingside pawns.

notes.explains: White builds a safe haven for the king on b2, but must be careful about move order because a premature king move could allow a checkmate. The move order is crucial.
notes.teaches: When creating a shelter for your king, always check for tactical shots like back-rank mates or other immediate threats.
notes.plans: White continues to consolidate the king's safety while maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's queen sally to c4 is overzealous; it tries to harass the white king but leaves Black's pieces uncoordinated. Better was to put the rook on c8 to pressure the c-file and maintain counterplay.
notes.teaches: Avoid overextending your queen in the middlegame; piece coordination and pressure on files are often more valuable than chasing the king.
notes.plans: Black should improve piece placement, perhaps by doubling rooks on the c-file, to create lasting pressure.

notes.explains: White's rook on e1 is dangerous because it can give a check on e8, and Black cannot capture due to losing the queen on f1. This forces Black to move the king, losing time.
notes.teaches: Active rooks on open files can create tactical threats that force the opponent to weaken their position.
notes.plans: White continues to exploit the active rook and the misplaced black queen.

notes.explains: White offers a queen trade, which Black declines, but the queen becomes awkward in the corner. White then uses the opportunity to improve the position and eventually force a favorable endgame.
notes.teaches: When your opponent declines a trade, their pieces may become misplaced; use that to improve your own position and keep the pressure.
notes.plans: White should continue to target the awkward queen and aim for the endgame.

notes.explains: After the queen exchange, White's king is much closer to the passed b-pawn than Black's king, and the rook is cut off from stopping the pawn. The pawn will promote.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the king's proximity to passed pawns and the activity of the rook are decisive. A cut-off rook cannot stop a pawn.
notes.plans: White should push the b-pawn with the king's support, while keeping the black rook cut off.

notes.explains: In the Rapport-Jobava System, White often plays differently than in the classical Queen's Gambit Declined, sometimes with bishop to f4 and c5. Here, White faces an early e3 from Black, leading to a structure where the c8 bishop can become problematic if Black plays e6, as it gets locked in.
notes.teaches: When facing the Rapport-Jobava, be mindful of your light-squared bishop's activity; playing e6 early can leave it passive, so consider developing it to g4 to exchange or activate it.
notes.plans: If Black has played e6, White can aim for a slow positional grind, possibly with knight e2, and later reposition pieces to target Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a choice of which rook to place on d1 and which on e1. The d4 pawn is weak because the knight on c3 doesn't defend it, so a rook on d1 supports it. Placing the rook on e1 instead would leave it less active, and the f4-f5 break is hard to achieve.
notes.teaches: Rook placement can decide the game; prioritize supporting weak pawns and placing rooks on open or semi-open files where they have influence.
notes.plans: White should put the rook on d1 to defend the d4 pawn, and the other rook on e1 to prepare potential central play.

notes.explains: After all pieces are developed, White must find a plan. The knight on e2 is poorly placed, so White repositions it to g3. Black's rook on c8 and queen on b6 are active, but White's move sets up a tactical idea based on the weakness of the bishop on e7.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions, look for your worst-placed piece and improve it. Also, identify the opponent's weaknesses; here, the bishop on e7 is defended only by pawns, making it a target for tactics.
notes.plans: White plays knight f5, attacking the bishop on e7. If Black takes, White can recapture with the rook, and if Black tries to win the rook, White has a brilliant resource like bishop h6, exploiting the exposed king.

notes.explains: In this attacking position, the defender's queen, knight, and rooks are all far away on the queenside, leaving the king with almost no defenders. The attacker exploits this by finding a move that is surprising but logical: a bishop sacrifice on h6, which rips open the king's shelter and brings the queen into the attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are committed to one side, look for sacrificial blows against the king even if they seem unpredictable. The key is to check whether the king has enough defenders; if not, a sacrifice can be decisive.
notes.plans: After the bishop sacrifice, the attacker intends to bring the queen to g5 with check, forcing the king to move and then winning material or delivering mate. The defender's king cannot run because the bishop on g7 and queen on g5 cover escape squares.

notes.explains: In the actual game, the defender did not play the best defensive move, and the attacker finished with a different but equally elegant mate. The final position shows that the defender's pieces are overloaded: the knight cannot return to defend because it would lose the bishop, and the f7 pawn is pinned. The attacker's heavy pieces (rook and queen) are lined up against the king, and a decisive rook sacrifice on e6 leads to mate on f7.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down by pins and overloaded, you can often finish with a direct attack using your heavy pieces. Look for sacrifices that remove the last defender or expose the king, and remember that pinned pieces cannot help.
notes.plans: The attacker plays rook e1, threatening to take on e6. If the defender tries to block or escape, the rook takes on e6 anyway, and the queen delivers mate on f7. The defender's resignation is justified because there is no way to prevent the mate.

notes.explains: In the Scotch Game, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4, Black's Qh4 (the Steinitz Variation) directly attacks the e4 pawn. White must decide how to defend it, but the f-pawn is pinned, so f3 is illegal.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is attacked, first check if the natural defender is pinned or otherwise unavailable. Recognize that a queen early attack often targets weak squares like c7.
notes.plans: White should consider developing moves that also address the attack, such as Nc3, or even ignoring the pawn to exploit Black's queen's absence from the queenside.

notes.explains: Defending the e4 pawn with Qd3 is passive; Black can simply play Nf6, and statistics show Black scores well. Similarly, Bd3 fails tactically to Nxd4, losing a piece.
notes.teaches: Passive defense of a pawn often allows the opponent to develop with tempo. Always consider tactical refutations like Nxd4 when placing pieces on vulnerable squares.
notes.plans: Avoid Qd3 and Bd3; instead, seek active development or counterplay.

notes.explains: White can ignore the hanging e4 pawn and play Nb5, targeting c7. This exploits the queen's absence from the queenside. However, Black can respond with Bc5, threatening mate, so White must be careful not to grab the rook immediately.
notes.teaches: Sometimes sacrificing a pawn for active piece play is justified, especially when the opponent's queen is misplaced. Always be alert to counter-threats like mate before grabbing material.
notes.plans: After Nb5, if Black plays Bc5, White should avoid taking c7 prematurely; instead, develop the queen (e.g., Qf3) to maintain pressure and avoid the mate threat.

notes.explains: In this sharp line, grabbing the pawn on c7 with the knight fails because Black's bishop on c5 threatens mate, forcing White to spend moves defending while the knight gets trapped, leaving White down material.
notes.teaches: Before taking a pawn, check if the piece becomes trapped or if the opponent's threats force you to lose time and material.
notes.plans: If White wants to keep pressure, develop the queen to f3, but be ready for Black's knight to d4 attacking the queen and eyeing c2.

notes.explains: After queen f3 and knight d4, White can trade on d4, but a more forcing idea is knight takes c7, giving check. Black must move the king to d8, then White plays queen f4, which defends against mate, is protected by the bishop, and supports the knight.
notes.teaches: When your queen is developed, look for squares where it can multitask: defend, attack, and support your pieces simultaneously.
notes.plans: If Black plays knight c2 check, White can allow the trade and both sides win a rook in the corner, leading to a balanced endgame with White having a slightly healthier structure.

notes.explains: In the main line with knight c3, Black plays bishop b4, pinning the knight and attacking e4 again. White must decide how to handle the pressure on e4, and many moves fail: queen e2 allows knight takes d4, knight e2 allows Black to simply take the pawn or continue developing with knight f6.
notes.teaches: When your center pawn is attacked, look for moves that defend it while also developing or maintaining the initiative, and be wary of moves that allow your opponent to win the pawn cheaply.
notes.plans: White needs to find a move that defends e4 without creating weaknesses, possibly by breaking the pin or counterattacking.

notes.explains: In this Scotch position, White's central pawn is under attack and cannot be defended by pushing it, since Black's knight would simply capture. White must choose a setup that either defends the pawn or accepts its loss while gaining compensation.
notes.teaches: When a central pawn is attacked and cannot be pushed, look for piece moves that defend it indirectly or accept the pawn sacrifice for activity and development.
notes.plans: White should consider moves like knight to e2 or bishop to e2, aiming to maintain a sound structure and develop pieces while keeping the position flexible.

notes.explains: White's queen to d2 is possible but blocks the dark-squared bishop, leaving it without a clear future. If Black captures on e4, White can recapture with the knight, and after bishop d2, recapture with the bishop, reaching an even position. However, Black is not forced to take on e4 and can instead capture on c3, leaving White still down a pawn.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that block your own bishop's development unless they offer concrete compensation; consider whether the opponent is forced to follow your plan.
notes.plans: If White plays queen d2, be ready for Black to avoid the main line and choose a different capture, so White should have a plan for that.

notes.explains: Bishop to d2 to break the pin fails because it also removes the defense of the knight on c3, allowing Black to simply capture on d4. This shows that breaking a pin must not leave another piece undefended.
notes.teaches: When breaking a pin, ensure that the piece you move does not abandon defense of another piece; otherwise the pin is not truly resolved.
notes.plans: White should reject bishop d2 and look for a move that both breaks the pin and maintains the knight's defense, such as castling or bishop e2.

notes.explains: Bishop to e2 is the move that leaves White with a healthy advantage. If Black captures on c3, White recaptures, and after queen e4, White can castle and then use the rook on e1 to pressure the queen and king. The bishop pair becomes significant compensation for the pawn because the board is open and Black's central pawns are still on their original squares, so the bishops have clear diagonals.
notes.teaches: The bishop pair can be strong compensation for a pawn in open positions, especially when the opponent's central pawns have not advanced to block the bishops.
notes.plans: After bishop e2, White should aim to castle quickly, then use the rook to e1 and possibly bring the bishop to a3, while keeping pressure on Black's queenside.

notes.explains: If Black instead plays knight g to e7, White can castle to break the pin and reconnect the knight to the pawn. If Black then captures on c3, White recaptures with the pawn, and after queen e4, White can choose bishop f3 to hit the queen, or rook e1. Bishop f3 is direct, and after the queen moves to h4, knight b5 threatens c7 and forces Black to give up castling rights, leaving the king in the center.
notes.teaches: Castling can be a powerful way to break a pin while also improving king safety; look for moves that combine defense with threats.
notes.plans: White should consider bishop f3 to harass the queen, then knight b5 to target c7, followed by rook e1 to control the open file.

notes.explains: If Black plays Qxg2, White has Bf3, forcing the queen to move, and then Nxc7 wins the rook. Alternatively, Nxc7 first is also possible, but Bf3 first is cleaner.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple tactical ideas, consider the order that forces your opponent to react and maintains your initiative.
notes.plans: After Bf3 and the queen retreats, White can continue with Nxc7 or develop the bishop to f4, keeping the c7 threat and improving the position.

notes.explains: White prefers Bf4 over immediately taking on c7 because it develops another piece and keeps the c7 pawn hanging. This allows ideas like O-O-O or Rook to d1, while Black cannot defend c7.
notes.teaches: When you have a material-winning tactic, sometimes it's better to first improve your position and keep the threat, rather than cash in immediately.
notes.plans: White can develop the bishop to f4, then consider castling queenside or bringing the rook to d1, maintaining pressure on c7.

notes.explains: If Black tries Qe5 to defend c7 and attack the knight, White can play f4, attacking the queen. The queen has no safe square that keeps c7 protected, so Black loses material.
notes.teaches: Sometimes pushing the f-pawn is justified when it gains time and exploits the opponent's queen being overloaded.
notes.plans: After f4, if the queen moves to c5, White plays Nxc7+ winning the exchange. The f-pawn push is a key tactical resource in this line.

notes.explains: When Black takes on c3 with check, White should recapture with the b-pawn, accepting doubled pawns, to keep the initiative and maintain the knight on b5. This is a common theme in the Steinitz Variation.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are often acceptable when they come with an attack or initiative; here the b-pawn recapture keeps the knight on b5 and the c7 threat alive.
notes.plans: After bxc3, White can castle, develop the knight to f6, and play Bg5, while the c7 threat remains. Black's best defense is Kd8, but White still has a strong attack.

notes.explains: In the Steinitz variation, after Black's king moves to d8 to defend the c7 pawn, White's play becomes straightforward: castle, develop the knight to f6, and then pin with bishop to g5. Black's alternative of playing a6 to hit the knight back is poor because it undoubles White's pawns, giving White the bishop pair and a lead in development.
notes.teaches: When your opponent offers to undouble your pawns, consider whether the resulting structural improvement is worth the concession. Here, Black's a6 move relieves White's doubled pawns, which were compensation for Black, so it's not recommended.
notes.plans: White should continue with natural development: castle, knight to f6, and bishop to g5, aiming for an easy game with the bishop pair and open files.

notes.explains: In the Steinitz variation, Black's move rook e8 is not accurate because White can play bishop d3, forcing the queen to retreat, and then queen h5, exploiting the pinned knight to target h7 and f7. The knight on b5 is supported by the bishop, so it's secure.
notes.teaches: When a knight is pinned, the squares it defends become vulnerable. Here, the pinned knight on f6 leaves h7 and f7 weak, so White can attack them with queen h5.
notes.plans: White should play bishop d3, then queen h5, creating threats against h7 and f7, while the knight on b5 remains safe.

notes.explains: In the Steinitz variation, after Black plays d6, the position is roughly equal with a slight edge for White (about +0.7). Black has opened the diagonal for their bishop, but White's position is still comfortable.
notes.teaches: Not every advantage is decisive; a small edge like +0.7 is meaningful only at high levels. For most players, such a difference is not significant, so Black can play this line without fear.
notes.plans: White can continue with natural development, while Black should aim to complete development and activate the bishop.

notes.explains: In the Scotch, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4, Black's queen can go to f6 instead of the more common h4. This line lacks a standard name, so it's often called the queen f6 line. White has several viable setups, and Black's position is generally easy to play, with fewer attacking chances against e4 compared to the queen h4 line.
notes.teaches: Recognize that queen f6 is a legitimate alternative in the Scotch, and be prepared for White's multiple possible replies. Black's development is often smoother here than in the queen h4 line.
notes.plans: Black should aim for natural development, often with ...Bc5 or ...Bb4, and be ready to meet White's attempts to exploit the queen's placement.

notes.explains: After queen f6, White can try Nb5. If Black responds with Bc5, this is more effective than in the queen h4 line because the bishop develops with a threat of mate on f2. White cannot simply capture on c7 because the knight would be trapped, so White must address the threat.
notes.teaches: When a developing move creates a concrete threat, the opponent must respond, often losing time. Compare similar positions to see why a move that was less good in one line can be strong in another.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bc5, and if White tries Qf3, Black can continue with ...Bb6, avoiding queen trades and keeping the position healthy.

notes.explains: In the Nb5 line, White's queen often goes to g3 to hit c7, but Black can stop this with ...d6. Black is not struggling with development as much as in the queen h4 line, and the position opens up faster. The move Qf3 is less favorable here because Black can simply retreat the bishop to b6, and neither side wants to trade queens prematurely.
notes.teaches: In queenless middlegames, development and piece activity matter more than material. Sometimes avoiding queen trades is beneficial for both sides, as each has reasons to keep queens on the board.
notes.plans: Black plays ...d6 to solidify, then continues development. White may need to find another plan if Qf3 is not effective.

notes.explains: The main move for White against Bc5 is Qe2, which scores very well statistically. Black retreats the bishop to b6 to prevent Nc7, and White develops the knight to c3. Black's knight goes to e7, and White plays Be3 to pressure the bishop on b6. Black's counterintuitive ...Ba5 moves the bishop again but avoids the pin and prepares to deal with threats.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must move a piece multiple times to maintain the best defensive setup. A move that looks like a loss of time can be justified if it prevents a stronger threat or improves your piece coordination.
notes.plans: White can castle queenside, which is unusual in this line, and Black should aim for ...a6 to kick the knight, then ...d6 and natural development.

notes.explains: After White castles queenside, Black's best is ...a6, forcing the knight back to d4. There may be trades on c3, opening the queenside, but Black's pieces are not well placed to exploit the exposed white king. White has the resource Kd2 to escape if needed. Black typically plays ...d6 and both sides develop naturally.
notes.teaches: When castling queenside, be aware of pawn weaknesses but also consider the opponent's piece activity. Sometimes an exposed king is safe if the opponent's pieces are not coordinated to attack.
notes.plans: White should be ready to move the king to d2 if necessary, while Black continues with ...d6 and development.

notes.explains: Another system for White is Nf3, and Black's most played response is ...Bb4. White blocks with c3, gaining a tempo, and the bishop retreats to c5. This seems to lose time, but Black's purpose is to prevent the knight from coming to c3, which is the natural square for the knight to go to d5 or b5, and also to protect e4.
notes.teaches: In the opening, a move that appears to lose time can be justified if it prevents the opponent's best piece placement or creates a long-term weakness. Here, ...Bb4 stops Nc3, which would both develop and protect e4.
notes.plans: After ...Bc5, White should develop normally, for example with Be2, and avoid moves like Nd2 that are passive. Black will play ...d6 and develop the knight to e7.

notes.explains: The knight on c3 is a natural developing move that also protects the e4 pawn, which would otherwise be a weakness. The knight can later go to d5 or b5, both useful ideas.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a piece, consider both its immediate activity and its defensive duties. A piece that protects a key pawn while also eyeing strong outposts is often ideal.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to c3, then look to place it on d5 or b5 depending on Black's setup.

notes.explains: After White plays c3 and Black plays Bc5, White should avoid passive moves like Nd2 and instead develop the bishop to e2, then castle and continue with normal development. Black's d6 prepares to develop the knight to e7, and White can still get queenside play with b4 and Bg5.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions, prioritize natural development and castling over artificial maneuvers. Don't be afraid to make simple, solid moves that improve your position.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e2, castle kingside, and then aim for queenside expansion with b4 and Bg5.

notes.explains: The move Bh4 is specifically prepared to meet Bh3 from Black. If Black plays Bh3, White can drop the bishop back to g3, and then Black's bishop on h3 is misplaced, allowing White to play Bg4 later.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a move's purpose is to anticipate and neutralize an opponent's plan. A bishop on h4 can be flexible, retreating to g3 to avoid being traded off.
notes.plans: If Black plays Bh3, retreat the bishop to g3, then consider Bg4 to pressure Black's position.

notes.explains: In a line where Black plays a5 and then Nxb4, White should not be greedy and try to hold the pawn. Instead, White can take on e7, forcing Black's king to move and lose castling rights, then develop the knight to c3 with future d5 in mind.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn grab, consider tactical responses that damage the opponent's king safety. Forcing the king to move can be worth more than a pawn.
notes.plans: After Nxb4, play Bxe7, then develop the knight to c3 and aim for d5.

notes.explains: If Black plays h6 to stop Bg5, White should not force the issue but instead play other natural moves like castling or Qc2. Qc2 is useful because it defends e4 and also puts pressure on Black, forcing a decision. If Black plays a5, White can develop the knight and later get play on the queenside with b4, a4, and b5.
notes.teaches: When your opponent prevents one plan, don't insist; switch to other useful moves that improve your position and keep the pressure on.
notes.plans: Play Qc2, castle, and then aim for queenside expansion with b4 and a4.

notes.explains: In the line with Nxc6, Black has the in-between move Bc5, which threatens a checkmate pattern. White must not be greedy and try to save the knight with Na5, as that leads to checkmate. Instead, White should protect the king with a move like Qd2, even though it blocks the bishop.
notes.teaches: Be alert to in-between moves that create threats. When your king is in danger, prioritize safety over material or piece activity.
notes.plans: Play Qd2 to defend the king, then continue development.

notes.explains: When Black has multiple ways to capture a pawn, the general rule is to capture towards the center, but here capturing away from the center is better. If Black captures towards the center, the light-squared bishop will be stuck on b7 or a6 and suffer. Capturing away from the center gives extra protection when castling queenside.
notes.teaches: The rule 'capture towards the center' has exceptions. Consider the resulting piece activity and king safety; sometimes capturing away from the center is superior.
notes.plans: Black captures away from the center, then castles queenside with extra protection.

notes.explains: Against the Scotch, White's bishop to e3 defends the knight and protects f2 while developing. Black's bishop to c5 attacks the knight, forcing White to play c3 to save it. The alternative knight b5 is dubious because it leads to doubled pawns and gives Black active play, as the queen can become very strong.
notes.teaches: When your opponent defends a piece, look for immediate tactical pressure like a bishop attacking the knight. Be wary of grabbing pawns if it damages your pawn structure and gives the opponent active pieces.
notes.plans: Black continues with knight to e7, preparing to castle, and then develops the bishop to c4, a strong square, while White solidifies with c3.

notes.explains: In the Scotch Gambit, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4, Black can check with Bb4+ to force c3, then the bishop retreats to e2. White allows this because the bishop's route via c4 to e2 sets a trap: if Black plays Nge7 and later ...Ng6, the knight on e5 may be lured, allowing White to play f4 with tempo.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a seemingly time-wasting bishop maneuver (Bc4-e2) is purposeful: it provokes a knight to e5, enabling a later f4 pawn thrust with gain of time.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...Qg6, White can castle and meet ...Nxe4 with Nd2, hitting the queen and developing. Alternatively, Nb5 is also viable. If Black plays ...Bb6, White can capture on e5, and Black's only defense is ...Qxe5.

notes.explains: Rather than allowing White free development, Black typically plays ...d6. White then has a choice between f3 and f4; f3 is more common, but f4 is an aggressive idea, especially after the bishop has been to c4 to lure the knight to e5.
notes.teaches: When facing a flexible setup, choose between solid (f3) and aggressive (f4) plans; the aggressive plan may be enabled by earlier provocation.
notes.plans: After ...d6, White can play f3, then after ...O-O, develop with Nd2, and if Black plays ...d5, White can meet ...exd4 with fxe4, opening the f-file for the rook. King h1 is a useful precaution.

notes.explains: In the Scotch with …Qf6, White has several options. Nb5 is the most scoring, but it leads to doubled c-pawns and potential queenside pressure. Nf3 is a less common but natural developing move. Capturing on c6 leads to opposite-side castling and a race. Be3 transposes to the classical Scotch.
notes.teaches: Against early queen sorties, White can choose between concrete attacking tries and solid development; each has its own positional trade-offs.
notes.plans: If White plays Nb5, Black should respond with ...Bc5, threatening mate, and White must address that before continuing. With Nf3, Black can develop naturally with ...Bc5 or ...Bb4. After exd6, both sides may castle queenside, with White having a kingside majority and Black extra queenside defense.

notes.explains: In the Petrov Defence, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6, Black attacks the e4 pawn. White's most common response is d4 or Nc3, but Nxe5 is a trap: if Black recaptures with …Nxe4, then Qe2! attacks the knight on e4 and also threatens the knight on e5, winning material. Therefore, Black must play …d6, forcing the knight back.
notes.teaches: In the Petrov, the move Nxe5 is a well-known trap that wins a piece if Black naively recaptures. The correct response is to attack the knight with …d6, maintaining the solid structure.
notes.plans: After …d6, White can choose between several setups, including d4, Nc3, or the game's Qe2, which aims for a slower build-up.

notes.explains: In the line e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6 Nxe5 d6 Nf3 Nxe4, White has several options. The most popular is Nc3, leading to the main lines. However, the game featured Qe2, which is less aggressive but still sound. After …Qe7, White played Nc3, and after …Nxc3 dxc3, the position is balanced, but White has the plan of playing Be3, Qd2, and long castling, aiming for opposite-side castling and a dynamic middlegame.
notes.teaches: In the Petrov, White can choose between different move orders. The setup with Qe2 and Nc3 leads to a solid but less forcing position, where the plan is to develop the bishop to e3, queen to d2, and castle long, creating unbalanced play with opposite-side castling.
notes.plans: White aims for Be3, Qd2, and 0-0-0, while Black will likely castle short, leading to a race of attacks on opposite wings.

notes.explains: In the position after the opening, White played g2-g4 with the idea of attacking the bishop on f6 with g5, and if the bishop retreats, then f4-f5 gains space on the kingside. Black's best response was to play ...Rfe8, preventing the knight from going to e4 and also preparing to challenge the center. The move ...Bf5 was inferior because it allows g4, forcing the bishop back and giving White a space advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage on one wing, pushing pawns to gain more space and drive back enemy pieces is a common plan. However, the opponent must find precise moves to prevent the pawn push from being too strong. In this case, ...Rfe8 was the best way to stop the knight from reaching e4 and to maintain the balance.
notes.plans: White continues with the plan of g4-g5, trying to win the bishop pair or gain space. Black must be careful to avoid allowing White to get a bind on the kingside.

notes.explains: The bishop pair is a long-term asset, especially in open positions. In the game, White tried to force Black to give up the bishop pair by attacking the bishop on f6 with g4-g5. Black had to decide whether to retreat or to trade. The move ...Bf5 was not good because it allowed g4, and after the bishop retreats, f4-f5 gives White a large space advantage. Instead, Black played ...Rfe8, which prevented the knight from going to e4 and kept the position balanced.
notes.teaches: The bishop pair is often worth a slight advantage, but its value depends on the position. When your opponent has the bishop pair, you should try to neutralize it by trading one of the bishops or by creating a position where the knights are better. Conversely, if you have the bishop pair, you should try to open the position and use the long-range power of the bishops.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain the pressure and possibly win the bishop pair. Black must find a way to coordinate the pieces and avoid falling into a passive position.

notes.explains: The bishop pair is a key asset in this position, so White must avoid trades that give it up cheaply. Moving the attacked bishop back to its original square wastes time, so finding a new active diagonal is important.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is attacked, look for a square that keeps it active and preserves the bishop pair rather than retreating passively.
notes.plans: Place the bishop on a good diagonal, such as b3, and maintain threats like occupying e4 with a knight.

notes.explains: Black's move ...g5 attacks the bishop and aims to reduce the danger of White's kingside pawn storm. The bishop can retreat to h2, and Black improves the king to g7.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn storm, countering in the center or improving your king's safety can neutralize the attack.
notes.plans: After ...g5 and Bh2, Black prepares to meet g4 with ...gxf4, keeping the position solid.

notes.explains: White's h3 prepares a kingside pawn expansion with g4, but Black must be careful. If Black plays passively, White can build up with f4 and g5, winning material.
notes.teaches: A pawn storm can be a decisive attacking plan when the opponent's pieces are poorly placed, but the opponent must seek active counterplay.
notes.plans: White intends g4, followed by f4 and g5, while Black should look for ways to challenge the center or trade pieces.

notes.explains: White's c4 is a central break that challenges Black's pawn structure. If Black captures, White can recapture and open lines, but if Black ignores it, White gains space.
notes.teaches: Central pawn breaks are essential when the opponent's pieces are tied down, but they must be timed correctly to avoid weakening your own position.
notes.plans: White plays c4 to create play in the center, while Black must decide whether to capture or maintain the tension.

notes.explains: When the bishop is placed on a strong diagonal and the opponent's pawn storm on the kingside is not dangerous, the defender can calmly improve the king and then challenge the center.
notes.teaches: A well-placed bishop can neutralize a pawn storm; improving the king before striking in the center is a common defensive resource.
notes.plans: After the king moves to g7, White can play c4 to prevent ...d5 and keep the bishop active.

notes.explains: If Black allows White to get the bishop pair and a solid pawn structure, Black may end up worse. White's plan is to improve the bishop via c3 and Bc2, giving White long-term chances.
notes.teaches: The bishop pair is a long-term asset; when the opponent has no counterplay, you can slowly improve your pieces and rely on the pair.
notes.plans: White can play c3 and Bc2 to bring the bishop back to life, then use the bishop pair to press.

notes.explains: In a sharp tactical melee, Black considers capturing on h3, but must calculate concrete variations. White's f4 can fork knight and bishop, but Black may have resources like ...Ng4 or ...f5 to refute it.
notes.teaches: When a capture looks tempting, calculate the forcing replies; a move like f4 can be met by a counter-fork or a pawn break that leaves the opponent's pieces hanging.
notes.plans: Black should look for active moves like ...Ng4 or ...f5 to create counterplay rather than accepting a passive position.

notes.explains: After a series of exchanges, Black's connected passed pawns on the queenside become extremely strong. Even if White wins one, the remaining pawns and threats like ...Rh8 or ...Bh4 can decide the game.
notes.teaches: Connected passed pawns are a decisive advantage; when they are supported, they can outweigh material deficits and create mating threats.
notes.plans: Black should push the passed pawns and use them to tie down White's pieces, then switch to kingside threats.
