notes.explains: When a knight is unstable on e5 because its support (d6) is removed, it becomes a target. White's rook must find the best square; retreating to e2 allows ...g4, while taking on c6 allows a pawn promotion threat.
notes.teaches: In dynamic positions, the only move may be a counterattacking one that creates threats of your own, rather than a passive retreat.
notes.plans: White plays Rf4 to create threats and avoid the immediate dangers, keeping the position complicated.

notes.explains: In this rook and bishop vs. rook and bishop endgame, the rook must find the most active and forcing square. Moving the rook forward is the only way to keep the initiative; retreating allows the opponent to attack the bishop and create dangerous passed pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity is paramount. A passive rook move can allow the opponent to seize the initiative and create decisive threats.
notes.plans: Place the rook on its most active file, pressuring the opponent's pieces and pawns, and be ready to support passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black faces a critical decision with the king. Several king moves are possible, but only one avoids the threat of f4, which would win a pawn. Moving to h8 is the only safe square because it avoids tactics involving the bishop being taken with check.
notes.teaches: When your opponent threatens a pawn break, you must find the only king move that neutralizes the threat and avoids tactical refutations.
notes.plans: After Kh8, if White plays f4, Black can respond with Ng4, creating counterplay and maintaining the balance.

notes.explains: White's bishop on h2 is hanging, and the natural retreat to g1 is actually losing due to a combination involving a knight fork and attacks on f2. White instead finds a resourceful move, Bxa4, sacrificing the bishop to win a pawn and create dangerous connected passed pawns.
notes.teaches: When your piece is attacked, look beyond the obvious retreat. Sometimes sacrificing material for active play and dangerous passed pawns is the best practical chance.
notes.plans: White aims to take on c6, attack the rook on e1, and push the passed pawns, especially the d-pawn, to create threats.

notes.explains: Black responds with a brilliant rook move, Rc8, leaving the rook on e1 en prise. If White takes the rook, Black's rook on d6 becomes extremely strong, and the back-rank threats are overwhelming. The rook on c8 also covers key squares, limiting White's rook mobility.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best defense is to ignore an attack and create a stronger counterthreat. A rook can be more valuable on an open file than the material it might lose.
notes.plans: Black's rook on c8 supports the d6 pawn and restricts White's rook, while maintaining threats of promotion and back-rank mates.

notes.explains: In a rook versus piece endgame, the side with the piece can often leave a rook en prise if capturing it allows a decisive counterattack. Here, leaving the rook on e8 is strong because if White takes it, Black's rook on d6 becomes very active, and the White rook has almost no safe squares due to threats of back-rank mate and queen promotion.
notes.teaches: When your rook is attacked, consider leaving it hanging if the opponent's capture allows you to activate your other rook or create mating threats. Rooks need open files and safe squares; if you can dominate the opponent's rook, material can be regained with interest.
notes.plans: Black should aim to keep the rook active on the d-file, supporting passed pawns and cutting off the White king, while using the bishop to control key squares.

notes.explains: With multiple passed pawns racing, the side with the piece must use the king and bishop to support the pawns and restrict the opponent's rook. Here, Black's bishop on c6 supports the passed pawns and the rook on d8, while the White rook is tied to passive defense.
notes.teaches: In rook versus piece endgames, the side with the piece should coordinate the king, bishop, and rook to create threats and keep the opponent's rook passive. Passed pawns are a major asset, but they need support.
notes.plans: Black should advance the passed pawns while keeping the bishop on a strong diagonal, and use the rook to cut off the White king or attack weak pawns.

notes.explains: When the opponent's rook is passive, a humble prophylactic move like c3 can be very effective, preventing the rook from coming to b4 and creating counterplay. This move also protects the b2 pawn and prepares to advance the a-pawn.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves that restrict the opponent's pieces are often the most powerful. Preventing the rook from reaching an active square can be more important than immediate material gains.
notes.plans: White should continue to advance the a-pawn, while keeping the rook active and the king safe. Black must find active counterplay, often by attacking the opponent's weak pawns.

notes.explains: In time trouble, players often miss the best defensive or attacking moves. Here, White missed a strong move like rook c6, which would have created threats against the Black king and bishop, while Black had to find precise moves to stay in the game.
notes.teaches: In rook versus piece endgames, look for moves that create threats against the king and pieces simultaneously. Even in time pressure, try to find the most active and forcing moves.
notes.plans: White should aim to activate the rook and create threats, while Black must keep the king safe and maintain the coordination of the pieces.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, both sides have dangerous passed pawns racing. The placement of the kings and rooks determines who promotes first, and a single king move can decide between winning and losing.
notes.teaches: When both sides have passed pawns, king activity and the ability to stop the opponent's pawn are critical. One king move can be the difference between winning and losing.
notes.plans: Push your passed pawns while using your rook to restrain the opponent's pawns and your king to support your own.

notes.explains: Here, the natural-looking king move is actually losing due to a tactical resource: the opponent can give up their rook for the promoted pawn and then win the queen back with a check, leaving them with a winning position.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, always check if the opponent can sacrifice material to stop your promotion and then regain the queen. The king's square matters for avoiding checks.
notes.plans: Choose the king move that avoids the opponent's tactical tricks, even if it looks less natural.

notes.explains: With both sides promoting threats, the side with the extra pawn and connected passed pawns is better, but only if the king is placed correctly to avoid the opponent's counterplay.
notes.teaches: Connected passed pawns are a huge advantage in endgames, but they must be supported by the king and protected from tactical blows.
notes.plans: Use the connected passed pawns to tie down the opponent's pieces and then infiltrate with the king.

notes.explains: When the opponent's pawn is about to promote, you may need to sacrifice a piece to eliminate the dangerous pawns, but you must evaluate if the resulting position is sufficient for counterplay.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up material to stop passed pawns is correct, but you must calculate whether the resulting endgame is defensible.
notes.plans: If you can sacrifice a bishop for two dangerous pawns, you may be able to hold or even win if the opponent's king is exposed.

notes.explains: A non-obvious pawn move can be the winning idea, creating threats that force the opponent's king to move and allowing your rook to penetrate.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for quiet pawn moves that create zugzwang or force the opponent's king to abandon key squares, enabling your rook to enter.
notes.plans: Advance the pawn to restrict the enemy king and then use your rook to target the opponent's weaknesses.

notes.explains: White played a surprising bishop move that appears to hang a rook. However, taking the rook allows a knight fork that wins material or delivers checkmate, so the rook is poisoned.
notes.teaches: A piece can be 'poisoned' if capturing it allows a tactical refutation. Always check for forks, checks, and mate threats before grabbing material.
notes.plans: Black must find the only move to avoid the tactic, often by covering key squares or creating a counter-threat.

notes.explains: In a rook and bishop vs rook endgame, activity is paramount. Even when material is equal, the side with the more active pieces has practical winning chances.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active rook placement and king penetration often outweigh material considerations. Use the rook to cut off the enemy king and create threats.
notes.plans: Black should aim to activate the rook, attack the weak pawns, and coordinate with the king to create mating threats.

notes.explains: A subtle king move decides the game. The king must stay on a square that maintains the rook's defense against back-rank mate threats and allows the bishop to interpose.
notes.teaches: In endgames, king placement is critical. Choose squares that keep your pieces coordinated and avoid allowing tactical shots like discovered checks or back-rank mates.
notes.plans: The winning side should use the king to support the advance of a passed pawn or to create a mating net, while the defender must find the only move to hold.

notes.explains: With a material advantage, the winning side must still be precise. A bridge-building maneuver with the bishop allows the rook to support the passed pawn and secure the win.
notes.teaches: When promoting a pawn, use pieces to create a 'bridge' that prevents the defender from stopping the pawn. This is a standard technique in rook endgames.
notes.plans: The winning side should advance the passed pawn, using the rook and bishop to control key squares and force the win.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, Black's connected passed pawns on the kingside are decisive. White's rook is tied to stopping them, so Black can use the king and rook to build a bridge, advancing the pawns to promotion.
notes.teaches: When you have connected passed pawns, the opponent's rook is often tied down to stopping them. Use your king and rook to support their advance, and if the opponent's rook leaves its defensive post, the pawns will queen.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawns with the support of the king and rook, using the rook to shield the king from checks if needed.

notes.explains: After Black wins a piece, the position is technically winning because Black has a material advantage and passed pawns. Even strong players would win this with Black.
notes.teaches: When you are a piece up with passed pawns, the win is usually straightforward: trade pieces, simplify, and promote. Avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Consolidate the material advantage, exchange pieces, and shepherd the passed pawns to promotion.

notes.explains: The game started as a solid Petrov Defense and turned into a wild endgame where White tried to create queens on the queenside while Black tried to queen on the kingside.
notes.teaches: In endgames with passed pawns on both sides, it becomes a race. Accurate calculation and king activity are crucial to determine who promotes first.

notes.explains: In rapid chess, the time control is faster than classical but slower than blitz, with an increment that adds time per move, allowing players to recover from time trouble by moving quickly.
notes.teaches: Understand the different time controls and how increments work, as they affect strategy and time management.

notes.explains: Psychologically, losing several games in a tournament can be hard to recover from, but strong players are skilled at bouncing back from bad losses.
notes.teaches: Maintain a resilient mindset after losses; focus on the current game rather than dwelling on past results.

notes.explains: Rook endings are notoriously complex, especially with extra pawns on the board, and are rarely straightforward wins even when one side is up a pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endings, active king play and pawn structure are crucial; do not assume a material advantage guarantees a win.

notes.explains: When both sides have passed pawns, the side with the more active king and better pawn support often has the winning chances, but counterplay must be respected.
notes.teaches: Evaluate passed pawn races carefully; consider king placement and the opponent's counterplay before committing to a plan.

notes.explains: In a rook ending, a tempo move like checking the opponent's king can force them to respond, disrupting their plan to queen a pawn.
notes.teaches: Use checks and threats to gain time and force the opponent to react, especially when both sides are racing to promote.

notes.explains: In this rook versus queen endgame, the side with the rook is trying to queen a pawn, but the queen can give perpetual check. The defender must keep the rook close to the king to avoid losing it to forks, and the attacker must find precise moves to make progress.
notes.teaches: When defending with a queen against a rook and passed pawn, perpetual check is a key resource. The rook must stay near the king to avoid being captured with check.
notes.plans: The side with the rook should try to advance the pawn while keeping the rook protected; the queen should look for checking squares that also attack the rook.

notes.explains: The rook can be placed on c1 or a1 to block the queen's checks along the file, allowing the king to escape. The choice of square matters: on c3, the rook is more active and can gain a tempo by checking when attacked.
notes.teaches: In rook versus queen endgames, rook placement is critical. A rook on a central file can both block checks and create counterplay, while a passive rook may be restricted.
notes.plans: Place the rook on a file that blocks the queen's checks and allows the king to move toward the pawn. If the rook is attacked, look for a checking opportunity to gain time.

notes.explains: The side with the rook must avoid repeating the position too many times, especially with increment, because a threefold repetition would draw. However, repeating twice can be useful to gain time on the clock when low on time.
notes.teaches: In endgames with increment, be aware of the threefold repetition rule. Repeating a position once or twice can be a practical way to gain time, but avoid a third repetition unless you want a draw.
notes.plans: If low on time, consider repeating the position once or twice to gain increment, but have a plan to deviate before the third repetition.

notes.explains: The queen can use the pawns on the board to restrict the enemy king's escape squares. By checking from certain squares, the queen can keep the king in a box and prevent it from approaching the pawn.
notes.teaches: In queen versus rook endgames, use your own pawns to limit the enemy king's mobility. The queen can often force perpetual check by confining the king to a small area.
notes.plans: Look for checking squares that also cut off the king's escape routes, using the pawns as natural barriers.

notes.explains: When the opponent has separated passed pawns and your king is close, the win is straightforward if you keep the enemy king out and get your rook behind the pawns. Trading queens and taking a pawn is fine, but you must avoid letting the enemy king support the pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames with passed pawns, place your rook behind the pawns to stop them, and use your king to shoulder the enemy king away. Keep your pieces active and avoid awkward placements.
notes.plans: Bring the rook behind the pawns (e.g., to the 8th rank) while the king approaches, preventing the enemy king from advancing. Then collect the pawns and convert.

notes.explains: If you allow the enemy king to get in front of the pawns and your pieces become awkward, the win may slip away. The key is to keep your king active and the enemy king out.
notes.teaches: When converting, prioritize king penetration and rook activity over material. Avoid moves that let the defender's king support the pawns.
notes.plans: Use checks and threats to keep the enemy king away, then bring your king to support your own pawns or attack the enemy pawns.

notes.explains: In a position with a king trapped in a box and a queen giving checks, the defender may have to block with the queen, leading to repetition. The attacker can use the presence of pawns to restrict the queen's mobility.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's king is exposed, look for ways to use your own pawns to limit the defender's queen's squares, making perpetual check harder to achieve.
notes.plans: Continue checking while improving your piece placement, and if the defender blocks with the queen, consider whether you can exploit the queen's restricted mobility.

notes.explains: In a winning position, it's easy to blunder by overcomplicating. Sometimes the simplest winning move is best, especially when you have a material advantage and a clear plan.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning advantage, look for the most forcing and safe continuation. Avoid unnecessary complications that could give the defender counterplay.
notes.plans: Calculate the simplest winning line and execute it confidently, keeping your pieces coordinated.

notes.explains: In the Scotch Opening (e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4), after …Nf6, White must protect the e4 pawn. Moving the bishop to d3 is bad because it blocks the queen's defense of the knight on f3, leaving it hanging.
notes.teaches: In the Scotch, be careful about developing the bishop to d3 before the queen has a clear path to defend the knight. Consider moves that maintain the defense of the e4 pawn and the knight.
notes.plans: Choose a move that protects e4, such as Nc3 or Qe2, keeping the knight defended and the position sound.

notes.explains: Recovering from a string of losses is extremely difficult, especially under public scrutiny and with ego involved. The psychological toll can affect performance.
notes.teaches: Resilience is a key skill in chess; players must learn to reset mentally after defeats and focus on the next game.

notes.explains: In the Four Knights Scotch, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6, White must defend the e4 pawn. Moving the bishop to d3 blocks the queen's defense, leaving the knight on d4 hanging. Playing Nc3 leads to the Four Knights, not a gambit.
notes.teaches: Recognize opening transpositions and avoid moves that block your queen's defense of key pawns.
notes.plans: Develop pieces harmoniously, maintaining pressure on the center.

notes.explains: In the main line, Black plays ...Qe7 to create a pin on the knight, and after White retreats, the point is to challenge the e5 pawn—whether it becomes a strength or a weakness. Black may sacrifice a pawn for activity.
notes.teaches: Pawn sacrifices must yield concrete compensation: lead in development, awkward opponent pieces, or long-term weaknesses.
notes.plans: After ...Qe7, Black aims to pressure the e5 pawn and exploit White's queen's awkward placement.

notes.explains: When evaluating a position, consider material, king safety, piece activity, and pawn structure. Some weaknesses are irrelevant if they cannot be attacked. Here, an isolated a7 pawn is not a real weakness because no white piece can easily attack it.
notes.teaches: Evaluate positions systematically, but prioritize factors that are actually relevant to the position.
notes.plans: In the endgame after queen trades, focus on piece activity and pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black's compensation for the pawn includes a lead in development and White's queen being misplaced. This advantage is temporary, so Black must act quickly before White catches up.
notes.teaches: Development advantages are temporary; capitalize on them before the opponent completes development.
notes.plans: Use the lead in development to create threats and prevent White from consolidating.

notes.explains: When the opponent is behind in development and their queen is misplaced, the side with the lead has compensation, but it is temporary. If the opponent catches up in development, the advantage disappears.
notes.teaches: A development advantage is fleeting; to make it count, you must keep the opponent from completing their development, often by attacking their pieces and creating threats.
notes.plans: Keep the pressure on the opponent's undeveloped pieces and awkward queen, preventing them from consolidating.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's pieces are all active and have natural squares, while White's pieces are passive and the queen is in trouble. This makes Black's position easy to play, whereas White must constantly solve problems.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are active and your opponent's are passive, it is practical to keep the tension and force your opponent to find difficult moves, especially in faster time controls where instinct matters.
notes.plans: Continue to create threats (e.g., attacking the queen, targeting weak pawns) to maintain the initiative and avoid giving the opponent time to reorganize.

notes.explains: White's queen is in trouble and the c4 pawn is weak. White tries to save the queen by exchanging pieces, which is a typical reaction when the opponent's pieces are more active.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are passive and the opponent's are active, exchanging pieces can relieve pressure, even if it costs material, because it reduces the opponent's attacking potential.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to exchange pieces and free the queen, even if it means giving up the weak pawn.

notes.explains: Black considers a tempo move like Rc8 to attack the queen and maintain the initiative. The idea is to keep the queen trapped and force White to spend moves on defense.
notes.teaches: Tempo moves that attack the opponent's pieces while improving your own position are a key way to maintain pressure and prevent the opponent from consolidating.
notes.plans: Look for moves that attack the queen or other valuable pieces while also developing or improving your own pieces.

notes.explains: In a line where White tries to save the queen, Black can choose between taking a pawn or first giving a check. The difference is the king's position: if the king is on h1 instead of g1, the rook might be unprotected, affecting tactics.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice between capturing material and giving a check, consider how the king's position changes the tactical landscape, especially regarding the safety of your own pieces.
notes.plans: Calculate the consequences of each move order, particularly how the king's placement affects the safety of your pieces and the opponent's counterplay.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has a strong pawn chain and control of key central squares, while White's pieces appear to be aiming at the king but are actually scattered and uncoordinated. The bishop on the long diagonal looks powerful, but a lone bishop cannot deliver checkmate; it needs the queen to support it, and the queen is currently unable to join the attack.
notes.teaches: When evaluating an attack, consider whether the pieces can cooperate. A single piece, no matter how well placed, is insufficient to break through; you need coordination and a way to bring reinforcements.
notes.plans: Black should continue to improve piece activity and maintain the pressure on White's weaknesses, while keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: The knight on d5 looks nice but is actually under attack and cannot directly threaten the black king. Black has a potential tactic: if the bishop can get to d4, it will line up with the queen and win material. The move Rook d8 creates a threat and prevents the knight from moving due to the bishop d4 fork.
notes.teaches: A piece that appears well-placed may be vulnerable or ineffective if it cannot participate in the attack. Always look for tactical motifs like forks and pins to exploit the opponent's piece placement.
notes.plans: Black should continue to create threats, such as the bishop d4 fork, and force White to defend while improving Black's own position.

notes.explains: The queen on c8 is a good square because it supports the bishop on a6, which is not doing much. The bishop would be better placed on the long diagonal aiming at the pawn on b7. The best move was queen g4, which threatens bishop b7 and keeps the bishop d4 threat alive.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a piece, consider its future potential and how it supports your other pieces. A piece that is not active should be repositioned to a more influential diagonal or file.
notes.plans: Black should aim to place the queen on g4, threatening bishop b7, and then continue to improve the bishop's activity.

notes.explains: White's worst piece is the knight, which is misplaced and not participating in the game. Black can attack it with moves like queen c6 or rook d7, which also doubles rooks and creates multiple threats. This forces White to defend and allows Black to win a pawn.
notes.teaches: Identify your opponent's worst piece and target it. Multi-purpose moves that attack a piece while improving your own position are often the most effective.
notes.plans: Black should continue to attack the knight, double rooks on the d-file, and then win the pawn, while maintaining the strong bishops.

notes.explains: After winning a pawn, Black has strong bishops on the long diagonals and a solid position. The bishop on the b-file is powerful, but there is an awkwardness about its placement, possibly due to the opponent's pieces or pawns. The game is at move 23, and the bishop has finally developed, but it may be obstructed.
notes.teaches: Even in a winning position, be aware of the harmony of your pieces. A bishop on a long diagonal is strong, but if it is blocked or awkwardly placed, it may not reach its full potential.
notes.plans: Black should consolidate the extra pawn, improve the bishop's placement, and continue to pressure White's weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black has won a pawn and has strong fianchettoed bishops. The queen is defending the bishop, so no other piece can attack it. The bishop on the other side is undeveloped, and its development is awkward because it lands on the same diagonal as the other bishop.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, improve your position by activating pieces and creating threats. Use tactics with tempo to force your opponent to respond, not giving them time to consolidate.
notes.plans: Continue to develop the undeveloped bishop, but be aware of awkward placements. Use the active pieces to create threats and maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: Black is attacking the white bishop. White cannot defend everything, so they are losing a piece. The rook on f3 can be met by retreating the bishop, and the rook is not available to defend because it is captured.
notes.teaches: When you are going to lose a piece, try to get compensation in the form of pawns or other material. Do not lose a piece for nothing.
notes.plans: If losing a piece is unavoidable, seek the best possible compensation, such as pawns or a strong attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Rook g3, which pins the white bishop. The alternative Rook h3 fails to Bishop g1. The pin is very strong and Black's pieces coordinate well.
notes.teaches: Pins are powerful tactical motifs that can immobilize enemy pieces. Always look for moves that create pins or other tactical threats to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Maintain the pin and continue to build pressure, forcing White to defend or lose material.

notes.explains: Black calculates a forced line: Bishop g2, King g1, and then Bishop f3, which leads to a winning endgame. The rook is hanging, but the threats are decisive.
notes.teaches: Always calculate forced lines first. If you find a forced win, take it. After calculating a line, evaluate the resulting position to ensure you are better or at least not worse.
notes.plans: Execute the forced line that leads to a winning position, then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: After the forced line, Black has a queen and bishop against three pawns, with the white king weak and pieces hanging. Black is completely winning.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, ensure your king is safe and your pieces are active. Convert the advantage efficiently, and if the opponent is clearly lost, they may resign.
notes.plans: Use the queen and bishop to create threats, win the hanging pieces, and promote a pawn or deliver mate.

notes.explains: In the warm-up position, White's pieces—queen on a4, rook on c1, bishop on f4, and knight—are poised to coordinate against the black king. The key is to open the c-file and exploit the alignment of the queen and king on the same diagonal, and the rooks on the same file.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for ways to open files and diagonals to bring all pieces into the attack. Sacrificing a pawn to open a file can be justified if it leads to a decisive exchange or checkmate threat.
notes.plans: White should play b4 to open the c-file, then consider moves like Nd6+ to exploit the geometry, or Nc7/Rxc6 as alternative winning tries.

notes.explains: After b4, if Black plays Nxb4, White can consider Nd6+ because the queen on a4 and king on e8 are on the same diagonal, and the rooks are aligned on the c-file. If the bishop on c5 captures on d6, White can exchange rooks on c8, winning material.
notes.teaches: In tactical combinations, always check the alignment of pieces on diagonals and files. A sacrifice can be used to deflect a defender or to force a favorable exchange.
notes.plans: If Black's king moves to e7, White should take the rook on c8. If the king moves to f8, White can play d7, followed by Nxc8 and Nxc8, winning.

notes.explains: If Black instead plays Bxb4, the situation differs because the bishop on b4 blocks the c-file for the rook. Then Nd6+ is less effective, so White should look for other ideas like Nc7 or Rxc6.
notes.teaches: When a planned tactic fails due to a piece blocking a key line, switch to alternative attacking ideas. Flexibility in calculation is crucial.
notes.plans: White can try Nc7, threatening to win the exchange, or Rxc6, both leading to winning positions.

notes.explains: In the Réti endgame position, White's king is out of the square of the h5 pawn, but White can use the idea of helping his own c6 pawn while also catching the opponent's pawn. The first move is Kg7, not Kh7, because Kh7 allows the h-pawn to advance.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, when your king cannot catch the opponent's pawn, try to get closer to your own pawn to support its promotion. The Réti idea shows how to create a dual threat: helping your pawn and stopping the opponent's.
notes.plans: White plays Kg7, then if Black plays Kb6, White continues Kf6, aiming to support the c-pawn while also threatening to catch the h-pawn.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn endgame, the white king must choose the correct path to stop the black pawns. The first move is Kg7, not Kh7, because Kh7 allows the h-pawn to advance and become unstoppable.
notes.teaches: When approaching passed pawns, the king must take the most direct route that prevents the pawn from advancing. Choosing the wrong square can allow the pawn to run.
notes.plans: White should play Kg7, then approach the c6 pawn while staying within the square of the h-pawn to stop it.

notes.explains: If black plays Kb6, white should respond with Kf6, approaching the c6 pawn. If black takes on c6, white goes Kg5, staying in the square of the h4 pawn. If black instead advances h4, white must find the precise move Ke5, which both approaches the c6 pawn and keeps the h-pawn under control.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, the king often has to serve two purposes: supporting your own pawn and stopping the opponent's. A single move can sometimes accomplish both if you calculate the geometry of the board.
notes.plans: White should aim to either capture the c6 pawn or force black to use tempi, while always keeping the h-pawn within the king's reach.

notes.explains: In a similar endgame, black appears to be winning, but white can draw by using the same idea: the king must approach the pawns with the right timing. The first move is Kg6, and if black plays Kb6, white must be careful not to take on c6 immediately, but instead play f5 or h5, which are the same idea.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice of captures, consider which pawn to take first. Sometimes you must take the pawn that keeps your king in the square of the other passed pawn, rather than the one that seems most natural.
notes.plans: White should play Kg6, then if black goes Kb6, white plays f5 (or h5) to create a passed pawn and keep the king active. If black takes on c6, white takes on f5 and remains in the square of the h6 pawn.

notes.explains: In rook endgames, when your king is being checked repeatedly and you cannot block the checks, you can use the 'umbrella' idea: hide your king behind the opponent's pawn. For example, if your pawn is on e3 and the opponent has a pawn on f5, you can trade your e-pawn for the f-pawn, creating a shelter for your king.
notes.teaches: The umbrella is a defensive resource in rook endgames: by trading your own pawn for the opponent's pawn, you create a shield for your king against rook checks, allowing you to promote your passed pawn.
notes.plans: If the rook checks from b2, the king should aim to get to f3, using the f5 pawn as cover. The key is to play Rook b2 and then King f3, which will bring success.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the side with the extra pawn must be careful about trading pieces because rook endgames are complex and require precise knowledge of theoretical positions.
notes.teaches: When you have extra material in a rook endgame, avoid unnecessary trades; instead, use your pawns to create tactical ideas like the 'umbrella' to block checks.
notes.plans: Use the pawn on f5 to trade for the opponent's f-pawn, creating an umbrella that blocks rook checks from the back rank, allowing your pawn to promote.

notes.explains: The key to winning is to get your rook to the second rank and your king to f3, creating a mating net or forcing promotion. The f-pawn is crucial because it prevents the enemy rook from checking from the back rank.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a pawn on f4 (or f5) can serve as an umbrella, blocking checks from the back rank and giving your king a safe path to support promotion.
notes.plans: Play Rook b2, then King f3, and if the enemy rook checks, use the umbrella pawn to block. If the enemy rook goes to a1, play Rook h2, forcing King g1, then Rook g2+ and continue with the promotion plan.

notes.explains: When the enemy rook tries to check from the side, you can use your pawn to block the file, but you must be precise. The f-pawn is essential because without it, the back-rank checks would be very hard to defend.
notes.teaches: In pawn promotion races, a pawn on f4 can act as a shield, preventing the enemy rook from checking along the rank. This gives you the tempo you need to promote.
notes.plans: If the rook checks from the side, move your king to the safe square, then use the umbrella pawn to block further checks. Continue with the promotion plan.

notes.explains: Lasker's idea, also called the 'elevator', is a technique to win a rook endgame that looks drawn. If black is to move, he would play King a7 to control b8 and b7, so white must prevent that.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, sometimes you need a precise first move to prevent the enemy king from reaching a key square. The 'elevator' idea involves moving your king to b8 to threaten promotion, forcing the enemy rook to give checks.
notes.plans: Play King b8, threatening to promote. If black checks, use the elevator technique to bring your king to the promotion square while your rook controls the necessary files.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the key is to promote the passed pawn. The defender's king tries to control the promotion squares, so the attacking king must be brought up to support the pawn.
notes.teaches: Use the king to support a passed pawn's promotion, and use the rook to cut off the defender's king or give checks to gain tempi.
notes.plans: Advance the king to support the pawn, using the rook to shield from checks and to force the defender's king away from the promotion square.

notes.explains: The defender's rook gives checks from the side to prevent the pawn from advancing. The attacker must find a way to neutralize these checks, often by using the king as a shield or by interposing the rook.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the defending rook checks from the side to stop the pawn. The attacker can use the king to block checks or create a 'bridge' to shelter the king from further checks.
notes.plans: Move the king to a square where it can both support the pawn and block the checking rook, or use the rook to interpose.

notes.explains: The attacker must be careful not to allow the defender's pawn (here on h2) to become dangerous. While focusing on promoting the c-pawn, the h-pawn can also queen if ignored.
notes.teaches: Always watch for counterplay from the opponent's passed pawns. Sometimes you must take time to eliminate them before proceeding with your own promotion.
notes.plans: If the defender's pawn is a threat, capture it or neutralize it before continuing the promotion plan.

notes.explains: The 'elevator' maneuver refers to the rook moving up and down the file to give checks and force the king back, while the attacker's king advances step by step. This is a common technique to make progress in rook endgames.
notes.teaches: The 'elevator' or 'ladder' technique: use the rook to give checks from a distance, forcing the enemy king to move, while your own king advances to support the pawn.
notes.plans: Coordinate the rook and king to gradually advance the pawn, using checks to gain tempi and push the defender's king away.

notes.explains: After a tactical sequence, the position has simplified dramatically, with few pieces left. Black has a rook on the second rank, which is an asset, but the reduced material means the advantage is not overwhelming, and rook endgames are often drawn.
notes.teaches: When material is reduced, the side with an advantage must be precise and avoid trades that lead to drawn endgames. Active rook placement on the seventh rank is valuable, but its impact diminishes as pieces are exchanged.
notes.plans: Black should seek to maintain activity and create concrete threats, while White should aim to simplify further to increase drawing chances.

notes.explains: Black plays a strong move to restrict White's counterplay, specifically taking away the b-file, which White desperately wants for rook activity. The rook on a3 is stranded and ineffective.
notes.teaches: In endgames, restricting the opponent's pieces is a key technique. Prophylactic moves that limit the opponent's options are often more valuable than immediate material gains.
notes.plans: Black will continue to improve the king and pawns while keeping White's rook passive. White should seek to activate the rook via the b-file if possible.

notes.explains: Black makes a prophylactic king move (King f8) rather than trading rooks, because trading would give White extra options and free counterplay. Black wants to see White's plan before committing.
notes.teaches: In endgames, avoid unnecessary trades that give the opponent additional possibilities. Patience and waiting moves are often the best way to maintain pressure.
notes.plans: Black will continue to gain space on the queenside with pawn advances, while keeping the rook active and the king centralized.

notes.explains: Black has created a situation where the white rook is boxed in and cannot move freely. The white rook is stuck on the fifth rank, and the a5 pawn has become a weakness. Black's pawns on the kingside are well-defended, and the rook is not yet winning but is clearly better.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, restricting the opponent's rook and creating weaknesses can yield a long-term advantage. Patience and unhurried play can force the opponent to make mistakes.
notes.plans: Black should continue to restrict white's pieces, avoid creating unnecessary weaknesses, and wait for the right moment to break through on the queenside or create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black has placed pawns on g3 and h6 to take away squares from the white rook, eventually trapping it on c5. The white rook has no good squares, and black is slowly improving the position. White's defensive strategy of waiting and not showing plans is also noted as a good defensive technique.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves can be used to restrict the opponent's pieces, especially rooks. In rook endgames, it's important to take away the opponent's rook's best squares and force it into passivity.
notes.plans: Black should continue to improve the king and prepare to create a passed pawn on the queenside by breaking with d6, while keeping the white rook trapped.

notes.explains: White, after being pressured for many moves, finally errs by exchanging rooks, but this turns out to be losing. The rook exchange was a mistake because it allowed black's pawns to become dangerous, and the resulting position is winning for black.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, exchanging rooks can be a double-edged sword; it may relieve pressure but can also activate the opponent's king and pawns. It's important to evaluate the resulting pawn endgame carefully before trading.
notes.plans: After the exchange, black should use the active king and better pawn structure to convert the win.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the side that just exchanged rooks made a critical error. The rook was terrible and the player was eager to trade it off, but the exchange actually loses. Keeping the rook on the board with a move like g5 would have preserved drawing chances, as the rook could later get behind the passed pawn.
notes.teaches: Do not rush to trade off a 'bad' piece if the resulting endgame is lost. Sometimes the active potential of that piece is more valuable than its current poor placement.
notes.plans: If the rook had stayed, the plan would be to activate it behind the passed pawn to create counterplay and drawing chances.

notes.explains: The critical moment was a king move that the defender missed. The king needed to get in front of the pawns quickly, but a slower king move allowed the opponent's king to take the opposition and then push the passed pawn to victory.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, king activity and opposition are paramount. A single tempo can decide the outcome, so calculate king routes carefully.
notes.plans: The winning side will use the king to support the passed pawn and force the opponent's king away, then promote.

notes.explains: In a balanced position, the opponent's best piece is a strong bishop on c4. It is a monster, and the first priority is to neutralize it. However, capturing it immediately with a pawn would lose material, so a different approach is needed.
notes.teaches: Identify the opponent's strongest piece and find a way to neutralize it without weakening your own position. Sometimes you must change plans if the direct approach fails.
notes.plans: The side with the weaker position must seek active counterplay rather than passively defending, because waiting will only allow the opponent to improve.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame, the placement of the rook is crucial. The player chose a square that restricts the opponent's rook, forcing it to a passive spot where it will be tied down to defending a pawn. This gives the active side lasting pressure.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, an active rook is essential. Place your rook to restrict the opponent's rook and create long-term pressure, even if it doesn't win immediately.
notes.plans: The active side will continue to press by advancing pawns and keeping the opponent's rook passive, aiming to create weaknesses.

notes.explains: A pawn move like g4 is committal because it permanently weakens the f4 square and also the h4 square, which the opponent's king can later exploit. Pawns cannot move backward, so such moves must be considered carefully.
notes.teaches: In endgames, pawn moves are often irreversible. Avoid creating permanent weaknesses unless they serve a clear purpose, and be aware of squares that become available to the opponent's king.
notes.plans: The opponent will use the weakened squares to infiltrate with the king and increase pressure on the pawns.

notes.explains: In rook endgames, the king's placement is critical. Here the white king is cut off on the first rank, which is dangerous because it cannot support the pawns or stop the enemy king from invading. The black rook is active, cutting off the white king, and black has a passed a-pawn, but that alone is not enough to win.
notes.teaches: A king stuck on the first rank is a severe liability in rook endgames. Active rooks are essential; if you have a chance to activate your rook, do so, because waiting can lead to running out of useful moves.
notes.plans: Black should aim to use the active rook and the passed pawn to create threats, while keeping the white king confined. White should try to free the king and activate the rook to counterplay.

notes.explains: When a rook is in front of a passed pawn, it often blocks the pawn's advance, making promotion difficult. Supporting the pawn from the side is more effective. Here, black's rook is in front of the a-pawn, so black must find a way to support the pawn from the side to make progress.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a rook in front of your own passed pawn can be a hindrance. Try to support the pawn from the side or behind to allow it to advance.
notes.plans: Black should maneuver the rook to the side of the pawn (e.g., to b-file or c-file) while the king supports the pawn's advance. White should try to keep the rook in front and bring the king to stop the pawn.

notes.explains: Black's plan is to march the king to the kingside to gobble up the pawns, specifically targeting h3 and g3. If the black king can get to g3, the game is winning. White must find a way to stop this invasion, but the white king is too far away.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the king's ability to invade and capture pawns is often decisive. If the opponent's king is far away, you can use your king as a strong attacking piece.
notes.plans: Black should aim to bring the king to h4 and then g3 to win the kingside pawns. White must try to create counterplay or use the rook to defend the pawns, but the king's distance makes it difficult.

notes.explains: White had a defensive resource: pushing the pawn and then defending it from the side with the rook, allowing the king to walk to b1 and save the game. But White played passively, allowing Black to invade. This shows the importance of active defense.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active defense is crucial. Sometimes you must give up a pawn to activate your pieces and free your king. Passive defense can lead to a slow death.
notes.plans: White should have looked for ways to activate the rook and bring the king into the game, even at the cost of a pawn. Black should prevent White from activating by keeping the rook passive and the king cut off.

notes.explains: The overarching theme in these endgames is restricting the opponent's pieces: keeping the rook passive and the king cut off. This restriction leads to a win even if the material is not overwhelming.
notes.teaches: Restriction is a powerful endgame technique. By limiting the opponent's piece activity, you can create a winning position even with minimal material advantage.
notes.plans: When you have an advantage, look for ways to restrict the opponent's pieces. In rook endgames, cut off the king and keep the rook passive.

notes.explains: The key to this position is that Black has restricted all of White's pieces: the rook on a2 is passive and the king is stuck on the first rank. White's pieces are tied down, so Black can build up without fear.
notes.teaches: Restricting the opponent's pieces is a powerful long-term strategy. Before launching your own plans, look for ways to limit the activity of every enemy piece.
notes.plans: Continue improving Black's position while maintaining the restrictions. Avoid unnecessary pawn breaks that open lines for White's passive pieces.

notes.explains: In this semi-closed position, White's bishop pair is not immediately useful, and Black's knights can find strong outposts. The f5 square is especially attractive for a black knight, so Black wants to prevent White from challenging it.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, piece activity matters more than material or the bishop pair. Identify key outposts and take measures to secure them for your pieces while denying them to the opponent.
notes.plans: Play g6 to solidify the f5 outpost, and first gain space on the queenside with b5 to prevent White's bishop from becoming active on that diagonal.

notes.explains: White's natural developing move (knight to d1) is not bad, but it is passive. White should instead look for active play, such as c4, to open the center and give the knight more scope, even if it means defending the e4 pawn.
notes.teaches: In the modern game, you must actively seek counterplay rather than just make natural moves. If your pieces are passive, look for pawn breaks to open lines and activate them.
notes.plans: White should consider c4 or e4 to create counterplay, but must be ready to defend the e4 pawn. Black will continue to restrict and build up on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black's pieces are all on the queenside, so it is logical to start a pawn expansion there. Black plays a5 to gain space and create targets, while also preparing to place a knight on c5.
notes.teaches: Align your plans with the placement of your pieces. If your forces are concentrated on one side, that is where you should seek to gain space and create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Continue the queenside expansion with a5, then b5, and aim to put a knight on c5. White's attempts to play c4 are prevented by Black's pawn on a6 and knight on b6.

notes.explains: Black is better but must remain precise. White's knight on d3 is well placed, but Black can push it back with c5-c4. Black also keeps an eye on the possibility of playing ...Nc5 at the right moment.
notes.teaches: Even when you are better, you must continue to improve your pieces and restrict the opponent's. Do not rush to force matters; instead, slowly squeeze the opponent by pushing back their active pieces.
notes.plans: Play Bishop d6 to reinforce the kingside and prepare to advance c5-c4, driving the knight back. Then place a knight on c5 to dominate the position.

notes.explains: Black has a stable advantage with a knight on d3 and pressure against White's position. The immediate push b4 would be premature; instead, Black improves piece placement and keeps threats in reserve.
notes.teaches: When you are better, you don't need to rush. Maintain tension and improve your worst pieces while keeping threats like b4 or c5 in the air.
notes.plans: Continue improving pieces, possibly with Ba6, preparing b4 while waiting for the right moment to strike.

notes.explains: Black's rook on f8 is flexible: it doesn't commit to a kingside break yet. If White gives up the b-file, Black can switch plans and exploit the open file instead.
notes.teaches: Keep your pieces flexible so you can adapt to your opponent's moves. Avoid committing to a plan prematurely if a better one may arise.
notes.plans: After Rf8, if White plays b4, Black can take and use the open b-file, changing the focus from kingside to queenside.

notes.explains: Black's knight is tied to defending the c3 pawn, and White's pieces are passive. Black restricts the knight further and prepares a kingside break with g5, aiming to create a passed pawn.
notes.teaches: Restrict your opponent's pieces by tying them to defensive duties. Then prepare a breakthrough on the side where you have space and pawn majority.
notes.plans: Play f6 and g5 to create a passed pawn on the kingside, while keeping the knight immobilized.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on f2 is powerful, and White's g4 pawn is weak. Black can push g5, and White's knight cannot move because it must defend the f3 pawn, so White is helpless.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are tied down, a decisive pawn break can be unstoppable. Ensure your king is not needed to defend before launching it.
notes.plans: Push g5 and then advance the h-pawn, while White's pieces remain spectators.

notes.explains: In the winning endgame, Black must avoid trading bishop for knight, as that would lead to opposite-colored bishops and a drawish position. The position is closed, so keeping pieces is key.
notes.teaches: In endgames, be aware of trades that change the character of the position. Opposite-colored bishops can be drawish even when you are a pawn up.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop and use it to support the passed pawn, while avoiding any exchange that would reduce winning chances.

notes.explains: In this endgame, the knight on the board is severely restricted and cannot move effectively. The king cannot come to defend against the threats because of this restriction. The position is closed, and there is a danger that trading the bishop for the knight would lead to opposite-colored bishops, which could result in a draw.
notes.teaches: When you have a material or positional advantage, avoid trades that lead to drawing mechanisms like opposite-colored bishop endgames. Keep the position closed to maintain the advantage.
notes.plans: Infiltrate the opponent's position with the king and pieces, while keeping the opponent's pieces restricted. Build up pressure gradually.

notes.explains: The bishop is placed on h3 instead of pushing the pawn to h3. This gives the option to push the pawn later, and it also restricts the development of the opponent's knight. The king cannot easily move to h8 because the bishop on h3 would control the diagonal and the opponent could capture the pawns.
notes.teaches: In endgames, piece placement should be flexible and serve multiple purposes: restricting the opponent's pieces and keeping options open for pawn pushes.
notes.plans: Continue to restrict the opponent's knight and king, and prepare to bring your own king forward to support the pawns.

notes.explains: The player demonstrates extreme patience by retreating the bishop to d7 after already achieving a lot. The opponent is in a near zugzwang, but instead of forcing the issue, the player retreats and comes up with a different plan. The king stays near the pawn to be ready to advance it at any moment.
notes.teaches: Patience is crucial in endgames. If you cannot make progress directly, retreat and find a new plan. Keep your king close to key pawns to maintain threats.
notes.plans: Bring the king up to support the pawns and put pressure on the opponent's weak pawns, such as the f3 pawn.

notes.explains: The final position is one of total domination. The opponent's pieces are completely tied up, and there are threats of checkmate and capturing the opponent's pieces. The opponent resigned because there is no way to meet all the threats.
notes.teaches: The ultimate goal in endgames is to restrict the opponent's pieces so much that they have no useful moves. This can lead to resignation or a decisive material gain.
notes.plans: When the opponent is in zugzwang, look for ways to deliver checkmate or win material by exploiting the lack of moves.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: In the King's Indian Defense, after the moves d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 Nf3 O-O, Black plays e5, which provokes White into closing the center with d5. This makes the position static, slowing the pace and giving both sides time to plan.
notes.teaches: The move e5 in the King's Indian is a typical way to force the center closed, leading to a strategic battle where each side attacks on opposite wings.
notes.plans: White will play on the queenside, Black on the kingside.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: White's move Ne1 serves two purposes: it unblocks the f-pawn for a future f3-f4 push, and it reroutes the knight to d3 or c2, where it can support queenside play by controlling c5.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, knights often reroute to better squares; here the knight goes back to e1 to reach d3, a classic maneuver in the King's Indian.
notes.plans: White will aim to play on the queenside, using the knight on d3 to support c5 and b4.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: Black's Nd7 mirrors White's idea: it unblocks the f-pawn so Black can play f5-f4 and launch a kingside attack. Both sides are preparing their respective pawn storms.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, Black often plays Nd7 to free the f-pawn for a kingside pawn advance, while White prepares queenside play.
notes.plans: Black will push f5-f4 and attack the white king; White will continue on the queenside.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: After the moves Be3 f5 f3 f4 Bf2 g5, Black has made aggressive pawn pushes but has not yet created concrete threats. The initiative is not yet his; it will come later.
notes.teaches: Pawn advances alone do not constitute an initiative; you need to create threats that force your opponent to respond.
notes.plans: Black will continue to build up on the kingside, while White continues on the queenside.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: Black's Rf7 is a multipurpose move: it protects the c7 pawn, and prepares to bring the rook to g7 and the bishop to f8, defending d6 and supporting the kingside attack.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the rook often comes to f7 to defend and then to g7 to join the attack, while the bishop goes to f8 to cover key squares.
notes.plans: Black will play Rg7 and Bf8, reinforcing the kingside attack.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: When White captures on c5, Black recaptures with the pawn to maintain a strong pawn center and avoid weakening the c5 square. This keeps the position solid.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, it is often better to recapture with a pawn to maintain central control and avoid creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will continue with his kingside plans, while White proceeds with queenside operations.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: After a series of moves where both sides ignored each other, the moment arrives when Black takes the initiative. The excerpt suggests Black makes a risky move that seizes the initiative.
notes.teaches: In a balanced static position, the player who first creates concrete threats gains the initiative. Sometimes you must take risks to seize it.
notes.plans: Black will launch a decisive attack on the kingside, exploiting the initiative.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: Black sacrifices a pawn on g3 to seize the initiative, and the position requires keeping the momentum with forcing moves.
notes.teaches: When you sacrifice material for an attack, you must maintain the initiative with forcing moves—checks, captures, and direct threats—to prevent the opponent from consolidating.
notes.plans: Continue with moves that create threats and force White to respond, such as Nh5 attacking the bishop.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: White defends against the Bg5 skewer with Nb1, and Black must find a way to keep the initiative.
notes.teaches: When a tactical threat is parried, look for another forcing move to keep the pressure; sometimes the most direct move is best, even if it seems simple.
notes.plans: Play Bg5, attacking the rook on c1 and activating the bishop to a powerful diagonal.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: Black's bishop, once passive on f8, becomes dominant on e3 after Bg5, while White's pieces are tied up.
notes.teaches: A seemingly bad piece can become powerful if you find the right route to an active square; also, avoid unnecessary trades when attacking, as exchanging pieces helps the defender.
notes.plans: Continue the attack, but be cautious about trading off your active pieces.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: In this attacking position, Black has multiple pieces aimed at the white king. The temptation to grab a knight is present, but trading pieces when you have the initiative is wrong because it reduces the number of attackers and helps the defender.
notes.teaches: When you are attacking, avoid unnecessary piece exchanges. Keep as many pieces on the board as possible to maintain the pressure and increase the chances of a decisive breakthrough.
notes.plans: Continue building the attack by bringing more pieces into the fray rather than trading off. Look for ways to add another attacker to the king-side assault.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: White is forced to play defensively, making moves like Bf1 to guard against threats. Black has been dictating the pace, and White's pieces are tied down to passive squares.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is on the defensive, keep creating threats and avoid giving them counterplay. Prevent their ideas even if they are not immediately dangerous, because it maintains your initiative.
notes.plans: Continue to improve your position and prevent White's freeing moves. Use moves like ...b5 to stop White's knight from reaching c4, and keep the pressure on.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: Black plays ...a6 to meet White's a4, maintaining the pawn structure and keeping the queenside stable. This is a simple way to keep the attack rolling without allowing White any counterplay.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to create counterplay, you can often neutralize it with a simple pawn move that maintains the status quo. This keeps your attacking pieces free to continue the assault.
notes.plans: After ...a6, continue the attack on the kingside. The rook on c7 is ready to join the action, and the white king is exposed.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: White plays Bh3, offering a sacrifice. Black cannot accept because after ...gxh3, White has a forced mate: Qg1+, Bxg1, Rxg1+, Kh2, and Nf3#. This shows the danger of opening lines when your king is exposed.
notes.teaches: Before capturing a piece, always check if the resulting open lines allow a mating net. Sometimes a piece is poisoned because taking it opens the king to a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Decline the sacrifice and continue the attack. The queen can go to e2, but White's knight will crash through anyway, leading to a winning position.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation, Aronin-Taimanov Defense
notes.explains: After some exchanges, Black plays Qh4, exploiting the fact that the white queen has very few safe squares. The g-file and h-file are covered, and many squares are forked by the knight.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is short of squares, you can use tactics like forks and pins to win material or force it to a bad square. Look for ways to restrict the most powerful piece.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with the queen and knight. The white king is exposed, and Black has a material advantage, so the win is just a matter of technique.

notes.explains: In the Scotch Game, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4, Black can choose ...g6, preparing ...Bg7 and ...Nf6. White's most solid response is Nc3, keeping the center flexible. Black's ...Qe6 is a common move, attacking the knight on d4, and White often replies with Qe4, maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: In open games, when the opponent attacks a central knight, it's often better to move the queen to a central square that keeps the pressure on rather than retreating passively.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain the strong knight on d4 and develop rapidly, while Black prepares to fianchetto the bishop and castle kingside.

notes.explains: After ...Bb4, White plays Bd2 to avoid doubled pawns on c3, which would give Black a superior pawn structure. Black then plays ...Ba6, attacking the c4 pawn. White must protect c4, and b3 is the most natural move, keeping the pawn chain intact and preparing to develop the bishop.
notes.teaches: Avoid doubled pawns unless you get a concrete compensation; here, keeping the pawn structure healthy is more important than winning a tempo. When a pawn is attacked, look for a move that both defends it and improves your position.
notes.plans: White will continue development, aiming to castle and then decide on the central pawn structure.

notes.explains: The critical position arises after Black threatens ...Bxc3 and ...d5. White must choose between taking on d5 or moving the queen. Taking on d5 fixes Black's pawns and gives White a chance to castle, but it also opens the position. The best move is Qh4, which puts pressure on the kingside and avoids the exchange of knights.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn break, consider whether capturing helps your opponent's pawn structure. Sometimes a queen move to the edge can be the most active, creating threats while keeping the center fluid.
notes.plans: White will follow up with development, possibly castling long or short, and use the queen on h4 to create kingside pressure.

notes.explains: After Qh4, if Black plays ...dxc4, White appears to lose a pawn, but the position is dynamic. White has compensation through the open lines and the exposed black king. The move b3 is not necessary immediately because Black's knight is pinned, so White can focus on development.
notes.teaches: Material is not always the most important factor; initiative and king safety can outweigh a pawn. Pins can restrict the opponent's options, allowing you to delay defensive moves.
notes.plans: White will continue developing, possibly with Be2 and long castling, while keeping the pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: With the center opened and the d5 pawn gone, the knight can jump to d5, creating strong pressure. If Black castles, White can place the knight on d5 and then support it with rooks to c1 or d1, targeting Black's weakened pawns.
notes.teaches: When a central pawn disappears, outposts like d5 become available for knights. Use them to dominate the position and create long-term pawn weaknesses.
notes.plans: After Black castles, jump the knight to d5 and prepare rooks on the c- or d-file to pressure the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black has several candidate moves: taking on c4, playing c5, or developing the bishop to d4. Some moves are unpleasant due to tactical replies like queen checks. The move g5 is tricky but risky because it weakens the kingside and allows queen d4, which is safe for White.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, evaluate candidate moves by checking tactical refutations and the resulting pawn structures. Avoid moves that create permanent weaknesses without compensation.
notes.plans: For White, after g5, consider queen d4 to maintain safety and pressure. For Black, taking on c4 is the best practical try despite the doubled pawns.

notes.explains: Grandmasters do not calculate every move from scratch; they rely on intuition and pattern recognition to narrow down candidates, then calculate only to verify. Beginners often over-calculate, wasting energy on irrelevant lines.
notes.teaches: Develop a feel for the position by studying typical patterns and plans. Use calculation selectively to confirm or refute intuitive moves, not to explore every possibility.

notes.explains: Black's best move is to take on c4, accepting doubled pawns, because other moves like bishop d7 allow White to castle and then use ideas like bishop b4-c5 to control the position and prevent Black from castling. The doubled pawns are inevitable and lead to a favorable endgame for White.
notes.teaches: Sometimes accepting a structural weakness is the best practical choice if alternatives lead to worse problems. Doubled pawns can be a long-term liability, but they may be the price for activity or safety.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit the doubled pawns by targeting them with rooks and pieces, and simplify to a favorable endgame.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's king is unsafe, so keeping queens on the board favors White's attack. Black's best practical chance is to trade queens and head to an endgame, where the king's safety matters less and White's pawn weaknesses are less relevant.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, consider forcing or allowing queen exchanges if it leads to a favorable endgame, especially if your own king is also vulnerable.
notes.plans: For Black: aim to exchange queens and simplify to an endgame. For White: if queens stay, use the initiative to attack the exposed king.

notes.explains: With the queens off, White chooses to castle long. This keeps the rook active and the king relatively safe, while also supporting a potential pawn storm. Tucking the king away on h1 would leave it passive and disconnected from the action.
notes.teaches: In endgames and simplified middlegames, castling long can be better than short when it activates a rook and keeps the king close enough to support play, as long as the king is not in immediate danger.
notes.plans: White: castle long, then bring the rook to the open file and target Black's weak pawns.

notes.explains: Black tries King g7 to find safety, but White brings the rook up. When Black offers a rook exchange, White accepts because after the rooks come off, Black's pawns become even more vulnerable and White's rook can penetrate more easily.
notes.teaches: Exchanging rooks can be good when your opponent's pawns are weak and your remaining rook will have clear entry points. Avoid exchanges only if you need the rooks for attack or defense.
notes.plans: White: exchange rooks, then use the remaining rook to attack Black's weak pawns, while the bishop controls key squares.

notes.explains: White has a strong bishop and Black's pawns are falling. White doesn't need to rush the pawn break; instead, improving the king with King c2 keeps harmony and prepares for the endgame. Black's attempts to save pawns are futile because White can simply target the other weaknesses.
notes.teaches: In a technically winning position, take your time to improve your pieces and king before executing the final breakthrough. Don't rush if the win is not going anywhere.
notes.plans: White: improve king to c2, then push the pawn break (e.g., f4) to win more material. Black: try to create counterplay, but the pawn weaknesses are decisive.

notes.explains: The knight on the board is very defensive, so exchanging it for the bishop can lead to an endgame where the opponent's chances are reduced. The move c5 aims to force this exchange and transition into a favorable endgame.
notes.teaches: When a piece is purely defensive, consider trading it to simplify into a better endgame. Look for moves that force favorable exchanges.
notes.plans: Play c5 to challenge the knight, and if the exchange occurs, proceed into the endgame with active pieces.

notes.explains: When in check, you cannot ignore it. Moving the king to b2 might allow the opponent to activate their rook and create threats, so it's better to capture the checking piece if possible.
notes.teaches: Always address checks, but evaluate which response gives the opponent the least counterplay. Capturing the checking piece is often best if it doesn't worsen your position.
notes.plans: Capture the knight to avoid giving the opponent rook activity, then continue with your plan.

notes.explains: After capturing the pawn, if the rook takes back, you can capture again, resulting in two passed pawns that support each other. This is stronger than having a single passed pawn because they are harder to stop.
notes.teaches: Connected passed pawns are a powerful endgame asset. They can advance together and support each other, often winning the game.
notes.plans: Aim to create connected passed pawns on the queenside and advance them while the king supports.

notes.explains: When the opponent plays King d7, you can finally play King d3 to block the opponent's king from invading. The threat of Rook e2 is strong, so the opponent cannot save the pawn, and you can maintain your advantage.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, king activity is crucial. Getting your king to an active square like d3 can prevent the opponent's king from penetrating and secure your pawns.
notes.plans: Place the king on d3 to control key squares, then use the rook to win the pawn on e5.

notes.explains: The rook's job is done on e4, so it should move to capture pawns. The move Rook e4 is interesting, but Rook e4 is better because it attacks the opponent's pawns and creates threats. The opponent's only logical move is c5, and you must calculate how to use it.
notes.teaches: In endgames, activate your rook by placing it on open files or ranks where it can attack pawns. Always calculate the opponent's most logical responses and prepare for them.
notes.plans: Move the rook to e4 to attack the e5 pawn, and after c5, find the best way to exploit the pawn structure, possibly with a check.

notes.explains: Giving a check with the rook can push the opponent's king forward, which might be unpleasant if it reaches d5. Instead, a different move like Rook e4 is better because it doesn't allow the king to advance and still wins the pawn.
notes.teaches: Be cautious with checks in endgames; they can sometimes help the opponent's king to a better square. Prefer moves that restrict the opponent's king while improving your own position.
notes.plans: Play Rook e4 to win the pawn, and if the opponent tries to save it, use your outside passed pawn to win the game.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, Black's king is trying to reach d5, which would be very unpleasant for White. White must prevent that and also watch for checks like c4 and King e6.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, king activity and outside passed pawns are decisive. Always calculate possible checks before committing.
notes.plans: White should aim to create passed pawns and keep the black king out of d5.

notes.explains: Black's best try is c4 check, forcing White to choose which pawn to take. Taking with the king to d4 gives Black more chances; taking with the pawn to c4 is better, allowing White to get to the second rank and attack Black's pawns.
notes.teaches: When facing a check, evaluate which recapture gives you the better pawn structure and king activity. Sometimes the less natural capture is superior.
notes.plans: After c4, White should aim to activate the rook and create passed pawns.

notes.explains: After Black plays King e6, White should check first and then push b5, creating two passed pawns. If the black king goes to d5, White can play a5 and head for a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: Creating multiple passed pawns can be decisive. Use checks to gain tempo and then push pawns to restrict the enemy king.
notes.plans: Push b5 and a5 to create connected passed pawns, then support them with the king and rook.

notes.explains: In the final phase, White must see the key move g4 to avoid being stuck. If the pawn were on g4, Black could play c4 and then d3, creating threats. The move g4 allows White to meet c4 with d3 and then use the rook to defend.
notes.teaches: In sharp endgames, you must calculate deeply, especially when the opponent threatens to create passed pawns. If you cannot see the full variation, choose a safer move that still keeps an advantage.
notes.plans: Play g4 to create luft and prevent Black's counterplay, then continue with the winning plan.

notes.explains: In the Scotch with ...Bc5, White's setup with Nb3 and Nc3 aims for a flexible development, often placing the bishop on e2 and the queen on e2, preparing to meet ...Nf6 with Bg5 or to play a simple development with Be3 and castling.
notes.teaches: The Scotch with ...Bc5 offers White a choice between sharp and solid setups; the Nb3/Nc3 system is a reliable way to play for a small advantage without taking excessive risks.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously, keep the king safe, and prepare to expand on the kingside with f3, g4, and h4 if Black allows.

notes.explains: After White plays Bg5, if Black tries h6, White can retreat to e3 and then castle long, creating a target on h6 for a future pawn storm. This provokes a weakness in Black's kingside.
notes.teaches: Provoking pawn moves like h6 can create permanent weaknesses that become targets for a later attack, especially when you can castle on the opposite side.
notes.plans: Castle long and prepare to advance the g- and h-pawns to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...Nxd4, White should recapture with the queen (Qxd4) rather than the pawn, because taking with the pawn exposes the king and weakens the pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In the Scotch, recapturing with the queen keeps the king safer and maintains a better pawn structure, even if it means developing the queen early.
notes.plans: After Qxd4, continue development and prepare to castle, keeping the position solid.

notes.explains: With the position after ...cxd4, White has a choice between aggressive moves like h4 or solid development like Be3. The solid choice is often better because it keeps pieces protected and prepares a pawn storm without hanging pieces.
notes.teaches: When you have more pieces, sacrifices can be considered, but if you lack attacking pieces, it's more logical to develop solidly and keep your pieces protected. Avoid leaving pieces hanging as it gives the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Be3, castle long, and then start pushing the g- and h-pawns to attack the black king.

notes.explains: Black's move ...g5 takes away White's g5 square, but it also weakens Black's kingside. White should be happy because Black's move is not the best, and White can continue with the planned pawn expansion.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the opponent's defensive moves create weaknesses that you can exploit later. Don't be discouraged if they stop one plan; look for new targets.
notes.plans: Continue with the kingside pawn push, using the weakened dark squares around Black's king.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a promising kingside attack with pawns on f3 and g4, and the time is right to push h4 and g5. Black's g5 move takes away White's g5 square, but it is not actually good for Black because White can simply capture on g5, keeping the attack alive. If White instead plays h5, it would close the position and reduce attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn storm on the flank, be willing to capture when the opponent tries to block your pawns; closing the position with your own pawn can blunt your attack.
