notes.teaches: In positions with central tension, look for the right moment to release it—when you gain the most from opening lines or when the opponent's pieces are poorly placed.
notes.plans: If Black doesn't take on d5 and instead plays ...b6, White should not give up the bishop but can capture a pawn, exploiting Black's weakened queenside.

notes.explains: If Black captures on b3, White can recapture with the knight, and after ...Rxb3, White's rook becomes active on the b-file, attacking Black's queenside. If Black tries to defend with a pawn, White has the resource c4, creating a passed pawn and tactical threats.
notes.teaches: When exchanging pieces, consider which recapture gives your remaining pieces the most activity; a rook on an open file can be worth more than a bishop on a diagonal.
notes.plans: After c4, if Black takes, White recaptures and then plays Bb5, attacking the queen; if Black doesn't take, White's knight remains strong and the rooks can double on the b-file.

notes.explains: Watching commentary on super-GM events is valuable for players under 2000 because commentators often explain ideas at a level that is accessible, not just for grandmasters.
notes.teaches: Expose yourself to high-level commentary and games; even unfamiliar positions can teach you calculation and strategic thinking.

notes.explains: In the English Opening, black's setup with b6, Bb7, and a knight on d7 or c6 aims to prepare the d5 break, though it can be difficult to achieve.
notes.teaches: Recognize typical plans in the English: black often fianchettoes the light-squared bishop and seeks central expansion with d5.
notes.plans: Black will develop the bishop to b7, then aim for d5, possibly with the knight going to d7 or c6 to support it.

notes.explains: In this bishop-for-bishop relationship, White's light-squared bishop is naturally defended by the king after castling, while Black's counterpart on b7 is undefended. This asymmetry creates latent tactical threats for White, such as knight moves or pawn breaks that hit the loose bishop.
notes.teaches: When evaluating opposite-side bishop positions, consider which bishop is easier to defend. A naturally defended bishop gives the owner free tactical opportunities, while an undefended one can restrict the opponent's plans.
notes.plans: White can look for ways to exploit the loose bishop with moves like a knight to e5 or a timely d4 break, gaining tempo on the bishop.

notes.explains: Black refrains from the natural central break d5 because the undefended bishop on b7 would hang, allowing White tactics like Nxe5 or a pawn push that pins the bishop. Black needs to consolidate and activate pieces before opening the center.
notes.teaches: Before initiating central pawn breaks, ensure your pieces are safe and coordinated. A loose piece can make a seemingly natural break too costly.
notes.plans: Black should play d6, finish development, and prepare a later break like d5 or b5 once the position is more solid.

notes.explains: White plays d4, and after the exchange, White gives up the light-squared bishop but gains central space. Black adopts a Hedgehog-like structure with d6, aiming to keep weaknesses minimal and later break in the center.
notes.teaches: In structures like the Hedgehog, one side trades space for solidity and counterplay. The side with more space should use it to attack, while the cramped side seeks timely breaks to free their pieces.
notes.plans: White will use the central space to expand, possibly with e4 and f4, to attack Black's king. Black will look for a well-timed d5 or b5 break to activate his pieces.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has a slightly weak pawn on d6, but the long-term plan is to break in the center with d5 or on the queenside with b5, which would neutralize that weakness and activate the pieces. White, on the other hand, aims to exploit the central space advantage, possibly by advancing the f-pawn to attack Black's king, and to prove that Black's weaknesses are real.
notes.teaches: When you have a spatial disadvantage, look for pawn breaks to challenge the opponent's center and create counterplay. The side with more space should try to use that space to launch an attack, often with a pawn storm.
notes.plans: Black should prepare and execute either d5 or b5 at the right moment. White should try to maintain the central bind and look for opportunities to push e5 or f4-f5.

notes.explains: Black, having less space, trades off pieces to free up squares for the remaining pieces. A knight on c6 that isn't doing much is exchanged for a strong knight on d4, simplifying the position and reducing White's attacking potential.
notes.teaches: When cramped, trading pieces is a common and effective strategy to relieve pressure and give your remaining pieces more room to maneuver.
notes.plans: Continue simplifying where possible, while keeping the position solid and preparing the pawn breaks.

notes.explains: Black's queen moves to b7, getting off the back rank and supporting the key squares d5 and b5, which are the targets for the planned pawn breaks. This is simple, principled development that sets up the long-term plan.
notes.teaches: Even in quiet positions, every move should serve a purpose. Developing pieces to squares that support your strategic goals is more valuable than flashy tactics.
notes.plans: Black will continue to prepare b5 or d5, while White tries to prove that the d6 pawn is weak.

notes.explains: Black plays a6 to prevent White from jumping into b5, and also prepares the b5 break. This is a prophylactic move that stops White's potential ideas and sets up Black's own plan.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves that prevent the opponent's ideas while preparing your own are a hallmark of strong play. Always consider what the opponent wants to do and stop it if possible.
notes.plans: Black will continue to prepare b5, and White will look for ways to exploit the queenside weaknesses.

notes.explains: White is planning to double or triple on the d6 pawn with moves like queen e6 or queen f4, and also looking to play e5 at an opportune moment. Black must consider the pawn breaks b5 and d5 on every turn, calculating if they work now and what is needed to prepare them.
notes.teaches: In positions with a fixed pawn structure, both sides should constantly evaluate the critical pawn breaks. The side under pressure must be ready to strike at the right moment to equalize.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play b5 or d5 when possible, while White will try to maintain the bind and increase pressure on d6.

notes.explains: In this position, Black is considering the pawn break b5, which would create tension in the center and potentially open lines. Both sides have pieces defending key squares, and the queens are aligned, so tactics are possible.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn break, calculate the forcing sequences that follow, including captures and recaptures, to see if the resulting position is favorable.
notes.plans: Black should evaluate b5 carefully, considering White's possible responses like e5, and whether the resulting exchanges lead to a good endgame or middlegame.

notes.explains: The exchange on b5 (cxb5) would remove a defender of the d5 square, which is a critical weakness in Black's position. White would prefer to avoid this exchange because it would free Black to play d5 later.
notes.teaches: Before initiating a pawn exchange, consider which pieces are defending key squares and whether the exchange improves your opponent's position by removing a defender.
notes.plans: White should avoid cxb5 and instead find a move that maintains the tension, such as Bb2, which also steps out of a potential fork.

notes.explains: Black wants to force White to open the a-file and remove the c4 defender. Adding pressure on c4 with moves like Rc8 or Qb6 can threaten to win the pawn, but Black must be careful about tactics on the long diagonal, especially with the queens aligned.
notes.teaches: To force a favorable pawn break, add pressure to the target pawn with multiple attackers, but always be alert to tactical motifs like pins and skewers along open diagonals.
notes.plans: Black can consider Rc7, which adds another attacker to c4 and forces White to respond, possibly by taking on b5, leading to the desired opening of the a-file.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has a weakness on d6, but it is well defended. Black's pieces are all active: the knight and queen target the c4 pawn, the rook pressures the b2 pawn, and another rook challenges the open file. The bishop, though seemingly passive, prevents White's counterplay against d6.
notes.teaches: A static weakness is acceptable if it is defended and your pieces are more active than the opponent's. Sometimes a 'bad' piece is actually crucial for restricting the opponent's plans.
notes.plans: Black should continue to pressure the c4 pawn and the b2 pawn, while keeping the d6 pawn defended. White may try to relieve pressure with moves like Rook to b4, but Black should be ready to meet it.

notes.explains: White considered adding a defender to c4, but the natural move (like Knight to e2) would retreat and remove a defender from another key square. The move that adds a defender to c4 also removes the defender of e4, forcing White to capture and open the a-file.
notes.teaches: When defending a weakness, check whether the defending piece is overworked. A move that appears to defend one square may abandon another, and the opponent can exploit the resulting tactical motifs.
notes.plans: Black should exploit the opened file and the weakened squares, while White must be careful not to allow Black's pieces to dominate.

notes.explains: Black played d5, a classic freeing move in the Hedgehog structure. This move opens the bishop and rook, but it also leaves the bishop on f8 attacked. White must respond with tempo, and after Bishop takes f8, Black has to find an in-between move rather than simply recapturing.
notes.teaches: In the Hedgehog, freeing moves like d5 or b5 are typical to activate pieces. When a piece is attacked, look for intermediate moves that create multiple threats before resolving the capture.
notes.plans: Black should consider taking on c4 as an in-between move, creating further complications. White must handle multiple hanging pieces, and the calculation becomes critical.

notes.explains: After the complications, Black has to calculate carefully. If Black simply recaptures, a counting puzzle shows that White has more defenders than attackers on a key square, so Black would lose material. Instead, Black must find a clever in-between move like taking on c4, leaving more pieces hanging.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, count attackers and defenders. If you are losing the counting race, look for an intermediate move that changes the tactical balance before recapturing.
notes.plans: Black should play the in-between move to create multiple threats. White must find a way to save the queen and rook, but may have to give up material.

notes.explains: In this sharp tactical position, White has multiple pieces hanging, including the queen and rook, and Black's threats are multiplying. White cannot save everything at once, and capturing the pawn on d7 would allow Black to recapture with check, leaving White's queen hanging.
notes.teaches: When many pieces are hanging, look for the move that addresses the most critical threats, often by creating counterplay or forcing trades that neutralize the opponent's initiative.
notes.plans: White should seek a forcing sequence that resolves the complications favorably, such as trading pieces to reach a calmer position.

notes.explains: After the tactical sequence, the position simplifies and approaches an endgame with queens still on the board. Black's b6 pawn is a potential weakness, but White has no clear way to attack it, and White has no targets either, so the position is equal.
notes.teaches: In balanced positions, static weaknesses are only meaningful if they can be attacked; otherwise, the position remains equal.
notes.plans: Both sides should improve piece placement and wait for the opponent to create a weakness.

notes.explains: White tries to break through with c5 to create play before the game fizzles out. Black trades queens because the white king on f8 is unsafe, and then Black has the choice of recapturing on c5 or moving the knight away. Keeping the knight is preferable because it has a natural square where it controls important squares in both camps.
notes.teaches: In queenless middlegames, the knight can be a strong piece if it has a stable outpost that controls key squares. Activate your king early in endgames.
notes.plans: Black should centralize the king and place the knight on its best square, while White tries to create pawn breaks.

notes.explains: Black plays a5 to prevent b4 and to defend the knight, but White eventually plays b4 anyway, creating a passed pawn. However, the passed pawn is not enough to win because Black's pieces control it well. The position remains balanced despite the pawn structure changes.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn is only a winning advantage if it can be supported and advanced; if the opponent can blockade it, it may not be decisive.
notes.plans: Both sides should continue improving piece placement and king activity, with Black keeping the passed pawn under control.

notes.explains: Black (Magnus) makes a critical mistake by leaving a knight and a rook loose (undefended). White exploits this by attacking both simultaneously with a move like Qg7, which wins material because Black cannot defend both. The tactic works because the loose pieces are vulnerable to a double attack.
notes.teaches: Always look for loose pieces in the opponent's camp; a double attack against two undefended pieces often wins material. Before moving, check if your own pieces are left hanging.
notes.plans: White should execute the double attack and then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Tactics often arise from loose pieces—pieces that are undefended or underdefended. In the game, both a knight and a rook were hanging, and a single move attacked both simultaneously, making it impossible to defend both.
notes.teaches: To find tactics, scan for loose pieces and look for moves that create double attacks or forks. If you can attack two undefended pieces at once, the opponent can only save one.
notes.plans: When you spot loose pieces, calculate forcing sequences that exploit them, such as checks or captures that gain material.

notes.explains: In the opening, the exchange of light-squared bishops can be a key theme. One side may give up a bishop for central space, which can be a fair trade if the resulting pawn center is strong. The opponent should be careful not to fall into a worse version of this structure.
notes.teaches: When considering an early bishop exchange, weigh the value of the bishop against the central space and pawn structure you gain. Simple, principled development and following natural plans can be enough to neutralize an opponent's play.
notes.plans: If you have central space from such an exchange, reinforce it with pawn moves and piece development, and avoid overextending.

notes.explains: In a Queen's Gambit Declined or Catalan-type setup, Black can accept the c4 pawn and later return it to gain time and space. After White recaptures, Black can use the queen to pressure the center and then expand on the queenside with b5, exploiting the queen's placement.
notes.teaches: Accepting a gambit pawn can be fine if you can return it under favorable circumstances, gaining development or space. Look for pawn breaks like b5 to challenge the opponent's setup and create queenside play.
notes.plans: After ...b5, continue with ...c5 to gain more space and create outposts for your pieces, such as the b6 square for the queen.

notes.explains: When the opponent's queenside pieces are loose, a move like a4 can try to exploit the weaknesses. Black's c5 pawn break not only controls key squares but also opens the b6 square for the queen, which helps coordinate the queenside and prevents tactics.
notes.teaches: Expanding with pawns gives your pieces more space and can create useful outposts. When your position is loose, find a square that coordinates your pieces and holds the structure together.
notes.plans: Play ...Qb6 to consolidate the queenside, keeping the pieces protected and ready to counter any threats.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's queenside pieces are somewhat loose, and White's bishop is well-defended while Black's counterpart is less so. Black needs to find a way to coordinate and defend the queenside.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are loose, look for a square that can serve multiple purposes: an outpost for a piece, a way to defend others, and control of key central squares.
notes.plans: Black can consider placing the queen on b6, which controls b5, supports pawn advances, indirectly eyes d4, and adds a defender to the bishop.

notes.explains: Black has a tactical way to defend a pawn with ...Nd5, which also creates threats. If White captures the pawn, Black has tactical resources like ...Nc3+ or an in-between check.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best defense is a tactical one that creates counterplay, rather than a passive block. Look for moves that defend while also attacking or creating threats.
notes.plans: Black can use the knight on d5 to defend the b6 pawn and potentially create threats, while also being ready to exploit pins like ...Bc6 if the knight is captured.

notes.explains: After the opening, White has a solid fortress but needs to create active play. Black has weaknesses on b5 and c5, which are targets for White.
notes.teaches: When unsure of a plan, examine the pawn structure for weaknesses. Pressure on weak pawns can tie down enemy pieces and create opportunities for expansion.
notes.plans: White should aim to pressure the b5 and c5 pawns, potentially with moves like d4, e5, or f4 to open lines and increase the pressure.

notes.explains: Black's pawns on b5 and c5 are advanced and can be used to gain space and create outposts. Black has already used the b4 outpost and may push to c4 to gain more space.
notes.teaches: In such pawn structures, the side with the advanced pawns should look to push them further to gain space and create outposts for pieces.
notes.plans: Black can aim to advance the c-pawn to c4, creating more space and potentially opening lines, while using the b4 outpost for a piece.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense: O'Kelly Variation, Maróczy Bind
notes.explains: In a position with a space advantage, the plan is to control the queenside, center, and kingside. The bishop is well placed on e2, and pushing b4 restricts the opponent's knight outposts. The rooks can be relocated to support the pawn pushes.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, use it to restrict the opponent's piece activity and slowly improve your own pieces, avoiding premature exchanges that relieve the pressure.
notes.plans: Push b4 to gain space, bring the bishop to e2, and prepare to double rooks on the open file. Avoid exchanging rooks until you have created weaknesses in the opponent's camp.

notes.explains: After pawn exchanges, the structure changes, and it's crucial to reevaluate who stands better. Here, Black's b-pawn is more vulnerable than White's c-pawn, making Black's position preferable.
notes.teaches: After any pawn exchange, reassess the position: compare weaknesses, piece activity, and long-term prospects.
notes.plans: White should consider playing b3 to trade off the weak b-pawn, while Black should aim to exploit the weakness on b2 and use the open files.

notes.explains: Black's advanced knight on b4 is a key piece, but it can be kicked. However, Black has counterplay with ideas like Nc2, targeting d3 and b2, and possibly using the b3 square for a bishop.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a strong outpost, look for ways to challenge it, but also consider the weaknesses that may arise if it moves.
notes.plans: Black should consider moves like Nc2 to create threats against d3 and b2, while White must defend these squares and possibly trade off the knight.

notes.explains: In the tactical phase, White offers a knight on d4, daring Black to take on b2. This is a tactical trick because the bishop on a4 is hanging, so Black cannot take immediately.
notes.teaches: Be wary of tactical offers: sometimes a piece is 'poisoned' because of a follow-up tactic. Always check if the capture is safe before taking.
notes.plans: Black should not rush to take on b2; instead, consider moves like Bishop a4 to create threats, but be prepared for complications.

notes.explains: In this sharp tactical line, White offers a pawn on b2 as a provocation, daring Black to take it. The bishop on g5 is en prise, and White's pieces are coordinated to punish premature captures.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices and pawn grabs in the opening/middlegame are often poisoned; before taking, check if the opponent has a tactical refutation like a pin or a fork.
notes.plans: If Black takes on b2, White can try to exploit the loose black queen and the pinned bishop with moves like Nc6, aiming to regain material or create threats.

notes.explains: White's bishop is running out of safe squares due to pawn forks and piece pressure. The knight on c2 is overworked, defending multiple key points, and Black exploits this by attacking it.
notes.teaches: When a piece is overworked, look for ways to overload it further or force it to abandon a critical defensive duty.
notes.plans: Black can continue to harass the knight, using tactics like Bb2 and Rxb1 to create threats that tie down White's pieces.

notes.explains: Black faces a choice: retreat the attacked bishop or counter-attack elsewhere. The best practical approach is often to ignore the threat and create a bigger one, as long as the hanging piece is not immediately lost.
notes.teaches: When your piece is attacked, consider counter-attacking rather than automatically retreating, especially if the opponent's threats are more dangerous.
notes.plans: Black can play a move like c3, attacking the white king and rook simultaneously, forcing White to respond to the check while Black's bishop remains safe.

notes.explains: In the actual game, Black played the spectacular Nc3, sacrificing a piece to force the bishop to capture, then using a fork on d1 to win material. This shows that even in chaotic positions, concrete calculation can reveal winning tactics.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be justified if they lead to a decisive fork or other tactical motif that regains more material than invested.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, Black must keep the initiative and ensure the king is safe while converting the material advantage.

notes.explains: White resigned when it became clear that there was no way to win back the sacrificed piece, and Black's material advantage was decisive.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a position is lost and avoid prolonging a hopeless defense; instead, focus on learning from the tactical patterns that led to the defeat.

notes.explains: In this game, White's pieces were tied up and Black had a material advantage, leading to resignation. Even if the tactics are too complex to follow in real time, the position can be understood through its key features.
notes.teaches: When analyzing a complicated position, break it down into essential elements: space, weaknesses, and piece activity. This makes evaluation manageable even without deep calculation.

notes.explains: The move c5 by Black grabs queenside space and supports the bishop on b4 or c5, helping to hold the position together. This relationship between pawn moves and piece placement is crucial.
notes.teaches: A pawn move like c5 can serve dual purposes: gaining space and preparing to support key pieces. Understanding these relationships helps in planning.
notes.plans: Black should aim to exploit the queenside space and target White's weaknesses, such as the b2 pawn.

notes.explains: Studying a single opening, even one you don't play, is valuable because it exposes you to new plans and ideas. Chess is fundamentally the same game regardless of the opening, so the ideas transfer.
notes.teaches: Use opening study to collect transferable plans and typical middlegame themes, not just memorized moves.

notes.explains: In the Nimzo-Indian, after d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4, the bishop pins the knight to the king and attacks c3, loosening White's control over e4. The main imbalance is that if Black takes on c3, White gets a doubled c-pawn but Black gives up the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Recognize the structural and material imbalances in the Nimzo: White's doubled pawns versus Black's bishop pair.

notes.explains: The f3 variation (f3) is a direct attempt to control e4 and prepare a central pawn expansion. It's not the most popular, but it sets up a clear fight for the center.
notes.teaches: A move like f3 can be a useful way to reinforce control of a key central square and prepare an aggressive pawn advance.
notes.plans: White intends to expand in the center, likely with e4, while Black must choose a plan to counter it.

notes.explains: Black's most natural response to f3 is …d5, challenging White's control of e4 directly. Many club players rely on this natural move without deeper preparation, which can lead to poor results.
notes.teaches: Natural moves are often correct, but in sharp openings you must understand the resulting positions, not just play automatically.
notes.plans: White will aim to exploit Black's lack of preparation after ...d5, often with a consistent plan that has proven effective.

notes.explains: Black's alternative …c5 attacks a dark square, while White's f3 controls light squares. This creates an imbalance: Black gets play on the dark squares, White gets a central light-square advantage and more space.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's setup targets one color complex, countering on the opposite color can create a healthy imbalance.
notes.plans: Black will aim to exploit the dark squares, while White will try to use the central space advantage.

notes.explains: Another natural developing move for Black is …Nc6, but this requires care because the knight can be vulnerable to tactics or pawn pushes.
notes.teaches: In the opening, natural developing moves are often good, but you must check for tactical refutations or pawn attacks.

notes.explains: In this pawn endgame, the position is delicate: the white king is one square away from stopping the black pawn, but the exact square matters. If the king goes to e5 or f5, black can promote with check and win the white queen, whereas king d5 is the only move that draws.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, the precise placement of the king is critical—one square can be the difference between a win, a draw, or a loss. Always calculate the promotion race with checks in mind.
notes.plans: With the king on d5, white can maintain the opposition or be in time to stop the pawn, ensuring a draw.

notes.explains: This is a classic triangulation position: white wants to reach the same position but with black to move, because then black must give way. The key is to maneuver the king between f1, g1, and g2 while keeping the pawn structure intact.
notes.teaches: Triangulation is a fundamental technique in king and pawn endgames to lose a tempo and force the opponent to move, thereby gaining a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: White will use the triangulation to force black's king away from the critical squares, then advance the f-pawn or b-pawn to create a passed pawn and win.

notes.explains: This is a famous rook endgame position. The immediate rook move to a5 fails because black can respond with g6 or h4, creating counterplay. The correct start is king h7, which avoids the h-pawn tricks and prepares to support the rook.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, king activity is often more important than rushing with the rook. Look for the most active king square first, and be wary of pawn breaks that can change the evaluation.
notes.plans: After king h7, white will bring the king to support the rook and the passed pawn, while neutralizing black's h-pawn counterplay.

notes.explains: In this pawn race, the placement of the king is critical. Starting with king h7 is precise because king g7 allows the opposing pawn to advance with tempo, changing the outcome. The presence of a pawn on g7 prevents the queen from checking along the diagonal, which would otherwise stop the rook.
notes.teaches: When both sides are promoting, the king's route must be chosen to avoid allowing the opponent's pawn to gain crucial tempi. The exact king move can be the difference between winning and drawing.
notes.plans: Advance the king to h7, then support the pawn's promotion while using the king to control key squares.

notes.explains: With a bishop versus a far-advanced pawn, the bishop must find the precise square to stop the pawn and also prevent the enemy king from approaching. Bishop d7 is the only winning move because it controls the critical diagonal and allows the bishop to later move to e8, where it can both stop the pawn and support the king's approach.
notes.teaches: In bishop-versus-pawn endgames, the bishop often needs to be placed on a specific diagonal that both blocks the pawn and restricts the enemy king. The exact square can be counterintuitive and requires deep calculation.
notes.plans: Play bishop d7, then after the pawn advances, reposition the bishop to e8 to maintain control and allow the king to come in.

notes.explains: In a knight versus pawns endgame, the knight must be maneuvered to a square where it can stop the pawns while the king comes to help. Knight b3 is the only move because it allows the knight to reach a1, where it can blockade the a-pawn and also support the king's entry.
notes.teaches: Knights are often clumsy in stopping outside passed pawns; the correct route is to place the knight on a square that both blocks the pawn and allows the king to approach. Sometimes the knight must go to the edge of the board to achieve this.
notes.plans: Play knight b3, then maneuver the knight to a1, while bringing the king to support the blockade and eventually win the pawns.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame with a passed pawn, the rook must be placed on the correct file to both support the pawn and prevent the enemy king from approaching. Rook g5 is the only move because it gives the king time to approach, while other rook moves allow the black king to get in front of the pawn or create counterplay.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the rook's placement is often about timing: you must prevent the enemy king from reaching a key square while also supporting your own pawn. The first move can be a waiting move that forces the opponent to commit.
notes.plans: Play rook g5, then bring the king to support the pawn, while using the rook to cut off the enemy king.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the placement of the rook and king determines whether a mating net exists. With the king on d4 and rook on g5, Black can play ...g6 to avoid the mate, whereas a different rook placement might force it.
notes.teaches: When trying to mate with rook and king, the rook must control the key escape squares; the defender can often slip out if the rook is not on the correct file or rank.
notes.plans: Look for the precise rook move that cuts off the enemy king's escape, even if it seems counterintuitive.

notes.explains: In a bishop endgame with opposite-colored bishops and two central pawns, the defender's ideal setup is to place the king in front of one pawn (e.g., e6) and the bishop on the long diagonal (e.g., b7) to restrain the other pawn and prevent the enemy king from infiltrating.
notes.teaches: With opposite-colored bishops, the defender should aim to blockade the pawns and keep the king active in front of them, while the bishop covers the other pawn's advance.
notes.plans: As the defender, set up the blockade before the pawns advance too far; as the attacker, try to break the blockade by forcing the bishop away or using the king.

notes.explains: In this opposite-colored bishop endgame, the move rook c7 is actually a mistake because it allows Black to trade rooks and reach a drawn bishop endgame. The key defensive resource is the a2 pawn, which gives Black enough counterplay to hold.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, even being a pawn up may not be enough to win; the defender should seek to simplify to a drawn bishop ending, and the attacker must avoid premature rook trades.
notes.plans: White should keep rooks on the board and use them to create threats, while Black should aim to exchange rooks and reach a known drawn bishop endgame.

notes.explains: In a queen versus rook endgame, there is a key winning position where the queen forces the rook away from the king, then wins it. The defender should keep the rook close to the king, but the attacker can use checks and threats to separate them.
notes.teaches: In queen vs rook, the stronger side should aim for a specific winning setup (often with the queen cutting off the king) and then use a maneuver to drive the rook away from its king.
notes.plans: The attacker should first bring the king closer, then use the queen to force the rook to a square where it can be won; the defender should try to keep the rook on the same rank or file as the king.

notes.explains: In a queen versus rook endgame, the key is to separate the defending rook from its king. By driving the enemy king to the edge or corner and using your own king to support the queen, you can create threats that win the rook.
notes.teaches: To win queen versus rook, first bring your king closer and force the enemy king to the edge, then use your queen to cut off the rook's connection to the king, eventually winning it.
notes.plans: Bring your king to a useful square like f3, then maneuver the queen to restrict the enemy king and rook, aiming to win the rook or force a checkmate.

notes.explains: In knight endgames, the side with a far-advanced passed pawn often has winning chances. The h-pawn for Black or the a-pawn for White can be decisive if supported correctly.
notes.teaches: In knight endgames, a distant passed pawn is a major asset; use it to tie down the enemy pieces and create zugzwang or entry points for your king.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawn, use the knight to support it, and bring the king to assist, while preventing the enemy knight from blockading.

notes.explains: In bishop versus knight endgames with pawns on both sides, the bishop is generally stronger because of its long-range influence. Here, Black's pawn structure is better, with a strong c5 pawn restricting White's queenside.
notes.teaches: When you have a bishop against a knight, place your pawns on the same color as the bishop to maximize its scope and restrict the knight's mobility.
notes.plans: Use the bishop to pressure the weak pawns and create passed pawns, while keeping the knight passive.

notes.explains: In rook versus bishop endgames, the result depends on the pawn placement. With a pawn on h4, the side with the rook can win by getting the king to h5 and g4, but with a pawn on h5, it's a draw because the king cannot penetrate.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop, the winning method often involves using your king to invade via the pawn's support. The exact pawn rank matters: a pawn on the 4th rank may allow a win, while on the 5th it may not.
notes.plans: If you have the rook, aim to get your king to the key squares (like h5 and g4) to support the pawn and force the bishop away. If defending, keep your king in the correct corner and use the bishop to control the promotion squares.

notes.explains: With a pawn on h4, the winning plan requires the white king to reach h5 and g4. If the king goes to g5 instead, the position is drawn even with a pawn on h6 and a bishop controlling h7, because the black king can stay on f8 and the rook can defend.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop endgames, the placement of the pawn and the king's route are critical. A pawn on h4 gives White the winning idea of invading with the king via h5 and g4, while a pawn on h5 may only draw.
notes.plans: White should aim to play Rg7, then Rg5, and later bring the king to h5 and g4 to create decisive threats. Black should try to keep the king on the correct side and avoid allowing the white king to penetrate.

notes.explains: In the losing line, the black king is on the wrong side, and the bishop is vulnerable to harassment by the rook. The rook can chase the bishop around the board, forcing it to abandon key squares, after which the rook can capture it or win the game.
notes.teaches: When defending with a bishop against a rook, the king must be placed on the correct side to avoid being driven into a lost position. The rook can use checks and threats to force the bishop to move to unfavorable squares.
notes.plans: Black should try to keep the bishop on squares that cover the king's escape routes and avoid allowing the rook to attack it repeatedly. White should continue to harass the bishop with rook moves like Rh1, Rh3, Rc3, and Ra3 to force it to a losing square.

notes.explains: The difference between a pawn on h4 and h5 is crucial in this endgame. With the pawn on h4, White can win by using the extra tempo to bring the king around, whereas with the pawn on h5, the position is drawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the exact pawn structure can change the evaluation dramatically. Always consider how the pawn's position affects the king's routes and the opponent's defensive resources.
notes.plans: When studying such endgames, compare the variations with the pawn on h4 and h5 to understand the subtle differences. In practice, aim to create the favorable pawn structure for your side.

notes.explains: In a pure rook versus bishop endgame with no pawns, the defender draws by placing the king in a corner opposite the color of the bishop. The bishop guards the two squares adjacent to the corner, preventing checkmate.
notes.teaches: The drawing method is to keep the king in the safe corner and maintain the bishop on the long diagonal, ready to interpose on the key square in front of the king.
notes.plans: The defender shuffles the king between the corner and the adjacent square, while the bishop stays on the diagonal, meeting any rook check with a block.

notes.explains: When the defending king is trapped in the wrong corner, the rook can use a series of checks and threats to force the bishop away from its ideal defensive squares. The key is to use the rook to challenge the bishop along files and diagonals, creating threats of mate that force the bishop to move to less favorable squares.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop endgames, if the defending king is confined to a corner, the attacking side can often win by using the rook to drive the bishop away from the king, eventually winning it or delivering mate. The defender's best hope is to keep the bishop close to the king to block checks, but the rook can force it out.
notes.plans: Use the rook to check the king and attack the bishop, forcing it to move to squares where it can be won or where mate is threatened. The goal is to drive the bishop to a file where the rook can both attack it and threaten mate on the back rank.

notes.explains: The defender's best drawing chance is to run the king away from the corner, even if it means giving up the bishop. If the king can escape the mating net, the rook cannot win against a lone king, so the game is drawn.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop, the defender should prioritize king activity. If the king can get out of the corner and avoid immediate mate, the bishop can often be sacrificed to reach a drawn rook versus king endgame.
notes.plans: If you are defending, look for opportunities to move the king toward the center or the opposite corner. Even if you lose the bishop, a rook versus king is a draw if the king is not in a mating net.

notes.explains: In this rook versus bishop endgame, the defender's bishop is sheltering behind its king, preventing the attacker from delivering checkmate. The immediate rook move to the e-file is wrong because it allows the defender to reach the wrong-corner drawing setup.
notes.teaches: When the enemy bishop hides behind its king, the winning idea is to evict it with a rook move that attacks the bishop while also threatening checkmate.
notes.plans: Play the rook to the third rank (e.g., g3) to force the bishop away, then coordinate the rook and king to win the bishop or deliver mate.

notes.explains: The defender's bishop must stay on the three files adjacent to its king to avoid immediate loss. If it leaves those files, the rook can attack it while also threatening mate.
notes.teaches: In these positions, the defender's bishop is tied to specific squares; the attacker should use zugzwang-like maneuvers to force it away.
notes.plans: Keep the rook active, use checks and threats to restrict the bishop, and when the bishop is forced off its safe files, capture it or mate.

notes.explains: If the bishop is on the same color as the kings, the win may still be possible but requires more precision, often by forcing the king to a square where the bishop can be captured.
notes.teaches: The color of the bishop relative to the kings determines the ease of the win; be alert to tactical captures when the king moves.
notes.plans: If the bishop is on the same color, look for a rook move that forces the king to step onto a square where the bishop becomes vulnerable.

notes.explains: When a pawn is added, the endgame is generally winning for the side with the rook, but the technique still relies on the same principles: restrict the enemy king and bishop, and use the pawn as a decoy or extra threat.
notes.teaches: Do not memorize every detail; instead, apply the core ideas of piece activity, restriction, and coordination to find the win.
notes.plans: Use the pawn to create threats and force the defender into passivity, then convert using the rook's power.

notes.explains: In this rook versus bishop endgame, the winning plan for the side with the rook is to force the king to one of two key squares, E5 or C5. These squares are crucial because from there the king can support the pawn's advance and avoid the bishop's checks.
notes.teaches: Identify the key squares that lead to a win and focus all efforts on reaching them, rather than aimlessly checking or attacking.
notes.plans: Use the rook to cut off the bishop and king, and maneuver your own king toward E5 or C5.

notes.explains: The defender's drawing technique is to keep the bishop on a diagonal that can check the enemy king away from the key squares. For example, if the king steps to C5, the bishop checks from F2; if it steps to E5, the bishop checks from C3. This prevents the king from reaching the winning squares.
notes.teaches: When defending, use the bishop to control the key squares from a distance, forcing the enemy king to retreat or lose time.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on a long diagonal that covers both key squares, and only move the king when necessary.

notes.explains: Advancing the pawn to D6 is often not winning because the defender can respond with King C6, placing pressure on the pawn and preventing the enemy king from approaching. If the enemy king tries to come to E6, the bishop can simply capture the pawn on D6.
notes.teaches: Do not rush to push the pawn; first secure the key squares for your king. Premature pawn advances can be neutralized by the defender's king and bishop coordination.
notes.plans: Instead of pushing the pawn, use the rook to restrict the bishop and slowly improve the king's position.

notes.explains: The defender's bishop is best placed on squares like B4 or B8, where it can both protect the pawn and deliver checks. If the bishop is on a bad square, the win becomes possible because the defender cannot maintain the drawing setup.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop endgames, the placement of the defending bishop is critical. Aim to keep it on a square that covers key entry points for the enemy king.
notes.plans: As the defender, keep the bishop on B4 or B8 if possible. As the attacker, try to force the bishop to a worse square.

notes.explains: When the defender's bishop is well-placed, the attacker must use precise rook maneuvers to make progress. For example, after King D4 and Bishop E1, only a few rook moves (like Rook G8) actually make progress. The idea is to force the defender's king to D6, then use the rook to take away squares from the bishop.
notes.teaches: In winning attempts, use the rook to restrict the bishop's available squares and force the defender into a passive position. Patience and tempo play are essential.
notes.plans: Maneuver the rook to the seventh rank or to the side to limit the bishop's diagonals, then bring the king to the key squares.

notes.explains: In rook versus bishop endgames with a pawn, the defender's bishop can control key squares and prevent the king from advancing. The winning method is to systematically take away the bishop's safe squares, forcing it to move to a worse square and allowing the king to penetrate.
notes.teaches: To win such endgames, you must use your rook to restrict the bishop's movement, often by controlling the squares it needs to retreat to. This can involve 'wasting' tempi to put the opponent in zugzwang, where any bishop move is bad.
notes.plans: Use the rook to check and force the king to a worse position, then use the rook to cut off the bishop's squares. Repeat this process until the bishop is forced to a square that allows your king to advance.

notes.explains: In rook versus bishop endgames with a bishop pawn, the same principles apply: push the king first, not the pawn. If the pawn is pushed prematurely, the win becomes much more difficult because the bishop can control key squares.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, it is generally better to advance your king before your pawn. Pushing the pawn too early gives the defender's pieces more targets and makes it harder to make progress.
notes.plans: Bring your king up to support the pawn, using the rook to control the bishop's squares. Only push the pawn when the king is in a position to support it.

notes.explains: The rook can be used to control key squares that the bishop needs to retreat to, such as the square in front of the pawn. For example, placing the rook on a file can prevent the bishop from going to a certain diagonal.
notes.teaches: In these endgames, the rook's power lies in its ability to control many squares at once. Use it to cut off the bishop's retreat squares, forcing it to move to less favorable positions.
notes.plans: Identify the squares the bishop needs to defend and use your rook to control them. This may involve placing the rook on a specific rank or file to limit the bishop's mobility.

notes.explains: The winning process in these endgames is often long and complex, requiring precise moves and patience. Even strong players may struggle to find the exact sequence, but the general method is to restrict the bishop and create zugzwang.
notes.teaches: Do not be discouraged by the complexity. Focus on the method: use your rook to take away the bishop's squares, and if the opponent has no good moves, they will be forced to allow your king through.
notes.plans: Continue to improve your king's position while using the rook to keep the bishop passive. Be patient and look for the moment when the bishop runs out of safe squares.

notes.explains: In rook versus bishop endgames with a knight pawn, the winning method is simpler than with bishop or center pawns. The key is to use the pawn as a sacrifice to reach a known winning position where the enemy king is trapped in the corner.
notes.teaches: When you have a knight pawn, you can often win by pushing the pawn to the seventh rank, even if the bishop captures it, because the resulting position is a forced mate or a won rook versus bishop endgame.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to the seventh rank, allow the bishop to take it, then use the rook to deliver checks and drive the enemy king to the corner, where the rook and king can mate.

notes.explains: With a rook pawn, the winning idea is different: you must first bring the rook to the side (e.g., g1) and advance the king, but you must avoid giving up the pawn carelessly. Instead, you use a rook check to gain tempo and drive the enemy king to the wrong corner.
notes.teaches: In rook-pawn endgames, you cannot simply sacrifice the pawn; you need to use the rook to check the king and force it to the corner, where it is trapped, allowing you to win the bishop or deliver mate.
notes.plans: Bring the rook to the side, advance the king, then use a rook check to push the enemy king to the corner, after which you can win the bishop or mate.

notes.explains: The difference between pawn types (knight pawn vs. rook pawn) in rook versus bishop endgames is crucial: knight pawns allow a direct sacrifice, while rook pawns require a more delicate approach to avoid losing the pawn for nothing.
notes.teaches: Always consider the pawn type in rook versus bishop endgames; the winning method changes significantly based on whether it is a knight pawn, bishop pawn, center pawn, or rook pawn.

notes.explains: When the pawn is not too far advanced, the defending king controls the squares immediately around it, so direct checks from the front or side are limited. Checking from behind forces the king to choose a side, leaving the other side vulnerable.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop endgames, if the pawn is not far advanced, prefer checking the enemy king from behind. This forces the king to commit to one side, allowing your rook to defend your own pawn and your king to advance.
notes.plans: Use the rook to check from behind, then bring the king up in front of the pawn to support its promotion.

notes.explains: With a rook pawn on the sixth rank, the defender can draw by heading to the safe corner (the corner opposite the pawn's promotion square). A careless pawn sacrifice or king move allows the bishop to set up a blockade.
notes.teaches: In rook vs. bishop endings, the defender's king must aim for the safe corner; the attacker must force the defender into the unsafe corner to have winning chances.
notes.plans: The attacker should use the rook to cut off the king and drive it toward the unsafe corner, while the defender tries to reach the safe corner.

notes.explains: With a bishop's pawn on the sixth rank, the position is a dead draw if the defender has blockaded, because the defender has just enough maneuvering room to maintain the blockade.
notes.teaches: Bishop's pawns are the worst for the attacker in these endings; the defender can hold the blockade more easily than against other pawns.
notes.plans: The defender should keep the blockade and head to the safe corner if the pawn advances; the attacker should avoid reaching this setup if possible.

notes.explains: With a knight's pawn on the sixth rank, the attacker can still win by returning to a known winning position, often by a rook check and king maneuver.
notes.teaches: Knight pawns offer winning chances even on the sixth rank, as the defender cannot always reach the safe corner.
notes.plans: The attacker should aim to transpose to a known winning position, using checks to force the defender's king to the wrong corner.

notes.explains: In a study by Troitzky, even with the white king far from the pawn, white can draw by staying in the 'king's shadow'—the file where the black king blocks the rook's check—and by preventing the black king from moving to a winning square.
notes.teaches: When the king is far from the pawn, the defender can sometimes draw by using the enemy king as a shield against rook checks, and by avoiding moves that allow the rook to free the pawn.
notes.plans: White should keep the king on the same file as the black king to avoid checks, and be ready to meet any king move with a counter that maintains the blockade.

notes.explains: In this rook-versus-bishop study, Black has two concrete winning threats: advancing the king to f2 and delivering a rook check on h1. White must find a move that addresses both ideas simultaneously.
notes.teaches: When defending a difficult endgame, identify all of the opponent's threats and look for a single move that neutralizes them all. A quiet move that controls a key square can be more effective than a flashy one.
notes.plans: White should play Bf3, preventing the black king from reaching f2. Then White keeps the bishop on the f3-e2 diagonal, staying in front of the black king, and repeats the position if necessary to hold the draw.

notes.explains: In rook-versus-bishop endgames, the defending side can often hold a draw by keeping the bishop on a diagonal that controls the squares the enemy king needs to cross. The bishop's long-range power compensates for the rook's material advantage.
notes.teaches: The bishop is a strong defensive piece when it can dominate a diagonal. Use it to restrict the enemy king's approach rather than to chase the rook.
notes.plans: Maintain the bishop on the f3-e2 diagonal, stepping back and forth as the black king probes. If the black king retreats, simply repeat the position; there is no need to force anything.

notes.explains: In certain endgame studies, the attacking side may have a hidden resource: if the defender has a pawn that can promote to a knight, the attacker might accidentally checkmate himself in a corner. This is a known tactical motif in composed positions.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of stalemate and self-mate possibilities in endgames. A pawn promotion to a knight can create unusual mating nets, even for the side that is nominally winning.

notes.explains: In this position, black has an extra pawn but several pieces are scattered and the bishop on c6 is passive despite attacking e4. Loose pieces in the opponent's camp are telltale signs of tactical opportunities.
notes.teaches: Always scan for loose pieces in the opponent's position; they often indicate that a tactical blow is available.

notes.explains: White chooses a forcing tactical sequence starting with Nh6+ rather than a quieter move like Qg4, because Fischer prefers forcing lines. After gxh6, Qg4+ double attacks the king and knight, winning material.
notes.teaches: When you have a tactical opportunity, prefer the most forcing continuation if it leads to a concrete gain. Double attacks are a powerful way to exploit a vulnerable king and loose pieces.
notes.plans: After winning the knight, white must consolidate while being down a pawn but with better structure.

notes.explains: Black defends tenaciously, creating multiple pins on the e-file. White must sidestep these threats carefully; capturing in the 'obvious' ways would lose.
notes.teaches: When facing pins, look for ways to sidestep the threat rather than resolving it by capture. Sometimes the best move is one that avoids the pin altogether.
notes.plans: White plays Qh5, a beautiful move that creates new threats and forces black's reply.

notes.explains: White finds a tricky knight maneuver to c3, which puts pressure on black. Black cannot capture the knight because the queen is under attack, so the move creates a tactical threat.
notes.teaches: In complex middlegames, look for moves that create multiple threats or exploit the opponent's pinned or overloaded pieces. Sometimes a quiet-looking move can be very strong if it sets up a tactical shot.
notes.plans: Black must carefully assess the position and find a move that addresses the threats, possibly by moving the king to a safer square.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a material deficit, so trading pieces is generally favorable to reduce Black's attacking potential and simplify toward an endgame where the extra pawns matter less.
notes.teaches: When you are down material, seek exchanges to decrease the opponent's advantage and increase drawing chances.
notes.plans: Look for forcing sequences that lead to queen trades or piece exchanges.

notes.explains: After exchanging queens, White still faces a pawn deficit, so the task is to find a plan that maximizes activity and creates counterplay despite being down pawns.
notes.teaches: Even in a worse endgame, active piece play and king centralization can create practical chances.
notes.plans: Activate the rooks, bring the king toward the center, and consider pawn moves that improve the structure without creating weaknesses.

notes.explains: The king can be brought to the center because the opponent cannot prevent it, and centralizing the king is a key resource in the endgame.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the king is a fighting piece; bring it to the center when safe.
notes.plans: Play Kf2, then Ke3, and aim to reach d4 to attack the enemy pawns.

notes.explains: Counting pawns is a simple way to assess material balance, but it is not the only factor; piece activity and king safety also matter.
notes.teaches: Use material count as a baseline, but always consider dynamic factors like piece activity and king safety.

notes.explains: In the endgame, central squares are like a power-up zone: whoever controls them gets a huge boost. The king's activity is a key part of this, but only once the endgame truly begins.
notes.teaches: Activate your king in the endgame, not the middlegame. Marching the king up too early can spoil your game even if it doesn't ruin your structure.

notes.explains: With both rooks active and the king entering, the position is about maximizing piece activity. White's king on e2 or f2 supports the center and keeps the kingside pawns defended.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activate the king before grabbing pawns. Keep your pieces defended and avoid moving the king to a square where it can be attacked by a bishop.
notes.plans: Bring the king to a safe central square, keep the rook active, and target weak enemy pawns.

notes.explains: Black's pawn structure is bad, with doubled pawns and weaknesses. White can exploit this by advancing central pawns and using the king to support them.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a bad pawn structure, use your king and pieces to target the weak pawns. Central pawn advances can be decisive.
notes.plans: Push the central pawns, use the king to support them, and force the opponent to defend weaknesses.

notes.explains: A move like bishop takes f5 would be a mistake because the rook is defended, so the attacker would lose material. Instead, the king should be brought in to support the attack.
notes.teaches: Before capturing, check if the target is defended. In endgames, it's often better to improve the king's position than to grab a pawn that is safely defended.
notes.plans: Improve the king's activity and keep pieces coordinated, avoiding tactics that lose material.

notes.explains: Black should take control of central squares with the king, as in king f6, to get closer to the pawns and the center. Moving the king to the wrong side can leave pieces loose and pawns falling.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, the king should head toward the center and the action, not the edge. Keep your army defended and avoid leaving pawns hanging.
notes.plans: Centralize the king, keep pieces defended, and prepare to attack weak pawns.

notes.explains: In this position, the king must be kept safe and the army coordinated. Moving the king to f2 keeps everything defended, whereas a move like bishop e4, while not losing, creates unnecessary discomfort and leaves the kingside loose.
notes.teaches: Prefer solid, safe moves that maintain full control over the position over flashy but troublesome alternatives. Avoid moves that create discomfort without clear gain.
notes.plans: Keep the king on f2, maintain the defense of the kingside, and wait for the opponent's plan before committing.

notes.explains: The bishop on e4 could become trapped after a pawn push like d5, leaving it stranded in the center. This is a concrete reason to avoid such a move.
notes.teaches: Before placing a piece on an active square, check if the opponent can chase it away with tempo and gain time.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on a safe square where it cannot be attacked by pawns.

notes.explains: When you have a material advantage (extra pawn) and pressure, the position is favorable. The immediate task is to address the attack on the rook and then find the best way to increase the pressure.
notes.teaches: When things are going well, don't just wait—look for ways to improve your position and nurture the advantage. Always be alert to your opponent's threats, even when winning.
notes.plans: First, move the rook to safety (e.g., h6, c5, or b6), then decide which pawn to attack, likely the b-pawn.

notes.explains: Choosing between rook moves like c5, b6, or h6 requires evaluating which target is most likely to fall. The rook on h6 attacks the h-pawn, which is a concrete weakness.
notes.teaches: Grandmasters use an internal statistical sense to weigh the probability of success for each candidate move. Prefer moves that attack the most vulnerable pawns.
notes.plans: Play rook h6 to attack the h-pawn, then follow up by converting the extra pawn into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: In the endgame, piece quality matters more than pawn count. A well-placed rook and active king are worth more than having extra pawns that are poorly placed.
notes.teaches: Aim for active, well-coordinated pieces over mere material. A passed pawn can be more dangerous than a cluster of weak pawns.
notes.plans: Trade pieces to reach a winning endgame, using the extra pawn and active pieces to push for victory.

notes.explains: In this endgame, a pawn is hanging, but taking it may allow the opponent's rook to infiltrate and become active. The player offering the pawn is prioritizing piece activity over material.
notes.teaches: Quality over quantity: in endgames, active pieces often outweigh extra pawns. Do not automatically grab material if it lets your opponent's pieces become powerful.
notes.plans: If your opponent offers a pawn, consider whether accepting it gives them active play. If so, decline and seek your own active piece placement.

notes.explains: The move rook h6 was chosen as a practical decision, not necessarily the computer's top choice, but one that preserves the advantage and limits the opponent's chances. This reflects a human approach to endgames: aim for the easiest path to victory, not the quickest or most flashy.
notes.teaches: In endgames, choose moves that are practical and maintain a clear advantage, even if they are not the absolute best. The goal is to convert the win reliably, considering time pressure and the opponent's resources.
notes.plans: Look for moves that simplify or restrict the opponent's counterplay, even if they are not the most forcing. Keep the advantage and nurse it to victory.

notes.explains: The position may have a check sequence leading to a draw, but one player chose to avoid it and instead allowed the opponent to activate their pieces, fighting for a win rather than settling for a draw.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the 'safe' drawing line is not the best practical choice if you have winning chances. Be willing to take risks and allow your opponent activity if you believe you can still win.
notes.plans: If you have a choice between a draw and a complex fight, consider your opponent's style and the tournament situation. If you need a win, avoid the draw and keep the game alive.

notes.explains: In this position, the player with a better position must still identify the dangers. With limited material, the main risk is that if the remaining pawns disappear, the bishop versus rook endgame could be a theoretical draw, especially if the pawns are on the wrong corner color.
notes.teaches: When you have a better position, always look for the opponent's drawing or swindling resources. In rook versus bishop endgames, be aware of the wrong-corner draw if all pawns are traded off.
notes.plans: Keep control of the position, avoid unnecessary pawn trades, and ensure the king can support the pawns.

notes.explains: The player used a few repetitions of moves to gain time on the clock, which was a common technique in the pre-increment era to reach time controls. However, this carries the risk of a threefold repetition draw.
notes.teaches: Using repetitions to gain time on the clock is a practical technique, but you must be careful not to allow a threefold repetition. Always have a backup plan if the opponent repeats moves.
notes.plans: If you need to gain time, choose repetitions that do not force a draw, and be ready to deviate if necessary.

notes.explains: In the endgame, the player with the extra pawn must be vigilant about not losing the f-pawn, because if that pawn falls, the resulting bishop versus rook endgame with only the wrong-colored rook pawn could be a draw.
notes.teaches: In rook versus bishop endgames, the side with the extra pawn must protect the pawns that are on the same color as the opponent's bishop, because trading them off can lead to a theoretical draw.
notes.plans: Keep the king active, defend the key pawns, and avoid trades that lead to a drawn pawn structure.

notes.explains: The winning technique here is to bring the king to e7 and then simply shuffle, avoiding any unnecessary risks. The opponent is helpless, so there is no need to rush.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, the most practical approach is to improve your pieces to their optimal squares, then slowly advance. Do not rush; just keep control and let the opponent run out of moves.
notes.plans: Bring the king to e7, then use the rook and king to force the opponent's pieces back, and finally promote a pawn.

notes.explains: In this king-and-pawn endgame, the winning side has a passed pawn and the opposing king is cut off. The defender's pieces are tied to stopping the pawn, so the attacker can improve their king's position without rushing.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive material or positional advantage, do not rush. Improve your king's position first, then force the issue at the right moment.
notes.plans: Bring the king to a key square like e7, then wait for the defender to commit, and strike with a decisive move such as bishop e6 to deflect the defender from controlling the queening square.

notes.explains: The defender is in a waiting pattern, forced to shuffle while the attacker maneuvers. The attacker can use triangulation or simply out-wait the defender to gain the opposition.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the opposition is a powerful tool to force the opponent's king out of position. Control key squares like f8 to ensure promotion.
notes.plans: Use the opposition to penetrate with the king, then support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: Even when the defender tries to prevent promotion by controlling the queening square, a tactical deflection can break the blockade. For example, a bishop move like e6 can force an exchange that removes the defender's control.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical resources to remove the defender's control of critical squares. Sometimes a sacrifice or exchange is necessary to clear the path for promotion.
notes.plans: If the defender controls the queening square, consider a deflection or exchange to eliminate that control, then promote.

notes.explains: The defender may try to create stalemate tricks, but if the attacker has a clear winning plan, these are not real threats. The attacker must remain precise and avoid careless moves that could allow stalemate.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of stalemate possibilities, but do not let them deter you from executing a winning plan. Calculate carefully to avoid blunders.
notes.plans: Continue the winning plan, ensuring that the final moves do not allow stalemate.

notes.explains: In composed puzzles, the position may be illegal (e.g., two dark-squared bishops with all pawns present), but that's acceptable for artistic purposes. The goal is to force a win through a long, forced sequence.
notes.teaches: Composed puzzles often use illegal positions to create artistic challenges; focus on the ideas, not legality.

notes.explains: Black's pieces are mostly immobilized: the rook on c8 is trapped by its own pieces, the bishop is similarly blocked, and the knight on g1 is the only mobile piece. White's checks force black to block, further restricting movement.
notes.teaches: In zugzwang puzzles, you often restrict the opponent's pieces until they have no useful moves, forcing them to weaken their position.
notes.plans: After the initial checks, white captures the knight on g1 and then sets up a zugzwang position, forcing black to move pawns.

notes.explains: The puzzle revolves around zugzwang: black is forced to move, but every move worsens their position. Because black has many pawns, each zugzwang only forces one pawn move, so the cycle must be repeated many times.
notes.teaches: Zugzwang can be used to force a long sequence of moves; when the opponent has many pawns, you repeat the zugzwang cycle until they run out of pawn moves.
notes.plans: White will find a cycle that forces black into zugzwang, black moves a pawn, then white repeats the cycle until all pawns are gone, eventually winning.

notes.explains: In this puzzle, black has several pawns that provide spare moves, so every time we force zugzwang, black just pushes a pawn. We need to repeat the zugzwang cycle until all those pawns are gone, then make progress elsewhere.
notes.teaches: When a position is nearly locked and the opponent has spare pawn moves, the winning method is to repeat a zugzwang cycle, forcing the opponent to burn their spare moves one by one.
notes.plans: Find a repeatable cycle that forces zugzwang, then repeat it until the opponent's pawn moves are exhausted.

notes.explains: The key to the position is to win the bishop on a8 so that we can promote on a8. The bishop is currently trapped because our king on b6 guards its only escape square.
notes.teaches: In locked positions, identify the opponent's immobile piece that is the key to your breakthrough; often it is a bishop or rook that can be captured once you control its only squares.
notes.plans: Aim to capture the bishop on a8 after forcing zugzwang, then promote the pawn.

notes.explains: If we move any of our pawns or the bishop, we break the lock and black escapes. The only movable pieces are the king and rook, but moving the rook gives the bishop a square to move to, so we need to use the king to cover that square.
notes.teaches: When you need to lose a tempo but your king is on a straight line with no triangulation squares, use your rook to triangulate while your king covers the opponent's freeing move.
notes.plans: Place the king on a square that covers the bishop's escape, then move the rook to lose a tempo, forcing black to push a pawn.

notes.explains: The position is a 290-move checkmate, and even Stockfish cannot see it because it is beyond its horizon. The solution is a precise sequence of zugzwang and tempo-losing maneuvers.
notes.teaches: Long forced wins are built from repeating small zugzwang cycles; you can solve them by identifying the cycle and then repeating it methodically.
notes.plans: Once the cycle is found, execute it repeatedly until the opponent's spare moves are gone, then finish the promotion.

notes.explains: In this position, the black bishop on d4 is a key defender, protecting two pawns that the white king might otherwise capture. If one of those pawns disappears, black is immediately mated in three moves, so the bishop's defensive role is critical.
notes.teaches: A piece can be immobilized not just by attacking it, but by making its moves lose to a tactical threat, such as a mate. Here, the bishop cannot move because it must keep guarding the pawns.
notes.plans: White should aim to force black into zugzwang, where black must move the bishop or push a pawn, allowing white to make progress.

notes.explains: White is trying to lose a tempo to gain the opposition or zugzwang, but black can simply pass with the bishop, moving it to squares like f6, g7, h8, c3, or e5. If white's king goes to c2 or b1, black can always return the bishop to d4, and white has not lost a tempo.
notes.teaches: To lose a tempo, you need a move that forces the opponent to respond, not just a quiet king move. If the opponent can pass, you cannot gain the tempo.
notes.plans: White must find a way to force black to commit the bishop to a square where it cannot return to d4, or find a move that creates a real threat.

notes.explains: When the white king is on d3, the black bishop on d4 can legally move, but that would expose a discovered attack by the king on something. However, black can still pass by moving the bishop to other squares, so the discovered attack is not enough to force progress.
notes.teaches: A discovered attack can be a powerful resource, but if the opponent has safe squares to move the piece, it may not create a decisive threat. You need to combine it with other ideas like zugzwang.
notes.plans: White should look for a way to restrict the bishop's safe squares, perhaps by using the king to control key squares.

notes.explains: If white sacrifices a pawn to open lines, black's pieces will flow out and white will be stuck. For example, after f6, white drops a pawn and black's pieces become active, so the sacrifice is not good.
notes.teaches: Before sacrificing material, consider whether the resulting piece activity for the opponent outweighs your own gains. A pawn sacrifice that only opens lines for the opponent is often bad.
notes.plans: White should avoid pawn sacrifices that give black counterplay; instead, maintain the closed position and seek a zugzwang.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on d4 is also preventing checkmate by controlling key squares. White wants black to be almost stalemated so that black is forced to push pawns, which will eventually allow white to mate.
notes.teaches: In zugzwang positions, you want to leave the opponent with only bad moves. Here, the bishop is overworked: it must stay on d4 to guard pawns, but if it moves, it allows mate.
notes.plans: White should aim to put black in a position where every legal move loses, either by moving the bishop or pushing a pawn.

notes.explains: In a position where the opponent has only a bishop and pawns left, the goal is to leave the opponent almost stalemated, forcing them into zugzwang so they must move their pawns.
notes.teaches: To force zugzwang, immobilize the opponent's pieces by placing your king on a key square that restricts their movement, then use a waiting move with a rook to lose a tempo.
notes.plans: Place the king on a square that immobilizes the bishop, then use the rook to pass the move back to the opponent, forcing them to push a pawn.

notes.explains: A specific pawn (e3) is critical because if it disappears, the opponent gets mated in three moves (e4, e5, mate). This pawn's presence ties down the bishop, which must protect it.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn is a 'guardian' that prevents a quick mate; by keeping it on the board, you restrict the opponent's pieces and maintain the zugzwang.
notes.plans: Keep the critical pawn protected and use the king to control the bishop's squares, forcing the bishop to stay put.

notes.explains: Once the king is placed on d3, the bishop is immobilized. If the bishop moves to c3, the king captures it and mates; if it moves elsewhere, the king captures the e3 pawn, still leading to mate.
notes.teaches: When a piece is overloaded (must protect a key pawn), you can use your king to capture it or the pawn, depending on where it moves, creating a mating net.
notes.plans: After the bishop moves, respond by capturing the bishop or the pawn, then deliver mate with the rook and king.

notes.explains: The solution involves repeating a cycle: the king travels from b6 to d3, the rook passes a move, and the king returns to b6, forcing black to move a pawn each cycle. This repeats until all black pawns are gone.
notes.teaches: Long puzzles are often built on repeating cycles that force the opponent to make weakening moves, one at a time, until a decisive advantage is reached.
notes.plans: Repeat the cycle: king to d3, rook pass, king back to b6, forcing a pawn move each time, until the pawns are exhausted.

notes.explains: At the end, white sacrifices the rook on d4 to avoid stalemate, then uses the king to keep the black king trapped, and finally promotes a pawn to queen, delivering mate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is nearly stalemated, you must give up material to give them a legal move, then use your remaining pieces to force mate.
notes.plans: Sacrifice the rook on d4, bring the king to b6 to confine the black king, promote the d-pawn, and deliver mate with the queen.

notes.explains: Long, forced wins often rely on a repeating cycle of moves that puts the defender in zugzwang, forcing them to make a pawn move or another concession. The cycle length matters for practical rules like the 50-move rule.
notes.teaches: Recognize cyclical zugzwang patterns: a repeated maneuver that forces the opponent to worsen their position each time. Count the moves in the cycle to see if it fits within rule limits.
notes.plans: Identify the cycle and the forced moves; execute the cycle until the opponent's pawns are exhausted or a decisive capture is possible.

notes.explains: In composed problems, a 'unique solution' means every white move is forced and any deviation leads to a longer mate. Some positions have alternative moves of equal length, but the longest legal unique mate has no such duals.
notes.teaches: When solving or composing, distinguish between unique solutions and those with duals; a unique solution is more elegant and often the goal in problem chess.

notes.explains: A self-mate is a puzzle where White forces Black to checkmate White against Black's will. Black tries to avoid giving mate, so White must create a zugzwang where every black move eventually leads to mate.
notes.teaches: In self-mates, think in terms of forcing the opponent into a position where their only legal moves are bad, and the final mate is delivered by the opponent.
notes.plans: Look for ways to restrict Black's moves and force a sequence that ends with Black delivering checkmate.

notes.explains: In a self-mate puzzle, the goal is reversed: White must force Black to checkmate the white king, while Black tries to avoid doing so. This creates a unique dynamic where White's moves are aimed at restricting Black's options and ultimately compelling the desired checkmate.
notes.teaches: Self-mate puzzles invert the usual objective, requiring you to think about forcing your opponent to deliver checkmate against you. This often involves zugzwang and precise maneuvering to eliminate Black's alternatives.

notes.explains: White's early moves in the puzzle are preparatory: capturing black pieces while giving check to prevent the black queen from escaping. This is necessary to set up the core position where the black queen is entombed.
notes.teaches: When a piece is trapped, you can often use checking moves to maintain control while you improve your position or capture material, as long as each check keeps the opponent's king on the move.

notes.explains: The core position has White successfully entombing the black queen, meaning it has no legal moves. If White can win the queen, the rest is straightforward. Black is reduced to shuffling the king with moves like ...Kb2, giving White free moves to make progress.
