notes.explains: After the queen trade on g7 and ...cxd4, White's center is falling apart, but White has a very good opposite-colored bishop endgame. The h6-pawn is a permanent weakness, and White's pieces are well placed to pressure the dark squares.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop positions, a permanent weakness on the opponent's side can be more important than a damaged pawn structure. Even without queens, an attack can be effective if the pieces coordinate well.
notes.plans: White will slowly improve the king and pieces, targeting the h6-pawn and the queenside, while Black struggles for counterplay because the f6-advance is no longer possible.

notes.explains: The move Rc3 is excellent because it prepares to improve the knight on e2 via d4. The immediate threat is Nb5, which would be very uncomfortable for Black. Black responds with ...f6 to undermine the e5-pawn and the d6-square.
notes.teaches: When a piece is poorly placed, look for a rook move that clears a path for it to reach a better square. A knight on d4 can create strong threats, especially with a rook behind it.
notes.plans: White will continue to press on the dark squares and the h6-pawn, while Black tries to generate counterplay with ...f5 and ...g3, but the position remains very difficult for Black.

notes.explains: In this type of pawn structure, White should generally avoid playing f4 and instead press on the queenside, especially since the b-file is open. The rook on h7 is tied to defense, and Black has very little counterplay after ...f5.
notes.teaches: When you have a lasting advantage, do not rush to force exchanges or create weaknesses. Slowly improve your position, and let the opponent's weaknesses (like the h6-pawn) become more significant over time.
notes.plans: White will continue to improve the king and pieces, maintaining pressure on the queenside and the h6-pawn, while Black remains passive and without counterplay.

notes.explains: White repeats moves to gain time on the clock while maintaining the attack. Black's h5 weakens the g5 square, allowing the white king to infiltrate.
notes.teaches: Repeating moves is a classic technique to gain time when you have an ongoing attack.
notes.plans: White brings the king to g5, preparing a decisive attack, possibly leading to checkmate.

notes.explains: In this position, White's king can march to h6 to support a mating attack, and Black has no reasonable way to prevent it. The king's participation is decisive despite few pieces remaining.
notes.teaches: In endgames with few pieces, the king can be a powerful attacking piece. Use it to join the attack when the opponent cannot stop it.
notes.plans: White should continue with the king march to h6, then use the rook to create mating threats, such as rook b7-b8.

notes.explains: Black tries to deflect the rook from the second rank with a6, but it's not necessary and White can simply capture. The mating attack persists even after material loss.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attack, don't be distracted by side issues. Keep the initiative and continue with the most direct threats.
notes.plans: White can capture on a6 and continue with the king march, maintaining the mating net.

notes.explains: Black tries to trade rooks to reach an opposite-colored bishop endgame, which is more defensible. White must decide whether to allow the trade or keep rooks on for the attack.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endings, material imbalances and passed pawns matter more than the bishops themselves. Keeping rooks can preserve winning chances.
notes.plans: White should avoid unnecessary trades and continue pressing with the rook, targeting weaknesses like the e6 pawn.

notes.explains: After a trade, the position becomes an opposite-colored bishop endgame. With no a-pawn, the black bishop on c6 is unassailable, and Black can defend the draw.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, the defender can often hold if the pawns are fixed on the same color as the defender's bishop. Passed pawns on the wrong color may not win.
notes.plans: White should try to create passed pawns on both flanks, but Black can set up a blockade.

notes.explains: When a player is hit with a novelty, the natural human reaction is to trade pieces and head for a safe-looking position, especially one with opposite-colored bishops, because such endgames are often drawish.
notes.teaches: A prepared novelty can be chosen precisely because the 'safe' response is deceptively difficult. The defender's instinct to simplify can walk into a worse endgame where the opponent's bishop is unassailable.

notes.explains: A move like Rh3 creates a concrete threat, making it more practical in human games than a computer-generated move that only offers a subtle edge.
notes.teaches: When preparing an opening, prioritize moves that create immediate threats and force the opponent to solve problems, as they are more effective in practice than engine-only ideas.

notes.explains: The prepared position with opposite-colored bishops is extremely deceptive: it looks safe for black, but in reality it is very dangerous, and the defender must navigate it precisely.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, material is not the only factor; the activity and safety of the bishops matter enormously. A seemingly equal position can be winning for the side with the more active bishop.

notes.explains: The novelties in this opening all tie into the same thematic idea: exploiting the dark squares and creating direct threats there.
notes.teaches: When preparing an opening, look for a unifying theme (like dark-square control) and choose novelties that reinforce that theme, making the preparation coherent and easier to remember.

notes.explains: In the Lucena position, the standard winning method is to build a bridge with the rook, but there are actually multiple winning plans. The key is to understand the underlying principles of king safety and rook activity.
notes.teaches: The Lucena position is a fundamental rook endgame where the side with the extra pawn can win by using the rook to shield the king from checks. Recognizing alternative winning methods deepens your understanding of rook endgames.
notes.plans: Start with a rook check to drive the enemy king away, then choose a winning setup: either build a bridge with the rook or use the rook to cut off the king and promote the pawn.

notes.explains: After Rg1+ Kh7, the immediate king move to get out of the pawn's way fails because of perpetual checks. The bridge-building move Rg4 provides a shelter for the king, allowing it to escape the checks and promote.
notes.teaches: In rook and pawn versus rook, the defending side often relies on checks to prevent promotion. The attacking side must use the rook to create a safe path for the king, either by blocking checks or by cutting off the enemy king.
notes.plans: After the rook check, if the king retreats to the h-file, play Rg4 to prepare the bridge. Then advance the king to f7, and when checked, step to e5 and block with the rook.

notes.explains: Alternative winning moves like Re1 or Rd1 also work in the Lucena position. These moves cut off the enemy king's approach, allowing the white king to simply walk out and promote the pawn.
notes.teaches: There is often more than one winning method in rook endgames. Understanding different approaches, such as cutting off the king versus building a bridge, gives you flexibility and a deeper grasp of the position.
notes.plans: After the rook check, if the king goes to h7, consider Re1 or Rd1 to prevent the black king from interfering. Then move the white king away from the pawn and promote.

notes.explains: Rook d1 is another winning idea: after black checks, the white king steps up, and when the rook checks again, white can block with the rook, then promote.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the rook can be used both to block checks and to support the pawn, so look for flexible rook placements that serve multiple purposes.
notes.plans: Play rook d1, then if black checks, move the king up and use the rook to block subsequent checks, finally promoting the pawn.

notes.explains: When the board is flipped and black is to move, the position is a draw due to the short side defense: black's king is on the short side, giving the rook enough space to check the white king indefinitely.
notes.teaches: The short side defense works when the defending king has at least three files of space to check the enemy king, preventing it from both protecting the pawn and escaping checks.
notes.plans: Black should keep checking from the side, using the three-file space to avoid the white king's interference, and only stop if the pawn is abandoned.

notes.explains: In a rook versus rook and pawn endgame where the defending king is cut off by three files, the defender can hold the draw by checking from the side. The key is that the king is too far away to both protect the pawn and block the checks, so the checks can continue indefinitely.
notes.teaches: When defending, use your rook to check from the side, keeping it at a distance so the enemy king cannot interfere. The number of files between the rook and the pawn matters: three files is enough, two is not.
notes.plans: Keep checking from the side, and if the enemy king leaves the pawn, the rook can capture it or continue checking.

notes.explains: With only two files between the rook and the pawn, the defending side cannot maintain the checks because the enemy king can step in and block the rook's access to the pawn, eventually winning.
notes.teaches: The defending rook needs at least three files of space to check effectively. With less space, the king can interfere and the defense fails.
notes.plans: If you are the defender and lack space, look for other drawing resources; if you are the attacker, exploit the lack of space to win.

notes.explains: When the defending rook is stuck on the eighth rank, it can still draw against a knight pawn. The rook prevents mate and stops the pawn from queening, and the attacker cannot make progress because the king has no shelter and the pawn cannot be pushed effectively.
notes.teaches: Passive defense—placing the rook on the back rank—is a valid drawing resource against a knight pawn. The defender should keep the rook on the eighth rank and only move the king to avoid mate.
notes.plans: Keep the rook on the eighth rank, shuffle the king, and do not allow the attacker to bring the king up. If the pawn advances, the rook can be sacrificed or the king can step in front.

notes.explains: Against a bishop's pawn, passive defense fails because the attacker has an extra file to use. The rook can check the king away, then use the extra space to create mating threats and force the pawn through.
notes.teaches: The file of the pawn matters: a bishop's pawn offers the attacker more room to maneuver than a knight pawn. In such positions, the defender must seek active checking from behind rather than relying on passive defense.
notes.plans: With a bishop's pawn, the attacker should use rook checks to drive the king to the edge, then advance the pawn with check, winning the defending rook.

notes.explains: Even against a bishop's pawn, there may be a surprising drawing resource if the defender can find the right move. The position is delicate, and the defender must choose between passive defense and a more active setup.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, always look for hidden drawing resources. A single extra file can change the evaluation, but sometimes the defender can still hold with precise play.
notes.plans: The defender should consider whether to keep the rook passive or to use it actively. The correct choice depends on the exact placement of the kings and the pawn.

notes.explains: A surprising drawing resource exists: a rook check that attacks the pawn while also threatening stalemate if captured. This works because capturing the rook would leave the defending king with no legal moves.
notes.teaches: Always look for stalemate tricks in rook endgames. A checking move that also attacks the pawn can be a saving resource when the king is trapped in front of the pawn.
notes.plans: If the defender can give such a check, the attacker must avoid the stalemate and may have to allow the draw.

notes.explains: Once the defender starts checking from behind, the draw is secure as long as the king has no shelter. The checking rook can keep the enemy king away from the pawn.
notes.teaches: Checking from behind is the surest drawing method in rook endgames when the pawn is advanced and the king is cut off from shelter.
notes.plans: The defender should immediately begin checking from behind and avoid letting the enemy king find shelter in front of the pawn.

notes.explains: In the flipped position with white to move, the simple winning method is to check the black king away with rook g2, then bring the king to f7 and achieve the Lucena position. This is the straightforward path to victory.
notes.teaches: When the defending king is cut off, a rook check can force the king away, allowing the attacking king to advance and support the pawn's promotion.
notes.plans: White should play rook g2 check, force the black king to h7, then move the king to f7, and after black's checks, reach the Lucena position to win.

notes.explains: After the simple winning method, the position after king e8 is still winning for white, but there is a more instructive method that demonstrates the underlying winning idea. Black's drawing attempts, such as king f6, are insufficient.
notes.teaches: In winning rook endgames, it's important to understand the key defensive ideas and why they fail, so you can choose the most reliable winning method.
notes.plans: White should look for the alternative winning method that avoids the need for the Lucena position, possibly by using the rook to cut off the black king more effectively.

notes.explains: When defending a rook endgame, the defender's king should go to the short side of the board (the side with fewer files between the king and the edge). This makes it easier to stop checks because the rook has less space to check from that side.
notes.teaches: Place your king on the short side to minimize the checking distance for the opponent's rook and to facilitate drawing checks.
notes.plans: Move the king to the short side (e.g., f8) rather than the long side (d8) to improve drawing chances.

notes.explains: When the attacker's rook is on the b-file, the defender can draw by moving the rook to a1, creating three files of separation. This prevents the attacker from making progress because the rook cannot leave the pawn without allowing checks.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the defender can draw by placing the rook on a file with sufficient separation from the pawn, making it impossible for the attacker to advance without losing the pawn.
notes.plans: If the opponent's rook is on the b-file, move your rook to a1 to achieve the drawing setup.

notes.explains: A check from f1 loses because the attacker's king can step to e6, and then the defender has no time to reorganize the rook to e1, allowing the pawn to advance. The defender must avoid checks that give the attacker time to improve the king's position.
notes.teaches: When defending, choose checks carefully; a check that allows the enemy king to step forward and support the pawn can be losing. Prefer moves that maintain the blockade.
notes.plans: Avoid rook f1 check; instead, keep the rook on e1 and the king on f7 to maintain the draw.

notes.explains: In this rook versus pawn endgame, the white rook must choose a square that maintains the opposition and controls the pawn's advance. Rook d2 is the precise waiting move because it loses a tempo while keeping the rook active, whereas rook d1 allows the black pawn to advance and the black king to seize the opposition.
notes.teaches: When defending against a passed pawn, use the rook to lose a tempo at the right moment, and keep the rook on a square that can later attack the pawn from the side. Opposition is a key tool in king and pawn endgames; the defender can use it to prevent the attacker's king from making progress.
notes.plans: After rook d2, if black advances the pawn, the white king approaches, and the rook will eventually capture the pawn from the side. The goal is to win the pawn and then promote the extra pawn.

notes.explains: In the position with the pawn on the g-file, the immediate winning tries like g6 or rook g7 check fail because the black rook can check from behind, and the white king lacks shelter.
notes.teaches: When the pawn is on the knight file, the attacker must find a precise maneuver to break the blockade. The key is to use the rook to give a check from the side, forcing the enemy king away, then bring the king to support the pawn.
notes.plans: For white: play rook a8 check, then king e7, then rook g8, breaking the blockade on g6. After that, the pawn can advance with support, leading to a win.

notes.explains: The winning idea works because the rook check from the side forces the enemy king to a square where it cannot defend the pawn's advance, and the attacking king can then approach.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a rook check from the side can be a decisive resource to drive the enemy king away and create a path for the pawn. This is a common winning pattern.
notes.plans: For the attacker: look for side checks that force the enemy king to a worse square, then use the king to support the pawn. For the defender: avoid allowing such checks by keeping the king on the correct side.

notes.explains: The term 'basic' in endgames refers to positions with minimal material, like a single pawn, but these can still be highly complex and require precise technique.
notes.teaches: Even simple-looking endgames can have deep nuances, and mastering the fundamental techniques is essential for converting or defending them correctly.

notes.explains: In this endgame, material is equal, but white's king on f3 is much more active than black's king on g8. The black king is not weak because it cannot be attacked effectively with so few pieces on the board; it is simply less active. White's king has several tempos over black's, which is a significant advantage.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, king activity is a crucial factor. A king that is centralized and active can support pawns and restrict the opponent's pieces, while a passive king can be a long-term liability.
notes.plans: White should aim to use the active king to penetrate into black's position, possibly targeting weak pawns or supporting a passed pawn. Black should try to activate the king and coordinate pieces to create counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's b7 pawn is a backward pawn, fixed by white's a4 pawn, and cannot advance to become a passed pawn. It must be defended by pieces, not pawns, making it a potential weakness. White's c3 pawn is better protected, and the bishop on d4 has more mobility than black's bishop on c7.
notes.teaches: A backward pawn on an open file is a structural weakness because it cannot be supported by other pawns and often requires piece defense. Pawn islands are not the only factor; the quality of pawns and their protection matter.
notes.plans: White should pressure the b7 pawn and exploit the better bishop mobility. Black must defend the weakness carefully and seek active piece play to compensate.

notes.explains: The position is close to equal, but white has practical winning chances due to small advantages: better king, better bishop, and a potentially weak black pawn. These factors accumulate if black does not play precisely.
notes.teaches: In endgames, small advantages can be accumulated and converted into a win if the opponent is not accurate. It is important to identify and press on the opponent's weaknesses while improving your own pieces.
notes.plans: White should play actively, improving piece placement and creating threats. Black should aim for solid defense and active counterplay to neutralize white's advantages.

notes.explains: A backwards pawn on b7 is a permanent weakness because it cannot be supported by another pawn and must be defended by pieces, tying them down. The bishop on d4 is more active than the one on c7, which has limited mobility.
notes.teaches: In same-colored bishop endgames, small positional factors like a backwards pawn and a better bishop accumulate into a decisive advantage if the defender does not find active play.
notes.plans: The side with the advantage should increase pressure on the weak pawn and improve piece activity, while the defender must seek counterplay.

notes.explains: In this opposite-colored bishop endgame, White is up two pawns, but the result is not straightforward. The black pawns are placed on light squares, the same color as White's bishop, making them difficult to attack. The connected passed pawns for White are not enough to force a win because the black bishop can blockade them.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, the defender should place their pawns on the color of the opponent's bishop to reduce their vulnerability. The attacker's extra pawns are often insufficient to win if the defender can establish a blockade.
notes.plans: Black should aim to set up a light-square blockade, while White should try to create weaknesses or penetrate with the king.

notes.explains: Black's first move H5 is important to gain space and prevent White from playing G4, which would be very annoying. If Black had played King E6 instead, White could play G4, making it hard for Black to set up a light-square blockade.
notes.teaches: In such endgames, the defender should proactively place pawns on the correct color and prevent the opponent from gaining space with pawn advances. A move like H5 can be crucial to stop a disruptive G4.
notes.plans: Black should continue with moves like Bishop D3 to force White's pawn to A7, then place the bishop on E4 to maintain the blockade.

notes.explains: After Black played b6, the bishop on c7 became tied to defending the b6 pawn, reducing its activity. White then played Rb1 to pressure the pawn, and Black's indirect defense via Rc8 is insufficient because if the pawn falls, the resulting rook vs bishop and pawns endgame is not winning for Black—the pawns will drop later.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is weak, tying a piece to its defense can leave that piece passive. In rook endgames, giving up the exchange for two pawns is often not enough if the remaining pawns are weak and the opponent's rook is active.
notes.plans: White should continue to increase pressure on the weak pawn and improve the rook's activity, while Black must find a way to activate the bishop and avoid further weaknesses.

notes.explains: White's rook on e4 is a strong centralizing move. It controls key squares and prepares to double rooks or invade. Trading rooks with Rb5 might be less effective because Black's rook can go to e6, protecting the pawn and cutting off the king, giving Black active defense.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, centralizing the rook and avoiding unnecessary trades that give the opponent active counterplay is often the best way to convert an advantage.
notes.plans: White should keep rooks on and use the active rook to penetrate Black's position, while maintaining pressure on the weak pawns.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the rook on e4 is strong because it protects the pawns and keeps the enemy king out. Trading rooks would let the white king penetrate and win the pawns, so Black avoids it.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, keep rooks on the board when your king is closer and your pawns are protected; trading can turn a win into a draw.
notes.plans: White can double rooks on the file or bring the king over, while keeping the rook active on e4.

notes.explains: After Black plays f5, White can trade rooks and then play Rb5, now protected by the e4 pawn. This threatens both b6 and a5, and Black cannot defend both.
notes.teaches: Subtle tactics in endgames matter: a protected rook can create double threats that decide the game.
notes.plans: White should execute the rook maneuver to win a pawn on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black's g6 weakens the h6 pawn and the light squares, allowing White's g4 to fix the h6 pawn on the bishop's color. This makes the position nearly lost for Black.
notes.teaches: In endgames, avoid pawn moves that create weaknesses without gaining something; fixed weaknesses on the bishop's color are easy targets.
notes.plans: White should play g4 to fix h6 and then attack it with the bishop and king.

notes.explains: Endgames require alertness and practical play; missing a small tactic can be fatal because there are fewer pieces to compensate.
notes.teaches: Stay focused in endgames and study endgame books to improve technique and avoid blunders.

notes.explains: In the endgame, tactical awareness is crucial. A move like f5 may look tempting but fails due to a tactical refutation. Instead, active rook play can win a pawn by exploiting the split pawns.
notes.teaches: Always calculate tactical lines in the endgame; a seemingly good move may have a hidden refutation. Active pieces can create threats that win material.
notes.plans: Use the rook to infiltrate and attack the weak h6 pawn, while keeping the king safe from counterplay.

notes.explains: The move h4 prepares h5, fixing the h6 pawn on the same color as the bishop. Once the pawn is fixed, White can trade pieces and then win the pawn, leading to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: In endgames with minor pieces, fixing your opponent's pawns on the color of your bishop creates a target. If you have a better pawn structure, you can force trades to reach a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Play h5 to fix the h6 pawn, then trade pieces and go after the pawn. Avoid lines where Black can create counterplay, such as bishop g7 ideas.

notes.explains: In this position, a tactical resource like bishop g7 might be tempting, but it fails because after king takes and rook takes, the bishop can take on h4, leaving an unclear endgame. This is why a move like bishop d7 doesn't work.
notes.teaches: Before committing to a tactical sequence, calculate the resulting endgame carefully. If the outcome is unclear or favorable for the opponent, the tactic is not worth it.
notes.plans: Instead, prefer a solid move like bishop d8, preparing to advance the h-pawn and activate the rook.

notes.explains: After bishop d8, white can continue with h5, and if black takes, rook to e7, then rook to g1, aiming for bishop g7 and later taking on h6. Black defends with rook c6, but white can improve with rook g4, then rook e6, and after rook g8, the king advances, and the other rook comes in, winning.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong initiative, keep improving your pieces and create threats. The rook lift to g1 is a typical maneuver to attack the king side.
notes.plans: Follow this plan: h5, rook e7, rook g1, bishop g7, and then bring the king up.

notes.explains: In the bishop endgame that arises, white has a winning position because the passed pawn on the a-file is unstoppable. The black bishop only has one long diagonal to stop the pawn, but white can use the king to support the pawn's advance, and the bishop cannot cover both key squares.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, a passed pawn on the edge is often winning if the defending bishop lacks a second diagonal to control the promotion square. The attacking king can help escort the pawn.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn, use the king to support it, and if the bishop tries to block, use the king to chase it away.

notes.explains: After bishop d4 and king f8, white's next step is to play f4, then f5, fixing the pawns on the opposite color of the bishop. This makes them immune to bishop attacks, and the rook alone cannot capture them.
notes.teaches: In endgames with bishops of opposite colors, place your pawns on the opposite color of your opponent's bishop to protect them from being attacked. This is a key principle for pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play f4, then f5, and continue to gain space and push black back.

notes.explains: In this rook-and-bishop endgame, White has a passed pawn on the g-file. The immediate plan is to activate the rook to g7 or g8 to support the pawn's promotion, while the bishop on e5 and king on d5 coordinate to restrain Black's pieces. This setup gives White a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn, prioritize bringing your rook behind it or to the seventh rank to support its advance, and use your king and bishop to control key squares.
notes.plans: Play Rg1, then Rg7 or Rg8, supporting the g-pawn. Keep the bishop on e5 and king on d5 to limit Black's activity.

notes.explains: After trades, the position reduces to a bishop endgame where White has a passed a-pawn. The critical choice is between Bb4 and Bc5. Bc5 allows Bxc5, Kxc5, and then Black's king reaches a8, drawing because the bishop is the wrong color for the a-pawn's promotion square.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, a rook pawn (a- or h-file) is drawn if the bishop cannot control the promotion square. Always check the bishop's color relative to the corner pawn.
notes.plans: Choose Bb4 to keep the bishop on the correct color to support the a-pawn's promotion, avoiding the drawing mechanism.

notes.explains: With a central pawn, the bishop can waste tempos to gain opposition and force the enemy king to the wrong side, allowing your king to penetrate and support the pawn. This is winning, unlike the rook-pawn case.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames with a central pawn, use the bishop to triangulate and gain opposition, forcing the king away and then entering with your own king.
notes.plans: If the pawn is central, maneuver the bishop to lose a tempo when needed, then bring the king to support the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: In the actual game, White played Bb4, then advanced the pawns to c6 and a6, forcing Black's king to a8. The next stage is to bring the king around to support the pawn's promotion, using the bishop to keep Black's king confined.
notes.teaches: Technical endgames often proceed in stages: first secure the pawns and confine the enemy king, then bring your king to assist the pawn. Knowing these stages prevents converting a win into a draw.
notes.plans: After pushing the king to a8, bring your king to c4, then to a5, and use the bishop to maintain the confinement while the king approaches the pawn.

notes.explains: In a bishop-and-pawn endgame, the winning method is to bring the king around to support the pawn while the bishop guards the queening square from a safe diagonal. The key is to avoid pushing the pawn too early, as that allows the defender to sacrifice the bishop and force stalemate.
notes.teaches: When promoting a pawn, first improve your king's position and use the bishop to control the promotion square. Do not rush the pawn push; a premature advance can throw away the win.
notes.plans: March the king toward the pawn's queening square, use the bishop to cover the promotion square from a long diagonal, and only push the pawn when the king is ready to support it.

notes.explains: Technical endgames are those where the result is theoretically known and the winning or drawing method can be memorized, such as rook and pawn versus rook. Practical endgames are less forced and require general principles and pawn-structure understanding.
notes.teaches: Study technical endgames thoroughly so you can execute the correct technique under time pressure. Practice them against a computer to internalize the method.

notes.explains: In equal endgames, playing passively to secure a draw gives the opponent chances to seize the initiative. Active moves keep the opponent under pressure and may induce mistakes.
notes.teaches: Do not play for a draw in equal endgames; play actively and try to win. If you are inferior, then it is correct to aim for a draw, but otherwise keep creating problems for the opponent.
notes.plans: Look for active king moves, piece activity, and pawn breaks to maintain pressure and avoid passive defense.

notes.explains: In equal endgames, players often aim for a draw and play passively, which can lead to missed opportunities and giving the opponent chances.
notes.teaches: Keep making active moves in endgames to pressure the opponent and induce mistakes, even against higher-rated players.
notes.plans: Look for ways to improve piece activity and create threats, rather than simplifying to a draw.

notes.explains: Planning in chess can feel intimidating, but it is not always necessary to have a grand, long-term plan. Sometimes the best approach is to focus on improving your pieces and placing them on their best squares, which naturally leads to good play.
notes.teaches: You do not need a detailed long-term plan to win; instead, make short-term, flexible improvements to your position, adapting as the game evolves.

notes.explains: In the second puzzle, it is black to move, and the position should be assessed by noting what is good and bad. The bishop is not well placed, and there are other imbalances to consider.
notes.teaches: Before choosing a plan, take a moment to evaluate the position: identify strong and weak pieces, pawn structure, and potential targets. This helps form a short-term plan.

notes.explains: Before choosing a plan, take a few minutes to survey the position: identify which pieces are poorly placed, which squares are weak, and what the opponent is trying to do.
notes.teaches: Always start by evaluating the position: note bad pieces, weak squares, and the opponent's intentions before deciding on a plan.

notes.explains: In this closed position, both sides have poorly placed bishops, and black's d6 pawn is weak. White's rooks are not connected, and white may aim for an outpost on d5 or a pawn break with f4.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, piece activity and outposts matter more than material; look for squares where your pieces can be improved and where the opponent's pieces are restricted.
notes.plans: Black should consider improving the bad bishop and finding a better square for the knight, while also addressing the weak d6 pawn and potentially preventing white's f4 break.

notes.explains: The bishop on h6 is powerful because it not only prevents f4 but also stops the knight from going to e3, which would control the d5 outpost. If the knight cannot reach d5, the outpost remains unused.
notes.teaches: A piece can be well-placed not just for its own activity but also for the squares it controls, denying the opponent key outposts.
notes.plans: Black should consider playing ...Bf8-h6 to control the e3 square and thereby limit white's knight from reaching d5, while also preparing to transfer the bishop to a better diagonal.

notes.explains: When considering moves, it's important to come up with at least two candidate moves, even if you have a strong preference for one. This avoids tunnel vision and ensures you consider alternatives.
notes.teaches: Always generate multiple candidate moves before deciding, to keep an open mind and avoid missing better options.

notes.explains: When evaluating a position, don't rush to judge who is better; instead, focus on finding the best plan for your side. Here, black's rooks cannot easily double, and the position may be more comfortable than it appears.
notes.teaches: In positional play, prioritize identifying the best idea for your position over arguing about the evaluation.
notes.plans: Consider transferring the knight to f4, doubling rooks, or advancing pawns to create pressure and restrict the opponent.

notes.explains: The move e6 is strong because it addresses two problems at once: it frees a square for the knight and gives the bishop a target if the pawn is taken. However, it is not immediately problematic because the pawn is hanging, but the resulting position is very comfortable for white.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that improve multiple pieces simultaneously, such as freeing a square for a knight and creating a target for a bishop.
notes.plans: After e6, if the pawn is taken, the bishop recaptures with pressure; otherwise, the knight can use the freed square, and the bishop may become dangerous.

notes.explains: In this position, white has a material advantage (queen up, rook down), so there is no rush to find the best move. The habit of searching for the best move can be replaced by calmly assessing the position and considering piece improvements.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, take your time and look for the most active placement of your pieces rather than forcing tactics.
notes.plans: Consider moves like c4 to activate the bishop, or e6 to free the knight, and evaluate whether opening files is beneficial.

notes.explains: The move c4 is a candidate because it activates the bishop and, if the opponent takes, the bishop recaptures and puts pressure on the file with the rook. However, if the opponent doesn't take, the move may not accomplish much.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn break, think about what happens if the opponent accepts or declines, and whether the resulting open file is actually good for you.
notes.plans: If c4 is played and taken, the bishop recaptures and the rook adds pressure; if not, the pawn may just create weaknesses.

notes.explains: In a comfortable position, even if the advantage is not yet decisive, there may be no better move than a quiet but purposeful one. Moves that merely develop a piece or improve a pawn without a concrete idea do not really accomplish anything.
notes.teaches: Every move should have a short-term plan or a real reason behind it. Avoid aimless moves that just look natural but lack a clear purpose.

notes.explains: Before choosing a move, take in the whole position: evaluate material balance, identify which pieces are good or bad, and notice weaknesses. In the given position, key observations include a weak pawn on d6, a potentially weak pawn on b2, a shaky bishop, a knight stuck defending a bishop, and a rook on an open file.
notes.teaches: Start your thinking process by assessing the position globally: material, piece activity, and weaknesses. Notice what captures your attention before diving into specific moves.

notes.explains: A tactical idea like capturing on d6 may look appealing, but when you try to calculate the continuation, the opponent has resources to neutralize it. For example, after captures, the opponent can defend or counterattack, and the initiative fades.
notes.teaches: Do not rely on intuition alone; support it with concrete calculation. If you cannot find a clear continuation that justifies your idea, set it aside and look for another plan. Later analysis can reveal if your intuition was correct but missed a resource.
notes.plans: If the capture on d6 does not lead to a clear advantage, consider other plans such as improving piece activity, targeting the weak d6 pawn with more pressure, or exploiting the open file.

notes.explains: Intuition can point to a promising idea, but the idea only becomes playable once calculation confirms it leads to a concrete advantage or at least a safe outcome. A flashy move that cannot be backed by a clear follow-up is not worth playing.
notes.teaches: Blindly following instinct or sacrificing material without verifying the end goal will not improve your chess in the long run. Always calculate the critical lines before committing.

notes.explains: In the referenced game, a knight on the rim (or a poorly placed knight) becomes a long-term liability. The side with the better minor piece can use it to dominate key squares and coordinate an attack, while the opponent's piece remains passive.
notes.teaches: A badly placed piece is a permanent weakness. Use your active pieces to restrict the opponent's bad piece and then exploit the extra freedom to build an attack.
notes.plans: Keep the opponent's knight out of the game by controlling its escape squares, then transfer your own knight to a strong outpost and target weaknesses like f7.

notes.explains: When the opponent's pieces are tied down and one piece is completely out of play, even equal material can feel like a decisive advantage. The active side can slowly improve, push a passed pawn, and create threats that the opponent cannot meet.
notes.teaches: Material equality is not the only measure of a position. Piece activity and coordination matter more; if you can keep the opponent's pieces passive, you can convert a static advantage into a win.
notes.plans: Improve your pieces to their best squares, advance a passed pawn, and force the opponent to defend while you keep creating new threats.

notes.explains: In the discussed position, the knight on the edge is badly placed, making all the light pieces for the side with the good knight effective. The key is to exploit the opponent's misplaced pieces rather than rushing into tactics.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a badly placed piece, your pieces gain relative value. Use that advantage by creating threats that force the opponent to keep the bad piece out of play.
notes.plans: Look for ways to attack the weak knight or its supporting squares, while keeping your own pieces active and coordinated.

notes.explains: In the exchange sacrifice line, the key move is to place the queen on a1, a quiet but powerful move that creates multiple threats. This forces the opponent to either retreat the knight or lose a pawn, and after the bishop comes to f4, the opponent's pieces become completely passive.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move in a tactical sequence is a quiet one that improves your position or creates a decisive threat. Look for moves that force the opponent to choose between two bad options.
notes.plans: After the queen goes to a1, follow up with the bishop to f4, maintaining pressure and preventing the opponent from developing their knight.

notes.explains: When solving a position, it's important to first take in the whole board and assess what is beautiful and what is horrible before calculating moves. In a real game, you arrive at a position gradually, so you already have context; in puzzles, you must build that context from scratch.
notes.teaches: Before calculating, pause to evaluate the position: identify strengths, weaknesses, and imbalances. This helps you form a plan and avoid jumping into random moves.

notes.explains: In the puzzle position, both kings are weak, but the white king is currently protected by a knight on f5 that defends the f2 pawn. The question is how long that knight can maintain its defensive role.
notes.teaches: When a piece is overloaded with defensive duties, look for ways to deflect it or undermine its support. The weakness of a king is often relative to the defender's ability to hold.
notes.plans: Consider moves that challenge the knight on f5 or create threats that force it away, exposing the white king.

notes.explains: Both kings are exposed, but the black king is the weaker one because it lacks a defender like the knight on f2 that shields the white king. The knight is currently holding the white position together by guarding f2, but it may not be able to do so forever.
notes.teaches: When both kings are vulnerable, compare the quality of their defenders. A piece that is tied to defense can become a liability if it is overloaded or can be driven away.
notes.plans: Look for ways to undermine the defender of the enemy king, perhaps by attacking the knight or creating threats that force it to move.

notes.explains: The knight on f2 is doing a great job defending the white king, but it is not doing much else. The question is whether to keep it there or reshuffle it to a better square, but moving it would expose f2.
notes.teaches: A piece that is purely defensive may be misplaced if it can be improved without compromising the king's safety. Evaluate whether the defensive duty is truly necessary or if the king can be made safe by other means.
notes.plans: Consider moves like h4 or knight e3 to improve the knight's activity, but only after ensuring the king's safety is not compromised.

notes.explains: In the game, White played queen c5, which led to a strong knight e3 by Black, kicking the queen and creating threats. After the pawn takes f3, the white king becomes very weak, and Black gets a powerful knight on f6. The position becomes unclear, but White has better options.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a dangerous piece that can be kicked, be wary of moves that allow it to jump into a strong outpost. Sometimes it is better to prevent the opponent's idea rather than to try to refute it later.
notes.plans: Instead of queen c5, consider king g1, which is a prophylactic move that prevents the knight from landing on f6 with tempo and keeps the king safer.

notes.explains: After the prophylactic king g1, Black's position is not so clear. If Black tries f5, White has a strong knight f6 move, which is forcing and leads to a powerful attack. Even though White is a piece down, the black king is so weak that White is winning.
notes.teaches: A king that is exposed and lacks defenders can be more valuable than material. When you have a lead in attack, forcing moves can create mating threats that outweigh a material deficit.
notes.plans: If Black plays f5, White can play knight f6, then follow up with rook g6 and queen d6, creating unstoppable mating threats. The key is to keep the initiative and not allow the opponent to consolidate.

notes.explains: Queen h5 is a natural active move, but it allows Black to play e3, which is a strong resource. After e3, White is in trouble because the knight can be kicked and the king becomes weak. The problem is that White often sees such moves but does not take them seriously enough.
notes.teaches: When you see a strong move for the opponent, do not dismiss it just because it looks scary. Take concrete measures to prevent it, even if it means playing a quieter move first.
notes.plans: Instead of queen h5, prefer a move like king g1 that prevents the opponent's key resource, even if it seems less active. This is a common pattern: prophylaxis before launching an attack.

notes.explains: The position is tense because the opponent can play e3, which is a strong move. The player must decide whether to take or avoid it, and there is a plan to play for a win with queen h5.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong move like e3, you don't have to react immediately; you can make a preparatory move like king g1 to stop it, then proceed with your own plan.
notes.plans: Consider playing king g1 to prevent e3, then continue with queen h5 and capture on the next move.

notes.explains: In this position, black has weaknesses: bad bishops, a weak g3 pawn, and a weak square. White has a passed b5 pawn that is a threat. Black must find a plan despite the unpleasant position.
notes.teaches: When your position is worse, focus on improving your worst piece. Identify the piece that can improve dramatically and reroute it to a better square.
notes.plans: Reroute the bishop to a better diagonal, possibly trading light-square pieces, and consider pushing d5 to activate pawns.

notes.explains: The idea of sacrificing a piece to open files is tempting, but without enough pieces to support the attack, it's not practical. The material investment is too high for the return.
notes.teaches: Before sacrificing material, ensure you have enough pieces to create a decisive attack. If the attack lacks support, the sacrifice is likely unsound.

notes.explains: In this position, the light-squared bishop on c8 is bad, and the pawn structure is fluid. Trading light-squared pieces and pushing d5 could make the pawns strong, but it's unclear how the structure will turn out. The open file and potential pins after trades add dynamic possibilities.
notes.teaches: When a piece is poorly placed, look for ways to improve it, even with a modest move like bishop c8. Improving a bad piece is often the best practical try, regardless of whether the position is objectively better or worse.
notes.plans: Consider moves that activate the bad bishop, such as bishop c8, and be ready to trade pieces to exploit open files and create pins.

notes.explains: After black's bishop c8, white's best response is queen f2, which preemptively addresses the threat of bishop takes h4 and the resulting pins. Moving the queen away immediately denies black the momentum of a tactical strike.
notes.teaches: When you anticipate a tactical threat, the best move is often to remove the target immediately, not give the opponent the chance to execute it. Prophylactic moves can be the strongest.
notes.plans: White should play queen f2 to avoid the pin and maintain control, then continue developing while keeping an eye on black's counterplay.

notes.explains: After the sequence with queen f2, bishop b7, and rook takes on h2, black plays d5 to eliminate the weakness and potentially create a passed pawn pair. If white captures, black recaptures and gets strong pawns; if white doesn't, black's pawns remain healthy.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn weakness, look for a move that either eliminates it or transforms the structure to your advantage. A pawn break like d5 can be a key resource to improve your position.
notes.plans: Black should play d5, aiming to either create a passed pawn pair or force white to ruin their own pawn structure.

notes.explains: When asked for a plan and feeling clueless, the pressure to find a brilliant long-term idea is self-imposed. Practical play rewards modest, incremental improvements over grand schemes.
notes.teaches: Break the game down into small, concrete improvements — one step at a time. You don't need a deep, distant plan; just find the next small thing that makes your position better.

notes.explains: Positional play can be approached from different angles, such as focusing on piece activity and small advantages rather than only long-term pawn structures.
notes.teaches: Study positional play from multiple perspectives to deepen understanding — for example, thinking about piece placement and short-term maneuvers.

notes.explains: In this position, the white king is trapped in the corner, which is a critical weakness. Black has a tactical opportunity to exploit the back rank and the king's lack of escape squares.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is confined, look for forcing moves that create threats against it, such as checks or captures that open lines. Even if a move seems obvious, verify that it leads to a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: Black should consider moves like Rxf3, which if accepted allows Qb1+ and then Bf4, winning the queen or mating. If White declines, Black still has a strong attack.

notes.explains: Black has a strong passed pawn and appears to be winning material, but White has a hidden resource. In any position, before assuming you are lost, look for tactical ideas, especially mating patterns.
notes.teaches: Always scan for mating patterns, even when the position seems hopeless. Imagine placing a piece on a key square to deliver mate, and then see if you can force that scenario.
notes.plans: White can play Rg5, threatening mate on g7. If Black tries to defend with Qd5+, White can respond with Rxd5, and the mate threat remains. This turns the tables and wins for White.

notes.explains: White has a breakthrough on the f-file, and Black's king is exposed. The immediate capture Rxf7 forces Black to recapture, after which White can use checks to drive the king into a mating net.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for a sequence of forcing moves that bring your pieces into the attack. Sacrifices that remove defenders or open lines are often the key.
notes.plans: White should continue with checks and threats, such as Nf7+ or Qe6+, to exploit the king's lack of shelter. The goal is to force mate or win material.

notes.explains: After the sacrifice on f7, the black king is exposed and must choose between fleeing to e8 or g8. The position demands aggressive play from White to convert the initiative into a win.
notes.teaches: When you have sacrificed material for an attack, you must keep the initiative and not allow the opponent to consolidate. Look for forcing moves that bring more pieces into the attack.
notes.plans: White should continue with checks and threats, such as queen checks, to drive the king into a worse position and then bring the knight to a dominant outpost like e6.

notes.explains: White has a strong move: placing the knight on e6, attacking the queen and creating a powerful outpost that suffocates Black's position. If Black captures the knight, White wins material; otherwise, the knight remains a monster.
notes.teaches: A knight on a strong outpost in the enemy camp can be worth more than a piece, as it restricts the opponent's pieces and creates tactical threats. Always consider such centralization even if it doesn't immediately win material.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the knight on e6, using it to tie down Black's pieces and create threats against the queen and other targets.

notes.explains: After winning material, White has a choice between an adventurous move like Qh4 and a stabilizing move like c4. The stabilizing move protects the base and ensures the advantage is converted without risk.
notes.teaches: When you have achieved a winning material advantage, it is often better to consolidate and simplify rather than go for risky continuations. In team events, converting a win reliably is crucial for the team's success.
notes.plans: White should play c4 to solidify the position, then proceed to convert the material advantage with simple, safe moves.

notes.explains: Black tries to defend with Rf7, but White can simply take and deliver mate on d8. The defense fails because the back rank is weak and the queen is overloaded.
notes.teaches: In the endgame of an attack, look for mating patterns on the back rank. A queen and rook can combine to deliver mate when the enemy king has no escape squares.
notes.plans: White should execute the mate by taking on f7 and then delivering mate on d8.

notes.explains: In a different game, Black has more central pawns and wants to roll them forward. The immediate d5 fails because the knight on e5 is attacked, so Black needs a preparatory move.
notes.teaches: When you have a central pawn majority, you should aim to advance it, but you must first deal with pieces that prevent the advance. Sometimes you need to sacrifice material to remove defenders and open lines for your pawns.
notes.plans: Black should consider a move like Rxc4 to deflect a defender, then follow up with the pawn break d5, using the central pawns to gain space and launch an attack.

notes.explains: In this position, the e5 pawn is under attack and the immediate push d5 fails because the opponent's pieces are covering it. The idea is to sacrifice the rook on c4 to open lines and start rolling the pawns, which is a sound attacking concept even if engines approve it.
notes.teaches: When your center is blocked, consider sacrificing material to open lines and create a pawn storm. Aggressive pawn pushes should be as far forward as possible, like a5 instead of a6, to maximize the initiative.
notes.plans: After the rook sacrifice on c4, black should continue with pawn pushes like a5, d5, and a4, aiming to promote and maintain a relentless attack.

notes.explains: In the Spanish opening, after a series of moves, white has a strategic edge and can play on both sides of the board. The position calls for a central break with d5 to challenge the opponent's center, and later a sacrifice on h6 to open the king's position.
notes.teaches: In the Spanish, if the opponent plays on the flanks, respond in the center. When attacking the king, bring more pieces to the attack to outnumber the defenders, as basic math favors the attacker.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack by bringing the queen to c1, targeting the h6 pawn, and then following up with Nxh6+ to expose the king.

notes.explains: In this attacking position, White's queen on c1 joins the attack on the h-pawn, creating threats that Black cannot fully defend. The knight on h6 delivers a check, and if Black recaptures with the bishop, White's queen takes on h6, leading to unstoppable mating threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in attack, bring all your pieces into the assault; a single extra attacker can make the defense collapse.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by focusing on the weakened kingside, using the queen and knight to create mating nets.

notes.explains: In this sharp Catalan position, White's attack is very strong after f5, and Black's pieces are not easily coming into the game. The position is simply dangerous for Black.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and a safer king, you can often launch a direct attack even if material is equal. The side with the initiative should look for ways to bring all pieces into the attack.
notes.plans: White can double rooks on the g-file, bring the queen to the kingside, and consider ideas like Qh6 or Bg6. The rook lift to a3 and then g3 is a key maneuver to join the attack.

notes.explains: When you are far ahead in development, material count matters less than piece activity. Here, White's pieces are all active while Black's rook on a8 is out of play, giving White overwhelming compensation.
notes.teaches: In positions with a big development lead, prioritize placing your pieces on their most active squares and attacking, rather than defending material.
notes.plans: Bring the knight into the attack (e.g., to c4) and use the rook on the open file to maintain pressure, ignoring material deficits.

notes.explains: Black's queen move to e6 creates an escape square for the king, avoiding the immediate threat of a knight check on d6. This shows the importance of king safety and prophylaxis.
notes.teaches: When your king is vulnerable to checks, look for a move that gives it a flight square while maintaining your own activity.
notes.plans: Black intends to consolidate and avoid the knight check, while White should continue to press with active pieces.

notes.explains: In the position, White's rook on d1 captures on b5, and the knight on c4 is hanging. The tempting rook trade on d6 would lose the knight, so White must find a way to keep the attack going.
notes.teaches: When attacking, bring extra pieces into the attack rather than trading off your active pieces. Avoid exchanges that leave your own pieces hanging.
notes.plans: White should seek to increase the pressure, possibly by activating the rook on the open file or finding a tactical resource.

notes.explains: White's knight on f5 is a strong outpost, and the threat is that if the queen goes to e5, the rook on e1 will trap it. Black responds with a counterattack on the rook, but White has a decisive resource.
notes.teaches: A well-placed knight can dominate the position, but always be alert to counterattacks. When you see a good move, look for an even better one—this is a key principle in chess.
notes.plans: White should continue with the most forcing and precise continuation, possibly sacrificing material to open lines against the king.

notes.explains: White finds a brilliant move with the pawn to f6, which moves the knight away and allows the rook to come to e1 with check. This is even stronger than the original plan, showing the value of looking for the best move.
notes.teaches: Even when you have a good move, there may be a better one. Always search for the most forcing and precise continuation, especially in attacking positions.
notes.plans: White's attack should break through, and the game should conclude with a decisive advantage, possibly leading to a mating net.

notes.explains: In the final phase, White plays queen g4, which wins, but later notes that queen e7 check would have been even faster, leading to a forced mate. This shows that even in winning positions, there may be a more efficient path.
notes.teaches: Always look for the most precise and quickest win. Self-critique after the game is valuable for improvement, as even strong players can miss the best move.
notes.plans: If the opportunity arises, choose the most forcing and mating continuation to finish the game efficiently.

notes.explains: In the French Defense structure (e4 e6 d4 d5 e5), White's pawns point toward the kingside, indicating that White's space advantage and attacking chances lie there. Black's pawns point toward the queenside, so Black should seek counterplay on that side.
notes.teaches: The direction of your pawn chain signals where your space advantage and attacking plans should be directed. Use your extra space to create weaknesses on your strong side, while being aware that your opponent will try to counter on the opposite wing.
notes.plans: White should focus on kingside play, using the extra space to maneuver pieces and create threats. Black should look for queenside counterplay to undermine White's center and create activity.

notes.explains: The knight on c2 in this French-like structure looks odd but is a modern idea: it supports d4 and can reroute to b4 or e3, maintaining control and flexibility. It also avoids blocking the bishop on c1.
notes.teaches: Sometimes unconventional piece placements are justified by the needs of the position. A knight on c2 can be a strong defender of the center and can later jump into the game via b4 or e3.
notes.plans: White should keep the knight on c2 to reinforce d4 and prepare to reroute it to a more active square if needed. Black should be aware of this defensive resource and plan accordingly.

notes.explains: In this position, White's bishop on b4 is attacked, and the natural capture would start trading pieces. However, the bishop on b4 is actually misplaced, as it blocks Black's own pieces and has limited prospects. White's king is safe on f2 because Black's queen and king are not coordinated to exploit it.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to avoid trades that relieve pressure, even if it means an unusual king move. A piece that is well-placed for the opponent can be left alone if it's actually hindering their development.
notes.plans: White should continue to develop and maintain the tension, aiming to use the space advantage to restrict Black's pieces.

notes.explains: White's king on g3 and later h3 looks risky, but it's safe because Black has no attacking forces on the kingside. White's rook on h1 is already developed, and the bishop on f1 is useful there. The center might explode, but White is prepared to handle it.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, the king can often find safety on the side where the opponent has no pieces. It's important to evaluate actual attacking potential, not just appearances.
notes.plans: White will continue to push forward on the kingside, using the space to squeeze Black's pieces.

notes.explains: Black has developed all pieces but has no useful plan: the bishop on b4 and queen on b6 are doing nothing. White's knight on c2 is a hero, preventing Black's counterplay against the center. White's ultimate goal is to smother Black and then attack if Black castles short.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, you must constantly think about taking away squares from the opponent's pieces. The opponent may have development, but if their pieces lack prospects, you are better.
notes.plans: White will play g4 to push back Black's pieces and then launch a kingside attack, using the space advantage to create threats.

notes.explains: In the French Defense, White's ultimate goal is to cramp Black's position and, if Black castles short, to launch a kingside attack. The knight on c2 is a key defensive piece, preventing Black's counterplay against the center.
notes.teaches: When playing against the French, aim to restrict Black's pieces and then attack the king if it castles short. A well-placed knight can be a silent hero in stopping counterplay.
notes.plans: White should continue to build up on the kingside, using the knight's control to keep Black passive.

notes.explains: White's attack with queen h5 looks beautiful but may be unsound. Black's defensive resource h6 is strong, and if White plays queen g6, Black can respond with rook f3, exchanging on d3 and surviving.
notes.teaches: Attacks that look crushing may have hidden defensive resources. Always check for counterplay before committing to a sacrificial attack.
notes.plans: Black should consider h6 to blunt the attack, and if queen g6 comes, use rook f3 to trade pieces and ease the pressure.

notes.explains: In a sharp position, White missed a winning continuation. After rook f7 and queen e7, White played rook g3, but rook g8 refuted the trick. The correct move was rook g4 or g5, followed by king g2, leading to a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, precision is crucial. A single move can turn a winning attack into a missed opportunity. Always look for the most forcing and accurate continuation.
notes.plans: White should have played rook g4 or g5, then king g2, to maintain the attack and win.

notes.explains: In another game from the same match, the players repeated similar ideas. Black played h5, and White responded with g3 and king g2, again aiming to run Black out of space.
notes.teaches: In the French, White often uses a king-side pawn storm and king safety to restrict Black's pieces. The same plans can recur across different games.
notes.plans: White should continue to expand on the kingside, while Black must find counterplay to avoid being squeezed.

notes.explains: In the French Defense, white's space advantage means the king is relatively safe and castling is not urgent. The priority is to maintain the space advantage and avoid trades that would relieve black's congestion.
notes.teaches: When you have more space, you should not rush to castle; instead, focus on expanding and restricting your opponent's pieces. The side with more space should avoid unnecessary exchanges.
notes.plans: White should aim to keep pieces on the board and expand on the kingside, while black seeks counterplay.

notes.explains: The move a3 followed by b4 in the French Advance is a paradoxical but effective idea. It appears to be a pawn storm on the queenside, but its real purpose is defensive: it prevents black from generating counterplay with moves like ...Na5 or ...a5, and it prepares to develop the bishop to b2 where it controls d4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn advance on the opponent's side of the board can be a defensive measure to restrict their piece activity. A bishop on b2 can control key central squares, similar to a knight on c2 in other variations.
notes.plans: White will continue to expand on the queenside with b4-b5 if needed, and develop the bishop to b2 to reinforce control of d4, then proceed to smother black's position.

notes.explains: In the French, black's pawn on e5 does not control any center squares, whereas white's pawns on e6 and d5 do. Thus, e5 is not about central control but about gaining space. This space can be a double-edged sword: it gives white more room but also creates targets and can be difficult to handle practically.
notes.teaches: A pawn advance that gains space does not necessarily improve your central control. Space advantages are valuable but require careful handling; they can be a liability if the opponent can undermine them.
notes.plans: White must be vigilant to maintain the space advantage and avoid pawn weaknesses, while black will try to challenge the center with moves like ...c5 or ...f6.

notes.explains: In a French structure, white's b5 pawn advance can be a serious mistake because it allows black to play ...c5, which gives the knight on c6 more activity and opens up the position for black's pieces. This is a typical way for black to get counterplay.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, avoid pawn moves that give your opponent's pieces more life. In the French, ...c5 is a key freeing move for black, so white should be cautious about advancing the b-pawn without preparation.
notes.plans: White should instead look for moves that maintain the bind, such as developing the bishop to b2 or preparing to support the center. Black will aim to play ...c5 to break free.

notes.explains: In this position, White's move B5 is a horrible mistake because it allows Black to play C5, giving the knight on C6 life and opening the queenside for Black. Black, as a French player, is often cramped, but if they can get play on the queenside, they can create counterplay before White's kingside initiative starts.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, be careful not to give your opponent counterplay by loosening your pawn structure. A move like B5 can be a mistake if it allows the opponent to undermine your center and activate their pieces.
notes.plans: Black should immediately play C5 to challenge White's center and activate the knight on C6, aiming for queenside counterplay.

notes.explains: White's knight on E3 is not the happiest move because it allows Black to trade bishops favorably: Bishop G6, Bishop D3, and then Bishop E4, turning Black's bad bishop into a good one. This simplifies to a position where Black's knight will go to C4, and White's king becomes weak.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, piece trades can be dangerous if they allow the opponent to improve their pieces and simplify into a favorable endgame. Be wary of allowing your opponent to trade off their bad pieces for your good ones.
notes.plans: Black should continue with the plan of trading bishops and placing the knight on C4, targeting the weakened white king.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black has an outside passed pawn, and the knight on D5 fully blockades White's pawns. Black's bishop is good, while White's dark-square bishop is poor. This is a textbook winning endgame for Black.
notes.teaches: An outside passed pawn can be a decisive advantage in the endgame, especially when it is supported by a well-placed knight and a good bishop. The side with the outside passed pawn should use it to tie down the opponent's pieces and create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black should advance the outside passed pawn, using the knight to blockade and the bishop to support, while White's pieces are tied down.

notes.explains: In another game, White plays A3 and B4, showing an incredible sense of confidence in the correctness of these quiet moves. This is a demonstration of the power of space, as White is slowly expanding and smothering Black.
notes.teaches: Quiet pawn moves like A3 and B4 can be powerful in the opening if they support a space advantage and prepare a favorable pawn structure. It requires confidence to play such moves, but they can be part of a deep plan.
notes.plans: White should continue expanding on the queenside, maintaining the space advantage and preparing to crack open the position.

notes.explains: In this position, White plays G5 to crack open the position, a common idea in French Defense structures. Black responds with A5, B5, and a trade, leading to a collapse of the center. This is similar to a variation with Knight takes D4, where Black collapses the center and creates chaos.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, you can often break open the position with a pawn thrust like G5. However, be aware that the opponent may counter in the center, leading to a mess where both sides have chances.
notes.plans: White should continue with the initiative, while Black should seek counterplay in the center.

notes.explains: The bishop on c2 in this setup looks appealing but can become a target; the king is safer than in previous lines, yet the piece may not be optimally placed.
notes.teaches: A piece that looks well-placed can still be a latent weakness if it's exposed to attack or lacks a clear role.
notes.plans: Black can consider taking on d4 and playing Nb4 to challenge the light-square bishop, aiming to exchange pieces and reduce White's attacking potential.

notes.explains: In this position, Black must break the center pawn chain; otherwise, his pieces will remain passive and White will build with Rook b1.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong pawn center, the defender must seek active counterplay or risk being slowly squeezed.
notes.plans: White should consider moves like g3 to solidify the kingside, while being wary of ...h5 and potential weaknesses. Black should aim to crack the center.

notes.explains: The game features high-level strategic plans, but tactical accuracy often decides the outcome; even with good plans, mistakes can turn the game.
notes.teaches: Strategy sets the stage, but tactics are the final arbiter; always be alert to concrete variations.

notes.explains: In this position, the knight on f7 is only preventing White's knight from going to g5, making it less effective. Black's pieces are active, and White's are not fully mobilized, so Black's pawn break is strong.
notes.teaches: A pawn break is only effective if your pieces are sufficiently mobilized to support it. If your pieces aren't involved, the break can backfire.
notes.plans: White should focus on completing development and strengthening the position before attempting any break, possibly with moves like bishop d3 and rook g1.

notes.explains: White's a3 move serves two purposes: preparing b4 and preventing Black's knight from coming to b4. Black's a5 only stops b4, so White gains a tempo in terms of useful moves.
notes.teaches: When choosing a move, consider if it can serve multiple purposes. A move that addresses two needs is often more valuable than one that addresses only one.
notes.plans: White should continue with a plan that exploits the slight advantage in useful moves, possibly by preparing a kingside attack or improving piece placement.

notes.explains: In this position, White's bishop on c2 is vulnerable to the rook on c8, and the knight on e5 trick works because the bishop on f2 is hanging. White must be careful not to leave pieces en prise.
notes.teaches: When considering a defensive sequence, always check if your pieces are left hanging. Sometimes you need to make an extra move like rook g2 to protect a piece before executing a plan.
notes.plans: White should consider moves like rook g2 to protect the bishop, then proceed with the plan of bishop f2, ensuring no pieces are undefended.

notes.explains: White's decision to play rook g1 and go for a direct attack is a practical choice, even if it might not be objectively best, because otherwise White risks being 'squished' by Black's space advantage.
notes.teaches: In difficult positions, it's often better to create active chances, even if they are not fully sound, than to passively allow your opponent to improve their position without resistance.
notes.plans: White should continue with the aggressive plan, looking for tactical opportunities to create threats against the black king, while being mindful of the weaknesses in their own camp.

notes.explains: In this position, white has a space advantage but black's pieces are well placed. White's minors on b1 and c1 are undeveloped and block the rook on h1, which is a serious issue. Black's bishop on c8 is like a prisoner, waiting to be freed with violent effect once the position opens.
notes.teaches: A space advantage is only useful if your pieces are actively involved. If your pieces are undeveloped or passive, a pawn break or space grab can backfire. Also, a 'bad' piece that is hemmed in can become very powerful once it is freed, so be careful about opening the position when your opponent has such a piece.
notes.plans: White should aim to develop the queenside pieces and bring the rook on h1 into play, perhaps via a2. Black should look to exchange pieces to reduce white's space advantage and target weaknesses like d4 and b3.

notes.explains: Black has just made a huge improvement by moving the knight from h6, which was terrible, to a better square. The idea is that by exchanging pieces, black can turn white's space advantage into a liability. If black trades off the bishop on d7 for a white piece, white will be left with weaknesses on d4 and b3.
notes.teaches: A space advantage can become a weakness if you exchange too many pieces, because the remaining pieces have more space to cover. The concept of 'capacity' means each position has a certain number of pieces it can support; if you trade pieces, the side with more space may find its pawns are overextended and vulnerable.
notes.plans: Black should seek exchanges, especially of the bishop on d7, to reduce white's attacking potential and expose weaknesses. White must avoid exchanges and try to keep pieces on the board to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: White has played a modern idea with rook to a2, swinging the rook over to the queenside. This is a way to activate the rook while the knights on b1 and c1 are still undeveloped. The bishop on e3 is protected, so the tactical trick with g5 is not available.
notes.teaches: Rook lifts to the second rank can be a powerful way to bring a rook into the game, especially when the back rank is blocked. Also, protecting key pieces can prevent tactical shots from the opponent.
notes.plans: White continues to probe black's position, looking for weaknesses. Black should be careful not to allow white's pieces to become too active.

notes.explains: After a single exchange of a bishop for a knight, the side with more space can be left with weaknesses, such as pawns on d4 and b3, while the opponent's pieces become active.
notes.teaches: Exchanges can transform a spatial advantage into concrete weaknesses; before trading, assess which side benefits from the resulting pawn structure.
notes.plans: If you have the space advantage, avoid trades that leave you with weak pawns; instead, keep pieces on the board to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: A bishop on a square like h5 can be very strong because it pins a knight and gains space, making it difficult for the opponent to develop harmoniously.
notes.teaches: In many openings, getting a bishop to an active square like h5 can be a key achievement, as it restricts the opponent's pieces and creates long-term pressure.
notes.plans: If you can place a bishop on such an active square, do so, and be ready to trade it off at the right moment to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: A knight on e7 can be poorly placed, blocking the bishop and lacking prospects, while the opponent has plenty of space to maneuver.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, the opponent's pieces often become tangled and passive; look for ways to exploit their lack of coordination.
notes.plans: Use your space to restrict the opponent's pieces, and consider tactical blows like knight takes e5 to break open the position if the opportunity arises.

notes.explains: In positions with a space advantage, the defender often has hidden tactical resources, such as a knight sacrifice on e5, that can create counterplay.
notes.teaches: Even when worse, look for dynamic tactical shots to complicate the position; the side with more space must remain vigilant against such counterpunches.
notes.plans: If you are the defender, seek active piece play and tactical blows; if you have the space, keep pieces coordinated and avoid giving the opponent targets.

notes.explains: White is a pawn down, but the extra pawn is a useless f-pawn while Black has two connected passed pawns. The saving grace is opposite-colored bishops, which give White defensive resources that would not exist with same-colored bishops.
