Black's queen on c7 is a natural developing move but also a 'sad point' because it can become a target.
notes.teaches: When assessing a position, look for concrete advantages: weak pawns, strong pieces, open files, and king safety. Even if the material is equal, these factors can justify a plan.
notes.plans: White can aim to increase pressure on the d4 pawn, use the bishop on c4 to support a kingside attack, and potentially exploit the queen's placement on c7.

notes.explains: Black's development is awkward: Queen e8 is impossible due to a pawn, and Queen f6 would be a blunder. Thus, Queen c7 is the only natural way to develop the queen, even though it may become a target. This shows that Black is under pressure and has limited good options.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are short on good squares, their 'natural' moves may come with drawbacks. Recognize when the opponent's development is constrained and look for ways to exploit the resulting weaknesses.
notes.plans: White can continue to improve piece placement, perhaps preparing to attack the queen on c7 or to increase pressure on the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: White's advantage is real but fleeting: the open rook file, active bishop, and space edge can evaporate if Black gets two quiet moves like ...Bd7 and ...Re8, turning White's edge into an 'imaginary' one.
notes.teaches: Assess a position dynamically: a static advantage is only meaningful if it can be converted before the opponent consolidates.
notes.plans: White should seek an energetic continuation to exploit the initiative before Black reorganizes.

notes.explains: Taking on f5 with the pawn is tempting but allows Black to use the e-file and the d5 square; the knight on g3 is poorly placed and needs redeployment.
notes.teaches: When a piece is badly placed, consider a multi-move maneuver to a better square, even if it costs time, because the improved piece activity is worth it.
notes.plans: White should play Nh1 and then Nf2-g4-g5, aiming at the weaknesses on h7 and f7.

notes.explains: After the knight reaches g5, Black's king is under pressure; if Black plays ...Bd7, White can continue with Re1, and Black's ...Re8 is bad because White can exchange rooks and then play Qd5, targeting the weak king.
notes.teaches: When attacking, keep pieces coordinated and be ready to exploit open files and weak squares around the enemy king; a simple plan like Qd5 can be decisive.
notes.plans: White should proceed with the knight maneuver to g5, then double on the e-file and use the queen to penetrate.

notes.explains: In this position, the queen on d5 is the strongest move because it directly threatens mate and keeps the initiative. The rook to e8 is weaker because it allows exchanges that reduce attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When you have a direct mating threat, prioritize it over slower positional moves. Look for the most forcing and simple continuation.
notes.plans: Play Qd5, then follow up by capturing weak pawns and preparing to bring the bishop to c3 to increase pressure on the weakened kingside.

notes.explains: The move h6 by Black is flawed because it does not address the underlying weakness of the g6 square. White can still play Qg6, and if the pawn on g5 is taken, Qxg5 leads to a mating attack.
notes.teaches: A pawn move like h6 does not eliminate the weakness of the square it was meant to defend; the square itself remains vulnerable. Always check if the opponent's defensive move actually covers the key squares.
notes.plans: If Black plays h6, White should respond with Qg6, threatening mate. If Black captures on g5, White recaptures with the queen and continues the attack.

notes.explains: After Black plays g6 to prevent Qg6, White must find a new plan. The immediate Qg6 is no longer possible, so White should look for other checks, captures, and threats. The move Bxf4 is undesirable because it allows the black queen to re-enter the game actively.
notes.teaches: When your primary plan is blocked, scan for alternative forcing moves: checks, captures, and threats. Avoid moves that bring the opponent's pieces back to life, even if they win material.
notes.plans: Consider moves like Rfe1 or other rook lifts to maintain pressure, while keeping the queen active and preventing Black from consolidating.

notes.explains: The move Bf4 is interesting because it creates threats that force Black to respond. If Black moves the rook, White can play Rae1, and if Black blocks with Bd6, White has Qg6, leading to a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece sacrifice or a move that seems to lose material can be strong if it creates unavoidable threats. Always consider moves that force the opponent to react to your attack.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, and after Black's response, continue with the rook to e1 or the queen to g6 to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: In this position, White's queen on g5 gives Black chances to slip away, so a quieter move like Bf4 is preferred. If Black doesn't move the rook, White can play Rae1, and if Black blocks with Bd6, then Qg6 wins the queen.
notes.teaches: When your queen is aggressively placed, consider whether it gives the opponent counterplay. Sometimes a quieter piece move maintains pressure while avoiding tactical complications.
notes.plans: Develop the rook to e1 and keep the queen centralized, ready to exploit any weakness on the g-file.

notes.explains: After Black plays h6, White's options are limited to Qh4 or Qh6. Qh6 allows Qg7, which lets the queen infiltrate the king's position, so Qh4 is preferred to keep the queen active without allowing that.
notes.teaches: When choosing between queen moves, consider not only your own threats but also the opponent's possible defensive resources. A move that allows the enemy queen to enter your position can be problematic.
notes.plans: Play Qh4 to maintain pressure and avoid the queen infiltration on g7.

notes.explains: There is a tactical trick: if Black plays Re8, White can capture on f6 and then play Qh6, threatening the rook on e8 and the knight. If the queen goes to g7, White picks up the rook.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical motifs where a queen can fork pieces or where a discovered attack can win material. Even if the opponent defends, you may gain a piece.
notes.plans: If Black plays Re8, capture on f6 and then Qh6, creating threats against the rook and knight.

notes.explains: After Black plays Kg7 to defend against Qh6, White's knight is better on h3 than g3 because it protects the f4 pawn and gives the queen room to regroup. The knight on h3 also supports the idea of removing the d4 pawn.
notes.teaches: Knight placement should be flexible: a knight on the edge can be useful for defense and for freeing squares for other pieces, especially when it supports central pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Consider moving the knight to h3 to protect f4 and allow the queen to reposition, then aim to open the center for the bishop.

notes.explains: Black has two ways to defend the d4 pawn: Qb6 or Nf6. Qb6 is passive, just defending without creating threats. If Black loses the d4 pawn, the game is essentially over because White's bishops become dominant.
notes.teaches: When defending a key pawn, prefer moves that also create counterplay. Passive defense can allow the opponent to build up pressure and win the pawn anyway.
notes.plans: If Black defends passively, continue to increase pressure on d4 with moves like Bc3 or Qb6, and be ready to exploit any inaccuracies.

notes.explains: White is attacking the d4 pawn and should bring more pieces to bear. Bc3 is a strong move, but Bc5 is also possible. If Black plays Bc5, White can capture on d4 and then Qd4, picking up the bishop. Also, Qb6 is a good idea, but Black must be careful because Bc3 and Bc5 are both strong.
notes.teaches: When attacking a pawn, coordinate your pieces to increase pressure. Look for moves that also create additional threats, such as attacking other pieces or squares.
notes.plans: Play Bc3 to increase pressure on d4, and if Black defends with Bc5, capture on d4 and then Qd4 to win the bishop.

notes.explains: If Black plays Qb6, White has several ideas, including Bc3, Bc5, and Qd4. If Black plays Bc5, White can play b4, forcing the bishop to e6, where it becomes passive and only defends the d4 pawn. The bishop was much more active on d6.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece is active, consider forcing it to a worse square. A bishop that is reduced to defending a pawn is often a sign of a positional advantage.
notes.plans: If Black plays Qb6, consider b4 to drive the bishop away, or Bc3 to maintain pressure on d4.

notes.explains: The bishop on b6 is passive compared to its previous post on d6, where it defended key squares like e7 and f5. Its retreat has weakened Black's kingside and left the queen as the main defender.
notes.teaches: A piece's activity is measured by the squares it controls and the defensive duties it fulfills; a retreat to a 'safe' square can leave other pieces overburdened.
notes.plans: White should exploit the bishop's passivity by targeting the weakened kingside, especially the h7 square.

notes.explains: The queen can be reactivated with Qh5, which has a direct impact on the kingside, attacking h7 and supporting the advance g5. This is more direct than other moves like Qe1, which are also interesting but less aggressive.
notes.teaches: When choosing between candidate moves, prioritize those that create immediate threats or improve your attacking potential, even if other moves are also good.
notes.plans: Play Qh5, preparing g5 to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: After Qh5, Black's rook on e8 is a target. White wants to place a rook on the seventh rank, but if Black plays Re8, White can consider g5, attacking h7. However, Black can respond with h6, so the best move is Rxe5, exploiting the weakness of the e5 pawn because Black cannot recapture due to the exposed king.
notes.teaches: When a king is exposed, tactical motifs like pins and discovered attacks become more potent; a piece that appears defended may be vulnerable because the defender is tied to the king.
notes.plans: Play Rxe5, winning a pawn and maintaining the attack, as Black's recapture is impossible due to the king's safety.

notes.explains: After the queen returns to attack d4 and forces the bishop to b6, White's pieces are optimally placed. The knight on g5 is finally achieved, attacking the queen and the h7 bishop, forcing Black's king to g8.
notes.teaches: Patience in maneuvering pieces to their ideal squares can create decisive threats; a well-timed knight jump can be the culmination of a long-term plan.
notes.plans: With the knight on g5, continue the attack by exchanging rooks and bringing the queen back to e1, preparing to activate the bishop on d2.

notes.explains: The bishop on d2 is still inactive, but White has a choice: either find a way to activate it on the long diagonal, or play safely by picking up material, like the bishop on b6, which is a risk-free way to win.
notes.teaches: When an attack is not fully conclusive, converting to a material advantage is a practical and safe way to win; you don't always need the most spectacular move.
notes.plans: If the bishop cannot be activated, capture the b6 bishop and simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: In this winning position, the opponent is down material and trying to prolong the game with moves like ...Qg7. The attacking side has a clear material advantage and can either force mate or simplify to a won endgame.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, the safest and most efficient way to convert is to take the free material and simplify, avoiding unnecessary complications that could allow counterplay.
notes.plans: Take the offered piece, then consolidate by relocating the knight to a strong square like c4, protecting pawns, and exchanging pieces to reach a technically winning endgame.

notes.explains: The move g6 is a powerful idea because it puts pressure on the opponent's king and threatens mate, while also restricting the enemy bishop's activity. It creates a mating net and makes the win much easier.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, look for moves that increase the pressure and create direct threats, such as mating threats, rather than just grabbing material. A move like g6 can be decisive because it limits the defender's options.
notes.plans: After g6, if the opponent tries to defend with ...h5, bring the bishop to the other diagonal to maintain the attack. The threat of mate on g7 forces the opponent to defend passively.

notes.explains: The opponent's king is exposed and under pressure. Moves like ...h5 are attempts to create luft, but they don't solve the fundamental problems of being down material and facing a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When your king is in danger, creating luft can be necessary, but it is often insufficient if the opponent has a sustained attack. You must also address the material deficit and the opponent's threats.
notes.plans: Continue the attack, using checks and threats to prevent the opponent from consolidating. If the opponent plays ...Bd5, respond with Qf6 to maintain the initiative and increase the pressure.

notes.explains: The speaker notes that the winning side did not need to move the king after castling, and the king remained safe on its original square. This highlights the importance of king safety and the fact that a castled king can often stay put while the attack unfolds.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, you don't need to move your king unnecessarily. Keep it safe and focus on the attack, as long as the king is not in immediate danger.
notes.plans: Maintain the king's safety while continuing to press the attack, using the extra material to force a win.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a material advantage and can simplify by exchanging pieces, which reduces Black's counterplay and makes the win easier to convert.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, aim to exchange pieces, especially the opponent's active ones, to reduce their chances and simplify the position.
notes.plans: Relocate the knight to a strong square like c4, protect the pawns, and then target and capture more pawns to increase the advantage.

notes.explains: White's king remained safe after castling, allowing the rest of the army to go on the offensive without concern.
notes.teaches: Once the king is safe, you can commit fully to an attack or active play, using all your pieces for the initiative.

notes.explains: In this line of the Englund Gambit (d4 e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf4), White's f4 move is dubious because Black can play f6, undermining the e5 pawn and wrecking White's kingside structure. The position resembles the Albin Countergambit but with a key difference: White's pawn is on f4, making the e3 pawn a target.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, be willing to return material to destroy the opponent's pawn structure and hinder their development. A weak pawn on e3 can become a long-term target.
notes.plans: Black should aim to develop quickly, castle long, and apply pressure on the e3 pawn, possibly with moves like ...Bc5 and ...Qd7, preparing to strike when White commits to b3.

notes.explains: Black has a strong position with the e3 pawn under attack. White's b3 move creates a tactical opportunity: Black can play ...Bc5, hitting e3, and if White defends, there may be a combination involving ...Nd4, ...Bxc2, and ...Re8, exploiting the dark-square weaknesses and the alignment of the white king and rook on the a1-h8 diagonal.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to wait for the opponent to commit to a move that weakens their position before striking. Look for tactical motifs like discovered attacks or checks that hit two pieces at once.
notes.plans: Black should continue to target the e3 pawn and the dark squares, possibly with ...Ng4 to double the attack, and be ready to sacrifice the exchange for a winning attack.

notes.explains: Black has a choice between castling and further development. Castling immediately would allow White to exchange knights on d5 and then play f4, creating attacking chances. By delaying castling and developing the knight to f6 first, Black keeps more options and avoids weakening the kingside.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to castle if it gives the opponent a target. Sometimes it's better to complete development first, keeping the king in the center temporarily, to avoid committing to a side that might become weak.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing with ...Nf6, ...Be7, and ...O-O, but only after ensuring that White's potential f4 advance is not dangerous. If White plays f4 prematurely, Black can respond with ...g6 and ...Bh6 to challenge the bishop.

notes.explains: In this position, Black delays castling to avoid allowing White to exchange knights on d5 and then exploit weaknesses with moves like g6 and Bh6, which would leave Black's position full of holes.
notes.teaches: Develop your pieces first before deciding whether to castle; castling too early can invite tactics that target your king's future shelter.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Nbd7 and ...Nf6, keeping the king in the center until the moment is safe, then castles once White's immediate threats are neutralized.

notes.explains: When White launches a flank attack with g4, Black correctly responds with the central break ...c5, because flank attacks must be countered in the center. If Black instead plays passively, White's attack would crush the king.
notes.teaches: Against a flank attack, seek active counterplay in the center rather than trying to keep the position closed.
notes.plans: Black plays ...c5, opening lines and creating counterplay, while White's attack loses momentum.

notes.explains: In the resulting opposite-colored bishop middlegame, Black's bishop on b7 proves stronger than White's on c3 because the attacking side's bishop is more active and supports the initiative.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop positions, the side with the more aggressive and active bishop often has the advantage, even if material is equal.
notes.plans: Black continues to press with ...Rook e3, restricting White's queen and preparing ...Qh1+ and ...Rf3, leading to a decisive attack.

notes.explains: In the first game, black kept the king on e8 and did not castle, which was safe because the position was closed. This allowed black to launch an attack on white's king, which was exposed on b1, while black's own king remained protected.
notes.teaches: Deciding whether to castle depends on the nature of the position: in closed positions, keeping the king in the center can be safe and even beneficial for launching an attack, but in open positions, the king becomes vulnerable and castling is usually necessary.
notes.plans: When the position is closed, consider delaying castling to use the extra tempo for attack, but be ready to castle if the position opens up.

notes.explains: In the second game, black played c5 prematurely, opening the position while the king was still in the center. White immediately opened the center with dxc5 and used a pin on the d7 knight to exploit black's uncastled king, leading to a material win.
notes.teaches: If you choose not to castle, you must avoid opening the position, as an exposed king in an open center is a serious liability. Open positions demand that the king be castled to safety.
notes.plans: When the opponent leaves their king in the center, look for ways to open the position and create pins or attacks against the uncastled king.

notes.explains: In the endgame-themed game, black faced development difficulties with pieces in each other's way. The move ...Ne7 was played, but an alternative exotic plan with ...Be3, ...Bd8, ...Bb2 was also possible. White's g4 push was not effective because black could respond ...Nh4, making the g4 pawn weak.
notes.teaches: When development is awkward, look for non-standard but sound ways to untangle, such as rerouting pieces through unusual squares. Avoid pawn pushes that create permanent weaknesses without clear benefit.
notes.plans: Develop harmoniously, aiming to castle kingside, and consider piece maneuvers like ...Nf5 and ...Bb7 to complete development.

notes.explains: In this position, developing the bishop to b7 is often the most natural way to complete development, while an early g4 pawn push can become a weakness if the opponent responds with Nh4, leaving the pawn exposed.
notes.teaches: Avoid creating pawn weaknesses in the opening unless there is a clear concrete benefit; prefer sound development over speculative pawn advances.
notes.plans: Develop pieces harmoniously, castle, and only consider flank pawn pushes when they support a concrete plan.

notes.explains: White's idea of playing f5 runs into tactical problems because after exf5 and Nxc5, the queen is exposed on the long diagonal, so White first plays Kh1 to sidestep potential checks and then proceeds with f5.
notes.teaches: Before initiating a pawn break, check for tactical refutations, especially along open diagonals; sometimes a preparatory king move is necessary to avoid harassment.
notes.plans: White aims to play f5 to gain space and activate pieces, but must first ensure the king is safe from diagonal attacks.

notes.explains: Black's Nb4 is a strong move, pinning the knight and attacking the c2 pawn. White wisely avoids c2 because it would allow Nxc2+ and the e3 square becomes weak, so White instead plays a3 to drive the knight away, though this costs time.
notes.teaches: When a knight jumps to b4, consider whether to allow it or to kick it with a3, but be careful not to create weaknesses on squares like c2 or e3; sometimes the pin is more dangerous than the pawn loss.
notes.plans: Black will try to exploit the weakened squares, while White must consolidate and find active play.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, Black is better because his king is more active and the knight is much stronger than the bishop, which is blocked by its own pawns on g5.
notes.teaches: In endgames and simplified middlegames, piece activity and king position often outweigh material; a knight can dominate a bad bishop that is hemmed in by its own pawns.
notes.plans: Black should seek to open the position to create entry points for the king, while White should try to keep the position closed and blockade.

notes.explains: Black's a6 was imprecise; the position is about to become closed, so Black should have played Kg6 to bring the king toward the center and prepare infiltration via f5. After White closes the queenside with a4 and b5, there are no entry points left, and even a protected passed pawn on d5 is not enough to win.
notes.teaches: In closed endgames, the king must be centralized and active early; once the opponent seals the position, it may be impossible to break through, so you must create entry points before the position locks up.
notes.plans: Black should have aimed for Kg6-f5 to infiltrate, while White's plan is to blockade all entry points and force a draw.

notes.explains: In the London system, White's Nc4 is a clever way to defend the b2 pawn, because if Black takes on b2, the rook on a1 would trap the queen, but here Black's bishop on f5 provides an escape square on c2, so the tactic is not fully effective.
notes.teaches: When defending a pawn, look for tactical resources that also develop pieces; but always check if the opponent has a resource to escape the trap.
notes.plans: White continues development and aims to maintain the center, while Black seeks counterplay on the queenside with a5 and b5.

notes.explains: When the opponent has an advantage in the center, you should seek counterplay on the flanks. Black does this with a5 and b5, trying to expand on the queenside and push White back.
notes.teaches: If you are worse in the center, don't fight there directly; instead, create play on the flanks to distract and undermine the opponent's central control.
notes.plans: Black will continue to advance the queenside pawns, while White must find a way to neutralize this expansion and maintain the center.

notes.explains: A tactical trick like Nc4 may threaten to trap the queen, but the presence of a bishop on f5 can give the queen an escape square, so the tactic fails.
notes.teaches: Before relying on a tactical motif, check if the opponent's pieces cover the key escape squares.

notes.explains: In the Sämisch King's Indian, after d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 f3 O-O Nge2, black's modern approach is …a6, preparing ...b5 to challenge the center and the c4 pawn. This is a relatively new and dynamic idea, aiming for quick counterplay rather than the traditional ...e5 or ...c5 structures.
notes.teaches: When facing a setup like the Sämisch, black can use a flank pawn move like ...a6 to provoke weaknesses and create immediate tension in the center. The key is to challenge the opponent's pawn chain before they consolidate.
notes.plans: Black plans to follow up with ...b5, sacrificing a pawn if necessary to open lines and develop rapid piece activity, especially on the queenside and center.

notes.explains: A knight on h5 can pressure a bishop, so White should consider h3 to give the bishop a retreat square on h2.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like h3 can prevent harassment of a bishop and keep it active.
notes.plans: Play h3 to secure the bishop and avoid losing tempo.

notes.explains: Taking with the f-pawn away from the center (exf4) leaves the pawn off-center, which is a structural concession.
notes.teaches: Pawns generally should capture toward the center to maintain central influence.

notes.explains: In the endgame, the king is the strongest piece. Here Black's king is much better placed than White's, giving Black a big advantage.
notes.teaches: Always evaluate king activity in the endgame; an active king is a decisive asset.
notes.plans: Activate the king and use it to support pawn advances.

notes.explains: When a pawn up, creating a passed pawn and exchanging rooks are key techniques to convert the advantage.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, aim to create a passed pawn and trade rooks to simplify.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn or exchange rooks to reach a winning pawn endgame.

notes.explains: White's ideal defensive setup is a pawn structure like h4, g3, f2, which creates a barricade that makes the position drawish.
notes.teaches: In a worse endgame, a solid pawn structure can hold the draw if the opponent has insufficient material.
notes.plans: White should try to play h4 and g3 to set up a fortress.

notes.explains: Black must prevent White from setting up the defensive structure, so he uses tempo moves and pawn breaks like g5 or f4 to cramp White.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a defensive plan, use active moves to disrupt it before it is established.
notes.plans: Play h5, rook checks, and pawn breaks to keep White from consolidating.

notes.explains: In this position, Black can consider moves like g5 or f4 to stop White's h4, but h4 is even stronger because it cramps White's position permanently and likely wins the game for Black.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, look for pawn pushes that restrict your opponent's pieces and create long-term weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play h4 to cramp White's kingside, then continue to improve your pieces and prepare to exploit the space advantage.

notes.explains: Black achieved a passed pawn, the white king is offside, and the white rook is far from the defense, attacking the black king instead. White tries to mate but fails, and Black's passed pawn rolls to promotion.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, a passed pawn is a decisive advantage, especially when the enemy king is out of the square and the rook is tied down.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawn with the king's support, while keeping the rook active to block checks and escort the pawn to promotion.

notes.explains: When you are a pawn up in an endgame, you need to open up the position and exchange pieces to convert the advantage, but you must keep some pawns on the board to have one to promote.
notes.teaches: To win a pawn-up endgame, trade pieces but not all pawns; keep enough pawns to create a passer and promote.
notes.plans: Aim to simplify into a winning pawn endgame by exchanging pieces while preserving a healthy pawn majority.

notes.explains: In this study, white has a bishop and pawn versus black's bishop, with the pawn heading toward a corner square that is the wrong color for white's bishop. Black's defensive task is to get his king to that corner, which would secure a draw because the bishop cannot force the pawn's promotion.
notes.teaches: Studies are valuable because they illustrate important chess ideas in a dramatic, concentrated form. Even if the exact position seems artificial, the underlying theme—here, the wrong-colored bishop and the defender's goal of reaching the corner—appears in real games.
notes.plans: White must find the only winning move, which involves using the bishop to control the key squares and prevent black's king from reaching the corner. Black, if given the move, would immediately head for the corner with his king.

notes.explains: The excerpt highlights that even strong players can struggle with studies, but they are a common training tool among top grandmasters. The difficulty lies in finding the single winning move, which often requires precise calculation and understanding of the theme.
notes.teaches: Solving studies improves calculation and pattern recognition. The best players use them to sharpen their skills, and the ability to solve them quickly comes with practice.

notes.explains: If it were black's turn in this position, black would play his king toward the corner (e.g., Kg1), threatening to reach the drawing square. If white's king moves instead of the bishop, black can simply take the pawn and draw.
notes.teaches: In bishop-and-pawn endgames, the defender's priority is to get the king to the queening square if it is the wrong color for the attacker's bishop. The attacker must use the bishop to cut off the king's path.
notes.plans: White must move the bishop to a square that prevents black's king from reaching the corner, while also supporting the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: With the black king near the corner and a lone pawn, the defender's king can head for the corner to force a draw. If the attacker's king is too far, the pawn cannot promote because the defender can shuffle in the corner.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn vs king, the defending king must run to the corner in front of the pawn. The attacker needs his king to support the pawn and control the promotion square.
notes.plans: The defender should move the king toward the corner (e.g., Kg1) and then stay in the corner, only moving when necessary to avoid stalemate.

notes.explains: When the pawn is on the rook file and the bishop is the wrong color (not controlling the promotion square), the defender can hold the draw by staying in the corner. The attacker cannot force the king out because any approach leads to stalemate.
notes.teaches: In bishop and pawn vs king, if the bishop does not control the promotion square and the defending king reaches the corner, the game is drawn. The attacker must have the bishop on the correct color to win.
notes.plans: The attacker should try to use the bishop to cut off the king's path to the corner, but if the bishop is the wrong color, the win is impossible.

notes.explains: The defender's king can stay in the corner, and if the attacker tries to bring his king closer, it results in stalemate. The attacker cannot force the king out because the defender has no legal moves when the king is in the corner.
notes.teaches: Stalemate is a key defensive resource in the endgame. When the defending king is trapped in the corner, the attacker must avoid stalemate while trying to promote.
notes.plans: The defender should aim to reach the corner and then only move when forced, maintaining the draw.

notes.explains: With a bishop and pawn against a lone king, if the defending king can reach the corner of the opposite color to the bishop, it can draw by heading to the corner and staying there. The attacking side cannot force the king out without risking stalemate.
notes.teaches: Recognize the drawing fortress: a king in the 'wrong' corner (the corner not controlled by the bishop's color) can hold a draw against a bishop and pawn if the pawn cannot be queened without stalemate.
notes.plans: If you are the defender, head for the safe corner and stay there. If you are the attacker, avoid allowing the king to reach that corner; use your bishop to control the key escape squares.

notes.explains: The key to winning with bishop and pawn is to use the bishop to cut off the defending king from the queening square or from the drawing corner. The bishop must be placed on the correct diagonal to control the critical square.
notes.teaches: In bishop-and-pawn endings, the bishop's role is to control the square the enemy king needs to cross. Identify the critical square and place the bishop on the diagonal that covers it.
notes.plans: Calculate the race: visualize the king's path to the corner, determine which square must be controlled, and position the bishop accordingly. Then advance the pawn with the king's support.

notes.explains: When the defending king is forced to move away from the pawn's path, the pawn can advance. The bishop's placement on the right diagonal forces the king to abandon its blockade.
notes.teaches: Use the bishop to create a zugzwang-like situation: the defender must move, allowing the pawn to advance. The bishop's diagonal should be chosen to restrict the king's options.
notes.plans: Once the bishop is on the correct diagonal, push the pawn step by step, using the king to support it, while the bishop keeps the enemy king away.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn versus king and bishop endgame, the black king is trying to reach the queening square to draw, while white aims to promote. The black king has two possible routes to the corner, and the defender must choose the right path to intercept the pawn.
notes.teaches: When defending, identify all possible paths for the enemy king to reach the queening square and ensure your own king can get into the 'box' to stop the pawn. The defending king must be able to catch the pawn if it advances.
notes.plans: Black should head towards the queening square, using the most direct route, while white should use the bishop to control key squares and support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: The white king is not yet able to support the pawn, so the bishop must be used to control the queening square and keep the black king away. The bishop can also be used to block the black king's path.
notes.teaches: In endgames with bishop and pawn, the bishop often needs to be deployed to cut off the enemy king's approach, while the pawn advances. The bishop can be sacrificed if it ensures promotion.
notes.plans: White should aim to place the bishop on a diagonal that controls the queening square, then advance the pawn, using the king to support when possible.

notes.explains: The black king is in the 'box' and can catch the pawn if it advances, so white must use the bishop to create a barrier. The black king's path is being contested, and both sides are maneuvering for control of key squares.
notes.teaches: When the defending king is in the box, the attacking side must use the bishop to restrict the king's movement, often by placing it on a diagonal that prevents the king from approaching the pawn's path.
notes.plans: White should continue to use the bishop to control squares like d6 and e5, while advancing the pawn when safe. Black should keep the king active and look for chances to blockade.

notes.explains: The pawn must be pushed immediately because the black king is racing to the corner. Moving the king first wastes time and allows the black king to get there.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, every tempo matters. Prioritize pawn advancement over king moves when the opponent's king is close to a key square.
notes.plans: Push the pawn as fast as possible, using the bishop to support its advance and to control the black king's entry squares.

notes.explains: White tries to cut off the black king's path to the corner. The bishop is used to control light squares, but the black king finds a way around, so white must find the precise square to block the king's progress.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, the bishop's color complex is crucial. Use the bishop to control the squares of the color that the enemy king needs to cross.
notes.plans: Place the bishop on a square that covers the key light squares, and coordinate with the pawn to create a barrier.

notes.explains: The black king is almost at the corner, but white finds a bishop move that cuts off the king's path, preventing further progress. This is the critical moment where the defense succeeds.
notes.teaches: A single bishop move can completely stop the enemy king's advance if it controls the right squares. Look for such moves when the king is near the corner.
notes.plans: Once the king is cut off, bring the white king closer to support the pawn's promotion, while keeping the bishop on the key diagonal.

notes.explains: In this pawn endgame, the winning idea is to use the king to support the pawn's advance. The defender's king must eventually move out of the way, allowing the pawn to push forward and promote.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn, your king should lead it up the board, staying close enough to support it. The defender's king will be forced to give way, and then you can advance the pawn.
notes.plans: Bring the king closer to the pawn, then push the pawn when the opposing king is forced to move aside.

notes.explains: The engine line shows that running behind the pawn or choosing certain squares can lead to a loss, while other moves like A5 or Bishop D6 work. The key is to find the correct path for the king.
notes.teaches: In endgames, precise king maneuvering is critical. A single wrong step can turn a win into a draw or loss, so you must calculate the king's route carefully.
notes.plans: Choose the correct king route to support the pawn, avoiding squares that allow the defender to stop the promotion.

notes.explains: These studies are simple in terms of piece count but can be extremely tricky. The challenge lies in finding the precise sequence of moves.
notes.teaches: Endgame studies are excellent training tools because they force you to think deeply about piece coordination and exact move orders. Solving them improves your overall chess understanding.

notes.explains: In the Two Knights Opening, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4, Black should play ...d5. The knight on c6 has few good squares, and if Black does nothing, White will build a strong center. Playing ...d5 strikes in the center, gains a tempo on the queen or bishop, and creates a safe square for the knight on f6 or d7.
notes.teaches: Understand the purpose of your opening moves rather than memorizing lines. When your opponent builds a center, you must challenge it. A move like ...d5 can be both a tempo move and a way to improve your piece placement.
notes.plans: After ...d5, if White captures, Black can recapture and later castle queenside, relying on the strong center and the closed e-file to keep the king safe.

notes.explains: In the position after ...d5, Black's king may appear stuck in the center if the e-file opens, but Black has not committed to castling kingside. Castling queenside is a viable option, and White is not developed enough to exploit the central king. The e-file can be closed, and Black has a strong center.
notes.teaches: Do not fear an open center if your king can find safety on the other side. Evaluate the opponent's development: if they are behind, your king may be safe even in the center for a few moves.
notes.plans: Black can castle queenside, develop the bishop to b6, and bring the queen out, with a comfortable position.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...d5, White may pin the knight with Bb5. Black should consider taking with the bishop rather than the knight, because recapturing with the knight loses a tempo and allows the bishop to escape. The resulting pawn structure is compromised for White, and the knight can be kicked away.
notes.teaches: In the Two Knights, the move ...d5 creates a safe square for the knight, but you must be careful about recapture choices. Avoid losing tempi in the opening; prefer moves that develop and maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: Black aims to exploit White's weak pawn structure and the misplaced knight, while completing development.

notes.explains: Black played ...Rb8, a move that makes developing the bishop to b7 more difficult, but it costs time. White can use this to gain a tempo by attacking the b-pawn with Nb3, forcing Black to respond. Black's kingside development is delayed, and the king remains in the center.
notes.teaches: Every move should have a purpose, but be wary of moves that are too slow. If you spend time on the queenside, your opponent may gain a tempo and accelerate their attack.
notes.plans: White will continue to develop and put pressure on Black's center, while Black must find a way to catch up in development and castle.

notes.explains: Black played ...f6 early, trying to open lines for the bishops, but this is risky because the king is still in the center. Opening the center when your king is uncastled is generally bad, as it gives the opponent targets. White should look to exploit the exposed king by opening lines.
notes.teaches: General rule: if your king is in the center, keep the center closed until you have castled. Do not voluntarily open the position when your king is vulnerable. Your opponent will play where your king is.
notes.plans: White can consider moves like Re1 to pressure the e-file, or prepare to open the center with f4 or d5, aiming at Black's king.

notes.explains: In positions with a weak king and weak dark squares, exchanging pieces that defend the dark squares can leave the opponent with a bad bishop and a vulnerable king.
notes.teaches: Identify which pieces are good for both sides. If you can trade off the opponent's good defender, your remaining pieces can dominate the weak squares.
notes.plans: Aim to place a knight on a strong outpost like c5, where it controls key dark squares and cannot be captured by the opponent's bad bishop.

notes.explains: A bishop on a7 can be a tempo move, forcing the rook to move and gaining time to improve your pieces while the opponent's king is still vulnerable.
notes.teaches: Use tempo moves to gain time for development and to improve your position while the opponent is forced to react.
notes.plans: After the bishop move, continue with artificial castling (king to f7, rook to g8) and then place a bishop on d4 to control the dark squares.

notes.explains: When you have two bishops, you need open positions to make them strong. Passive play wastes their potential.
notes.teaches: With the bishop pair, strive for active piece play and pawn breaks (like c5, d4) to open the position and give the bishops scope.
notes.plans: Consider rook lifts like Rook b4 to create threats (e.g., Rook g4) and keep the initiative, rather than playing passively.

notes.explains: A knight on b3 can be strong when it supports a c5 outpost, but becomes bad if the pawn structure changes (e.g., if c5 is pushed).
notes.teaches: Evaluate pieces dynamically: a piece's value depends on the pawn structure and the squares it can control.
notes.plans: If the opponent's knight is bad, try to exploit its poor placement by targeting weak squares and using your active pieces.

notes.explains: Before pushing a pawn like c4, consider whether it weakens your own pawns or gives the opponent a strong central outpost.
notes.teaches: Pawn breaks must be timed carefully; avoid moves that create weaknesses or allow the opponent's pieces to become active.
notes.plans: Calculate concrete tactics before committing to a pawn push, and look for moves that improve your pieces first.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's pieces are not yet coordinated enough to justify an immediate rook lift like Rg2. The bishop on h3 lacks a follow-up, so the attack stalls.
notes.teaches: Before committing to an aggressive move, ensure your pieces are coordinated and you have a concrete follow-up. A flashy move without support is often a waste of tempo.
notes.plans: Develop naturally and improve piece placement before starting a direct attack.

notes.explains: Black's pawn on c5 is a key defender, keeping the knight out of d4. Playing c4 would allow the knight to jump to d4, giving Black a strong centralized piece.
notes.teaches: Do not weaken your pawn structure or open lines for the opponent's pieces without a very specific reason. Pawns often serve as guardians of key squares.
notes.plans: Keep the c5 pawn intact to restrict the enemy knight's access to d4.

notes.explains: Black's initiative and the bishop pair are significant advantages. The bishop on e6 is better than on c6 because it keeps the h3 diagonal open, preserving tactical ideas like Bh3.
notes.teaches: When choosing between two good squares for a piece, consider which one leaves more options open for future tactical motifs. Flexibility is a key asset.
notes.plans: Place the bishop on e6 to maintain pressure and keep the h3 diagonal available.

notes.explains: Black's worst piece is the bishop on d8, but after the pawn structure changes, it can go to g5, threatening to jump to e3 and suffocate White's position. This creates long-term pressure.
notes.teaches: In a closed or semi-closed position, find a way to activate your worst piece. A bishop that can dominate a long diagonal can be worth more than a pawn.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g5, aiming for e3 to restrict White's pieces and increase pressure.

notes.explains: White's queen is overworked, trying to defend multiple key points. Black's pieces are all aimed at the king, so it's time to look for tactics. The move Qg3 is strong because it gives White the fewest options and maintains the mating threat.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is overloaded, look for tactical blows that exploit the overload. Choose the most forcing and least risky continuation to keep the initiative.
notes.plans: Play Qg3, threatening mate and forcing White into a helpless position.

notes.explains: Black sacrificed a pawn for long-term compensation: active pieces and a lasting attack. There is no need to rush to prove the sacrifice correct; the positional pressure is enough.
notes.teaches: When you have long-term compensation for material, you don't need to force immediate tactics. Let the opponent struggle to coordinate while your pieces dominate.
notes.plans: Maintain the pressure and slowly improve piece placement, converting the initiative into a win.

notes.explains: After sacrificing a pawn, the compensation is long-term: the opponent's knight is out of play, the bishop on e5 is isolated and unsupported, and the queen is offside. The pieces are scattered, so there is no immediate need to force tactics.
notes.teaches: When you have long-term compensation for a pawn, you should improve your pieces calmly rather than rush to justify the sacrifice. Give your opponent time to stumble while you build up pressure.
notes.plans: Keep improving piece placement, target the weak squares, and avoid forcing lines until the accumulated pressure breaks through.

notes.explains: The opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated: the bishop on e5 is alone and aiming at a defended square, the queen is out of the game, and the knight is useless. White should have tried to break the pawn chain with c3 but played too slowly.
notes.teaches: When facing a cramped or scattered position, look for pawn breaks to undermine the opponent's structure before they can consolidate. Delay allows the opponent to improve all their pieces to ideal squares.
notes.plans: If you are White, prioritize c3 to challenge the pawn chain; if you are Black, continue improving without rushing.

notes.explains: In a closed Italian-like position, the choice of recapture after an exchange on e4 depends on the rook's placement. If the rook has already moved to f1, taking with the pawn opens the f-file and gives the rook a clear path; otherwise, taking with the knight or queen is also playable.
notes.teaches: When deciding how to recapture, consider which file you open and whether your rook is ready to use it. In closed positions, you often have time to reroute pieces, so both recaptures can be fine.
notes.plans: If you took with the pawn, plan to play Nf1, then Rf1, using the open f-file. Black can aim for d4 to challenge the center.

notes.explains: The position is close and not much is happening, so White has time to reroute pieces. Black has a better center with e5 versus d3, and the d3 pawn is a weakness. White's pieces are cramped.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, central pawn majorities and weak enemy pawns are long-term assets. Use the time to improve your pieces and prepare breaks like d4.
notes.plans: Black can play moves like Nf6, Rf1, and prepare d4. White should try to activate the knight and control e4.

notes.explains: A specific move like b4 stands out because it attacks a piece and puts pressure on the e-file, creating a concrete threat. General moves like Rd1 are less forcing.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice between a general improvement and a specific attacking move, look for the move that creates immediate threats or exploits a tactical weakness.
notes.plans: Continue with the plan of pressuring the e-pawn and preparing d4, while using the b4 move to gain tempo.

notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez, the bishop on c2 can look active but often attacks only defended points. The real pressure is on e5, defended by the knight and queen. To make progress, you need to target the defenders themselves.
notes.teaches: A piece that attacks a defended point is not necessarily useful; look for ways to increase pressure on the defenders or redirect your pieces to more effective squares.
notes.plans: Consider moves like b4 to attack the knight on c6, or a4-a5 to place the bishop on a4, increasing pressure on the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: When White plays d4 and Black captures, recapturing with the knight (instead of the pawn) can look weakening, but here it opens the e-file and prepares a knight maneuver to f5. The idea is to have both knights access f5, a key outpost.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you make a move that seems to violate general principles (like closing a rook's file) because you have a concrete long-term plan. Always have a specific reason for such moves.
notes.plans: After Nxd4, play Nf5 if possible, and then Qg3 to target h6 and g7, provoking weaknesses.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and can simplify to an endgame if the attack fizzles. The pressure on Black's position makes it easy for Black to blunder, as seen when Black collapses under the sustained attack.
notes.teaches: If your attack doesn't break through, you can still be up material and win the endgame. Also, sustained pressure often induces blunders from the defender.
notes.plans: Keep the initiative, maintain the pin, and bring the remaining knight to f5. If Black blunders, take the piece.

notes.explains: The move fxe3 (or similar) goes against general principles because it closes the rook's file, but White has a long-term plan to bring the rook back and play d4 later. This illustrates the importance of keeping an open mind and not being dogmatic about rules.
notes.teaches: Always evaluate moves based on concrete plans, not just general principles. Sometimes you must break rules to achieve a deeper idea.

notes.explains: Playing f3 with a rook on e1 closes the rook's file, which seems wrong, but White has a long-term plan to bring the rook back and push d4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must break general principles (like keeping files open) if you have a concrete long-term plan that justifies it.
notes.plans: Rook returns to f1 or similar, then d4 to strike in the center.

notes.explains: After White played b4, the game shifted to the queenside, and the bishop on a4 created pressure on f5. This shows that the position was not one-sided.
notes.teaches: Always keep an open mind and consider the whole board, not just one side. Opportunities can arise on the flank you least expect.
notes.plans: Keep monitoring both wings and be ready to switch the focus of the attack.

notes.explains: Playing Nd4 to capture is ugly and creates a weakness, but it was done for a specific tactical reason. The move is justified if the calculation works.
notes.teaches: You can intentionally create weaknesses if you have a concrete tactical justification. But if you play such moves without calculation, your intuition is flawed.
notes.plans: Follow up on the tactical idea that justified the move, then proceed to win the pawns.

notes.explains: This game, Lasker vs Capablanca from St. Petersburg 1914, is a strategic masterpiece where Lasker outplays Capablanca in the middlegame and endgame. The point is not to nitpick computer variations but to appreciate the overall plan and execution.
notes.teaches: When studying classic games, focus on the strategic ideas and the flow of the game rather than getting lost in engine analysis. The beauty lies in the conception and execution of a plan.

notes.explains: After the exchange of queens, White has a central pawn majority (four vs three) which Lasker tries to utilize with f4 and e5. Black's move ...Re8 is fine, but Kasparov and Dr. Tarrasch preferred ...f5 to immediately undermine the center. White's e5 is natural, but Black's counterplay with ...Bc5 and ...b6 gives him chances.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn majority, it's often crucial to challenge it immediately with pawn breaks like ...f5. A strong-looking center can be undermined if you act quickly. Also, opposite-colored bishops can offer defensive resources and counterplay.
notes.plans: Black plans ...c5 and ...Bb7, activating the bishop and creating pressure on the queenside, while White tries to maintain the central bind.

notes.explains: The pawn on e5 looks strong, but black's counterintuitive capture and subsequent b6 to stop the bishop's pin can leave black very much in the game. Opposite-colored bishops can reduce white's attacking potential.
notes.teaches: A strong-looking center pawn can be neutralized by precise counterplay, and opposite-colored bishops often favor the defender in the middlegame.
notes.plans: Black aims to develop the bishop to b7 and play c5, challenging white's center.

notes.explains: When the opponent threatens to push e5, and you cannot prevent it directly, you must work around it. The move f5 is a radical way to challenge the center, even if it seems to leave e5 weak forever.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must abandon conventional square control and create dynamic imbalances to solve positional problems.
notes.plans: After f5, white aims to undermine black's center and create play on the kingside or in the center.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on b7 allows white to double black's pawns, but this trades one advantage for another: the pawn structure a6-b6-c6-d6 becomes vulnerable, and the squares around it weak.
notes.teaches: Doubling pawns is not always bad; it can be a defensive asset, but it may create long-term weaknesses in the pawn chain.
notes.plans: White will target the weak pawns and squares, while black must defend carefully.

notes.explains: A knight on e6 can be a 'thorn in the side'—a very strong piece that is hard to dislodge. Black's attempt to activate the rook and defend the d-pawn may not address the knight's power.
notes.teaches: A well-placed knight in the enemy position can be worth more than material; you must often take measures to evict it or neutralize it.
notes.plans: White will build on the knight's dominance, while black should consider retreating the bishop to c8 to challenge it.

notes.explains: In this game, the position after the buildup is where the real action begins. Black's position may look similar, but white's pieces have improved dramatically, especially the knight.
notes.teaches: Positional advantages are built gradually; the final position may look similar to the initial one, but the piece placement and pawn structure tell the real story.
notes.plans: White continues to exploit the knight's strength and the weaknesses in black's camp.

notes.explains: A knight on e6 is a powerful outpost, acting as a thorn in the opponent's side and restricting their pieces. The position is closed, and White has a serious positional advantage.
notes.teaches: A well-supported knight deep in enemy territory can be worth more than its nominal value, tying down pieces and limiting activity.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the knight on e6 while improving other pieces and preparing a pawn break to open lines.

notes.explains: Black faces a critical decision: whether to sacrifice the exchange (rook for knight and pawn) to open the position and activate pieces. The engine recommends taking on e6, but it's a difficult human decision due to material concerns.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, material can be less important than activity; sometimes sacrificing the exchange is necessary to activate your pieces and create counterplay.
notes.plans: If Black declines the sacrifice, they must find other ways to generate activity, but passive play will likely lead to a slow loss.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on a8 is passive, and the rook on a7 is stuck on a dead-end file. White is preparing g4-g5 to open the position, and Black's pieces are poorly placed.
notes.teaches: Avoid placing pieces on squares where they have no future; a passive piece is a serious liability. Also, when the opponent is better developed, opening the position can be dangerous.
notes.plans: White should continue with the pawn push g5 to open lines and exploit Black's passive pieces. Black should seek active piece play, even if it means material concessions.

notes.explains: Black's last chance is to take on h4, even though the pawn will come back, to create some activity. Instead, Black plays Nb6, which allows White to consolidate and maintain control.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must make uncomfortable moves to create counterplay; allowing the opponent to keep a bind can be fatal. Also, avoid allowing counterplay when you have a winning advantage.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve pieces and control files, while Black must try to activate the knight and rook, even at material cost.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's pieces are passive and White has control of the open files. The rook on h8 is active, and the knight can maneuver to e5 or d6, creating strong threats. Black is struggling to find counterplay.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are passive, you should avoid unnecessary risks and maintain pressure by controlling open files and improving your pieces to their best squares.
notes.plans: Continue to control the open files with rooks, improve the knight to a strong central outpost, and prepare to exploit Black's lack of activity.

notes.explains: White has a winning position, but instead of playing a prosaic winning move, White finds a brilliant sacrifice to vacate the e4 square for the knight, leading to a family fork and decisive material gain.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the most forcing or obvious continuation is not the best; look for tactical resources that improve your piece coordination and create greater threats.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, the knight goes to e4, threatening a fork on f6. If Black defends, the knight can continue to c5, winning material.

notes.explains: Against a tactical, aggressive opponent like Marshall, Lasker chooses a quiet move (Qe2) that invites an early queen trade, steering the game into an endgame where Black's tactical chances are minimized.
notes.teaches: Adjust your opening choices to your opponent's style. If your opponent thrives in complex tactical battles, consider simplifying to a position where their strengths are neutralized.
notes.plans: After the queen trade, White aims for a solid, slightly better endgame with no counterplay for Black.

notes.explains: Black avoids trading queens and instead plays for complications, but this leads to an asymmetrical position with dangers. Black's bishop on g3 can be taken, but rushing to take it opens the h-file and creates a pin against the rook, tying down the queen.
notes.teaches: Do not rush to capture a piece if it is not going anywhere. Consider the consequences of the resulting pawn structure and open lines before taking.
notes.plans: White can use the open h-file and the pin to create pressure, while Black must be careful not to overextend.

notes.explains: Black's move d5 is an inaccuracy. If Black had played Nb6, the game might have been dull, but d5 gives White a target. Black is one move away from castling, which would solve his problems, but White has a strong plan to prevent it.
notes.teaches: In the opening/middlegame, look for ways to prevent the opponent from castling and to create weaknesses in their pawn structure.
notes.plans: White should seek a plan to exploit the d5 pawn and keep the black king in the center.

notes.explains: White chooses a plan starting with a move that looks strong, forcing a response, then Qb5, attacking both b7 and d5. At first it seems White wins a pawn, but Black can castle, and the d5 pawn is poisoned because of tactical tricks: if White takes, Black can respond with Qg5+ forking king and queen, and the knight cannot move due to the undefended rook on h1.
notes.teaches: Be wary of 'poisoned pawns' – a pawn that appears free to take but is protected by tactical resources. Always calculate the consequences of capturing before grabbing material.
notes.plans: White should not take the d5 pawn but instead continue with the attack, using the queen to create threats.

notes.explains: White plays Qa5, attacking a7 and creating serious threats. Black cannot defend passively; giving up the pawn and hoping to survive the ending is not humanly acceptable. Kb8 would lose to Nb5 with a double attack on a7 and c7, so Black tries a6.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a strong attack, sometimes material must be sacrificed to survive, but it is often better to seek active counterplay rather than passively defend.
notes.plans: White continues the attack, exploiting the weaknesses on the queenside and the black king's exposure.

notes.explains: In this position, the pawn on a7 is attacked, and while computers might suggest giving it up and entering a defensive endgame, a human player cannot accept such a passive approach. The immediate king move to b8 fails to a knight fork on b5 hitting both a7 and c7.
notes.teaches: When defending, prefer active resistance over passive pawn sacrifices, even if engines suggest survival is possible. Always check for tactical refutations like forks before committing to a defensive move.
notes.plans: Black should seek a way to defend the pawn while maintaining piece activity, possibly by advancing the a-pawn or repositioning pieces to cover key squares.

notes.explains: Black plays a6 to avoid the fork, but White sacrifices the bishop on a6 to expose the king, forcing bxa6 and then Kb8. White's knight on b5 then threatens mate on a7 and c7, and after black's knight goes to b6 to cover c7, White finds the key move Rd3, preparing Rook to b3 and an eventual a4-a5 breakthrough.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be justified by creating multiple threats and tying down the opponent's pieces to defense. The rook lift to d3 is a classic maneuver to bring the rook into the attack while maintaining pressure on the c-file.
notes.plans: White continues with a4, Rook b3, and a5 to open lines against the black king, while black is forced to defend against the constant mate threats.

notes.explains: Black tries to defend with checks and piece moves, but White's attack is overwhelming. The move Rook b3 is winning despite appearances, and even alternative moves like f4 are possible. Black's attempts to block the c-file with Bishop d6 fail to the knight taking on d6.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, keep the initiative by giving checks and maintaining threats. Even if the opponent finds defensive resources, the attacker should look for ways to increase pressure, such as opening more lines.
notes.plans: White continues to press with the rook on b3 and the pawn advance a4-a5, eventually forcing mate or winning material.

notes.explains: The game concludes with White's a-pawn advancing to a5, a knight on a7 threatening mate on c6, and after black defends, a5 breaks through. The final sequence involves a queen sacrifice on d2, king moves, and a decisive knight on b5 leading to mate.
notes.teaches: A successful attack often involves a pawn storm against the castled king, combined with piece sacrifices to remove defenders. The attacker must be relentless, using every check and threat to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: White finishes with a mating net, forcing resignation after the queen and knight coordinate.

notes.explains: In the opening, White plays f4, and Black responds with d5. The ideal setup for White is f4, Nf3, and b3, but the move order matters: if White plays Nf3 too early, Black can play g6, and if White plays b3 first, Black can play Bg4 pinning the knight. Therefore, White plays e3 first to prepare the setup.
notes.teaches: In the opening, move order is crucial to achieve the desired setup. Anticipate your opponent's responses and choose a move order that prevents them from disrupting your plans.
notes.plans: White aims to develop the knight to f3 and the bishop to b2, creating pressure on the center and kingside.

notes.explains: In this opening, White aims for a setup with f4, Nf3, and b3, which supports a fianchettoed bishop and controls key central squares. If White delays b3, Black can play ...g6, and if White plays b3 immediately, ...Bg4 can pin the knight. The move ...Bf5 is a natural development before committing the bishop to e7, avoiding burying it.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize developing pieces to active squares before committing to a passive setup. Be aware of timing: if you intend a fianchetto, play it before your opponent can exploit the pin or the pawn push.
notes.plans: White should aim to complete development harmoniously, perhaps with e3, Nf3, b3, and Bb2, while Black should consider ...Bf5 to develop the bishop actively before it gets trapped.

notes.explains: White's setup with a bishop on d3 and pawn on b2 is unusual because the bishop on b2 is blocked by its own pawn and cannot influence the center effectively. White avoided d4 because then the bishop on b2 would be biting on granite against the pawn on e5, which is already well supported.
notes.teaches: A fianchettoed bishop needs open diagonals; if your own pawns block it, the setup may be passive. Avoid placing pieces where they are ineffective, and consider whether a pawn push like d4 would open lines or just create a blockade.
notes.plans: White should seek to open the position or reposition the bishop to a more active diagonal, while Black should maintain the central pawn structure to limit the bishop's scope.

notes.explains: Black played ...Bb7, but a more active idea was ...Ba6, trading off the bishop that x-rays towards the king's intended position. This trade would reduce Black's chances of getting mated. Although ...Bb7 is not a mistake, it misses a chance to simplify.
notes.teaches: In the middlegame, consider trading off pieces that are well-placed against your king. Prophylactic trades can reduce attacking chances and are often worth considering even if not immediately forcing.
notes.plans: Black should look for opportunities to exchange the bishop on d3 or other attacking pieces, while White continues to build up pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: White shifted pieces towards the kingside with Ne2, intending an attack. Black had a chance to play ...Nc5, attacking the bishop on d3, which would have been strong. ...Ne4 was also good, as the knight on e4 would be difficult to dislodge because the f-pawn has moved. Black instead played ...c5, which was natural but not as good.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is preparing an attack, active counterplay in the center or against the attacking pieces can be more effective than passive defense. Look for moves that challenge the opponent's key pieces or create your own threats.
notes.plans: Black should consider ...Nc5 or ...Ne4 to disrupt White's setup, while White continues with Ng3 and Ne5 to build the attack.

notes.explains: Black missed the last chance to play ...g6, which would have created a defensive shield against White's kingside attack. Instead, Black played ...Qc7 and later ...a6, allowing White to launch the attack. White's pieces are massed, and Black's pieces are somewhat misplaced.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like ...g6 can be crucial before the attack starts. It's often better to anticipate threats and prepare defenses early rather than waiting until the attack is in full swing. Sometimes you must play defensively even if you are not yet under direct threat.
notes.plans: Black should have played ...g6 to blunt White's attack, but now White can proceed with the attack, possibly with Nh5 and sacrifices. Black must defend accurately.

notes.explains: White played Nh5, a move that requires deep understanding of the follow-up. If Black takes the knight, White recaptures with the bishop, threatening the rook on a1. This shows how White maximizes the potential of the minor pieces and creates threats.
notes.teaches: Some attacking moves are only playable if you see the follow-up. Before making a sacrifice or a piece offer, calculate the consequences and ensure you have a concrete continuation. Also, look for ways to coordinate your pieces to create multiple threats.
notes.plans: White continues the attack, possibly with sacrifices on h5 or g6, while Black must find the best defense under pressure.

notes.explains: White's minor pieces are all actively placed and ready for an attack, while some black pieces are offside. The key is to eliminate the defenders of the black king.
notes.teaches: Before launching an attack, ensure your pieces are coordinated and identify the opponent's key defenders. A sacrifice to remove those defenders can be decisive.
notes.plans: Play a move like Nh5, attacking the bishop on g7 and the knight on f6, forcing black to deal with multiple threats.

notes.explains: After Nh5, black is in serious trouble. The knight on f6 is a key defender, and the bishop on g7 is also important. Black must resort to desperate measures to survive.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a strong attack, sometimes you must give up material or accept a compromised position to survive. Practical chances may be slim, but you must try.
notes.plans: Black might try to move the f-rook to allow the king to escape, or accept the loss of the f7 pawn.

notes.explains: White's attack is overwhelming. The combination of Bxh7+ and Qxh5+ strips the king of its defenders, and then Bxg7+ further exposes it. The rook on f3 joins the attack.
notes.teaches: A successful attack often involves a series of sacrifices to expose the enemy king. Even if the material is not immediately recovered, the initiative and attacking chances can be worth it.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with Rf3, threatening mate or winning material. If black gives back the piece, white wins back the investment and more.

notes.explains: After the dust settles, white has won a queen for a rook, but has invested two bishops. However, a simple fork with Qd7 wins one of the bishops, leaving white with a decisive material advantage.
notes.teaches: Even when the immediate attack fades, look for tactical resources to convert the initiative into material gains. Forks and other tactics can secure the win.
notes.plans: Play Qd7, forking the bishops, and then convert the material advantage in the endgame.

notes.explains: In this attacking position, the attacker refrains from capturing the d5 pawn immediately because doing so would open lines for the defender's rook, giving it activity. The rooks currently have no open files, so the attack is best conducted with the queen, which can create mischief and coordinate with other pieces.
notes.teaches: When attacking a castled king, avoid premature captures that open lines for the opponent's pieces. Keep the position closed to your opponent's rooks while using your queen to generate threats.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with the queen, aiming to open the f-file for your rook and deliver a decisive check. The final combination will win material and crush the defense.

notes.explains: In the critical position, after the knight captures on h5, the queen must not recapture because of the tactical resource f5. The black king appears safe behind a classic three-pawn shelter, but within two moves, after a series of exchanges and checks, the shelter is stripped away and the king is left exposed.
notes.teaches: A seemingly solid pawn shield around the king can be dismantled quickly through forcing moves. Always consider tactical resources like f5 that prevent the opponent from recapturing with the queen.
notes.plans: Execute the forcing sequence that removes the pawn shelter and delivers check, forcing the defender to give back material and leaving them lost.

notes.explains: A young player who is already near 2500 at 13 shows maturity by not relying on memorized ideas but composing his own plans in the opening.
notes.teaches: Strong players develop their own understanding of positions rather than just following known lines. This independence is a sign of true chess strength.

notes.explains: In the Sicilian, the setup with ...Nc6, ...Be7, ...Qc7 is a classical system, as seen in the famous Kasparov–Karpov 1985 game 24. The usual plan involves a kingside attack with g4, but the move order and piece placement matter.
notes.teaches: Knowing the typical plans in a system is essential, but you must also be aware of tactical nuances like losing tempi or misplaced pieces. The evaluation of a position can change if the opponent can exploit development issues.
notes.plans: If black has lost time with a knight, white can aim to prevent the standard attack and exploit the lead in development.

notes.explains: In this game, black's idea of playing ...g7-g5 was deemed dubious because it allowed white to force f3, stopping the attack. Black's knight on c5 was misplaced, and black fell behind in development.
notes.teaches: When launching a kingside attack, ensure your pieces are harmoniously placed and you are not neglecting development. A premature attack can backfire if the opponent can consolidate and exploit your weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and aim to punish black's lack of coordination, perhaps by opening the center or targeting the misplaced knight.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has lost time with the knight on c5, which is misplaced and not doing much. Black is behind in development, and although the knight attacks e4, it is itself under attack, allowing White to gain more tempi.
notes.teaches: Development and tempi are critical; a misplaced piece that invites attacks can cost you time and allow the opponent to build an attack.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and pressuring Black's position, while Black needs to catch up in development and find a way to neutralize White's initiative.

notes.explains: White plays Qe1, a famous idea with a pawn on f4, aiming to transfer the queen to g3 where it will pressure g7 and keep Black's bishop stuck on f8. Black's attempts to free the position are met with concrete replies, and Black's lack of development remains a major issue.
notes.teaches: In sharp opening lines, a queen maneuver can be a powerful way to maintain pressure and restrict the opponent's piece activity.
notes.plans: White will continue to develop and maintain the bind, while Black must find a way to complete development and challenge White's control.

notes.explains: Black has a big problem: lack of development. If Black can get the bishop out and castle, the position would be fine, but White's rook on d1 is strong, preventing Black from starting kingside play. Black's usual queenside plan with b5 and Rc8 is available, but White has no kingside attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is underdeveloped, you should seek to open the position or create concrete threats to exploit the lead in development.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to undermine Black's position, possibly by targeting the knight on c5 or creating weaknesses.

notes.explains: White finds a creative idea: playing a4-a5 to undermine the knight on c5, which is vulnerable and has insufficient defenders. This leads to a sequence where Black's pieces become overloaded, and White wins material due to pins and checks.
notes.teaches: Creativity in chess involves finding moves that undermine the opponent's key pieces, even if they seem unconventional. Accuracy in calculation is essential to convert advantages.
notes.plans: White continues the attack, forcing Black into a losing position, eventually winning a piece and delivering a back-rank mate.

notes.explains: Elite players have done their homework and know the key ideas in their openings. In this game, the player was on top of the theory, playing the newest fashion h4, and later found a strong move c4, creating permanent weaknesses in Black's camp.
notes.teaches: Preparation and deep understanding of opening theory are essential for high-level play. Identifying and exploiting permanent weaknesses is a key skill.
notes.plans: Continue to apply pressure on the weaknesses created, maintaining the advantage.

notes.explains: In this line, White's h4 is the latest theoretical trend, and the move c4 is strong because it fixes the black c-pawns as permanent weaknesses, killing Black's counterplay and making the bishop on c8 and the other bishop passive.
notes.teaches: Fixing a weakness in the opponent's pawn structure can be a long-term strategic goal, even at the cost of a pawn, if it removes all counterplay.
notes.plans: White will aim to exploit the weak c-pawns and the passive bishops, while Black will try to generate activity with moves like ...h5-h6 and ...Ng6.

notes.explains: After the exchange of rooks, White reaches a pleasant endgame with a good knight versus a bad bishop. The knight will land on f4, attacking the weak f-pawn, and the bishop on c8 is dead unless Black plays ...f6 and ...e5, which would create more weaknesses.
notes.teaches: In fixed pawn structures, you should know which pieces you need to win: here, a good knight versus a bad bishop is a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: White will maneuver the knight to f4, attack the f-pawn, and gradually increase pressure, while Black is tied to defense.

notes.explains: In the endgame, White has a winning position due to the pawn structure: Black's pawns are weak and there are many targets. The bishop on a5 is active but has no real targets, while White's pieces are better placed.
notes.teaches: In rook and bishop versus rook and knight endgames, the bishop and rook combination is often better than knight and rook, so one goal is to trade rooks and reach a winning pawn-up endgame.
notes.plans: White should trade rooks, then create a passed pawn on the kingside, exploiting Black's weak pawns.
