notes.explains: After the moves Nc3, Nc7, Be3, Rb8, Rc1, b4, Ne2, Rb6, Nf4, g6, Qf3, Qd7, the position is balanced. Both sides have chances: White has a potential kingside attack, while Black has a solid setup and counterplay.
notes.teaches: In equal positions, it's important to keep pieces flexible and look for plans that create imbalances, such as attacking on one side while the opponent has counterplay on the other.
notes.plans: White can continue with Ng3 and then Qh5 or Qf3, aiming at the kingside. Black can consider ...d5 or ...c5 breaks to challenge the center.

notes.explains: In king and pawn endgames, a key square is one that, if the king reaches it, the game is won regardless of the opponent's king placement. Identifying all key squares is the first step in solving corresponding squares positions.
notes.teaches: Always start by identifying the key squares—the squares whose occupation by your king guarantees a win. These are often squares from which you can capture decisive pawns or promote.
notes.plans: Find all key squares in the position before considering corresponding squares.

notes.explains: In an eight-square corresponding squares system, each square in one set corresponds to exactly one square in the other set, with no overlaps. This one-to-one mapping is essential for precise king maneuvering.
notes.teaches: When you have an eight-square system, every square corresponds uniquely to another. Use this to outmaneuver the opponent by stepping onto the square that matches their king's square.
notes.plans: Once the eight-square system is identified, use it to triangulate or gain opposition to reach a key square.

notes.explains: In king and pawn endgames, corresponding squares form a one-to-one mapping between squares for White and Black. When the kings are on corresponding squares, the side to move is at a disadvantage because any move allows the opponent to step to a corresponding square and maintain the opposition.
notes.teaches: Build a system of corresponding squares from the shortest path between the kings, extending it by leapfrogging to other squares. Use this system to find the winning move: step to the square that corresponds to the opponent's current square, denying them access.
notes.plans: When the opponent is on a square that corresponds to a square you can reach, move there to force them away from the critical path and win the race to the key squares.

notes.explains: The eight-square system requires many available squares for both kings. When pawns block access to some squares, the system may not be constructible, so a simpler quadratic (four-square) system is used instead.
notes.teaches: Use the eight-square system whenever possible; only fall back to the quadratic system when the eight-square system is unavailable due to restricted mobility.
notes.plans: Identify the shortest path and the available squares; if the full eight-square system cannot be built, construct a two-by-two square system based on the same base triangle.

notes.explains: In this endgame, corresponding squares form a system where each key square for one king has a matching square for the other. The mapping is built from the shortest path between key squares, and it can be extended by 'leapfrogging'—if d4 corresponds to f7, then b4 corresponds to d4, and so on.
notes.teaches: Corresponding squares are a general framework that underlies opposition; opposition is just one instance. To use them, identify the key squares, map their corresponding squares, and extend the pattern outward.
notes.plans: When the opponent's king is on a square, step to its corresponding square. If the opponent cannot step to your corresponding square, you can approach closer.

notes.explains: The decision of when to approach closer depends on whether the opponent can step to a corresponding square. For example, after king b2 and black king g7, approaching to c3 is unsafe because black can step to g8, the corresponding square. But after king b3 and black king g8, black cannot step to g8 again, so c3 becomes winning.
notes.teaches: Approach closer only when the opponent has no corresponding square available. This is the practical application of the corresponding-square system.
notes.plans: Use the mapping to find the winning move: if the opponent is on a square that corresponds to a square you can step to, do so; otherwise, you may be able to gain opposition.

notes.explains: In this pawn endgame, the e5 square is a key square because if the white king can attack it, White can push the pawn to e5 and win one of Black's pawns regardless of where the black king is.
notes.teaches: Identify key squares by looking for squares where a pawn push or king entry guarantees a win.
notes.plans: White should aim to occupy or attack the key square e5.

notes.explains: When Black tries to rush to f6 or g6, White uses the corresponding squares (d4 for f6, d3 for g6) to step to the matching square (d2 or e3) and force Black to give way, allowing the e5 breakthrough.
notes.teaches: Use the corresponding squares to maintain the opposition and force the opponent to move away from key squares.
notes.plans: If Black heads to f6, White plays Kd2; if Black heads to g6, White plays Kd3, then after Black chooses, White steps to the corresponding square and wins.

notes.explains: Visualizing the eight-square system is feasible by remembering the pattern of corresponding squares and extending them as needed, as demonstrated by playing against a strong engine.
notes.teaches: With practice, you can visualize corresponding squares systems without physical markers.
notes.plans: Practice by setting up the position and playing through the system against an engine.

notes.explains: In corresponding squares, the shortest paths for both kings often contain ambiguous squares where the defender has multiple equivalent replies, which weakens the system.
notes.teaches: When building a corresponding-square system, choose squares with the least ambiguity — squares where the opponent's response is forced — rather than squares where they have options.

notes.explains: A key square is one that, if the king reaches it, wins the game (e.g., by capturing a decisive pawn). Here, b5, g5, and h5 are key squares.
notes.teaches: Identify the key squares first; they define the goal of the corresponding-square system.

notes.explains: When building an eight-square system, you often cannot use the outside because a pawn defends that side, so you need a linking square and a two-by-two block.
notes.teaches: Build the two-by-two square on the side of the base triangle that is not defended by enemy pawns, ensuring it is closely connected to the triangle.

notes.explains: Some squares are irrelevant because an easier key square already exists; for example, c6 might be winning but b5 is simpler to reach.
notes.teaches: Focus on the most accessible key square; ignore squares that are redundant or harder to achieve.

notes.explains: In this corresponding-squares endgame, the defender's pawn on a5 controls one side of the base triangle, so the attacker must use the bottom side instead. The key is to build a system of four corresponding squares for each king, where each square maps to a unique square for the opponent.
notes.teaches: When one side of a base triangle is blocked by a pawn, choose the other side that is still connected to the triangle. Build a set of corresponding squares to navigate the opposition.
notes.plans: Identify the base triangle and the available sides; then map out the corresponding squares for both kings to find the winning path.

notes.explains: When the opponent steps to a square that is an extension of a base-square (like b7), you must step to the extension of its corresponding square (c3 becomes c1). The pattern continues: each move must match the opponent's square to its corresponding partner.
notes.teaches: Always respond to the opponent's king move by moving to the square that corresponds to their new square, maintaining the mapping.
notes.plans: Follow the correspondence table: if the opponent moves to a square that maps to yours, move to that mapped square.

notes.explains: In this corresponding-squares endgame, the choice of which square to step to depends on the distance to the shortest path to the key squares. For black, d8 does not work as an extension of b8 because black is farther from the shortest path on the queenside, so the correspondence breaks down.
notes.teaches: When extending corresponding squares, you must account for the distance to the shortest path; if one side's path is longer, the extension may fail.
notes.plans: White should maintain the correspondence by stepping to the square that matches black's move, keeping black from invading.

notes.explains: In corresponding squares, the shortest paths for both kings define the correspondence: squares equidistant along those paths correspond. Here, the key squares form a system where each side's path length is equal, and the linking squares are determined by the base of the triangle.
notes.teaches: To build a system of corresponding squares, first identify the shortest path for each king, then choose two squares on each path of equal length. The correspondence is based on equal distance from the starting point.
notes.plans: Use the chosen squares to construct the full set of corresponding squares, extending the system as needed.

notes.explains: When choosing which squares to use for the system, multiple pairs may work if they lead to the same four key squares. For example, d3 and e2 or e2 and f1 both yield the same set of four squares for white, because the board's edge or obstruction prevents an eight-square system but allows the same base.
notes.teaches: Flexibility in choosing corresponding squares: different pairs can be equivalent if they produce the same critical squares. The goal is to find a consistent mapping that covers all relevant positions.
notes.plans: Select the pair that gives the most accurate correspondence, often the one that keeps options open for the winning side.

notes.explains: With white to move, the most accurate first move is to step to the square that corresponds to the opponent's potential entry square. For instance, if black's key square is a8, white's corresponding square is d1 (the back corner relative to the shortest path). This maintains the correspondence and keeps both options open.
notes.teaches: The most accurate move in a corresponding squares position is to step to the square that corresponds to the opponent's most likely move, thereby maintaining the mapping and preventing the opponent from making progress.
notes.plans: After white's accurate move, if black steps to b8, white goes to c1; if black steps to a7, white goes to d2, and so on, always mirroring the correspondence to win the pawn.

notes.explains: If black deviates from the shortest path, he abandons the correspondence and allows white to win the pawn directly. For example, if black steps too far away, white can simply take the pawn because black is no longer covering the critical squares.
notes.teaches: In corresponding squares, the defender must stay on the corresponding squares to prevent progress. If the defender leaves the system, the attacker can immediately capitalize by capturing material or advancing.
notes.plans: White should be alert to any deviation by black and punish it by taking the pawn or penetrating.

notes.explains: Even if the defender's path were shorter, the attacker could still draw or win by leaving the king to guard the pawn, because the defender must stay to prevent the attacker's king from invading. The attacker's path length is not the only factor; the defender's obligations matter.
notes.teaches: In corresponding squares, the relative path lengths are not decisive by themselves. The defender's need to stay near the pawn can allow the attacker to draw or win even with a longer path.
notes.plans: When analyzing such positions, consider the defender's constraints, not just the geometric path lengths.

notes.explains: When a king-and-pawn endgame has a passed pawn on the sixth rank, the defending king must occupy specific corresponding squares to prevent the attacker's king from invading. For example, if the white king goes to d6, the black king must go to d8 to meet the threat of c7, which would otherwise win.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, a pawn on the sixth rank creates a 'checkmate threat' that forces the defending king to a precise square. Recognizing these key squares is essential for evaluating the position.
notes.plans: If the white king can reach d6 while the black king is not on d8, then c7+ will win. Otherwise, the defender holds the draw by maintaining the correspondence.

notes.explains: When constructing a system of corresponding squares, sometimes there isn't enough board space for the full eight-square or quadratic systems. Here, the black king runs out of room, and a pawn on c6 takes away a key square, so a simpler triangular system of three squares (d5-c8, c5-c7, d6-d8) is used.
notes.teaches: The triangular system is a minimal set of corresponding squares used when space is limited. It is the basic building block for positions where the defender has only three critical squares to cover.
notes.plans: White can use triangulation to force black to move first from a corresponding square, gaining a tempo to invade.

notes.explains: In this triangular setup, the white king can step back to d4, and the square c4 also corresponds to d6 because from c4 the king threatens to go to the same two squares as from d4. This creates an 'ambiguous' backward square for white, while black has only one such square (b8).
notes.teaches: Triangulation works when one side has an extra 'waiting' square that the other side cannot match. The side with the extra tempo can force the opponent to leave a corresponding square, allowing invasion.
notes.plans: White steps back to d4, then after black chooses a corresponding square, white steps to the other green square, leaving black with a losing choice between two squares.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn endgame, White wins by triangulation: the king steps back and forth between two squares that are equivalent for White, while Black has only one matching square and must commit to it, allowing White to gain the opposition.
notes.teaches: Triangulation is a key technique in corresponding squares: if one side has an extra spare move (a 'triangulation square') and the other does not, the side with the extra tempo can force the opponent to move into a losing position.
notes.plans: White uses the ambiguous squares (e.g., c4/d4) to pass the move, then steps to the corresponding square that forces Black into a zugzwang, eventually penetrating with the king.

notes.explains: Corresponding squares systems come in three basic types: the quadratic (four-square), the eight-square, and the six-square (which is two quadratics sharing a file). More complex systems are combinations of these basics.
notes.teaches: Recognize the fundamental corresponding-square patterns; most studies reduce to one of these three systems, and complex positions are just interlinked versions of them.
notes.plans: When facing a corresponding-squares position, identify which basic system applies, then use the spare tempo or the opposition to force the opponent into a losing move.

notes.explains: Corresponding squares can be made more complex by giving both sides extra tempi, allowing transpositions between systems, and there are rare oddball studies where the system shifts slightly, but these are exceptions.
notes.teaches: Master the three basic systems and their combinations; they cover the vast majority of corresponding-squares endgames, and the exceptions are rare enough to be handled case-by-case.
notes.plans: When analyzing a corresponding-squares position, first look for the basic patterns; only if they don't fit should you consider unusual shifts or extra tempi.

notes.explains: Corresponding squares are a key concept in pawn endgames, and different authors have proposed different methods for finding them. Verretsky's approach is case-by-case and requires examining the whole position, while the system from Zarin and Offerbox is more systematic: you recognize a pattern and build a system from it.
notes.teaches: When studying corresponding squares, prefer a systematic method that lets you recognize patterns and extend them, rather than relying on ad-hoc analysis for each position.

notes.explains: In positions with a strong light-squared bishop on the d3-h7 diagonal, a move like h6 can appear to defend the kingside but often creates long-term weaknesses. The h6 pawn can become a target if the bishop captures it, and it weakens the g6 square, making it hard to blunt a mating battery on the h-file.
notes.teaches: When considering h6, weigh the immediate defensive benefits against the permanent weakening of the kingside, especially when the opponent has a bishop on d3 or similar diagonal.
notes.plans: If you have a bishop on d3 and the opponent plays h6, consider building a battery with the queen on d3 to threaten mate on h7, exploiting the weakened g6 square.

notes.explains: Placing the queen on d3 in coordination with the bishop on d3 creates a battery that pressures h7. If the black knight moves, the queen can go to h7, winning pawns and creating threats, even if not an immediate mate.
notes.teaches: A queen and bishop battery on the same diagonal can create direct threats against the king, forcing the opponent to keep pieces on defensive squares.
notes.plans: Continue developing while maintaining the battery, and be ready to exploit any knight move by taking on h7 and picking off pawns.

notes.explains: A move like c5 may look positionally suspect because it leaves a backward pawn, but it can be played for tactical reasons to seize the initiative and create immediate threats. The positional weakness gives the opponent a nice square for a knight, but the tactical gains may outweigh that.
notes.teaches: Sometimes tactical opportunities justify positional concessions; evaluate whether the initiative and concrete threats compensate for structural weaknesses.
notes.plans: If playing c5, follow up with active piece play to maintain the initiative before the opponent can exploit the backward pawn or the outpost.

notes.explains: A move like c5 can be positionally suspect because it creates a backward pawn, which gives the opponent a nice square for a knight, such as d5. Even if the knight cannot go there immediately due to tactical threats, the long-term structural weakness remains.
notes.teaches: When evaluating pawn moves, consider the pawn structure and the squares it gives up to the opponent. A backward pawn often provides a permanent outpost for an enemy piece.
notes.plans: If you have a backward pawn, try to trade it or use it as a base for counterplay, but be aware of the opponent's potential piece placement.

notes.explains: In a position with a strong attack, a common tactic is to remove the defender of a key square or piece. Here, the knight on f6 is a defender, and distracting it can lead to a decisive tactic.
notes.teaches: Look for ways to eliminate or deflect the defender of a critical point. This is known as removal of the guard or decoy, and it often enables a checkmate or wins material.
notes.plans: If you have a knight that can move to a square where it attacks the defender, consider that move even if it sacrifices material, as it may lead to a stronger attack.

notes.explains: When attacking a castled king, it is often more effective to use pieces rather than pawns, especially when you already have many pieces coordinated. A pawn move like g4 can be slow and may not be necessary if you have a direct piece attack.
notes.teaches: In king-side attacks, prioritize piece play over pawn pushes unless the pawn move is essential for opening lines or driving away defenders. Avoid slow moves when you have a ready-made attack.
notes.plans: If you have a strong attacking position, look for immediate tactical blows with pieces, such as sacrifices or checks, rather than spending time on pawn advances.

notes.explains: In this position, White already has many pieces aimed at the black king, and Black has only one defender. A pawn move like g4 is slow and unnecessary when the attack can be conducted with pieces directly.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong piece attack, prefer direct piece moves over slow pawn advances. Pawn storms are often not needed if your pieces are already coordinated.
notes.plans: Look for immediate tactical blows, such as captures or checks, to exploit the lack of defenders.

notes.explains: This is a critical moment where you must decide whether to play automatically or to invest time in deep calculation. The presence of loose pieces and tactical opportunities signals that you should pause and analyze all captures and checks.
notes.teaches: Develop the ability to recognize when a position requires deep calculation versus when you can rely on instinct. This skill separates strong players from the rest.

notes.explains: After a knight takes on g4, there is a checkmate threat on h2, but queen to h7 is not mate because the king can escape to f8. The difference is that the bishop on f8 would have covered that square, but it has moved.
notes.teaches: Always check the king's escape squares before assuming a queen check is mate. A check that only drives the king to safety is not as strong as a mating threat.

notes.explains: Knight takes f7 is a desperado sacrifice: since the knight is lost anyway after taking on c5, White gets material for it, including a crucial defensive pawn. This leads to material equality and a fantastic position with two bishops and a exposed black king.
notes.teaches: A desperado is a tactic where you use a piece that is doomed anyway to gain compensation. Even a small amount of material can be valuable if it weakens the opponent's king.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, continue the attack with the bishops and the king's exposed position.

notes.explains: The move bishop takes h6 is a sacrifice that exploits the looseness of Black's pieces. If Black recaptures, White has a powerful tactic: queen g3 check, and if the king goes to f8 or h8, knight g6 is a discovered attack on the unprotected queen on c7.
notes.teaches: Loose pieces drop off: when you see unprotected enemy pieces, look for sharp tactics like sacrifices and discovered attacks. A discovered attack can win material or even the game.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, follow up with queen g3 check and knight g6, using the discovered attack to win the queen.

notes.explains: A knight on g6 can deliver a discovered attack on an unprotected queen on c7, creating a 'boo' moment. The same idea works if the king is on f8, but a knight check from d7 is weaker because the queen can simply capture it.
notes.teaches: When considering checks, always evaluate whether the checking piece is safe from capture. A discovered attack on a queen is powerful, but only if the attacking piece cannot be taken.

notes.explains: Black avoided the immediate threat by trading on d4, but the attack remains strong because White has only sacrificed one pawn. The king is exposed and White's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: A material deficit of one pawn is often acceptable when the opponent's king is vulnerable and your pieces are coordinating well.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing more pieces to bear on the king, using the open lines created by the pawn sacrifice.

notes.explains: In a position with a knight on d5 protecting the queen on c7, the move queen g3 no longer wins the queen because the knight defends it. Instead, White played a move that sets up a common tactical pattern.
notes.teaches: Always check if the opponent's pieces are defended before assuming a tactic works. A piece that appears undefended may be protected by a distant piece.

notes.explains: Before diving into a forcing line like queen h7 check, consider all candidate moves, especially other checks. In this position, bishop h7 check is the correct one, forcing the king to h8 and setting up the mate.
notes.teaches: Most chess errors come from not considering enough options, not from miscalculating deep variations. Always list all checks and forcing moves before committing.

notes.explains: When you have multiple checks, only one may be good. However, you might be able to repeat moves to gain time, but be careful not to repeat too many times and accidentally draw.
notes.teaches: Repetition of moves can be used to gain time on the clock, but it carries the risk of a threefold repetition draw. Use it sparingly and keep track of the number of repetitions.

notes.explains: A queen on h6 supported by a bishop on the long diagonal creates a classic mating net. The defender's best try is to bring the queen back to defend, but the attacker can keep the pressure by adding more pieces.
notes.teaches: Recognize the pattern where a queen and bishop coordinate to deliver mate. When attacking, look to bring additional pieces, like rooks, into the attack to increase the pressure.
notes.plans: If the defender plays a move like ...f6 to block, the attacker can push the f-pawn to open lines for the rook. The rook then joins the attack on the g-file, threatening mate.

notes.explains: Defending with the queen is crucial when under attack. The defender should consider moves like ...Qg7 to offer a trade or create defensive resources, even if the attacker can continue with threats.
notes.teaches: In defense, use the queen to cover key squares and potentially trade off the attacker's active pieces. Always look for defensive moves that also create counterplay.
notes.plans: If the attacker plays Qh5 hitting a rook, the defender must decide whether to move the rook or allow further attack. The attacker continues with the rook lift to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: When the defender tries to protect against one threat, the attacker can find an even quicker winning move. Here, a pawn push to g6 creates a decisive mating net, exploiting the pinned queen and the coordination of knight and bishop.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical shots that exploit the opponent's pieces being tied to defense. A pawn break can open lines or create threats that overload the defense.
notes.plans: After the pawn push, if the rook captures, the queen delivers mate on h8, and if the king moves, the queen mates on f7, with the knight protected by the bishop.

notes.explains: Chess problems and studies are composed positions that highlight the power of pieces and train creativity. They often feature unusual mates and are useful for improving tactical vision.
notes.teaches: Study composed positions to develop creativity and tactical awareness. They can reveal patterns that occur in real games, even if the exact position is artificial.

notes.explains: With only kings and pawns left, the position looks lost for White because the black pawn seems unstoppable and the white king appears too far away to catch it. The key is to find a way to create counterplay with the white pawn while also getting the king into the square of the black pawn.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, never assume a lost position based on first impressions; look for ways to create mutual promotion threats or to get the king into the square of the enemy pawn. The concept of the 'square of the pawn' is crucial for evaluating whether a king can stop a passer.
notes.plans: White should aim to advance the c-pawn while simultaneously bringing the king toward the black pawn, creating a double threat that forces Black to choose between stopping one or the other, leading to a draw.

notes.explains: The position illustrates a double attack in its purest form: White's king move creates two simultaneous threats—one to catch the black pawn and one to support the white pawn's promotion. This is the essence of the tactic, even though it doesn't look like a typical double attack at first.
notes.teaches: Double attacks are not limited to forks with pieces; in endgames, a single king move can create two threats that the opponent cannot parry simultaneously. Recognizing these geometric motifs is key to finding saving resources.
notes.plans: White should choose king moves that maximize the dual threats, such as heading toward the black pawn while also supporting the c-pawn, forcing Black into a drawn pawn race.

notes.explains: Chess studies and problems often fall into two categories: those that are simple in appearance but hide deep ideas, and those that are complex but contain a simple underlying point. This position belongs to the first category—minimal material, yet a stunning resource.
notes.teaches: Appreciate the beauty of simplicity in chess: even with few pieces, there can be profound tactical ideas. Training on such positions improves creativity and tactical vision, which transfers to real games.

notes.explains: In this position, many candidate moves appear to give checkmate but fail because of a defensive resource: a bishop can capture, the king can flee to a square, or a pinned piece can interpose. The difficulty comes from the abundance of checks and captures available.
notes.teaches: When solving a mate-in-one, systematically examine all checks and captures first, but verify each candidate against every possible defense. The solution is often a quiet-looking move that covers all escape squares and prevents captures.
notes.plans: Continue searching for the mating move by considering all checks and captures, then look for a move that addresses the king's flight squares and the defenders' captures.

notes.explains: The position is unrealistic because many pawns have promoted to bishops, leading to a clutter of light-squared bishops that interfere with each other. This makes it hard to see the mating move because the board is full of pieces that seem to cover squares but also block lines.
notes.teaches: In composed problems, the solution often involves a paradoxical or surprising move, such as an underpromotion or a quiet move, rather than an obvious capture or check. Expect the unexpected and look beyond the first ideas.
notes.plans: When stuck, consider unconventional moves like underpromotions or moves that seem to ignore material, as they may be the key.

notes.explains: The group tried many plausible moves that failed, such as knight checks that get captured or bishop moves that allow the king to escape. The winning move, Queen to a3, is a quiet move that delivers mate by covering all escape squares and avoiding capture.
notes.teaches: A common reason for missing a winning move is not overlooking a long variation but simply not considering a quiet move that is right in front of you. Always scan for non-checking moves that create a mating net.
notes.plans: After finding the mate, reflect on why the obvious checks failed and how the quiet move succeeded, to improve pattern recognition for future problems.

notes.explains: The difficulty of this mate-in-one stems from the high number of checks available, which distracts from the actual solution. Counting the checks reveals why the position is so challenging.
notes.teaches: In positions with many forcing moves, it's easy to get lost in the noise. A systematic approach—listing all checks and captures, then testing each—helps filter out false leads and find the true solution.
notes.plans: As an exercise, count all the checks in the position to understand the complexity, then use that to appreciate the value of a systematic search.

notes.explains: White has several options against ...a6, including Bg5 and Be3. Be3 is considered slightly better because it controls the center more effectively. If white plays Nf3 instead of Nge2, the ...b5 idea is less effective because after cxb5 axb5 Bxb5, white is just a pawn up with no compensation for black.
notes.teaches: The placement of the knight matters: a knight on e2 supports the center differently than on f3. When a pawn sacrifice is offered, evaluate whether the resulting activity truly compensates for the material deficit.
notes.plans: White should consider Nf3 to blunt black's ...b5 idea, while black must find alternative plans if the knight is on f3.

notes.explains: If white plays Ng3, black can respond with ...h5, attacking the knight and preventing it from settling. White has two main replies: Bd3, intending to retreat the knight to e2 if ...h4, or Bg5, which stops ...h4 altogether. After Bg5, black should play ...Nc6, exploiting the fact that the knight on g3 is not well placed and the d4 pawn is not defended by it.
notes.teaches: When a knight is placed on g3, it can become a target for a pawn storm with ...h5-h4. The defender must decide whether to allow the advance or prevent it, and the attacker should look for ways to exploit the knight's poor placement.
notes.plans: Black plans to follow up with ...Nc6, ...Qd7, ...Nh7, and ...Bd7, preparing ...e5 and ...d5 to establish a strong knight on d4. White must find a way to develop harmoniously despite the pressure.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Nc6, black should not rush ...e5. If black plays ...e5 immediately, white can respond with d5, and after ...Nd4, white can play Ne2 to challenge the knight. This is undesirable for black, so instead black plays ...Bd7 first, preparing ...e5 and ...d5 under better circumstances.
notes.teaches: Timing is crucial in the opening: a central break like ...e5 should be prepared carefully, ensuring that the resulting pawn structure and piece placement favor you. Sometimes a quiet developing move is better than an immediate break.
notes.plans: Black aims to play ...Bd7, then ...e5 and ...d5, creating a strong outpost on d4 for the knight. White must find a way to prevent or neutralize this central expansion.

notes.explains: In this King's Indian Defense setup, Black delays central pawn breaks like e5 because after e5, d5, and knight d4, White can challenge the knight with knight e2, which is undesirable for Black. Instead, bishop d7 prepares the e5 and d5 breaks under better circumstances.
notes.teaches: When a central break allows the opponent to challenge your strong piece favorably, consider a preparatory move that improves your piece placement before executing the break.
notes.plans: After bishop e2, play e5 and d5, aiming for a strong knight on d4 that is less easily challenged.

notes.explains: The move a6 is useful because it prepares b5, challenging White's pawn on c4 in Benoni/Benko-style positions. If White plays d5, Black can quickly play b5 and open the queenside, creating counterplay.
notes.teaches: In Benoni-type structures, a6 is a key preparatory move to enable b5, which undermines White's pawn chain and opens lines for Black's pieces.
notes.plans: After d5, play b5 to challenge the c4 pawn and open the queenside, aiming for active piece play.

notes.explains: In a line where White has an extra pawn after a sacrifice on b5, Black's compensation comes from reduced central control by White. With the c4 pawn gone, Black can challenge the center more efficiently and fight for initiative.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing a pawn, the key is to remove the opponent's central pawn, which weakens their center and gives you dynamic chances to seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Play c6 to solidify the queenside, then develop pieces to active squares like e5 and a6, aiming for long-term pressure.

notes.explains: In this King's Indian Defense Sämisch variation, Black plays an early a6 and b5 to challenge White's center. After White captures on b5 and Black recaptures, Black plays c6, and White has two knight moves: Nc3 or Na3. Na3 looks odd because the knight goes to the edge, but it can later reroute to c4. However, Black gets dynamic play.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, you must play actively and dynamically; passive moves allow White to keep the extra pawn and develop comfortably. Black should immediately challenge the center with c5, exploiting the misplaced knight on a3.
notes.plans: Black plays c5 to attack the center. If White takes on c5, Black can respond with Qa5, creating tactical threats. If White doesn't take, Black can continue with Nc6 and e6, reaching a Benoni-like structure with good chances.

notes.explains: After Black plays c5, White has several options. If White plays Qd2, Black can play Nc6, and after d5, Nb4 is strong, with ideas of Ba6 and e6, transforming into a Benoni-like position that is great for Black. White's knight on a3 is misplaced, and Black's play is very comfortable.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a piece on the rim, you should immediately strike in the center to exploit its poor placement. A knight on a3 is often a long-term weakness because it is out of play.
notes.plans: Black aims for a Benoni structure with c5, Nc6, e6, and d5, challenging White's center and gaining active piece play. The knight on b4 can be a strong outpost.

notes.explains: If White instead plays Nc3, Black can play cxd4, Nxd4, and then e5, followed by d5, opening the center and challenging White's control. This leads to dynamic play where Black has good chances. White's knight on a3 is again a liability.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, Black should seek to open the center when White's pieces are poorly coordinated. A timely d5 break can give Black a strong initiative.
notes.plans: Black plays cxd4, Nxd4, e5, and d5, aiming to open the center and activate the pieces. If White doesn't take on d5, Black may play d4 himself.

notes.explains: If White takes on c5, Black can play Qa5, attacking the c5 pawn and creating threats. After Qd2, Black can trade queens and then play Nxc4, winning a pawn. The resulting position, with White's king exposed and pieces undeveloped, is fine for Black despite the material imbalance.
notes.teaches: Tactical shots like Qa5 can punish White's pawn grabs. Even after queen trades, Black can have good compensation due to White's weaknesses and lack of development.
notes.plans: Black plays Qa5, and after Qd2, Qxd2+ and Nxc4, winning a pawn. Black is not worse despite the material imbalance because White's king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped.

notes.explains: The King's Indian Defense is a very flexible opening that can be played against many setups, including the English or London. However, White can avoid d4, so Black must be prepared for different structures. The key is to play dynamically and aggressively, as passive play leads to a worse position.
notes.teaches: The King's Indian is a dynamic opening that requires active play. You can play it against almost any setup, but you must be ready to adapt if White avoids the main lines.
notes.plans: Against setups without d4, Black should still aim for a KID structure with Nf6, g6, Bg7, d6, and O-O, but be flexible in the move order.

notes.explains: In this position, White's king is exposed on e1 and the queen on a7 controls key squares, preventing easy castling. Black has traded a rook for two minor pieces and has two pawns, giving dynamic compensation despite being down material.
notes.teaches: Material imbalances like rook versus two minor pieces can favor the side with better piece activity and king safety. A queen on a long diagonal can restrict the enemy king's escape routes.
notes.plans: Black should continue to exploit White's uncastled king and lack of development, aiming to create threats before White can consolidate.

notes.explains: After White plays Nbc3, Black's move Nbd7 prepares central action. The immediate ...e5 is not played yet, but the knight supports the central break ...d5, which is strong because White's c4 pawn has been traded off.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian Defense, when White's c-pawn is absent, Black can aim for ...d5 to challenge the center directly. This is especially effective when White's king is still uncastled.
notes.plans: Black should follow up with ...e5 and then ...d5, creating dynamic central tension and exploiting White's lag in development.

notes.explains: In the game continuation, after trades on e5 and d4, Black's knight on e5 is strongly placed, and the bishop on g7 pressures b2. The absence of Black's queenside pawns is irrelevant because the b-file and the long diagonal give Black active play.
notes.teaches: A strong centralized knight and a bishop on a long diagonal can outweigh an extra pawn, especially when the opponent's pawns are difficult to convert into an advantage.
notes.plans: Black should continue to play actively, targeting White's weaknesses (like b2) and avoiding passive moves that allow White to consolidate.

notes.explains: Black chooses a dynamic move like Ng4 to prevent White's bishop from going to g5, which would be annoying. This proactive approach avoids wasting time on natural but passive moves like ...Be6.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, it's important to anticipate and prevent the opponent's threats. Sometimes a move that seems unnatural is necessary to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: Black should continue to create threats and keep White off balance, not allowing White to stabilize.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on g7 is attacked along the diagonal, and White's extra pawn is not a real advantage if Black can generate active play. The pin by White's bishop on g5 is a potential problem, so Black must address it.
notes.teaches: When facing a pin or a threat, prefer active moves that create counterplay over passive defensive moves. A dynamic move like ...Ng4 can challenge the opponent's plans and force them to react.
notes.plans: Black should continue to develop actively, aiming to use the g7 bishop and create weaknesses in White's camp.

notes.explains: After the sequence, Black has sacrificed a pawn but has strong compensation: the bishop on g7 is powerful, and White's pawns on the kingside are vulnerable. Black's pieces are well-placed to attack.
notes.teaches: Material is not always the most important factor; dynamic compensation such as piece activity, attacking chances, and weaknesses in the opponent's position can outweigh a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press on the kingside, possibly with moves like ...g4 to create weaknesses (e.g., h2) and open lines for the rooks.

notes.explains: In this line of the King's Indian Defense, Black aims to play ...e5 and ...d5 to challenge the center, especially since White's pawn is not on c4. This central advance gives Black good play.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pawn structure lacks a key central pawn (like c4), you can often 'charge the center' with pawn breaks to gain space and activity.
notes.plans: Black should look for opportunities to play ...e5 and ...d5, and if White plays Bg5, Black can consider ...Bxh6 and ...Qxh6 to trade pieces and simplify, or find other active continuations.

notes.explains: In this King's Indian position with a pawn on f3, Black can consider Nxe4, removing the f6 knight to enable Qh4, which creates a double attack on h6 and e1.
notes.teaches: When the f-pawn is on f3, the e4 square is weakened, and Nxe4 is a typical tactical resource to exploit it, often leading to a double attack.
notes.plans: After Nxe4, Black aims for Qh4, and if White plays g3, Qxh6, followed by Nd6, with the pair of bishops and better development giving Black good chances.

notes.explains: White may try d5 to close the center and keep the extra pawn, but Black can challenge with Nb6, and the missing queenside pawn is not important because the active fight in the center matters more.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a pawn deficit can be irrelevant if you have active piece play and the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Black can play Nb6, and after dxc6, Nc4, then Bxe6, aiming to recapture the c6 pawn with Qc7 or Qa5, and later play d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: White's Rd1 is a natural move to control the center, but Black can respond with d5, opening the position and exposing White's king, especially if White castles long.
notes.teaches: Long castling is risky when the center and queenside are open; the king is safer on the kingside.
notes.plans: After Rd1, Black plays d5, and after exd5, Nxd5, cxd5, Black has compensation due to White's king being in the center.

notes.explains: White has two main approaches: develop normally with Nc3, Bf1-e2, and short castling, or take on e5 to pressure the d5 pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have an extra pawn, you can either consolidate and finish development or immediately challenge the opponent's central pawn.
notes.plans: If White plays dxe5, Nxe5, Nc3, Black can consider Qxd5, Nxa2, or Nc4, keeping the initiative.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, White has two plausible setups: develop the knight to c3 and aim for a quick castling, or capture on e5 to pressure the d5 pawn. The choice hinges on whether the extra pawn matters or whether immediate pressure is better.
notes.teaches: When facing a dynamic imbalance, weigh solid development against immediate tactical pressure; both can be valid, but the initiative often matters more.
notes.plans: If developing, bring the bishop to e2 and castle short; if capturing, use the open e-file to create threats.

notes.explains: After White plays Nc3 and prepares Be2, Black can generate counterplay with Re8, forcing the king to f2, and then Qh4, chasing the king. The bishop on e2 becomes vulnerable to tactics on the e-file, such as Bc4 or Qh4, exploiting the pin.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, prioritize attacking it over material; pins and open files can create decisive threats.
notes.plans: Black should aim to keep the initiative, possibly with Qh4 and Bc4, to prevent White from consolidating.

notes.explains: In the line with Kf2, Black can play Nc4, and if Bxc4, then Qh4 creates strong pressure. The bishop on e3 is pinned and cannot be defended adequately, leading to material gain or a continuing attack.
notes.teaches: A knight fork or a pin on a bishop can be a decisive tactical motif; look for ways to exploit the opponent's king exposure.
notes.plans: Black should continue with Qh4 and consider Rxe3 if the king moves, maintaining the attack.

notes.explains: After White plays Kf3, Black can play Qh4, and if g3, then Qf6, putting pressure on the f3 square. White's bishop is forced to f4 to defend, but then Black can play g5 to undermine it, or Nxf3 to open the position.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use queen checks and pawn pushes to disrupt the defense; opening lines is often the key to a successful attack.
notes.plans: Black should consider Nxf3, opening the position, or g5 to drive away the bishop, then continue the attack.

notes.explains: If White plays Nxf3, Black can play d4, opening the diagonal for the bishop to b7, which crashes through. The king is exposed and the bishop on c8 becomes a powerful attacking piece.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a piece to open lines against a exposed king can be decisive; the resulting attack is often worth more than the material.
notes.plans: After Nxf3, play d4, then Bb7, and continue the attack with the queen and rooks.

notes.explains: The move Qe4 is tempting but fails to Qh1, Bg2, after which white is much better. Instead, Rxa2 is stronger because it keeps all threats alive and leaves white with no good moves.
notes.teaches: When choosing between moves, prefer the one that preserves multiple threats and gives the opponent no clear defense, rather than a forcing line that allows them to consolidate.
notes.plans: Start with Rxa2, and only later employ ideas like Qe4 or Bxb2, when they are more effective.

notes.explains: If white tries to prevent black's central play by capturing the pawn, black still gets central play and the white king remains in the center, nearly checkmated by move 20. A better try for white is Nc3, but then black can play Re8 and after Kf2, black's knight is less active, but black can still play e4 and get good compensation.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's king is stuck in the center, you can often sacrifice a pawn to open lines and develop an attack, even if your pieces are not perfectly placed.
notes.plans: Develop quickly, play e4, and target the weak king on g1, using the open files and diagonals.

notes.explains: White's move Ng3 aims to support e4 and anticipate d5, but the knight on g3 has no bright future; it only performs defensive tasks. Black's best response is d5, which is stronger than taking on d4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a defensive move, look for a central pawn break to challenge their setup and open the position for your pieces.
notes.plans: Play d5, and if white takes, recapture with the bishop and bring the knight to c5 and e6 to continue the initiative.

notes.explains: After White plays Ng3, Black has two main approaches. The first is to play d5 immediately, which is the most natural and best choice. The alternative is to take on d4, followed by ...Nc5 and ...Ne6, aiming to play ...d5 later. Both options give Black good play, and the white king remains in the center, which is a significant drawback for White.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian Defense, when White deviates with moves like Ng3, Black should look for the most natural central break, often ...d5, to challenge White's center and exploit the king's exposure.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play ...d5, either immediately or after preparatory moves like ...Nc5 and ...Ne6, to open the position and create active piece play.

notes.explains: In the line where White plays Be2 after ...d5, Black can play ...h5, a typical idea in the King's Indian when White has a knight on g3. This move can transpose to other lines and creates pressure against the white king, even after White castles. The position becomes very complicated and unclear, with Black having good practical chances.
notes.teaches: The ...h5 pawn thrust is a standard resource in the King's Indian when White has a knight on g3, as it can open lines against the king and create long-term attacking chances.
notes.plans: Black should consider ...h5 to provoke weaknesses and generate initiative, even if the position remains balanced with best play.

notes.explains: In the Sämisch variation, the move …a6 is a recommended line for Black, preparing ...b5 and a pawn sacrifice to fight for the center. After the sacrifice, Black gets perfect piece development and the white king remains exposed, giving Black excellent compensation even a pawn down.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, a pawn sacrifice for rapid development and an attack on the king can be a powerful practical weapon, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Black should play ...a6, then ...b5, and if White takes, recapture with the king or develop pieces with tempo, aiming for a strong initiative.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has sacrificed a pawn but has achieved perfect piece development, while the white king on g2 is exposed despite having castled. The weakness of the king and Black's active pieces give Black excellent compensation.
notes.teaches: A pawn sacrifice can be justified if it leads to a lead in development and exposes the opponent's king. Even a castled king can be vulnerable if the surrounding pawns are compromised.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press the attack against the exposed king, using the lead in development to create threats and prevent White from consolidating.

notes.explains: The line with …a6 in the King's Indian Defense, Sämisch Variation, leads to a sharp and interesting position where Black gets good chances to fight for the initiative. It is not necessarily better for Black, but it poses practical problems for White.
notes.teaches: Choosing a sharp, less common line can be a practical weapon, especially if it forces the opponent to find precise moves. Even if the line is objectively balanced, it can create winning chances if the opponent is unprepared.
notes.plans: If playing this line, aim for dynamic play and attacking chances, while being aware that the position requires accurate handling.

notes.explains: In the King's Gambit, after e4 e5 f4, black can capture the f4 pawn. White's response with Bc4 is aggressive but leaves the h4 and g5 squares unguarded, allowing black to play Qh4+ and force the white king to move, preventing castling.
notes.teaches: When playing gambits, prioritize rapid development and activity over material. The immediate attack on the king can be tempting, but maintaining initiative and piece activity is often more important than regaining the pawn.
notes.plans: White should continue developing naturally, aiming to use the lead in development to create threats against the black king, which is now exposed in the center.

notes.explains: Black's Qh4+ and d6 attempt to hold onto the extra pawn and prevent white from castling, but this greedy approach can backfire. White's natural development with Nc3 is instructive, as it focuses on piece activity rather than immediate material recovery.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, avoid being greedy with material if it allows the opponent to develop freely. Instead, consider returning the pawn for quick development and central control, as seen in alternatives like Nf6 or d5.
notes.plans: White will continue to develop pieces and use the exposed black king as a target, while black must be careful not to fall behind in development.

notes.explains: In this gambit line, White has sacrificed a pawn on f4 but is prioritizing rapid development over immediate attack. The move Nc3 is a natural developing move that supports the center and prepares to bring pieces out quickly.
notes.teaches: The primary goal of a gambit is not to checkmate immediately but to achieve rapid development and active piece play. Amateurs often err by trying to force a quick attack instead of developing naturally.
notes.plans: Continue developing pieces harmoniously, aiming to build a strong center and create threats against Black's king while maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: Black has made concessions to hold the extra pawn, such as moving the queen to h4 and then retreating, and playing d6 instead of challenging the center. These concessions have given White a central pawn duo and active pieces.
notes.teaches: When you make concessions to keep material, you must remain consistent and not later give back the pawn without compensation. Consistency in your plan is crucial.
notes.plans: Black should consider moves that maintain the pawn on f4, such as g5, rather than developing with Nf6 which would allow White to regain the pawn and consolidate.

notes.explains: White's queen on e2 is active and not easily attacked by Black's minor pieces, making the early queen development justified. Black avoided trading bishops because it would activate White's queen further.
notes.teaches: The principle of not developing the queen early has an exception: if the queen cannot be harassed by minor pieces, it can be a powerful attacking piece. Evaluate whether the opponent can exploit its early development.
notes.plans: White aims to keep pieces on the board and use the queen's activity to increase pressure, while Black must find a way to neutralize White's initiative without giving back the pawn.

notes.explains: In the King's Gambit, when Black accepts the pawn and then tries to hold it with moves like g5, White must not allow Black to consolidate. The central pawn duo and development advantage are White's compensation, but they must be used actively or Black will catch up.
notes.teaches: If you have sacrificed a pawn for central control and development, you must play actively to justify it. Passive moves allow the opponent to consolidate and keep the extra material.
notes.plans: White should look for central breaks like e5 or d5 to exploit the pawn center, rather than flank attacks that may not involve all pieces.

notes.explains: A move like h4 in this position is tempting to attack the g5 pawn, but it can be met by g4, trapping the knight if it goes to g5. The knight and queen are not well placed to support a kingside attack, so flank play is premature.
notes.teaches: Before launching a flank attack, ensure your pieces are coordinated to support it. If the attack can be repulsed with a simple pawn push, it may not be the right plan.
notes.plans: Instead of h4, White should focus on central pawn breaks to open the position and use the active pieces.

notes.explains: Black, having accepted the gambit and lagging in development, must keep the center closed to avoid opening lines for White's better-developed pieces. Moves like d5 are natural to block the center, while capturing on e5 would open the position.
notes.teaches: When behind in development, keep the center closed to minimize the opponent's attacking chances. When ahead in development, open the center to exploit the lead.
notes.plans: Black should maintain the closed center and aim to complete development with moves like Bg7, Na6, and Nf6, while keeping the extra pawn.

notes.explains: White's queen can go to b3 to inhibit Black's development, as it attacks b7 and prevents ...Nd7. This is a more active option than retreating to d3 or e2, and it keeps pressure on Black's position.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space and development advantage, look for moves that restrict the opponent's natural developing moves. A queen move to b3 can be strong if it hits a weak pawn and prevents a knight from developing.
notes.plans: White continues to build pressure, possibly following up with central pawn advances or exploiting Black's cramped position.

notes.explains: With a central pawn wedge on e5, White has more space on the kingside, while Black's pieces are somewhat restricted. The queenside is difficult to open because White's own pawns block the knight from influencing that side.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage on one side, direct your pieces toward that side and seek a pawn break there. Reorganize your pieces to support the attack before initiating it.
notes.plans: Prepare the h4 break by rerouting pieces from the queenside to the kingside, e.g., moving the knight to e2 and supporting with c3.

notes.explains: The queen has a choice between central squares like d3 or e2, or a more provocative b3. Queen b3 inhibits Black's development by attacking b7, but queen d3 is consistent with central control.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for the queen, weigh the benefits of centralization against the potential to create concrete threats that hinder the opponent's development.
notes.plans: After queen d3, continue with the plan of preparing h4, while being aware of potential tactical ideas against the queen's safety.

notes.explains: Black's knight maneuver (a6-b4) gains tempi on the queen but wastes time, allowing White to fully organize his forces for the kingside attack. White's pieces become harmoniously placed while Black's are scattered.
notes.teaches: Avoid spending time on repetitive maneuvers that don't improve your position; instead, focus on completing development and coordinating your pieces for the plan you have chosen.
notes.plans: White proceeds with h4, having all available pieces pointing toward the kingside, while Black's pieces are poorly coordinated.

notes.explains: In the resulting sharp position, multiple pawns are hanging (g4, f4, h4). The position becomes tactical, and concrete calculation is required rather than relying on general principles.
notes.teaches: In complex tactical positions, you must calculate specific variations carefully; there are no shortcuts. Look for moves that maintain the tension or create counterplay.
notes.plans: Black may play h5 to give back the f4 pawn but cement the g4 pawn, locking the position and reducing White's attacking potential.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, several pawns are hanging, including the h4 pawn. The evaluation hinges on whether Black should grab it, but the key is piece activity versus material.
notes.teaches: When multiple pawns are hanging, calculate concretely; there are no general principles. Material gains can be meaningless if they allow the opponent's pieces to activate.
notes.plans: Black should consider moves that maintain the blockade of White's pieces, such as stepping the queen away to avoid tactical checks, rather than capturing the h4 pawn.

notes.explains: After Black captures on h4, White's rook on h1 becomes active along the h-file, and the knight and queen also spring to life. The previously contained white pieces are now free.
notes.teaches: A seemingly greedy pawn capture can open lines for the opponent's pieces. Always consider how your capture improves the opponent's activity.
notes.plans: White should aim to activate all pieces, for example by moving the king to g1 to free the f1 square for the knight, then bring the knight into play.

notes.explains: White's advantage after ...Qxh4 is not a tactical knockout but a positional one: all white pieces become active, while Black's pieces remain passive.
notes.teaches: Advantages can be purely positional, based on piece activity and coordination, not just material or direct threats.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve piece placement, using the h-file and central squares to increase pressure.

notes.explains: A better move for Black would have been to avoid taking on h4 and instead maintain the containment of White's pieces, for example by moving the queen to d7 to avoid tactical checks.
notes.teaches: When you have a good positional grip, avoid moves that release the tension and give the opponent counterplay. Keep the opponent's pieces tied down.
notes.plans: Black should continue with simple development, keeping the knight on f5 and maintaining the blockade, accepting a slightly worse but defensible position.

notes.explains: In this sharp opening line, White's pieces are cramped and passive, while Black has grabbed material. The key is that White's king on g1, though slightly odd-looking, vacates f1 for the knight and defends the rook, unpinning the knight and preparing active play.
notes.teaches: Activity is paramount in unbalanced positions; sometimes a quiet king move that improves piece coordination outweighs immediate material considerations.
notes.plans: White aims to activate the knight via f1, then target the h5 pawn and open lines, while Black struggles to develop.

notes.explains: After the h-pawns are traded, White's pieces suddenly become active: the rook on the h-file, the knight coming to f4, and the queen on a strong diagonal. Black's pieces remain passive, and White's pressure builds to a decisive level.
notes.teaches: Trading pawns can transform a position; evaluate the resulting piece activity, not just the material balance.
notes.plans: White continues to improve piece placement, eventually trapping a black piece and winning material.

notes.explains: Black tried to hold on to every material gain, but this gave White too much activity. Chess requires concessions; you cannot take everything without giving something back.
notes.teaches: Material greed without regard for activity often backfires. Aim for dynamic compensation and piece play.

notes.explains: In this fianchetto setup with pawns on d4 and d5, both bishops are often blocked by their own pawns. The bishops on g7 and g2 can become passive if the center remains closed.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a fianchettoed bishop is likely to be bad. In symmetrical central structures, both bishops may be limited, so activating them becomes a key plan.
notes.plans: Both sides should look for ways to activate their fianchettoed bishops, either by opening the center or rerouting the bishop to a better diagonal.

notes.explains: White plays e3 to support d4 and keep the g7 bishop locked in. Black avoids e6 and instead castles, keeping the option to push e5 later. White tries to activate the bishop via Nge2-f4, aiming at d5.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is bad, you can either support the center to keep the opponent's bishop bad, or find a way to reroute your own bishop to a better square. Sometimes delaying pawn moves keeps flexibility.
notes.plans: White may try to pressure d5 with pieces; black should seek counterplay by activating the g7 bishop, possibly with e5.

notes.explains: Black plays b6 and Ba6, trading the light-squared bishops. This is a good decision because the bishop on g2 is not a good piece; it's blocked by its own pawns. Black's bishop on a6 is more active, eyeing the d3 square and the queenside.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically trade pieces just because they are 'opposite colored' or seem annoying. Evaluate which bishop is actually better. A 'bad' bishop can be left on the board if it's not doing much, while you activate your own.
notes.plans: Black has improved his bishop to a6, gaining a tempo and making White's bishop on g2 look passive. Black should continue to improve piece activity.

notes.explains: After developing all minor pieces, the position is balanced. The open c-file is the only open file, but both sides need a plan to improve their pieces. Black considers Re8 to prepare e5, activating the g7 bishop.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions, look for pawn breaks that open lines for your pieces. A rook on e8 supports a central push like e5, which can free a fianchettoed bishop.
notes.plans: Black plays Re8, then pushes e5, sacrificing a pawn for active pieces. White may capture, but Black gets a strong knight on e5 and the g7 bishop becomes powerful.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, giving White a better pawn structure (isolated d-pawn) but gaining active pieces. The knight on e5 and the g7 bishop become very strong, and Black's pieces are all well-placed.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can trade a structural advantage for piece activity. If your pieces become more active, they can compensate for a weak pawn. This is a common theme in Fischer's games.
notes.plans: Black should continue to exploit the active pieces, possibly targeting the d4 pawn or the kingside. White must be careful not to fall to tactics.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has accepted a slightly weak pawn on e5 in exchange for active piece play, with a bishop on g7 and a knight on e5. The position is good for Black because all pieces are springing to life.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn sacrifice or structural weakness, evaluate the compensation in terms of piece activity and attacking chances.
notes.plans: Black should continue to develop and increase pressure, looking for tactical opportunities.

notes.explains: It is too early for Black to capture on d5 because the white queen is overworked. If Black grabs the pawn, White can respond with tactics that leave Black worse off.
notes.teaches: Before taking a pawn, check if the opponent's pieces are overloaded and if the capture allows a tactical refutation.
notes.plans: Black should avoid premature captures and instead maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: White must choose which rook to bring to d1. The f-rook is more natural because it moves off the a6-bishop's line, but the a-rook is correct due to subtle tactical reasons.
notes.teaches: When choosing between two similar moves, consider the tactical consequences of each, especially regarding pins and potential sacrifices.
notes.plans: White should play Rad1 to avoid the tactical sequence that follows Rfd1.

notes.explains: After Rfd1, Black plays Nd3, seemingly bad because the knight is attacked twice, but it sets up a forced sequence: Nxf2, Ng4+, Nxe3, and eventually Nxg2, removing the bishop that defends the king.
notes.teaches: A piece can be sacrificed to open up the king's defenses, even if the immediate move looks poor. Calculate forced sequences to see the full idea.
notes.plans: Black should follow through with the sacrifice to expose the white king.

notes.explains: After the knight sacrifice, Black plays d4 to remove the defender of the knight on e2, allowing a decisive rook invasion. The final move is queen f6, delivering mate.
notes.teaches: When attacking, remove the defenders of key pieces to enable decisive tactics. Look for quiet moves that set up unstoppable threats.
notes.plans: Black should continue the attack with d4 and then deliver the final blow with Qf6.

notes.explains: In this position, the knight on e2 is a key defender, and removing it allows a decisive rook capture. The move d4 is a simple removal of the defender, forcing the knight to move or be captured, which opens lines for the attack.
notes.teaches: When a key defender is blocking a winning capture, consider a move that forces that defender away or captures it, even if it seems like a quiet move.
notes.plans: After the defender is removed, continue the attack by exploiting the weakened squares and the exposed king.

notes.explains: After the queen moves to d7, the threat is queen h3 check, which forces the king to g1, setting up a mating net. The key is to use a distraction sacrifice on e1 to deflect the queen from guarding g2.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is defending a key mating square, a sacrifice on a square that forces the queen to capture can deflect it, allowing a back-rank mate or a decisive material gain.
notes.plans: Play rook e1 check, and if the queen takes, queen g2 is mate; if the rook takes, bishop takes d4, winning the queen.

notes.explains: The move e5 is a positional sacrifice that gives up a structural weakness (a pawn) in exchange for activity and piece coordination. This understanding of dynamic compensation over static structure is what separates top players.
notes.teaches: In chess, activity and initiative can be worth more than material or pawn structure. Look for moves that give your pieces maximum activity, even if they create weaknesses.
notes.plans: After e5, develop the pieces actively and use the open lines to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: In this position, black is considering b6, which opens a second diagonal for the bishop. The key is that the new diagonal is more valuable because it pressures the knight and rook and controls d3, while the original diagonal is less relevant. White's g3 and e3 have weakened the light squares, making black's plan even more effective.
notes.teaches: When deciding whether to spend a tempo on a move like b6, weigh the value of the new diagonal against the cost of weakening squares and the tempo spent. If the position is quiet and the opponent has no immediate threats, such a move can be justified.
notes.plans: Black should aim to develop the bishop to the long diagonal and maintain pressure on the knight and rook, while controlling key squares like d3.

notes.explains: White's opening was timid, and although most moves were fine, white missed chances to improve. After rook to d1, white could still hold, but after knight d3, white needed to defend f2 with moves like knight f4. The key was to spot the threat to f2 and address it before it became fatal.
notes.teaches: In a slightly worse but defensible position, look for ways to neutralize the opponent's activity while maintaining your structural advantages. Always be alert to tactical threats like the one on f2 and address them promptly.
notes.plans: White should consider rook to d1, followed by knight f4 or knight d4 to challenge black's pawn and blockade, aiming to stabilize the position.

notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez, black's early b5 and a6 are concessions that draw the pawns forward, but they also create immediate pressure on the bishop with knight a5. White's bishop e3 is a non-main line; castling is more common today.
notes.teaches: In the Ruy Lopez, black's pawn advances are a double-edged sword: they gain time on the bishop but create potential weaknesses. Understanding the trade-off between activity and long-term pawn structure is crucial.
notes.plans: Black will continue to develop and target the bishop, while white should aim to castle and consolidate, possibly exploiting the weakened queenside pawns later.

notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez, Black's early ...b5 is a slight concession, drawing the queenside pawns forward so they can later be targets. White's bishop on b3 is then attacked by ...Na5, and White responds by breaking in the center with d4, challenging Black's e5 pawn.
notes.teaches: The Ruy Lopez aims to provoke ...a6 and ...b5, creating potential weaknesses in Black's queenside pawn structure. When the bishop is attacked, central play with d4 is a common and principled response.
notes.plans: After ...exd4 and Qxd4, Black develops with ...Ne7, avoiding ...Nf6 because of the possible e5 push, and instead prepares to develop the bishop to b7.

notes.explains: White's bishop on f4 is a loose piece, as it is not defended and can be attacked with tempo. This allows Black to play ...d5, striking in the center, even though Black is behind in castling. If White captures on d5, Black recaptures with the knight, and the bishop on f4 remains a problem.
notes.teaches: Loose pieces create tactical opportunities. When your opponent has a loose piece, look for ways to exploit it, either by gaining time with attacks or by opening the position to increase its vulnerability.
notes.plans: Black can play ...d5, and if White takes, recapture with the knight, then follow up with ...Be7 and castling, enjoying the two bishops and open center. Alternatively, ...Ng6 attacking the bishop is also good.

notes.explains: The moral is to avoid creating loose pieces and to exploit your opponent's. Here, White's bishop on f4 is loose, and Black's ...d5 is justified because White must spend time dealing with the bishop, allowing Black to use the open e-file.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for loose pieces in the opponent's camp. They can be the basis for tactics and for seizing the initiative, even if you are behind in development.
notes.plans: If White plays a move like castling instead of addressing the bishop, then ...d5 is less effective, so Black should consider other ways to exploit the loose piece, such as ...Ng6.

notes.explains: In this position, black's bishop on f4 is loose, and white's pieces are not well-coordinated. Black can exploit this by attacking the loose piece with knight g6, gaining time, or by opening the center with d5, which is strong because the bishop on f4 is vulnerable.
notes.teaches: Loose pieces are a major weakness. Always look for ways to exploit your opponent's loose pieces, either by attacking them to gain tempo or by opening the position to increase their vulnerability.
notes.plans: If white castles kingside, d5 becomes less effective because the open file allows white to defend. Instead, black should consider other ways to pressure the loose bishop.

notes.explains: After white plays e5 to prevent the knight from reaching d5, black finds c5, attacking the bishop on f4 again. If white's queen takes on c5, black has a winning tactic: knight f5 traps the queen in the center because all escape squares are defended.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's queen is exposed, look for tactical motifs like trapping it with a knight fork or a discovered attack. Even in the center, a queen can be vulnerable if the surrounding squares are controlled.
notes.plans: If white avoids the tactic, black continues to pressure the bishop, forcing white to lose tempo with moves like bishop g3, while black develops and maintains the initiative.

notes.explains: Black has a space advantage on the queenside and a strong center. The plan is to maintain the space and prepare a break with d4, which would open the bishop and the d-file. Castling is natural, but black chooses a more aggressive plan: rerouting the knight to e6 to blockade the d-pawn and support d4, then expanding on the kingside with g5 and h5.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, you can often expand on both sides of the board to create multiple threats. However, such pawn advances create weaknesses, so they must be timed carefully and only when the king is safe.
notes.plans: Black will continue to improve piece placement, perhaps with queen b6 to avoid the rook's file, and prepare breaks like d4, g4, or a4 to keep white off balance.

notes.explains: When the opponent is attacking on all sides, it can be uncomfortable, but such aggression often creates weaknesses and carries risk.
notes.teaches: Aggressive pawn moves like h5 and g5 can win games but also lose some; be prepared for the risk if you adopt them.

notes.explains: The queen was moved to b6 to improve its position, getting off the same file as the rook and preparing ideas like Rd8 if needed.
notes.teaches: Improving the queen to a better square can also prepare tactical resources like a rook lift or a central break.

notes.explains: After White's knight retreated to f1, Black decided it was time to break through with d4, since the c-pawn is not hanging due to the tactical resource of Rd8.
notes.teaches: A central pawn break can be justified when the opponent's pieces are poorly placed and tactical resources protect your pawns.
notes.plans: After d4, Black aims to open the center and exploit White's passive pieces.

notes.explains: White's move Nd2 was confusing because the knight had just gone to f1, and if the idea was to play Ne4, why not use the other knight? Nd2 does step out of the way of g4, but then the knight on h4 would be better placed to go to f5.
notes.teaches: Piece coordination matters: avoid redundant maneuvers that waste time; choose the most active square for each piece.

notes.explains: In the resulting queenless position, Black's king improved to d7, rooks went to the queenside, and Black picked off pawns on both sides and the center, leaving White unable to hold everything together.
notes.teaches: In a queenless middlegame, the king can become an active piece, and rooks should target multiple weaknesses simultaneously.
notes.plans: Black will continue to collect weak pawns, using the king's centralization and rook activity to convert the advantage.

notes.explains: This game is a classic example of creating a weakness on one side, then creating a second weakness on the other side rather than playing simple moves like castling kingside.
notes.teaches: Instead of just defending or making obvious moves, look for ways to create additional weaknesses in the opponent's position.

notes.explains: Zugzwang is a position where the player to move has no good moves; it is most common in king and pawn endgames but can occur in any phase, including the middlegame, though it is rarer with many pieces on the board.
notes.teaches: Recognize zugzwang by noticing that any move worsens your position; in endgames, it often decides the outcome.

notes.explains: In a king and pawn endgame with corresponding squares, the kings are tied to defending their pawns. If the defender must move first, they may lose the pawn because no adjacent square allows them to keep both attacking and defending.
notes.teaches: When kings are in a mutual opposition or corresponding squares, the side to move may be in zugzwang; look for waiting moves or pawn moves to shift the burden.

notes.explains: If the defender moves the king away, the attacker captures the pawn and, with extra pawns on the other side, can win by sacrificing a pawn to gain access to the remaining pawns.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, an extra pawn is often winning if there are pawns on both sides, because you can create a passed pawn or use a diversion.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawn to deflect the enemy king, then gobble the remaining pawns.
