notes.explains: Another key idea is circling around with the king: by shouldering the opponent's king and pushing it down, you can eventually return to grab the material. This is a favorite technique in king and pawn endgames.
notes.teaches: The 'circle around' technique: use your king to shoulder the opponent's king away, then come back to capture pawns. This is a powerful way to win material.
notes.plans: White circles around the black king, forcing it down, then returns to capture the pawns and win.

notes.explains: In king and pawn endgames, the race of passed pawns is decided by whose king is faster to support the pawn. Here, giving up a pawn to let the black g-pawn run is hopeless because black's pawn is much faster than anything white can do.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a pawn race, count the moves each side needs to queen, and check whether the defending king can catch the passer. If the opponent's pawn is faster, do not rely on a race; look for other resources.
notes.plans: If white tries to stop the pawn with the king, black can use the king to shoulder white's king away and then return to grab the material.

notes.explains: The key winning idea is to use the king to 'circle around' the opponent's king, shouldering it away from the pawns. By pushing the defending king down, the attacking king can then come back to win the pawns.
notes.teaches: Outflanking (or circling) is a fundamental king maneuver in king and pawn endgames: use your king to push the opponent's king sideways, then return to the critical squares.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play ...c5, then ...b5 to trade pawns and maintain the opposition, keeping the win.

notes.explains: The opposition is a powerful tool: by maintaining the opposition, black can prevent white's king from making progress, even though white has an extra pawn. White cannot break through because any attempt to go around is met by ...b4, which is not effective since black's b-pawn is more advanced.
notes.teaches: The opposition is a defensive and offensive resource: if you can keep the opposition, you can freeze the opponent's king and control the key squares.
notes.plans: Black keeps the opposition and follows the white king, never allowing it to infiltrate.

notes.explains: When white is in zugzwang, any move loses. If white pushes the pawn, black's king is faster and will take both pawns. If white moves the king away, black wins the pawn.
notes.teaches: Zugzwang is a recurring theme in king and pawn endgames: sometimes the side to move is forced to weaken their position. Recognize when the opponent has no good moves.
notes.plans: Black uses zugzwang to force white to give up the pawn, then wins the resulting king and pawn endgame.

notes.explains: Beautiful ideas can occur at any level of play, not just in games between top grandmasters. The endgame examples here illustrate that even simple positions can contain deep and elegant maneuvers.
notes.teaches: Chess beauty is accessible to everyone; you don't need to be a top player to create or appreciate a beautiful idea. Enjoy the game and the learning process.

notes.explains: Beauty in chess is not reserved for top players; even games between weaker players can contain instructive and beautiful positions. The value of a position comes from the ideas it teaches, not the rating of the players.
notes.teaches: Always look for the instructive content in any game, regardless of the players' strength. Enjoy the game for its ideas.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn endgame, both kings are active and pawns are on the same side. The position looks deceptively simple, but the evaluation is not obvious: it is a draw, but only with one precise move for White. Natural moves like Ke7 or Ke5 are actually blunders.
notes.teaches: Do not trust first impressions in king-pawn endgames; the activity of the kings and the race to capture pawns require precise calculation. The side to move may have only one drawing move.
notes.plans: White must find the only drawing move (g4) to hold; other natural king moves lose.

notes.explains: After the natural Ke7, Black pushes the pawn and wins the race because White's weakness (the h-pawn) is closer to Black's king than Black's weakness is to White's. When Black captures, the correct target is the h-pawn, not the g-pawn, because taking the g-pawn allows White to create a passed h-pawn and draw.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, capture the opponent's pawn that is closer to promoting or that can create a dangerous passed pawn. Always take the pawn that bothers you the most.
notes.plans: Black captures the h-pawn, then uses the extra pawn to win the endgame.

notes.explains: If White tries to deviate with king moves like Kf6 or Kg7, Black continues to target the weak pawns and the f-pawn marches. White's attempts to create counterplay with g4 or f4 fail because Black has an extra pawn and can win.
notes.teaches: When defending a worse endgame, you must find the precise defensive resource; otherwise, the opponent's extra pawn will decide. Keep your king close to the opponent's pawns to stop them.
notes.plans: White's only hope is the immediate g4 push; otherwise Black wins.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn endgame, the white king must choose the only move that draws. Pushing the wrong pawn or moving the king to the wrong square allows Black's distant passed pawn to win.
notes.teaches: When facing a distant passed pawn, the king must stay close enough to stop it, while also being able to support your own pawns. Every tempo matters.
notes.plans: White should play g4 to keep the black king far from the kingside, then use the time to bring the king back to defend.

notes.explains: The move f5 is correct because it trades off a pawn and creates a passed pawn, while king e5 would waste time and allow Black to win.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, you must use your pawns to create counterplay, not just move the king aimlessly. A pawn break can be the only way to draw.
notes.plans: After f5, White trades pawns and then uses the resulting passed pawn to force a draw.

notes.explains: The move h5 is crucial for Black to draw. If Black pushes the g-pawn instead, White's king gets too close and can create mating threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a queen vs. pawns, the defending side must keep the enemy king far from the queening square. Pushing the wrong pawn can allow the king to approach.
notes.plans: Black plays h5 to keep the white king away, ensuring a draw even if White promotes.

notes.explains: In the final phase, White must choose king e7, not f6. King e7 gets the king to the opposition and prevents Black from winning the h-pawn.
notes.teaches: When defending against a king and pawn, you must take the opposition to stop the enemy king from penetrating. Do not push your pawns prematurely; they can be captured quickly.
notes.plans: White circles around to take the opposition, forcing a draw.

notes.explains: In king and pawn endgames, pushing a pawn too early can be a blunder because the opponent can simply take it and promote. The correct technique is to bring the king around and take the opposition, not to chase the pawn directly.
notes.teaches: Do not rush pawn pushes in king and pawn endgames; use the king to gain opposition and control key squares before advancing pawns.
notes.plans: Circle the king around to take the opposition and force the opponent's king away, then advance the pawn when it is safe.

notes.explains: In a specific position, the correct move was king e7, not pushing the f-pawn. Pushing f6 would allow the opponent to take it quickly and win. By playing king e7, white maintains the defense and can later take opposition.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, prioritize king activity and opposition over pawn pushes. Calculate whether a pawn push is safe before making it.
notes.plans: Play king e7, then use the king to control key squares and eventually draw or win depending on the position.

notes.explains: The concept of 'mine squares' is introduced: in some king and pawn endgames, the player who steps onto a certain square first loses. This is a critical tactical motif that can decide the game.
notes.teaches: Be aware of 'mine squares' in king and pawn endgames; sometimes you must avoid moving to a square because the opponent can then force a win.
notes.plans: Recognize mine squares and maneuver the king to avoid them, forcing the opponent to step on them first.

notes.explains: In a position with a protected passed pawn, the defender may be in zugzwang: any move worsens their position. The correct move for the attacker is to put the defender in zugzwang, forcing them to move their king and lose the pawn.
notes.teaches: Use zugzwang in king and pawn endgames to force the opponent's king away from defending a pawn, then capture it.
notes.plans: Play h5 to put the opponent in zugzwang, forcing their king to move, then capture the f6 pawn and win.

notes.explains: In a different position, the correct move for white was g4 to maintain the balance and draw. Other moves like king e4 would allow f4, giving black counterplay. The choice of king move matters because it affects the opponent's pawn breaks.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, choose king moves that restrict the opponent's pawn breaks and maintain the balance. Sometimes a quiet move like g4 is better than an aggressive king move.
notes.plans: Play g4 to keep the position balanced and aim for a draw.

notes.explains: In a position with multiple pawns, the correct move for black was f5, not f3, because f3 would allow white to be faster. The key is to calculate the race and ensure your pawn advances first.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, calculate which pawn promotes first. Sometimes the less obvious move is correct because it gains a tempo.
notes.plans: Play f5 to ensure the pawn promotes before white's, leading to a win.

notes.explains: In any position, the 'right' move is simply the one that wins; there is no single correct method. You must identify your goal and find the fastest route to it.
notes.teaches: Always evaluate moves by their practical outcome, not by abstract rules. Choose the move that most efficiently leads to a win.

notes.explains: In king and pawn endgames, getting your king to the center quickly is crucial. Here, Black managed to bring their king to d5 first, gaining a tempo advantage.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, king activity and centralization are paramount. Every tempo matters, so avoid unnecessary pawn moves that waste time.
notes.plans: White should focus on activating the king and creating passed pawns, while Black must use their central king to restrict White's progress.

notes.explains: Black missed a drawing resource: playing b4 to blockade the queenside pawns. This creates a fortress where White's king has no entry points, and despite being a pawn up, White cannot win.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, blockade the opponent's pawns to create a fortress. If you can prevent the enemy king from penetrating, the game may be drawn even with a material deficit.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade pawns and maintain the opposition to keep White's king out. White must find a way to break the blockade, but if Black plays accurately, it's a draw.

notes.explains: In king and pawn endgames with pawns on both sides, the opposition is a key resource. Taking the opposition can hold a draw, but the defender must be precise about which square to move to when the attacking king advances.
notes.teaches: When defending, do not automatically head for the 'important' square; check whether the position is fully fixed or whether the attacker can outflank you. A wrong king move can allow the opponent to enter and win a pawn.
notes.plans: If the defender keeps the opposition correctly, the result is a draw. The defender should maintain the opposition and avoid moving the king to a square that lets the attacker infiltrate.

notes.explains: In positions with pawns on both sides, a reserve tempo (an extra pawn move) can be decisive. By choosing the right pawn move (e.g., b5 instead of g5), Black keeps a spare tempo to maintain the opposition later.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple pawn moves available, think about which one preserves a useful extra tempo. A well-timed pawn move can give you the opposition when needed.
notes.plans: Black should play b5 to keep the extra tempo, then later decide between g6 or g5 depending on White's play. This maintains the option to take the opposition and draw.

notes.explains: In the actual game, Black erred by playing h4 instead of the correct b5, allowing White to enter and win. Even strong players make such mistakes in complex pawn endgames.
notes.teaches: In endgames with many pawn pushes, it is easy to misjudge which pawn move is critical. Always double-check that your move does not give the opponent a decisive entry.
notes.plans: Black should have played b5 to keep the position solid and maintain the draw. After the mistake, White can win by entering and grabbing the pawn.

notes.explains: White has a winning plan by using a king triangulation (e.g., Kh2) to lose a tempo and put Black in zugzwang. Black is forced to move and eventually must give way, allowing White's king to penetrate.
notes.teaches: When the defender is waiting, you can use triangulation or extra pawn moves to pass the move to the opponent. This forces them to weaken their position, allowing your king to enter.
notes.plans: White should play Kh2, then use pawn moves (like f3, f4, g5) to force Black's king away. Once White's king penetrates, the win is straightforward.

notes.explains: If Black tries to restrict White's king by advancing on the kingside (e.g., e5), White should respond with a4 on the queenside. This move loses two tempi but stops Black's queenside pawns from becoming a distraction.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must spend tempi to neutralize the opponent's pawns on the other side. This allows you to focus on the main plan of penetrating with your king.
notes.plans: White plays a4 to fix the queenside pawns, then proceeds with the king penetration on the other side. Black's counterplay is neutralized.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn endgame, White's extra tempi are decisive. By playing a4, White voluntarily loses two tempi but stops Black's queenside pawns from creating counterplay, leaving White with more waiting moves.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, it's often worth sacrificing tempi to fix the opponent's pawns and preserve your own extra waiting moves. The side with more pawn moves can use them to force the opponent to move their king and lose the opposition.
notes.plans: White should use the extra tempi to wait, then create a passed pawn on the queenside to deflect the black king, after which White's king can invade and win the h-pawn.

notes.explains: When Black tries to keep the position solid and not push pawns, White can gain space on the kingside, forcing Black to eventually push pawns and run out of moves. White's king can also enter via h2 instead of the more natural f1, landing on the better square f4.
notes.teaches: King routes are not always direct; sometimes a longer path leads to a better square. Also, advancing your own pawns can restrict the opponent's king and create more tempi.
notes.plans: White should push the kingside pawns to gain space, then use the extra tempi to force Black's king to move and allow White's king to penetrate.

notes.explains: In this bishop-versus-pawns endgame, White's extra bishop does not guarantee a win. If White's king is tied to stopping Black's connected passed pawns, the bishop alone cannot support the f-pawn, and Black can hold a draw by keeping the king active and the pawns protected.
notes.teaches: Connected passed pawns can create a fortress that neutralizes an extra bishop, especially when the stronger side's king is passive. Always check for defensive resources like pawn sacrifices and king activity before assuming a win.
notes.plans: White should look for a way to activate the king or reposition the bishop to create threats, rather than passively defending.

notes.explains: The move bishop d5 is a key resource: it improves the bishop's placement while exploiting a tactical idea. If Black captures, they lose material, so the bishop gets to a better square.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for tactical ways to improve your pieces. A bishop can often find a more active diagonal while creating threats that force the opponent to allow the improvement.
notes.plans: After bishop d5, White aims to use the bishop to control key squares and support the f-pawn while keeping Black's pawns in check.

notes.explains: After the sequence where White captures on b4 and c6, the position appears winning, but it is actually a fortress. Black's king and pawns coordinate to prevent White's king from supporting the f-pawn, and the bishop cannot win the pawns alone.
notes.teaches: Even with an extra piece, if the opponent can set up a fortress where your king is locked out, the game may be drawn. Recognize fortress patterns and avoid simplifying into them.
notes.plans: White must find a way to break the fortress, often by repositioning the bishop to create zugzwang or by finding a different entry point for the king.

notes.explains: The move bishop b7 is the winning idea. It forces Black to push pawns, and then White can create a fortress of their own, putting Black's king in zugzwang. Black's king cannot approach the f-pawn, and White will eventually win the pawns and support the f-pawn with the king.
notes.teaches: In endgames, sometimes the winning idea is to create a fortress of your own, restricting the opponent's king. Zugzwang can force the opponent to weaken their pawn structure, allowing you to win them.
notes.plans: White plays bishop b7, then after Black's pawn pushes, White uses the bishop to control the pawns while bringing the king to support the f-pawn, securing a win.

notes.explains: In this bishop-and-pawn versus pawns endgame, the key is to create a fortress where the bishop stops the enemy pawns while the king supports the passed f-pawn. If the black king cannot approach the f-pawn, White's extra bishop should win.
notes.teaches: A fortress can be built by placing the bishop on a diagonal that both blocks enemy pawns and prevents the enemy king from approaching your passed pawn. The king then supports the passed pawn, and the bishop handles the rest.
notes.plans: White should aim to place the bishop on a key diagonal (like b7 or d5) to stop the a- and b-pawns, while the king advances to support the f-pawn. If the black king gets close, use a waiting move with the bishop to put Black in zugzwang.

notes.explains: The correct move for White is king to a3, forcing Black's king to move away, allowing White's king to advance. This puts Black in zugzwang because any pawn move loses a pawn, and any king move allows White to improve.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a waiting move (often with the bishop) can force the opponent into zugzwang. The bishop is ideal for this because it can make a waiting move while the knight cannot.
notes.plans: After king a3, if Black plays b6, the bishop retreats; if Black goes back, White pushes f4. The fortress remains, and White can eventually win the enemy pawns.

notes.explains: When the black king is close to the f-pawn, White must not rush to push the pawn. Instead, a waiting move with the bishop gives Black the move, forcing them to weaken their position. If White pushes prematurely, Black can draw by deflecting the bishop.
notes.teaches: Do not rush to push a passed pawn if the enemy king is near. Use a waiting move to maintain the fortress and keep the opponent passive. The bishop's ability to make a waiting move is crucial.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on the correct diagonal, make waiting moves, and only push the f-pawn when the black king is far enough away. Then the king can support the pawn to promotion.

notes.explains: The bishop must stay on the correct diagonal to stop the enemy pawns from promoting and to keep the fortress. If the bishop leaves the diagonal, the pawns can advance and deflect it, leading to a draw.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, the bishop's diagonal is often the most important asset. It can simultaneously stop passed pawns, support your own pawn, and restrict the enemy king.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on the key diagonal (e.g., d5 or b7). If Black pushes a pawn, reposition the bishop to maintain the blockade. Then bring the king to win the pawns and the game.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn endgame, the bishop's placement on the correct diagonal is critical: it both stops the enemy pawn from promoting and supports our own pawn's advance.
notes.teaches: When defending against a passed pawn, place your bishop on the diagonal that controls its promotion square, even if it means giving up a tempo with a bishop move.
notes.plans: Move the king to c3 to maintain opposition and prevent the enemy king from approaching the pawn, while the bishop controls the promotion square.

notes.explains: The position is a study-like fortress: the bishop and king coordinate to create a barrier that prevents the enemy king from approaching the pawn, while the bishop also supports the pawn's advance.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a well-placed bishop can create a fortress that restricts the enemy king's movement, even when material is equal or slightly worse.
notes.plans: Maintain the fortress by keeping the bishop on the correct diagonal and using the king to control key squares, then advance the pawn when safe.

notes.explains: The position appears simple but has only one correct solution, requiring precise calculation and understanding of the underlying ideas.
notes.teaches: Endgame studies often have a single winning idea; take time to find the exact move rather than relying on general principles.

notes.explains: In a king and pawn endgame, when the two kings stand directly opposite each other with one square between them, the side to move is at a disadvantage because moving the king gives ground. This is the opposition, and it often decides whether the position is winning or drawing.
notes.teaches: The opposition is a fundamental tool: if it is your opponent's turn to move in such a standoff, you gain the advantage; if it is your turn, you may be forced to give way.
notes.plans: If you have the opposition, use it to penetrate with your king or to support your pawn's advance. If you are defending, try to maintain the opposition to hold the draw.

notes.explains: When defending a king and pawn endgame, the drawing move is often to step straight back behind the pawn, keeping the king ready to block the pawn's path. This avoids allowing the enemy king to get in front of the pawn.
notes.teaches: A common defensive technique is to move the king directly behind the pawn, so that if the pawn advances with check, the king can step aside and still stop promotion.
notes.plans: As the defender, retreat the king along the pawn's file to maintain the opposition and force the attacker to find a precise winning plan.

notes.explains: When the attacking king reaches the sixth rank in front of its pawn, the win is usually assured regardless of whose turn it is. The king controls key squares and can shepherd the pawn to promotion.
notes.teaches: A king on the sixth rank in front of its pawn is a decisive advantage: the pawn will promote even if the opponent has the move.
notes.plans: Aim to get your king to the sixth rank in front of the pawn. If the enemy king is cut off, use your king to escort the pawn, or if necessary, give up the opposition because the king's position is already winning.

notes.explains: In a queen versus pawn endgame, the queen often cannot stop the pawn from promoting if the pawn is far advanced and the defending king is nearby. The queen must use checks and pins to bring its own king closer.
notes.teaches: Against a lone pawn, the queen should first pin the pawn to prevent its advance, then use checks to force the enemy king in front of the pawn, buying time to bring the queen's king into the action.
notes.plans: Start by pinning the pawn with the queen, then give checks to drive the enemy king to a square where it blocks the pawn. Use that time to approach with your king, aiming to support the queen in forcing the pawn's capture.

notes.explains: In a queen versus pawn endgame, the queen must get as close as possible to the enemy king to restrict its movement and force it to block its own pawn. The key position often involves the queen checking from a square that controls the pawn's advance squares.
notes.teaches: When defending against a lone pawn, the queen should approach the king to create a mating net or force the king to step in front of the pawn, allowing the queen to win the pawn or bring the king closer.
notes.plans: Use checks to drive the king to the side of the board, then bring the king up to support the queen in capturing the pawn.

notes.explains: The position of the pawn matters: a pawn on f2 (central files) may be a draw if the defending king is far away, because the queen cannot force the king away from the pawn without stalemate. The queen must keep checking to avoid stalemate, but the king can shuttle between f1 and g1.
notes.teaches: In queen vs pawn, the file of the pawn and the distance of the attacking king determine whether it's a win or draw. For a central pawn, if the attacking king is far, the defender can draw by heading to the corner.
notes.plans: If the pawn is on f2 and the king is far, the queen should keep checking to prevent the king from approaching, but the result is a draw.

notes.explains: With a pawn on g2 (near the edge), the queen can win by pinning the pawn with Qf3, forcing the king to step aside, then bringing the king up. The key is to avoid stalemate by not taking the pawn when the king is in the corner.
notes.teaches: For a pawn on the knight file, the queen can often win by pinning the pawn and bringing the king, but must be careful of stalemate if the king is trapped in the corner.
notes.plans: Play Qf3 to pin the pawn, then bring the king to support the capture. If the king goes to h1, use Qh4 to force it away.

notes.explains: With a pawn on h2 (rook file), the queen cannot win if the defending king reaches the corner, because taking the pawn is stalemate. The queen must zigzag to force the king out, but if the attacking king is far, it's a draw.
notes.teaches: A rook pawn is a draw if the defending king can reach the corner, unless the attacking king is close enough to give support. The queen must use checks to drive the king away from the corner.
notes.plans: Use checks to force the king to h1, then bring the king up. If the king goes to g2, the queen must find a way to give checks without stalemating.

notes.explains: In a queen versus king endgame, the king must be brought close to support the queen for checkmate, but the timing matters: if the king approaches too early, the defending king can give checks that lead to a draw. The queen must first restrict the enemy king, often by moving to the second rank, before the king advances.
notes.teaches: Coordinate the queen and king: use the queen to confine the enemy king, then bring your king to a key square (like g3) to deliver mate. The king should be two squares away from the critical mating square to maintain control.
notes.plans: Place the queen on the second rank to cut off the enemy king, then bring the king to the key square (e.g., g3) to force mate. If the enemy king moves, reposition the queen to maintain the net.

notes.explains: When a king is near the edge, stalemate is a constant danger. The stronger side must avoid checks that allow the king to escape or that lead to stalemate; instead, the queen should be placed to control squares while the king approaches.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, always be alert to stalemate possibilities. Use the queen to reduce the enemy king's mobility without giving check until the mating net is ready.
notes.plans: If the enemy king is on the edge, place the queen a knight's move away to control escape squares, then bring the king to deliver mate.

notes.explains: In a pawn race, the rule of the square is a quick way to determine if the enemy king can catch a passed pawn. Here, the black king is inside the square of the a4-pawn, so it can stop the pawn. Therefore, pushing the pawn is not winning.
notes.teaches: Use the rule of the square: draw a diagonal from the pawn to its promotion square, then complete the square. If the enemy king can enter that square, it can catch the pawn; otherwise, the pawn promotes.
notes.plans: If the pawn cannot promote, look for other moves, such as using the king to cut off the enemy king or to support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: When several candidate moves exist, use the process of elimination. Here, pushing the pawn fails because the black king is in time, and moving the king to e1 also fails because black can stop the pawn and win the resulting pawn endgame. The remaining move is the one to play.
notes.teaches: In any position, first generate candidate moves, then eliminate those that are clearly bad. This narrows the choice and often reveals the correct move.
notes.plans: After eliminating the bad candidates, play the remaining move, which should be the one that best improves your position, such as activating the king or supporting the passed pawn.

notes.explains: In this pawn endgame, two connected passed pawns supported by the king are extremely powerful; the opponent's king cannot capture them because they protect each other, forming a shield.
notes.teaches: Connected passed pawns are often decisive because they defend each other and can force promotion if the defending king is too far away.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawns together, using the king to support them, and force the opponent to block or capture, creating a winning position.

notes.explains: The rule of the square helps determine if a king can catch a passed pawn. The square is drawn from the pawn to its promotion square; if the enemy king is inside, it can catch the pawn. The rule works symmetrically on both sides of the board.
notes.teaches: Use the rule of the square to quickly assess whether a king can stop a passed pawn; remember the square is mirrored for pawns on the other side.
notes.plans: When evaluating a pawn race, draw the square mentally and check if the enemy king can enter it; if not, the pawn promotes.

notes.explains: In queen vs pawn endgames, the result (win or draw) is mirrored on the left side of the board. For example, a pawn on the b-file may be winning, while a pawn on the a-file draws, and this pattern repeats symmetrically.
notes.teaches: Memorize the mirror symmetry in queen vs pawn endgames: edge pawns often draw, while knight-file pawns may win, and the same applies on the opposite side.
notes.plans: When facing a queen vs pawn, recall the mirror pattern to know whether to push for a win or settle for a draw.

notes.explains: In a puzzle with material deficit, look for forcing moves: checks, captures, and threats, in that order. A check may lead to a fork or promotion, but must be calculated carefully; if it fails, consider other threats.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, prioritize candidate moves: checks first, then captures, then threats. This systematic approach helps find winning combinations.
notes.plans: Calculate each forcing move deeply, and if the first idea fails, look for alternative threats or defensive resources.

notes.explains: Underpromotion can be a winning resource when promoting to a queen is not necessary or when a knight or rook is needed for a specific tactic, such as a fork or to stop a pawn on the right color.
notes.teaches: Consider underpromotion when a queen would be insufficient or when a minor piece delivers a decisive tactic; also note that bishop color matters in endgames.
notes.plans: In promotions, evaluate whether a queen is best or if a knight/rook/bishop achieves a specific goal like a fork or controlling key squares.

notes.explains: In a complex position with many tactical possibilities, the first step is to generate candidate moves, prioritizing checks, captures, and threats in that order. This systematic approach ensures that forcing moves are considered before quieter options.
notes.teaches: When facing a tactical puzzle, always start by looking for checks, then captures, then threats. This ordering helps avoid missing key tactical resources.
notes.plans: After identifying candidate moves, evaluate each one by considering the opponent's possible replies and the resulting position.

notes.explains: In a position where white is a rook down but has strong connected passed pawns, the only viable move is to push the pawn that creates a direct threat. Other moves allow black to neutralize the pawns or maintain the material advantage.
notes.teaches: When material down, look for forcing moves that create immediate threats, especially pawn promotions, to turn the tables.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to the seventh rank, forcing black to respond. If the pawn is captured, recapture and promote; if not, promote to a queen or underpromote as needed.

notes.explains: Underpromotion can be necessary to avoid immediate checkmate. In this case, promoting to a queen allows a back-rank mate, so promoting to a knight is the only way to give check and prevent the mate.
notes.teaches: Always consider underpromotion when a queen promotion allows a tactical refutation, such as a back-rank mate or a fork.
notes.plans: Promote to a knight with check, forcing the king to move, then deliver mate with the knight or other pieces.

notes.explains: In a bishop versus pawns endgame, the side with the bishop may be forced to give it up for a pawn, leading to a pawn race. The key is to calculate the opposition and king activity to determine if a draw is achievable.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, the opposition and king activity are crucial. Use checks to force the opponent's king to unfavorable squares and gain tempo.
notes.plans: After the bishop is captured, use the king to stop the passed pawns, aiming for opposition to secure a draw or even a win.

notes.explains: When defending against passed pawns, the king must choose the correct route to stop them. Moving to the wrong file allows the pawns to advance and win.
notes.teaches: In pawn endings, the king must take the most direct path to blockade passed pawns, often using opposition to maintain control.
notes.plans: Place the king on a square that prevents the enemy king from supporting the pawns, then capture the pawns when possible.

notes.explains: In this pawn endgame, the king must choose between two squares to stop the passed pawn. Going to the e-file would allow the opposing king to escape, so the correct square is on the f-file, either f3 or f4, both of which keep the king from coming out via g4.
notes.teaches: When defending against a passed pawn, prioritize squares that both stop the pawn and restrict the enemy king's escape routes. Use process of elimination among candidate moves, especially under time pressure.
notes.plans: Place the king on f3 or f4 to contain the enemy king, then push the pawn to force a favorable exchange and win the h-pawn.

notes.explains: The position is difficult to see from the initial setup, but the method is to generate candidate moves and eliminate them systematically.
notes.teaches: When low on time, rely on a process of elimination: list the plausible moves, then discard those that fail to the opponent's best replies.

notes.explains: Improvement in chess comes from home study and practice, not just from watching lessons.
notes.teaches: To improve, dedicate time to solving puzzles and practicing on your own.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's idea of Rook G4 looks like it wins the queen due to a discovered attack, but White can simply capture the rook. The combination of the knight and rook then leads to checkmate for White, turning the tables.
notes.teaches: Before committing to a tactical blow, check whether the opponent has a resource that turns the tables, such as a mating net. A move that appears to win material may be refuted by a stronger counter-threat.
notes.plans: Black must find a way to renew the threat without allowing the refutation.

notes.explains: Black plays Bishop C5 instead of Bishop A3 because it attacks the rook rather than just a pawn. This move is more powerful as it creates a direct threat against White's rook while also preparing the idea of Rook G4, but White's counterplay is strong because Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a strong threat, look for a move that both addresses the threat and creates a counter-threat. Attacking a more valuable piece (rook vs pawn) can be more effective than a lesser gain.
notes.plans: Black should aim to carry out the Rook G4 idea after White deals with the bishop threat, while being mindful of the king's safety.

notes.explains: White tries D5 to block the diagonal and save the queen, but Black continues with Queen E8, Rook C7, and Rook F4, launching an attack because White's king is also unsafe. The game proceeds with forcing moves, and Black's extra pawns and attack on the king decide the game.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, keep the initiative by making forcing moves—checks, captures, and threats. When your opponent's king is exposed, use your pieces to create threats that cannot be ignored.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press the attack, using the queen and rook to create mating threats while maintaining the extra material.

notes.explains: In the final phase, Black has two checks available, but starting with the rook check runs out of steam after King G2. Starting with the queen check allows a follow-up with Rook G4, Rook H4, etc., eventually winning the opponent's queen.
notes.teaches: When calculating forcing sequences, consider the order of checks carefully. A check that forces the king to a square where the attack can continue is better than one that leads to a dead end. Once you see a clear win of the opponent's queen, you can stop calculating.
notes.plans: Black should execute the winning sequence starting with the queen check, then use the rook to continue the attack and win the queen.

notes.explains: The key lesson from this game is to notice the opponent's main ideas and understand why a tempting move like Rook G4 fails. Then, find a move that renews the idea without the refutation.
notes.teaches: In chess, don't give up on your ideas just because the immediate execution fails. Look for ways to improve the move or change the move order to make the idea work, while also respecting the opponent's resources.

notes.explains: When a candidate move like Rg4 is refuted, the task is not to abandon the underlying idea but to find a way to renew it, possibly with a preparatory move.
notes.teaches: In chess, persist with your ideas: if a direct attempt fails, look for a way to set it up again, often by improving your position first.
notes.plans: Look for a move that addresses the refutation while keeping the threat alive, such as a rook lift or king maneuver.

notes.explains: In bishop endgames, fixing pawns on the same color as the opponent's bishop makes them permanent targets for your bishop, which is a powerful strategic weapon.
notes.teaches: Aim to fix your opponent's pawns on the color of your bishop, so they become attackable and can be won.
notes.plans: Identify pawns that can be fixed and use your bishop to attack them, while keeping your own pawns on the opposite color.

notes.explains: In endgames, pawn structure becomes more important than tactical motifs; weak pawns provide ready-made plans.
notes.teaches: Evaluate pawn placement carefully: pawns on the same color as the opponent's bishop are vulnerable, while those on the opposite color are safe.
notes.plans: Create targets by fixing opponent's pawns, then attack them with your pieces.

notes.explains: A seemingly small move like Bf8 can lose control over a key square, allowing the opponent to fix a target pawn, which can be decisive.
notes.teaches: In endgames, every move matters: losing control over a square can let the opponent fix your pawns and create a winning target.
notes.plans: Keep your king and bishop active to prevent the opponent from fixing your pawns on a bad color.

notes.explains: Placing your own pawns on the color your opponent's bishop cannot attack is a sound strategy, but sometimes there is a deeper point, such as creating a passed pawn or zugzwang.
notes.teaches: When putting pawns on safe squares, consider the deeper consequences: the move may also serve to create a passed pawn or restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: In the given position, after f3, black must find a plan; white's idea is to create a passed pawn on the queenside while keeping black's bishop passive.

notes.explains: In this bishop endgame, White's f3 move places Black in zugzwang: Black's pieces are optimally placed, with the bishop defending the key pawn and invasion square, and the pawns restraining the enemy king. Any move Black makes weakens his position.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a waiting move that forces the opponent to disturb a perfectly arranged defense can be decisive. Recognize when the opponent has no useful moves and create zugzwang.
notes.plans: After Black is forced to move, White's king advances toward the pawns, exploiting the weaknesses created.

notes.explains: White's f3 also places pawns on squares of the same color as the opponent's bishop, making them immune to attack by that bishop. This is a deeper point: the pawns become permanent fixtures that restrict Black's bishop.
notes.teaches: Putting pawns on the color of the opponent's bishop can neutralize that bishop, as it cannot attack them. This is a common strategy in bishop endgames.
notes.plans: Use the fixed pawn structure to create a target, such as the h6 pawn, which White later wins.

notes.explains: In the final phase, White wins by using his bishop to stop Black's passed pawns on the dark squares while advancing his own pawn. The key is to keep the bishop on the correct diagonal to block the pawns until it's too late for Black to stop White's promotion.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, the bishop's ability to stop enemy pawns on the color it controls is crucial. Timing the advance of your own pawn while using the bishop to restrain the opponent's is a fundamental technique.
notes.plans: White advances his g-pawn, using the bishop to control the promotion square, and sacrifices the bishop if necessary to win the race.

notes.explains: In a position where White has sacrificed a pawn for the bishop pair and initiative, the tempting move is to win back the pawn. However, the stronger move is c4, which establishes a positional advantage by fixing the pawn structure and enhancing the dark-squared bishop's scope.
notes.teaches: Do not rush to regain material if the pawn is not going anywhere. Look for moves that improve your position, especially in endgames where a small positional edge can be decisive.
notes.plans: Play c4 to fix the pawns on dark squares, then use the bishop pair to create long-term pressure.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, White has a chance to win a pawn back immediately, but the pawn is not going anywhere. The stronger move is to play c4, placing a pawn on a light square while Black's dark-squared bishop is stuck on b6, blocked by its own pawns. This keeps the bishop passive and fixes the pawn structure favorably for White.
notes.teaches: Before grabbing material, consider whether the material is stable and if there are more useful positional moves available. A pawn move that restricts the opponent's bishop can be more valuable than winning a pawn.
notes.plans: White can follow up by winning the pawn on b7 while maintaining the positional bind, then proceed to a favorable endgame.

notes.explains: If White delays c4 and instead takes on b7, Black gets the chance to play c4 himself, opening the bishop and creating counterplay. This shows the importance of seizing the opportunity to fix the pawn structure before it's too late.
notes.teaches: Always look for active moves for your opponent; if you have a move that prevents their counterplay, do it immediately. A bishop staring at its own pawns is a bad piece, so you must avoid allowing it to be freed.
notes.plans: White should play c4 first to prevent Black's freeing move, then proceed with the plan to win the b7 pawn.

notes.explains: When considering trading rooks to enter a king and pawn endgame, one must carefully evaluate the resulting pawn structure. Here, White has a 3-on-2 pawn majority on the queenside, which could potentially create an outside passed pawn. However, in this specific position, the pawns are too close and White's king cannot get active, so the outside passed pawn is not enough to win.
notes.teaches: Before trading into a king and pawn endgame, assess the potential for an outside passed pawn and whether the king can support it. Sometimes the side with the majority cannot convert because the king is cut off or the pawns are too close.
notes.plans: Black can safely trade rooks and enter the king and pawn endgame, as the draw is secure. Keeping rooks on might be worse for Black because White's active rook can attack the weak pawns.

notes.explains: In the rook endgame, if Black keeps rooks on, White can play Rc7, attacking the c4 and b5 pawns, creating a double attack. This would put Black in trouble because White's rook activity is decisive.
notes.teaches: Rook activity is crucial in rook endgames. A rook that can attack multiple weak pawns simultaneously can create winning chances even if the pawn structure is balanced.
notes.plans: Black should prefer to trade rooks to avoid the active rook, as the resulting king and pawn endgame is drawn.

notes.explains: With rooks on the board, White's active rook can create serious pressure on Black's weak pawns, such as by attacking c4 and b5 simultaneously. This activity gives White strong winning chances, so Black should avoid entering such a rook endgame if possible.
notes.teaches: Rook activity is paramount in rook endgames; an active rook can dominate passive pawns and create decisive threats.
notes.plans: If White, aim to use the rook to attack Black's weak pawns and maintain pressure. If Black, seek to trade rooks or activate your own rook to neutralize White's activity.

notes.explains: In this position, White has no immediate breakthrough, and Black's c4 move provides solid counterplay. The game is not lost for Black, but Black must suffer and defend accurately.
notes.teaches: Patience and subtlety are valuable in chess; not every position requires forcing moves. Appreciate the long-term effects of pawn moves that restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to improve piece activity without allowing counterplay. Black should consolidate the improved pawn structure and aim for a draw.

notes.explains: The most important first step in chess is learning how to checkmate right after learning piece movement. The easiest checkmates involve two major pieces (two rooks, queen and rook, or two queens), then king and queen vs king, and king and rook vs king. These are prerequisites for more advanced endgames.
notes.teaches: Before studying complex endgames, master the basic checkmates. They are the foundation for converting advantages.
notes.plans: Ensure you can checkmate with two major pieces, queen and king, and rook and king before proceeding.

notes.explains: Capablanca's quote emphasizes studying endgames first. Once you know how to checkmate with a queen, you can aim to promote a pawn to reach that winning position. Endgames build on each other: learn the simpler checkmates first, then use them as goals in more complex positions.
notes.teaches: Work backwards from known checkmates to figure out how to win endgames. The ultimate goal is often to promote a pawn to a queen.
notes.plans: In any endgame, identify the simplest checkmate you can reach and aim for that.

notes.explains: In a position with white having a pawn and knight against a lone black king, the winning plan is to promote the pawn. The knight and king must work together to push the enemy king away from the pawn's path.
notes.teaches: Use all your pieces to support pawn promotion. The knight can control key squares to drive the enemy king away.
notes.plans: Use the knight to check the king and force it to move, then advance the pawn step by step.

notes.explains: In a king and pawn versus king endgame, the defending king blocks the pawn's path. The attacking king alone cannot force the pawn through, so the extra piece must be used to control the key squares in front of the pawn and drive the defending king away.
notes.teaches: Use the extra piece to control the square directly in front of the pawn, forcing the enemy king to step aside. Then advance the pawn, and repeat this process one square at a time.
notes.plans: Bring the king up to support the pawn, use the knight to check or attack the enemy king to gain control of the critical square, then push the pawn when the square is secured.

notes.explains: When promoting the pawn, it is crucial to avoid stalemate. A natural-looking king move that controls all the enemy king's escape squares can accidentally leave the enemy king with no legal moves but not in check, resulting in a draw.
notes.teaches: Before making a move, check whether the enemy king will have any legal moves. If not, and it is not in check, the game is drawn by stalemate. Prefer a check that forces the king away while allowing the pawn to promote.
notes.plans: When the pawn is one square from promotion, use a check from the knight to drive the king away, then promote the pawn with support from the king.

notes.explains: When two kings stand directly opposite each other with one square between them, the side to move is at a disadvantage because moving the king allows the opponent to outflank. This is called opposition. The opponent can also be in zugzwang if every move worsens their position.
notes.teaches: Use opposition to your advantage: if your opponent must move their king, you can outflank and penetrate. Recognize zugzwang positions where the side to move is forced to weaken their position.
notes.plans: In king and pawn endgames, use opposition to force the enemy king away from key squares, allowing your king to advance.

notes.explains: Zugzwang is a German term meaning every legal move makes your position worse. In king and pawn endgames, when kings face each other with one square between them (opposition), the side to move must give ground, allowing the opponent to outflank and gain space.
notes.teaches: Recognize zugzwang positions where you want to force your opponent to move, not move yourself. Use a spare tempo (like a bishop move) to transfer the move to the opponent.

notes.explains: With a bishop and pawn versus king, the bishop can be used to control key squares (like g5) to restrict the enemy king, and also to waste a tempo when needed. The goal is to force the enemy king away from defending its pawn, then capture it and promote.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, use spare moves with a piece to maintain the opposition and make progress. Control the squares the enemy king needs to approach.
notes.plans: Advance your king step by step, using the bishop to give the move to the opponent when the opposition is against you. Eventually force the enemy king away, capture the pawn, and promote.

notes.explains: In endgames where you have an extra piece, converting a won position is a key skill. The fastest way to improve is to consistently win easily won positions.
notes.teaches: Focus on converting winning endgames reliably; this is a quick path to improvement.

notes.explains: In positions with multiple pawns, the side with the extra piece often has an easier win by targeting an undefended pawn. Here, the a-pawn is undefended because the enemy king is far away.
notes.teaches: Look for the easiest way to create a passed pawn; target pawns that are not defended by the king.
notes.plans: Bring a knight to attack the undefended a-pawn, capture it, and then promote the passed pawn.

notes.explains: In a king and pawn endgame, when the enemy king is too far to defend a pawn, that pawn becomes a target. The easiest way to win is to attack and capture that undefended pawn with a piece, here a knight, which can approach quickly.
notes.teaches: Identify undefended enemy pawns that are out of the king's reach; use a piece to capture them, creating a passed pawn.
notes.plans: Bring the knight closer to the target pawn, capture it, and then support the resulting passed pawn.

notes.explains: With a knight and a passed pawn, the two pieces can defend each other: the knight directly defends the pawn, while the pawn's promotion threat prevents the enemy king from attacking the knight. This mutual defense makes it hard for the king to win either piece.
notes.teaches: In endgames, pieces and pawns can cooperate defensively; a passed pawn's promotion threat can shield a piece from king attacks.
notes.plans: Place the knight so it defends the passed pawn, and use the pawn's promotion threat to keep the enemy king at bay, then bring the king to support.

notes.explains: After winning the a-pawn and creating a passed pawn, the immediate goal is not necessarily to promote it. Instead, the passed pawn acts as a decoy, forcing the enemy king to stay near it, which leaves the other enemy pawns undefended and vulnerable to our king.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn can be used as a distraction to tie down the enemy king, allowing your own king to capture other pawns and win the game.
notes.plans: Keep the passed pawn and knight as a decoy, march the king to the other side to capture the remaining enemy pawns, then promote.

notes.explains: The same decoy idea works even with equal material when one side has an outside passed pawn—a pawn far from the main action. Even if the enemy has a passed pawn too, the outside passed pawn can be more valuable because it pulls the enemy king away from the other pawns.
notes.teaches: An outside passed pawn is a powerful advantage because it distracts the enemy king, allowing your king to win the remaining pawns on the other side.
notes.plans: Use the outside passed pawn to lure the enemy king away, then capture the enemy pawns with your king and promote.

notes.explains: When the attacking king is in front of the pawn, there are winning chances. The key is to use the opposition: if the kings are facing each other with one square between them, the side to move is at a disadvantage. By taking the opposition, you force the enemy king to move away, then you can outflank and advance your king to support the pawn.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, the opposition is a fundamental tool to gain control of key squares. Outflanking (shouldering) allows you to shepherd the pawn to promotion.
notes.plans: Consider moves that put your king in front of the pawn, such as moving to the square directly in front or to the side. Use the opposition to force the enemy king aside, then advance your king and pawn together.

notes.explains: In a king and pawn endgame, the position of the king relative to the pawn is decisive. If the king is behind the pawn, the game is a draw; if the king is in front, there are winning chances because the king controls the promotion square before the enemy king.
notes.teaches: Always advance your king ahead of your pawn in king and pawn endgames. The king's placement in front of the pawn is crucial for controlling key squares and promoting.
notes.plans: Maneuver the king to a square in front of the pawn, using opposition to force the enemy king to give ground.

notes.explains: When the king is in front of the pawn, the immediate move to step directly in front (e.g., king e4) may allow the enemy king to take the opposition, resulting in a draw. Instead, a preparatory move (e.g., king d4) takes the opposition first, forcing the enemy king to move, and then stepping in front maintains the opposition.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, use the opposition to force the enemy king to give way. If you can take the opposition first, you can then advance your king and maintain control.
notes.plans: Play the opposition-taking move first, then step in front of the pawn, and after the enemy king moves, occupy the square it vacated.

notes.explains: This endgame is a fundamental winning technique. Once mastered, you can trade down into this position to win many games. The key is to maintain opposition and keep your king in front of the pawn.
notes.teaches: Mastering this king and pawn endgame is essential because it appears frequently after trades. The winning method is to use opposition to force the enemy king back and then promote.
notes.plans: Practice this technique to recognize and execute it in games.

notes.explains: In this endgame, White has an outside passed pawn on the queenside. The key is to use it as a decoy to pull the enemy king and pieces away from the kingside, where White can then invade with the king to win the remaining pawns. The opponent's bishop on c7 is currently preventing the white king from breaking through on the kingside.
notes.teaches: An outside passed pawn is a powerful advantage because it can distract the defender's forces to one side of the board, leaving the other side vulnerable to infiltration.
notes.plans: White should aim to use the passed pawn to draw the enemy king away, then find a way to eliminate the bishops or bypass the bishop's control to invade the kingside.

notes.explains: The move b6 is counterintuitive because it appears to hang the pawn, but it is a powerful resource. If Black captures the pawn, White can trade bishops, and then the black king is too far away to stop the white king from sweeping up the kingside pawns. If Black declines, the bishop is driven away, weakening its control over key squares.
notes.teaches: Sometimes offering a pawn is justified if it forces a favorable trade or creates a decisive infiltration. The threat of a winning bishop trade can be used as a lever to improve your position.
notes.plans: Play b6 to drive the bishop away, then use the threat of trading bishops to gain entry for the white king on the kingside.

notes.explains: After the bishop is driven away, White can challenge the bishop's diagonal with moves like g3 and Bf4 (or similar). If Black trades bishops, the resulting king and pawn endgame is winning for White because the black king is still far from the kingside. If Black avoids the trade, White can use the pawn to kick the bishop and invade.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning endgame after a trade, you can use the threat of that trade to force your opponent into a worse position or to gain time for your own king to advance.
notes.plans: Use the bishop to challenge the enemy bishop's diagonal, and if the bishops come off, the white king will march to the kingside and win the pawns.

notes.explains: In rook endgames with two connected passed pawns, the main challenge is that the enemy rook can check the king endlessly, preventing progress. The key is to use the pawns as shelter from checks and the rook to drive away the enemy king.
notes.teaches: When you have two connected passed pawns and rooks, prioritize preventing enemy rook checks by using your pawns as shields, and place your rook on the side of the board to control key squares in front of the pawns.
notes.plans: Start by advancing the pawns (e.g., g4), then bring the rook to the side (e.g., Rb1) to challenge the enemy king. Push the pawns forward, using them to shelter the king from checks, and use the rook to drive the enemy king away.

notes.explains: The pawns themselves can serve as shelter for the king against enemy rook checks. For example, the g-pawn can protect from behind and the f-pawn from the side, limiting the enemy rook's checking squares.
notes.teaches: When advancing passed pawns, use them to create a shield for your king, reducing the effectiveness of enemy rook checks. This allows your king to support the pawns safely.
notes.plans: Push the pawns in a coordinated way (e.g., f5, g5) to create a shelter for the king. If the enemy rook checks, move the king behind the pawns, and continue advancing.

notes.explains: If the technique is not applied correctly—by not using the pawns as shelter and not bringing the rook to the side—the enemy rook can create perpetual checks and prevent progress, making the win much harder.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames with passed pawns, failing to use your pawns as shelter and your rook actively can allow the defender to hold the position. Always prioritize king safety and rook activity.
notes.plans: Avoid passive rook placement and leaving the king exposed. Instead, follow the proper technique: advance pawns, place rook on the side, and use pawns to shield the king.

notes.explains: In a pawn endgame with connected passed pawns, the pawns can be unstoppable if they are supported by the king and shielded from rook checks. When the pawns are pushed without king support, the enemy king can get in front of them and blockade them, turning a win into a draw.
notes.teaches: Always advance pawns with the king in support and use the pawns to shelter the king from side checks. If the enemy king gets in front of your pawns, the endgame is likely drawn.
notes.plans: Push the pawns together, keeping the king in front or beside them, and use the rook to cut off the enemy king from the queening squares.

notes.explains: This position is not common, but it illustrates a general principle: relate unfamiliar endgames to ones you already know. Here, the goal is to force a trade of rooks to reach a winning king and pawn endgame.
notes.teaches: When facing an unfamiliar endgame, look for a way to simplify to a known winning endgame. Use your rook to control key squares and force favorable trades.
notes.plans: Identify the winning endgame you are aiming for (e.g., king and pawn vs king) and work backward to see how to force the trade.

notes.explains: When choosing between rook moves like Rook B1 or Rook A1, the exact square often doesn't matter as long as the rook reaches the sixth rank to deliver effective side checks. The goal is to get the rook active on the side where it can harass the enemy king.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, prioritize getting your rook to an active rank or file for checking distance over minor differences in move order. The key is the rook's activity, not the precise path.
notes.plans: Continue with the plan of advancing the pawn and using the rook to check the king from the side, eventually forcing the defender to give up material or allow promotion.

notes.explains: Basic endgames, like king and rook versus king, are building blocks for more complex positions. When you are up material, you can trade down to a simpler winning endgame if you recognize the pattern.
notes.teaches: Learn the fundamental checkmates and endgame techniques so you can convert material advantages by trading down to positions you know how to win. This connects simple endgames to complex ones.
notes.plans: When ahead in material, look for opportunities to exchange pieces and reach a theoretically winning endgame, using the techniques from basic endgames.

notes.explains: When the opening ends and you have no specific preparation, you must rely on general principles and the concrete features of the position to form a plan.
notes.teaches: In the early middlegame, if you lack opening knowledge, focus on identifying weaknesses, piece activity, and pawn structure to guide your decisions.

notes.explains: In a King's Indian Defense structure with a black pawn on e5 and white pawn on d4, the central tension can be resolved in different ways. Here, the queen on e7 is not ideally placed because it may have to move again to defend the c7 pawn after exchanges.
notes.teaches: When choosing between central pawn moves (d5 or dxe5), consider the resulting piece placements and potential weaknesses. A queen on e7 can become a target if the center opens.
notes.plans: After dxe5, follow up with Nbd5 to attack the queen and the c7 weakness, then deal with the e-pawn by supporting it or recapturing appropriately.

notes.explains: The position offers a choice between playing d5 (maintaining central tension) or taking on e5 (opening the center). The decision should be based on which resulting structure you are more comfortable with and which gives you concrete chances.
notes.teaches: When facing an unfamiliar position, try to visualize a few moves ahead and assess the resulting pawn structures and piece activity. Choose the option that leads to a position you understand better or that gives you clear targets.
notes.plans: If you take on e5, aim to exploit the c7 weakness and the misplaced queen, while being prepared to handle counterplay against your e-pawn.

notes.explains: White has just captured on c5, gaining access to the weakness on c7, but Black will generate counterplay against the e-pawn. White must decide how to defend it, choosing between moves like Qc2, Nd2, or Nc3, each with different implications.
notes.teaches: When you create a weakness in the opponent's camp, be ready to handle their counterplay against your own vulnerable points. Defending a pawn can be done in multiple ways; pick the one that best fits your long-term plans.
notes.plans: Defend the e-pawn while maintaining the pressure on c7 and keeping flexibility for piece placement.

notes.explains: After a few developing moves, White has gained tempi because Black's pieces are awkwardly placed, but now White must formulate a concrete plan. The e5 pawn is annoying, but removing it could activate Black's bishop, so it's not necessarily a target.
notes.teaches: In quiet middlegame positions, if you can't find your own plan, look at your opponent's intentions and play against them. This is often easier and can guide your move selection.
notes.plans: Identify Black's most likely plan (knight to d4 via c5-e6) and find ways to prevent it, such as Nb3 or a4.

notes.explains: Black's queen on e7 and the open d-file suggest pressure on the d-file, but the more pressing threat is the knight maneuver to d4. White must decide between moves like Nb3, which directly stops it, or a4, which prepares queenside expansion while also addressing the threat.
notes.teaches: When considering prophylactic moves, weigh the immediate stop of the threat against long-term positional goals. Sometimes a move that addresses both is available, even if it's less direct.
notes.plans: Choose a move that prevents Black's knight from reaching d4 while also preparing queenside expansion with b4, if possible.

notes.explains: In this position, the opponent's knight is eyeing c5, a strong square that would challenge White's space and piece activity. White's knights and space advantage point toward a queenside expansion with b4, but that move is not immediately possible.
notes.teaches: When unsure of a plan, identify the opponent's most threatening idea and find a way to prevent it. This often reveals the best move.
notes.plans: Stop the opponent's knight from reaching c5, then prepare b4 to expand on the queenside.

notes.explains: The move Qa4 is a clever way to stop the knight from landing on c5: it pins the knight to the queen if it moves there, a rare queen-versus-queen pin. This move also prepares b4, serving both defensive and offensive purposes.
notes.teaches: A single move can both prevent the opponent's counterplay and advance your own plan. Look for such multi-purpose moves.
notes.plans: After Qa4, continue with b4 to gain space, and later consider c5 to control weak squares like d6.

notes.explains: The opponent responded with a5 to stop b4, but White found c5, taking control of weak squares and potentially creating a d6 outpost. The same tactical motif remains: if the knight goes to c5, Qa3 pins it.
notes.teaches: When your plan is blocked, look for alternative ways to improve your position, such as gaining space or controlling key squares. Keep the opponent's counterplay in mind.
notes.plans: Play c5 to secure a space advantage and eye the d6 outpost. If the opponent takes on c5, recapture and continue developing.

notes.explains: After the opponent fell into the trap and took on c5, White's pieces coordinated to increase pressure. The knight maneuvered to b3 and then a4, attacking the pinned knight, and eventually won material.
notes.teaches: Once you have a positional advantage, convert it by improving your pieces and increasing pressure on the opponent's weaknesses. Simple development and open-file play can be decisive.
notes.plans: Bring the rook to the open file, attack the pinned knight, and then exploit the resulting material gain.

notes.explains: In a position where the opponent has a strong bishop and you have a chance to trade it off, doing so can be desirable, but the follow-up must be sound. Here the intended bishop d4 idea fails tactically because after trades the opponent can play queen h4 and then c5, leaving the queen no good way to defend f2.
notes.teaches: When aiming to trade off a strong piece, verify that the resulting tactical sequence does not leave your own position vulnerable; a failed trade can leave your pieces misplaced.

notes.explains: After a suboptimal sequence, the position may be worse but not lost. The key is to avoid panicking and to find simple, solid moves that address immediate threats, such as defending a hanging pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have no clear plan, play simply: defend weaknesses and ask the opponent to show their plan. Then try to slow down or stop that plan.
notes.plans: Continue with simple developing moves, keep the position solid, and wait for the opponent's plan to become concrete so you can counter it.

notes.explains: Improving pieces to central squares and placing them on safe posts is a reliable fallback when no concrete plan exists. This approach keeps the position sound and avoids creating weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When in doubt, bring your pieces toward the center and put them on the most secure squares available. This improves your position without committing to risky ideas.
notes.plans: Look for opportunities to activate pieces further once the immediate threats are neutralized.

notes.explains: When you simply respond to the opponent's threats with natural moves, you avoid making serious errors. The opponent's plan often forces them to make decisions, while you can play straightforwardly.
notes.teaches: You don't need a grand plan to avoid losing; just play solid, natural moves that meet the demands of the position. Mistakes usually come from overcomplicating or ignoring threats.
notes.plans: Keep defending and improving, waiting for the opponent's initiative to run out.

notes.explains: Facing a direct threat like rook h5, you can choose between creating a luft with h3 or repositioning the king to h1. The latter avoids creating a weakness while still addressing the threat.
notes.teaches: When dealing with threats, prefer moves that don't create permanent weaknesses. Sometimes a king move is more solid than a pawn move.
notes.plans: After the threat is parried, continue to improve piece placement and look for counterplay.

notes.explains: After a period of passive defense, the opponent's pieces may become overextended. The knight that was pressuring your position cannot stay forever, and you can start to activate your own pieces once the pressure eases.
notes.teaches: Patience in defense can pay off: if you hold solidly, the opponent's attacking pieces may have to retreat, giving you the chance to seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Begin to challenge the opponent's well-placed pieces and improve your own activity.

notes.explains: In this position, White has been improving pieces and responding to threats, but after the opponent's last move, White loses urgency and plays a slow move (a3) that doesn't address the ongoing attack. The opponent's queen move (Qe7) looks like a retreat but actually prepares a mating net.
notes.teaches: Never relax just because the opponent's move seems passive; maintain the same urgency and look for active, freeing moves even when you think you're safe.
notes.plans: Instead of a3, White should consider immediate queen moves (Qe2 or Qc2) to keep the initiative and avoid wasting time.

notes.explains: White's best move is g4, a freeing move that attacks the knight and creates threats. The point is that if Black captures on g4, White can recapture with the rook, leaving Black's rook with no good squares. This move is counterintuitive but nearly winning for White.
notes.teaches: Look for freeing pawn moves that create threats and improve your piece activity, even if they seem risky. Sometimes the best move is one that your opponent cannot easily refute.
notes.plans: After g4, White follows up with f4, creating forks and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Black has a three-step plan leading to checkmate: moving the queen out of the way, then bringing the knight to a key square, and then delivering mate. White must find a way to stop this plan, but the position is already very difficult.
notes.teaches: When you can't find your own plan, play against your opponent's plan. Identify their threats and make prophylactic moves to prevent them, even if it means giving up material or making a defensive move like h3 to create a flight square.
notes.plans: White should play h3 to give the king a flight square, but even that may not be enough to save the game.

notes.explains: In the early middlegame, when you are unfamiliar with the position, the two guiding principles are: respond to the opponent's plan and improve your own pieces. Here, black's rook on e8 signals the intention to push e5, supported by the rook.
notes.teaches: Read the opponent's last move as a clue to their plan. A rook on an open file often supports a pawn break.
notes.plans: Keep the opponent's e5 break in mind while looking for ways to improve your pieces and neutralize their threats.

notes.explains: White's c3 pawn is backward on a half-open file and is a target. In a perfect world, white would play c4 and trade it off, but that allows e5 and complications due to pins and hanging pawns.
notes.teaches: A backward pawn on a half-open file is a weakness. Sometimes the immediate fix creates other problems, so you must weigh the consequences.
notes.plans: If c4 is not playable, keep the pawn on c3 to discourage e5, since black's e5 would then allow c4 or other favorable reactions.

notes.explains: The minority attack is a strategy where you advance a smaller number of pawns against a larger pawn majority to create weaknesses in the opponent's structure.
notes.teaches: Even with fewer pawns on one side, you can use them to provoke weaknesses and open files for your rooks.
notes.plans: Consider opening files on the queenside for your rooks, possibly via a minority attack.

notes.explains: The threat of ...e5 is not real because the pawn on c3 supports d4, so taking on d4 would only help White. This means White can focus on other plans without worrying about that pawn break.
notes.teaches: When evaluating threats, consider whether the opponent's move actually helps you. If a capture would improve your position, it may not be a real threat.
notes.plans: Look for ways to improve pieces and open files for rooks, especially on the queenside.

notes.explains: White has a pawn minority (one pawn vs. two) on the queenside. The lone a-pawn is weak because it cannot be defended by another pawn, so White can use it to attack the majority and create weaknesses in Black's camp.
notes.teaches: The minority attack is a common plan: use your fewer pawns to provoke weaknesses in the opponent's pawn majority, forcing them to use pieces to defend.
notes.plans: Play a4 to attack the b-pawn, creating a target that Black must defend with pieces.

notes.explains: After White played Rc1 and Black responded with e5, White played a4 with the same minority attack idea. Black then played e4 attacking the bishop, and White had to choose a retreat square carefully because some squares would allow Black to fix the weakness on c3.
notes.teaches: When choosing a retreat square, consider whether the opponent can use the tempo to improve their position or fix their weaknesses. Also, control key squares like c4 to prevent pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Play Bb5 to avoid allowing Black to control c4 with a bishop on a6, which would permanently fix the c3 weakness.

notes.explains: In the forcing line, Black played a6, White traded the bishop for the knight, and after recapturing, White could play c4 immediately, fixing the weakness. The resulting position has an isolated passed pawn for Black on a6, but it is not dangerous because it is not advanced.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn can be a weakness if it is isolated and not advanced. The evaluation depends on the bishop color complex: opposite-colored bishops often lead to draws because each bishop controls different squares, making blockades possible.
notes.plans: Use the dark-squared bishop to blockade the a-pawn, preventing its advance. The light-squared bishop for Black cannot attack the dark-squared bishop, so the pawn is effectively stopped.

notes.explains: Opposite-colored bishops operate on different color complexes, so they can never directly attack each other. This makes it easy to blockade enemy pawns on the bishop's color, as the opposing bishop cannot challenge that blockade.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop positions, a blockade on the color of your bishop can be nearly permanent, often leading to a draw if the opponent has no other winning chances.
notes.plans: Use your bishop to control key squares on its color, preventing enemy pawn advances and simplifying to a drawn endgame.

notes.explains: When the opponent threatens to push a pawn (like e4) that would close the position and limit your bishop, it's often worth investing a move to prevent that push. Defending the square (e.g., with f3) stops the pawn break and keeps your pieces active.
notes.teaches: If you can stop your opponent's plan with a simple defensive move, it's usually a good investment, even if it seems passive. Preventing a pawn break that would worsen your position is a key middlegame skill.
notes.plans: Consider moves like f3 to control the key square and maintain a healthy pawn structure, preserving your bishop's activity.

notes.explains: In the rook and bishop endgame, the bishop controls a key square (like a5) that the opponent needs to penetrate. As long as that square is covered, the opponent can't make progress, leading to a static position.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a single piece can dominate a key entry point, and as long as that point is controlled, the opponent's king or pawns are stuck. Recognize when a position is drawish due to such control.
notes.plans: Maintain control of the key square with the bishop, and if the opponent tries to challenge it, be ready to trade down to a drawn pawn endgame or sacrifice the bishop for the last pawn.

notes.explains: When the opponent's king is closer to your pawns, creating your own passed pawn can distract the king and give you drawing chances. Even if the opponent's pawn is far advanced, a passed pawn of your own can create counterplay.
