notes.teaches: Even in sharp lines, maintaining piece activity and central control is key. A single inaccuracy may not ruin the position if the structure is sound.
notes.plans: Black develops harmoniously, keeps the queen active, and prepares ...Rd8 or ...b5.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has active counterplay with moves like Nc2, Ng4, or Rb8, ensuring compensation. After dxe5 dxe5 Qb3, Black can play Qe7 and already has a great position. White's Rd1 is met by Black's simple development, and Black's ideas like Nc5 give a comfortable game.
notes.teaches: When the center is fluid, active piece play and counterplay can compensate for structural concessions. Look for moves that create immediate threats and improve piece activity.
notes.plans: Black should aim for Nc5, controlling key squares and preparing pawn breaks like a5 and e4. White should try to consolidate and exploit any inaccuracies.

notes.explains: Black's move h6 was a mistake because it allowed White to play Be3, preventing Black's knight from reaching c5. The correct move was Nbd7, preparing h6 later and keeping the knight flexible for c5. After the mistake, White can get a somewhat better position, though unclear.
notes.teaches: In flexible positions, avoid committing pawn moves that weaken your control over key squares. Develop pieces first and keep options open.
notes.plans: Black should have played Nbd7, then h6, and later aim for Nc5. White should use the opportunity to play Be3 and restrict Black's knight.

notes.explains: In the game, Black solved problems by bringing the knight to e6, followed by a5 and e4, achieving a good position. After trading rooks and bishops, Black's knight and queen cooperate better than White's queen and bishop, and Black has access to c5, controls the d-file, and has more space.
notes.teaches: In endgames and simplified middlegames, piece cooperation matters. A knight can be superior to a bishop when it has strong outposts and the pawn structure favors it.
notes.plans: Black should use the knight on c5, control the d-file, and expand on the queenside. White should seek active piece play and try to create counterplay.

notes.explains: After White plays Ne1, preparing e4, Black has the option of Be6 or the modern e5. The idea behind e5 is to challenge the center immediately, exploiting the passive knight on e1. After Ng5, Black plays d5, and after cxd5 cxd5, a5 follows, with the plan of Na6, Bd7, and b5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a passively placed piece, challenge the center immediately to exploit its poor placement. Use pawn breaks to open lines and create activity.
notes.plans: Black should play e5, then after Ng5, d5, and follow with a5, Na6, Bd7, and b5. White must find a way to activate the knight on e1.

notes.explains: In the line with Nf3 and Bf5, Black should avoid allowing White to build a strong center with c4 and e4. If White plays c4, Black can play e5 immediately, changing the center. After dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8+ Kxd8, the endgame is equal, but Black has better perspectives because White's c4 pawn is misplaced.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prevent your opponent from establishing a dominant center. If they do, seek immediate central breaks. In endgames, pawn structure matters: a pawn on c4 can be a weakness if it cannot be supported.
notes.plans: Black should play e5 after c4, and if the endgame arises, aim to exploit the c4 pawn weakness. White should try to keep the center fluid and avoid structural weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this endgame, the position is equal, but black may have slightly better prospects because white's c4 pawn is misplaced; it would be better on c2. The c4 pawn gives black easier access to dark squares on the queenside, such as c5, and the black king on d8 is not a liability since castling is not needed in the endgame.
notes.teaches: In endgames, pawn structure and king safety matter more than castling rights. A pawn on c4 can be a target or give the opponent squares, so consider whether advancing it is truly beneficial.
notes.plans: Black can aim to place the king on c6 or e7, develop the bishop to e6 and knight to d7, and use the dark squares on the queenside. White should be cautious about the c4 pawn becoming weak.

notes.explains: In one line, after white plays h3, black can try f5. If white takes, black recaptures with the bishop, and white gains control of e4, but black can quickly develop the bishop to h6 or g7 and knight to f6, aiming for e4. White is slightly behind in development.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, pawn breaks like f5 can create counterplay. Even if the opponent gets a strong square, you can use your undeveloped pieces to challenge it.
notes.plans: Black should continue with Bh6 or Bg7 and Nf6, targeting e4. White needs to complete development and watch for black's activity.

notes.explains: Another idea for black is to play h5 immediately. This move stops white from playing g4 to expand on the kingside, and it prepares a future bishop move, likely to g4 or h6.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like h5 can prevent the opponent's pawn expansion and create luft for your own pieces. It's a useful way to gain space and restrict the opponent's plans.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with bishop development, possibly to g4 or h6, and continue with a flexible setup. White must consider how to handle the kingside tension.

notes.explains: After White plays d5 early in a King's Indian setup, Black has several promising setups. One is to develop the bishop to g7 and knight to f6, aiming for ...e5. Another, chosen here, is to play ...h5, which prevents White from playing g4 to expand on the kingside, and prepares ...Bh6 to trade off the dark-squared bishops.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, when White advances d5 prematurely, Black can often benefit by trading dark-squared bishops and gaining a favorable version of the structure. The move ...h5 is a useful prophylactic against White's kingside expansion.
notes.plans: Black can develop the knight to f6, play ...Nc5, and aim for ...f5 to challenge White's center. The trade of dark-squared bishops and a pair of knights reduces White's attacking potential.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, White has more space due to the pawns on d5 and e4, but this is irrelevant because Black's pieces have good squares. Black has already traded the dark-squared bishops and a pair of knights, making White's space less meaningful. Black's pieces are active and have room to maneuver.
notes.teaches: Space advantage only matters if the pieces can exploit it. After trades, the side with less space can often be fine if their pieces are active and have good prospects.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play ...f5 to challenge White's center. The rook on h7 and king on e8 are awkward, but Black can improve piece placement before committing to ...f5.

notes.explains: When White plays f4, Black can capture on f4 and then consider strong moves like ...Bxh3 or ...Qg5. In the game, ...Qg5 was played, but ...Bxh3 was even more direct. After White's queen goes to f1, ...Bxh3 wins a pawn and gives Black a decisive advantage due to control of the dark squares.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, look for tactical blows that exploit the opponent's king safety and piece coordination. A move like ...Bxh3 can open the king and win material if the opponent cannot defend adequately.
notes.plans: After ...Bxh3, Black wins a pawn and maintains a strong attack. The queen can come to e5, and Black's control of dark squares ensures a lasting advantage.

notes.explains: Another setup for Black after White's early d5 is to play ...Bh6, trade bishops, and then develop the knight to f6. Black can also play ...h5 and ...Nc5, aiming for a favorable version of the King's Indian. White's early d5 gives Black extra time to organize this.
notes.teaches: When the opponent advances a pawn too early, use the time to improve your pieces and trade off key defenders. In the King's Indian, trading the dark-squared bishops is often a key plan.
notes.plans: Black can castle short, prepare ...f5, and use the half-open f-file. The move ...h4 can create weaknesses in White's kingside.

notes.explains: In the game, Black prepared ...f5 over several moves, using moves like ...Qf6, ...Qg7, and ...b6 to improve the position. When White played f3, Black finally played ...f5, achieving the desired central break. After trades, Black's bishop on f5 is strong, and White cannot recapture due to the pin on the g-pawn.
notes.teaches: Patience in preparing a central break is crucial. Use preparatory moves to improve your pieces and create the right conditions before striking.
notes.plans: After ...f5, Black has a comfortable position with a strong bishop and active pieces. White's king is stuck in the center, and Black can continue to press.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian Defense, if White advances d5 too early, Black can adopt flexible setups. The pawn on h4 can become loose, and White's king may be stuck in the center, giving Black counterplay.
notes.teaches: Early central pawn advances by White can create weaknesses and give Black dynamic chances. Black should aim to prepare moves like f5 to challenge White's center.
notes.plans: Black castles short, prepares f5, and uses moves like Qg7 to support the break. If White captures on f5, Black can recapture with the bishop, exploiting tactics on the h5 square.

notes.explains: After the f5 break, Black's pieces become active, and White's king is exposed. Tactical motifs like Qg6 or Qe4 can punish White's inaccuracies, potentially winning material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is weak, look for tactical blows that exploit loose pieces and open lines. A safer king is a significant advantage.
notes.plans: Black continues to attack, using moves like Rf4 and g5 to increase pressure. White must defend precisely to avoid losing material.

notes.explains: Against Nf3, Black can quickly play e4, creating an imbalance and gaining space on the kingside. This is a logical approach based on central control.
notes.teaches: In the Pirc/King's Indian setup with d6 and e5, if White allows e4, Black should generally take it to gain space and initiative.
notes.plans: Black supports the e4 pawn with f5, builds a strong center, and develops pieces harmoniously. White may try to challenge with Ng5, but Black can respond with typical ideas like h6, a6, and later d5.

notes.explains: In the resulting structure, Black aims to solidify the center and prepare d5. Moves like a6 and Nc7 are typical to avoid weakening the kingside with h6, which could allow Nh5 and Nf4.
notes.teaches: Be cautious with pawn moves on the side where your king will castle; they can create weaknesses. Instead, use flexible moves like a6 to prepare development.
notes.plans: Black develops the bishop to e6 or f7, then plays d5 to challenge White's center. If White plays h5, Black can respond with Nd7 or Nf6, maintaining a solid position.

notes.explains: After the knight retreats, Black can develop the bishop to e6 and then aim for d5, building a strong central pawn presence. The position is complex and both sides have chances, but Black's setup is playable and avoids mainstream theory.
notes.teaches: In the opening, if you can achieve a strong central pawn duo (like d5 and e4) without compromising your position, you can claim good chances. Avoiding main lines can lead to playable positions with hidden potential.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e6, then play d5, possibly supporting with knight d7 and bishop f6. If White plays g3, Black can still aim for d5 after appropriate preparation.

notes.explains: If White plays knight h3 instead of h4, Black can still play knight f6. White's king side is not weakened, but White wants to play f3, which is not dangerous as long as Black can play d5. The position remains balanced.
notes.teaches: When evaluating an opponent's setup, focus on whether they can achieve their strategic goals (like f3) without allowing you to counter in the center. If you can always play d5, their plan is not threatening.
notes.plans: Continue with the plan of playing d5, possibly via knight d7 and knight d5, to secure a strong center.

notes.explains: After White plays knight c3 and takes on d4, Black recaptures with the queen, gaining tempi as White's queen is chased by knight c6. The best move for White is queen d2. Black has not yet committed the bishop from e5, keeping options open for development to g7 or staying on the diagonal.
notes.teaches: In the opening, recapturing with the queen can gain time if the opponent's queen becomes exposed. Keeping your pieces flexible (like the bishop) forces the opponent to commit first.
notes.plans: Black should play knight f6, maintaining flexibility with the bishop. White has three main plans: e4 with quick development, b3 with bishop b2, or g3 with bishop g2. Black will respond accordingly.

notes.explains: In this opening setup, Black keeps both castling options open, often choosing kingside but not committing prematurely. The queen on c7 supports a future d5 break, and if d5 is played, the e-pawn is protected, allowing e5 to advance.
notes.teaches: Keep your options open in the opening when the position allows; don't commit your king until you see where your opponent's plans lead. A queen on c7 can support central pawn breaks while also preparing to defend key squares.
notes.plans: Black may develop kingside and castle short, but can also consider queenside castling if the center remains closed and White's attack is slow. The immediate plan is to complete development and prepare the d5 break.

notes.explains: White's queen on d2 is oddly placed; normally the knight would be on d4 and queen on d1. This gives Black time for dynamic play.
notes.teaches: Exploit opponent's misplaced pieces by creating immediate threats or imbalances.
notes.plans: Black should aim for active piece play to punish White's slow development.

notes.explains: Black has a lead in development, so must play dynamically before White consolidates. If White develops all pieces, White's space advantage will squeeze Black.
notes.teaches: When ahead in development, open the position and create concrete threats; otherwise the opponent's space advantage becomes decisive.
notes.plans: Black should seek active counterplay, such as the a6-b5 pawn sacrifice, to disrupt White's development.

notes.explains: After White plays Bd3, intending Ne2 and O-O, Black can play a6 and b5, sacrificing a pawn. If White takes on b5, Black gets the bishop pair and opens the a6-f1 diagonal for the bishop to harass White's pieces.
notes.teaches: A pawn sacrifice can be justified by long-term compensation: open lines, bishop pair, and attacking chances against the opponent's king.
notes.plans: Black plays a6, b5, and if accepted, develops the bishop to a6, pressuring White's loose knights and center.

notes.explains: If White plays f3 to stabilize the center, Black can play a5 to challenge the queenside, creating counterplay there.
notes.teaches: When the opponent solidifies the center, seek counterplay on the flank to avoid being suffocated.
notes.plans: Black plays a5, aiming to undermine White's queenside pawn structure and open lines.

notes.explains: In this position, the center is stabilized and the pawn on e4 is not immediately vulnerable, so Black can seek counterplay on the queenside instead of reacting directly in the center.
notes.teaches: When the center is stable, look for play on the flank where you can create weaknesses or dynamic chances.
notes.plans: Play a5 and prepare a4 to challenge White's queenside structure, aiming for active piece play.

notes.explains: After a4, tactical shots like Nxa4, Rxa4, Nxe4 can arise, leading to material imbalance where Black sacrifices the exchange but gains the bishop pair and strong control of e5.
notes.teaches: Material is not the only factor; compensation in the form of the bishop pair and central control can justify an exchange sacrifice.
notes.plans: If White takes on a4, be ready to recapture and then exploit the long-term advantages of the bishops and the e5 outpost.

notes.explains: When White plays b3, Black should avoid passive development like Be7 and O-O, because that allows White to complete development comfortably. Instead, Black should immediately play a5 and aim for a4.
notes.teaches: In the opening, if the opponent's setup is slow, you must create immediate imbalances or pressure to prevent them from consolidating.
notes.plans: Play a5-a4, and if White takes the pawn, consider sacrificing it to activate the bishop to b4 and generate strong central play.

notes.explains: If White cannot take on a4, Black's rook on a8 becomes well-placed, and after axb3 axb3, the rook can later become active on the a-file, for example with Ra2.
notes.teaches: Even if a pawn push does not win material, it can open files for your rooks and improve your piece activity.
notes.plans: Keep the rook on the a-file and look for opportunities to invade or pressure White's queenside.

notes.explains: After White plays g3, Black can continue with g6 and Bg7, developing normally while maintaining dynamic possibilities like a6-b5 or Nf6-d5.
notes.teaches: Even in a solid setup, you must keep the tension and look for ways to create play, not just develop passively.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g7, keep the center flexible, and be ready to strike on the queenside with b5 or in the center with Nd5.

notes.explains: With the rook on a8 and a knight on d5, Black has latent activity along the a-file; moves like Ra2 become possible if the knight moves, giving the rook a useful role.
notes.teaches: A rook on its original square can still be active if the file opens or if it can swing to a useful rank; consider such resources before committing to development.
notes.plans: Keep the rook on a8 flexible; if the knight leaves d5, evaluate Ra2 to pressure the queenside.

notes.explains: After ...g6 and ...Bg7, Black has active pieces and quick development, with no problems. If White plays Qg5, Black can choose between simplifying to an equal endgame with ...Nxd5 or playing ambitiously with ...Nh5, which after Qxd8+ Kxd8 leaves Black with a development advantage and Ra3 coming.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, you can often choose between safe equality and a more aggressive continuation that exploits the opponent's uncastled king.
notes.plans: If White plays Qg5, consider ...Nh5 to force trades that leave Black with better piece activity and the rook entering on a3.

notes.explains: Against White's b3 idea, Black can respond with ...a5 and ...a4, immediately pressuring the queenside. If White plays Nxa4, the ...d5 break is always in the air.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens the queenside with b3, a quick ...a5-a4 can create concrete pressure and a permanent hook for a central break.
notes.plans: Play ...a5-a4 to challenge the b3 pawn; if the knight takes on a4, be ready to strike with ...d5.

notes.explains: After White plays g3, Black can develop the bishop to e6 to attack the c4 pawn instead of committing to ...g6 and ...Bg7. This forces White to address the pressure on c4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is better to delay fianchettoing and instead put immediate pressure on a weak pawn, forcing the opponent to react.
notes.plans: Play ...Be6 to attack c4; if White plays e3, prepare ...d5 to undermine the center.

notes.explains: In the line with White's knight on d5 and bishop on g2, Black can consider ...Nxd5 immediately to attack the d5 pawn, since White's knight on f3 does not support it well. Alternatively, ...Nf4 or ...Ne5 are also good ideas.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's knight is not well supported, you can often win a pawn or create weaknesses by capturing it; also look for knight maneuvers to strong squares.
notes.plans: Consider ...Nxd5 to win the d5 pawn, or ...Nf4/...Ne5 to improve your pieces and maintain pressure.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Ne5, after ...b6, ...g6, ...Qf6, and ...Bb2, Black must prevent White's ...a4 by playing ...g5, a novelty that puts pressure on the bishop on b2. Then ...Bg7 follows, and Black can win the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn move like ...g5 is necessary to stop a dangerous pawn advance, and it can also create long-term pressure on a diagonal.
notes.plans: Play ...g5 to stop ...a4, then ...Bg7 to pressure the b2 bishop; aim to win the bishop pair.

notes.explains: After White plays e3, Black's main idea is to attack c4 and then play ...d5, because White is not in time to bring the bishop to g2. If White plays Nxd5, Black recaptures and White's queen on d2 becomes awkward, with ...Bb4 a serious threat.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are awkwardly placed (like a queen on d2), you can often create threats that win material or force concessions.
notes.plans: Play ...d5 to open the center; if White takes, recapture and follow up with ...Bb4 to exploit the queen's position.

notes.explains: In this line, White's attempt to stop ...d5 with d5 is met by Nxd5, and because the e3 pawn has already advanced to d5, Black's knight lands on d5 with great effect. White's queen on d2 is awkwardly placed, and Black has perfect development, with the threat of ...Bb4 looming.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pawn structure has a hole like d5, a knight on that outpost can be decisive, especially if the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated.
notes.plans: Black should look to exploit the d5 outpost and the awkward queen on d2 by generating threats like ...Bb4.

notes.explains: After a sequence of tactical blows, Black wins material by forcing the knight to c2, which wins the rook. White must play Kg2 to avoid immediate loss, but Black then plays Bg4, preventing the white king from escaping to those squares and preparing to castle long.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, keep the opponent's king restricted and coordinate your pieces to launch a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Black castles long, then plays g5 to open lines and bring the bishop to g7, targeting the hanging f4 pawn and creating mating threats.

notes.explains: The game ends quickly after Rook d3, because White's king is exposed and Black has mating threats: if the king goes to c4, Nxa5 is mate, and if it goes elsewhere, Nb5 is mate. The position is hopeless for White.
notes.teaches: A well-coordinated attack can force resignation even without a large material advantage, especially when the opponent's king is trapped.
notes.plans: Black simply finishes the game with the mating net.

notes.explains: This game illustrates the dangers White faces in this line, especially if unfamiliar with the theory. While White may be objectively better with correct play, Black has excellent counter-chances and is not suffering.
notes.teaches: Choosing a less theoretical opening like d4 d6 can be a practical way to avoid mainline theory (King's Indian, Grünfeld, Nimzo-Indian, Slav) and reach a playable position quickly, especially if your opponent only plays d4.
notes.plans: Black can rely on this opening to get dynamic play and avoid heavy preparation.

notes.explains: In the French Defense, Black's early capture on e4 with the queen can be risky because it brings the queen out prematurely, where it can become a target for White's developing pieces.
notes.teaches: When your opponent brings their queen out early, look for ways to develop while attacking it, gaining time and initiative.
notes.plans: White should continue development with moves like Nf3 and Bg5, hitting the queen and forcing it to move again.

notes.explains: White's decision to capture the knight on f6 is an exception to the general rule against early trades, because it forces Black's queen to a square where it can be harassed.
notes.teaches: Trades that bring the opponent's queen out can be beneficial if you can then attack the queen and gain time.
notes.plans: White should aim to develop pieces with threats against the queen, such as Bg5, to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: Black's move ...Nc6 is a serious mistake because it allows White to play Bg5 with tempo, hitting the queen and gaining a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is exposed, you should look for developing moves that also attack it, forcing it to lose time.
notes.plans: White should play Bg5, forcing the queen to move again, and then continue development with moves like Bd3, also with tempo.

notes.explains: Black's queen on g4 is vulnerable to a pawn attack, and White can use this to gain further time and open lines.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is on a square where it can be attacked by pawns, use that to gain time and create weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should play h3, attacking the queen and forcing it to move, while also preparing to open lines against Black's king.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's knight on c6 is a serious mistake because it allows White to play bishop g5, which pins the knight and creates severe pressure on the f6 square, making the queen vulnerable.
notes.teaches: When facing the move bishop g5 in similar positions, Black often needs to play h6 to prevent the pin and avoid exposing the queen to tactics.
notes.plans: Black should consider playing h6 to stop bishop g5, or avoid the knight c6 move altogether if it allows such pins.

notes.explains: After the queen captures on g2, the natural rook g1 fails because the queen can escape with queen takes h3. Instead, the move rook h2 is strong because it keeps control and traps the queen completely.
notes.teaches: When trapping a queen, look for moves that maintain control of all escape squares, even if they seem less natural. The rook on h2 covers the h-file and supports the trap.
notes.plans: After trapping the queen, White should continue to consolidate and convert the material advantage, possibly by forcing further weaknesses.

notes.explains: After winning the queen, White still needs to force resignation. The move bishop b5 check is decisive because it threatens queen d8 mate, leaving Black with no good defense.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for forcing moves that create immediate threats, such as checkmate patterns, to convert the win efficiently.
notes.plans: White should deliver the final blow with bishop b5 check, forcing mate or resignation.

notes.explains: In the Queen's Gambit Declined, White's move c5 is an ambitious pawn push that aims to gain space and cramp Black's position. However, it can also be risky if not followed up correctly.
notes.teaches: Pawn pushes like c5 in the Queen's Gambit can be powerful when they restrict the opponent, but they require precise handling to avoid weakening your own position.
notes.plans: White should follow up the c5 push with rapid development and pressure on Black's center, while Black should aim to challenge the pawn and free their pieces.

notes.explains: White's c4-c5 push grabs space on the queenside and can suffocate Black if Black doesn't react energetically. The pawn on c5 cramps Black's position, and White aims to follow up with b4, a4, and piece pressure to keep Black's pieces passive.
notes.teaches: A space-gaining pawn push like c4-c5 can be very effective if the opponent fails to challenge it immediately. The side with more space should use it to restrict the opponent's piece activity.
notes.plans: White will support the c5 pawn with b4, then expand further with a4-a5, and use the space to maneuver pieces to active squares while Black's pieces remain stuck.

notes.explains: Black's best response to c4-c5 is to immediately challenge the head of the pawn chain with b7-b6. This attacks the c5 pawn and fights for queenside squares. If White captures on b6, Black recaptures with the a-pawn, opening the a-file and gaining central control.
notes.teaches: When facing an overextended pawn chain, attack its base or head to undermine it. Challenging a space-gaining pawn immediately prevents White from consolidating.
notes.plans: After b6, if White supports with b4, Black can continue with a5 to further pressure the queenside and force White to overextend.

notes.explains: After White plays b4 to support c5, Black should play a5 immediately. This keeps the tension and forces White to either capture or advance to a3. Black doesn't need to capture right away; the threat is enough to keep White's pawns overextended.
notes.teaches: In such positions, it's often better to maintain tension and force the opponent to commit. Playing a5 before capturing on b4 or c5 gives Black the option to recapture favorably later.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with moves like Nf6-e4, targeting the c3 knight, and develop the bishop to b7, creating active piece play against White's weakened pawns.

notes.explains: If Black captures on c5 too early, White never has to resolve the tension and can maintain the pawn structure. Black's pieces may become active, but White's pawns remain solid and Black misses the chance to force White to overextend.
notes.teaches: Don't release tension prematurely if the opponent cannot force you to. Waiting can be a powerful resource; the side that has to commit first often ends up worse.
notes.plans: Black should keep the pressure on the queenside and only capture when it gains a concrete advantage, such as fracturing White's pawns or opening lines.

notes.explains: In this position, black has a queenside pawn tension where white cannot easily capture on c5 or b4 without weakening themselves. Black can maintain this tension indefinitely, forcing white to make reactive pawn moves that neglect development and king safety.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a static weakness or tension they cannot resolve, you can delay capturing and use the threat to provoke further weaknesses or gain time for development.
notes.plans: Keep the tension on the queenside, develop pieces, and prepare to open the center when favorable.

notes.explains: White has made many pawn moves and neglected development, leaving the king uncastled. Black should seek to open lines to exploit this. The move d4 is strong because it attacks the center and creates tactical threats based on the queenside tension.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is behind in development and king safety, look for central pawn breaks that open lines and create tactical opportunities, even if they seem premature.
notes.plans: Play d4, and if the knight captures, use the queenside tension to win the b-pawn and collapse white's pawns.

notes.explains: After d4, if white plays Nxd4, black can capture on b4 because the knight on d4 is pinned to the queen or otherwise vulnerable, making it impossible to recapture. This wins material and destroys white's pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Tactical motifs like pins and overloaded pieces can make otherwise impossible captures work. Always check if the opponent's recapture is actually possible.
notes.plans: After winning the b-pawn, continue to attack the weakened queenside pawns and the uncastled king.

notes.explains: Alternative moves like Nc6 or Ne4 are less effective. Nc6 allows b5, and Ne4 allows queen trades, which reduces attacking chances. The direct d4 is best because it forces the issue and maintains the initiative.
notes.teaches: When you have a tactical resource, prefer the most forcing move that keeps the initiative, rather than solid developing moves that allow the opponent to consolidate.
notes.plans: Play d4 and follow up with e5 to further open the position and attack the king.

notes.explains: In this position, black has just played e5, striking at the center while white has been pushing on the queenside. White's pawn on d4 is the base of the pawn chain, and if black can undermine it, white's center collapses.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks on the flank, counter in the center. A central pawn break like e5 can be more powerful than a wing attack because it strikes at the opponent's pawn chain.
notes.plans: Black should continue to develop pieces and maintain pressure on the center, aiming to exploit the weakness of the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: Black has developed the bishop to e6, neutralizing threats on the queenside. White's pieces are tied down to defending the weak c5 pawn, and black's pieces are more active.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has weaknesses, develop pieces to put pressure on them. Neutralizing threats and improving piece activity can create a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: Black should continue to pressure the c5 pawn and look for ways to open the position to exploit white's cramped pieces.

notes.explains: Black has just played d3, a central pawn push that creates a passed pawn and restricts white's pieces. White's queen is tied to defending the knight, and there is no good way to contest the black queen.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is undeveloped and cramped, a central pawn push can be decisive. It creates weaknesses and opens lines for your pieces.
notes.plans: Black should continue to push the d-pawn and use the queen to create threats, while white struggles to find active play.

notes.explains: White has played e3 to block the d-pawn, but black responds with e4, gaining even more space. White's pieces are cramped, and black's pawns are rolling forward.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, use it to restrict your opponent's pieces. Push pawns to gain more space and create a bind.
notes.plans: Black should continue to advance the pawns and prepare to break through, while white tries to find counterplay.

notes.explains: In this game, White's early c5 pawn push in the opening led to a cramped position after Black responded actively with b6 and later e5, gaining space and central control.
notes.teaches: When your opponent grabs space with a pawn push, counter immediately in the center and on the flank to prevent them from consolidating.
notes.plans: Black should continue to expand and maintain pressure, targeting White's weakened pawns and king safety.

notes.explains: Black's advanced d3 pawn became a key asset because White could not trade it off due to the vulnerability of his king, which had been forced to castle late and under pressure.
notes.teaches: A far-advanced passed pawn can be a permanent advantage if the opponent cannot eliminate it; use it to restrict their pieces and as a basis for attack.
notes.plans: Black should use the d3 pawn to support piece activity and prepare a breakthrough in the center.

notes.explains: Black's rook to e8 seemed passive but later proved crucial, supporting the e-pawn's advance and giving the rook a clear file once the center opened.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet rook move is a deep preparatory idea; place rooks on files where pawn breaks will occur.
notes.plans: Black will aim to push the e-pawn, using the rook's support to create a decisive passed pawn.

notes.explains: After White played f3 to challenge the center, Black found the crushing knight to d4, attacking the e3 pawn and creating threats. The point was not to win material but to open the e-file and promote the e-pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have a powerful pawn center, sacrifices to open lines and promote pawns can be more valuable than winning pieces.
notes.plans: Black should continue to push the e-pawn, using the knight and bishop to coordinate an attack on White's king and force promotion.

notes.explains: After the knight was captured, Black recaptured with check, then pushed e3, devastating White. The rook on e8 was perfectly placed, and all black pieces coordinated to queen a pawn.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, keep pieces coordinated and focus on the most direct plan—here, queening a pawn—rather than grabbing material.
notes.plans: Black will continue to advance the e-pawn, using the rook and bishop to support it, while White's pieces are tied down.

notes.explains: In this line, black's immediate b6 and a5 create queenside counterplay, while the e5 break is a key resource. White's c5 advance can be met by these active responses, making it a double-edged choice.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn advance like c5, look for immediate counterplay with b6 and a5, and keep the e5 break in mind as a central lever.
notes.plans: Black should aim to complete development and prepare the e5 break, while white must decide whether to maintain the tension or capture on c5.

notes.explains: Comparing bishop f4 and bishop g5 setups: with the bishop on f4, white controls e5 and is fully developed, reducing the effectiveness of black's knight e4 tactics. With the bishop on g5, black's e5 break gains strength.
notes.teaches: The placement of the bishop affects control of key central squares and the viability of tactical motifs like knight e4. Full development can neutralize such tactics.
notes.plans: White should aim for a fully developed position with the bishop on f4 to maintain control over e5, while black must seek counterplay through b6, a5, and possibly e5.

notes.explains: In the Panov-Botvinnik Attack, the pawn structure differs: black has committed to e6, so the e5 break is not available in one tempo, and white's c-pawn is passed. This changes the evaluation of c5.
notes.teaches: The same move (c5) can be good or bad depending on the pawn structure and the opponent's ability to generate counterplay. In the Panov, black's lack of a quick e5 makes c5 more viable for white.
notes.plans: Black should aim for timely counterplay with b6 and a5, while white can exploit the passed c-pawn and the absence of black's central break.

notes.explains: In this game, black chooses dxc4 instead of allowing c5, leading to a different line. Black then plays c5 to strike in the center and aim for quick equality.
notes.teaches: There are multiple ways to handle the opening; capturing on c4 can be a valid alternative to allow central counterplay with c5.
notes.plans: Black should continue with natural development and aim to complete equalization, while white must decide how to recapture and maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: Black's early ...dxc4 followed by ...c5 trades off the central pawns, removing White's space advantage and aiming for immediate equality.
notes.teaches: When facing a space-gaining opening, trading the central pawns can neutralize White's advantage and simplify the position.
notes.plans: After the pawn trades, Black develops naturally and prepares to challenge the isolated queen's pawn.

notes.explains: Black chooses ...Nbd7 over ...Nc6 to reach d5. ...Nc6 would pressure the pawn but allows White to play a3, forcing the knight to reroute. ...Nbd7 is a more reliable path to d5.
notes.teaches: When aiming for a specific outpost, choose the most direct and robust route, even if it looks less active initially.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Nb6 and ...Nd5, establishing a strong knight on the blockade square.

notes.explains: White's setup with Qe2 and Bb3 supports the d-pawn and prepares attacking ideas, including potential sacrifices on e6. Black's knight on d5 pressures the bishop on f4 and disrupts White's coordination.
notes.teaches: The side with the IQP should avoid trading minor pieces, as they are needed for the attack. The defender should use the blockade to create counterplay.
notes.plans: Black maintains the knight on d5, while White seeks to use the extra space to launch an attack with pieces like the knight on e5 and bishop pressure on h7.

notes.explains: With an isolated queen's pawn (IQP), the side playing against it wants to avoid trading minor pieces because those pieces are the ammunition for the attack. The knight on d5 is a key outpost pressuring the bishop on f4, and the side with the IQP wants to use the extra space to put the knight on e5 and the bishop on the h7 diagonal.
notes.teaches: When you have an IQP, keep minor pieces on the board to sustain attacking chances; trading them off reduces your firepower and leaves you with a static weakness.
notes.plans: From this position, the side with the IQP should aim to play the knight to e5, use the bishop to pressure h7, and possibly jump the knight to e4 to remove defenders.

notes.explains: Black's queen to a5 is a useful move because the queen often gets in the way in these structures; the bishop on g5 takes away c7 and d6, and the c-file is open, so c7 is not comfortable. The queen pressures the knight on c3 while also getting out of the way.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, look for ways to reroute pieces to better squares, even if it means moving the queen early to avoid future congestion.
notes.plans: Black can continue with rook to c1 (by White) and then develop the bishop to d7, aiming for a flexible setup.

notes.explains: Black's bishop maneuver to d7 and then back to e8 is a defensive idea. It heads not to c6 but to e8, where it controls the f7 square and supports the d5 outpost. This conservative approach keeps all pieces harmoniously placed, giving Black solid control over key squares while White struggles to create play.
notes.teaches: Bishops need not always go to the most active diagonal; a bishop can serve a vital defensive role, especially in positions where the opponent has a space advantage or a weakness to attack.
notes.plans: Black should maintain the blockade on d5 and keep the position solid, waiting for White to overextend or fail to make progress.

notes.explains: When facing an IQP, it is tempting to avoid trading pieces to keep the pawn isolated forever, but in practice you often end up taking the knight on c3. After bxc3, White's d4 pawn is more solidly supported, but White gains new weaknesses, such as the c3 pawn, and must watch both pawns if he pushes c4.
notes.teaches: Do not fear changing the structure by trading pieces against an IQP; the resulting weaknesses (like a backward c-pawn) can be just as exploitable as the original isolated pawn.
notes.plans: If White pushes c4, Black should be ready to pressure both the c4 and d4 pawns, possibly with moves like ...c5 or ...b5 to undermine.

notes.explains: After the knight is captured on c3, white's d4 pawn is supported, but c3 becomes a permanent weakness. Pushing c2-c4 creates a hanging pawn pair on c4 and d4, which are connected but isolated from the rest of the pawns.
notes.teaches: Hanging pawns are a double-edged sword: they control key central squares and can advance, but they are also targets and require constant attention.
notes.plans: White must decide whether to maintain the pawns or push one to create a breakthrough, while black should pressure them and aim to trade pieces.

notes.explains: Black retreats the queen to c7, unpinning the knight, and later plays ...Nbd7 to trade pieces. White's queen on d3 supports both pawns, but black repeatedly seeks to trade minor pieces against the hanging pawns.
notes.teaches: When facing hanging pawns, the side with the pawns should avoid unnecessary piece trades, while the opponent should actively trade to reduce the attacker's resources.
notes.plans: Black should continue to pressure d4 and c4, while white should keep pieces on the board to maintain attacking chances.

notes.explains: White captures on d5 with the bishop, trading off a minor piece. This is a positional mistake because it reduces white's attacking potential. White could have played c4 instead, keeping the knight active and maintaining more pieces.
notes.teaches: In structures with hanging pawns, preserving minor pieces is often more important than winning a pawn or simplifying, because the pawns need support to create a breakthrough.
notes.plans: White should avoid further trades and seek to advance d5 or c5 with piece support.

notes.explains: After further trades, black gains freedom to make weakening moves like ...f6 because white lacks the pieces to exploit them. The bishop that was passive now gets scope, and black's pieces coordinate well.
notes.teaches: When you trade off pieces, the defender's weaknesses become less exploitable. Conversely, the side with more pieces can often afford to make pawn moves that create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black should continue to improve piece activity and target the d4 pawn, while white must find active counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's pieces all take attacking roles, and the bishop comes to e4, trapping the rook on g6. White's rook is lost, and the position is winning for black.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied to defense, look for tactical motifs like trapping a piece. Also, a seemingly active rook can become overextended if it lacks support.
notes.plans: Black should convert the material advantage by simplifying or continuing the attack.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has strong pressure against White's central pawns, and White's rook on g6 becomes trapped after ...Be4 and ...Kh7, making it a decisive mistake.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece becomes trapped, it can be the turning point of the game; always look for ways to exploit such tactical weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black should continue to increase pressure on White's position, using the trapped rook to gain material or force a winning attack.

notes.explains: Black's rook takes on c5 initiates a sequence that leads to a decisive attack, as White's replies are met with checks and threats that bring all Black's pieces into the game.
notes.teaches: A single tactical blow can open the position for your pieces; when you have the initiative, keep the pressure on with checks and threats.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing the remaining pieces into play, aiming for a mating net or material gain.

notes.explains: In this English Opening, White plays an early e3 instead of the more common g3, aiming for a setup that can transpose into Grünfeld-like positions. Black's early Nf6 and d5 lead to a standard Grünfeld structure, but with e3 played instead of e4, it's an anti-Grünfeld approach.
notes.teaches: Recognize that different move orders can lead to the same pawn structure, and that playing e3 instead of e4 can avoid some mainline Grünfeld theory while still pressuring Black's center.
notes.plans: White will use the queen to pressure the d5 pawn, while Black will aim to defend it and complete development.

notes.explains: White plays Qb3 to pressure the d5 pawn, a common idea in Grünfeld positions. Black must be careful not to capture on c4 prematurely, as that would allow Bxc4, creating a dangerous battery against the kingside.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is under pressure, it's often better to let it be captured temporarily if it's on a half-open file and can be recaptured or attacked later, rather than weakening your position to defend it immediately.
notes.plans: Black will allow White to take on d5 if necessary, and will instead focus on developing pieces and preparing to attack the pawn with moves like Na6-c7.

notes.explains: Black plays Na6, a roundabout route to c7, to attack the d5 pawn from a different angle. This is an offbeat but interesting idea, as the knight will pressure the pawn without allowing White to easily defend it.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the most direct route to a target isn't the best; using a knight to attack a pawn from a different square can be more effective, especially if it also supports other plans.
notes.plans: Black will continue to develop and aim to undermine White's defense of the d5 pawn, possibly with moves like Bg4 to pin or trade off defenders.

notes.explains: The move Bg4 is not ideal because while it removes a defender of d5, it also temporarily removes the attacker, allowing White to develop comfortably. The bishop ends up retreating, wasting time.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that only temporarily address the position's needs; if you remove a defender, ensure you still maintain pressure or gain another advantage.
notes.plans: Instead, consider more forcing moves like b5, which creates immediate threats and cannot be easily ignored.

notes.explains: If White ignores the b5 sacrifice, Black should continue with b4 to break down the defense of the d5 pawn. This is more forcing than other moves like Rook b8, which allows White to develop comfortably.
notes.teaches: When you have a concrete plan, execute it with forcing moves; don't give the opponent time to consolidate.
notes.plans: Play b4 to undermine the d5 pawn's defenders, and be ready to meet Knight b5 with moves like Queen d7, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: After Black plays Rook b8 instead of the stronger b4, White can develop with Bishop f4, hitting the rook and gaining a tempo. This shows the importance of choosing the most forcing continuation.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, prefer moves that maintain the initiative and force the opponent to react, rather than allowing them to develop freely.
notes.plans: If White captures on b5 later, Black must be aware of the differences in the position, such as the rook's placement and the potential for tactics.

notes.explains: In this position, White has just played Bishop f4, hitting the rook on b8 and developing with tempo. Black's natural response is to move the rook to e8, keeping the position flexible. White then captures on b5, assuming the bishop on f4 controls the c7 square, preventing Black from kicking the knight away with Knight c7.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, look for a developing move that also creates a threat, gaining time. Also, when considering capturing a pawn, verify that the square you are relying on to retreat or defend is truly controlled.
notes.plans: Black should look for a way to exploit the pinned or overloaded bishop on f4. The move g5 is a direct challenge, attacking the bishop and threatening g4, which would trap the bishop on f3 with no squares.

notes.explains: Black plays g5, attacking the bishop on f4 and threatening g4, which would trap the bishop on f3. White is forced to capture on g5, after which Black plays Knight c7, hitting the knight on b5. White cannot save the knight, so Black wins a piece.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece is short on squares, use pawn moves to attack it and create threats that force concessions. Look for moves that have multiple purposes, such as attacking a piece and preparing a trap.
notes.plans: After winning the piece, Black should consolidate the material advantage while maintaining activity. White must seek compensation through active piece play.

notes.explains: White is down a piece and must find a way to maximize activity for the remaining pieces. The bishop on f3 is currently passive, so White plays d6, opening the diagonal for the bishop and creating a threat. Black must capture on d6, allowing White to castle and get the king safe.
notes.teaches: When material down, prioritize piece activity over pawn structure. Look for moves that open lines for your pieces and create counterplay, even if they involve pawn sacrifices.
notes.plans: White should continue to activate the bishop and create threats against Black's position, hoping to generate enough compensation for the lost piece.

notes.explains: When you are down significant material, the opponent's king may be too safe for a direct attack, so you need another source of counterplay.
notes.teaches: In materially worse positions, look for something concrete to play for—a passed pawn, active pieces, or complications—rather than hoping for a cheap tactic.

notes.explains: Here, pushing the a-pawn forward, supported by an active bishop, gives White real winning chances despite being down a piece.
notes.teaches: When down material, keep pieces on the board and create complications; avoid simplifying because that lets the material advantage shine.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn with the support of the bishop, aiming to promote or tie down black's pieces.

notes.explains: A move like a5 keeps the rook file closed and preserves the a-pawn's promotion potential, which is exactly the kind of resource needed when down material.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that maintain your counterplay—like advancing a passed pawn—rather than trades that simplify into a lost endgame.
notes.plans: Continue advancing the a-pawn, using the bishop to support it, while keeping the position complex.

notes.explains: When the opponent offers a repetition, deviating shows confidence in outplaying them despite being down material, but it also risks losing the draw.
notes.teaches: In a worse position, you may choose to avoid a draw if you believe you can create practical chances, but you must be willing to accept the risk.
notes.plans: Keep the game going by avoiding repetition and continuing to push the a-pawn, forcing the opponent to find precise moves.

notes.explains: When you are up material, trading pieces is often good, but here the best move (Knight takes f3) is good not just because it trades a bishop, but because it allows a strong follow-up.
notes.teaches: When up material, look for trades that also create tactical opportunities or improve your position, not just trades for their own sake.
notes.plans: If possible, trade off the active bishop and then use the resulting initiative to consolidate the material advantage.

notes.explains: When you are up material, trading pieces simplifies the position and reduces the opponent's counterplay; when down material, you want to keep pieces on to create complications.
notes.teaches: Use trades as a lever: trade when ahead to convert, avoid trades when behind to maximize swindling chances.

notes.explains: In a position where the opponent's bishop is pinning along a long diagonal, a move like ...d5 can block the diagonal and neutralize the bishop's activity, making the position easier to handle.
notes.teaches: Look for pawn moves that shut down your opponent's active pieces, especially long-range bishops.
notes.plans: After ...d5, the bishop is cut off, and Black can proceed with simplifying trades and advancing the queenside pawn.

notes.explains: In a position where the opponent's king is exposed, even when down material, creating direct threats against the king can be the best practical chance.
notes.teaches: When material down, look for attacking chances against the enemy king to complicate the game.
notes.plans: Use checks and threats to force the king into the open and create perpetual check or mating nets.

notes.explains: When one side has threats on one flank, the defender may solve them, but the attacker can then switch to the other flank to create new problems. Here, the player under pressure eventually blundered after repeated switching.
notes.teaches: In chess, keep the initiative by shifting the point of attack from one side of the board to the other, forcing the defender to constantly re-evaluate and find new resources.
notes.plans: If you have a space or activity advantage, look for ways to create threats on both wings to overload the opponent's defense.

notes.explains: In a sharp position, a forcing sequence may lead to a draw by repetition or perpetual check, even if it looks dangerous for the defender. The defender can often find a fortress-like setup where the attacker cannot make progress.
notes.teaches: When defending, look for ways to force a draw by repetition or by creating a fortress, especially when material is equal but the opponent has active pieces.
notes.plans: If you are the defender, aim to simplify into a drawn endgame or force a perpetual check. If you are the attacker, avoid premature forcing lines that allow the defender to escape.

notes.explains: In a critical position, a single move can turn the game. Here, the defender missed a winning move (Bishop d5) that would have exploited the pin on the queen and the fork on the knight, but instead played a different move that allowed the attacker to turn the tables.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical resources that exploit pins, forks, and the vulnerability of the king. In time pressure, it's easy to miss such moves, so practice calculating forcing sequences.
notes.plans: When you have a chance to win material or checkmate, calculate carefully, considering all defensive resources for the opponent.

notes.explains: After the defender missed the win, the attacker capitalized on the weakened position by creating threats against the king and the a-pawn, leading to a decisive material gain.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a mistake, be alert to the new weaknesses and immediately create threats that exploit them. Keep the pressure on and do not give the opponent time to recover.
notes.plans: If you have a material or positional advantage, convert it by combining threats against the king with advancing passed pawns.

notes.explains: In the endgame, having an active rook and a passed pawn can be decisive. Here, the player sacrificed a pawn to activate the rook and eventually won the game by promoting the h-pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity is paramount. Sometimes sacrificing a pawn to activate your rook and create a passed pawn is the fastest route to victory.
notes.plans: If you have a passed pawn, use your rook to support its advance and cut off the opponent's king. Avoid allowing the opponent to queen if you can win more efficiently.

notes.explains: In the final position, one extra knight is sufficient to convert the win in the endgame, even if the game could have continued a bit longer.
notes.teaches: Material advantages like an extra minor piece are often enough to win an endgame if technique is sound.
notes.plans: Use the extra piece to create threats, trade down to a simpler winning endgame, and avoid unnecessary risks.

notes.explains: The game featured an interesting opening idea and a tactic that won material, but the opponent kept the game alive with moves like d6 to open the bishop and a5 to maintain chances.
notes.teaches: When behind in material, look for moves that activate pieces and create counterplay rather than passively defending.
notes.plans: Keep the position dynamic, switch play between wings to stretch the opponent's pieces, and force mistakes.

notes.explains: In the Scotch Game, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bc5 Be3, Black's Qf6 is the main line, challenging the knight and controlling e5, whereas Nf6 would allow Nxc6 with too many threats.
notes.teaches: In the Scotch, Qf6 is a solid developing move that avoids tactics and keeps an eye on key central squares.
notes.plans: Black aims to complete development, castle, and prepare to challenge the center with moves like ...Nge7 and ...d6.

notes.explains: White's Bb5 is less common than Bc4 in the Scotch, but it's not a mistake; it's difficult to be much worse with White in the Scotch even after a slightly unusual move.
notes.teaches: In the Scotch, White has flexibility in bishop placement; minor inaccuracies don't lead to a clear disadvantage.
notes.plans: Continue with normal development, castle, and maintain central presence.

notes.explains: In faster time controls, players often rely on solid principles like keeping pieces defended, as loose pieces drop off and tactics become more likely.
notes.teaches: In blitz or rapid, prioritize sound piece placement and avoid loose pieces; in slower games, you can afford to look for exceptions to principles.
notes.plans: Keep all pieces defended, avoid creating weaknesses, and be alert to tactical opportunities.

notes.explains: Black's ...Be6 and ...Qg6 challenge the e4 pawn and prepare ...Nf4, while White's Bd3 defends the pawn and opposes the queen. After ...Bxd4, cxd4, ...Nb4 is the key follow-up, regaining the bishop pair and challenging the center.
notes.teaches: When giving up a bishop for a knight, ensure you have a follow-up that compensates, like gaining the bishop pair or attacking the center.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Nb4 to trade off the bishop and then focus on central control; White must handle the pressure on e4 and the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: After the sequence with ...d4 and ...Nf4, White's bishop takes on d4 is a major concession: it gives up the dark-squared bishop and the bishop pair, and hands Black a strong central pawn duo. The only compensation is the follow-up ...Nb4 to regain the bishop pair, but the central space remains a long-term problem.
notes.teaches: When you give your opponent a big center, you must contest it quickly; otherwise, the space advantage becomes overwhelming.
notes.plans: Black should aim to challenge the center with ...d5 as soon as possible, rather than making slow developing moves.

notes.explains: In this structure where Black has traded the c-pawn for White's e-pawn, White's full center (pawns on d4 and e4) is very pleasant. Black's ...d5 is the only move to contest the center; moves like ...d6 or ...b6 are insufficient because they leave the center uncontested, allowing White to consolidate and press.
notes.teaches: Against a big center, you must challenge it immediately with a pawn break, not just develop pieces around it.
notes.plans: Black plays ...d5, and White supports with f3, maintaining a strong center and a comfortable advantage.

notes.explains: Black's ...f6 is a forced move to prevent White from playing e5, which would be followed by f4, g4, h3, and a kingside pawn storm that could run Black over. Without ...f6, White's central pawns would roll forward and create a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong center, you must prevent the opponent's central pawn breaks, even at the cost of weakening your own pawn structure.
notes.plans: Black plays ...f6 to stop e5, and White must find a plan to use the center advantage, considering moves like Nf4, g4, or a minority attack.

notes.explains: In a position with a strong center, White has many possible plans: Nf4 to trade on e6, kingside expansion with g4, a queenside minority attack, trading in the center, or pushing e5. The key is to choose a plan and execute it consistently.
notes.teaches: Having a big center gives you an advantage, but you must convert it by picking a concrete plan and playing with purpose.
notes.plans: White should evaluate each candidate move and select a plan that maximizes the central space advantage.

notes.explains: In this type of central pawn structure, White has several plausible moves: switching to the queenside for a minority attack, trading in the center, or pushing with e5. The key is not which move is chosen but that it is part of a coherent plan.
notes.teaches: Always choose moves that fit a concrete plan rather than playing aimless moves. Even if multiple moves are playable, the one that gives you a clear follow-up is preferable.
notes.plans: If playing e5, anticipate that Black may capture, leading to a central pawn on e5 and a half-open d-file. Then plan to use the d4 square for a knight, the c-file for rooks, and support the e5 pawn with f4 if needed.

notes.explains: A move like Nf4, while tempting to win a pawn, may not lead to a clear plan. After exchanges, you might be left with the same positional questions, so it's not a real plan.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that win material but leave you without a strategic direction. A good move should improve your position or create a concrete threat that fits your overall plan.

notes.explains: When considering a plan like playing b4 and Bf4 to control dark squares, you must ask what you are actually achieving. If the opponent can simply defend and then activate their pieces, your plan may not be effective.
notes.teaches: Evaluate your plans by asking what concrete gains you achieve. If your opponent can neutralize your ideas easily, consider a more forcing or direct approach.

notes.explains: The move e5 is combative and poses a question to the opponent. If they allow it to remain, White can expand with f4 and build a strong center. Black is practically forced to capture, leading to a clear structure for White.
notes.teaches: A strong center is a long-term asset that forces the opponent to react. By playing a move that creates a threat, you can anticipate the opponent's response and calculate the resulting position.
notes.plans: After e5 and recapture, White has a passed pawn on e5, a half-open c-file, and a d4 outpost for a knight. The plan is to prevent c5 with b4 and then transfer pieces to the queenside to pressure Black.

notes.explains: White has a strong center with a pawn on e5, a half-open c-file, and a d4 square for the knight. The dark-square pressure and the passed e-pawn give White a clear advantage if Black cannot challenge with c5.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and a passed pawn, prevent your opponent's freeing breaks (like c5) to maintain the pressure and keep your plan rolling.
notes.plans: Play b4 to stop c5, then transfer pieces to the queenside and keep the e5 pawn defended (e.g., with f4 if needed).

notes.explains: In the game, White played a5 to undermine Black's a7-b6 pawn structure, creating a direct threat once the knight moves. This is more effective than just repositioning the bishop.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are already well placed, look for pawn moves that create concrete threats and worsen your opponent's structure.
notes.plans: After a5, continue with moves like Rfe1 and Qe2, maintaining pressure on c6 and preparing a kingside expansion.

notes.explains: Black's only real idea is to push c5, so White must always be alert to prevent it. A momentary lapse (like Bf2) allowed Black to create a nuisance with Bh3.
notes.teaches: In positions where you have a bind, your number one priority is to keep the opponent's freeing break bad. Never relax your vigilance.
notes.plans: Keep the c5 square covered and continue improving your pieces, but always be ready to meet any attempt at c5.

notes.explains: This position illustrates a crossroad moment where deep understanding is required. Analyzing your own games after playing them helps you learn from such moments.
notes.teaches: After your games, review critical positions and ask what would have happened if you had chosen a different plan. This builds the intuition needed to spot these ideas over the board.

notes.explains: Black's only real plan in this position is to push c5, so White's top priority is to keep that square covered. Moving the bishop away from f2, where it defends c5, is a mistake that lets Black's main idea become playable.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has one clear freeing or counterplay move, every move you make should keep that move in check. Don't voluntarily abandon the key defensive square.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on f2 to defend c5, and consider Qf1 followed by Kh1 to prevent Bxh3 and keep control.

notes.explains: After White errs and Black plays c5, Black gains active play but also concedes the b5 square. White can occupy b5, which then gives access to d6, so the position remains pleasant for White even though Black has achieved the break.
notes.teaches: Every pawn break has a downside—here c5 weakens b5. When your opponent gets their desired break, look for the new weaknesses they created and occupy them with your pieces.
notes.plans: Occupy b5 with a piece, aiming to infiltrate via d6 and keep pressure on Black's position.

notes.explains: Black's rook to a8 fails to solve the problem on c5, allowing White to capture on e5 and eventually win material. The only way to keep the balance was to play c4, addressing the c5 weakness directly.
notes.teaches: When your position has a structural weakness, you must address it directly with a concrete move rather than a passive regrouping. Sometimes the only solution is to give back material or change the pawn structure.
notes.plans: If Black had played c4, the material would stay balanced; instead, White captures on e5 and invades with the queen on the queenside, winning a piece.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian Defense, White aims to establish a large pawn center with e4 and d4, gaining space on the queenside. Black deliberately allows this, planning to counterstrike later.
notes.teaches: The King's Indian Defense is a hypermodern opening: Black lets White build a big center, then attacks it with pieces and pawn breaks.
notes.plans: White will develop the knight to c3 and play e4, while Black prepares to challenge the center with moves like ...e5 or ...c5.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian Defense, White builds a big center with e4 and d4, and Black allows it, planning to counterstrike later. Black's main move is d6, preventing White from kicking the knight away with e5.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, Black voluntarily concedes central space to White, aiming for a later counterattack. The move d6 is essential to maintain the knight on f6 and control the e5 square.
notes.plans: White will aim to expand on the queenside, while Black will prepare a kingside attack with moves like f5 and g5.

notes.explains: When Black has fianchettoed with g6, White's light-squared bishop is better placed on e2 than d3. On d3, it is blocked by the pawn on g6, but on e2 it can prevent Black from bringing a knight to g4 or other squares.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchettoed setup, place the bishop on e2 to avoid aiming at a wall and to maintain control over key squares.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e2, castle, and prepare queenside expansion.

notes.explains: In the Exchange variation, if White grabs the pawn on d5, Black can play Nxe4, exploiting the open d-file and the powerful bishop on g7. This leads to tactical tricks for Black.
notes.teaches: When the center opens, beware of tactics involving the fianchettoed bishop and central pawn grabs. Always consider the opponent's counterplay before taking material.
notes.plans: If playing the Exchange variation, castle first and develop normally rather than grabbing the pawn.

notes.explains: Black can also play d5, gaining space and planning to bring a knight to c5, supported by a5 to prevent b4 kicking it away. This gives Black a solid central presence.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, Black has multiple setups; the knight on c5 can be a strong outpost, and a5 is a useful preparatory move to keep it there.
notes.plans: Black will aim to maintain the knight on c5 and pressure the center.

notes.explains: After the main line with Nc6 and d5, White has more space on the queenside, while Black has more on the kingside. White's plan is to break through with c5, while Black attacks with f5 and g5.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, both sides have opposing plans: White on the queenside, Black on the kingside. The race is often decisive.
notes.plans: White should prepare c5 with b4 or piece support; Black should launch a kingside pawn storm.

notes.explains: In this sharp King's Indian setup, Black gains space on the kingside and commits to a direct attack with pawns like f5 and g5, while White aims for a queenside breakthrough with c5. The game is often decided by whether Black's attack lands first or White's queenside pressure wins.
notes.teaches: Recognize the fundamental imbalance: one side attacks on the kingside, the other on the queenside. The player who executes their plan more efficiently usually wins.
notes.plans: Black: push f5 and g5, prepare a kingside assault. White: prepare c5 with b4 or piece support, then break through on the queenside.

notes.explains: White's Knight to e1 is a key defensive move: it prevents Black's knight from going to h5 (where it could be captured), and it clears the way for the bishop to retreat to f2, where it defends the king and also eyes the queenside.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, a knight on e1 can serve multiple purposes: blocking enemy knight jumps, allowing a bishop retreat to f2, and later rerouting to d3 or f2 to support the c5 break.
notes.plans: White: after Ne1, aim to place the bishop on f2, then bring the knight to d3 or f2 to support c5. Black: develop the knight to d7 or e8, and prepare f5.

notes.explains: Black's typical sacrifice of the bishop on h3 is a critical motif: if White has a pawn on h3, Black may sacrifice the bishop to open the kingside and expose the king. Both sides must be alert to this possibility.
notes.teaches: Be aware of the bishop sacrifice on h3 in the King's Indian: it's a common attacking resource that can rip open the king's position. Defenders should avoid creating the hook (h3) unless necessary.
notes.plans: Black: look for opportunities to play Bxh3 if White plays h3. White: keep the kingside solid, avoid weakening pawn moves, and keep pieces near the king for defense.

notes.explains: White's bishop on f2 sits on a strong diagonal, defending the king and also supporting the queenside break. Meanwhile, Black continues to bring pieces to the kingside, like the knight to g6, preparing pawn breaks.
notes.teaches: A well-placed piece can serve both defense and offense. The bishop on f2 in the King's Indian is a classic example: it guards the king and also eyes the queenside.
notes.plans: White: play c5 to create queenside pressure, and consider rerouting the knight to f2 to guard the key g4 square. Black: continue attacking with pieces and pawns, aiming for breaks like f4 or g4.

notes.explains: In this King's Indian structure, White's play on the queenside revolves around creating weaknesses, especially by fixing and attacking the d6 pawn. The key entry point is the c7 square, which White tries to invade with pieces like a knight on b5 or a rook.
notes.teaches: When facing a King's Indian, White should aim to create a permanent weakness on the queenside (like an isolated d6 pawn) and then target it with pieces, using outposts and open files.
notes.plans: White plans to play c5, then take on d6 to isolate the pawn, and then bring a knight to b5 and rooks to the c-file to attack c7.

notes.explains: Black's counterplay often involves sacrificing material on the queenside to gain time for a kingside attack. For example, allowing White to take the a7 pawn can be part of Black's strategy, as it deflects White's pieces from the main action.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings like the King's Indian, material is often secondary to initiative and attacking chances. It can be strategically sound to give up a pawn to buy time for a devastating attack.
notes.plans: Black continues to build up on the kingside with moves like h5, g4, and breaks to open lines against the white king.

notes.explains: Black must proactively defend the c7 square, as it is White's main entry point. Moves like Rf7 or dropping the knight back to e8 are typical ways to control that key square and prevent White's invasion.
notes.teaches: Identifying and defending your opponent's key invasion squares is crucial. Sometimes you need to make prophylactic moves to stop threats before they materialize.
notes.plans: Black prepares to meet White's queenside pressure by reinforcing c7 and continuing with kingside operations.

notes.explains: White's knight on b5 is a typical outpost, but Black can often expel it with a6 and b5. To prevent this, White may play a4 first, ensuring the knight remains on b5 and maintains pressure on the queenside.
notes.teaches: When placing a piece on an outpost, consider whether the opponent can easily kick it away. Sometimes you need to make preparatory moves to secure the outpost permanently.
notes.plans: White aims to establish a knight on b5 (or later c4) to exploit weakened dark squares, while Black tries to undermine it with pawn moves.

notes.explains: After the knight is kicked back, White can reorganize it to c4 or a3 to target the weakened dark squares on the queenside. Black's pawn moves (like b5) create weaknesses on both dark and light squares, such as c6, which White can occupy with a rook or knight.
notes.teaches: When your piece is driven back, look for alternative squares that still exert pressure on the opponent's weaknesses. The opponent's pawn advances often create new weaknesses that you can exploit.
notes.plans: White will try to place a piece on c6 (likely a rook) to increase pressure, while Black continues the kingside attack, hoping to break through before White's queenside play becomes decisive.

notes.explains: White has created weaknesses on both dark and light squares, notably c6, and can invade with a rook or knight. The rook on c6 attacks multiple targets, but black's kingside attack is fast and dangerous.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, a queenside invasion must be backed by concrete threats; otherwise, black's kingside attack can crash through first.
notes.plans: White should consider keeping the rook on c6 and preparing to meet black's kingside pawn storm, rather than retreating the rook prematurely.

notes.explains: Black plays Qf8 to defend the d6 pawn and enable Bh6, which supports typical knight sacrifices on the kingside. This setup is unusual but effective.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the queen can defend key pawns while the bishop goes to h6 to prepare sacrifices on the pawn chain.
notes.plans: Black aims to play Bh6, then consider sacrifices on e4 or on the kingside to open lines against the white king.

notes.explains: White's rook is attacked, and retreating it is a mistake. The rook belongs on c6, and sacrificing the exchange is common to maintain pressure and counterplay.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, material is often less important than the initiative; an exchange sacrifice can be correct to keep the attack going.
notes.plans: White should consider leaving the rook on c6 or even sacrificing it, rather than retreating, to maintain queenside pressure.

notes.explains: In this sharp King's Indian position, White has offered a pawn to open lines and generate attacking chances. Taking it can be risky because Black's pieces remain active and the initiative matters more than material.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit in the King's Indian, weigh the cost of accepting material against the opponent's compensation in development and attacking potential. Sometimes declining or returning material is wiser.
notes.plans: Black should focus on completing development and maintaining a solid pawn structure, while being ready to counterattack in the center or on the kingside.

notes.explains: White's move f3 opens the f-file and prepares to pile pressure on Black's position. The bishop on g7 remains a powerful attacking piece, so White is not interested in winning the exchange if it means removing that bishop.
notes.teaches: In positions with opposite-side castling or open files, piece activity and attacking potential often outweigh material gains. A powerful bishop can be worth more than a rook.
notes.plans: White will continue to open lines and create threats against Black's king, while Black must find active counterplay to avoid being overwhelmed.

notes.explains: After a series of tactical blows, Black has a rook on f1 giving check, and White's king is exposed. The rook is untouchable because capturing it would allow a mating net.
notes.teaches: In wild tactical positions, always check for mating threats before capturing material. A seemingly free rook can be a trap if the opponent has a forced mate.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press the attack, using checks and threats to drive the king into the open and bring more pieces into the attack.

notes.explains: Black's queen on h6 threatens discovered checks and creates a mating net. White is forced to give up material to avoid immediate checkmate, and the king is forced to march up the board.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use your queen and minor pieces to create threats that force concessions. Discovered checks and mating threats are powerful tools.
notes.plans: Black should continue to coordinate pieces to deliver a decisive attack, possibly bringing the rook into the attack with tempo.
