notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In the Deferred Steinitz, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 d6, Black often plays ...Bd7 and ...Be7, aiming for a solid setup. White cannot win a pawn immediately because after d4 exd4, Black recaptures with the knight and gets comfortable play.
notes.teaches: Recognize that in the Deferred Steinitz, White's main plan is to build a center with d4, but must be patient because Black's structure is solid and counterplay is available.
notes.plans: White should develop harmoniously, possibly with d5 or Bc2, and prepare to challenge Black's setup.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: The position after d5 and Bc2 resembles a King's Indian setup, but with a key difference: Black's bishop on e7 is passive and should ideally be on g7. White has a choice between Bxd7 and Bc2, each with pros and cons.
notes.teaches: When choosing between exchanges and retreats, weigh the value of the bishop pair, the opponent's weaknesses, and your own attacking chances. Here, Bc2 keeps the bishop active and pressures f5, while Bxd7 removes a good defender but gives up a strong piece.
notes.plans: If White plays Bc2, ideas include attacking h7 or pressuring f5, while also defending e4. If Bxd7, White simplifies but must find other ways to exploit Black's passive bishop.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: Black's early ...Bg4 is premature because White can play h3 and force Black to make a decision before Black is ready. If Black takes on f3, White gets the bishop pair and strong pressure; if Black retreats, the bishop ends up misplaced, as on g6.
notes.teaches: Avoid committing your bishop early if your opponent can gain tempo and force it to a bad square. Keep flexibility in development, especially with bishops, until the optimal moment.
notes.plans: Black should have kept the bishop on c8 to decide later whether to bring it to the kingside or keep it for defense. After ...Bg4 and h3, Black's bishop becomes a long-term liability.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: After Black's bishop is stuck on g6, Black's position is passive. The bishop on e7 is also bad, but at least it has some potential to be rerouted. The bishop on g6 is hopeless and will remain a target.
notes.teaches: In strategic positions, identify the opponent's worst piece and aim to keep it that way. A permanently bad bishop can be a decisive long-term weakness.
notes.plans: White should continue developing, perhaps with Qe2, Bd2, and Kg2, preparing to exploit Black's lack of activity and the bad bishop on g6.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White's move Kg2 is a typical human move that hides intentions while improving the king's safety. It prepares to bring the rook to the e-file or f-file and supports a potential f4 break.
notes.teaches: Sometimes quiet king moves are strong because they improve your position without revealing your plans. They can also prepare for central or kingside operations.
notes.plans: White aims to use the king's position to support a pawn storm or piece pressure, while Black remains passive.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In this position, black's bishop is passively placed on g6 and has no prospects, while white has a clear space advantage. Black's attempt to close the position with h4-g5 is generally bad because it leaves black without counterplay and forces a passive defense.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, avoid allowing your opponent to close the position if it gives them no counterplay; instead, keep the tension and slowly improve your pieces.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve piece placement and prepare a breakthrough on the kingside, while black must seek active defense rather than closing the position.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White plays a patient, ambiguous move like Kg2, which keeps multiple plans alive: it hints at a kingside pawn storm with Rh1-h4-g5, but also keeps queenside options open. This ambiguity makes it harder for black to decide how to defend.
notes.teaches: In strategic positions, playing moves that preserve multiple threats and hide your true intentions can be more effective than committing to one plan, as it forces the opponent to guess and defend against everything.
notes.plans: White should keep the opponent guessing and only commit to a breakthrough when the moment is right.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White plays Nf5 to prevent black's knight from reaching g6 and then f4, which would give black counterplay. By exchanging on f5, white secures the important g6 square and eliminates black's potential active piece.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a piece that could jump into a strong outpost, it's often worth spending time to prevent it, even if it means exchanging pieces. Controlling key squares can stifle all counterplay.
notes.plans: After securing the kingside, white can continue to build pressure and look for a decisive breakthrough.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White plays a mysterious move like Bd1, which has the long-term idea of transferring the bishop to h5 and g6 to support a kingside attack. This shows that even in a winning position, piece maneuvering can be more effective than forcing immediate action.
notes.teaches: In strategic positions, a piece can be repositioned over several moves to a better square, even if the path is not obvious. Patience and maneuvering are key to maximizing your piece activity.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve piece placement and only strike when the pieces are optimally coordinated.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In a winning position, exchanges generally favor the stronger side, but you must keep enough material to convert the advantage.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, look for exchanges that simplify the position while retaining a decisive material or positional edge.
notes.plans: Continue to trade pieces selectively, avoiding trades that leave you with insufficient mating material.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: A key move like d6 can be the most forcing way to win, creating threats that overload the opponent's defenses.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, prefer the most forcing continuation that maintains the initiative and avoids unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawn or create mating threats, as in the example where the pawn promotes or the bishop delivers mate.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In the Steinitz Deferred, after the typical moves, you can choose between different plans: closing the center with d5 or developing pieces classically.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, undeveloped pieces can sometimes be a resource, as they allow flexible defensive setups like ...f6 and ...Nh6.
notes.plans: Consider both central expansion and piece play; for example, Bg5 to provoke weaknesses or a classical setup with Re1 and Be3.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez structure, the bishop on b3 is powerful on the a2-g8 diagonal, and moves like d4 can be a tactical threat.
notes.teaches: Be alert to tactical shots like ...d4, which can win material if the opponent is careless; keep the bishop on a strong diagonal.
notes.plans: Maintain the bishop on b3 and prepare central breaks or pressure on e7, as in the idea of Bc5 after exchanges.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In the Steinitz Deferred, the bishop on b3 is powerful along the a2-g8 diagonal, pressuring e7 and supporting central breaks. Black's pieces on d7 and e7 can become cramped, giving White a slight space advantage.
notes.teaches: A bishop on b3 in the Ruy Lopez exerts lasting pressure on Black's kingside and e7 square, often forcing Black into passive piece placement.
notes.plans: White can aim to increase pressure with moves like Bishop c5 or Bishop a3, exploiting the diagonal and Black's cramped setup.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: Black's move b6 is a good defensive resource to stop White's immediate threats along the diagonal, but it doesn't solve all problems. The position remains close to equal with White having a slight pull.
notes.teaches: When facing pressure on a diagonal, a well-timed pawn move like b6 can neutralize immediate threats, but you must remain alert to long-term weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black should look for active counterplay, possibly with f5 or g5, while White continues to probe for weaknesses.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In these half-open structures, Black's f5 break is risky because White can open the position favorably. If Black manages f4, it could lead to a strong attack, but White can prevent that by taking on f5.
notes.teaches: In half-open positions, pawn breaks like f5 must be carefully timed; if the opponent can open the position to their advantage, the break can backfire.
notes.plans: White should aim to open the position when Black's pieces are passive, while Black must ensure his pieces are coordinated before initiating such breaks.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: Black's attempt to play f5 in this position leads to a tactical sequence where White can sacrifice on e7 or use the open file to win material. Black's pieces are too disorganized to defend effectively.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are uncoordinated, tactical blows like sacrifices on key squares can be decisive, even if material is temporarily given up.
notes.plans: White should look for concrete tactics to exploit Black's lack of coordination, such as opening lines and targeting weak points.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In these half-open King's Indian structures, a typical tactical idea involves sacrificing on h6. Here, the absence of the bishop on g7 is critical because the queen can go to g5, and the rook can take on e7, leaving the enemy king exposed on h6 while the white king is safe.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and their pieces are uncoordinated, even a material deficit can be compensated by active pieces and a safer king.
notes.plans: White should continue activating pieces and creating threats, such as queen to g7 or g6, while maintaining pressure on the exposed king.

notes.explains: White is down two pawns but has strong pressure on d6, which compensates for the material deficit. The black bishop on c8 is still locked in, and the black king remains on e8, making the position dangerous for Black.
notes.teaches: Material deficits can be offset by dynamic factors like piece activity, king safety, and control of key squares. In such positions, every move must be precise because a single mistake can tip the balance.
notes.plans: Maintain pressure on d6 and keep the black bishop restricted. Look for ways to increase the initiative without allowing Black to free their position.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In this King's Indian position, White has a space advantage with the c4-d4 pawn structure, but Black is well developed and ready for a kingside attack with f5. The absence of the dark-squared bishops favors White, as Black loses attacking chances.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the trade of dark-squared bishops can reduce Black's attacking potential, favoring White's space advantage.
notes.plans: Black must play h6 before f5 to prevent a knight jump to g5 and e6. White should aim to consolidate the space advantage and prepare for Black's f5 break.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In this structure, the absence of bishops changes the evaluation: it usually favors White because Black's chances are reduced, though Black's well-placed knights on d7 and e7 support play on both wings.
notes.teaches: When bishops are traded off, the side with better central control and piece activity often gains; knights on d7 and e7 can be flexible for supporting kingside or queenside operations.
notes.plans: Black should look for opportunities to use the knights to support pawn breaks or piece pressure on either side.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: The move Qb3 looks attractive and may be the engine's choice, but it is not part of a coherent human plan; the queen is better placed on c2, where it supports central and queenside operations.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for the queen, consider long-term plans: a queen on c2 often supports b4 breaks and keeps the queen safer from tactical tricks.
notes.plans: Prefer Qc2 over Qb3 in similar structures, as it prepares b4 and avoids exposing the queen.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: The a4-a5 plan is strong in this structure because it fixes a weakness on a6 and prepares a later b4 break, which can open lines on the queenside.
notes.teaches: In King's Indian-like structures, advancing the a-pawn to a5 can create long-term pressure on the queenside, especially if it fixes a pawn on a6.
notes.plans: Use a4-a5 to fix the a6 pawn, then prepare b4 to open the b-file or create passed pawns.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: Taking on e4 would give White a powerful outpost on e4 and allow a quick b4 break, leading to a strategically winning position for White; therefore Black avoids it.
notes.teaches: Before capturing a central pawn, consider whether the opponent gains an outpost or a free hand for a pawn break; sometimes it is better to maintain tension.
notes.plans: Black should keep the e4 pawn under pressure but not capture it, to avoid giving White a strong knight outpost.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: The move g7-g7 (likely g7-g6? but as given) is a committal decision because it releases the grip on the e4 pawn; that pawn is a key square in these structures, and White needs to defend it, so neither side wants to release the tension.
notes.teaches: In positions with a central pawn tension, the side that releases it may lose control of key squares; it is often better to maintain the tension until the right moment.
notes.plans: Black should avoid releasing the tension on e4 without a concrete plan, as it gives White more freedom.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: The knight maneuver to f2 and then d3 is typical in King's Indian structures: the knight is excellently placed on d3, supporting b4 and c5 breaks and eyeing potential sacrifices.
notes.teaches: In King's Indian setups, rerouting a knight to d3 can be a strong plan, as it supports queenside pawn advances and central control.
notes.plans: White should aim for the knight maneuver to d3, then prepare b4 and c5 to open lines.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: The move Kh1 is useful to avoid checks on the c1-h6 diagonal, especially if Black plays Bc5 or similar, and it also prepares for potential back-rank issues.
notes.teaches: A quiet king move like Kh1 can be prophylactic, preventing tactical checks and making future plans safer.
notes.plans: White should consider Kh1 before starting a pawn storm, to avoid interruptions.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In this position, moving the king to h1 is useful because it gets out of potential checks, such as queen c5 checks, that could occur after certain maneuvers. It's a prophylactic move that avoids future harassment.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic king moves to h1 can prevent annoying checks and are often useful when the opponent has latent tactical threats.
notes.plans: Continue with the planned maneuvers, knowing the king is safe from checks.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White gave up the center and played knight f1, a typical way to destroy a King's Indian structure. Black gained space but also weaknesses, particularly the f5 and h5 pawns. The e-pawn is well protected, so the main targets are the f5 and h5 pawns.
notes.teaches: When giving up the center, you can target the resulting weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure, especially doubled or isolated pawns.
notes.plans: White aims to attack the weak f5 and h5 pawns, possibly with a knight on g3 double-attacking them.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White has a brutal threat of a knight on g3 double-attacking both f5 and h5 pawns. Black cannot easily defend because moving the knight away allows b4 ideas, and the position crumbles.
notes.teaches: Double attacks on weak pawns can be decisive; if the opponent's pieces are tied to defense, they may be overloaded.
notes.plans: White will execute the knight maneuver to g3 and win material.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In this King's Indian setup, white's bishop on c2 supports the pawn on d3, which controls the f5 square. White comes up with a novel idea of knight a3, planning to reroute to c4 and then to a5 or b5, attacking the weak f5 square.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a knight maneuver to a seemingly odd square can be a concrete plan to exploit a weakness, even if it's not human-like.
notes.plans: White will play knight a3-c4, aiming at f5, and if black plays b5 to stop it, white can play a4 to undermine.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White plays g3 to smother the knight on g6 and also to prepare h4-h5, but mainly to take away the f4 square, which is pivotal. This prevents black from using f4 for counterplay.
notes.teaches: A pawn move like g3 can have multiple purposes: restricting enemy pieces, preparing a pawn storm, and controlling key squares.
notes.plans: White will continue with h4-h5 and a kingside attack.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White plays bishop h3, planning to play g4 and launch a kingside attack. The bishop on h3 supports the pawn push to g4 and also eyes the h5 square.
notes.teaches: A bishop on h3 can support a pawn storm with g4, and also prepare queen to h5 for attacking purposes.
notes.plans: White will play g4, h4, and launch a full-scale kingside assault.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White plays f3 to take away the g4 square from black, preventing counterplay. Later, white maneuvers a knight to f2, getting rid of black's only active piece (the bishop on g4) by trading it off.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like f3 can restrict the opponent's pieces, and trading off active defenders can simplify to a winning position.
notes.plans: White will continue developing and preparing the kingside attack, while black struggles to develop.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: After a series of maneuvers, white has the center, everything ready for a kingside attack, while black is struggling to develop. White plays f4, signaling that he is playing for two results: win or draw, but black must fight hard to draw.
notes.teaches: When you have a clear advantage, you can play for a win with a direct plan, and the opponent must defend precisely.
notes.plans: White will continue with f5 and a kingside pawn storm, aiming to break through.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In this position, White has a dominant center and all pieces ready for a kingside attack, while Black is struggling to develop. Black's moves like ...f7-f5 and ...b7-b6 are somewhat passive, allowing White to build up.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and better development, you should aim to open lines and bring more pieces to the attack, not allow your opponent to consolidate.
notes.plans: White should continue improving piece placement, targeting key squares like g5, and prepare a pawn storm with g4-g5 to open the kingside.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In this variation of the Steinitz Deferred, Black's knight on f6 is misplaced; it would be better on e7. This gives White a comfortable edge with a strong center and easier development.
notes.teaches: In the opening, piece placement matters. A knight on the edge or a passive square can give the opponent a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the center and exploit Black's slightly awkward piece placement by preparing a queenside expansion or a central break.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: After Black plays ...cxd5, White recaptures with the c-pawn to avoid weakening the c4-pawn, which could become a target. Black might otherwise get counterplay with ...f5-f4.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn structure gives you a solid center and avoids creating weaknesses that the opponent can exploit.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and look to exploit Black's weak b5-pawn with a4, while keeping the center stable.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: White sacrifices the bishop for pawns on the queenside, gaining a material advantage and eliminating Black's counterplay. Even though the bishop is powerful, the two pawns are worth more in this position.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is practical to trade a strong piece for pawns if it secures a decisive material advantage and removes the opponent's active pieces.
notes.plans: After winning the pawns, White should consolidate, exchange queens, and use the extra pawns to create a passed pawn on the a-file.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: In the resulting endgame, Black is lost because the white a-pawn cannot be stopped. The plan is to advance a6, then a7, supporting the pawn with the rook.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, a far-advanced passed pawn supported by the king or rook often forces resignation because the defender cannot stop promotion.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn to a7, use the rook to support it, and force promotion or win more material.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Steinitz Deferred
notes.explains: The excerpt references a historical match between world champions, illustrating that even the strongest players face decisive endgame conversions.
notes.teaches: Study games between top players to see how they convert small advantages into wins; the technique is transferable to your own games.

notes.explains: An isolated pawn is an asset in the opening or middlegame because it grants space and dynamic play, but in the endgame it becomes a weakness. The side with the isolated pawn must activate pieces and avoid creating a second weakness.
notes.teaches: Evaluate the isolated pawn differently depending on the phase: in the endgame, it is a liability, so the defender should aim to blockade it and create additional weaknesses.
notes.plans: The side with the isolated pawn should seek active piece play and avoid further weaknesses; the opponent should blockade the pawn and prepare to create a second weakness.

notes.explains: To play against an isolated pawn, you should block it to stop its advance, simplify by exchanging pieces, but choose which pieces to exchange carefully—especially remove the opponent's active pieces. The open file is also important.
notes.teaches: In endgames with an isolated pawn, the defender should blockade the pawn, trade off the opponent's active pieces, and use open files to create pressure.
notes.plans: Create a second weakness (e.g., by advancing pawns like f3-g4) because winning with only one weakness is difficult.

notes.explains: Blockading the isolated pawn gives control of key squares (like c2) to prevent rook infiltration, but then you cannot directly attack the pawn. This is a trade-off.
notes.teaches: When blockading an isolated pawn, you gain control of important squares but may lose the ability to attack the pawn directly; you must find other plans like seizing files or creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: If the pawn is well defended, focus on other targets: open files, second weaknesses, or piece activity.

notes.explains: In a specific position, the knight can jump to f5, which is strong because it is active and prevents black from playing g6 to kick it away. If the knight goes to f4 instead, black can play g6 and then exchange the bishop, giving black the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: In positions with an isolated pawn, piece activity is paramount; you should seize opportunities to place pieces on strong outposts before the opponent can prevent them.
notes.plans: Play the knight to f5 immediately, before black can play g6. If black plays g6, the knight can be exchanged for the bishop, eliminating a defender of the pawn.

notes.explains: Black played king f8 to defend the bishop, but white's idea is to play g6, attacking the bishop and also activating the king if the bishop is taken. This eliminates the 'bad' bishop that defends the isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's piece defends a weakness, try to eliminate that defender, even if it means exchanging a good piece for a 'bad' one. Also, use pawn moves to gain tempo and activate your king.
notes.plans: Play g6 to attack the bishop; if black takes, recapture and activate the king. This removes a key defender of the isolated pawn.

notes.explains: In this rook and minor piece ending with an isolated pawn, the side with the extra pawn must activate all pieces and create multiple weaknesses. The bishop on the same color as the isolated pawn is 'bad' but can be exchanged favorably, and the rook can use open files to pressure.
notes.teaches: In endings with an isolated pawn, the defender's pieces can be passive, so the attacker should seek to trade off the 'good' defender pieces and use activity to convert the extra pawn.
notes.plans: Exchange pieces favorably, use the rook on open files, and gradually improve king position.

notes.explains: After the bishop is eliminated, the knight becomes very strong on a central outpost, pinning the enemy knight and controlling key squares. The opponent's pieces are tied to defense, but one weakness is not enough to win.
notes.teaches: A single weakness (like an isolated pawn) is often insufficient to win; you must create a second weakness on the other side of the board to stretch the defense.
notes.plans: Use the active knight and bishop to maintain pressure, then expand on the kingside with f3, g4, h4, and bring the king to the center.

notes.explains: When the defender tries to unpin or create counterplay, the attacker can calmly reposition pieces, maintaining the bind. The defender may be forced to give up a pawn to relieve the pressure.
notes.teaches: In a superior position, patience is key: keep improving piece placement and avoid rushing; the opponent will eventually crack under the pressure.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece coordination, keep the pin, and be ready to win material when the defender cracks.

notes.explains: In this critical middlegame position, White has a choice between entering an opposite-colored bishop ending by trading knights on e6, or keeping pieces on with a move like Nb3. The opposite-colored bishop ending offers practical winning chances but is not theoretically straightforward, while keeping pieces may preserve a more clear advantage.
notes.teaches: When facing a choice between entering an opposite-colored bishop ending and keeping pieces on, consider that opposite-colored bishop endings are notoriously drawish even with extra pawns, so if you have a clear advantage, it may be better to avoid the trade and keep the position complex.
notes.plans: If White keeps pieces on with Nb3, the threats include Bxe5 and ideas like Rd2 or Ne5, maintaining pressure. If entering the ending, White must be ready to use the extra pawn actively, but should be aware that the win is not trivial.

notes.explains: After entering the opposite-colored bishop ending, White has an isolated pawn but it is not weak because the bishop can defend it and the rook is active. Black tries to activate with ...d4, but this gives up a pawn, leaving White two pawns up in an ending where the extra pawns can create passed pawns.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endings, even a one-pawn advantage may not be enough to win, but multiple extra pawns can create decisive passed pawns, especially if you can create two passed pawns on different flanks.
notes.plans: White should aim to create passed pawns by advancing the kingside pawns, using the bishop to support them, and bringing the king to the center to help.

notes.explains: In the opposite-colored bishop ending, Black's defensive idea is to place the bishop on a good diagonal (like d3 or c4) to attack White's pawns from behind, and to advance queenside pawns (a5-a4) to create counterplay. This can hold the draw even when down pawns.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endings, the defender should seek active bishop placement to attack the opponent's pawns, and use pawn moves to create counterplay, as the bishop can often compensate for material deficit.
notes.plans: Black should aim for ...Ke7 to free the bishop, then ...Bd3 or ...Bc4 to attack the f3 pawn, and consider ...a5-a4 to create a passed pawn or distract White.

notes.explains: In this rook and bishop versus rook and knight ending with an isolated pawn on d5, the bishop is well placed to attack the white pawns on the kingside, especially the f3 pawn, if the white king advances. Black can use the bishop to create counterplay against the pawns while defending the isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: In endings with an isolated pawn, the side with the bishop should look for active placement to attack enemy pawns, even if it means giving up the isolated pawn, as long as the resulting position is drawn or better.
notes.plans: Black should aim to block the pawns and control key squares like f5, while white should try to make progress without allowing the bishop to become active.

notes.explains: When white has an isolated pawn on d5, the side with the knight can try to gain space with g4 and h4, aiming to disrupt the knight and then capture the pawn. However, immediate g5 might allow the knight to go to h7 and attack the g5 pawn, so preparation is needed.
notes.teaches: In rook and knight versus rook and bishop endings, space-gaining pawn moves like g4 and h4 can be used to restrict the bishop and create weaknesses, but they must be timed correctly to avoid counterplay.
notes.plans: White should improve the king's position, then play h4 and g5 when the king can support the pawn, allowing the knight to reroute to f5 and attack the isolated pawn.

notes.explains: Black's idea of playing g5 to disrupt the white knight and then reroute the knight to e7 (defending d5 and controlling f5) is a typical defensive resource. White must avoid allowing the knight to settle on d4, as that would stop the attack on the isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: When defending an isolated pawn, the defender should seek to place pieces on squares that both defend the pawn and control key outposts, such as e7 for the knight to control f5.
notes.plans: Black should aim to consolidate the knight on e7, while white should continue to improve the king and prepare to break through with g5, possibly after rerouting the knight to f5.

notes.explains: The knight on e7 defends the d5 pawn and controls the f5 square, making it hard for White to attack the isolated pawn directly. Black's plan is to activate the rook via d6 and h6, creating counterplay on the h-file.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are well-coordinated to defend a weakness, direct pressure may not suffice; you need to create a second weakness elsewhere.
notes.plans: White should consider pushing f4 to gain space on the kingside and create a second weakness, as the knight on e7 does not control e4.

notes.explains: Black's position is difficult to defend, and exchanging pawns would have been advisable to reduce White's attacking potential. Instead, Black played king g6, missing the chance to simplify.
notes.teaches: When defending a worse position, it is often beneficial to exchange pawns and pieces to reduce the opponent's attacking chances and increase drawing possibilities.
notes.plans: White should exploit Black's mistake by playing f5 with check, followed by knight f3, aiming for e4 to break through.

notes.explains: White missed a strong opportunity: f5 with check, then knight f3, preparing e4. If Black plays king f6, knight f3 with the idea of e4 is strong. This would have given White a large, probably winning advantage.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, look for pawn breaks that create threats and restrict the opponent's king, often leading to a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Play f5+ and then knight f3, with the idea of e4, breaking through in the center.

notes.explains: After missing f5, White played knight f3, and Black was able to take on f6, making the position less clear. White still has an advantage but the win is no longer straightforward.
notes.teaches: Precise calculation is crucial; a missed tactical opportunity can allow the defender to consolidate and reduce the attacker's advantage.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve piece placement, possibly with knight e4 to reach e6, and maintain pressure on the weak d5 pawn.

notes.explains: In rook and knight endgames with an isolated pawn, piece activity and king centralization are paramount. The knight on e6 can challenge the opponent's knight on d4, and the fight for the c-file is critical.
notes.teaches: When fighting for an open file, ensure your pieces are placed to contest it; a well-placed knight can neutralize the opponent's control of the file.
notes.plans: Develop the king towards the center and use the knight to challenge key central squares, while preparing to double rooks on the open file if possible.

notes.explains: In the rook and knight ending, the king's activity is decisive. White's king on g4 is well placed to support the passed pawn and restrict black's king. Black must find precise defensive moves to hold the draw.
notes.teaches: In rook endings, the king's activity often outweighs material considerations. Active king play can create winning chances or hold difficult positions.
notes.plans: Use the king to support pawn advances and cut off the opponent's king. In defense, seek active counterplay with the rook and knight to create perpetual check or counter-threats.

notes.explains: Black's move d4 is a mistake because it weakens the pawn structure and allows white to win the pawn. Better defensive moves like rook c4 or knight d5 could have held the draw, but precision is required.
notes.teaches: In endgames, avoid pawn moves that create permanent weaknesses unless they generate concrete counterplay. Always look for active defensive setups that maintain material equality.
notes.plans: If defending, aim to keep the rook active behind the passed pawn and use the knight to block or harass the opponent's pieces. Seek to trade down to a drawn pawn ending if possible.

notes.explains: In rook endings, the activity of the pieces often outweighs material considerations. Here, exchanging rooks can give up the c-file, allowing the opponent's rook to become active, which can be more important than holding onto an isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: When considering rook exchanges, evaluate the resulting piece activity. Giving up a file can be worse than losing a pawn.

notes.explains: A rook on c8 can be a powerful resource, creating tactical threats such as trapping a knight or winning pawns. In this position, rook c8 is strong because it attacks the knight and the a7 pawn, leading to a collapse of Black's position.
notes.teaches: In rook endings, look for active rook moves that create multiple threats, especially against poorly placed enemy pieces.

notes.explains: When facing an isolated pawn, the side with the pawn can try to advance it to eliminate the weakness, but this may allow the opponent's pieces to become more active. Here, Black played d4 to get rid of the isolated pawn, but White's pieces remained better placed.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's worth giving up an isolated pawn to activate your pieces, but only if the resulting position is favorable.

notes.explains: In king and pawn endings, the placement of the kings is often decisive. Here, White's king is more active and can penetrate into Black's position, while Black's king is passive. This activity is more important than the material balance.
notes.teaches: In king endings, prioritize king activity. A centralized king can create winning threats, even if material is equal.

notes.explains: In this ending, White's knight is well placed and can attack Black's queenside pawns, while the white king is active. Black's pieces are passive, and White can gradually improve the position by pushing pawns and restricting Black's moves.
notes.teaches: In knight endings, a well-placed knight can dominate a passive opponent. Use your king to support pawn advances and create zugzwang.
notes.plans: Push the h-pawn to create weaknesses, then use the king to invade and win material.

notes.explains: In this ending, the black king is misplaced and lacks a clear destination, while the white pieces coordinate to target the f7 pawn. Black's counterplay with the h-pawn is too slow because White's passed pawn on the kingside is faster.
notes.teaches: In endgames with an isolated pawn, the activity and placement of the kings is often decisive. A passive king can be a permanent weakness, while an active king supports pawn advances and piece coordination.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve the king and pieces, push the passed pawn, and force Black to defend passively. Black should seek active counterplay, but here it is insufficient.

notes.explains: The key ideas for the stronger side against an isolated pawn in the ending are: block the pawn to prevent its advance, exchange active pieces to reduce counterplay, create a second weakness, and gain space on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When playing with an isolated pawn in the endgame, the stronger side should follow a systematic plan: block the pawn, trade off active defenders, create multiple weaknesses, and expand on the side where you have space advantage.
notes.plans: Implement these principles: first block the isolated pawn, then exchange pieces that are actively placed, then create a second weakness (e.g., on the kingside), and finally use your space advantage to penetrate.

notes.explains: Throughout all examples, the activity of the pieces was the decisive factor. Even small differences in piece activity can turn a drawn ending into a win.
notes.teaches: In endgames, piece activity is paramount. Always seek the most active squares for your pieces, and restrict your opponent's pieces to passive roles.
notes.plans: When evaluating an endgame, compare the activity of both sides' pieces. Aim to improve your worst piece and limit your opponent's best piece.

notes.explains: In the Smith-Morra Gambit, after White's bishop goes to f4 and Black plays ...Ng7, the position offers a choice of castling. Castling long is unconventional and risky because the c-file is open and the king on c1 can face pressure, but it sets up an attacking plan.
notes.teaches: When considering castling, weigh the safety of the king against the attacking potential. Sometimes an 'unusual' castling choice can be viable if it supports a direct attack, even if it looks risky.
notes.plans: If castling long, White aims to launch a pawn storm with h4-h5 and f4-f5, targeting the black king's position and the weak d6 pawn.

notes.explains: After long castling, White's plan is to push h4-h5 to drive away the knight on g7 and then bring the knight to g5, attacking the e6 and f7 squares. The pawn sacrifice is not a concern; the goal is to generate attacking chances.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, material is secondary to initiative. A knight on g5 can be a powerful attacking piece, and pawn pushes like h4-h5 and f4-f5 can break through the opponent's defenses.
notes.plans: White should continue with h4-h5, then knight g5, and aim for f4-f5 to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: In the stem game, Black tried to simplify by trading pieces, but that doesn't help because the black king remains in the center and White's f4-f5 push is still possible. Even castling into the attack would be dangerous.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is attacking, trading pieces may not relieve the pressure if the king is still vulnerable. The attacking side should keep the initiative and not be distracted by material.
notes.plans: White continues with f4-f5, and if Black trades on g5, White recaptures with the h-pawn, maintaining the attack.

notes.explains: White plays queen e3 instead of queen f3, a typical Velimirovic-style move. The queen on e3 supports a knight jump to b6 and then d5, creating a 'backflip' maneuver to attack. It also avoids simple harassment of the queen.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, queen placement is key. A queen on e3 can support central knight maneuvers and avoid being chased, while maintaining pressure on the opponent's position.
notes.plans: White aims to play knight b6, then knight d5, using the knight to create threats and possibly win material or continue the attack.

notes.explains: In this Smith-Morra Gambit subvariation, White willingly sacrifices material to gain attacking chances. The king is safely tucked on b1 after long castling, while Black's king remains on e8, making it a target.
notes.teaches: When playing gambit lines, prioritize king safety and rapid development over material. A safe king and active pieces can outweigh a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: White should aim to castle long quickly, then launch an attack against Black's uncastled king, often targeting the f7 pawn.

notes.explains: The move Qe3 prepares to plant a knight on b6 or maneuver it to d5, creating threats. It also sidesteps potential attacks on the queen. The f7 pawn is a key weakness, and Qf3 doubles the attack on it, forcing Black to defend.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for ways to create multiple threats and target the weakest point in the opponent's camp. Prophylactic moves that also prepare threats are valuable.
notes.plans: White should continue to increase pressure on f7 and the d6 square, using pieces to support the attack while keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: When Black plays Bb4, castling long becomes too risky because the bishop pins or attacks the king's path. Instead, White should continue developing with Bf4, pressuring d6.
notes.teaches: Always reassess castling safety based on the opponent's resources. If a piece can harass your king after castling, consider alternative plans.
notes.plans: White should maintain the pressure on d6 and continue development, possibly sacrificing more pawns to keep the initiative.

notes.explains: Even after losing a second pawn, White's position is playable because Black's pieces are still undeveloped (bishop on c8, rook on a8, king on e8). The pressure on d6 is strong, and White's activity compensates for the material deficit.
notes.teaches: Material is not the only factor; activity and the opponent's lack of development can justify further sacrifices. Keep the initiative and trust the dynamic compensation.
notes.plans: White should continue to build pressure on d6 and the king side, looking for ways to open lines and bring more pieces into the attack.

notes.explains: Rook b1 is preferred over rook c1 because it keeps the bishop on c3 as a target without forcing it to move to a better square. The bishop is not well placed on c3, and White would rather have it on b4 to support a future d6 break, even at the cost of a pawn.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better not to chase a piece immediately if it is already poorly placed. Instead, you can keep it as a target and gain time later, while preparing a more important plan.
notes.plans: Play rook b1 to maintain the pressure on the bishop and prepare to attack the king. If the bishop moves, it may go to a worse square or lose time.

notes.explains: The computer evaluation shows Black is only slightly better despite being two pawns up, indicating that White's compensation is real. The black bishop on c8 is so bad that even three pawns may not be enough to compensate for White's active pieces.
notes.teaches: Evaluations based on material alone can be misleading. A severely bad piece can outweigh a material advantage, so it's important to assess the position dynamically.
notes.plans: Continue to exploit the bad bishop and the exposed black king. Keep the initiative and avoid allowing Black to activate their pieces.

notes.explains: After rook b1 and castling, White has a firm grip on d6. The black bishop is still stuck on c8, giving White extra time to attack. The next move should be a decisive break, and queen d3 is the correct choice because it prepares to transfer the queen to h3, attacking h7.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, it's important to choose moves that have a clear purpose and set up future threats. Queen d3 is better than queen c2 because it allows the queen to go to h3, increasing the pressure on the king.
notes.plans: Play queen d3, then knight g5 to attack h7. If the bishop moves, continue with queen h3, forcing h5 and leaving Black with only one move to avoid checkmate.

notes.explains: The position resembles a pyramid, and White is dominating. The opponent's structure has holes (Swiss cheese), but that alone isn't enough. The move knight e4 is strong because it dominates key squares and continues the attack, whereas g4 would move a pawn in front of the king and could be risky.
notes.teaches: When attacking, it's often better to use pieces to control important squares rather than pushing pawns in front of your own king. Pawn moves can create weaknesses and give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play knight e4 to increase control and prepare further invasion. Avoid unnecessary pawn moves like g4 that could expose the king.

notes.explains: In a dominating position where the opponent's structure is compromised, the priority is to control key central squares rather than launching speculative pawn storms. Moving pawns in front of the king can be risky, even if it might work.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional grip, prefer moves that increase pressure and control important squares over risky pawn pushes. Solid centralization often leads to a win without unnecessary risk.
notes.plans: Place a knight on a strong central outpost to maintain pressure, then look for ways to tighten the bind, such as pinning pieces or targeting weaknesses.

notes.explains: A bishop that is far from the action (e.g., on a5) is effectively out of play, leaving the opponent's king vulnerable. The attacking side can use this to build a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: Identify enemy pieces that are offside and exploit their absence by focusing your forces on the king. A piece that is not defending is as good as missing.
notes.plans: Continue to improve your pieces, aiming to create threats that force the opponent to defend with their misplaced pieces, further weakening their position.

notes.explains: When the opponent's king is exposed and your pieces are well-placed, a sacrifice can be the most efficient way to break through, even if material is offered. The pressure from the bishops and queen can be overwhelming.
notes.teaches: In a dominating attack, be alert to tactical shots that give up material to expose the king. If the attack is unstoppable, the sacrifice is sound.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, continue with checks and threats to force mate or win back material with interest.

notes.explains: In the Smith-Morra Gambit, after the opponent develops normally, it's important to play aggressively to maintain initiative. Moves like h4 are typical to start a pawn storm against the castled king.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, you must be willing to push pawns to open lines and create attacking chances. The initiative is worth more than material.
notes.plans: Follow up with pieces to support the pawn storm, such as bringing the knight to g5 and the queen to h5, aiming for a direct attack on the king.

notes.explains: When the opponent makes a mistake that weakens their kingside, it's crucial to capitalize immediately. A move like Qh5 can create an unstoppable attack.
notes.teaches: Always be on the lookout for tactical opportunities when the opponent's king becomes exposed. A single mistake can be enough to decide the game.
notes.plans: Bring the heavy pieces to bear on the weakened squares, and look for sacrifices to remove defenders or open lines.

notes.explains: In this attacking position, the king on g8 is exposed and the f-pawn is weak. The bishop on e7 blocks the e7 square, making the king more vulnerable to mating threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for ways to exploit the weakness of the pawns in front of it, especially the f-pawn. A piece that blocks a key escape square can be a decisive factor.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing the queen to h5, creating threats on h7 and f7, and preparing to break through with sacrifices if necessary.

notes.explains: In this tabiya, white has long castled and black is still uncastled. White's pieces are actively placed, and black's king is still in the center, which is a target.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is still in the center, you should open lines and create threats against it, often by sacrificing material for initiative.
notes.plans: Consider moves like rook c1 to pressure the queen, or a knight sacrifice on d5 to open the center and expose the black king.

notes.explains: White has a strong attacking setup with the knight on g5, aiming at the f7 and h7 squares. Black's pawns on e6 and f7 form a chain that can be undermined.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, you can sacrifice material to break the opponent's pawn chain and open lines for your pieces. It's important to keep the initiative and not worry about material deficits if the attack is decisive.
notes.plans: Play f4 to undermine the e6-f7 pawn chain, and if black takes the knight, recapture with the h-pawn and bring the queen to h5 to launch a mating attack.

notes.explains: After a series of forcing moves, white has a winning attack. The black king is trapped on g8, and the bishop on e7 blocks the e7 escape square, allowing a mating net.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent's king is in a mating net. A piece that blocks an escape square can be the key to delivering checkmate.
notes.plans: Deliver checkmate with queen h7+, queen h8+, and rook h8#.

notes.explains: The black king on g8 appears safe, but the bishop on e7 is a liability because it occupies the e7 square, blocking the king's escape route. This makes the king vulnerable to a mating attack.
notes.teaches: A piece that seems to defend can actually be a 'dummy' that traps its own king by occupying a vital escape square. Always check whether the defender is truly helping or hindering.
notes.plans: If the position allows, consider a queen check on h7, forcing the king to f8, followed by queen h8 check, and if the rook takes, recapture with the rook for checkmate.

notes.explains: The position arises from the Smith-Morra Gambit, specifically the long castle variation, sometimes called the 'Pokimane' subvariation. This line involves castling long and launching a direct attack on the black king.
notes.teaches: In gambit openings like the Smith-Morra, rapid development and castling long can set up a powerful kingside attack, often at the cost of material. The initiative and attacking chances can outweigh the pawn deficit.
notes.plans: If playing this variation, aim to quickly develop pieces, castle long, and prepare a pawn storm or piece attack against the black king, using the open files and diagonals created by the gambit.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: In this position, White's pieces are aimed at the kingside: the bishops are on strong diagonals, the queen and knight are ready to join, while Black's pieces are far from their king. This imbalance justifies a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are concentrated on one side and the opponent's are absent, that is the side to attack. Look for a preponderance of force.
notes.plans: Play an immediate attacking move like Nh5, creating threats against the kingside pawn structure.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: After Nh5, Black may capture the knight. Recapturing with the queen is too slow because Black can play f5, blocking the bishop and bringing the queen to defense with tempo, which can defuse the attack.
notes.teaches: When attacking, avoid slow recaptures that allow the opponent to consolidate. Look for more forcing continuations that maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: Consider a double bishop sacrifice to demolish the kingside pawns, followed by Qxh5+ forcing the king to g8.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: If White only sacrifices one bishop and tries to lift the rook, Black can defend with ...f6, which prevents any mate on the h-file and gives the king an escape square. This defense is common against queen and rook attacks on the h-file.
notes.teaches: When defending against a kingside attack, ...f6 can be a key resource to blunt the attack and create luft. Attackers often need a piece that can deal with this ...f6 defense, such as a knight on g5 or a bishop on g6.
notes.plans: In this position, the double bishop sacrifice is the precise way to break through, as it removes the f6 defender and opens lines.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: When attacking with queen and rook on the h-file, the defender's f6 move is a key defensive resource that prevents typical h-file checkmates like Qh7 or Qh8.
notes.teaches: Always check the opponent's defensive resources before committing to an attack; f6 is a common defense that blocks h-file mates.
notes.plans: If f6 is played, consider using a knight on g5, a light-squared bishop on g6, or a pawn on g6 to challenge the f7 square and maintain attacking chances.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: After a double bishop sacrifice, the king is exposed but you are down material, so the attack must be fast and precise. Simply bringing the rook in with Rf3 can be too slow if the opponent has defensive resources.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing material for an attack, you must check the opponent's defensive ideas and find the most forcing moves to keep the initiative.
notes.plans: Look for in-between moves that prevent the king's escape routes before committing to the rook lift.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: After Qg4, the king is forced to the h-file, and then Rf3 threatens mate. Black's only defense is e5, but after the rook check and Qh6, Black must give up the queen. The resulting material balance is queen and two pawns for rook and two bishops, which is not terrible for Black, so White must continue accurately.
notes.teaches: When calculating a combination, read until the position stabilizes and you can evaluate the material balance and king safety. Do not stop just because you win the queen.
notes.plans: Continue the attack: after Qf5+ and Kg7, play Qd7 to fork the bishops and win one back, leaving White with a winning material advantage.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: Once the position stabilizes with White having queen and two pawns for rook and bishop, plus Black's king unsafe and pawns hanging, White has a comfortably winning advantage.
notes.teaches: There is a cutoff point in calculation where you can stop and evaluate; if the material and positional factors are clearly in your favor, you don't need to calculate further.
notes.plans: Convert the winning position by exploiting the extra material and Black's unsafe king.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: This is a double bishop sacrifice, an extreme version of the Greek gift, which is an advanced but memorable attacking pattern. The first step is recognizing that such an idea exists.
notes.teaches: Knowing typical attacking patterns like the double bishop sacrifice is essential before attempting them; they don't always work, but awareness is the first step.
notes.plans: Look for opportunities to execute similar sacrifices when the opponent's king is vulnerable.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: In this 1914 game, White played Bd3, a reasonable developing move, but it allows Black to force a tempo loss: after ...cxd4, exd4, and ...a6, White's bishop has moved twice (f1-d3-c4) while in the modern QGA line, the bishop goes straight to c4 and White gets a free move to castle.
notes.teaches: Be mindful of move orders and tempo in the opening; developing a bishop to d3 can lose a tempo if it later goes to c4, whereas playing Nc3 or taking on d5 first avoids this.
notes.plans: In similar positions, prefer moves like Nc3 or cxd5 to avoid losing tempo, or consider taking on d5 and playing Bb5+.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: Both sides in this old game developed pieces and controlled the center logically but not in the most precise order, leading to tempo losses. The modern approach in the QGA is more efficient.
notes.teaches: General principle: avoid passive moves like e3 before Black has taken on d4, as it can cost a tempo; strive for accurate move orders to gain or avoid losing tempi.
notes.plans: Study modern opening lines to see more efficient move orders and apply those ideas.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: In this Queen's Gambit Accepted-style position, both sides have developed naturally without precise move orders. White's bishop has moved twice, giving Black a free tempo. The position is not bad for White, but Black has gained a small edge in development.
notes.teaches: Avoid moving the same piece twice in the opening if possible; if you can force your opponent to do so, you gain a tempo. Be aware of concrete move orders to avoid such issues.
notes.plans: Black should either play a6 to prepare b5 and Bb7, or simply take on c4 and develop, maintaining the extra tempo. White should consider alternatives like taking on d5 or Bb5 to avoid the tempo loss.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: In these positions, a6 is often useful to control b5, preparing b5 and Bb7 with tempo. However, here a6 is less useful because if Black takes on c4, White recaptures with the pawn, so b5 doesn't gain tempo. Instead, Black plays b6 and fianchettoes the bishop.
notes.teaches: The purpose of a6 is to prepare b5 and Bb7, but its value depends on the specific pawn structure. If the c-pawn is recaptured by a pawn, b5 may not be effective, so consider other development like b6.
notes.plans: Black develops with b6 and Bb7, aiming for a symmetrical structure. White may try to claim space with e4, but must be careful about Black's counterplay.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: White wants to play e4 to gain space and improve the bishop, but Black can prevent it with a double-purpose move: Nb4, which uncovers the bishop's attack on e4 and also targets the bishop on c2. This creates a three-to-two advantage on e4 and a simultaneous threat, making e4 impossible for White.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that serve multiple purposes, such as attacking a pawn while creating another threat. This can prevent your opponent's plans and create concrete problems.
notes.plans: Black should consider Nb4 to stop e4 and target the bishop. White may need to play Rc1 to prepare Bb1, dealing with the threat and setting up a battery on h7, while also preparing for open files.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: In this symmetrical setup, the rooks belong on the open c-file, and the knight on d2 is more active than on c3 because it keeps the bishop on d3 unobstructed, allowing ideas like Ne5 and later Nf3 to reinforce that square.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a knight, consider whether it blocks a bishop's diagonal; a knight on d2 can be more flexible than on c3 if it keeps the bishop active.
notes.plans: Develop the rook to c1, then aim for Ne5, using the e5 outpost, and potentially Nf3 to support it.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: After Black plays Nb4, White can retreat the bishop to b1, which is not passive because the bishop's long range means it still exerts influence across the board, and the a3 idea can later kick the knight back.
notes.teaches: A bishop on a long diagonal can be effective even from its original square; retreating a piece to avoid a threat is often fine if it retains activity.
notes.plans: Use the bishop on b1 to pressure both sides if the position opens, and prepare a3 to drive the knight away.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: Nimzovich's idea of Nh4 aims to trade on f5 for the bishop, leaving White with dark-square control, but it induces a weakening of the diagonal and leaves the knight on the rim, which is often poor.
notes.teaches: A knight on the rim is generally badly placed; inducing a weakness with a knight move is only good if the knight can find a strong square, otherwise it may just be misplaced.
notes.plans: After Nh4, Black should consider how to exploit the knight's poor placement, while White can play Nf3 to neutralize it.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: The trade on d5 gives Black a bad bishop on b7 for the moment, but the capture is not always bad; it depends on the position. Here, Black's pawns on the fourth rank and the control of e5 give Black some compensation.
notes.teaches: Trading a bishop for a knight is not inherently good or bad; evaluate the resulting pawn structure and piece activity before deciding.
notes.plans: Black should use the control of e5 and the open files to pressure White, while White must find a way to activate the pieces.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: The pair of pawns on the fourth rank, called hanging pawns, give the side owning them a space advantage and room for active play, but they can also be weak. Here, Black's hanging pawns have created a serious space advantage and a development lead, while White's pieces are poorly placed, especially the knight on f3 blocked by its own pawn.
notes.teaches: Hanging pawns are a double-edged sword: they provide space and activity but can become targets. Recognize when the opponent's hanging pawns give them a space edge, and avoid leaving your own pieces passive.
notes.plans: White should seek to challenge Black's space advantage, possibly by trading pieces or targeting the hanging pawns with moves like b4, but must be careful not to fall behind in development.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: Black's active center pawns and unopposed light-squared bishop on the long diagonal give Black a strong initiative. White's queen is passive, and White lacks the space to exploit the diagonal for a mating attack, whereas Black can use the diagonal to target White's king.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and a well-placed bishop on a long diagonal, look for pawn breaks like d4 to open lines and create threats against the enemy king. The side with more space often has the initiative.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play d4 to open the diagonal and create threats like Bxf3, ripping apart White's kingside defenses. White must be ready to make concessions to prevent this.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: Black has a beautiful bishop pair aimed at White's king, which has too little defense. The threat of d4 and then Bxf3 is very dangerous, and Black can also consider sacrificial ideas on the kingside, such as Bxh2, to expose the king.
notes.teaches: When you have a bishop pair on open diagonals and the enemy king is exposed, look for tactical blows like bishop sacrifices to rip open the king's defenses. Prepare such sacrifices with moves that increase the pressure, like d4.
notes.plans: Black should continue to build pressure with d4, and if White captures, be ready to unleash a sacrificial attack on the kingside.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: The bishop pair on open diagonals targets the enemy king, which has insufficient defensive pieces around it. The immediate threat is a sacrifice on h2 to expose the king.
notes.teaches: A powerful bishop pair combined with a vulnerable king creates a tactical opportunity to launch a kingside attack, often starting with a sacrifice.
notes.plans: Prepare the sacrifice with moves like d4 to open lines, then consider bishop takes h2 to initiate the attack.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: White's defensive tries include e4 to reinforce the kingside, but if White takes on d4, Black's attack gains momentum. The combination begins with bishop takes h2, then queen h4, and bishop takes g2, forcing the king to the h-file.
notes.teaches: The double bishop sacrifice is a classic attacking motif that rips open the king's shield, often leading to a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After the sacrifices, use queen g4 to drive the king to the h-file, then lift the rook to d5 to threaten mate.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: White has a defensive resource: queen takes c5, which covers the mate threat. However, Black can still win material by exploiting the loose knight and the exposed king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is open and pieces are hanging, tactics often work out for the side with the better position and fewer weaknesses.
notes.plans: Use checks to win the queen and then capture the loose knight, converting to a winning material advantage.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: White's knight on d2 was misplaced; it should have gone to f3 and e5 to defend the kingside. White also has a defensive idea with f3 to block the bishop's diagonal, a common resource in such positions.
notes.teaches: Piece placement matters: a knight on f3 can defend key squares and prevent sacrifices. Also, f3 can be a defensive move to blunt a bishop's attack on h2.
notes.plans: If White plays f3, Black should look for other ways to continue the attack, possibly with e3 or other breaks.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: White's knight on d2 has been ineffective; it would have been better placed on f3 or e5 to support the attack. Black's attack is overwhelming, and White's defensive resources are limited.
notes.teaches: Piece placement matters: a knight on d2 can be passive, while on f3 or e5 it controls key squares and supports the attack.
notes.plans: White should seek counterplay, but Black's attack is decisive.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: Black threatens mate on h1 after taking on g2. White has a defensive idea with f3, giving the king an escape square on f2, but Black can still maintain the attack.
notes.teaches: When facing a mating threat, look for ways to give the king an escape square, but be aware that the attack may continue.
notes.plans: Black should reinforce the attack, e.g., by bringing the rook to e8, rather than rushing to take material.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: Black's rook on e8 cuts off the king's escape and supports the mate threat. White's knight on d2 is overloaded: it must guard the queen, so it cannot recapture on g2.
notes.teaches: An overloaded piece cannot fulfill multiple defensive duties; use this to your advantage in the attack.
notes.plans: Black continues the attack, aiming for mate or material gain.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: White tries d5 and queen c3 to create counterplay, but Black's attack is too strong. Black plays f5 to maintain the initiative, and White's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When facing a strong attack, creating counterplay is better than passive defense, but you must be accurate.
notes.plans: Black should continue quickly, not allowing White to consolidate.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: Black finds a forcing checkmate sequence: queen g3 check, forcing the king to d2, then queen f2 check, etc. The key is to use the most forcing moves to restrict the opponent's options.
notes.teaches: When looking for checkmate, start with the most forcing checks and consider how they restrict the opponent's king moves.
notes.plans: Execute the mating sequence.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: When the opponent's king is exposed and your material is overwhelming, the fastest win is often a forcing sequence of checks that drives the king into a mating net, rather than a slower material-gathering approach.
notes.teaches: Look for the most forcing moves first—checks that restrict the opponent's options and lead to a forced mate, even if other moves also win.
notes.plans: Identify a sequence of checks that shepherd the enemy king to a square where it can be mated, covering all escape squares with your pieces.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: A 'perfect mate' occurs when every square the king could flee to is covered exactly once by the attacking side, making the mate aesthetically pleasing and fully controlled.
notes.teaches: Recognize the aesthetic and practical value of a mate where each escape square is defended precisely once—this demonstrates full control of the position.

notes.opening: Philidor Defense: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
notes.explains: When the opponent has a lot of material but a wandering king, the king's safety is compromised, and the attacker can often chase it into a mating net.
notes.teaches: Do not be afraid to pursue a king that has advanced into your territory; a king with no pawn shield is vulnerable to a coordinated attack.
notes.plans: Use checks to drive the king to a square where your pieces can deliver mate, even if it takes several moves.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a powerful bishop on d6, supported by pawns on e5 and f4, which is immune to capture because taking it would cost a rook for a bishop and pawn. White also has more space, and the black bishop is blocked by its own pawns on c6 and f5, which sit on light squares, restricting its mobility. The material is even, but White has a clear positional advantage.
notes.teaches: A well-supported bishop deep in enemy territory can be a decisive asset, especially when the opponent's pieces are cramped and their bishop is hindered by its own pawns. Recognize when a piece is 'immune' due to the material cost of capture.
notes.plans: Black should seek counterplay by advancing pawns, particularly the h-pawn, to attack White's kingside and create weaknesses.

notes.explains: The bishops are of opposite colors: White's bishop operates on dark squares, Black's on light squares. This often leads to draws because each side attacks only one color complex, and the other side can defend the opposite color. Here, White's bishop is active in front of its pawns, while Black's is behind its pawns, making White's bishop more effective.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop positions, the side with the more active bishop and better pawn structure often has a lasting initiative, but the defense can hold if it finds counterplay. Pawns should generally be placed on the opposite color of your own bishop to avoid blocking it.
notes.plans: Black must use its pawns to open lines and create counterplay, especially against White's king.

notes.explains: Black doubles rooks on the d-file, and the rook on d7 is a strong defensive piece. White also doubles rooks on the d-file to reinforce the advanced bishop. Black then advances the pawn to c5, opening the diagonal toward the white king, with the idea of playing queen to c6 check and then queen to g2, which would be checkmate, protected by the advanced pawn. This forces white to keep a piece watching the g2 square, tying down white's pieces.
notes.teaches: An advanced pawn can provide a safe square for the queen to deliver checkmate. Creating threats against the king can tie down the opponent's pieces, preventing them from pursuing their own plans.
notes.plans: Black should continue to threaten the king, while white must keep a rook or piece on the second rank to prevent the mate, limiting white's activity.

notes.explains: White moves the king to avoid the check on the diagonal, and black doubles rooks. White moves the queen to a3, threatening to take the pawn on a7. However, white cannot take immediately because of a tactic: if white takes, black can respond with queen takes queen, then bishop takes queen, opening the d-file for the rooks to win a rook on d2. Black anticipates this by moving the pawn from a7 to a6, so that the pawn is protected by the pawn on b7, allowing the queen to move away in the future without losing the pawn.
notes.teaches: Before capturing a pawn, consider the tactical consequences, such as pins or discovered attacks. Moving a pawn to a protected square can allow a piece to leave its defensive duty without material loss.
notes.plans: Black should aim to move the queen to c6 to continue the attack, while white must be careful not to fall into tactical traps.

notes.explains: After a series of exchanges, the position has equal pawns (six each), but White has a passed pawn. Black must neutralize this passed pawn. Black can place the queen with check, then bring the king up to block the pawn's advance. The king and queen can work together to win the pawn, and White may not have time to bring the king to defend.
notes.teaches: In queen and pawn endgames, a passed pawn can be a decisive advantage if it is supported by the king. The defending side must use the queen to give checks and bring the king to blockade the pawn.
notes.plans: Black should aim to blockade the passed pawn with the king and queen, then win it, possibly leading to a winning king and pawn ending.

notes.explains: White has a resource: he can give up on the d5 pawn but take the f6 pawn with check. Black considers queen takes pawn but it doesn't work, so he takes with the king. Now the position has five pawns each side, and White may be able to get a perpetual check because the black king is exposed in the middle of the board.
notes.teaches: When facing a lost pawn, look for counterplay that can lead to a perpetual check or a drawn ending. A centralized king can be vulnerable to perpetual check.
notes.plans: White should aim for a perpetual check or trade queens to reach a drawn king and pawn ending.

notes.explains: Black tries to bring the king in to attack White's pawns and king. White gives checks to keep the black king from making progress. At one point, White's king blocks certain squares, and the threat of a checkmate prevents Black from taking a pawn. White must keep checking to maintain the balance.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, giving perpetual checks can be a drawing resource when the opponent's king is exposed. The defending side must keep the checks coming to avoid losing.
notes.plans: White should continue to give checks and try to force a draw, either by perpetual check or by trading queens into a drawn pawn ending.

notes.explains: In this queen endgame, the white king is exposed and black's queen can deliver perpetual check or create mate threats. White must keep checking to avoid losing, while black tries to win pawns and secure a draw or win.
notes.teaches: When your king is exposed, perpetual check is a valuable resource to save a draw. Use your queen to keep checking and prevent the opponent from consolidating.
notes.plans: White should look for perpetual check or a way to eliminate black's dangerous pawns. Black should try to win pawns while maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: Black's queen on c6 defends both pawns, and white's attempt to protect a pawn with Queen f7 fails because it leaves the h2 pawn undefended, allowing black's queen to infiltrate and win material.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, every move must consider the opponent's counterplay. Protecting one weakness can create another; always check if your queen is overworked.
notes.plans: White should seek a better defensive setup, possibly with the queen on b4, which the computer suggests gives winning chances.

notes.explains: White's move to d3 was a blunder because it allowed black to win a pawn and create a mate threat (Queen g2 checkmate). The computer evaluation shows that Queen b4 would have been much better, giving White an advantage.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, a single inaccurate move can turn a draw into a loss. Use engine evaluations to identify critical moments and find the most active square for your queen.
notes.plans: White should have played Queen b4, which would have given active play and possibly winning chances.

notes.explains: White advances the e-pawn to attack black's king, but black uses the h-pawn to break up white's pawn shield and create counterplay. Black's knight on d6 is a sacrifice because after e5 wins the knight, black's queen can infiltrate on the light squares and threaten mate on g2.
notes.teaches: When attacking, be aware of counterplay against your own king. A pawn break can open lines for the opponent's queen, turning a winning attack into a defensive struggle.
notes.plans: Black should aim to get the queen to g2 to force mate or perpetual check. White must find the only move, Rook f2, to stop the mate threat.

notes.explains: In this position, the queen must move to a white square, allowing it to target g2 and threaten checkmate. The only way to stop the mate is to place a rook on the f-file, because the queen cannot drop back to defend due to the black queen's control, and no other piece can guard the g2 square.
notes.teaches: When facing a mating threat, look for the only defensive move that parries the threat, even if it seems passive. Also, recognize that a queen can create mating threats by moving to squares that align with the enemy king.
