notes.plans: After the rook goes to f-file, the defender must keep checking or maintain the threat of mate to force a repetition or perpetual check, as the king cannot move.

notes.explains: Advanced pawns can be a double-edged sword: they can provide attacking chances or counterattacking chances. In this case, the advanced pawns create threats that lead to a perpetual check or a draw.
notes.teaches: Always consider the dynamic potential of advanced pawns. They can be used to generate counterplay even when the position seems lost.

notes.explains: The target is the queen knight six square (b6 in algebraic notation), which is currently not under attack. The plan is to prepare an attack on that square by doubling rooks, opening the knight file, and eventually winning a weak pawn on that file.
notes.teaches: When targeting a weak square, you need to prepare the attack by improving piece placement and creating pawn breaks. A pawn that is not defended by other pawns becomes a long-term target for rooks and queen.
notes.plans: Black will double rooks on the knight file, open the file with pawn exchanges, and then bring the queen and rooks to bear on the b6 square to win the pawn.

notes.explains: In the sequence, white makes a mistake by moving the bishop to h2 instead of keeping it on a better square. The bishop should be placed behind the pawn to give it more options and to avoid blocking the pawn's advance.
notes.teaches: Piece placement matters: a bishop should be placed on squares where it has flexibility and does not impede your own pawns. When planning a pawn storm, ensure your pieces support the advance rather than block it.
notes.plans: White should have moved the bishop back to g3 to keep the queen on f3, protecting both the pawn and the bishop, and giving the bishop future squares.

notes.explains: Black's attack on the queenside is not a kingside attack; it is a plan to win a pawn on the b-file. The pawn on b3 is weak because it is not defended by any other pawn, so black uses rooks and queen to target it.
notes.teaches: In the middlegame, you can attack a weak pawn with major pieces. A pawn that is isolated or not defended by other pawns is a permanent weakness that can be exploited.
notes.plans: Black will continue to pressure the b3 pawn with rooks and queen, forcing white to defend it, and eventually win it or gain other concessions.

notes.explains: The rook is tied to defending the f5 pawn, so it must first prepare its move with g6. If the rook moved immediately, the queen could capture the pawn and then threaten the knight.
notes.teaches: Before moving a piece that is defending a pawn, ensure the pawn is protected by another piece or a pawn move.
notes.plans: After g6, the rook can move to d2 to chase the queen, and the queen will reposition to support the rook's invasion.

notes.explains: The queen retreats all the way to the back rank so that when the rook comes over, the queen is behind it, supporting the rook's entry into the opponent's position.
notes.teaches: Place your queen behind a rook to create a battery that can penetrate the enemy position.
notes.plans: The rook will jump to a7, using the queen's support to create threats.

notes.explains: After the rook reaches b2, it attacks a pawn that is defended by the opponent's rook. The key is to find a piece that can join the attack on that pawn.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is defended by a rook, a knight can often be the right piece to add pressure, especially if the pawn is on a square of the opposite color to the opponent's bishops.
notes.plans: The knight will maneuver around to attack the pawn, and with the rook, they will overwhelm the defense.

notes.explains: Black makes a purposeless bishop move because it doesn't have the support of a pawn to capture the bishop if it moves. The knight ends up on a bad square on the side of the board.
notes.teaches: Before making a move that seems to attack, ensure it has a concrete purpose and that your pieces are not left on poor squares.
notes.plans: White will continue the queenside pawn storm, breaking down Black's defenses.

notes.explains: White's queenside pawn attack culminates in a breakthrough, where pawns advance to undermine the defense and open lines for the rooks.
notes.teaches: A pawn majority on the flank can be used to create passed pawns and open files for rooks.
notes.plans: White will push pawns to create threats like pawn takes pawn, followed by rook infiltration.

notes.explains: In this position, the queenside pawn structure is being liquidated to create weaknesses in Black's camp. Black's bishop on c7 was annoying, so he retreated it, allowing White to proceed with the attack.
notes.teaches: When a defender's piece is misplaced, use the tempo gained to improve your own pieces and increase pressure on the opponent's weak points.
notes.plans: Continue the queenside attack by targeting the isolated pawn and preparing to bring the queen and rooks into the attack.

notes.explains: Black played b6 to avoid allowing pawn takes pawn, but this was a mistake. White can take on c6, liquidating the pawn, and then take on b6. If Black recaptures with the pawn, the knight can jump to b5, pinning the bishop and creating a dangerous passed pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent creates a pawn weakness, exploit it by forcing recaptures that leave their pieces tied down or create passed pawns.
notes.plans: After the pawn liquidation, use the knight on b5 to maintain pressure and force Black to recapture with the queen, which allows White to activate the rook with tempo.

notes.explains: White's knight reaches the key central square, attacking the unprotected bishop, while the rooks are active. Black is forced to retreat the bishop, and White can take it because it guards important queenside squares.
notes.teaches: Centralized knights on strong squares can dominate the position, especially when they attack undefended pieces and support the advance of your own pieces.
notes.plans: Capture the bishop and then focus on winning the key pawn on h7, which will give White a material advantage and a winning endgame.

notes.explains: White wins the h7 pawn because the knight was protecting it. Now White is a pawn up, Black's kingside is weak, and White dominates the queenside. White pulls the bishop back to avoid being blocked by g6.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify the position by trading off pieces while maintaining pressure on the opponent's weak points.
notes.plans: Proceed to trade off Black's active pieces, then double rooks on the seventh rank to create decisive threats.

notes.explains: Black tries to defend with rook moves, but White's rooks penetrate to the seventh rank, attacking the queen and pawns. Black's counterattacks fail because White has an escape square, and the bishop guards key squares.
notes.teaches: When your rooks reach the seventh rank, they create multiple threats that are often decisive. Always ensure your king has an escape square to avoid back-rank mates.
notes.plans: Finish the game by bringing the queen to deliver checkmate, using the bishop to cover the escape squares.

notes.explains: When a player with White absolutely must win, e4 is the standard practical choice because it offers the most direct chances to fight for an advantage, even though other moves like d4, c4, or Nf3 are also viable.
notes.teaches: In must-win situations with White, prefer openings that create immediate imbalance and winning chances over solid but drawish setups.

notes.explains: Black, needing only a draw, chose the Sicilian (c5) instead of a more solid option like the Petroff or Berlin. This is defensible because at a high level, getting a familiar and comfortable position is more important than aiming for a dead draw, especially against a strong opponent.
notes.teaches: When a draw is sufficient, it's often better to play lines you know well than to force a drawish line that might be outside your repertoire.

notes.explains: The game entered the Accelerated Dragon, where Black delays d6 to play d5 in one move. White played Bc4 to control d5, and Black chose the sideline Re8, which is less common than transposing to the normal Dragon or playing a5.
notes.teaches: The Accelerated Dragon's key idea is the immediate d5 break, and sidelines like Re8 can be viable if they support that plan.
notes.plans: After f3, Black can aim for d5, leading to forcing play where Black regains the pawn.

notes.explains: In the Dragon, Black's rook to e8 prepares to meet f3 with d5, aiming for a forcing line where Black regains the pawn and reaches a drawish position. This is a known plan for Black.
notes.teaches: When facing the Yugoslav Attack, Black's ...Re8 is a useful waiting move that keeps the option of ...d5 alive, forcing White to decide how to handle the center.
notes.plans: Black intends to play ...d5 if White plays f3, entering a forcing sequence that leads to equality.

notes.explains: White's f4 is a novelty that Black may not have analyzed deeply, even though it is a natural move. This highlights the danger of repeating the same lines against top players who prepare surprises.
notes.teaches: At the highest level, consistent repetition of the same opening lines makes you vulnerable to prepared novelties. Always check natural moves even if they are untried.
notes.plans: Black responds with ...d6, and White follows with Qf3, keeping the king uncastled to retain flexibility.

notes.explains: White's delayed castling is a key idea: by not committing the king, White can choose to castle kingside or queenside depending on Black's moves. If Black plays ...d5, White can meet it with e5, and the bishop can go to g1 to defend the knight, which would not be possible if White had already castled kingside.
notes.teaches: Delaying castling can be a powerful tool to keep options open and punish premature central breaks. The king's placement should be flexible until the opponent's plan is clear.
notes.plans: White waits for Black to commit, then chooses the best side to castle based on Black's setup.

notes.explains: Black's ...Bd7 is a waiting move that is not the most useful; it gives White a tempo to launch a stronger attack. White castles kingside, and Black plays ...Ng4, but White is better prepared because the king is already safe.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings like the Dragon, every tempo matters. Avoid passive waiting moves that allow the opponent to improve their position for free.
notes.plans: White castles kingside, then meets ...Ng4 with Nxc6 and Bd2, maintaining a comfortable position.

notes.explains: After White castles and Black plays ...Ng4, White is comfortable playing d5, and Black has options like capturing on d5, but the bishop on g7 remains a target, causing some awkwardness for Black.
notes.teaches: In the Dragon, the bishop on g7 is a key piece; even when Black gets a central break, the bishop's activity can be a long-term concern.
notes.plans: Black may capture on d5, but must handle the pressure on the long diagonal.

notes.explains: In this line, after the early knight sortie to g4 and the bishop retreat to e2, White has castled and developed, making it safe to play d5. Black's options include capturing on d5, but recapturing can be awkward because the bishop on g4 may target b2, creating compensation for the pawn.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn capture in the opening, check whether the opponent's resulting piece activity or pressure on your weak points (like b2) gives them enough compensation to make the capture unattractive.
notes.plans: If Black captures on d5, White should be aware of the potential bishop pressure on b2 and consider whether to recapture or decline to avoid awkwardness.

notes.explains: Black also has the option of playing f5, a sharp move that immediately challenges White's center and creates kingside pressure. White can respond with h3 to gain a tempo on the bishop before committing to a plan. After f5, Black's position becomes uncomfortable if White can break through on the f6 square.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, a move like f5 can be a strong way to seize the initiative, but it requires precise follow-up. A tempo move like h3 can be useful to improve your position before making key decisions.
notes.plans: White should aim to target the f6 square, possibly by repositioning the queen to f2 and preparing f5 or f6 breaks.

notes.explains: After Black plays f5, White's best response is to accept the pawn and continue attacking. Black's attempt to defend with Ne5 is flawed because it leaves the f6 square critical. White can reposition the queen to f2 to maintain pressure on f6, and if Black plays a6, White can break through with f6.
notes.teaches: When attacking, identify a critical square (like f6) and keep pressure on it. A defensive setup that ignores that square can quickly collapse.
notes.plans: White should continue to target f6, possibly with f6 itself, and then use the open f-file to create a decisive attack.

notes.explains: In the game, Black's a6 allowed White to play f6, and after Ng4, the move Qf3 is devastating because it maintains the attack on f6 and prepares e5, opening the f-file. Black's attempts to defend, like Qxf6, fail to tactics such as Qg4+ and Qd4+, winning material.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for moves that maintain pressure on the key square while also creating additional threats. Tactical sequences often involve checks and captures that force the opponent into a losing position.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack by exploiting the f-file and the weakened kingside, eventually winning material or checkmating.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, Black's attempt to win material with Qxf6 backfires because White has a tactical resource: Qg4+ followed by Qd4+ and Qxe4, regaining the piece while keeping the initiative. The pin on the bishop and the exposed king make Black's position collapse.
notes.teaches: When your opponent grabs material, look for forcing checks and captures that exploit your lead in development or the opponent's king safety. A material advantage is meaningless if your king is vulnerable and your pieces are hanging.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack, using the lead in development and the exposed black king to create threats, while Black must find a way to neutralize the initiative or return material to stabilize.

notes.explains: The line with Re8, f4, and Qf3 poses serious problems for Black. The suggested defensive idea is Ng4, and after Nxc6 bxc6, the move Nf6 is worth considering. This retreats the knight to a solid square, preparing to meet d5 with e5, and if White castles kingside, Black can play d5 with less fear because f5 is not as strong after dxe4, Nxc4, and Bxf5.
notes.teaches: In sharp opening lines, sometimes the best defense is to return a piece to its original square or to a passive-looking post if it neutralizes the opponent's attacking plans. Prophylactic thinking—anticipating the opponent's breaks like f5—can guide piece placement.
notes.plans: Black should consider Nf6 to solidify the center and prepare counterplay with d5 or e5, while White may try h3 to prevent Ng4 and delay castling, aiming for a quick g4 and f5 attack.

notes.explains: In must-win situations, players often choose aggressive and sharp openings, even if they are not objectively the most sound, to create winning chances. Here, Black opts for a Benoni structure, which leads to unbalanced and complex positions.
notes.teaches: When you need a win, you should steer the game into positions with clear winning potential, even at the cost of some objective soundness. Playing solid but drawish lines reduces your chances of scoring a full point.
notes.plans: Both sides should play for the initiative and look for ways to create imbalances, such as pawn structure weaknesses or attacking chances, rather than simplifying.

notes.explains: In this Benoni, Black delays playing d6 for several moves, which is an unusual but interesting approach. This keeps the center more flexible and avoids committing the d-pawn early, potentially allowing for different pawn breaks.
notes.teaches: Delaying a central pawn move can be a way to keep the opponent guessing and maintain flexibility. However, it also risks falling behind in development if not handled precisely, so it's a double-edged strategy.
notes.plans: Black should aim to complete development while keeping the tension in the center, and be ready to strike with d5 or e5 at the right moment. White should try to exploit the delay by building a strong center or launching an attack.

notes.explains: In a must-win situation, the player with White chose the most contesting opening lines to maximize winning chances, even if slightly risky. Black delayed d6 for several moves, which is unusual in the Benoni, but White responded by developing normally and not trying to punish it immediately.
notes.teaches: When you need a win, you should select sharp, critical lines that offer the best practical chances, rather than solid but drawish ones. If your opponent makes an unusual move, don't panic or try to refute it immediately; just continue with sound development and trust that the position will offer chances.
notes.plans: White continued developing naturally, playing h3 to prevent ...Bg4, and soon the game returned to a normal Benoni structure, with Black having spent a tempo on ...Re8.

notes.explains: Black's early ...Re8 limited his options because ...Bg4 was no longer available after White's h3. Black then played c4, a pawn sacrifice to open lines, but White accepted it and forced a sequence that left Black's rook misplaced.
notes.teaches: In the Benoni, delaying d6 can restrict your own piece play, especially the bishop on g7. When your opponent offers a pawn, you must evaluate whether accepting it leads to a clear advantage or just gives them counterplay; here, accepting was correct because it left Black's rook awkward.
notes.plans: White played Bc2, then captured on c4, forcing ...Nxe4, and after Rxe4 the bishop on d3 becomes strong, and the rook on e8 is misplaced. White then played Bg5, Qa4, and Nxg5 to create threats.

notes.explains: After the tactical sequence, Black is in a tough spot. The best try is to continue development with ...Nf7, but White can meet it with ...Ng4, creating a strong threat. Black's alternatives like ...Nc5 fail due to a second threat, so ...Rc5 is forced, leading to an uncomfortable position.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a lead in development and active pieces, you must be precise to avoid falling into a lost position. Sometimes you have to make a move that looks awkward (like ...Rc5) to meet immediate threats, even if it costs time.
notes.plans: White's winning sequence involves a rook lift or queen move to exploit the pin on the knight and the weakness of the e-file. The exact move is left as an exercise.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, a tempting queen move to f4 fails tactically because after the opponent's accurate reply, the queen becomes vulnerable and the knight is lost. The key defensive resource is to attack the queen while also defending the critical e8 square.
notes.teaches: Before committing to an aggressive queen move, check for intermediate replies that attack the queen or defend key squares, turning your initiative into a loss.
notes.plans: Look for a more forcing move, such as f4, which creates threats that are harder to meet.

notes.explains: The move f4 is strong because it threatens f5, which would open lines and be devastating. Black is forced to take on d5 to prevent this, but then white's queen c4 is decisive, as black's pieces are overloaded and the white squares become weak.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn break that opens the position, it can force concessions; if the opponent cannot meet it, your attack crashes through.
notes.plans: After f4, if black takes on d5, play queen c4, targeting the weaknesses and preparing to invade on the light squares.

notes.explains: In a winning position, the priority is to safeguard the king and prevent counterplay. By playing rook f2 and bishop f1, white covers all squares on the second rank and prepares to defend the king, while also limiting black's activity with moves like b3 to deny the c4 square.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, first ensure your king is safe and your pieces are harmoniously placed; then slowly convert your advantage without taking risks.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece activity, target weak pawns (like d6), and avoid unnecessary complications.

notes.explains: White finds a tactical blow: bishop c4 interferes with the connection between black's queen and rook, adding an attacker to the d5 pawn. The pawn cannot be captured because that would allow queen takes c3.
notes.teaches: Interference tactics can win material by cutting off a defender; look for such moves when pieces are aligned.
notes.plans: After winning the d5 pawn, the game is effectively over; continue to press with all pieces.

notes.explains: At the end, white delivers a final tactical blow: rook takes c6, which leads to a quick checkmate if the rook is captured, because the queen and rook coordinate to mate the black king.
notes.teaches: Even in a winning position, stay alert for mating combinations; a single tactical shot can end the game immediately.
notes.plans: Execute the combination and deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: In this position, the rook on c6 is a decisive sacrifice because if the queen recaptures, a fork on e7 wins material, and if the pawn recaptures, a queen check on f7 followed by a rook checkmate on f8 or f7 ends the game.
notes.teaches: When a sacrifice leads to a forced mate or a decisive material gain, it is often the fastest way to convert a winning position.
notes.plans: Execute the rook sacrifice on c6 and follow up with the mating net.

notes.explains: In this English Opening, Black's early d5 is a principled attempt to equalize immediately by seizing the center, challenging White to prove an advantage.
notes.teaches: When facing a setup that doesn't directly attack the center, Black can often equalize with the most principled central moves.
notes.plans: White must find concrete play to justify the opening, while Black aims for a solid, equal position.

notes.explains: White delays Nf3 and uses the bishop to tempt Black into playing Nc6, which would allow White to capture the bishop and double Black's pawns, leading to a favorable endgame.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a move that looks natural for the opponent can be a trap; delaying development can lure the opponent into a structural weakness.
notes.plans: White continues to pressure Black's structure, while Black avoids the trap and develops normally.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd7 instead of the natural f6, keeping the kingside pawns intact and avoiding any weaknesses, even at the cost of a tempo because White also moves the bishop again.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a move that appears to lose a tempo is not a loss if the opponent also has to move a piece again; keeping a solid pawn structure can be worth more.
notes.plans: Black maintains a solid structure and aims for a comfortable game, while White continues to probe for weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this opening, a move that appears to lose a tempo by blocking the bishop is not actually bad because the opponent also spends a tempo moving the queen again. Both sides are effectively losing a tempo, so the relative value is neutral.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a move that seems to lose time, consider whether the opponent also has to spend time to reposition their pieces. If both sides are 'losing' a tempo, the move may be perfectly playable.

notes.explains: In a position where both sides have improved their pieces to the maximum, the game becomes a waiting game. Whoever makes a committal pawn move first might create weaknesses. White's ideas like e4 are not immediately possible due to tactical issues, and preparing them can worsen white's own pieces.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions, patience is key. Avoid making pawn moves that create permanent weaknesses unless you are sure they improve your position. Sometimes the best move is a waiting move that maintains flexibility.
notes.plans: Both sides should look for ways to improve their pieces without creating weaknesses. If white plays e4, black can potentially exploit the d4 square. Black might consider moves like Be7 or Ra8 to maintain the balance.

notes.explains: Black plays g4 as a concrete attempt to solve all problems and claim that white has more issues. The idea is that after Nxd4 and exd4, the e-pawn could become a weak backward pawn. However, white is able to strike back immediately with Nxg4 and exd4, seizing the initiative.
notes.teaches: Concrete pawn moves can be double-edged. They may solve your problems but can also create new weaknesses or give the opponent tactical opportunities. Always check the immediate tactical consequences before committing.
notes.plans: After white's response, black must deal with the initiative and the potential weaknesses created by the g4 move.

notes.explains: Black's attempt to solve all problems with c6 gives up key central squares like d4 and e4, and also weakens b6. White's pieces spring to life on these squares, and the bishop on c5 becomes a powerful defender of the weakened dark squares.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to simplify by exchanging pawns and pieces, be alert to the squares they abandon. A seemingly solid move like c6 can create permanent weaknesses that your pieces can occupy.
notes.plans: White should aim to occupy the weakened squares (d4, e4, b6) with pieces and keep pressure on the dark squares, especially by trading off the bishop that guards them.

notes.explains: After Black's c6, the bishop on c5 is crucial because it guards the weakened dark squares. Black would love to trade light-squared bishops, but the same principle applies: removing the defender of weak squares makes them even weaker.
notes.teaches: In positions with pawns fixed on light squares, the opponent's dark-squared bishop is often the key defender. Trading it off can expose fatal weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should seek to exchange the bishop on c5 for Black's dark-squared bishop, then exploit the dark-square holes with knights and queen.

notes.explains: White's d4 pawn is untouchable because capturing it allows Qxh6+ and Re8+ tactics. Black is frozen, unable to move, and any attempt to relieve pressure leads to a lost endgame or immediate tactics.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn is protected by tactical threats rather than pieces. Recognize such 'poisoned' pawns and use them to restrict the opponent's moves.
notes.plans: White should continue to improve piece activity and maintain the threats, forcing Black to defend passively until a decisive breakthrough appears.

notes.explains: In this position, White's attack is overwhelming. The rook on e8 check is devastating, and Black's defensive resources are insufficient. If Black captures with the knight, White has an unstoppable mate threat, and if Black tries other moves, the queen is lost or mate follows.
notes.teaches: When you have a powerful attack, look for forcing moves like rook checks that create unavoidable threats. Sometimes the opponent's best defense still loses material or allows mate.
notes.plans: White should continue with the forcing sequence, using checks and threats to drive the attack home, ultimately winning the queen or delivering mate.

notes.explains: After winning material, White has a technically winning endgame with two extra pawns. The pawns are far advanced and supported, making the win straightforward. Black's attempts to create counterplay around the white king are easily neutralized.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, simplify when possible, but keep an eye on the opponent's counterplay. Advance your passed pawns and use the king actively to support them.
notes.plans: White should trade down to a simple pawn endgame or use the extra pawns to create a decisive passed pawn, while keeping the king safe from any tricks.

notes.explains: In the similar game discussed, White delayed the development of the knight to f3, which allowed Black to play ...d5 and reach a different structure. The bishop on e6 leaves the b7 pawn undefended, which can be a target. Black's setup with ...Qd7 and ...Rfd8 is a more solid alternative to the one chosen in the main game.
notes.teaches: In the opening, the order of moves matters. Delaying a natural developing move can allow the opponent to equalize or reach a different pawn structure. Be aware of the weaknesses created by each move, such as undefended pawns.
notes.plans: White should consider the implications of move order and look for ways to exploit any weaknesses, such as attacking the b7 pawn or gaining a tempo with moves like a3 and Bf4.

notes.explains: In this line, White aims to establish a powerful bishop on g2 along the long diagonal. Black's early bishop to d5 contests that bishop, preventing White from getting a free roll on the diagonal.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to dominate a long diagonal, contesting the bishop immediately can neutralize their plan and leave them with nothing for their efforts.
notes.plans: If White's bishop is contested, consider whether to exchange or reposition; if Black's bishop remains, White may need to challenge it later with pawn breaks or piece play.

notes.explains: The move e4 is generally risky for White in these structures, but it becomes playable when it can be immediately followed by d4, establishing a strong pawn center. If Black cannot prevent both pawns, White gets a very advantageous setup.
notes.teaches: A central pawn break is often only justified if you can follow up with a second pawn to support the center; otherwise, you may just weaken your own position.
notes.plans: If White can play e4 and d4 in quick succession, the center pawns can cramp Black and open lines for the bishops. If not, White should avoid the break and seek other plans.

notes.explains: After Black forces White to play b5 and then exchanges knights on d4, White's e4 break is no longer viable because several pawns are hanging. White must instead play defensively, allowing Black to gain the two bishops and central space with a d4 pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has multiple threats, you must prioritize defense over ambitious pawn breaks. Sometimes you have to concede a structural advantage to avoid immediate material loss.
notes.plans: White should aim to minimize Black's advantage by trading pieces and seeking counterplay on the queenside or along open files.

notes.explains: Black has a pleasant position with the two bishops and a strong d4 pawn. Instead of keeping the bishops, Black might have been better off exchanging on g2 and simplifying to a very comfortable endgame. Keeping the bishops can backfire if White gets counterplay.
notes.teaches: When you have a structural advantage, sometimes it's better to simplify and convert than to keep pieces on the board and allow your opponent chances to complicate.
notes.plans: Black could consider exchanging bishops to reduce White's activity, then use the d4 pawn and open files to press for a win.

notes.explains: White trades rooks on the open file, giving Black a protected passed pawn on b4 in exchange for the file. This is a practical decision from a worse position: White gets counterplay on the file, while Black has a strong pawn but must be careful not to lose the initiative.
notes.teaches: When objectively worse, it's often wise to trade a structural disadvantage for active play, such as an open file, to create practical chances.
notes.plans: White should use the open file to pressure Black's back rank and pieces, while Black must consolidate the passed pawn and avoid letting White's activity become dangerous.

notes.explains: Black's nonchalant queen move allows White to activate the rook and create threats against Black's pawns. After exchanges, White's knight reaches b3, attacking multiple pawns, and Black's position becomes difficult to defend.
notes.teaches: In positions with a material or structural advantage, you must stay alert to tactical shots. One careless move can allow your opponent to generate strong counterplay.
notes.plans: White should continue to target Black's weak pawns and coordinate pieces for an attack, while Black must find accurate defensive moves to survive.

notes.explains: A slightly careless queen move leaves several pawns hanging, and the opponent can immediately exploit it by trading rooks and attacking the loose pawns.
notes.teaches: Every move must be checked for tactical vulnerabilities; a single nonchalant move can turn a playable position into one where all your pawns are targets.
notes.plans: If you have hung pawns, look for active counterplay rather than passive defense.

notes.explains: After the opponent's attack fizzles, the player with the extra pawn must be careful not to overextend; the defender can use checks and threats to force the king to shuffle and gain tempi.
notes.teaches: In king-and-pawn endgames or queen endings, perpetual check and king maneuvers can be used to gain time and improve the position.
notes.plans: Use checks to force the opponent's king to awkward squares, then improve your own pieces.

notes.explains: The winning side methodically advances the passed pawn, using the queen to support it and the king to avoid checks, while the defender runs out of useful checks.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, the king must be sheltered from checks while the passed pawn is pushed; sometimes a 'ring-around-the-rosie' maneuver gains a crucial tempo.
notes.plans: Support the passed pawn with the queen, keep the king safe, and force the defender to resign when the pawn promotes.

notes.explains: In the Nimzo-Indian, after d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4, White's move Nf3 can lead to the Kasparov variation with g3, but here White played e3 instead. Black has castled, which is a reasonable alternative to the main move c5.
notes.teaches: Recognize the Nimzo-Indian setup and understand that castling early is a legitimate option, though c5 is the most common.
notes.plans: Black should aim to create central tension with c5 or d5, exploiting the lead in development.

notes.explains: When Black has already castled, White's bishop on g5 can be a strong piece because Black's h6 and g5 pawn pushes would weaken the kingside. Here White played e3 instead of developing the bishop to g5, missing this opportunity.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, if Black has castled, consider developing the bishop to g5 to pressure the knight and restrict Black's pawn moves.
notes.plans: White should develop the bishop to g5 before playing e3, to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Black played b6, which is good because it prepares to develop the bishop to b7, adding pressure on e4. White is planning to play Bd3, and Black will have another defender of e4.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, Black often fights for control of e4; b6 and Bb7 is a natural way to do that.
notes.plans: Black should continue with Bb7, then possibly d5 or c5 to challenge the center.

notes.explains: White played d5, which gives up the c5 square, a great outpost for Black's knight. This is strategically dubious; White should prefer Bd3 and castling.
notes.teaches: Avoid pawn moves that create permanent weaknesses like weak squares; here d5 weakens c5.
notes.plans: White should develop with Bd3 and castle, keeping the position solid.

notes.explains: Black captured on d5, but it might be better to play d6 and recapture with the pawn to open the file. Capturing with the knight helps White and leaves the pawn overextended.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece should recapture to maintain pawn structure and open files for rooks.
notes.plans: Black should consider d6 and recapturing with the pawn to open the c-file.

notes.explains: Black played d6, which is fine, but it creates light-squared weaknesses on the queenside. If the light-squared bishop disappears and a knight lands on c5, Black could have problems.
notes.teaches: Be aware of the weaknesses created by pawn moves; here d6 weakens light squares, but it's not immediately exploitable.
notes.plans: Black intends to maneuver the knight to c5, using the outpost.

notes.explains: White played h3, preventing a pin on the knight. Black might not want to trade the light-squared bishop, so this move might be unnecessary.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary prophylactic moves if they don't address real threats; consider if the opponent really wants to make that trade.
notes.plans: White should continue development, perhaps with Bd3 and castling.

notes.explains: In the Semi-Slav, the triangle pawn formation with pawns on c6 and e6 supports the center and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop, though it temporarily blocks the knight's natural square on c6.
notes.teaches: The Semi-Slav is a rich opening that offers both dynamic tactical and solid positional play, requiring deep theoretical knowledge and strong positional understanding.
notes.plans: Black aims to complete development, often with ...Nf6, ...Be7, ...O-O, and may later seek central breaks with ...e5 or ...c5, depending on White's setup.

notes.explains: Move order matters: starting with ...c6 (the pure Slav) avoids the Exchange Slav but allows the Catalan if White plays g3, while starting with ...e6 avoids the Catalan but allows the Exchange Slav. Each choice has its own theoretical requirements.
notes.teaches: When choosing an opening move order, be aware of the resulting alternatives for both sides and be prepared to face the corresponding lines.
notes.plans: If playing the pure Slav order, be ready for the Catalan; if playing ...e6 first, be ready for the Exchange Slav. Choose based on your preferences and preparation.

notes.explains: If White plays Nc3 before Nf3, Black has extra options: the Winawer Countergambit (d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3 e5) is a sharp surprise weapon, and Black can also aim for the Noteboom or a Stonewall setup. These lines require specific knowledge.
notes.teaches: When White deviates from the main move order, Black should know the alternative setups and be ready to exploit them.
notes.plans: Against Nc3, consider the Winawer Countergambit if prepared, or transpose to the Semi-Slav with ...e6 and ...Nf6. Also be aware of the Marshall Gambit if White plays e4.

notes.explains: The move ...e6 in the Semi-Slav is common, and the pawn on c6, while blocking the knight, supports a future ...d5xc4 and ...b5 expansion, and also supports the center if White captures on d5.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves in the opening often have dual purposes: they may restrict your own pieces but also support key central or flank advances.
notes.plans: Black will typically develop the knight to f6, the bishop to e7 or d6, castle, and then aim for ...e5 or ...c5 breaks, depending on White's setup.

notes.explains: In the classical King's Indian, after White castles, Black chooses between ...Nc6, ...Na6, or ...Nbd7. The main line is ...Nc6, attacking the d4 pawn. White must decide whether to defend, capture on e5, or push d5. The critical choice is d5, forcing the knight back to e7.
notes.teaches: Black's knight moves in the King's Indian are aimed at pressuring d4 and preparing ...c5 or ...e5 breaks. White's d5 push is a key central clamp, gaining space and restricting Black's pieces.
notes.plans: After ...Nc6, White plays d5, and after ...Ne7, White prepares a kingside pawn storm with f4, while Black will try to play ...f5.

notes.explains: The move Ne1 is a classical setup for White in the King's Indian, preparing f4 and keeping the center flexible. Black often gets ...f5 in, but White counters on the queenside with a pawn majority and space.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, both sides race on opposite wings: Black attacks on the kingside, White on the queenside. White should not fear Black's kingside play if White can create counterplay on the other side.
notes.plans: White will aim for f4, then possibly f5 or a queenside expansion with b4 and c5, while Black tries to break with ...f5 and ...e4.

notes.explains: Black's knight to d7 prepares f5 and controls key squares. White develops the bishop and plays f3 to defend the e4 pawn and give the bishop space. Black plays f4, and White's bishop goes to f2.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, Black's plan is to push f5-f4 and attack on the kingside, while White must make defensive moves like f3 to maintain the center.
notes.plans: Black continues with g5 to support the pawn storm. White prepares to defend and counter on the queenside.

notes.explains: After g5, White has several options. The recommended move is Rc1, as played by Wesley So. Black plays Ng6. White can also consider Nd3 or an immediate c5.
notes.teaches: In this line, White should choose the most flexible and aggressive setup, often Rc1, to prepare the c5 break. Black must be ready for various white setups.
notes.plans: White aims to play c5 and open the queenside. Black continues with the kingside attack, possibly preparing ...f4 and ...g4.

notes.explains: If White plays c5 immediately, Black can capture, but White's idea is to open the b-file and use the knight to b5. However, Black can respond with a6, which seems good for Black.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn break, look for tactical resources like Nb5 to exploit the open file, but be aware of Black's defensive moves like a6 that can neutralize the attack.
notes.plans: White should consider other ways to prepare the c5 break, perhaps with Rc1 first. Black can use a6 to prevent Nb5 and maintain the kingside initiative.

notes.explains: In this sharp line, white has sacrificed a pawn on b4 to lure the black knight to a passive square. The key is that black cannot comfortably return the knight to d7 because white can then play Bc5, attacking the rook on f8 and winning material. Thus, black is forced to play the unnatural ...Na6, leaving the knight misplaced.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing a pawn to kick a piece back, ensure the piece cannot retreat to its best square. The success of the pawn sacrifice often hinges on the opponent's piece being forced to a bad square.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and preparing to exploit the misplaced knight, likely by playing Nd3 to defend the b4 pawn and then Nb5 to attack the c7 pawn.

notes.explains: The bishop on g5 is a crucial defender of the kingside, particularly controlling the g4 square. If black can play ...Ng4 and then ...g5-g4, they will gain a strong attack against the white king. Therefore, moving this bishop away, such as to b5, weakens the defense of g4 and is undesirable.
notes.teaches: Before moving a defender, consider the squares it controls that are vital to your king's safety. Sometimes a piece's defensive role outweighs its attacking potential.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on g5 to restrain black's kingside expansion, and instead use the knight to probe on the queenside.

notes.explains: After white plays b4 and black is forced to play ...Na6, white's knight can go to d3 and then to b5, attacking the c7 pawn. Black cannot defend it because the rook on f8 is tied to the defense of the knight on a6, and ...Rf7 is impossible due to the knight's position. This leads to winning the c7 pawn and trapping the rook.
notes.teaches: A misplaced knight can leave weaknesses in the opponent's camp. Use your pieces to target those weaknesses and create concrete threats that are difficult to meet.
notes.plans: White should proceed with Nd3, then Nb5, and after ...Rf8, Nxc7 wins the pawn and traps the rook on a8, leading to a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: In this King's Indian line, Black's knight is forced to the unnatural a6 square to defend a key point, leaving it horribly misplaced and slowing down Black's kingside attack. This gives White time to build on the queenside.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece is badly placed, you gain time to pursue your own plans; don't rush to punish it immediately, but use the tempo to improve your position.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and expanding on the queenside, exploiting Black's passive knight.

notes.explains: Black spends a tempo on b6 to stop a threat, but this weakens the queenside pawns and the diagonal, and it's a waste of time because White's space advantage means Black can't stop everything anyway.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, you must prioritize which threats to meet; sometimes you have to give up something to keep your plan rolling.
notes.plans: Black should have accepted the loss of the a-pawn and continued with the kingside attack, rather than weakening the queenside.

notes.explains: White plays the maneuver Be1 to reroute the bishop and bring the knight to f2, where it controls the key g4 square. This is a common idea in the King's Indian: pieces are often better on different squares than they initially appear.
notes.teaches: Look for piece maneuvers that improve your control of critical squares, even if the first move looks unnatural. A knight on f2 can be more valuable than a bishop there.
notes.plans: White aims to complete the knight maneuver to f2 to stifle Black's kingside play, then continue on the queenside.

notes.explains: White's queen goes to a4 and then a3, which is unusual because normally the queen stays on d1 to defend against g4. But with Black's knight stuck on a6, White doesn't need to worry as much about that break, so the queen can join the queenside action.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are misplaced, you can deviate from standard defensive setups and use your pieces more aggressively.
notes.plans: White's queen on a3 supports the queenside pawns and adds defense on the third rank, while Black's attack is slowed.

notes.explains: In this King's Indian structure, White's b4 break is the key queenside plan, but it must be prepared carefully. The immediate a3 can be met by a4, locking the queenside and stopping White's pawn storm. Playing b3 first keeps the option of b4 while maintaining flexibility.
notes.teaches: When preparing a pawn break, consider the opponent's possible responses that could freeze your pawns. A flexible move order (b3 before a3) can preserve your options and avoid a permanent blockade.
notes.plans: White should aim to play b4 to kick the black knight away and open lines on the queenside, using the rook to support the advance if needed.

notes.explains: Black's a4 is a pawn sacrifice to force White's hand on the queenside. If White accepts, he gets a clear extra pawn, but Black hopes to gain activity. If White instead plays f4, Black can use the tempo to improve his pieces, but White's queenside play accelerates.
notes.teaches: Pawn sacrifices are often about forcing the opponent to take time or to accept a structural weakness. When deciding whether to accept, count defenders and attackers, and evaluate whether the resulting activity compensates for the material.
notes.plans: White can accept the pawn and then continue with b4, or if Black plays f4, White can use the time to strengthen his queenside pressure.

notes.explains: Black's knight on c5 is his main asset, but it is not enough to compensate for his lack of space and pawn breaks. White simply captures it when it becomes convenient, showing that a single good piece cannot outweigh a positional advantage.
notes.teaches: A good piece is valuable, but if the rest of the position is bad, it may not be enough. Sometimes you must be willing to trade off your opponent's best piece to consolidate your advantage.
notes.plans: White trades off the knight on c5 and continues to press with his extra pawn and queenside majority.

notes.explains: In this King's Indian structure, white has a space advantage on the queenside and is up a pawn. Black's counterplay on the kingside has fizzled out, leaving white free to pursue his queenside plans without concern.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's counterplay on one side has been neutralized, you can proceed with your own plans on the other side, especially if you have a material advantage.
notes.plans: White should continue to advance on the queenside, using his extra pawn to create passed pawns or force weaknesses in black's camp.

notes.explains: In the final position, white has two passed pawns on files far apart, and black's bishop cannot cover both. The black king or bishop must move, allowing white to advance a pawn and win.
notes.teaches: In bishop endgames, two passed pawns on opposite sides of the board are often winning because the defending bishop cannot control both fronts simultaneously.
notes.plans: White should advance the pawn that is not being blockaded, forcing the black bishop to choose which pawn to stop, then use the other pawn to create a decisive breakthrough.

notes.explains: Black's failure to generate kingside play, despite playing f5, allowed white to dominate on the queenside. Black spent too much time trying to stop white's queenside expansion instead of creating his own counterplay.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side attacks, you must play actively on the side where you have the advantage; spending too much time defending on the opponent's strong side will lead to a slow defeat.
notes.plans: Black should have sought more dynamic kingside play, such as a timely pawn sacrifice or piece activity, to create real threats before white's queenside breakthrough.

notes.explains: With the knight on d7 instead of c6, black puts less pressure on d4, so white does not need to play d5 immediately. White can instead develop the bishop to e3, but must be aware of the tactical resource ...Ng4 attacking the bishop.
notes.teaches: The choice of knight development in the King's Indian affects whether white should play d5 early. If black doesn't pressure d4, white can delay the advance and develop harmoniously.
notes.plans: White should consider moves like Be3 to reinforce d4, but be ready to respond to ...Ng4 by moving the bishop or playing h3 to prevent the pin.

notes.explains: After black plays c6 and then c5, the structure becomes a closed King's Indian with pawns on c5, d6, e5 for black and c4, d5, e4 for white. This structure is more solid for black because it prevents the c5 break for white.
notes.teaches: The c5 break is a key lever for white in the King's Indian; if black can prevent it by playing ...c5 himself, he reduces white's queenside play and gains a more solid position.
notes.plans: White can still try to create play with b4 and a minority attack, but it will be less effective than the c5 break. Black should aim to complete development and prepare ...f5 or ...b5 for counterplay.

notes.explains: In this King's Indian structure, black has played c6 and c5, which prevents white's c5 break but costs time. Black's knight is also on a suboptimal square, having to reroute to e7 or d7. This gives white a lead in development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent spends time on pawn moves and piece shuffling, you should use your lead in development to create immediate threats or seize space, rather than allowing them to consolidate.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit the time advantage by launching a quick attack or creating weaknesses, possibly on the kingside, before black can fully coordinate.

notes.explains: White plays Ne1 to prevent the black knight from advancing to d7, forcing it back to e8. This maneuver also prepares f4 or other central breaks, but the key is to restrict black's pieces.
notes.teaches: A knight maneuver like Ne1 can be used to control key squares and force the opponent's pieces to awkward squares, gaining time and space.
notes.plans: After Ne1, white can consider f4, but must be careful not to improve black's bishop. The immediate plan is to prevent black's f5 break.

notes.explains: White considers f4 and g3, but both moves allow black's bishop to become active and support the f5 break. Black's plan is centered on playing f5, and if white can prevent it, white should be better.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, black's f5 break is a key source of counterplay. If you can prevent it without weakening your own position, you may gain a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: White plays g4 to stop f5 once and for all, even at the cost of weakening the kingside, because black has wasted time and cannot punish it immediately.

notes.explains: White plays g4, a typical idea when black has wasted time. Black responds Qh4, but white can move the king and continue with Rg1, threatening to trap the queen with g5. Black must retreat the queen.
notes.teaches: A pawn thrust like g4 can be a powerful way to seize the initiative, but you must be prepared to meet counterattacks. Sometimes you can allow a queen sortie if you can trap it or gain time.
notes.plans: White continues with a3 and b4, expanding on the queenside while maintaining the clamp on the kingside. The immediate threat of g5 forces black's queen back.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian, when Black spends tempi on moves like c6 and c5, White can seize the initiative with g4, aiming to challenge Black's kingside setup and gain space.
notes.teaches: Punish slow or time-wasting moves by striking immediately on the side where you have a lead in development.
notes.plans: After g4, follow up with Qh4 and rook to g1 to create threats against Black's king.

notes.explains: White's g5 advance takes away key squares (f6 and h6) that Black's pieces would like to use, restricting their activity and slowing down Black's typical f5 break.
notes.teaches: Identify the squares your opponent's pieces need and take them away; this can be more valuable than material.
notes.plans: Continue to restrict Black's pieces while building up on the queenside.

notes.explains: White's play on the kingside (g4, g5) is ultimately in service of the queenside plan, where White's real advantage lies.
notes.teaches: In many openings, actions on one wing are a means to create weaknesses or gain time to pursue the main plan on the other wing.
notes.plans: After securing the kingside, transfer pieces to the queenside and advance pawns there.

notes.explains: Black's bishop to f6 is a serious error because it gives up a piece for insufficient compensation; White declines the capture and continues to improve his position.
notes.teaches: Do not give up material without clear compensation; sometimes the best way to punish a mistake is to ignore the bait and improve your position.
notes.plans: Maintain the extra piece and coordinate pieces for a decisive attack.

notes.explains: In the classical line of the King's Indian, the c5 pawn sacrifice is a key idea to sideline Black's knight, after which White plays on the queenside.
notes.teaches: Know the typical pawn sacrifices in your openings; they often aim to improve piece activity or create a lasting structural advantage.
notes.plans: After the c5 sacrifice, focus on queenside play, using moves like a3 and a4 to prevent structural weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this classical line against the King's Indian, the main idea is to sacrifice the c5 pawn to deflect Black's knight from its active post, then build pressure on the queenside.
notes.teaches: A pawn sacrifice can be used to remove a key defender or active piece, even at the cost of material, to gain positional control.
notes.plans: After the c5 sacrifice, focus on queenside play, using the open files and space advantage to create threats.

notes.explains: When Black opts for a defensive setup, avoiding an immediate kingside assault and instead trying to solidify a knight on c5, White should still direct play toward the queenside.
notes.teaches: Against a solid defensive setup, maintain your own plan rather than reacting; here, the queenside remains the correct theater of operations.
notes.plans: Continue queenside expansion, but be careful not to create structural weaknesses like the a3-a4 pawn formation that could be exploited.

notes.explains: If Black wastes time with moves like c6 and then c5, White should use that extra tempo to implement a concrete plan to disrupt Black's setup, such as playing g4 to gain space and challenge Black's pieces.
notes.teaches: When your opponent spends moves on pawn advances that don't develop, you must seize the initiative with a concrete action, often a pawn thrust that restricts their pieces.
notes.plans: Look for the most forcing or space-gaining move that exploits Black's slow play; in some positions, g4 is the move, but it may require preparatory moves like moving a knight to defend the pawn.

notes.explains: White's typical plan after g4 d5 is Bg2, hoping that if Black captures on g4, White can play c4 and Qb3 to attack Black's light squares. However, Black can safely take the pawn with …Bxg4, because the resulting complications are favorable for Black.
notes.teaches: Do not be afraid to take a free pawn if you can handle the subsequent pressure. In this line, Black's extra pawn is worth more than White's attacking chances.
notes.plans: If White plays c4, Black should be prepared to meet the attack on the light squares. If White does not play the tricky line and instead develops normally, Black just continues development while being up a clean pawn.

notes.explains: If White avoids the tricky lines and plays a normal move like d4, Black gets a standard d4 opening position but with an extra pawn, because White is missing the g-pawn that would normally be on g3. This is essentially playing with pawn odds.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's opening move is a mistake, you can often transpose into a familiar opening with a better version for you. Here, Black is simply better by a pawn.
notes.plans: Black should develop normally, defend the extra pawn, and aim to consolidate the material advantage. Moves like Nf3, e3, and Bf4 by White can be met with simple development by Black.

notes.explains: In the Grob, if White plays the bishop to g2 and then draws the light-squared bishop out with Bxg4, the key idea is to target the weakened light squares on Black's queenside with c4. Black's most natural response is c6, preventing the bishop from landing on b7 and keeping it out of the game.
notes.teaches: When your opponent voluntarily gives up a pawn to lure a defender away, consider whether the resulting weaknesses are worth more than the material. Here, Black's light-squared bishop is drawn out, but White's bishop on g2 becomes a long-term threat to b7.
notes.plans: Black should aim to keep the d-pawn, as it controls the center and blocks the bishop on g2. If White plays cxd5 and Qb3, Black should prioritize defending the d-pawn over the b-pawn, possibly with Nf6 or e6.

notes.explains: After White's queen goes pawn-hunting on b7, Black can develop the knight to d7 to defend the rook. If White plays d4, Black can exploit White's lack of development and the queen's exposure with a tactic starting with Rb8.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen ventures deep into your position, look for tactical blows that target the queen's lack of safety and the opponent's undeveloped pieces. A move like Rb8 can create threats that force the queen to move, gaining time.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing while harassing the white queen. If White plays Qc6, Black can respond with Rc8, attacking the queen and the undefended bishop on c1, winning material.

notes.explains: In this position, black's queen on a7 is vulnerable, and white's bishop on c1 is undefended. Black can exploit both weaknesses with the move Qc8, which attacks the bishop and threatens mate, while also preparing Rxa8 to trap the queen.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen goes pawn hunting, look for tactical blows that target both the queen and other weak pieces. A queen on the rim can be trapped with a rook lift.
notes.plans: After Qc8, if white plays Bf4 to defend, black plays e5, attacking the bishop and maintaining the threat of Rxa8. This forces white into a losing position.

notes.explains: After white plays e5, if white captures with dxe5, black can continue with Rxa8, and after the queen moves to e3, black has the tactic Bc5, driving the queen to a square where it is attacked, followed by Rb4 hitting two pieces.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is short of squares, use piece play to force it to a worse square, then hit multiple targets with a rook or bishop.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by taking on f4 and f2, leading to a decisive material gain.

notes.explains: If white instead plays Qa6, black can still play e5, exploiting the queen's poor placement. After dxe5, Nc5 traps the queen, and if the queen goes to a3, Nbd7 or Nb3 attacks the queen and rook.
notes.teaches: Even when the opponent avoids the immediate trap, the same thematic ideas (e5, Nc5) can be used to punish a misplaced queen.
notes.plans: Use the activity of the pieces to win the queen or gain a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: In the main line with Nc3, white has defended the c1 bishop and the d5 pawn is under attack. Black can choose to play e6 to solidify the center and be slightly better, but to refute the Grob, black can still play e5, leading to a tactical battle.
notes.teaches: When the opponent improves their setup, you can either consolidate your advantage or continue with aggressive play if you have a concrete follow-up.
notes.plans: If playing e5, be prepared for complications; otherwise, e6 and development gives a comfortable edge.

notes.explains: In this position, black has a strong center and white's pieces are poorly coordinated. The move e5 is available and aims to take over the center completely, putting white in a tough spot.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are uncoordinated, seize the center with pawn breaks to gain a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: Play e5, and if white doesn't take on d5, continue with Bc5, developing with tempo and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: After e5, if white captures on d5, black recaptures with the bishop, and then Bc5 comes with tempo. White's queen is misplaced and has few safe squares, leading to a very good position for black.
notes.teaches: Develop pieces with tempo and exploit the opponent's queen's vulnerability by attacking it while developing.
notes.plans: Continue development with Bc5, and if the queen attacks the bishop, retreat it while maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Black castles kingside, creating a threat against white's king. White cannot castle due to tactical threats, and the queen is still short of safe squares. White's best move is Qh4, but it's still very bad for white.
notes.teaches: Castling can be a tactical move that creates threats, and when the opponent's king is stuck in the center, you should aim to open lines and attack.
notes.plans: After Qh4, play Be7 to avoid queen trades, then defend the e5 pawn with Bf6, maintaining a large advantage.

notes.explains: Black has a winning position and can choose among several strong moves. The idea of h5 is less effective because black already captured white's g-pawn, so the typical h5-h4 plan is unnecessary. Instead, a rook lift along the sixth rank is a simple and forcing way to win.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is missing a pawn, consider whether pawn storms like h5 are still useful; if the pawn is already gone, focus on other attacking plans like rook lifts.
notes.plans: Consider moves like Rb4 or e4, which are strong, but the recommended plan is to bring the rook to the sixth rank to create threats against the king.

notes.explains: In this sharp opening line, black's early development and pawn structure aim to create immediate threats against white's king, exploiting weak light squares and lack of coordination in white's camp.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, prioritize rapid piece play and direct threats over material gains; use forcing moves to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: Continue developing pieces to active squares, keep pressure on white's weaknesses, and prepare to open lines against the king.

notes.explains: In this position, black has a serious attack, and the threat of ...Rf3 followed by ...Ng2# is a real mating net. White must be careful not to allow such tactics, as the king is still in the center and the pawn structure is compromised.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's king is exposed, look for mating patterns involving heavy pieces and knights. A rook lift to the third rank can be a powerful attacking resource, especially when combined with a knight checkmate.
notes.plans: For black, aim to execute the mating net by bringing the rook to f3 and the knight to g2. For white, try to create luft or block the threats, but the position may already be lost.

notes.explains: When white plays knight e1 to give the queen an escape square, black switches to a different plan: rook b6, bishop moves, and rook g6 again, showing the flexibility of the attack. The idea of bishop h3 is a key tactical resource to deflect the queen.
notes.teaches: If one attacking plan is parried, have a backup plan that reuses the same pieces to create new threats; look for deflection tactics to remove the defender of a key square.
notes.plans: Proceed with rook b6, move the bishop, and then play rook g6; if white tries to defend, use bishop h3 to force the queen to h1, then continue the attack.

notes.explains: After black wins the queen, the material advantage is decisive, but the key is that white's pieces are poorly placed and black's attack continues. Black can choose between several winning plans, such as advancing the h-pawn to mate or switching to a queenside attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive material advantage, still look for the most forcing continuation to convert, but also be aware that multiple plans may win; choose the one that is simplest and safest.
notes.plans: Play h5-h4 with the idea of hxg3, or use the queen to create mating threats; either way, black is completely winning.

notes.explains: In the Grob (g4), black's response d5 is straightforward: attack the pawn and take it if possible. After white plays Bg2, black takes the pawn, and when white plays c4, black plays c6 to support the d5 pawn and restrict the bishop.
notes.teaches: In the opening, punish pawn weaknesses by attacking them, and support your central pawns with pawn moves that also limit the opponent's piece activity.
notes.plans: Continue with Nf6 to defend the d5 pawn, keeping the option of e5 in reserve, and consider developing the bishop to a good square.

notes.explains: After the queen moves to b3, the d-pawn is under attack, so we defend it with Nf6. We avoid e6 to keep the e5 break available and to allow the bishop to return to c5 later.
notes.teaches: When choosing between pawn moves, consider which ones keep your options open. Sometimes delaying a pawn move like e6 preserves a useful break (e5) and keeps the bishop's diagonal free.
notes.plans: Defend the d-pawn, then develop the knight to d7, and prepare to challenge the center with e5 after dealing with the queen's pressure.

notes.explains: With the queen on b7, we must defend the rook and develop, so we play Nd7. Then, before playing e5, we first distract the queen with Rb8, forcing it to a7, and only then play e5.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong central break, sometimes it's better to first improve your position or force the opponent's pieces to worse squares before executing the break. This is a form of prophylaxis and timing.
notes.plans: After e5, if White captures on d5, recapture with the knight, then develop the bishop to c5 with tempo, and continue to harass the queen while castling.

notes.explains: After the queen retreats to a4 and we develop with Nf3, White castles and threatens Nb6. We respond with Qh4, but we don't trade queens; instead we play Be7 with tempo, keeping the initiative. When the queen goes to g3 attacking our pawn, we defend with f6, then castle.
notes.teaches: In the middlegame, keep the initiative by making moves that create threats (tempo moves) rather than trading pieces. Defend when necessary, but look for ways to maintain pressure.
notes.plans: After castling, aim to play Nc5, targeting the bishop, then Ne4 to misplace the queen, and finally Qc8 to prepare a decisive rook lift to b6 and g6.

notes.explains: The plan culminates in Nc5, forcing the bishop to move, then Ne4, hitting the queen and misplacing it. After the queen goes to c8, White must play Ne1, and then we finish with Rb6, moving the bishop, and Rg6, winning the game.
notes.teaches: A well-coordinated attack can force the opponent's pieces to awkward squares. The rook lift to b6 and g6 is a classic pattern to exploit the weakened kingside.
notes.plans: Execute the rook lift: Rb6, then after the bishop moves, Rg6, delivering a decisive attack.

notes.explains: If White tries to avoid the rook lift by playing Qf3, we can still win by simple means: give check, force the king to move, and if the knight goes to g2, we play Bh3, which is very strong. After the king moves to h1, we can move the knight to safety, and then continue with Rg1, Bg4, and the queen has no squares on the diagonal.
notes.teaches: Even if the opponent tries to sidestep your main threat, there are often other tactical resources. Look for checks, pins, and ways to exploit the opponent's queen's lack of squares.
notes.plans: If White plays Qf3, respond with a check, then use Bh3 to create threats, and continue to harass the queen until you are winning material or checkmate.

notes.explains: In this line after queen b3, black plays e6 to prepare developing the knight to e7, keeping the c6 pawn defended and avoiding the knight to d5 complications from the main line.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen attacks b7, it's often worth delaying natural development (like Nf6) to keep the pawn structure solid and prevent tactical tricks.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to e7, then after cxd5 recapture with the e-pawn to keep the bishop on g4 bad and maintain a solid center.

notes.explains: After black's setup, the plan is to harass the queen on b7 with rook to b8, forcing it to awkward squares. If the queen goes to a7, black can trap it with rook to a8 after queen c8, and if it goes to a6, rook to b6 continues the harassment.
notes.teaches: A queen that ventures deep into enemy territory can become a target; use rooks to drive it back and gain time while developing.
notes.plans: Play rook to b8, then if queen a6, rook b6; if queen a7, use the queen c8 idea to trap it. Develop pieces harmoniously while white's king remains in the center.

notes.explains: In the line where white plays bishop f4, black can simply capture on b2, winning a pawn and gaining a strong position. The material is even, but black has all the activity and white has no plan.
notes.teaches: Sometimes grabbing a pawn is correct when it comes with active play and the opponent has no compensation.
notes.plans: After taking on b2, continue with knight g6 and bishop b4 to increase pressure, or simply castle and enjoy the better position.

notes.explains: If white avoids the queen traps and retreats to d3, black develops normally: knight g6, bishop d6, castles, achieving harmonious development while white's king is stuck in the center due to the missing g-pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has compromised their kingside (missing g-pawn), their king safety is poor; focus on rapid development and central control.
notes.plans: Complete development with knight g6, bishop d6, and castle, then prepare to exploit white's weak king and lack of plan.

notes.explains: In the Grob, after White plays g4 and Bg2, Black's d5 and c6 set up a solid center while stunting White's bishop. The key is to keep the c6 pawn to support a later e5 break, which challenges White's center and leaves the bishop on g2 bad.
notes.teaches: Against flank openings, a central pawn duo (d5 and e5) is a powerful way to seize space and restrict the opponent's pieces. Prioritize maintaining your pawn structure over developing minor pieces if it keeps the opponent's bishop passive.
notes.plans: Continue with Nf6, Be7, O-O, and then aim for the e5 break when appropriate, keeping the c6 pawn to support it.

notes.explains: When White plays Qb3, Black should not rush Nf6 if White hasn't committed to capturing on c6. Instead, keep the c6 pawn and develop with Nbd7 and Ne7, defending the pawn and preparing to challenge the center with e5.
notes.teaches: In the face of pressure on a pawn, it's often better to defend it with a piece that also develops, rather than moving the same pawn again. This maintains your structure and keeps your options open.
notes.plans: After White plays cxd5, recapture with e5, then develop naturally with Be7, O-O, and later aim for Nf4 to exploit the weakened dark squares around White's king.

notes.explains: If White captures on c6 prematurely, Black can respond with Rc8, Rxc4, and Nf6, achieving easy development and central control while White's pieces remain undeveloped and the king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent grabs a pawn at the cost of development, you can often sacrifice the pawn back to accelerate your own development and seize the initiative. A lead in development and central control can outweigh a material deficit.
notes.plans: Continue developing with Be7, O-O, and use the open c-file to pressure White's position, while White's king remains vulnerable.

notes.explains: In the H3 lines of the Grob, White plays two moves (h3 and g4) that do nothing for development, while Black's d5 and e5 control the center. This leaves White effectively two tempi down and without a plan.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that don't contribute to development or central control, especially in the opening. Each move should either develop a piece, fight for the center, or improve your king's safety; otherwise, you're giving your opponent a free advantage.
notes.plans: Black should continue with natural development (Nf6, Be7, O-O) and then exploit White's lack of coordination by opening the center or attacking the weakened kingside.

notes.explains: After White plays g4 and Black responds d5, White's h3 is a wasted tempo that does nothing for the center, allowing Black to seize space with e5. White's subsequent g4 further weakens the kingside and leaves White down two tempi.
notes.teaches: In the Grob, moves like h3 and g4 are often pointless and create permanent weaknesses. Strike in the center immediately with d5 and e5 to gain a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing quickly, aiming to exploit White's weakened kingside and lack of central control.

notes.explains: With White's pawn on g4, the f4 square is permanently weakened. Black can reroute a knight to e7 and later to g6, eyeing f4 or h4 as outposts. Also, Black can attack the g4 pawn with h5, which is more effective than f5 because it avoids weakening Black's own kingside.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates a pawn weakness, plan to occupy the weakened squares with your knights. Also, attack a forward pawn with a flank pawn push (h5) to force concessions, especially when your knight is not on f6 to be hit by g5.
notes.plans: Play h5 to force White to respond to the threat, then develop the bishop to e6 and prepare to castle queenside.

notes.explains: After Black plays h5, White must address the threat, but Black's development continues smoothly. Black can play Be6, overprotecting the pawn and freeing the knight, then shore up the center with f6. The resulting position is already very good for Black, with easy development and a clear plan.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize rapid development and central control. When the opponent's moves are passive, you can calmly finish development and then choose the most favorable plan.
notes.plans: Play Qd7, castle queenside, and then decide where to place the remaining pieces. Black's position is so comfortable that many moves are good, such as Nf5, Rg8, or e4.

notes.explains: The line g4 d5, h3 e5, Bg2 Nc6, Nc3 Nge7, and now h5 is a recommended setup. White's pawn on g4 is a target, and Black's pieces are well placed to pressure it. The computer evaluates this as clearly better for Black.
notes.teaches: Against the Grob, a solid setup with d5, e5, Nc6, Nge7, and h5 gives Black a comfortable advantage. The key is to create weaknesses in White's camp and then develop naturally.
notes.plans: Continue with Be6, f6, Qd7, and O-O-O. After that, Black can choose among several good plans, such as Nf5, Rg8, or e4, depending on White's setup.

notes.explains: After g4 d5, White's e3 defends the g4-pawn while also controlling the center. Black can respond with e5, taking space, and then develop the knight to c6. If White plays Nc3, Black defends the e5-pawn with Be6, keeping the knight on g8 for a later jump to f6.
notes.teaches: When facing an unusual opening, prioritize central control and flexible development. Keeping the knight on g8 can be useful if it needs to reroute to f6 to recapture a pawn.
notes.plans: If White plays d4, Black should play e4, creating a French-like structure where White's early g4, Bg2, and Nc3 are misplaced. Then aim to castle queenside and expand with f5.

notes.explains: In the line after e3 e5 Bg2 Nc6 Nc3 Be6 d4 e4, White has a poor version of the French Defense: the knight on c3 blocks the c4 break, the bishop on g2 is passive, and the g4-pawn is a weakness. Black's plan is to target the h5-pawn after White plays h3 and h5, using the knight from g8 to f6 to recapture.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent's moves are inconsistent with standard plans in a familiar structure. Exploit weaknesses like overextended pawns by targeting them with pieces.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, Be7, h3, h5, then Nf6 to recapture on h5. Follow with queenside castling and a kingside pawn storm with f5, using the central majority to crush White.

notes.explains: Against g4 d5 g5, Black should again play e5 to control the center. If White tries d4, Black can capture and after Qxd4, c5 is strong, developing with tempo and leaving White's g5-pawn misplaced.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a pawn move that doesn't contribute to development, seize the center and open lines to exploit the weakness.
notes.plans: After e5, if White plays d4, take with exd4. If White recaptures with the queen, play c5 and develop the knight to c6 and bishop to f5. If White recaptures with the knight, play c5, then after c3 take with the pawn, and follow with d4 to keep control.

notes.explains: After White's early pawn thrusts in the Grob, Black can often meet Qxd4 with c5, striking at the center and developing naturally. The g5 pawn becomes a liability for White, giving Black a comfortable edge without material deficit.
notes.teaches: When facing an unorthodox opening, prioritize rapid development and central control over grabbing pawns. A misplaced enemy pawn can be left alone if it doesn't contribute to their position.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to c6, bishop to f5, and maintain the central pawn duo. If White tries to recapture the pawn, continue with c5 and recapture on c3, then solidify with d4.

notes.explains: The g5 pawn, though annoying, can be dealt with by playing h6, forcing White to either trade or waste time. If White tries to open the king with g6, Black can simply capture and emerge with a clean extra pawn.
