notes.teaches: In rook endgames, it's often important to fix the pawn structure to prevent the opponent from creating passed pawns. Also, creating luft for the king is a standard precaution.
notes.plans: Black should keep the king active to block any pawn pushes and use the rook to defend the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black sees a repetition possibility with king d7 and rook c2, but also notes that playing king e6 would be a mistake because it allows rook f8, giving White counterplay. Black must be precise with king moves.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, every king move matters. A seemingly natural move can allow the opponent's rook to become active, so always check for rook invasions.
notes.plans: Black should choose king moves that keep the rook from invading and maintain the blockade.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the black king is close enough to neutralize the a-pawn push. If White tries a5, Black can capture b6 and then bring the king to b8, securing the pawn and maintaining a draw.
notes.teaches: When defending against an outside passed pawn, the king's proximity can render the pawn push ineffective. Always check if the king can stop the pawn before committing to a plan.
notes.plans: Black should aim to keep the king active and support the b6 pawn, while avoiding passive rook placements.

notes.explains: White's rook to c3 creates a threat of rook c6 attacking the b6 pawn. Black has multiple good replies, but the abundance of choices can be psychologically challenging, especially under time pressure.
notes.teaches: In time trouble, it's important to have a clear method to evaluate candidate moves. Sometimes the simplest move that maintains the balance is best, even if others are also viable.
notes.plans: Black can choose between active moves like rook e1, rook c5, or rook g5, each with its own merits. The key is to find a move that keeps the position safe without requiring deep calculation.

notes.explains: Rook c5 is a committal move because it may lead to a pawn endgame. If Black plays king d5 and then king c7, the c5 pawn is supported by b6, and White cannot make progress, resulting in a draw.
notes.teaches: When considering a move that forces a pawn endgame, you must accurately evaluate the resulting king and pawn structure. A supported passed pawn can secure a draw even if the opponent has a more active king.
notes.plans: If Black plays rook c5, the plan is to centralize the king and support the c-pawn, ensuring the position remains drawn.

notes.explains: White's a5 push is risky because Black can give up the a-pawn to gain king activity. After a5 bxa5, Black's king is closer to the center and the kingside, making it potentially winning for Black.
notes.teaches: The power of an outside passed pawn is not just in promotion but in the ability to deflect the opponent's king. Giving up the pawn can lead to a faster king march to the other side.
notes.plans: Black should be alert to such opportunities and be willing to sacrifice the outside pawn to activate the king.

notes.explains: After rook e1, Black must play rook d1 to kick the white king away from the center. If Black instead plays rook a1, White can win the b6 pawn and then invade with the king to d5, winning material.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, controlling the king's access to key central squares is crucial. A rook check can force the king back and prevent it from supporting pawn advances.
notes.plans: Black should use the rook to harass the white king and keep it away from the center, while maintaining the defense of the b6 pawn.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame, the activity of the kings is decisive. The rook on d1 gives a check that forces the enemy king away from the center, preventing it from reaching d5, where it would dominate and win pawns.
notes.teaches: Use checking moves to keep the enemy king out of the center. A centralized king is a huge asset in rook endgames, so every tempo that delays its advance is valuable.
notes.plans: After the king is driven back, continue with rook checks to maintain the king's passivity, then activate your own rook and king.

notes.explains: The natural move d5 allows the enemy rook to go to c6, which lets the enemy king reach e5. That king becomes very active, and even though you win the a4 pawn, the enemy king will recapture it soon, leaving you with a passive king and an active opponent.
notes.teaches: Before advancing a pawn, check whether it opens a path for the enemy king to become active. Sometimes the most natural move is a practical trap because it gives the opponent a hidden resource.
notes.plans: If you have already played d5 and the opponent responds with Rc6, look for ways to activate your own king or trade rooks to neutralize the opponent's activity.

notes.explains: An alternative was to play Ke6, activating the king. This also leads to a draw, but it is tricky because the opponent can create a dangerous passed pawn on the b-file. There is a brilliant resource: Rb5, which prepares to bring the king to f6 and also supports the d-pawn's advance, ensuring a trade of rooks or a perpetual check.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a rook on the fifth rank can be a powerful defensive resource, both cutting off the enemy king and supporting your own passed pawn. Look for such active defensive setups.
notes.plans: If the opponent threatens to queen a pawn, use your rook to give checks and force a trade of rooks, simplifying to a drawn pawn endgame with an active king.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, Black has an extra pawn but is passive. The key is to simplify by trading pawns, as the defender's drawing chances increase when fewer pawns remain.
notes.teaches: A rule of thumb in rook endgames: trade as many pawns as possible when defending, because the opponent will have fewer attacking resources.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade pawns and simplify the position, ideally by playing d4 to create counterplay and force pawn trades.

notes.explains: Black played h4, intending to trade pawns, but the immediate rook move to b4 was based on a miscalculation. The correct defensive resource was d4, which would have forced favorable trades.
notes.teaches: In time pressure, rely on concrete calculation rather than instinct; a move that seems to win a pawn may allow the opponent's rook to become active.
notes.plans: Instead of grabbing the g3 pawn, Black should have played d4, creating a passed pawn that distracts the white rook and king.

notes.explains: After the correct d4, Black's king can approach the queenside, and the white rook cannot both stop the d-pawn and defend the b5 pawn. This leads to a draw.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a passed pawn can serve as a deflection: if the opponent's rook leaves to capture it, other pawns become vulnerable.
notes.plans: Black should advance the d-pawn and use the king to support it, forcing White to choose between stopping the pawn and defending the b-pawn.

notes.explains: The seemingly drawn position after pawn trades is actually winning for White because the black king is cut off on the c-file, and White can build a bridge to promote the b-pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the defending king must be close enough to the passed pawn; being cut off by the enemy rook can turn a drawn position into a loss.
notes.plans: White should use the rook to cut off the black king and then employ the 'bridge' technique to shield the king from checks and promote the pawn.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, White has a passed b-pawn that is close to promotion, but the defending king is nearby. The key is to coordinate the rook and king to support the pawn while keeping the opponent's rook passive.
notes.teaches: The 'bridge' technique is a fundamental winning method in rook and pawn vs. rook endgames: the rook moves to the fourth rank to shield the king from checks, allowing the pawn to advance and promote.
notes.plans: White should aim to place the rook on the fourth rank (e.g., d4) to build the bridge, then advance the king and pawn to force promotion.

notes.explains: The defender can hold the draw by reaching the Philidor position, where the rook stays on the sixth rank (or even the eighth for a b-pawn) to prevent the king from approaching the pawn. This is a reliable drawing method.
notes.teaches: The Philidor position is a key drawing resource in rook endgames: keep the rook on the third or sixth rank to cut off the enemy king, and only use it to check from afar when necessary.
notes.plans: The defender should aim to place the rook on the sixth rank (or eighth for a b-pawn) and keep the king close to the pawn, ensuring the draw.

notes.explains: A seemingly small difference in checking squares can be decisive. Here, checking from d6 is winning because it forces the enemy king to a worse square, whereas checking from e7 allows the king to stay active and maintain the draw.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the choice of checking square matters: you want to drive the enemy king away from the pawn and keep your own rook active. Always consider which check gives the opponent the most limited options.
notes.plans: If given the chance, White should play the winning check (e.g., Rd6) to force the king away and then use the rook to protect the pawns and advance.

notes.explains: The winning method in this endgame involves using the king and rook to support the passed pawn, while the defender's rook is tied to blocking the pawn. The key is to advance the pawn with the support of the king, and if the defender tries to capture the pawn, the rook can deliver a decisive check or mate.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the king's activity is crucial. Use your king to support the passed pawn and to cut off the enemy king. If the defender's king is far away, you can often win by advancing the pawn and using your rook to protect it from behind.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawn with the support of your king. If the defender's rook tries to stop the pawn from the side, use your rook to shield the pawn and drive the enemy king away.

notes.explains: Even simple rook endgames contain hidden resources and pitfalls. The game showed that a natural move (Rg4) could have been met with a winning reply, while a different check would have lost the win.
notes.teaches: Always play endgames to the end, even seemingly simple ones, because there is always room for error. Look for the most precise moves, especially checks and rook placements, to avoid letting the opponent escape.

notes.explains: In the middlegame, a single mistake allowed the opponent to escape into a rook endgame with less material but active pieces, making conversion difficult.
notes.teaches: Even when winning, active pieces for the defender can create practical difficulties; conversion requires precise play.

notes.explains: In the rook endgame, black has two extra pawns, but white's active rooks and vulnerable black pawns (like b6 and f3) make the win non-trivial. The h7 passed pawn is not enough alone.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity and pawn weaknesses matter more than material count; simplifying trades can increase drawing chances for the defender.
notes.plans: Black should seek to stabilize the position, defend the weak pawns, and create a passed pawn while avoiding pawn trades that lead to simplification.

notes.explains: The move b5 was a mistake because it allowed a4, undermining the queenside pawn structure and increasing the likelihood of further pawn trades, which favors the defender.
notes.teaches: Avoid advancing pawns that can be undermined, especially when your pawns are already under attack; keep the structure solid.
notes.plans: Instead, play e5, which covers the b6 pawn with the rook on f6 and prevents the undermining with a4.

notes.explains: e5 was the best move because it maintains the pawn structure and covers b6, while the e5 pawn can be defended easily (e.g., with Re1, Re8, Re3, Rf5).
notes.teaches: When converting, choose moves that preserve your pawn structure and keep your pieces coordinated, even if they seem passive.
notes.plans: After e5, black can defend the e5 pawn and continue to improve the rook, keeping winning chances alive.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the choice between advancing the e-pawn or the b-pawn is critical. Advancing the b-pawn allows White to undermine the queenside pawn structure with a4, while e5 keeps the b6 pawn protected by the rook on f6 and avoids that weakness.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice of pawn breaks, consider which one leaves your pawn structure more solid and less vulnerable to undermining. Sometimes the move that seems to create a weakness (e5) is actually safer because it keeps your other pawns protected.
notes.plans: Play e5 to secure the b6 pawn, then use the rook to defend the e5 pawn if needed, and prepare to advance the h-pawn to create a passed pawn and distract the enemy king.

notes.explains: When defending, White can try to activate the rook to attack Black's pawns, for example with Rb3. Black must ensure all pawns are protected before making progress; otherwise, they will be constantly under attack.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the defender's active rook can create counterplay. The attacker must first stabilize the pawn structure and ensure every pawn is defended before trying to improve the position.
notes.plans: Black should play moves like Re6, Kg7, and then slowly improve, possibly trading rooks or advancing the c-pawn. White should look for active rook moves to harass Black's pawns.

notes.explains: With only one extra pawn and reduced material, the win is not clear over the board. The engine suggests h5 gives decent chances, but the position is complex and requires precise calculation.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames with a single extra pawn, the win is not automatic. You must create concrete threats, such as advancing the h-pawn, and be ready to calculate variations carefully.
notes.plans: Play h5 to create a passed pawn and generate winning chances, but be aware that the defender has resources. Continue to improve the king and rook while maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, black has only one extra pawn, and the reduced material means the win is not guaranteed. The engine suggests h5 gives black decent chances, but over the board it's unclear if it's winning because the pawns can easily be traded off.
notes.teaches: When material is reduced, even an extra pawn may not be enough to win if the opponent can force pawn trades. Assess the winning potential realistically, especially in rook endgames where drawing margins are wide.
notes.plans: Black should aim to keep the extra pawn and avoid trades that liquidate to a drawn pawn ending.

notes.explains: Black's plan was to play e5, Re8, a5, and Re6 to protect all pawns, then trade rooks and improve the king. But playing b5 allowed white's a4, which would force an immediate draw. White missed it, but later black's premature rook move led to losing a pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, before making a pawn move, check if it weakens your pawn structure or allows the opponent to force favorable trades. Protecting all pawns first is a sound strategy before improving the king.
notes.plans: Black should have kept the rook on c6 to protect the b-pawn and avoid the rook being attacked by Rd6.

notes.explains: After the mistake, black's pawns fell, and the game became a draw. The key difference was that if the black pawn were on f6 instead of g5, black could play f3, sacrificing a pawn to kick the white king away from g2 and h2, allowing checks from the side or back.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the placement of your pawns determines whether you can create mating nets or force the enemy king away. A pawn on f6 (or f5) can be used as a lever to open lines for the rook, while a pawn on g5 may not offer such resources.
notes.plans: If the pawn were on f6, black could aim for f3 to dislodge the white king and then use the rook to deliver checks.

notes.explains: The game continued for many moves with only kings and pawns, but the position was a theoretical draw, so the players agreed to a draw.
notes.teaches: In endgames, recognizing when a position is drawn is crucial to avoid unnecessary risk and to save half a point.
notes.plans: When you have a drawn endgame, simplify to a known drawn position and offer or accept a draw.

notes.explains: The speaker mentions that other games from the tournament were also interesting and educational, indicating a broader set of instructive endgames.
notes.teaches: Studying a variety of endgame positions, especially from high-level play, helps build pattern recognition and practical technique.
notes.plans: Review your own games and those of strong players to identify instructive endgame moments and learn from them.

notes.explains: Preparation should include studying your opponent's recent games and identifying their weaknesses, not just calculating opening lines. In this game, the player chose f4 in the Sicilian because the opponent had poor results against it.
notes.teaches: Understanding your opponent's weaknesses and your own strengths is as important as opening preparation. Use databases to find patterns in their play and choose openings that exploit them.
notes.plans: Before a game, review your opponent's recent games to spot recurring issues and select a line that targets those weaknesses.

notes.explains: In the Sicilian, after e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6, the move f4 is a sideline compared to more popular moves like Bg5 or Be3. The idea behind a4 is to prevent b5 and prepare Bc4, keeping the position in preparation.
notes.teaches: Early f4 in the Sicilian can be a viable surprise weapon, but be aware that theory evolves; check recent games to ensure your line is still sound.
notes.plans: If you play f4, follow up with a4 to restrain b5 and then develop the bishop to c4, aiming for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: In the resulting position after f4 and exchanges, there is a weak pawn on e5 and a weak square (likely d5) that Black can occupy. The question is whether to capture on e5 or maintain tension.
notes.teaches: When there is a weak pawn or square, consider whether capturing fixes the opponent's problems or gives them activity. Sometimes it's better to maintain pressure than to resolve the tension.
notes.plans: Instead of taking on e5, consider moves like Bb3 to keep the pressure and avoid giving the opponent's bishop a free diagonal.

notes.explains: In this position, taking on e5 with the bishop is unattractive because it fixes Black's weak pawn and opens a diagonal for Black's bishop, giving the opponent free gifts.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that solve your opponent's problems or grant them free activity; look for moves that maintain tension and keep their pieces passive.
notes.plans: Consider bishop b3 or bishop d5 to keep pressure and provoke weaknesses.

notes.explains: Bishop d5 is a provocative move: it offers a trade that Black should decline because taking allows White to recapture with the knight, attacking the queen and winning a pawn. Black's best is to ignore it and continue development, like castling.
notes.teaches: Use provocative moves to tempt the opponent into mistakes; if they decline, you still have a good position with active pieces.
notes.plans: If Black doesn't take on d5, continue developing and prepare to increase pressure.

notes.explains: After Black plays bishop g4, taking on e5 is still not desirable for the same reasons: it fixes Black's bad pawn and gives the bishop a good diagonal. Instead, king h1 is a useful prophylactic move, avoiding pins and preparing rook g1.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like king h1 can be strong because they prevent future tactics and prepare active plans like rook g1.
notes.plans: Play king h1, then prepare rook g1 to pressure the g-file and support a future pawn push.

notes.explains: In the game, White played queen f2, a provocative move inviting Black to take on d5. When Black did take, White recaptured and later played rook g1, creating serious pressure. Black's bishop e6 was an attempt to avoid worse, but White's pressure continued.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can provoke the opponent into taking a 'free' piece when the recapture gives you a strong initiative. Intermediate moves and pressure can be more valuable than material.
notes.plans: After recapturing on d5, continue with rook g1 and look for intermediate moves like bishop h6 to maintain the attack.

notes.explains: When White has a choice of recaptures, intermediate moves are crucial. Queen g3 is tempting but fails to knight h5, so bishop h6 is better, forcing g6 and creating further weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Always look for intermediate moves (checks, threats) before recapturing; they can improve your position or force concessions.
notes.plans: Play bishop h6, forcing g6, then decide whether to take on d5 or f8 based on the resulting position.

notes.explains: In this Najdorf position, the move Qg3 is tempting but flawed because Black can respond with Nh5, attacking the queen and disrupting White's plans. If White then plays Qg4, Black can play Be6, and even if White captures, g6 follows, leaving White's position undesirable.
notes.teaches: When considering a queen sortie, always check for tactical refutations like a knight fork or a pawn thrust that can harass the queen and gain time. Prefer moves that maintain harmony and avoid giving the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Instead of Qg3, consider Bh6, which forces g6 and then allows White to choose between taking on d5 or f8, with the latter being stronger.

notes.explains: In the game, Black played Qxc2, exchanging queens, which was a harsh decision. A better try was Qc4, keeping pressure on d5 and c2, and if White plays Rad1, Black can consider taking on a4. White would still be better, but Black would have more fighting chances.
notes.teaches: When behind, avoid simplifying into a worse endgame. Instead, keep pieces on the board and create imbalances or counterplay, even if the position remains difficult.
notes.plans: If Black had played Qc4, White could respond with Qd2, maintaining an edge while allowing Black some activity.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, White got everything desired: Rc1 and Black took on b2, which was a gift. White then went after the back rank. Black tried Rc2 to free the bishop, but White should have played Rb1, which would have been best, as after b5 and exchanges, White could push. Instead, White played a5, hoping to promote the a-pawn by eating b7 and a6.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, sometimes the most direct plan is to create a passed pawn and push it, but be careful not to neglect the opponent's counterplay. Rook activity on the b-file can be decisive.
notes.plans: White's plan is to advance the a-pawn, supported by the rook, aiming to create a passed pawn and eventually promote.

notes.explains: In the endgame, White brought the king closer to avoid checks and used a psychological trick by repeating moves, giving the opponent hope of a draw, but White had no intention of drawing. The win was straightforward: win the rook and then deliver checkmate.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, centralize your king and avoid unnecessary risks. Repeating moves can be a psychological tool to lull the opponent into false hope, but ensure you maintain the win.
notes.plans: Continue to improve the king, target the opponent's pawns, and force the exchange of rooks to reach a winning pawn endgame or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: In the Najdorf, White has a wide range of setup choices, including moves like Be3, Bg5, g4, h3, f4, Qf3, and others, depending on whether you plan to castle short or long. The speaker prepared a specific line with Be3, Bd3, Qf3, and Qh3, intending to castle short and push f4.
notes.teaches: When facing the Najdorf, it's important to have a concrete plan and be prepared for various black responses. The choice of setup should align with your intended castling side and pawn breaks.
notes.plans: White aims to develop with Be3, Bd3, Qf3, and Qh3, then castle short and play f4 to launch a kingside attack.

notes.explains: After Black plays b5 and b4, the knight on c3 is kicked back. The bishop on d3 is not ideally placed but is in a defensive role, guarding a weak pawn. The speaker notes that one piece often lags behind, and here it's the bishop on d3.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, it's common to have a piece that is temporarily passive. Recognize which piece is underperforming and either redeploy it or use it defensively while the rest of your pieces coordinate.
notes.plans: White should consider playing f3 to support the bishop on d3 and prepare for future pawn advances, or find a way to activate the bishop later.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf5, and White should not capture because Black recaptures with the knight, giving Black control of the d5 square. This is a common theme in the Sicilian: avoiding trades that hand your opponent key central squares.
notes.teaches: Be cautious about exchanging pieces if it allows your opponent to occupy a strong outpost like d5. In the Sicilian, the d5 square is often a critical weakness for White, so avoid giving it up without a concrete reason.
notes.plans: Instead of capturing on f5, White should retreat the knight, for example to g3, maintaining pressure and keeping control of key squares.

notes.explains: Black plays g6 and Bg7, fianchettoing the bishop. The speaker considers d5 and f5 as potential moves for Black, but notes that f5 is interesting for White if Black plays d5, as White can respond with Bg5. Also, if Black tries h5-h4, White can still push f5 or play Nc4 to create play.
notes.teaches: In the Najdorf, Black often aims for d5 as a freeing break. White should be alert to this and have responses ready, such as Bg5 to pin or pressure. Also, when Black fianchettoes, White can still pursue a kingside pawn storm with f5.
notes.plans: White considers playing f5 as a pawn break, but is wary of Black's possible d5 or castling. Alternatively, White can play a normal move like castling, or try a tricky idea to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: In the Najdorf Sicilian, Black's d5 break is a key thematic move that Black wants to achieve. White must be aware of this and take measures to prevent or punish it.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, especially the Najdorf, always respect Black's d5 break. If you allow it without preparation, Black can free their position and gain counterplay.
notes.plans: Consider moves that either prevent d5 or make it costly, such as playing a move that attacks the d5 square or prepares to meet d5 with exd5.

notes.explains: White played Nc4 to attack the d6 pawn, setting a trap: if Black plays d5, White can capture on d5. Black wisely avoided this by playing Qc7, a flexible move that defends d6 and keeps options open.
notes.teaches: When you attack a pawn, you may set traps, but be prepared for your opponent to avoid them. Always have a plan if they don't fall for it.
notes.plans: After Nc4 and Qc7, White should castle short, as long casting would leave the king vulnerable to Black's attack, which is more advanced.

notes.explains: In the position after short castle, Black threatens d5, which would be strong. White must take this threat seriously. Playing f5 would allow d5, and after exd5, the bishop on g7 is hanging, so White would have to play Qe2, but then the bishop is still trapped. Therefore, White should simply take on e5 with the f-pawn.
notes.teaches: Always consider your opponent's threats. If they have a strong move like d5, you must address it. Sometimes the best way is to capture a central pawn, even if it seems simple.
notes.plans: Play fxe5, removing the d5 threat and opening lines. Then develop and improve your pieces.

notes.explains: After fxe5, White should look to improve their position. The move a3 is best because it prepares to expand on the queenside, creating weaknesses in Black's camp. If Black captures on a3, White recaptures and gains a target to attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development or a space advantage, look for ways to open files for your rooks. Pawn moves like a3 can provoke weaknesses and create targets.
notes.plans: Play a3, and if Black plays a5, then consider taking on a5 and following up with Bd2, aiming to open the a-file for the rook.

notes.explains: After a3 a5, White can take on a5 and then play Bd2. Black has a tricky resource: b3. If White takes on a1, Black can recapture and later play Nc5, targeting weaknesses. This shows that even when you think you are winning material, you must be alert to counterplay.
notes.teaches: When you win material, be aware of your opponent's counterplay. Sometimes they can create weaknesses or threats that make the material gain less significant.
notes.plans: After a3 a5, consider taking on a5 and then Bd2, but be ready for Black's b3 idea. If Black plays b3, you may need to recapture on a1 and then deal with the resulting weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this position, the queen on c5 is misplaced because it is exposed and can be harassed, even if it defends a pawn. The defender's task is to exploit such awkward placement.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's queen is misplaced, look for ways to gain time by attacking it, even if it means not immediately recapturing or defending a pawn.
notes.plans: Consider moves that attack the queen and create weaknesses in the opponent's camp, such as b3 to undermine the pawn structure.

notes.explains: When your bishop is attacked, you don't have to retreat it one square. There might be a stronger intermediate move that creates a greater threat or improves your position.
notes.teaches: Always look for intermediate moves (zwischenzugs) before automatically retreating an attacked piece. A move that forces the opponent to respond can be more valuable than a passive retreat.
notes.plans: Consider moves like b3 that create weaknesses or attack the opponent's pieces, rather than simply moving the bishop back.

notes.explains: In this position, the bishop on e4 is a monster attacking the king, and even if material is equal, the activity of that bishop makes the position unpleasant for the defender.
notes.teaches: Piece activity can outweigh material considerations. When your opponent has a powerfully placed piece, look for ways to neutralize it or avoid allowing it to settle.
notes.plans: Consider intermediate moves to prevent the opponent from establishing a strong piece on an outpost like e4.

notes.explains: In this rook and bishop endgame, the position is likely drawn but requires precise play. The presence of weaknesses and the activity of the bishops matter.
notes.teaches: In endgames with bishops of opposite colors (or similar), precise play is essential; even drawn positions can be lost if you are not careful. Look for ways to activate your pieces and create threats.
notes.plans: Consider pushing pawns to create weaknesses, or bringing the king into the game. Avoid moves that allow the opponent's pieces to become active.

notes.explains: In this endgame, the move b3 is strong because it creates a passed pawn or a threat, and if the opponent doesn't take, you can follow up with rook e3. The key is to create a concrete threat that forces the opponent's response.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for pawn breaks that create passed pawns or weaknesses. Sometimes it's better to make a waiting move that sets up a threat rather than an immediate capture.
notes.plans: Play b3 to create a passed pawn or a threat, and if the opponent doesn't take, follow up with rook e3 to support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the white rook on b1 is passive but solid: it prevents black from making progress, while black's king cannot penetrate. The key is to keep the rook inactive but well-placed, and only activate it when black commits.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a passive rook is the best defense; it can restrain the opponent's pawns and king without needing to be active. Patience and waiting moves are often the correct strategy in rook endgames.
notes.plans: Place the king on e2, keep the rook on b1, and wait. If black moves the rook away, then advance the b-pawn to b4 and b5.

notes.explains: After black takes on b2, white must choose between giving up the pawn or allowing the black king to infiltrate. The decision is based on calculation: white can give up the pawn if the resulting position is a draw.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, you must calculate concrete variations when deciding whether to hold a pawn or give it up for activity. Sometimes sacrificing a pawn is necessary to activate your pieces and reach a drawn position.
notes.plans: Play Rc5 to activate the rook, and if the black king goes to f6, consider taking on e4 or playing g4, depending on the precise calculation.

notes.explains: When white has a rook and pawns versus rook, the defender can often hold by creating a fortress-like structure. The key is to keep the king active and the rook ready to counterattack.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the defender should aim to create a position where the opponent cannot make progress, often by using the king to blockade pawns and the rook to cut off the opponent's king.
notes.plans: If black pushes h3, play Kf4 and then Kg4 to pick up the pawn, while keeping the rook active to prevent promotion.

notes.explains: After rook takes on h2, white can use the king to attack the pawns, creating a zugzwang-like situation where black's moves worsen their position. The white king on g4 ties down the black rook and pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the king can be a powerful attacking piece against pawns. By creating threats, you can force the opponent into zugzwang, where any move loses material or allows progress.
notes.plans: Move the king to g4 to attack the h-pawn, and use the rook to control key files. If black moves the rook, pick up the pawns.

notes.explains: In this rook-and-pawn endgame, the position is nearly drawn because both kings are cut off and the remaining pawn is a g-pawn, which offers little winning chances. The defender can hold by keeping the king close to the pawn and waiting.
notes.teaches: When defending a pawn-down rook endgame, keep your king in front of the pawn and use waiting moves with the rook to maintain the cut-off. Recognize that a g-pawn (or edge pawn) often makes the defense easier because the attacking king has less room.
notes.plans: The defender should keep the king near the pawn, use rook checks from the side, and be ready to give up the pawn at the right moment to reach a drawn king-and-pawn versus king endgame.

notes.explains: After the exchange on e4, Black has a choice between h3 and hxg3. Taking on g3 leads to a position where White must return the king to f2, and Black will win the g2 pawn anyway, but the resulting endgame is a draw because the kings are cut off and the pawn is a g-pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, sometimes it is better to win a pawn even if it leads to a drawn position, rather than risk a losing pawn structure. Evaluate whether the resulting endgame is drawn before committing to a capture.
notes.plans: If Black takes on g3, White should play Kf2, then use the rook to harass Black's king while keeping the king close to the pawn. The game will likely end in a draw after the pawn falls.

notes.explains: In the game, Black played h3, and White responded with Kf3 to keep the king close to the pawn. Black then played Kg4, a strong move that threatens to penetrate with the king if White doesn't respond accurately. White missed the best defense, Kg4, which would have kept the draw.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, king activity is paramount. Even when defending, the king must stay close to the pawn to prevent the opponent's king from infiltrating. A missed king move can turn a drawn position into a lost one.
notes.plans: White should aim to keep the king on f2 or f3, ready to approach the pawn if needed. Black should use the king to support the pawn's advance, but must be careful not to allow counterplay.

notes.explains: The endgame is very drawish because the pawn is on the fifth rank and the defending king is well placed. The attacking side can keep pushing the pawn, but the defender has an easy time holding with accurate king and rook placement.
notes.teaches: Recognize when an endgame is a 'super draw' and simplify accordingly. Even if the opponent keeps pushing, as long as you maintain the correct defensive setup, you can force the draw.
notes.plans: The defender should continue to give checks and keep the king in front of the pawn. Eventually, the pawn can be given up to reach a drawn king and pawn endgame.

notes.explains: In a queen versus pawn endgame where the pawn is one step from queening, the queen alone cannot permanently stop the pawn or make progress by checking or blockading. The defending king can always threaten promotion, so the queen must use a specific technique to win.
notes.teaches: The queen cannot win such positions by just checking or trying to blockade; the king must be brought closer to support the queen in capturing the pawn.
notes.plans: Use the queen to force the enemy king to a square where the pawn cannot promote, then bring your own king closer step by step.

notes.explains: The key winning method is to force the enemy king to a specific square (here, g8) where the pawn cannot promote because the king blocks it. This gives the attacking side a free tempo to move their king closer.
notes.teaches: By forcing the enemy king to block its own pawn, you gain a tempo to bring your king closer. This is the fundamental 'check procedure' in queen vs pawn endgames.
notes.plans: Use queen checks and threats to drive the enemy king to the square in front of the pawn, then advance your king.

notes.explains: The attacking king should stay away from the pawn initially. If the king steps too close (e.g., to g8) prematurely, the defending king can step closer, gaining time. Instead, the king should approach from squares that do not allow the defender to approach.
notes.teaches: In queen versus pawn, the attacking king must avoid moving to squares that allow the defending king to gain opposition or approach the pawn.
notes.plans: Move the king to squares like e7, f7, g6, h7, etc., while the queen controls the key squares.

notes.explains: When the queen is close enough, the key move is to place it on the rank directly behind the pawn (e.g., queen g6). This prevents the pawn from promoting because the king has stepped away, and it also sets up a decisive check.
notes.teaches: The queen should often be placed on the rank behind the pawn to cut off the pawn's advance and prepare a mating net.
notes.plans: After queen g6, the defending king is forced to f8, then queen f6 check wins the pawn or forces mate.

notes.explains: Once the queen is on g6, the check queen f6 is powerful because it also attacks the pawn on g7. The defending king cannot step away from the pawn without losing it, so it is forced to g8, allowing the attacking king to approach.
notes.teaches: Look for checks that also attack the pawn; this restricts the defender's options and forces the king to a favorable square.
notes.plans: Repeat the checking procedure to drive the king back and bring your king closer each time.

notes.explains: There is a faster method once the queen is close: queen f7. This move threatens mate and forces the king to h8 or h6, after which the queen can deliver mate or win the pawn.
notes.teaches: When the queen is close, look for direct mating threats that force the king to a corner, simplifying the win.
notes.plans: If king h6, queen g8 mate; if king h8, queen h5 check forces g8, then bring the king.

notes.explains: If the defending king tries to promote to a knight, the queen and king can still force mate. The knight is no escape because the queen controls key squares and the king supports.
notes.teaches: Even if the pawn promotes to a knight, the queen versus knight endgame is winning with proper technique.
notes.plans: Use the queen to check and drive the king to the corner, then mate with the king's support.

notes.explains: When the enemy king is very close to the pawn, precise calculation is needed. There is a risk of stalemate if you are careless, so you must always ensure the enemy king has a legal move when you are not giving check.
notes.teaches: In queen versus pawn endgames, when the king is near the pawn, avoid moves that stalemate the opponent. Calculate carefully to give checks that maintain the opponent's legal moves while you improve your king.
notes.plans: Calculate the sequence of checks and king moves to force checkmate, ensuring the enemy king always has a legal move until the final checkmate.

notes.explains: In time scrambles, you don't need to win the pawn; you can just keep checking the enemy king until the opponent runs out of time. Also, the 50-move rule is not a concern because the win is always achievable within the limit.
notes.teaches: In blitz, if you have a queen versus pawn, you can simply give perpetual checks to run the clock. The technique is always fast enough to avoid the 50-move rule.
notes.plans: If low on time, focus on giving checks rather than trying to win the pawn, and trust that the win is achievable well within 50 moves.

notes.explains: The technique for queen versus pawn works for pawns on the knight, bishop, center, and queen files due to board symmetry. However, it fails for rook's pawns because the corner of the board creates a stalemate fortress.
notes.teaches: Recognize that the queen-versus-pawn technique is symmetric for most files, but rook's pawns are a special drawing fortress if the defender plays correctly.
notes.plans: When facing a rook's pawn, be aware that the win is not possible if the defender keeps the king in the corner; instead, seek other winning chances or accept the draw.

notes.explains: With a rook pawn on the seventh rank and the defending king in the corner, the attacking king cannot advance because the game ends in stalemate. The defender simply shuffles the king between the corner and the adjacent square, and the attacker can make no progress.
notes.teaches: In queen versus rook pawn on the seventh rank, if the defending king reaches the corner, the game is a draw due to stalemate. The attacker cannot force the king out of the corner, and any attempt to bring the queen closer fails because the defender can either stay in the corner or move to a square that attacks the queen.
notes.plans: If you are the defender, keep your king in the corner and only move to the adjacent square when necessary. If you are the attacker, recognize the draw and look for exceptions where the defending king is not in the corner.

notes.explains: The rook pawn and bishop pawn cases are symmetric: the same drawing ideas apply on both sides of the board. The defender's king can run to either corner (a8 or h8) and use the stalemate trick.
notes.teaches: When defending against a queen with a pawn on the seventh rank, always aim for the corner that is the same file as the pawn. The stalemate resource is available on both wings.
notes.plans: In similar positions, remember the symmetry and apply the same defensive ideas regardless of which side of the board the pawn is on.

notes.explains: In rook-pawn endgames, the defending king can often reach the corner and force a draw via stalemate ideas, especially with a bishop's pawn. The drawing mechanism is symmetric: the defender heads to the corner square in front of the pawn.
notes.teaches: Recognize the stalemate resource in rook-pawn endgames: the defender aims to get to the corner, and if the attacker cannot avoid the stalemate, it's a draw.
notes.plans: As the defender, rush the king to the corner (e.g., h8 or a8) to set up stalemate chances.

notes.explains: When the attacking king is far from the pawn, direct pawn promotion is not enough; the queen must be used to create mating threats. The queen needs to be placed actively, often by checking and then inching closer to the enemy king, to support the king's approach.
notes.teaches: In queen vs pawn endgames, use the queen to give checks and gradually improve its position, forcing the defending king to move and allowing your own king to advance.
notes.plans: Start with a check (e.g., Qg4+), then bring the queen closer (e.g., Qf5, Qg5) while the king advances, aiming to reach a key square that delivers mate or wins the pawn.

notes.explains: The ultimate winning idea is a checkmate pattern where the attacking king steps to a square like f7, cutting off the defending king's escape and creating unavoidable mate threats. This position is a key pattern to remember.
notes.teaches: Memorize the mating pattern: with the queen on f5 and the king on e6, stepping to f7 can be decisive, as it threatens mate and leaves the defender with no useful checks.
notes.plans: Aim to reach that mating net: queen on f5, king on e6, then Kf7! when the pawn queens, leading to mate or winning the queen.

notes.explains: With the queen on f5 and the black king near the queening square, the black king can step to e6, and after White promotes, the queen and king coordinate to deliver mate. The key defensive square for Black is f7, where the king is safe from checks and the mating net is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: In queen versus pawn endgames, the stronger side must use the king to support the queen in a mating net, often stepping to a square like f7 that covers all checking squares and threatens mate.
notes.plans: From the initial position, play Qg4+ Kf7, Qf5+ Kg7, then Ke6, followed by Qg5+ and Kf7, setting up the mating net.

notes.explains: If the black king is on h8 instead, Black can transpose back to the known winning idea with Qf5 and Ke6, or use Qd7 with the idea of Ke6 and mate on f7. The simplest is to return to the familiar pattern.
notes.teaches: When the opponent deviates, look for transpositions to known winning setups rather than improvising.
notes.plans: After Kh8, play Qf5, then Ke6, and proceed with the same mating net as before.

notes.explains: The four squares f7, g6, and their counterparts are crucial because from them the black king can reach the mating net. Squares like d4 are too far away, so the king cannot get to the key squares in time.
notes.teaches: In queen versus pawn endgames, the stronger king must be within a 'box' of key squares to win; otherwise the defender can draw by stalemate or other resources.
notes.plans: Aim to get the king to one of the four key squares before the pawn promotes.

notes.explains: For the rook pawn, even if the king cannot reach the most comfortable key square (e6), reaching a slightly less ideal square (e7) works just as well because the critical square is f7. The winning idea is identical.
notes.teaches: In these endgames, the exact key square reached matters less than being able to touch the critical squares. Don't be deterred by awkward king positions if you can still reach the essential squares.
notes.plans: If the king is on e7, play queen f5 and then king e7, following the same plan as from e6.

notes.explains: For the bishop pawn, the winning technique is more complex. The key is to get the king to g6. If the king can reach g6, black can force a checkmate even after white promotes, using the queen to trap the king.
notes.teaches: Bishop pawn endgames have different key squares than rook pawns. Here, reaching g6 is essential for the win; if you cannot get there, the position is likely drawn.
notes.plans: With black to move, play king f5, then after white's king move, play queen g5 check, and then king g6 to set up the mating net.

notes.explains: In the bishop pawn endgame, if it is white to move, the position is a draw because white can step out of the way and prevent black from reaching g6. Black's checks are insufficient because the white king escapes.
notes.teaches: The evaluation of these endgames can depend on whose turn it is. If the defender can prevent the attacker from reaching the key square, the result changes.
notes.plans: If white to move, step the king away to avoid the key square and aim for a draw. If black to move, immediately head for g6.

notes.explains: When the stronger side's king is far from the pawn, a single move may not suffice; a precise sequence is needed. In the given puzzle, the winning idea is to play the king to b5, which prevents the enemy king from crossing to the other side of the board, thereby cutting off its escape route.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the key is not to approach the pawn directly but to restrict the enemy king's movement. A distant king move can be decisive if it denies the opponent access to a drawing zone.
notes.plans: After king b5, if the enemy king tries to promote, use checks to drive it away, but be ready to switch to the king-side mating net if the opponent tries to escape.

notes.explains: In these positions, the defender may have drawing resources by running to the side of the board where the stronger side's king is far away. For example, if the stronger side's king is on the long side, the defender can sometimes hide on the short side, avoiding the mating net.
notes.teaches: When defending, look for ways to flee to the side of the board where the enemy king is less effective. The defender's goal is to avoid being checkmated and to force a draw by reaching a stalemate or perpetual check.
notes.plans: If the stronger side tries to bring the king closer, the defender should run to the opposite side, using the pawn as a shield and seeking a draw.

notes.explains: In a queen vs. pawn endgame, the defending king's path to the corner for stalemate is critical. If the queen can cut off access to that corner, the defender's drawing resource disappears.
notes.teaches: When the defender cannot reach the stalemating corner, the attacking side wins if they can control the key squares that prevent the king's approach. The square c6 is often the critical control point.
notes.plans: The attacker should aim to place the queen to control the key squares, then bring the king closer to support the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: With a lone a-pawn on the seventh rank, the defender's king can hide in front of the pawn, creating stalemate threats. The winning method is to use the queen's diagonal power to force the enemy king in front of the pawn, then deliver mate using the pawn as a shield.
notes.teaches: When the pawn is on the seventh, aim to force the defending king to the corner in front of the pawn, then use checks along the diagonal to drive it to the edge and mate.
notes.plans: Play Qh6, forcing Kg8, then Qg6+ Kh8, and Qf7#.

notes.explains: Choosing the wrong first move (e.g., Qf1) allows the defending king to approach the pawn and reach the sixth rank, where it can set up a stalemate defense. The correct move (Qf5) prevents the king from getting close and wins.
notes.teaches: In queen vs pawn, the queen must cut off the enemy king's approach to the pawn. A distant queen can be harassed, allowing the king to reach a drawing fortress.
notes.plans: Place the queen on a square that controls the key escape routes, preventing the king from approaching the pawn.

notes.explains: When the defending king reaches the sixth rank in front of the pawn, the attacker must be careful: if the queen takes the pawn, the king can be stalemated. The defender can sacrifice the pawn to force a draw.
notes.teaches: Recognize stalemate patterns: if the queen captures the pawn and the enemy king has no legal moves, it's a draw. Sometimes the defender can give up the pawn to reach a stalemate.
notes.plans: If the king is on h6 and the pawn on a7, avoid taking the pawn immediately; instead, use checks to drive the king away before capturing.

notes.explains: In queen versus pawn endgames, when the pawn is not on the seventh rank, the stronger side can often use checks to bring the king closer and win the pawn. If the defending king tries to hold the pawn, the queen can blockade it, and if the pawn is on the seventh rank, there may be mating threats.
notes.teaches: Use checking sequences to improve your king's position and force the enemy king away from the pawn. When the pawn is on the seventh rank, look for mating patterns rather than just trying to stop the pawn.
notes.plans: Bring the king up to support the queen, using checks to drive the enemy king away, then capture the pawn or deliver mate.

notes.explains: If the pawn is on the seventh rank, stalemate is not a concern for the stronger side; instead, the defending king may be in zugzwang, forced to move to a worse square, allowing the queen to infiltrate and win the pawn.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the defender is in zugzwang and use it to your advantage. In queen versus pawn, the seventh-rank pawn often gives the stronger side winning chances because the defender's king has limited moves.
notes.plans: Force the defending king to move to a square where the queen can capture the pawn or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: In queen versus pawn endgames, the key is to prevent the pawn from queening while also avoiding stalemate. The stronger side should use the queen to control key squares and bring the king into the action.
notes.teaches: Master the basic technique of queen versus pawn: use checks to improve your king's position, blockade the pawn, and then bring the king up to win the pawn. Be aware of tricky cases where the pawn is far advanced or the defending king is close.
notes.plans: Practice these endgames to recognize the winning methods and avoid common pitfalls.

notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez Marshall Attack, the move order matters: Black must castle before playing d5, because if d6 is played first, White can avoid the Marshall. Castling first keeps the option of d5 in one move.
notes.teaches: When preparing an opening as Black, pay attention to move order to ensure your intended setup is available. Delaying a key pawn break can allow the opponent to sidestep it.
notes.plans: After ...O-O, if White plays c3, Black can play ...d5, entering the Marshall Attack. If White avoids it with a4 or other moves, Black should be ready for a different type of game.

notes.explains: After the main Marshall moves, White faces a critical choice between d3 and d4. The old main line with d4 allows Black's ...g5 idea after Rook e4, which creates counterplay and gains space, making White's rook awkward.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, a single tempo can be decisive. Black's ...g5 in the Marshall not only prevents Rook h4 but also prepares ...Bf5, attacking the rook and gaining time.
notes.plans: If White plays d4, Black should look for ...g5 and ...Bf5 to harass the rook. If White plays d3, the rook is protected, so Black needs a different plan, often with ...Bf5 immediately.

notes.explains: The shift from d4 to d3 in the Marshall is because after d3, if Black tries the same ...g5 idea, White's rook on e4 is protected by the pawn, so Black's tactics don't work. This makes d3 more solid for White.
notes.teaches: When choosing between similar moves, consider how they affect your opponent's tactical resources. A small difference like a pawn protecting a piece can change the evaluation of a line.
notes.plans: White's d3 aims to neutralize Black's ...g5 resource. Black must then find alternative plans, such as ...Bf5, to develop and create pressure.

notes.explains: White is an exchange down but has two dangerous connected passed pawns on e5 and f6. Straightforward pawn pushes fail because the black rook can stop them: e6 allows Rxe6, f7 allows Rf4, and king moves like Ke3 allow Rxe5 followed by Rf4, covering the queening square.
notes.teaches: In rook versus pawns endgames, the side with pawns must coordinate king and pawns; the rook's ability to attack pawns from the side or rear is powerful. A quiet move that brings a piece to a key square can be stronger than an immediate pawn advance.
notes.plans: Play Nc3, preparing to centralize the knight on d5 or e3 to support the pawns and block the rook's checks. Then advance the pawns with the king's support.

notes.explains: After Nc3, if Black plays Rf4, White is forced to play Nd5. If Black then plays Re4, attacking the e5 pawn, White must choose the correct king move. Kf3 fails because after Rxe5, the rook can go to f5 and stop the f-pawn. The correct move is Kd3, because if Black takes on e5, White has the stunning f7, and if the rook goes to f5, White has Ne7+ forking the king and rook.
notes.teaches: King placement is critical in pawn races: the king must support the pawns and avoid squares where the rook can both attack the pawn and cover the promotion square. A tactical resource like a fork can turn the tables when the rook tries to stop a pawn.
notes.plans: After Kd3, if Rxe5, play f7; if Rf5, play Ne7+ winning the rook. Then promote the f-pawn.

notes.explains: In the other main line, after Nc3 Black plays Ra5, attacking the e5 pawn from the side. White's natural e6 fails to Rxe5, so White must find a deeper idea: play f7, and when Black plays Rf5 to stop the pawn, White has a beautiful resource that saves the game.
notes.teaches: When a rook attacks a pawn from the side, the pawns can still advance if the king or other pieces can create tactical threats. Look for moves that create dual threats: advancing a pawn while also preparing a fork or check.
notes.plans: After f7 and Rf5, find the winning move (likely a knight fork or a king move that wins the rook). Then promote the pawn.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, the rook is tied to defending the e6 pawn, and the white king is trying to penetrate. The key is to use the king and rook in coordination to create threats that overload the defense.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's rook is passively defending a pawn, look for ways to use your king to support an advance or create a fork. A well-timed knight move can exploit the rook's immobility.
notes.plans: Play f7 to force the rook to react, then use the knight to create a fork if the rook captures. If the rook takes the knight, the king can recapture and the pawn promotes.

notes.explains: With a passed pawn on the h-file, the immediate bishop to b8 fails because the black king can catch the pawn and the d5 pawn falls, leading to a draw. The winning idea is to use the bishop to create mating threats or win the queen.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, sometimes the direct approach is insufficient; look for tactical resources that involve the king's position. A bishop can be sacrificed to deflect the king or to set up a skewer.
notes.plans: Play d6 to force a capture. If the pawn captures, use the bishop to give check and then promote with mate threats. If the king captures, use the bishop to control light squares and force the king to a square where a skewer wins the queen.

notes.explains: After the king captures on d6, the bishop must be placed on e8, not d5, because d5 allows the black king to escape to c6 and avoid the skewer. The bishop on e8 controls the light squares and forces the king to d5, where the skewer works.
notes.teaches: When setting up a skewer, the placement of the piece is critical. You must control the escape squares of the enemy king to force it into the skewer.
notes.plans: Play bishop e8, then after the pawn promotes, if the king goes to d5, play bishop c6 to force the king to take and then queen a8 wins the queen. If the king tries e5, there is a decisive move.

notes.explains: In this composed endgame, White's king and bishop coordinate to force the black king onto light squares, where it becomes vulnerable to a decisive bishop check or a skewer that wins the queen. The key is to restrict the black king's movement and drive it to the wrong-colored squares.
notes.teaches: Artistic endgames often require forcing the opponent's king to specific squares by controlling the escape squares with your pieces. Look for ways to use checks and threats to herd the king into a mating net or a tactical shot.
notes.plans: Continue to use checks and threats to force the black king to light squares, then deliver the final bishop move that wins the queen or checkmates.

notes.explains: In a pawn race, White's only winning idea is to push the pawn, but Black can stop it by placing the bishop on the diagonal. The critical moment comes when White must find a deflection to remove the bishop from the promotion square's control.
notes.teaches: When promoting a pawn, always consider deflection tactics to remove the defender from the key square. A bishop that controls the promotion square can be deflected by a check or a threat that forces it to move.
notes.plans: Push the pawn, and when the bishop blocks the path, use a bishop move to deflect it, then promote with check if possible.

notes.explains: In this position, the natural-looking pawn push h6 fails because the black king can approach and capture the pawn, drawing. Instead, the winning idea is to use the bishop to control the key diagonal, preventing the king from stopping the pawn.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, the placement of the bishop is crucial. Sometimes the obvious pawn move is wrong because it allows the enemy king to get in front of the pawn; instead, use the bishop to control the squares the king needs to cross.
notes.plans: Place the bishop on a diagonal that prevents the black king from approaching the pawn, then support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: The bishop on d6 is the key defensive piece for Black, stopping the passed h-pawn and covering critical squares. White's winning attempts fail if this bishop remains active.
notes.teaches: In endgames with passed pawns, identify the defender's key piece and look for ways to deflect or eliminate it.
notes.plans: White should seek a deflection tactic to remove the bishop from d6, enabling the h-pawn to advance.

notes.explains: Candidate moves like bishop d2, bishop e1, h4, and bishop b4 fail because Black's bishop on d6 can still stop the pawn or White's king is not close enough to support.
notes.teaches: When calculating, consider all defensive resources of the opponent, especially the bishop's ability to control key squares from a distance.
notes.plans: Reject insufficient moves and search for a more forcing idea that removes the bishop from d6.

notes.explains: The move c5 is a deflection: if Black's bishop takes on c5, White's h-pawn can advance; if it doesn't, White's c-pawn promotes. This forces the bishop away from its ideal defensive post.
notes.teaches: Deflection tactics can force the defender's piece to abandon a key square, allowing your passed pawn to advance.
notes.plans: After c5, if the bishop takes, push h6 and support the pawn; if the bishop declines, push c6 and c7.

notes.explains: Against bishop d4, Black threatens ...Kg5 and ...Kh6 to capture the h-pawn. White must find a move that both stops this plan and keeps the pawn rolling. The winning idea is to use the bishop to control the key squares from a different angle.
notes.teaches: When the opponent threatens to approach your passed pawn with the king, you must either create counterplay or use your pieces to control the squares the king needs.
notes.plans: Play a move that prevents ...Kg5, such as a bishop check or a move that covers g5, while maintaining the h-pawn's advance.

notes.explains: In this endgame, the bishop is tied to the long diagonal, and a pin on that diagonal prevents it from leaving. The pawn on h7 is far advanced, so even if the black king checks, the pawn cannot be stopped from promoting.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is on the seventh rank, a pin can immobilize the defender, making promotion unstoppable. Look for pins that restrict the enemy piece's ability to stop the pawn.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to promotion, using the pin to keep the bishop from interfering.

notes.explains: White's d-pawn is about to promote, but black has a defensive resource: g4, which covers key squares and prepares a fork on g6 if the knight goes to c5. This resource must be seen before committing to d7.
notes.teaches: Before pushing a passed pawn, calculate the opponent's defensive resources, including counterplay that can fork the queen or force a drawn opposite-colored bishop endgame.
notes.plans: White should consider h6 to prevent black's defensive setup, while black uses g4 and g6 to create counterplay.

notes.explains: Promoting to a knight is insufficient because black can force a trade into an opposite-colored bishop endgame, which is a theoretical draw. The bishop on the wrong color (light-squared) with a dark h8 promotion square means no winning chances.
notes.teaches: When promoting, consider the resulting endgame. If the promotion square is the wrong color for the bishop, the position may be drawn even with an extra piece.
notes.plans: White must find a way to promote to a queen while avoiding black's drawing resources.

notes.explains: In this endgame, even without the extra pawn the position is a theoretical draw, so precise play is required to keep winning chances. The knight on d8 is not possible, and the bishop on c8 is the wrong color, so black can neutralize threats like knight takes e7.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a material advantage is not enough to win; the bishop's color and the placement of pieces determine whether a position is winning or drawn.
notes.plans: White should look for forcing moves that restrict the black king and create threats, such as h6 to prevent the king from returning to the eighth rank, and then consider checks like bishop e4.

notes.explains: After bishop e4 check, black has several king moves, but only one square avoids the fork. Moving to f5 or f4 allows knight c5 or knight d6 to stop the pawn, while g4 and h5 allow knight f6, which is winning for black. The only safe square is h7 (or similar) where no fork is possible.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn vs knight endgames, the king must choose squares that avoid knight forks and allow the pawn to promote. Always calculate the opponent's knight checks and forks before moving the king.
notes.plans: White should aim to promote the pawn while keeping the black king cut off, and black should try to get the king to a square where it can stop the pawn without being forked.

notes.explains: In the next puzzle, the first move is h5 to create a passed pawn and clear the way for the e or g pawn. If black plays king takes e3, h6 is tempting but black can take on e5 and cover h8, so it's not good. Instead, white should push the passed pawns, but not e6 immediately because bishop a3 stops it. The correct sequence involves knight c5 check to deflect the bishop, then e6.
notes.teaches: Passed pawns must be pushed, but timing is crucial. Sometimes a check or a deflection is needed to clear the path for the pawn. Avoid moves that allow the opponent to blockade the pawn.
notes.plans: White should play h5, then after black's response, use knight c5 check to force the king away, then push e6 to promote.

notes.explains: In this endgame, White's passed pawns on the e- and g-files are the main threats, but Black's bishop can stop them from specific squares like a3. The key is to find a move that creates a decisive passed pawn while also neutralizing the bishop's defensive role.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple passed pawns, look for a move that not only advances one but also restricts the opponent's defensive pieces. Sometimes the most forcing move is not the most obvious one.
notes.plans: White should aim to create a passed pawn on the e-file or g-file, but must first deal with the bishop's ability to block. A move like knight c5 might be a resource to deflect the bishop or support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: After Black captures on h5, White has a choice: create a passed pawn on the g-file with g6 or on the e-file with e6. The engine might not immediately see the winning idea, but human understanding of pawn majorities and outside passed pawns is crucial.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, creating an outside passed pawn can be decisive because it pulls the opponent's king away. Even if the engine doesn't immediately show it, the principle of the most distant passed pawn is a powerful guide.
notes.plans: White should play g6 to create a passed pawn on the g-file, which will distract Black's king and bishop, allowing White's other pawns to advance.

notes.explains: Black's bishop is well placed on e3, controlling key squares and stopping the e-pawn. White's knight is not fast enough on b8, and the position might be a draw if White only focuses on the e- and g-pawns. However, White has a hidden resource: the a-pawn.
notes.teaches: When the obvious plans fail, look for less obvious pawns that can become passed. A pawn on the opposite wing can be the key to winning because it forces the opponent to split their defenses.
notes.plans: White should use the a-pawn as a decoy. A move like knight b4 might force Black to capture, after which a4 creates a passed pawn that the bishop cannot stop alone.

notes.explains: In the final phase, White's a-pawn is racing against Black's d-pawn. White must find precise moves to avoid Black's promotion. The only winning move is a quiet queen move like queen a2, which prevents Black's checks and supports the a-pawn's promotion.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, the placement of the queen is critical. A quiet move that maintains control and avoids perpetual check can be the only way to win. Always check for the opponent's defensive resources before promoting.
notes.plans: White should play queen a2, then answer Black's king moves with king e1, and finally promote the a-pawn, ensuring no checks from Black's queen.

notes.explains: In this composed endgame, the queen is the only move to maintain the win, and the king must be placed carefully to avoid checks and support the pawn's promotion.
notes.teaches: In queen vs. pawn endgames, precise king placement is crucial to avoid perpetual check and to support the pawn's promotion.
notes.plans: Place the king on g2 to control key squares and prepare the pawn's advance, while using the queen to cut off the enemy king.

notes.explains: After Bc3, Black's best defense is Kg8. White must find a way to make progress. The move Bc4 is the only try, as it sacrifices a piece to deflect the knight and allow the a-pawn to advance.
notes.teaches: In endgames, sometimes you must sacrifice material to remove obstacles and create a decisive passed pawn. The sacrifice is justified if it leads to promotion.
notes.plans: After Bc4, if Nxe4, then a6. If Black plays b5, White must cover b6. The correct move is Ba5, sacrificing a second piece to keep the pawn rolling.

notes.explains: The natural-looking Bd4 to cover b6 is a trap: Black plays c5, and after a7, Nb6, Bxc5, Bb6, Black stops the pawn. The correct move is Ba5, which covers b6 and also prevents the knight from reaching the key square.
notes.teaches: When covering a key square, look for the move that also restricts the enemy pieces' activity. Sometimes the most natural move is not the best; consider sacrifices that maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: Play Ba5, sacrificing the bishop. If Nxa5, then a7 wins. If c5, then Bxd5, and the knight cannot stop the pawn.

notes.explains: In this composed endgame, White's c6 pawn is under attack and must be advanced or supported. The immediate c7 push fails because Black can coordinate the bishop and king to stop the pawn, as the bishop can be deflected or the king can approach. The key is to find a waiting move that preserves the pawn's advance while avoiding Black's defensive resources.
notes.teaches: In pawn races and composed endgames, the first move that seems natural (like pushing the pawn) may be a trap. Look for a preparatory move that improves your piece's position or removes a defensive resource before committing to the pawn advance.
notes.plans: White should choose a bishop move that both gives check (if possible) and places the bishop on a square where it can support the pawn's promotion after the king approaches. The winning idea involves a precise bishop placement that prevents Black's bishop from stopping the pawn.

notes.explains: The bishop on h1 is the winning move because it avoids the tactical resource Black has on h5. If the bishop goes to f3 or g2, Black can use the h5 pawn to create a discovered check or deflect the bishop, allowing the black king to stop the pawn. The h1 square is safe and keeps the bishop on a diagonal that controls the key squares.
notes.teaches: Every piece on the board, even one that seems irrelevant, can have a purpose. In composed studies, the placement of every piece is deliberate, and you must account for all tactical resources, including distant pawns that might enable checks or deflections.
notes.plans: After bishop h1, if Black plays king d6, White advances c7, and if Black captures the bishop, the pawn promotes with check or without interference. The bishop on h1 also supports the pawn's promotion square, ensuring that the new queen is protected.

notes.explains: The puzzle demonstrates that in endgames with passed pawns, the defender's king can often stop the pawn if the attacking pieces are not coordinated. The attacker must use the bishop to control the promotion square or to deflect the defender's bishop, but must also be wary of checks that allow the king to get in front of the pawn.
notes.teaches: When advancing a passed pawn, consider the defender's possible checks and deflections. A bishop can be a powerful supporter, but only if it is placed on a square where it cannot be harassed and where it controls the critical promotion square.
notes.plans: The winning plan is to first place the bishop on h1, then advance the pawn when the black king approaches, because the bishop will be able to recapture on h1 if the black bishop takes it, and the pawn will promote safely.

notes.explains: Solving composed endgame studies is a training method that stretches the imagination and forces the solver to look beyond routine moves.
notes.teaches: Regularly solving puzzles and studies builds creative thinking that carries over into practical play.

notes.explains: In this game, White deliberately steers into a position with a small structural edge rather than a sharp theoretical battle. The resulting structure is close to an isolated pawn for Black, which requires precise handling.
notes.teaches: A player can choose lines that offer a small but lasting edge, relying on the opponent's need to defend accurately. Such positions may not be spectacular but are effective in match play.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain pressure against the isolated pawn and exploit any inaccuracies in Black's defense.

notes.explains: Black's move order with ...Qd7 before castling is precise because it prevents White from playing h3 and forcing the bishop on g4 to retreat. If Black castled first, White could play h3, and the bishop would have to choose a less active diagonal, while ...Qd7 keeps the queen and bishop aligned on the same diagonal.
notes.teaches: Move orders matter in the opening; sometimes delaying castling to preserve a pin or maintain piece activity is more important than rushing to safety.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with castling, having secured the bishop's active post on g4.

notes.explains: White's choice of Nd2 instead of Nc3 is tied to the isolated pawn structure. The knight on d4 already blockades the pawn, and Nd2 reinforces that central outpost, whereas Nc3 would not support d4 as directly.
notes.teaches: When facing an isolated pawn, blockading it with a knight is a key strategy. Supporting that blockade with another piece can be more important than routine development.
notes.plans: White will continue to pressure the isolated pawn and the squares around it, while keeping the blockade intact.

notes.explains: In this isolated queen pawn position, the knight on d4 blockades the pawn, and the second knight on d2 can reinforce d4 or go to f3/b3. Blockading prevents the pawn from being traded off, which is key for the side playing against it.
notes.teaches: To handle an isolated pawn, blockade it with a knight and reinforce the blockade with another piece. This keeps the pawn fixed and prevents the opponent from relieving the weakness.
notes.plans: White aims to keep the blockade and slowly improve, while black should avoid trades and seek active counterplay.

notes.explains: Black should not take on d4 because that would help white by allowing recapture with the knight and activating the bishop on g2. Keeping pieces on the board makes it harder for white to play positionally against the isolated pawn, as there are tactical chances.
notes.teaches: When defending against an isolated pawn, avoid trades that relieve the pressure. Keep pieces on the board to create tactical complications and make the opponent's positional task harder.
notes.plans: Black should maintain tension and look for active moves, while white tries to provoke a favorable simplification.

notes.explains: White plays natural moves like c3 and queen f1 to keep the tension and prepare h3. White wants to provoke black into clarifying the position, but black responds with waiting moves like h6, asking white to improve. The bishop on g2 is not fully active, so white wants to create a favorable structure.
notes.teaches: In positions with an isolated pawn, the side with the pawn should keep the tension and avoid premature trades, while the opponent tries to force a favorable simplification. Waiting moves can be useful to ask the opponent to commit.
notes.plans: White plans h3 and possibly queen b5 to trade pieces and focus on the d5 pawn. Black should avoid trades and keep the position flexible.

notes.explains: Black has to be careful not to trade off too many pieces, as that helps white. Moves like knight e4 or rook c8/d8 are decent, but black must avoid knight takes d4. The position is messy but playable for black if they keep the tension.
notes.teaches: When defending against an isolated pawn, avoid trades that simplify into a favorable endgame for the opponent. Keep pieces on the board and seek active counterplay, even if the position is uncomfortable.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing and look for a plan, while white tries to provoke a mistake and eventually target the d5 pawn.

notes.explains: In this position, white has made all the natural waiting moves (h3, rooks to the center, queen to f1) and is running out of useful moves. Black has been playing solidly, so white must decide whether to force a structural change or continue maneuvering.
notes.teaches: When you have no more useful waiting moves, you must either create a plan or force a favorable structural change. Simply shuffling pieces without a plan allows the opponent to equalize comfortably.
notes.plans: White considers playing c4 or knight takes c6 to change the pawn structure, aiming for a slight pull.

notes.explains: White plays knight takes c6, and black recaptures with the b-pawn, transforming the isolated pawn into a different structure. The resulting position still has weaknesses for black (isolated a-pawn, potential weak c6 square), but it's less clear-cut than a pure isolated queen's pawn.
notes.teaches: An isolated pawn alone is not enough to win; it's a target that makes the opponent's position uncomfortable, leading to mistakes. You should not sacrifice a good position just to create an isolated pawn—the overall position must remain favorable.
notes.plans: White continues with c4, aiming to exploit black's slightly weaker pawn structure and create more targets.
