notes.explains: After winning the rook, Black tries to defend with moves like f5 and g4, but White's pieces are so active that Black's resources are tied down. The final tactic involves bishop takes h6, and if Black recaptures, bishop g5 wins the game due to mate threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and an ongoing attack, keep the pressure on. Use the activity of your pieces to create threats that overload the defender, and look for mating nets.
notes.plans: Continue attacking the king, using rook checks and bishop sacrifices to force mate or win more material.

notes.explains: In the position, all of Black's pieces are tied down, and Black tries to trap the White queen with g4, but it doesn't matter because White can capture on h6. If Black recaptures, White has a decisive tactic with bishop g5, exploiting the king's lack of escape squares and the threat of rook c6 mate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, a temporary queen trap may be irrelevant if you have a stronger tactical resource. Look for checks and mating threats that exploit the opponent's king's limited mobility.
notes.plans: After the tactical sequence, White should choose the recapture that avoids perpetual check and maintains the material advantage, leading to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: In a Slav/Catalan-type opening, White sacrifices a pawn for long-term pressure. The engine may prefer Black due to the extra pawn, but practically it's easier to play White because the plans are clear and Black must defend accurately.
notes.teaches: A pawn sacrifice for initiative can be practically more difficult to defend than to play, even if the engine evaluation is balanced. Clear plans matter more than raw material.
notes.plans: White aims to open the position and use the bishop pair to infiltrate on the c-file, while Black must find precise defensive moves.

notes.explains: White trades knights on d5 and gives up another pawn to open the position, keeping both bishops for the purpose of infiltrating on the c-file with the rook. This is position-specific because usually you keep knights in closed positions, but here the bishops are more valuable for the attack.
notes.teaches: The decision to trade pieces depends on the pawn structure and your long-term plan. In open positions, bishops can be more effective than knights for infiltrating and attacking.
notes.plans: White uses the bishop to support rook infiltration on c7, while Black may create counterplay with a passed pawn, so White must act quickly.

notes.explains: Black has a passed pawn that White cannot ignore, which may have prompted White's aggressive sacrifice. Black's counterplay revolves around this pawn, forcing White to address it.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn is a powerful asset that can create counterplay and distract the opponent from their own attack.
notes.plans: Black should aim to connect rooks and use the passed pawn to tie down White's pieces, while seeking active play.

notes.explains: White has a battery on a diagonal and a favorable pawn structure with pawns on c4 and d4. The best move is d5, even if it costs a pawn, because White will win it back and gain initiative.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development or a better piece activity, a pawn break can open lines and create threats, even at material cost.
notes.plans: White should play d5 to open the position and exploit the diagonal battery, but must be careful because Black has many pieces near the king.

notes.explains: In the position after White's queen b6, White has massed pieces on the queenside, while Black has a concentration of pieces on the kingside. Black's connected central pawns and kingside pieces suggest a potential attack.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has committed forces to one side, you should seek counterplay on the opposite side, especially if you have a space advantage or better piece placement.
notes.plans: Black should initiate an attack on the kingside, using the central pawns to support the advance.

notes.explains: Black has a concentration of pieces on the kingside while White's forces are scattered, with only one piece on the queenside. This imbalance suggests an attack is the right plan.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are massed on one side and the opponent's are far away, look for a direct attack before they can reorganize.
notes.plans: Begin the attack by opening lines on the kingside, such as with e3, to expose the enemy king.

notes.explains: After White defends with Nf3, Black should not play Ne4 immediately because White has the resource Be1, which neutralizes the attack and leaves Black worse. Instead, Black should take on e3, exploiting the fact that both the f3 knight and the c3 bishop are hanging.
notes.teaches: When the opponent defends, look for a capture that creates multiple threats or leaves multiple pieces hanging, so they cannot save everything.
notes.plans: Capture on e3 with the knight, winning material because White cannot defend both the knight on f3 and the bishop on c3.

notes.explains: After winning material, Black has two pieces for a rook, which is a significant advantage, and the White king remains exposed. White must try something aggressive to avoid losing, but Black should still be winning if they play accurately.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and the opponent's king is weak, you can often simplify or trade down to a winning endgame, but be careful of tactical tricks.
notes.plans: Consolidate the material advantage, avoid unnecessary complications, and aim to simplify into a winning position.

notes.explains: In this position, black has a winning tactic with h4, but it is complicated and risky. White can simplify and possibly escape, so black should not spend time on it when there is a clearer path to victory.
notes.teaches: When you have a material or positional advantage, prefer the simplest, most forcing winning method over a flashy but complicated tactic. Avoid unnecessary risk when a clear win exists.
notes.plans: Look for a straightforward way to convert the advantage, such as trading pieces and simplifying into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Black's queen on g7 is pressuring, and the knight on h5 defends while preparing to join the attack via g3. White's rook on b8 creates a direct threat based on the pinned bishop: queen takes c6 would exploit the pin.
notes.teaches: A pinned piece can be a decisive tactical weakness. Use your pieces to create threats that exploit pins, and be alert to your opponent's similar threats.
notes.plans: Black moves the king to h7 to avoid back-rank issues, then continues the attack. White must address the threat on c6.

notes.explains: After trades, black begins a knight maneuver to f4, then to e4, aiming to block the only defender of the checkmate threat. The knight on e4 is decisive, and knight e2 also works because it threatens the mate on g1.
notes.teaches: When a single piece is the only defender against a mating net, target that piece. A knight can be an excellent blocker or deflector in such cases.
notes.plans: Black plays the knight to e4 to neutralize the queen's defense, forcing mate or material loss.

notes.explains: The examples show that sacrificing material for long-term piece activity can be effective, even if the compensation takes several moves to materialize. The 'long run' may be only four or five moves, but sometimes longer.
notes.teaches: Don't be overly materialistic. If a piece is badly placed, consider giving it up to activate the rest of your army. Active pieces often outweigh a static material advantage.
notes.plans: When considering a sacrifice, calculate whether you can improve your pieces and regain the initiative or material within a reasonable number of moves.

notes.explains: In the Queen's Gambit Declined, after d4 d5 c4, Black's early a6 is a surprise move that prepares to capture on c4 and then support the pawn with b5, transposing to a favorable Queen's Gambit Accepted structure. The move also prevents White from playing b5 in some lines.
notes.teaches: When surprised by an unusual move, pause and ask what the opponent's move accomplishes and how it affects your plans. Here, a6's immediate point is to defend b5, enabling ...dxc4 and ...b5.
notes.plans: White should consider playing a4 to prevent ...b5, either immediately or after developing the knight to f3.

notes.explains: A trap exists if White tries to win the pawn on c4 after ...dxc4: Black can play ...b5, and if White captures, Black pins the knight with ...Bf5 or similar, winning material. This illustrates the tactical justification for Black's a6-b5 plan.
notes.teaches: Even in quiet opening positions, be alert to tactical resources that support the opponent's strategic ideas. A seemingly simple pawn move can set up pins and traps.
notes.plans: White should avoid greedily recapturing on c4 and instead prevent ...b5 with a4.

notes.explains: After Black plays a6 in the Queen's Gambit Declined, the immediate threat is b5, attacking the c4 pawn. If White allows b5, Black can win a pawn with Bxb5, so White must address this.
notes.teaches: When an opponent plays a move like a6 to prepare b5, you should consider whether you can neutralize the plan immediately or whether you should play around it.
notes.plans: White can consider a4 to prevent b5, or simply take on d5 to relieve the tension and make a6 less useful.

notes.explains: Taking on d5 after a6 is a simple solution: Black must recapture with the pawn, and then a6 becomes a wasted move because the b5 idea is no longer available. This is compared to the main line where Black plays Nf6 and White plays Bg5, pinning the knight.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the simplest move is best; taking on d5 removes the tension and makes the opponent's preparatory move look silly.
notes.plans: After cxd5, White can continue with normal development, e.g., Nf3, e3, Bd3, and the position is a standard QGD with Black having wasted a tempo on a6.

notes.explains: Playing Nf3 and a4 is also fine, but it gives Black what he wants: a6 becomes useful because it induces a4, which is a tempo loss for White. Black's a6 is a useful waiting move, controlling b5 and delaying Nf6 to avoid Bg5.
notes.teaches: Be wary of playing into your opponent's preparation; if a move like a6 is designed to provoke a response, consider whether that response is really necessary or if you can ignore it.
notes.plans: Instead of a4, White can take on d5 to make a6 less relevant, or play Bf4 to develop the bishop to a good square.

notes.explains: With a6 played instead of Nf6, the normal Bg5 pin is not available because the knight is still on g8. White can develop the bishop to f4 instead, which is a slight concession but acceptable. However, the move order matters: playing Nf3 first is more accurate because it prevents Black from playing c5 in one go.
notes.teaches: Move order is crucial in the opening; a small change like Nf3 before Bf4 can deny the opponent a key freeing move like c5.
notes.plans: White should play Nf3 first, then Bf4, and if Black tries c5, White can take and leave Black's d-pawn weak. If Black plays Nf6 first, White can switch to Bg5, pinning the knight.

notes.explains: When Black delays the c5 break, White can meet it with a timely capture on d5, exploiting the loose d-pawn. The move order matters: if Black prepares c5 with Nf6, White can choose Bg5 instead of Bf4 to maintain pressure on d5.
notes.teaches: In the Queen's Gambit Declined, the timing of Black's c5 break is critical; White can punish an immediate c5 by taking on d5, and can use Bg5 to keep the d5 pawn under pressure if Black tries to prepare it.
notes.plans: If Black plays c5 prematurely, capture on d5 and recapture, winning a pawn. If Black prepares with Nf6, pin the knight with Bg5 and maintain the tension.

notes.explains: Black's early c4 is an unusual move that prevents White's bishop from developing to d3 and signals a queenside pawn storm with b5, a5, b4, and possibly c3. White must reassess the plan and consider both the queenside pressure and the fate of the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When surprised in the opening, take time to evaluate the dynamic position: identify the opponent's plan, the weaknesses created, and your own pieces that need redeployment.
notes.plans: White should consider central breaks like e4 to challenge Black's overextended c4 pawn, and also look for ways to activate the light-squared bishop.

notes.explains: In this position, attacking the c4 pawn with b3 is a typical idea, but it weakens the dark squares because the bishop is locked outside the pawn chain and cannot defend them. Moves like Bb4, Qa5, and Ne4 then create serious problems around the c3 square.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn break like b3, check whether it weakens squares that your own pieces can no longer defend. A normal idea can be bad in a specific structure if it over-weakens key squares.
notes.plans: Avoid b3 for now; look for other ways to handle the c4 pawn or improve the position before considering it.

notes.explains: The bishop on c1 needs to be developed to support the e4 break. Moving it to e2 is possible but it blocks the rook from the e-file and is not the final destination. The long diagonal is ideal because after e4, the d-pawn disappears and the bishop becomes powerful on the open diagonal, pressuring Black's queenside expansion.
notes.teaches: When planning a central break like e4, develop pieces to squares that support that break and will be useful after it. The long diagonal is often the right home for a bishop in such structures.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to the long diagonal, either via b2 or through a maneuver like Be2-f3, to support e4 and create pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: There are multiple ways to get the bishop to the long diagonal, such as Be2 followed by Bf3, or directly to b2. The move g3 is also possible, but the speaker prefers a different plan. Queen c2 is a decent move to include, but it can be delayed. Knight d2 is too slow because Black will play b5 and then Bb4, creating problems on the diagonal.
notes.teaches: When choosing a development plan, consider the speed of your moves relative to your opponent's counterplay. A move that is too slow allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Choose a concrete way to get the bishop to the long diagonal that is fast enough to keep Black from getting in b5 and Bb4 first.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's early b5 aims to gain space on the queenside and preempt White's b3. White's knight on d2 is slow and doesn't address the immediate pressure on the diagonal, allowing Black to continue with ideas like Bb4, Qa5, and Ne4. Even if White isn't losing material, Black's play is comfortable and White faces ongoing problems.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is actively gaining space, avoid slow, passive moves that don't meet the immediate needs of the position. Consider whether your move addresses the opponent's threats or just supports your own plans.
notes.plans: White should look for more active moves that challenge Black's setup, perhaps by contesting the center or preparing to break with e4 under better conditions.

notes.explains: White plays Ne5 to defend g4 twice, preparing to push g4 and fianchetto the bishop to g2. This flank attack is justified because the center is closed—Black is not taking on d4—so the files remain closed and the king is safe. If the pawn were on c5 instead of c4, the center could open, and g4 would be risky.
notes.teaches: Flank pawn pushes are safer when the center is closed. If the center is fluid, such moves can expose your king. Always assess the center before launching a flank attack.
notes.plans: White intends to push g4, develop the bishop to g2, and gain space on the kingside, while the closed center keeps the king safe.

notes.explains: In the game, Black played b5, and White responded with a3 to prevent Bb4. Black then played Bb7, anticipating pressure on the diagonal. White chose g4 over g3 because g4 gives the bishop a flight square on g2 and avoids the risk of the bishop being trapped on the fourth rank. The computer suggests g3 is also fine, but White preferred g4 for safety and to continue the kingside expansion.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is on the fourth rank, ensure it has retreat squares to avoid being trapped by pawn advances or knight attacks. A pawn move like g4 can provide that flight square while also supporting a space-gaining plan.
notes.plans: White will develop the bishop to g2, continue pushing kingside pawns, and keep the center closed to maintain safety.

notes.explains: Black played Ne4, anticipating that the knight might be kicked by g5. White considered capturing but worried about weakening the dark squares, so instead played Bg2 first. Black then played Qa5, which the engine considers a mistake, but White's choice was also not optimal.
notes.teaches: When your opponent posts a knight in the center, consider whether capturing it is beneficial or whether it's better to maintain tension and develop. Be wary of weakening squares that could become targets.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and look for ways to challenge Black's queen on a5, perhaps by preparing b4 or other active moves.

notes.explains: After the opponent plays Ne4, the immediate capture is possible, but the bishop on g2 is important for controlling the dark squares and the long diagonal. Moving the bishop to g2 first is a practical choice, even if the engine prefers something else.
notes.teaches: In the Catalan or similar setups, the bishop on g2 is a key piece; don't give it up lightly. Consider developing it before engaging in tactics.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g2, then continue with natural development and castling.

notes.explains: Black's queen to a5 is a mistake, giving White a significant advantage. The engine suggests options that give Black the advantage, but they are scary to play.
notes.teaches: Be alert to opponent's queen sorties; they can be inaccuracies. Look for ways to exploit the queen's early activity.
notes.plans: Find the best continuation to punish Qa5, possibly by attacking the queen or exploiting the weakened squares.

notes.explains: If Black plays h5 to stop g4, White can respond with Be2 or even Bf3, and the plan of g4 or h5 can still be pursued later. h5 creates weaknesses for Black.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid of pawn moves that seem to stop your plan; they often create weaknesses. Have flexible plans (like Be2 or Bf3) to continue.
notes.plans: If h5, consider Be2 targeting the knight, or later bring the bishop to f3.

notes.explains: Black is threatening something, and White has several options: capture the knight, defend the knight, or ignore it. The simple move Qc1 defends the knight and avoids tactics.
notes.teaches: Always look for a simple, solid move that deals with the threat without creating new weaknesses. It's a good practical choice in complex positions.
notes.plans: Play Qc1, defending the knight and keeping the position solid.

notes.explains: Other moves like Qc2 or Rc1 can run into tactical problems, such as the rook on a1 being stranded or pins along the file. Bxc4 might be okay but gives up the bishop for a knight, which is not ideal in a tactical position.
notes.teaches: Be wary of giving up a bishop for a knight in dynamic positions. Also, watch out for common tactical motifs like pins and stranded rooks.
notes.plans: Avoid Qc2 and Rc1; prefer the simple Qc1 or possibly Bxe4 if the position is clear.

notes.explains: In a fluid tactical position, trading a bishop for a knight is a major concession, especially when the opponent retains the bishop pair and your own knight can become misplaced.
notes.teaches: Be cautious about giving up a bishop for a knight unless you have concrete compensation; the bishop pair is a long-term asset.
notes.plans: Avoid such trades unless you can immediately justify them with activity or structure.

notes.explains: A knight on e5 can be a target or a trap if it cannot retreat; advancing a pawn to e4 requires readiness to deal with the resulting tension, such as being developed and castled.
notes.teaches: Only push central pawns when you can support the ensuing complications; otherwise, the pawn advance can leave weaknesses.
notes.plans: Delay pawn breaks until your pieces are coordinated and your king is safe.

notes.explains: When facing a threat, you have options: counterattack, ignore it and play a useful move, or address it directly. The computer may prefer aggressive continuations, but practical play often favors solid moves that maintain the position's trumps.
notes.teaches: In unclear positions, you can choose between concrete aggression and quiet consolidation; both can be valid, but you must weigh the risks.
notes.plans: If you choose a quiet move, ensure your pieces remain active and your structure sound.

notes.explains: After the opponent's queen goes to a5, it can become misplaced, unable to influence the kingside; meanwhile, your queen can become more relevant if central pawns are exchanged.
notes.teaches: Queen placement matters: a queen on the flank can be out of play if the action shifts to the other side.
notes.plans: Look to exploit the opponent's queen's poor placement by opening the center or attacking on the side where your queen is active.

notes.explains: In the c4-b5 structure, the opponent's long-term plans revolve around the pawn structure; understanding what each side wants from the structure is key to evaluating moves like queenside castling.
notes.teaches: Always recall the typical plans and weaknesses of the pawn structure you are playing; this guides your evaluation of unusual moves.
notes.plans: Assess the opponent's move in light of the structure's demands; if it doesn't fit, it is likely suspect.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has just played queenside castling, which looks unnatural because the king becomes exposed and, more importantly, it contradicts Black's own strategic plan of pushing queenside pawns (a5-b4) to gain space and attack. With the king on c8, those pawn pushes are no longer viable, so Black has essentially denied himself his main plan.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a move, consider whether it fits with the overall strategic plan of the position. A move that prevents you from executing your own plan is often anti-positional, even if it seems active.
notes.plans: White should continue with the central plan of playing e4, supported by moves like Qc2 or Nd2, to open the center and exploit Black's misplaced king.

notes.explains: White's pieces are well placed to support the e4 break, and Black's queenside castling has left the king vulnerable. White can prepare e4 with Qc2 or Nd2, both of which are strong. Nd2 has the extra benefit of allowing the bishop to see more of the board.
notes.teaches: When you have a central pawn break in mind, use your pieces to support it efficiently. Moves that both prepare the break and improve piece activity are often the best.
notes.plans: Play e4 to open the center, then follow up with active piece play, targeting Black's exposed king and weak squares.

notes.explains: White has just played a move that attacks a black piece twice, and Black can only defend it once, so White will win material back. The expected continuation involves Black trying to reposition with ...Ne7 and ...Ne4, but White can maintain pressure with moves like Nd5 and Bg3.
notes.teaches: When you attack a piece multiple times, the defender can only respond once per move, so you can often win material or force concessions. Look for such tactical motifs in the middlegame.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn back, White should continue developing and improving piece placement, aiming for squares like c4 or e4 for the knight, and keeping the bishops active on long diagonals.

notes.explains: In this position, White has achieved the desired central break and opened the center. The bishops are raking along open diagonals, and the knight is centrally placed, serving both offensive and defensive roles. The key is to activate these pieces further.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and open diagonals, prioritize bringing your pieces to their most active squares. A knight in the center can be both an attacking and a defensive asset.
notes.plans: Consider moves like Rc1 to open the c-file and pressure the c-pawn, or a4 to undermine Black's queenside pawn structure and open lines.

notes.explains: Black has castled on the queenside where they have pushed pawns, creating targets. White can exploit this by advancing a4 to break up the pawn shield and open files against the king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent castles into a side where they have advanced pawns, use pawn breaks like a4 to open lines and create attacking chances. This is often stronger than a slow buildup.
notes.plans: Play a4, and if Black captures, recapture with the pawn to open the a-file for the rook.

notes.explains: Black has ignored the center to launch a kingside pawn attack with g5 and h5. However, this does not address the central threats. White can now strike in the center with exd5, which is both tactically sound and desirable.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, always ask two questions: 'Can I do this?' (check for tactics) and 'Do I want to do this?' (evaluate the resulting position). Sometimes a move that seems to lose material is actually good because it opens lines and improves your piece activity.
notes.plans: Play exd5, and if Black recaptures, continue with moves like Be5 to exchange pieces and highlight Black's weak pawns and exposed king.

notes.explains: Black is forced to play g7 to defend against threats, but White must respond to Black's counterplay. The move h4 is tempting but tactically unsound; instead, White should consider h3 or gxh5 to handle the threat.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a threat, organize your thoughts: identify the threat, list candidate responses, and compare them. Avoid moves that close the position when you want to open lines against the king.
notes.plans: Choose between h3 and gxh5, evaluating which gives better long-term chances. h3 may allow Black to open the h-file, while gxh5 might lead to a more favorable recapture.

notes.explains: In opposite-side castling positions, the defender must choose between responding to the opponent's threat or continuing their own attack. Here, after the opponent's threat, the choice is between h3 and gxh5. h3 opens the file and gives the opponent another tempo to bring the knight to f4, while gxh5 invites the rook to h5, which spends the opponent's turn and allows the defender to resume their own plan.
notes.teaches: When facing a threat in a race, prefer the response that forces the opponent to spend a move, allowing you to keep the initiative. In opposite-side castling, urgency and being the first to land a decisive blow are paramount.
notes.plans: After gxh5, if the opponent plays Rh5, the defender can continue with their own plan, such as R a1-a4, to open the a-file and attack the enemy king.

notes.explains: The opponent's knight on d5 is a key defender; if it is captured, the defender loses material because the f5 square becomes undefended. The defender must be careful not to allow the opponent to open lines or create counterplay, so the knight must be maintained or captured only when it is safe.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, identify which enemy pieces are crucial for defense and consider whether capturing them immediately is necessary or if you can first improve your own position to increase the pressure.
notes.plans: After the opponent's bishop takes on d5, the defender can play a4 to open the a-file and continue the attack, while the opponent's queen is far from the action.

notes.explains: With the a-file open and the bishop on the long diagonal, the defender has a winning attack, but must find the right way to invade. Direct moves like Bh3 are not ideal because they allow counterplay such as g4 and f5, which can create threats against the defender's own pieces. The key is to use the a2 square to double heavy pieces and then invade on the a-file.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied to defense, look for ways to bring extra pieces to the attack, such as using a rook or queen to a2, and then to a1 or a7, to create unavoidable threats. Avoid placing pieces on squares where they can be harassed.
notes.plans: Play Ra2, then Qa1 or Ra7, with the idea of checkmating on the a-file. The opponent's pieces are overloaded, so the attack is decisive.

notes.explains: In this position, White's attack on the a-file and kingside is overwhelming. Black's counterplay, like rook a2, is too slow and does not address the immediate threats. The key is that White's major pieces can deliver checkmate before Black can organize defense.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive attack, do not be distracted by your opponent's threats if they are not immediate. Prioritize your own mating threats over preserving material.
notes.plans: Continue with the attack, using the rook on the a-file and queen to deliver checkmate, ignoring Black's attempts to create counterplay.

notes.explains: White hesitated to play the strongest moves (like rook a2 or queen a1) because they involved sacrificing material, but the computer shows that these sacrifices are winning because Black's king is too exposed and White's pieces coordinate perfectly.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must be willing to sacrifice material to maintain a mating attack. If you can calculate that the attack is unstoppable, do not shy away from it.
notes.plans: Play the sacrificial line that leads to checkmate, even if it means giving up a piece.

notes.explains: White played defensive moves like knight d2 and bishop e5 to keep pieces, but these allowed Black to relieve pressure. The computer's suggestion was to continue the attack with rook a5 and queen a1, ignoring the bishop.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, do not over-defend. If your opponent's threats are not decisive, continue improving your own attacking pieces.
notes.plans: Focus on the attack, not on preserving material. Use the rook and queen to create threats that Black cannot meet.

notes.explains: Black played f5 to lock out the bishop, but White's attack is so strong that the bishop is not needed. The computer suggests ignoring the bishop and continuing with rook a5 and queen a1, leading to checkmate.
notes.teaches: Do not be attached to your pieces. If a piece is not essential to the attack, be willing to abandon it to keep the initiative.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with the rook and queen, even if it means losing the bishop.

notes.explains: White finally played rook a7 after dealing with threats, but the opponent played knight d5 to block the rook and threaten knight e3. White then had a chance to play the heroic queen a5, but instead played rook e1, giving away most of the advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, you must be alert to the moment to strike. Delaying the decisive blow can allow the opponent to consolidate and escape.
notes.plans: Play the decisive queen a5, which leads to a forced win, rather than a quiet move that lets Black defend.

notes.explains: After White missed the best move, Black had a chance to play rook d7 to defend, but instead played knight f4, counterattacking. White then took the knight and finally played queen a1, and Black's position collapsed.
notes.teaches: When your opponent misses a chance, you must punish it by continuing your attack with maximum energy. Do not let them off the hook.
notes.plans: Take the knight and play queen a1, using the rook to cut off the king's escape and the queen to deliver mate.

notes.explains: Black tried to defend with bishop d6, but White can give checks with rook a6 and queen a5, encircling the king. Black's attempt with bishop a3 to stop rook a8 was nonsense, and White has a forced mate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use checks to drive it into a mating net. Do not be afraid to give up material to keep the initiative.
notes.plans: Use the rook and queen to give checks and force the king to a square where it can be mated.

notes.explains: The black king is exposed and the white pieces are coordinating to encircle it. A queen check forces the king into a mating net, and any attempt to block or escape is met with decisive tactics.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for forcing checks that drive it into a smaller and smaller box, and calculate the escape squares before committing.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing more pieces to the king's vicinity and using checks to restrict its movement.

notes.explains: The opponent plays a desperate move to stop a threat, but it allows a tactical sequence that leads to checkmate if the king goes to the wrong square. The correct square avoids the mate and leaves the opponent's attack failing.
notes.teaches: When defending against a mating attack, always identify the safe squares for the king and choose the one that avoids the immediate mate, even if it looks passive.
notes.plans: After escaping the mate, consolidate and use the extra material or positional advantage to win.

notes.explains: After the king escapes, the opponent's checks run out because the knight defends key squares, and the attacker has no perpetual check. The position is winning for the side with the extra material.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, ensure your king is safe and that the opponent cannot force a perpetual check; use your pieces to cover the checking squares.
notes.plans: Trade down to a winning endgame or use the extra material to press the attack.

notes.explains: When surprised in the opening, it's important to think dynamically about how the position changes with each move rather than relying on automatic moves. This game involved a surprise with a6, and the player spent time understanding the new plans.
notes.teaches: In the opening, if your opponent plays an unexpected move, reassess the position and adjust your plans accordingly; don't just play 'normal' moves.
notes.plans: Use the opening principles to navigate the unfamiliar position and look for opportunities to punish any inaccuracies.

notes.explains: When the opponent made a critical mistake by castling queenside, the player knew to open the position and attack the king. Despite tactical mistakes, the attack was successful.
notes.teaches: If the opponent castles into a weakened position, open lines and coordinate pieces to attack the king; even if you miss some tactics, the initiative can carry you through.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with piece pressure and pawn breaks to expose the king.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian setup, Black's early ...a5 is unusual and doesn't address the central tension. White has completed development and castled, while Black's king is still in the center. The e-file is half-open and can be opened fully, creating attacking chances against the uncastled king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is still in the center and you have a lead in development, look for ways to open lines, especially files that point at the enemy king.
notes.plans: White should aim to open the center with d4, and if Black captures, recapture to open the e-file, then bring pieces to bear on the king.

notes.explains: Black's ...a5 is a move that tries to restrict White's queenside expansion but neglects the center and development. It is more typical in the English opening with ...e5, but here it leaves Black's kingside undeveloped and the king vulnerable.
notes.teaches: In the opening, moves that are not aimed at controlling the center or developing pieces can be punished by energetic central play.
notes.plans: White should proceed with d4, opening the position before Black can consolidate.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has just captured on d4 with the e-pawn, but capturing with the c-pawn was preferable because it keeps the knight on f6, which helps protect the d5 square and supports the d6-pawn push. The e-pawn capture leaves Black with doubled pawns and a knight that is less active.
notes.teaches: When recapturing in the center, consider which pawn recapture maintains piece coordination and supports future pawn breaks. Keeping the knight on f6 can be crucial for defending key squares and facilitating d6-d5.
notes.plans: Black should aim to play d5 to trade off the doubled pawn and reach a balanced, symmetrical position. White should seek to exploit the slight weakness in Black's structure by developing with tempo and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: White has sacrificed a pawn to gain the initiative. The bishop on b5 is vulnerable to a6 and b5, so White must act quickly to develop with tempo rather than waste time moving the bishop again. The idea is to use the lead in development to create threats before Black can consolidate.
notes.teaches: When you sacrifice a pawn, you must gain the initiative and develop with tempo. Avoid retreating pieces unnecessarily; instead, find moves that create threats and force your opponent to react.
notes.plans: White should continue developing, possibly with Nc3 and Bg5, while keeping the bishop on b5 for now. The outpost on d5 is valuable, and White can use it to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Black's d7 pawn is a structural weakness: it is isolated, blocks the c8 bishop, and restricts Black's overall development, making it hard to get rooks into play. Black's main plan is to get rid of this pawn, often by pushing it to d6.
notes.teaches: Identify the key weakness in the opponent's camp and understand that their plans revolve around fixing it. If you can keep that weakness in place, you restrict their development and activity.
notes.plans: White should maintain pressure on the d7 pawn and avoid allowing Black to easily advance it to d6.

notes.explains: Black chose a materialistic approach by capturing a pawn, but this led to a worse position. The alternative was to prioritize development and equality. Comparing the resulting positions is crucial before grabbing material.
notes.teaches: Material gains must be weighed against positional factors. A pawn can be less valuable than the activity and safety you give up to win it.
notes.plans: When considering a material grab, evaluate the resulting position for both sides, especially development and king safety.

notes.explains: After Black's blunder of capturing a pawn, White has strong attacking chances. White can choose the order of captures to maximize pressure, and there are mating threats or winning the queen. Black has defensive resources, but they must be found precisely.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, calculate forcing sequences carefully. Look for checks, captures, and threats, and be aware of defensive resources for the opponent.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack, possibly by bringing more pieces to bear on the king, while Black must find accurate defensive moves to avoid immediate loss.

notes.explains: White has a slightly better position due to Black's weak pawns and poor bishop diagonals, even though Black has the bishop pair. White can improve by playing on the c-file and repositioning the knight to a better square.
notes.teaches: The bishop pair is not automatically an advantage if the bishops lack good diagonals. Pawn structure and piece activity matter more.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit the c-file, improve piece placement, and maintain pressure on Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: When attacking, it is important to bring another piece into the attack rather than making pointless pawn moves that give up the initiative. White has threats involving the bishop and rook, and possibly a rook sacrifice to expose the king.
notes.teaches: In attack, every move should increase the pressure or bring a new piece to the attack. Avoid moves that do not create threats or improve your position.
notes.plans: White should continue with moves that create concrete threats, such as bishop to c3, and be alert to sacrificial ideas to open lines against the king.

notes.explains: In this attacking position, the defender's bishop on g7 is crucial for king safety. Removing it weakens the king's shelter, and the attacker can then use rook and knight sacrifices to open lines.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is a key defender, consider removing it even at material cost, because the resulting attack on the weakened king can be decisive.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing more pieces to bear on the king, using threats like rook takes e5 and bishop c6 to create mating nets.

notes.explains: Black's failure to develop the bishop and push the d-pawn left the king vulnerable. White invested tempi and gave up a pawn to accelerate the attack, which is justified when there is a serious mating threat.
notes.teaches: Do not shy away from material sacrifices if they bring your pieces rapidly into an attack against the enemy king. Development and king safety outweigh material in such positions.
notes.plans: Keep the initiative by not allowing the opponent to consolidate; continue to create threats that force the defender to react.

notes.explains: When the opponent tries to trade pieces to relieve pressure, it is often better to avoid the trade and instead keep pieces on the board to sustain the attack. Giving up a bishop for a knight is usually not favorable, especially when the bishop is more active.
notes.teaches: Before trading, ask who benefits. In attacking positions, keep as many pieces as possible to maintain pressure, and let the opponent spend time to capture rather than initiating trades yourself.
notes.plans: If the bishop is attacked, move it or ignore it, allowing the opponent to waste time capturing, while you continue building the attack.

notes.explains: With the queen and other pieces converging on the king, moves like queen h6 can create immediate threats. The defender's pieces are far from the action, making it impossible to parry all threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a majority of pieces attacking the king, look for the most forcing and direct moves, such as queen checks or threats of mate, rather than routine captures.
notes.plans: Bring the queen to h6 to threaten mate, and use the rook to cut off the king's escape, ensuring the attack cannot be repelled.

notes.explains: In the featured game, Black's bishop on c8 and another piece remained undeveloped, leaving the king vulnerable. White exploited this by sacrificing the queen on f8, leading to a forced mate.
notes.teaches: Punish an opponent's lag in development by opening lines and sacrificing material to expose the king. A king stuck in the center with pieces undeveloped is a fatal weakness.
notes.plans: When the opponent's king is exposed and their pieces are not ready to defend, look for forcing moves and sacrifices to break through.

notes.explains: In the opening, Black's early move of the bishop from g7 to d6 (or similar) removed a key defender of the king, leaving the king vulnerable. Keeping the knight on c6 and the bishop on g7 would have allowed Black to castle and reach safety.
notes.teaches: Do not move pieces away from the defense of your king prematurely. Maintain the integrity of your pawn structure and keep key defenders in place until your king is safe.
notes.plans: Prioritize castling and completing development before initiating tactical operations.

notes.explains: The Berlin Defense is a solid opening choice for Black, often leading to a drawish endgame. It was famously used by Kramnik to neutralize Kasparov's white attacks.
notes.teaches: The Berlin Wall is a reliable way to reach a tenable endgame with Black, but it requires precise knowledge and can be passive if not handled actively.
notes.plans: If playing the Berlin, be ready to defend accurately and transition to a favorable endgame.

notes.explains: The Berlin Defense was chosen by Kasparov in this 2002 game, a choice with historical weight since it was used against him in his title loss. The opening has gone through reputation cycles: once highly respected, then criticized, and now again considered solid for Black.
notes.teaches: Opening reputations fluctuate; a defense that was once considered refuted can become fashionable again. Choosing a solid, well-analyzed opening like the Berlin can be a practical weapon for Black.
notes.plans: If playing the Berlin, be prepared for both the main lines and the opponent's attempts to avoid it, such as with d3.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a kingside pawn majority (4 vs 3) while Black's queenside majority is blocked due to doubled pawns, making it nearly impossible for Black to create a passed pawn there. Black's compensation is the pair of bishops.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a pawn structure, consider the potential for creating passed pawns. A blocked majority is less valuable than an active one, and the bishop pair can offset structural weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should aim to expand on the kingside, using the pawn majority to gain space and potentially create a passed pawn. Black should seek to activate the bishops and counter on the queenside if possible.

notes.explains: After White played g4, Black played Bh7, and White continued with g5, gaining a space advantage on the kingside. The position is better for White because the king is stuck in the center, and White can create a passed pawn by pushing e6 at some point.
notes.teaches: In positions with queens traded, the king's safety becomes a relative concern; a centralized king can be a weakness if the opponent can open lines. Space advantage on one wing can be converted into a passed pawn.
notes.plans: White should continue to expand on the kingside, aiming to create a passed pawn and exploit Black's king's lack of safety. Black should try to activate the bishops and find counterplay.

notes.explains: In the game, Black played Nh4, and White had the option to trade or centralize. The speaker notes that Judith would not play for a draw, showing her fighting ambition. Also, a move like Bf5 would be a blunder because the bishop gets trapped.
notes.teaches: Always develop pieces and avoid trapping your own pieces. In positions with limited activity, look for ways to improve your pieces, but be careful not to lose material.
notes.plans: If playing Black, ensure that your pieces have safe squares and avoid moves that allow them to be trapped. Consider centralizing knights or activating bishops.

notes.explains: A bishop on e4 can be an annoying piece for the side that traded it away, as it becomes active and controls important squares. The position favors White because of a potential kingside pawn majority and the ability to create a passed pawn by pushing e6.
notes.teaches: When considering a trade, evaluate the resulting activity of the opponent's piece. A seemingly equal trade can leave your opponent with a well-placed piece.
notes.plans: White aims to create a passed pawn on the kingside and improve piece placement, while Black must find a way to activate their pieces and deal with the king's safety.

notes.explains: With queens traded, the king becomes a target and castling is less urgent. Black struggles to find a safe square for the king, as the natural squares like f8 and d7 are unavailable or awkward. White can improve the position of pieces without rushing, exploiting Black's cramped setup.
notes.teaches: In queenless middlegames, king safety remains crucial, but the king can also become an active piece. Use the opponent's king's lack of a safe haven to restrict their piece play.
notes.plans: White continues to improve piece coordination and restrict Black's rook from entering the game, while Black seeks any opportunity to activate the rook and relieve the pressure.

notes.explains: White uses a king maneuver to chase away the rook and prevent it from becoming active. Black's pieces remain passive, and White's position improves with simple moves, showing how a small space advantage can grow into a decisive one.
notes.teaches: Even small advantages can be converted by steadily improving your pieces and denying the opponent counterplay. Patience and prophylaxis are key.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain the initiative, possibly pushing g5 to further restrict Black, while Black must find a way to break out, perhaps by trying to get the rook to d8.

notes.explains: In a tactical sequence, White gives up a rook for a bishop to ensure the king doesn't escape to a better square, and then pushes g5, which is unstoppable. This leads to a decisive attack. The trade is fine for Black, but White's active pieces and Black's passive ones make the difference.
notes.teaches: When calculating trades, consider the resulting king safety and piece activity. Sometimes sacrificing material to maintain the initiative or expose the king is worth it.
notes.plans: White continues the attack, using the passed pawn and active pieces to break through, while Black tries to defend against the threats.

notes.explains: In the Two Knights Defense, the most aggressive and dynamic approach for White is the immediate knight attack on f7 with Ng5, exploiting the weakness of the f7 square, which is only defended by the king.
notes.teaches: When facing a position with a vulnerable point like f7, the most active plan is to attack it directly with a piece, even at the cost of a pawn, rather than playing quiet developing moves.
notes.plans: After Ng5, Black must respond with d5 to block the bishop's diagonal to f7, leading to sharp tactical play.

notes.explains: After Black plays d5 and White takes on d5, Black should not recapture the pawn immediately because White's lead in development makes the position dangerous. Instead, Black should consider sacrificing a piece with Nxd5? leading to the Fried Liver Attack (Nxf7).
notes.teaches: Material should not be regained automatically if it allows the opponent to launch a devastating attack. Recognize when development and initiative outweigh material.
notes.plans: If Black recaptures, White can play Nxf7, sacrificing the knight for a powerful attack on the king, forcing the king to move and exposing it to the rest of White's pieces.

notes.explains: In the Fried Liver Attack, after White plays Nxf7+ and the king takes, White plays Qf3+, forking the king and the knight on a5, forcing the king to move up the board. White then plays Nc3, bringing another piece into the attack, while Black must use a knight to defend the attacked knight.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing material for an attack, coordinate your pieces to create multiple threats, such as checks and forks, to keep the initiative and prevent the opponent from consolidating.
notes.plans: White continues to develop and attack, while Black must defend carefully, often having to make awkward moves to survive.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, Black plays a strange move like c6 instead of the natural Bd7 to block the check. This move gives up another pawn but aims to create a peculiar pawn structure and possibly trap the white bishop.
notes.teaches: Sometimes unconventional moves that sacrifice material can be justified by long-term positional goals, such as creating weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure or gaining time. Keep an open mind to non-standard ideas.
notes.plans: White takes the pawn on c6, and Black recaptures with the pawn (not the knight, to avoid the bishop returning to c4 with threats on f7), leading to a unique pawn structure.

notes.explains: In this gambit line, White has sacrificed a pawn for development and activity. Black has a funny pawn structure and a knight on g5 that is causing White trouble, forcing White to respond to threats instead of developing.
notes.teaches: When you sacrifice a pawn for initiative, every move should create a threat that forces your opponent to react, gaining time for your own development.
notes.plans: Black should continue to develop with tempo, maintaining pressure on White's position, and look to exploit the weak pawns and active pieces.

notes.explains: Black has just castled, and White has finally had a chance to develop. Black is down a pawn but has active pieces and a semi-open file for the rook.
notes.teaches: When you are down material, you should avoid passive play and seek to activate your pieces, especially rooks on open or semi-open files, to create counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should consider moves like c5 to attack the center and open lines, and later activate the rook to b8, putting pressure on White's weak pawns.

notes.explains: Black has played c5, attacking White's central pawn on d4. If White ignores this, Black can capture on d4 and then play Bc5, skewering White's queen and rook.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn on a weak square, use it to attack the opponent's center and create tactical threats. Look for skewers and other tactics that exploit the opponent's piece placement.
notes.plans: Black should continue to pressure White's center and look for ways to increase the activity of the rook, such as Rb8, targeting the b-pawn and tying down White's pieces.

notes.explains: The rook move to b8 activates the rook and puts pressure on the b-pawn, while also supporting the center. The bishop cannot easily move because it is defending that pawn.
notes.teaches: Rooks belong on open or semi-open files and can be activated to pressure weak pawns. A piece that is tied to defending a pawn is not truly free to move.
notes.plans: Black's rook on b8 eyes the b-pawn, and the bishop remains on its square to keep guarding it.

notes.explains: White, facing the threat to the b-pawn, considers developing the knight. Developing to a3 threatens a fork on b5, attacking the queen and bishop, which looks appealing.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are undeveloped, look for active development that creates immediate threats. A knight on a3 can jump to b5 with a fork.
notes.plans: White plays Na3, threatening Nb5 forking the queen and bishop.

notes.explains: Black had a simple recapture with cxd4, but instead set a trap. White naively fell into it by playing Nb5, thinking his threat was bigger. Black then played Rxb5, sacrificing the exchange for a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: Not every threat must be answered mechanically. Sometimes you can ignore a threat if you have a bigger one, but you must calculate carefully. Also, be wary of traps: a move that looks like a strong fork may be met by a sacrifice that leaves you worse.
notes.plans: Black sacrifices the exchange (rook for knight) to gain a powerful attack, with queen to b6 coming.

notes.explains: After Rxb5, Black plays Qb6, hitting the bishop and creating a discovered attack along the diagonal towards the king. The pawn on d4 is ready to advance with check.
notes.teaches: A queen can create multiple threats simultaneously. A discovered attack can be a decisive resource, especially when the queen is lined up with the king.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with d3+ or similar, exploiting the discovered attack and the loose bishop.

notes.explains: Black's queen move to b6 creates a double threat: it attacks the bishop and sets up a discovered attack along the diagonal against the white king, ready to be unleashed by a pawn move.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that combine an attack on a piece with a latent discovered check or attack on the king.
notes.plans: Black should exploit the discovered attack by advancing the d-pawn with check, forcing the king to move and gaining time.

notes.explains: White must address the threat to the bishop. Moving it to e2 allows d3+ and the pawn captures the bishop, so White instead plays a4, a useful waiting move that maintains the bishop's safety.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, consider moves that preserve it while also creating other threats or improving your position.
notes.plans: White's a4 prepares to meet the coming pawn push, possibly by supporting the bishop or creating counterplay.

notes.explains: Black has a strong pawn duo on e4 and d3, but the d-pawn is the key. Pushing it gives check, but Black must choose the right moment. Taking the a-pawn with the d-pawn is tempting but wrong because it separates the pawns and weakens the duo.
notes.teaches: In positions with a powerful pawn duo, avoid breaking them up for material gain; the duo's strength outweighs a single pawn.
notes.plans: Black should first play a6 to prevent the bishop from sacrificing itself for the pawns, then proceed with the pawn push.

notes.explains: Black's inaccurate move allows White's bishop to sacrifice itself for the two pawns, which would be a good deal for White. By playing a6 first, Black would have prevented that sacrifice, forcing the bishop to remain clumsy.
notes.teaches: Before executing a plan, check if the opponent has a resource that can undermine it; a small preparatory move can neutralize it.
notes.plans: Black should have played a6 to keep the bishop trapped, then continue with the pawn push.

notes.explains: The tempting move Knight g4 threatens smothered mate, but it only involves the knight. The bishop on c8 is still passive and should be activated first.
notes.teaches: Before starting a tactical operation, improve the placement of all your pieces, not just the one delivering the threat.
notes.plans: Black should develop the bishop to a good square (like g4 or f5) to increase the pressure, then consider the knight maneuver.

notes.explains: The bishop on c8 is passive and needs to be developed to a better square. The ideal square is e2, where it can support the attack and control important diagonals.
notes.teaches: In any position, look for your worst-placed piece and find the best square for it. Improving piece activity is a key middlegame goal.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e2, possibly after forcing the queen to move, and then bring the rook to e1 to support the bishop and control the e-file.

notes.explains: The black queen is attacked by the bishop, so it must move. The queen should stay on the diagonal to maintain pressure, and also consider squares that keep it active and near the king for defense.
notes.teaches: When your queen is attacked, choose a square that preserves its activity and also keeps it close to the king for defensive purposes. Activity is important, but safety and coordination matter too.
notes.plans: Move the queen to a square like e1, which is both active and defensive, rather than to a4 where it is offside.

notes.explains: After the queen moves, the bishop can go to e2 and the rook to e1, completing the development of the pieces. The position is good for Black: the king is safe, pawns are well placed, and the bishop on e2 is excellent.
notes.teaches: A well-coordinated attack requires all pieces to participate. Even if one piece is doing a great job, the others need to support it.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing the knight to g4, creating threats against the white king, such as a potential mate with knight h3 and f2.

notes.explains: The knight on g4 creates a concrete threat of mate, forcing White to respond. White tries to create an escape square for the king and attacks the knight, but Black can continue to press.
notes.teaches: When you have a threat, keep the pressure on. Even if the opponent defends, look for ways to increase activity and create new threats.
notes.plans: After White's response, continue to improve piece placement and seek more space and threats against the white king.

notes.explains: The white king is exposed and isolated, with its own pieces far away and unable to defend. Black has a strong attack with the knight, queen, and bishops converging on the king.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a threat, don't automatically respond to it. Look for a bigger threat of your own that improves your position and creates more serious problems for the opponent.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by bringing more pieces into the attack, such as the queen, while maintaining the pressure on the king.

notes.explains: Black has a choice between trading the active knight on g4 for the undeveloped bishop on c1. The knight is much more valuable in the attack, so trading it off would be a mistake.
notes.teaches: Don't trade your active, well-placed pieces for your opponent's passive ones unless you gain a concrete advantage. Keep your best pieces to maintain the attack.
notes.plans: Keep the knight on g4 and find a way to increase the pressure, such as playing Qf2, which attacks the rook on e1 and joins the attack.

notes.explains: Black has many winning moves, but the key is to find the most forcing and direct continuation. The queen can be brought into the attack with threats of mate, and the knight can support.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, look for the most forcing moves that create immediate threats, such as checkmate threats, and use all your pieces in coordination.
notes.plans: Play Qf2, attacking the rook on e1 and threatening mate. If White defends, continue with moves like Nf2 or Bf3 to maintain the attack.

notes.explains: White is desperate and tries a last trick with Bxf7+ check, hoping to bring the queen into the game. Black can simply move the king to h8, ignoring the pawn, and White has no follow-up.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a desperate sacrifice, don't be greedy. Simply sidestep the threat and maintain your winning position. The king can often move to a safe square, and the attack continues.
notes.plans: Play Kh8, avoiding the check and keeping the material and positional advantage. White's attack fizzles out, and Black can proceed with the mating net.

notes.explains: Black is about to deliver mate, but White has just played a check with a bishop to bring the queen into the attack. The black king was safe before, but now White threatens annoying checks, possibly a perpetual.
notes.teaches: When you are winning and the opponent gives a check, do not automatically capture or block; consider moving the king to a safe square that avoids all further checks, preserving your winning advantage.
notes.plans: Play Kh8, ignoring the pawn, and maintain the mating net.

notes.explains: In a knight ending with equal pawns, Black has a beautiful pawn chain while White has doubled pawns and a poorly placed knight on d1 that has no safe moves. The black knight is attacked but has several squares.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a badly placed piece can be a decisive weakness; use your pawns to restrict it and improve your own pieces before pushing for a passed pawn.
notes.plans: Black should aim to create a passed pawn and queen it, but must first improve the knight and fix the pawn structure.

notes.explains: In this endgame, the immediate win is not by checkmate but by promoting a pawn. The defender's pieces are tied up, and the attacker has a clear path to queening.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, convert by advancing a passed pawn toward promotion, especially if the opponent's pieces cannot stop it.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawn, using tactics to eliminate any defenders that could intercept it.

notes.explains: The move ...Nc3 is a surprising sacrifice of a knight for a pawn, but it is justified because it creates an unstoppable passed pawn. The knight on c3 attacks the enemy knight, which is immobile and undefended, and if the knight is captured, the pawn recaptures and advances.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a piece sacrifice can be correct if it clears the path for a pawn to promote, especially when the opponent's pieces are poorly placed.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, the attacker's plan is to push the a-pawn, using the threat of promotion to force the opponent into a losing defense.

notes.explains: The defender tries to stop the pawn by bringing the knight back, but the attacker prevents that by capturing or blocking the knight's path. The pawn continues to advance, and the defender's attempts to blockade fail.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is far advanced, the defender must find a way to block it, but if the attacker can control the key squares, the pawn cannot be stopped.
notes.plans: The attacker keeps pushing the pawn, ignoring other distractions, and the defender eventually resigns because the promotion is inevitable.

notes.explains: In a two-game knockout match, having the white pieces is a significant asset because you have limited chances to convert your opening advantage into a win.
notes.teaches: When you have white in a short match, aim to be aggressive and try to gain an edge from the opening, as you may not get many opportunities to outplay your opponent.

notes.explains: Building a repertoire is more effective when you stick to one opening and follow games of players who specialize in it, as they provide reliable models for the lines you play.
notes.teaches: Choose an opening that fits your style and study key games from experts in that line to internalize the plans and typical ideas.

notes.explains: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, the move ...Nc6 is a subtle deviation from the more common ...a6, which keeps the knight flexible and avoids some lines where White can annoy Black with a capture on c4.
notes.teaches: Small deviations in well-known openings can be a practical surprise, especially if your opponent has prepared for your usual move order.
notes.plans: Black aims to develop harmoniously with ...e6, ...Bxc5, and ...Nc6, keeping the bishop's diagonal open and preparing to castle.

notes.explains: Repeating the same opening in consecutive games at a high level can be risky because your opponent may have prepared specifically for it, giving them comfort and possibly an edge.
notes.teaches: Varying your opening choices, even slightly, can prevent your opponent from relying on deep preparation and force them to think over the board.

notes.explains: Repeating the same opening line can be dangerous because it signals your intentions, allowing the opponent to prepare and feel comfortable in known positions. A slight move-order change, like ...Nc6 instead of the main line, can create surprise and unsettle the opponent.
notes.teaches: Avoid being too predictable in your opening choices; small deviations can disrupt your opponent's preparation and give you psychological or practical advantages.
notes.plans: Consider using move-order nuances to steer the game into positions where your opponent is less comfortable.

notes.explains: In the position after ...a6, White has the option of a3 as a waiting move, intending to later play b4 and Bb2 for quick development. This setup doesn't give a clear advantage but can lead to positions where White is more comfortable, especially if Black is unfamiliar with the strategic nuances.
notes.teaches: Waiting moves can be a useful tool to provoke weaknesses or gain a tempo in development, but they often yield only a slight edge, so they require precise follow-up.
notes.plans: If White plays a3, follow up with b4 and Bb2, aiming for rapid development and central control.

notes.explains: Black's solid setup with ...Bd7, ...Rc8, and ...Rd8 leaves no immediate weaknesses. The bishop on d7 can retreat to e8 if needed, and Black is happy to trade pieces, even leading to a balanced endgame. This shows that Black has already achieved equality in the opening.
notes.teaches: In the opening, if you can reach a comfortable, solid position with no weaknesses, you have already succeeded; don't overpress for an advantage that isn't there.
notes.plans: Maintain flexibility with pieces, be ready to trade into equal endgames, and avoid creating weaknesses.

notes.explains: In the game, White chose Nc3 and after ...a6, dxe5, the position simplified into an endgame without queens. This was a strategic mistake in the context of a match where White only has the white pieces once; wasting that chance to push for an advantage can be costly.
notes.teaches: When you have the white pieces in a match, you should consider the match situation and try to create winning chances, rather than settling for a drawish endgame early on.
notes.plans: If you have the white pieces, look for lines that maintain tension and offer chances to outplay your opponent, especially in a match format.

notes.explains: In the endgame after Qxd1 Rxd1 Bxc5, White's knight on f3 goes to d2 and then b3, regrouping to target weak squares. This is a different regrouping than when the knight was still on b1, showing that the knight's path depends on the piece placement.
notes.teaches: In endgames, piece regrouping is crucial; knights often reroute to better squares to control key points or attack weaknesses.
notes.plans: Look for knight maneuvers to strong outposts or to pressure opponent's pawns, even if it takes a few moves.

notes.explains: Black plays e5 to gain space and develop the bishop to b7 on the long diagonal, challenging White's central control. This leads to a structure resembling a Sicilian queenside pawn structure, but with the roles reversed.
notes.teaches: Gaining space with a pawn push like e5 can be a double-edged sword; it creates space but also potential weaknesses. Always consider whether the pawn advances create hooks or holes that the opponent can exploit later.
notes.plans: Black will develop the bishop to b7 and aim for a comfortable position, while White may look for breaks like a4 to challenge Black's structure.

notes.explains: White plays bishop takes c6, trading a bishop for a knight and doubling Black's pawns. This damages Black's structure but gives White the bishop pair, which can be a long-term asset, especially in endgames.
notes.teaches: When considering a trade that damages the opponent's pawn structure, weigh the compensation. The bishop pair can often compensate for a compromised structure because of their long-range control, especially in open positions.
notes.plans: White will aim to use the bishop pair to control the board and target Black's weak pawns, while Black will try to activate the knights and exploit the open files.

notes.explains: In endgames, the bishop pair can be especially powerful because bishops control many squares across open diagonals, while knights are short-range. A bishop that lacks good squares is a long-term problem.
notes.teaches: Value the bishop pair in open endgames and look to activate bishops; a passive bishop can be a permanent weakness.

notes.explains: White tried to create an advantage from the opening, but Black equalized comfortably. White's further attempts to find weaknesses only made things worse, giving Black chances.
notes.teaches: Don't force an advantage when the opponent has equalized; overpressing can backfire.

notes.explains: Black's pieces are well placed, with rooks on open files and a knight on a5 that attacks key squares. White's most active piece is the knight on c3, but its jumps are mostly controlled, so Black can kick it away with a simple move like bishop to b4.
notes.teaches: Identify the opponent's most active piece and find ways to neutralize it, even if it costs a tempo.
notes.plans: Play bishop to b4 to force the knight away, then follow up with rook to b5 to control the c5 square and prevent the knight from reaching an outpost.

notes.explains: Black trades the bishop pair for initiative: after bishop takes c4 and b takes c4, White's c-pawn becomes weak, and Black gains control of the b-file. The position offers only small edges, but Black is the one with chances to improve.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up the bishop pair is worth it to create weaknesses and seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Use the b-file and the weak c4 pawn to increase pressure, while keeping the knight on c3 restricted by the c6 pawn and the king on e7.

notes.explains: The pawn on c6, though isolated, does a great job controlling the knight's possible jumps, especially with the king on e7 covering d5. This prevents White from activating the knight.
notes.teaches: Pawns can be strong even if weak-looking, as they restrict enemy pieces; coordinate your king and pawns to control key squares.
notes.plans: Keep the c6 pawn in place to limit the knight, and proceed with the plan of improving Black's position while White's pieces remain passive.

notes.explains: In this position, Black's bishop on b4 is more active than White's bishop on e1, and Black's king is slightly better placed than White's on f1. The pawn on e5 gives Black more space than White's pawn on e3. These small advantages accumulate, and Black is the side improving.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a position, look for small advantages: better-placed pieces, safer king, more space. These tiny edges can add up to a clear plus.
notes.plans: Black should continue improving piece placement and increasing pressure, while White must find active play to counter Black's growing advantage.

notes.explains: White considered playing Ne4 to control the c5 square, but Black could respond with ...f5, gaining more space and kicking the knight away. After ...Bh4+ and exchanges, Black would still have a slight edge due to the doubled pawns being hard to attack.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a piece that can be kicked with a pawn advance, that piece may not be well placed. Consider pawn breaks to gain space and disrupt the opponent's plans.
notes.plans: If White plays Ne4, Black should play ...f5 to gain space and then continue with ...Bh4+ and exchanges to maintain the edge.

notes.explains: Black chose ...Nc5 instead of ...Nb6. The move ...Nb6 might allow White to play c5, and if Bxc5, then ...Ne4 could be a tactic. Also, the pawn on c5 is annoying for White because it blocks the c-file and prevents White from doubling rooks against c6.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to restrict your opponent's position than to go for immediate material. A pawn that blocks your opponent's pieces can be very valuable.
notes.plans: Black should keep the c5 pawn in place to restrict White's play, while continuing to improve piece activity.

notes.explains: If White tries to capture the knight on c5 with the bishop, Black has tactical resources: after ...Rxe1+ (check), the king must respond, then Black can recapture on c5. This would result in Black having two pieces for a rook, which is usually good.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are attacked, look for tactical defenses that involve checks and captures. Having two pieces for a rook is often a favorable trade.
notes.plans: If White plays Bxc5, Black should respond with ...Rxe1+ and then recapture on c5, securing a material advantage.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has sacrificed a rook for two pieces, and the resulting material balance is favorable because the two minor pieces cover more ground and coordinate better than the lone rook. The knight on c5 is a powerful outpost, and the pawn on c4 is weak because it is overextended and cannot control the d4 square, while Black's pawn on c6 perfectly controls the knight's jumps.
notes.teaches: When you have two pieces for a rook, the activity and coordination of your pieces often outweigh the material deficit. Look for outposts and weak pawns to justify the trade.
notes.plans: Black should continue to centralize the king, improve the rook, and target White's weak pawns and passive pieces.

notes.explains: White's position is difficult to play because almost every move creates new weaknesses. For example, pushing e4 gives Black the d4 square and ideas of Nf6-e6, while the pawn on c4 remains weak and the bishop on e1 is passive. Black's pieces are all active, while White's are struggling.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is cramped, avoid pawn moves that create permanent weaknesses. Instead, seek trades to relieve pressure, but be aware that even trades may not solve all problems if the opponent's pieces remain dominant.
notes.plans: White should look for ways to trade pieces and simplify, but must be careful not to allow Black's pieces to infiltrate.

notes.explains: White's move Rc2-a1 is a strange attempt to prepare a3 and provoke Black's bishop, but it fails to address the fundamental issues. Black can simply play f5, and if White plays a3, the b3 square becomes weak, allowing Nc5-b3. If White tries to defend with Rb1, Black can use tactical tricks like Nc5-d4+ to win the exchange.
notes.teaches: Every pawn move leaves a weakness behind. Before pushing a pawn, ask yourself which squares become weak and whether the opponent can exploit them. Also, when you have a space advantage, look for tactical motifs like forks and discovered attacks to convert the pressure.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press, using the weak b3 square and tactical threats to increase the advantage.

notes.explains: When one side has been pressing for a long time, the defender often cracks under the cumulative pressure, and tactical tricks become inevitable. In this position, Black's pieces are well placed, the e5 pawn is protected, and Black has more space, making White's defensive task very difficult.
notes.teaches: Prolonged pressure can force errors; maintain the pressure and look for ways to improve your position while denying the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should continue to improve piece placement and restrict White's activity, avoiding unnecessary trades that give White breathing room.

notes.explains: White tried a3 to create luft or prevent a pin, but it was not effective because Black can simply retreat the bishop and still have all the improvements. White then chose rook to d1 to simplify, hoping to hold the endgame, but after the exchange, Black's position remains superior.
notes.teaches: When defending, simplifying can be a practical try, but only if the resulting endgame is holdable; otherwise, you may be trading into a worse ending.
notes.plans: Black should keep the initiative and avoid trades that reduce the advantage; White must seek active defense and counterplay.

notes.explains: Black played e4, gaining even more space and potentially using d3 for a knight, supported by the pawn. Unlike a3, the weaknesses created (d4 and f4) are not easily exploitable by White because their pieces cannot get there effectively.
notes.teaches: When creating pawn weaknesses, ensure the opponent cannot easily occupy them; space gains can be worth structural concessions if the opponent's pieces are poorly placed.
notes.plans: Black should continue to expand and improve piece coordination, using the extra space to restrict White's options.

notes.explains: Black played rook to b7, a patient move, recognizing that the advantage is static and not dependent on quick tactics. The structure is fixed, no pawn breaks are possible, so Black can take time to improve the position little by little.
notes.teaches: Static advantages (like better pawn structure or piece activity) do not require immediate action; you can slowly increase the pressure without fear of the advantage disappearing.
notes.plans: Black should gradually improve piece placement, double rooks on open files, and create threats at the right moment.

notes.explains: When considering trades, Black must avoid exchanges that improve White's pieces. For example, bishop takes on d3 would allow the knight to move to a better square. Instead, Black can trade on e5, opening the a-file and creating targets, while keeping the knight out of play.
notes.teaches: Before trading, evaluate whether the exchange improves your opponent's pieces; avoid trades that help the opponent activate.
notes.plans: Black should seek trades that open lines for their rooks and keep White's pieces passive.
