notes.explains: Playing a3 to gain space on the queenside is a good idea because Black has more space there; it also forces White to make a decision between defending the b-pawn or acting on the kingside.
notes.teaches: Gaining space with pawn moves like a3 or h3 can be good even if you can't calculate all the consequences; it's a positional move that increases your options and forces the opponent to choose.
notes.plans: After a3, if White doesn't defend b3, Black can play b3 and then follow up with tactics against the weakened queenside.

notes.explains: Knight to e6 is an alternative that also puts pressure on White, but it allows White to play Kg2 to stop the knight fork on f3; a3 is more flexible because it creates a threat that White must address.
notes.teaches: When choosing between moves, prefer the one that gives your opponent more problems and forces them to make a difficult choice.
notes.plans: If White plays Kg2, Black can capture on f3 and then play Be6, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: White's f4 push weakens the king side and creates targets, making the position more unstable for White. Black has a solid position and should avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their own position, you don't need to rush into tactics; simply maintain your solid structure and let their weaknesses remain.
notes.plans: Bring the knight back to d7, then maneuver to b4 to pressure the queen side.

notes.explains: Black is better on the queen side and center, so it makes sense to bring pieces to that side. If Black attacks the queen side, White will counter on the king side, so Black should be prepared for that.
notes.teaches: Align your piece placement with your planned attack. If you intend to play on one side, bring your pieces there, and be ready for the opponent's counterplay on the other side.
notes.plans: Continue with knight to b4 and prepare to poke White's queen side.

notes.explains: The knight on d7 is a valuable piece that could become a beautiful sacrifice later, but it's safer to keep it and reposition it to b4. The knight belongs on b4, not back to c7.
notes.teaches: Don't give up a piece without clear compensation. Sometimes a piece is better placed on an active square like b4, even if it means a maneuver.
notes.plans: Play Nb4, then continue to pressure the queen side.

notes.explains: White's Rook to e3 is a strange move; a more natural plan would be g4 to start a king side attack. White's position is otherwise somewhat compromised.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a passive or awkward move, it's a sign that their position may be difficult to handle. Look for ways to exploit the lack of coordination.
notes.plans: Proceed with Nb4, then continue to improve piece placement and prepare queen side action.

notes.explains: In this position, Black has a choice between the aggressive f5 and the solid Bd7. The f5 push is tempting but commits too early; White can respond with g4 or Bg2, keeping many options. Bd7 is a flexible developing move that keeps the tension and invites White to show their plan.
notes.teaches: Avoid premature pawn advances that commit your structure and give the opponent clear targets. Prefer flexible moves that maintain tension and let the opponent make the first error.
notes.plans: Play Bd7, intending to follow up with b5, e5, or f5 depending on White's setup. Keep the position flexible and wait for White to commit.

notes.explains: The line with Bd4 and Nb3 leads to Qxa2, but then Rxd6 leaves Black in an inferior endgame despite having extra activity. The endgame is worse for Black, so this tactical idea is not appealing.
notes.teaches: Before entering a tactical sequence, evaluate the resulting endgame. Activity can be outweighed by structural weaknesses or a worse pawn structure.
notes.plans: Avoid the Bd4/Nb3 line; instead, keep pieces on the board and maintain dynamic chances.

notes.explains: After White plays e5 and Black captures, White's attack is less promising than with g4. Black's bishop on d7 is somewhat passive, but the rook on a8 is not doing much, so bringing it to d8 defends the bishop and improves the rook.
notes.teaches: When a piece is passive, look for ways to improve it while also defending. Rooks often belong on open or semi-open files, and moving them to active squares can solve multiple problems.
notes.plans: Play Rd8 to defend the bishop on d7 and activate the rook. Continue with natural development and wait for White's next move.

notes.explains: The bishop on d7 is blocked by the rook on d8, so the rook should move to d8 to defend the bishop and activate the rook, which is not doing much on a8.
notes.teaches: When a piece is passively placed, consider repositioning it to a more active square, even if it means moving a piece that has already been developed.
notes.plans: Play Rd8 to defend the bishop and prepare to activate the rook along the d-file.

notes.explains: Black has a stable position, so White must seek dynamic play to create winning chances. Rushing moves can lead to mistakes, as seen when White played g4 prematurely.
notes.teaches: When facing a solid position, avoid rushing; instead, improve your pieces and look for dynamic breaks, but only when they are fully prepared.
notes.plans: Continue improving piece placement and wait for the right moment to strike.

notes.explains: After White's g4, Black should continue rearranging pieces. The knight on f6 has done its job and should retreat to h5, attacking the pawn on g4 and preparing to reroute to f4.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a piece has fulfilled its role and be willing to retreat it to a better square, even if it seems counterintuitive.
notes.plans: Play Nh5, attacking the g4 pawn and eyeing the f4 square.

notes.explains: After Qc5 and Re4, Black plays Be6, opening up the position and increasing piece activity. This move is strong because it sacrifices the rook on d8, but after Rxd8+ Bxd8, Black gets Rook d2 coming, giving dynamic counterplay.
notes.teaches: Sometimes sacrificing material for activity and initiative is the best way to maintain the advantage, especially in dynamic positions.
notes.plans: Play Be6, offering the rook to activate the bishop and create threats against White's king.

notes.explains: In this position, the bishop on e6 is strong because it opens lines and creates dynamic threats, such as the coming rook to d2, rather than being a simple sacrifice.
notes.teaches: A move can be powerful not because it wins material, but because it activates pieces and creates lasting pressure.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece activity and coordinate rooks and bishops on open files.

notes.explains: Black's knight is misplaced and useless, but by opening lines and regrouping, black can bring it to better squares like e6, which would be very unpleasant for white.
notes.teaches: When a piece is poorly placed, look for ways to regroup and reroute it to a stronger outpost.
notes.plans: Regroup the knight to e6 or another strong square, and reposition the bishop to f5 or e6.

notes.explains: Rook f8 is the best move here because it prepares to bring the bishop to d4 and the queen to f5, creating one-move threats that keep white on the defensive.
notes.teaches: One-move threats are effective when they improve your position and maintain dynamic pressure.
notes.plans: Play Rf8, then Bd4 and Qf5, keeping the initiative with constant threats.

notes.explains: White's position is weak: the g5 pawn is falling, the a3 pawn is weak on the queenside, and black's bishops are far superior.
notes.teaches: In dynamic positions, compare the relative activity of pieces and identify weak pawns to target.
notes.plans: Capture the weak pawns, keep the queens on to maintain pressure, and use the bishops to dominate the board.

notes.explains: Black is clearly better, but the win requires technique: avoid blunders, keep activity, and don't rush to exchange queens.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, maintain piece activity and use the king actively before trading down to a favorable endgame.
notes.plans: Poke around with the queen, drive the enemy king back, bring your own king forward, and only then consider queen exchanges.

notes.explains: In this queen endgame, Black is winning, but the win is not immediate. The key is to avoid rushing and to keep the initiative while the queens remain on the board.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning endgame, don't rush to simplify if you can first improve your position. Keeping the queens can allow you to create threats and increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Black should aim to improve the king's position, gain space, and only exchange queens when it is most favorable, such as when the king can penetrate to b2.

notes.explains: The threat of mate (e.g., Qh2# if the king goes to g2) is a useful tool to force the opponent's king to a worse square, even in an endgame.
notes.teaches: In endgames, mating threats can be used to drive the enemy king to a less favorable position, even if the mate itself is not immediately delivered.
notes.plans: Use the queen to create threats that force the white king to move to a square where Black can then improve its own position.

notes.explains: There are multiple winning methods in this endgame. One straightforward approach is to bring the king to a5, exchange queens, and then march the king to b2 to capture the pawn.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, there is often more than one path to victory. It is important to choose the most practical and reliable method.
notes.plans: Consider the plan of king to a5, queen exchange, and king to b2 to win the pawn, but also be flexible to other winning ideas.

notes.explains: White's early pawn push e5 was premature and led to a worse position. The move g4 might have been more flexible, keeping the tension.
notes.teaches: In the opening, avoid rushing with pawn advances that create weaknesses or allow the opponent to seize the initiative. Sometimes it is better to maintain flexibility.
notes.plans: If you are White, consider more restrained moves like g4 instead of e5 to keep the position balanced.

notes.explains: Bxc6 is a strong move because it removes the knight that defends the dark squares, allowing the white king to enter. If Black recaptures with the rook, White can continue with Rd3, and if with the king, White can still penetrate.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is worth giving up a good bishop to eliminate a key defender, especially when the resulting king penetration is decisive.
notes.plans: After Bxc6, aim to bring the king to c5 or d4, creating threats and winning material.

notes.explains: With the knight gone, White's king has two ways to penetrate: via b4 and d4. Black cannot stop both, so the position becomes winning.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a centralized king is extremely powerful, especially when the opponent has weaknesses on both flanks.
notes.plans: March the king to c5, then capture the weak pawns on the queenside.

notes.explains: In this rook and minor piece endgame, the activity of the king is the dominant factor. If the white king can penetrate to a square like c5, black's position collapses because the pawns become vulnerable and the coordination of black's pieces is disrupted.
notes.teaches: In endgames with rooks and minor pieces, prioritize king centralization and penetration. A centralized king can support pawn advances and create threats that tie down the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: White should aim to bring the king to c5 or similar central squares, using the rook to control open files and the knight to cover key squares. Black must try to prevent this by placing pieces to block the king's entry.

notes.explains: Black's knight is not on d4, which means the white king has two possible entry routes into black's position. This makes it very difficult for black to stop the infiltration, as the king can choose the path of least resistance.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are not optimally placed to control key squares, the king can often find multiple entry points. Use this to your advantage by keeping the opponent's pieces tied down and unable to cover all avenues.
notes.plans: White should probe both entry points and switch to the one that black leaves unguarded. Black must coordinate pieces to cover both potential king entries.

notes.explains: White's rook is active on the c-file, and this activity is a key factor in maintaining the advantage. The rook controls the open file and restricts black's pieces, while the king can support the advance.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, an active rook is a powerful asset. It can dominate the opponent's pieces, control key files, and support the king's penetration. Keep your rook active and avoid passive defense.
notes.plans: White should keep the rook on the c-file to maintain pressure and support the king's advance. Black should try to challenge the rook's activity by contesting the file or creating counterplay.

notes.explains: Black is considering moves like f6 or g6, but these are 'good-looking' moves that don't actually accomplish much. They don't address the main issue of the king's penetration and may even weaken squares.
notes.teaches: Avoid moves that look natural but don't address the key strategic needs of the position. In endgames, every move should have a purpose, such as improving your pieces, preventing the opponent's plan, or creating counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should focus on preventing the white king's entry and improving piece coordination, rather than making pawn moves that don't contribute. White should continue to improve the king and rook.

notes.explains: Black is trying to exchange pieces, specifically the knight for the bishop, to increase drawing chances. Exchanging down reduces white's attacking potential and makes it harder for white to convert the advantage.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the defender often seeks to exchange pieces to reach a drawn pawn endgame or a simpler position. The attacker must be aware of this and avoid unnecessary exchanges that reduce winning chances.
notes.plans: Black should look for opportunities to trade minor pieces, especially if it leads to a rook endgame with fewer pawns. White should avoid such exchanges and keep pieces on the board to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: White is not in a hurry because black has no threats and is almost paralyzed. This allows white to improve the position methodically without rushing into complications.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has no active counterplay, take your time to improve your pieces and strengthen your position. Avoid unnecessary complications that could give the opponent chances.
notes.plans: White should slowly improve the king and rook, and only then consider concrete breakthroughs. Black should try to create counterplay to force white into less favorable lines.

notes.explains: In this rook and minor piece endgame, White's pieces are active while Black's are passive. Black's king is almost paralyzed, and there are no immediate threats, so White can take time to improve the position without rushing.
notes.teaches: When you have a dominant position, you do not need to hurry. Look for ways to improve your pieces and create weaknesses in the opponent's camp.
notes.plans: Continue to fix weaknesses on the kingside, such as advancing pawns to g4 and h4 to create targets like h6.

notes.explains: The move g4 serves two purposes: it prepares to use f4 as an entry square for the king if the h6 pawn moves, and it starts a pawn march (g4-h4-h5) to create weaknesses in Black's kingside. After h5, the threat of Nf6-g8 becomes significant, and the h6 pawn becomes immobile.
notes.teaches: In endgames, use pawn advances to create weaknesses and to open entry squares for your king. Fix your opponent's weaknesses before attacking them.
notes.plans: Play h4 and h5 to fix the h6 weakness, then bring the knight to f6 to attack it.

notes.explains: The knight on d6 is well placed but not attacking any weaknesses. It is important to give purpose to every piece. The plan is to continue improving the position by fixing weaknesses first, then finding better squares for the knight.
notes.teaches: A piece can look good but still be ineffective if it is not attacking anything. Always try to give your pieces a concrete task.
notes.plans: Continue the pawn march on the kingside, then reposition the knight to a more active square.

notes.explains: White plays g4 to open a new front and add tension, creating more weaknesses in Black's position. After h4 and f3-f5, Black seeks counterplay, but White can avoid unnecessary complications by not allowing any counterplay if possible.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, avoid allowing counterplay. Sometimes you must accept some, but if you can prevent it without risk, do so.
notes.plans: Use moves like Rc7 or Re7 to prepare an attack on the sixth rank, and after killing Black's counterplay, improve all pieces together.

notes.explains: The move g3 is suggested to 'pacify' the opponent's pieces, likely by limiting the knight's outposts or reducing the bishop's scope. After that, the plan is to improve all white pieces together, keeping the opponent's pieces extremely restricted.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a quiet move like g3 can be a strong prophylactic measure, preventing the opponent from gaining activity. It's important to keep the opponent's pieces restricted while you slowly improve your own.
notes.plans: Play g3 to limit the opponent's knight or bishop, then bring the king to c4 to keep it active and flexible. Avoid closing the position too much, as that can reduce your entry squares.

notes.explains: The speaker warns against advancing the king too far, as the opponent can start checking and plant a rook on g3, creating counterplay. The move King d6 is met with Rook a8, an interesting defensive idea, but the speaker prefers King d7 to maintain flexibility.
notes.teaches: In endgames, be cautious about overextending your king; the opponent can use checks to create counterplay. Sometimes a slight retreat or sideways move keeps your king safe while maintaining pressure.
notes.plans: Keep the king active but not overextended. If the opponent tries to create counterplay, be ready to redirect your rook to the kingside, where you have more space to attack.

notes.explains: The speaker emphasizes that going after the f3 pawn is a mistake, as it allows the opponent to activate their pieces. Instead, the rook should be redirected to the kingside, where there is more space to attack the opponent's position.
notes.teaches: In endgames, avoid grabbing pawns if it allows the opponent to activate their pieces. Redirect your pieces to the side where you have more space and can create threats.
notes.plans: Redirect the rook to h1, then to h7, to attack the opponent's kingside. This keeps the opponent passive and prepares to bring the knight into the game.

notes.explains: The threat of Knight xb6 wins the d6 pawn, forcing the opponent's king to d7. After the exchange, the knight is placed on g4, and the bishop is pinned, leading to a completely winning position. The opponent's pieces are passive, and the extra pawns will decide.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, use threats to force the opponent into passivity. A well-timed knight maneuver can create decisive threats while keeping the opponent's pieces tied down.
notes.plans: Execute the knight fork on b6 to win the pawn, then place the knight on g4 to maintain pressure. Continue to improve the king and rook, and convert the extra pawns.

notes.explains: In the rook versus knight endgame, the speaker discusses the importance of keeping the rook behind the passed pawn. If the rook is placed in front of the pawn, the defender can draw by giving checks. The king's distance is critical: if the king is too far, the defender can hold.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the rook belongs behind the passed pawn, not in front. The defending side can draw if the attacking king is too far away, so it's crucial to bring the king up to support the pawn.
notes.plans: Keep the rook behind the pawn and advance the pawn with the king's support. If the opponent tries to give checks, use the rook to block or the king to approach.

notes.explains: When promoting a pawn, you can use the rook to build a 'bridge'—a defensive shield against checks. By placing the rook on a square that blocks the enemy rook's checks, you can safely escort the pawn to promotion. This is a standard technique in rook endgames.
notes.teaches: The 'bridge' (or Lucena) technique is essential for converting a pawn advantage when the defending king is cut off. Place your rook on the fourth rank to block checks, then bring your king out.
notes.plans: If you have a pawn on the seventh rank and your rook is on the board, aim to build the bridge by moving the rook to the fourth rank and then using the king to support the pawn.

notes.explains: In rook versus minor piece endings, the side with the rook often has winning chances if the enemy king is far from the action. Here, the white king is too far to help, but the rook can still win by exploiting the knight's lack of stability. The defender's best hope is to exchange minor pieces, which would simplify to a drawn rook ending.
notes.teaches: When you have a rook against a knight, try to keep the knight passive and use your rook to attack pawns. If you are the defender, look for chances to exchange the knight for the rook or to reach a drawn pawn structure.
notes.plans: The side with the rook should target the enemy pawns and try to create connected passed pawns. The defender should seek to trade off the minor piece or activate the king.

notes.explains: In this position, the bishop on e3 is well placed, controlling key squares and supporting the knight. The opponent tries to displace it with a pawn push to f4, but that would weaken their own position. By preventing that with g3, the bishop remains strong and the knight is protected.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to your opponent's threats, even while executing your own plan. A well-placed piece can be worth more than material, so defend it against pawn attacks.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on its strong diagonal, and use the rook to attack the opponent's weak pawns. If the opponent tries to push f4, respond with g3 to maintain the bishop's post.

notes.explains: When you have a material advantage, the simplest winning method is often to create connected passed pawns. Here, the rook can capture a pawn on e4, leading to two connected passed pawns, which are very powerful and usually win easily.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, aim to create connected passed pawns. They support each other and are much harder to stop than isolated pawns.
notes.plans: Use the rook to capture enemy pawns and create a pair of connected passed pawns. Then advance them together, using the rook to protect them from behind.

notes.explains: In rook and minor piece endgames, forcing the exchange of minor pieces can simplify to a rook endgame that may still be winning but is much harder to convert. The defender can use the extra piece to create counterplay.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary simplifications when you have a material advantage; keep pieces on the board to maintain pressure and limit the defender's activity.
notes.plans: If the opponent offers a trade of minor pieces, evaluate whether the resulting rook endgame is clearly winning. If not, keep the pieces and improve your position.

notes.explains: Keeping more pawns on the board increases the number of weaknesses and gives the stronger side more targets to attack. Exchanging pawns can reduce winning chances.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, preserve pawns to create multiple threats and keep the defender tied down.
notes.plans: Avoid pawn exchanges that reduce your attacking potential; instead, use your pieces to create threats and force the defender into passivity.

notes.explains: Centralizing the king is crucial in endgames. A centralized king supports pawn advances, restricts the opponent's king, and helps in converting advantages.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, bring your king toward the center before pushing pawns or engaging in tactics.
notes.plans: Move the king to a central square (e.g., d5 or c4) to support your pawns and limit the opponent's counterplay.

notes.explains: The defender's best practical chances often come from active piece play and trying to exchange the last pawn. If the stronger side can prevent this, the win is easier.
notes.teaches: When defending, aim to exchange pawns and activate your pieces to create drawing chances. When attacking, prevent the exchange of the last pawn.
notes.plans: If defending, try to trade off the remaining pawns and centralize your king. If attacking, use your pieces to control key squares and avoid pawn trades.

notes.explains: In rook and bishop vs. rook and knight, the bishop can be a strong defensive piece, protecting key pawns and controlling important diagonals. The knight may struggle to find good squares.
notes.teaches: Use the bishop to defend weaknesses and restrict the opponent's pieces. In such endgames, the bishop often outperforms the knight due to its long-range influence.
notes.plans: Place the bishop on a strong diagonal to protect your pawns and prevent the opponent's knight from becoming active.

notes.explains: The defender played a knight move with the idea of exchanging the last pawn, but the king was too far away to support that plan. The attacker then prevented the exchange by placing the bishop on a square that controls the pawn's path, keeping the last pawn on the board.
notes.teaches: In these endgames, the attacker should use the bishop to restrain the defender's pawns and prevent the exchange of the last pawn, as keeping a pawn often secures the win.
notes.plans: Use the bishop to control key squares around the remaining pawn, avoiding its exchange, then use the pawn as a bait to win material or force the opponent's pieces into passivity.

notes.explains: The game ended with the knight trapped because it had no safe squares; the bishop controlled the escape routes, and the rook or king covered the rest. The defender resigned because the knight was lost for sure.
notes.teaches: In these endgames, look for ways to trap the enemy knight by using the bishop to control its flight squares and the rook/king to restrict its movement, often leading to a decisive material gain.
notes.plans: Coordinate the bishop and rook to encircle the enemy knight, cutting off its escape squares, and then win it.

notes.explains: In knight endgames, the side with a pawn up often faces a defender whose king can approach the pawns. If the defender's king is close, sacrificing the knight for the pawns may lead to a draw, but when the pawns are far apart on opposite wings, the defender's task becomes harder.
notes.teaches: Knight endgames resemble king and pawn endgames in that king activity and pawn structure are decisive, but the knight's unique movement can create tactical opportunities for domination.

notes.explains: In the study, white has pawns on both edges of the board. The a-pawn is doomed because the black king can capture it, but the h-pawn may be the winning resource. The key is to choose the correct king move to support the h-pawn while restricting the black knight.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is lost, focus on the remaining pawn and use the king to support it while also attacking the enemy knight. The correct king move can make the difference between a win and a draw.
notes.plans: White should play the king to e7, attacking the knight and preparing to advance the h-pawn. If the king goes to d7, black can regroup and draw.

notes.explains: After the correct king move, black's knight has limited squares. Moves like knight f4 or knight d4 stop the h-pawn from advancing, but white can still make progress. The knight is often tied to defending key squares, and white must exploit that.
notes.teaches: In knight endgames, the defending knight can be overloaded. Use your king to attack the knight while pushing the pawn, forcing the defender to give ground.
notes.plans: White should continue by advancing the h-pawn, using the king to support it and keeping the black knight passive.

notes.explains: In this knight endgame, black's knight is trying to stop the h-pawn. The knight must be dominated or traded to allow the pawn to advance. White's king and knight work together to restrict the black knight's squares and keep the black king away from the pawn's path.
notes.teaches: In knight endgames, a lone knight can often stop a pawn if it can get in front of it. The stronger side must use its king and knight to drive the defending knight away from key squares, while also keeping the defending king from approaching the pawn.
notes.plans: White should aim to place the knight on a strong square like c5, defending the pawn from behind, while the king supports the pawn's advance. If the black knight is traded, the pawn will win on the other side.

notes.explains: When the black knight tries to stop the pawn from a different square, white can still use the king and knight to dominate it. The key is to keep the black king out of the pawn's path and restrict the knight's options.
notes.teaches: In such positions, the stronger side should use the king to support the pawn and the knight to control the squares the defending knight needs. A knight can be dominated if it has no safe squares to move to.
notes.plans: White should march the king to support the pawn, while the knight restricts the black knight's squares. If the black knight is forced to move, the pawn can advance.

notes.explains: A key idea is to push the pawn whenever possible, rather than moving the king first. In one line, white considered king f5 but realized that h5 was stronger, because it makes immediate progress and the king can follow later.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, push the pawn when you can, as it gains space and forces the defender to react. Moving the king first may allow the defender to reposition and prevent progress.
notes.plans: Push the h-pawn as far as possible, using the king to chase away the knight. The black king is too far to stop the pawn.

notes.explains: A beautiful tactical idea is to sacrifice the knight to deflect the black knight, allowing the h-pawn to run. After the sacrifice, the black king is misplaced, and the pawn cannot be stopped.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a knight sacrifice is justified if it removes the defender of a passed pawn. The resulting pawn promotion is worth more than the knight.
notes.plans: Play knight to d4, inviting the trade. After the knight is captured, push the h-pawn, using the king's placement to prevent the black knight from getting back in time.

notes.explains: In this endgame, white's king on f6 is perfectly placed to support the h-pawn's promotion. Black's knight is too far away to stop the pawn, and any check it can give takes too many moves, allowing white to promote first.
notes.teaches: A king can dominate a knight by occupying key squares and restricting its movement, effectively neutralizing it. Sacrificing material to clear the path for a passed pawn is often decisive when the opponent's pieces are out of play.
notes.plans: White should push the h-pawn, using the king to control critical squares and prevent the knight from getting in front of the pawn.

notes.explains: In a similar position with the knight on b8, white must move the knight because it's attacked and unprotected. The correct move is knight c6, not knight d7, because after knight d7, black can play knight g5 check and stop the h-pawn. Knight c6 allows white to push h4 and maintain the threat.
notes.teaches: When your piece is attacked, look for a square that maintains your strategic goals. Sometimes the best move is not the most obvious one, but the one that keeps the opponent's pieces restricted.
notes.plans: White should play knight c6, then push h4, using the king to dominate the black knight and promote the pawn.

notes.explains: In this position, White must choose between knight to c6 and knight to d7; only one works because the other allows the black knight to stop the h-pawn effectively. The immediate push of the h-pawn is critical to restrict the black knight's strong squares.
notes.teaches: When a passed pawn races against a knight, the timing of pushing the pawn matters—push it immediately to restrict the knight's mobility before the king can come to help.
notes.plans: Play knight to c6, then after Black takes the pawn, push h4. The goal is to use the pawn to chase the knight and eventually deflect it from controlling the promotion square.

notes.explains: If White delays the pawn push and tries to dominate the knight with the king, the knight can jump around and the black king can come in to hold, so that approach fails. The correct method is to use the pawn to restrict the knight's strong square.
notes.teaches: Domination of a knight requires restricting its best squares with pawns, not just chasing with the king; otherwise the knight's agility allows it to escape.
notes.plans: After pushing the pawn, chase the knight with the king, using the pawn to control key squares, and aim to deflect the knight from the h-pawn's path.

notes.explains: The key move is knight to e2, not other knight moves, because it sets up a deflection: if Black captures, the knight gets trapped, and White can then push the pawn. Other moves allow Black to keep the knight on g3 and draw.
notes.teaches: In knight vs. pawn races, look for deflection tactics that force the enemy knight away from the promotion square, even at the cost of the knight.
notes.plans: Play knight to e2, and if Black captures, push h5 and bring the king in, using the knight to threaten g5 and deflect the black knight.

notes.explains: King and pawn endgames are ideal for teaching calculation and visualization because they involve minimal material and force precise calculation. Solving studies, especially blindfolded, improves pattern recognition and board visualization.
notes.teaches: To improve calculation, practice king and pawn endgames and solve studies blindfolded to enhance visualization and pattern recognition.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn endgame, White is a pawn down, and the natural evaluation is that Black's distant a-pawns should win. However, White also has a passed c-pawn, which changes the dynamics and gives real counterplay.
notes.teaches: When evaluating an endgame, consider all passed pawns, not just the opponent's. A passed pawn of your own can offset a material deficit if it can be pushed with the king's support.
notes.plans: White should aim to advance the c-pawn while placing the king in an optimal supporting square.

notes.explains: White cannot simply go after Black's a-pawns because the king is too far away; by the time it gets there, Black will have created counterplay, likely leading to a draw or worse. The idea of running to the queenside is a dead end.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, the king must prioritize supporting its own passed pawn over chasing distant pawns, especially when the opponent's king is active.
notes.plans: Reject the plan of going to the queenside; instead, focus on the c-pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: For the c-pawn to promote, the king must be in front of it to support the final pushes. The ideal squares are b7 or d7, with d7 being superior because it restricts Black's king and creates mating/checking ideas with the queen.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, the king should lead the pawn, occupying a square directly in front of it (or one step ahead) to escort it to promotion. The choice of which side can also limit the opponent's king.
notes.plans: Place the king on d7 to support the c-pawn and restrict Black's king.

notes.explains: Pushing the c-pawn immediately (c4) is a mistake because it gives Black time to bring the king to stop the pawn. Even if White promotes, the king is too far away to create any winning chances, so the game ends in a draw.
notes.teaches: Timing is crucial in pawn races: pushing too early can allow the opponent's king to catch the pawn. The king must be placed first to support the pawn's advance.
notes.plans: Play the king to d7 first, then push the c-pawn at the right moment.

notes.explains: A tempting alternative to supporting the c-pawn with the king is to use the king to capture Black's pawns, but this fails because Black's king is better placed and can create winning threats, such as a g-pawn breakthrough.
notes.teaches: Avoid decentralizing the king to grab pawns when the opponent's king is more active. In king and pawn endgames, the king's position is often more important than material.
notes.plans: Keep the king on d7 and avoid wandering to the kingside.

notes.explains: In this king and pawn endgame, the placement of the kings is decisive. The side whose king is better placed can create threats like pushing g5, while the opponent must be careful not to allow the king to infiltrate and win pawns.
notes.teaches: King activity is paramount in pawn endgames. A well-placed king can support passed pawns and create mating threats, so always consider king position before making pawn moves.
notes.plans: Move the king to the optimal square (e.g., d7) to stop the opponent's passed pawn and support your own. Use waiting moves to force the opponent into zugzwang.

notes.explains: In a blocked position with an extra knight, the win is not straightforward. The knight may need to be sacrificed, but the resulting passed pawn must be supported by the king, which is difficult due to the closed nature of the position.
notes.teaches: In closed endgames, piece maneuvering is key. You must find a plan to improve your pieces, often by rerouting the knight to a key square, even if it takes many moves.
notes.plans: Start by moving the king away to free a square for the knight, then maneuver the knight to a strong outpost like h4, from where it can create threats or be sacrificed to win a pawn.

notes.explains: The knight cannot reach h4 directly due to the pawn structure, so it must take a longer route. The king must also be repositioned to support the plan, even though it may not seem to win anything immediately.
notes.teaches: In endgames, sometimes you must make preparatory moves that seem slow but are necessary to achieve a favorable piece placement. Patience and precise calculation are required.
notes.plans: First move the king to g2 to free the square, then bring the knight to h3, and later to a4, before finally reaching h4. The king will then be ready to support the resulting passed pawn.

notes.explains: The placement of the pawns prevents the knight from reaching h4 directly, and bringing the king to the queenside does not win material because if the knight is sacrificed for a pawn, the opponent's king can stop the passed pawn while your own king cannot enter.
notes.teaches: In knight endgames, the knight's route to a key square may be blocked by pawn structure; the king must be used to support the knight's maneuver.
notes.plans: Bring the king over to support the knight's journey toward h4, using waiting moves to force the opponent's king to move and allow the knight to advance.

notes.explains: The knight cannot go to b6 immediately because the opponent will capture it; a waiting move with the king forces the opponent's king to move to keep the pawn protected, allowing the knight to reach b6.
notes.teaches: Use triangulation or waiting moves to gain the opposition and create a tempo to reposition the knight to a better square.
notes.plans: Play a king waiting move, then move the knight to b6, and continue to c7, using checks to drive the opponent's king away.

notes.explains: From b6, the knight cannot jump directly to h4; it must go through c7, and then to b5, but from b5 it is stuck. The king must come to b2 to support the knight's move to a3, where if captured, the king recaptures and enters the position.
notes.teaches: In endgames, the king often must escort the knight to a new route; sacrificing the knight for a pawn is only good if the king can recapture and penetrate.
notes.plans: Bring the king to b2, then play the knight to a3, and if captured, recapture with the king, then advance the b-pawn to create a winning king and pawn endgame.

notes.explains: After the knight reaches h4, the opponent rushes the king to f6 to be ready to capture if the knight is sacrificed, but white plays it anyway because if the knight is taken, the king enters and eventually wins the pawn due to zugzwang.
notes.teaches: A knight sacrifice can be correct if it opens the door for the king to enter and create a decisive advantage, even if the opponent's king is nearby.
notes.plans: Play the knight to h4, and if it is captured, bring the king in, use zugzwang to win the pawn, then push the g-pawn to promote or win the opponent's pieces.

notes.explains: In this king-and-pawn endgame, the key is to create a zugzwang: the defender's king is tied to protecting a pawn, so any waiting move forces it to give way, allowing the attacker to win the pawn and then the game.
notes.teaches: Use waiting moves to put the opponent in zugzwang when their king is tied to defending a pawn. If they cannot move without losing material, they must concede.
notes.plans: Make waiting moves with the king to force the opponent's king away, then capture the pawn. After that, promote or use the extra pawn to win.

notes.explains: The 50-move rule can be a real threat in long endgames; even if you reach a winning position, you might not have enough moves left to convert, so you must be efficient.
notes.teaches: Be aware of the move count in technical endgames. Convert advantages as quickly as possible to avoid a draw claim under the 50-move rule.
notes.plans: When you have a winning endgame, prioritize making progress every move, and avoid unnecessary shuffling.

notes.explains: In a position with a knight and pawns, the defender's king can be stuck defending a pawn, giving the attacker time to maneuver the knight to a better square and win material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is tied down, use your knight to probe for weaknesses and create threats that force the opponent to give ground.
notes.plans: Bring the knight to an active square, make a waiting move to put the opponent in zugzwang, then capture the pawn. After that, use the extra pawn to win.

notes.explains: In a blocked position with a bishop and knight, the defender's king may be restricted, and the attacker can use tactics to win a pawn and then convert with the minor pieces.
notes.teaches: In bishop-and-knight endgames, look for ways to exploit the opponent's restricted king to win a pawn. Then use the standard winning technique with bishop and knight.
notes.plans: Play a move that forces the opponent's king to a worse square, then win the pawn. After that, use the bishop and knight to win the remaining pawns and the game.

notes.explains: Grandmasters often win such blocked positions by maneuvering pieces until the opponent makes a mistake, rather than forcing an immediate breakthrough.
notes.teaches: In positions with no immediate breakthrough, improve your piece placement and create threats that force the opponent to weaken their position. Patience is key.
notes.plans: Keep maneuvering, maintain pressure, and wait for the opponent to err. Then capitalize on the mistake.

notes.explains: In this bishop-and-knight versus king endgame, the immediate check forces the black king to a corner square, which is essential for the mating net. The bishop then protects key squares while the knight maneuvers to deliver mate.
notes.teaches: When coordinating bishop and knight to mate a lone king, first drive the king to the correct corner and use the bishop to control escape squares.
notes.plans: Continue with the standard W-maneuver of the knight to herd the king, then bring the bishop to support the mating square.

notes.explains: The knight should follow a W-shaped path from the second to fourth rank, not jump from first to third, because that would block the king's path and prevent the mate. Keeping the knight on a2 preserves the option to reach g3.
notes.teaches: In bishop-and-knight mates, the knight's route matters: avoid moves that block your own king; plan the knight's jumps to maintain flexibility.
notes.plans: Keep the knight on a2, then play bishop to f2 and knight to g3 to threaten mate.

notes.explains: When the opponent has a passed pawn, you must blockade it with your bishop while keeping the king restricted. If you give the opponent a chance to trade bishops, you may not win the resulting pawn endgame.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, avoid unnecessary piece trades that could lead to a drawn pawn endgame; instead, maintain the mating net while dealing with passed pawns.
notes.plans: Use the bishop to blockade the passed pawn, then continue the mating threats.

notes.explains: The final maneuver involves a waiting move with the bishop to put the opponent in zugzwang. By chasing the enemy bishop away and threatening mate, you force the opponent to move a pawn, which you then blockade, leaving them with no good moves.
notes.teaches: Use waiting moves and zugzwang to force the opponent to weaken their position, then deliver mate.
notes.plans: Play bishop to g1, then after the opponent's reply, move the bishop to d4 to blockade the pawn, and finally deliver knight g3 mate.

notes.explains: In this endgame, black's king is trapped and the bishop is tied down, so black is forced to push the pawn. White can blockade the pawn with the bishop, leaving black with no useful moves and eventually delivering checkmate with the knight.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has no good moves, you can use zugzwang to force them to worsen their position. Blockading a passed pawn with a bishop can be a key technique to maintain control.
notes.plans: Keep the blockade, give black the move, and use the knight to deliver checkmate while the king is stuck.

notes.explains: If black chooses a different pawn move, white does not need to take it immediately; keeping the pawn on the board can prevent stalemate and maintain winning chances.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, avoid taking material if it allows the opponent to force stalemate. Sometimes it's better to leave a pawn and keep the position fluid.
notes.plans: Maintain the bind and continue to restrict black's moves, avoiding premature captures.

notes.explains: In a position with opposite-colored bishops and an extra pawn, material is not the only factor; the activity and safety of the pieces matter. Black threatens the c7 pawn, but white has a powerful resource.
notes.teaches: Opposite-colored bishops can favor the attacker because the defender's bishop cannot contest the same color squares. Sacrifices can be justified if they create unstoppable threats.
notes.plans: Consider a queen sacrifice to deflect the enemy pieces and promote the c-pawn.

notes.explains: The queen sacrifice Qe8+ is decisive because black must capture, after which white's king moves to b6, threatening to win the queen with Bc6 and promote the pawn. Black has no adequate checks to stop this.
notes.teaches: A queen sacrifice can be correct if it leads to a forced promotion or wins the queen back with interest. When evaluating sacrifices, consider the resulting endgame and whether the threats are unstoppable.
notes.plans: After Qe8+ and forced capture, play Kb6, then Bc6 to win the queen and promote.

notes.explains: In this endgame, the white bishop is stuck on a1, unable to participate, while the h-pawn is outside the black king's square. Black's pieces are tied up, and the bishop on a1 cannot stop the pawn's advance.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is outside the opponent's king's square and the opponent's pieces are immobilized, the pawn can decide the game. Always check if the defending king can catch the pawn.
notes.plans: Push the h-pawn, ignoring attacks on the bishop, and promote. The opponent's own promotion is too slow.

notes.explains: Black may try to block the pawns with the bishop, but white can sacrifice all the pawns on the kingside to deflect the bishop, allowing the d-pawn to promote. The black bishop cannot control both the d-pawn and the h-pawn from the same diagonal.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, sacrificing pawns to deflect the defender's pieces is a key technique. The defender's bishop may be overloaded if it must stop two passed pawns on different diagonals.
notes.plans: If black blocks with the bishop, sacrifice the f- and e-pawns to pull the bishop away, then push the d-pawn. The black bishop will have to be given up for the d-pawn, and the black king will reach the corner for a draw.

notes.explains: Black's attempt to play bishop c3 to stop the pawns is too slow. White can simply push the h-pawn, and the bishop on c3 cannot catch it. The black king is also out of the square.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a dangerous passed pawn, you must calculate whether your pieces can actually stop it. A bishop on a distant diagonal may be too slow if the pawn is far advanced.
notes.plans: Continue pushing the h-pawn; the bishop on c3 is irrelevant.

notes.explains: In a variation where black promotes, the white king is on mate. White can deliver checkmate with bishop g6 or f5, also attacking the black pawn. Black has no time to stop the mate.
notes.teaches: When your opponent promotes, look for mating nets before they can consolidate. A check that also attacks the new queen can be decisive.
notes.plans: If black promotes, play bishop g6 check, forcing mate or winning the queen.

notes.explains: In this study, material is equal, and a normal move would likely draw. The black rook on a7 is badly placed, trapped by its own pawns, which is a key feature to exploit.
notes.teaches: In endgame studies, every piece is placed for a reason; look for poorly placed enemy pieces and try to keep them restricted.
notes.plans: White should seek a way to exploit the trapped rook rather than immediately capturing pawns.

notes.explains: The first move is rook h8, a precise move that keeps the black rook restricted. Black cannot go to the corner due to mate, so must play king c8.
notes.teaches: When a piece is trapped, use precise moves to maintain the trap and force the opponent's king to awkward squares.
notes.plans: After king c8, White can check and continue to restrict the rook, aiming to win it or gain material.

notes.explains: If White tries to capture the a5 pawn, Black has a resource: king c6, threatening to trap the rook. If White then tries to trap the rook, Black can give a check and free the rook, likely to a light square (opposite color of the bishop).
notes.teaches: In rook vs rook and bishop endings, place your rook on the opposite color of the enemy bishop to avoid harassment. Also, be alert to tactical resources that free trapped pieces.
notes.plans: If no better line exists, White can still capture pawns and try to win on technique, though it should be a draw with best defense.

notes.explains: In this rook-and-bishop endgame, black's rook is trapped and white has two extra pawns, but white cannot easily win because black's king can attack the pieces and force favorable trades. The key is that black must avoid the trap of capturing the bishop, which allows white's king to trap the rook and create mating threats.
notes.teaches: When your rook is trapped, do not grab material if it allows the opponent to activate their pieces and create mating threats. Instead, find the move that keeps your pieces coordinated and forces the opponent to retreat.
notes.plans: Black should play the move that avoids the trap, such as moving the king to d8, after which the bishop becomes trapped and must retreat, leading to a draw.

notes.explains: White's attempt with bishop f4 does not win because black can escape with the rook. The winning idea is to stop black's pawn push with bishop d8 check, forcing black to block with b6, and then create a zugzwang position where black's rook has no moves and the king is restricted.
notes.teaches: In endgames, zugzwang can be decisive when the opponent's pieces are short on moves. Restrict the enemy king's squares and force them to make a weakening move.
notes.plans: White should play bishop d8 check, then after black blocks with b6, use the king to restrict black's king on the c-file, leaving black with only one legal move that loses.

notes.explains: A far-advanced passed pawn is the main winning asset; if it falls, the winning chances often vanish. Here the pawn is attacked, and the rook must stay on d8 to keep it under pressure.
notes.teaches: In endgames, protect and support an advanced passed pawn with the king rather than giving it up. Keep the pawn as long as possible because it is the primary source of winning chances.
notes.plans: Bring the king to support the pawn's promotion, while keeping the rook active to defend it.

notes.explains: When the rook is forced to stay on d8, the bishop can be sacrificed to deflect the rook or gain a tempo. The move bishop c5 protects the pawn and forces black to capture, after which white's king can chase the rook and promote.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up a piece to keep the passed pawn alive is correct. A sacrifice that deflects the opponent's pieces from stopping the pawn can be decisive.
notes.plans: After bishop c5, if black captures, use the king to attack the rook and promote the pawn.

notes.explains: The king can perform a triangle maneuver to approach the rook while maintaining opposition and supporting the pawn. This is a typical technique to force the rook away and promote.
notes.teaches: Learn the king triangle: by checking and moving the king in a triangular pattern, you can drive the enemy rook away from the pawn's promotion square.
notes.plans: Use checks to force the enemy king away, then advance the pawn with the king's support.

notes.explains: After the bishop and pawn are given up, the remaining pawn becomes the new passed pawn. The rook is trapped, and the king must choose between stopping the pawn or defending the rook.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a pawn majority on the other side can become a decisive passed pawn after sacrifices. The opponent's king may be overloaded trying to stop both the pawn and defend the rook.
notes.plans: Push the b-pawn to promote, while the rook remains trapped. If the king goes to c5, continue pushing; if to e5, use the rook to win the pawns.

notes.explains: In this rook endgame, White sacrifices a bishop and a pawn to trap Black's rook and promote a pawn. The key is that Black's rook is stuck, and White's pawn is far advanced, creating a winning position despite being down material.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up material to activate your pawns and restrict the opponent's pieces can lead to a win, even when you are technically behind.
notes.plans: White should push the passed pawn, using the king to support it, while keeping Black's king and rook tied down.

notes.explains: Black has two defensive ideas: keep the king on c5 to stop the pawn, or go to e5. If Black goes to c5, White pushes b4 to create threats. If Black goes to e5, White plays f4 to restrict the king. In both cases, White's plan is to force Black into zugzwang.
notes.teaches: In endgames, you can use pawn pushes to restrict the opponent's king and force them into zugzwang, where any move worsens their position.
notes.plans: White should aim to force Black's king to a square where it must move, allowing White to advance the pawn or win the rook.

notes.explains: The position becomes zugzwang: Black's rook has no safe squares, and the king is restricted to protecting the rook. Black is forced to push the h-pawn, which White can capture, maintaining the zugzwang.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent has no good moves; use your pieces to restrict their activity and force them to weaken their own position.
notes.plans: White should maintain the zugzwang by making waiting moves with the king or pawns, forcing Black to move the h-pawn and eventually lose it.

notes.explains: In this position, White must support the c-pawn's promotion. The tempting rook move to win the a2 pawn fails because Black's knight can fork the rook and another piece, and even if White wins the pawn, Black's bishop can stop the pawn push, possibly sacrificing the knight to draw.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn, prioritize supporting its advance over winning material on the other side. A move that wins a pawn but allows the opponent to blockade your passer is often a mistake.
notes.plans: Play the correct move: king to b7 to support the c-pawn, threatening c7. Then handle Black's defensive resources like bishop to e5.

notes.explains: Black has an alternative defense: bishop to d6, preventing f4 from coming with tempo. If White tries f4 anyway, Black can reposition, and White must be careful not to run out of tempo. Pushing pawns carelessly can lead to zugzwang for White, allowing Black to draw.
notes.teaches: In endgames, tempo counting is crucial. You must choose pawn moves carefully so that you are the one who gives the final check or forces the opponent into zugzwang, not yourself.
notes.plans: If Black plays bishop d6, consider moves like h4 or f4, but calculate the tempo sequence to ensure you maintain the initiative and avoid zugzwang.

notes.explains: In this pawn race, every tempo matters. The side that can force the opponent to move first into a zugzwang position gains the decisive advantage.
notes.teaches: When pushing pawns in king-pawn endgames, count tempi carefully and try to leave yourself the final waiting move that puts the opponent in zugzwang.
notes.plans: Push pawns only when they force the opponent's king or pieces to give ground, and use your king to control key squares.

notes.explains: A knight on the rim is poorly placed. Here, the white knight dominates the black knight by keeping it trapped in the corner, while the white king makes progress.
notes.teaches: Avoid placing knights on the edge of the board; a centralized knight can dominate an opponent's piece and restrict its activity.
notes.plans: Use the dominant knight to restrain the enemy knight while the king advances to collect pawns.

notes.explains: White has a winning material advantage, but must find the precise move to convert. The king must be brought close enough to support the knight in protecting the passed pawn.
notes.teaches: In king and knight vs king and pawn endgames, coordinate your king and knight so that the knight can defend the passed pawn while the king goes to win the remaining pawns.
notes.plans: Move the knight to a square where it both protects the pawn and is protected by the king, then march the king to capture the h-pawn.

notes.explains: Black has dangerous passed pawns and threatens promotion. White's only chance is to use the king to create a mating net, not to try to stop the pawns directly.
notes.teaches: When facing multiple passed pawns, sometimes the only resource is a mating attack with the king and rook, rather than trying to defend against promotion.
notes.plans: Bring the king to a square that threatens back-rank mate, forcing black to deal with the mate instead of promoting.

notes.explains: The idea of using the king to threaten back-rank mate works differently depending on whether the promoted piece is a queen or a rook. With a queen, the rook can give check and the queen must block, but with a rook, the situation changes.
notes.teaches: In king and rook vs king and queen endgames with a pawn on the seventh, the back-rank mate threat can be decisive, but the exact technique differs from queen-versus-rook scenarios.
notes.plans: Use the rook to give check and force the queen to interpose, then exploit the resulting position.

notes.explains: In a queen versus rook and pawn endgame, the defending side's rook can often stop mate by interposing or giving check. But when the pawn is far advanced and the king is cut off, the queen can deliver mate because the rook has no safe square to control the mating square.
notes.teaches: Recognize when a queen can force mate against a rook and pawn: if the rook cannot interpose or give a meaningful check, the queen's mating net is decisive.
notes.plans: Use the queen to drive the enemy king to the edge and deliver mate, while keeping the rook and pawn immobilized.

notes.explains: Promoting to a knight can sometimes be the only way to give check and avoid immediate mate, but the knight often becomes trapped in the corner and cannot escape, allowing the stronger side to round up the remaining pawns and win.
notes.teaches: In queen versus rook and pawn, consider underpromotion to a knight to gain a tempo, but be aware that the knight may be trapped and lost.
notes.plans: If the opponent underpromotes to a knight, use the king to confine it and eventually capture it or win the other pawns.

notes.explains: The defending side may try to sacrifice or push pawns to create counterplay, but the stronger side must avoid careless captures that allow the pawn to promote with check and escape the mating net.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning mating net, do not take every offered pawn; sometimes you must ignore a pawn to maintain the mate threat.
notes.plans: Keep the king and queen coordinated to maintain the mate threat, and only take pawns when it does not release the pressure.

notes.explains: In a rook versus knight endgame, the knight can be dominated if it is confined to the corner. The stronger side uses a waiting maneuver to put the opponent in zugzwang, forcing them to push pawns and eventually run out of moves.
notes.teaches: Use triangulation and waiting moves to put the defender in zugzwang, forcing them to weaken their pawn structure while the knight remains trapped.
notes.plans: Repeat the same position with the opponent to move, forcing them to push pawns until they are exhausted, then capture the pawns and win the trapped knight.

notes.explains: When the knight is trapped in the corner, the stronger side must be careful not to allow the knight to escape with check or by a tactical trick, as that could turn a win into a draw.
notes.teaches: In rook versus knight, always keep the knight confined; avoid moves that allow the knight to jump out with tempo.
notes.plans: Maintain the cage around the knight, and only give check when it does not allow the knight to escape.

notes.explains: In this endgame study, the key is that black's knight is far from its king and can be dominated by the white king and rook. The knight has few safe squares, and by restricting its movement, it becomes trapped.
notes.teaches: To win against a lone knight, restrict its available squares with your rook and king, then bring the king closer to trap it. Always consider where the knight can go next and cut off those squares.
notes.plans: Use the rook to control the knight's escape routes, then advance the king to attack the knight. If the knight sacrifices pawns, take them and continue restricting.

notes.explains: The knight is far from the black king, so it cannot be rescued. The white king can approach and eventually win the knight once it is trapped.
notes.teaches: A knight far from its own king is vulnerable to being trapped by the opposing king and rook. Patience is required to slowly reduce its squares.
notes.plans: Keep the knight restricted, bring the king to attack it, and be prepared to take pawns when offered.

notes.explains: In a position with queens and minor pieces, the queen can be restricted by the opponent's pieces. Here, the queen is somewhat trapped, and white must find a way to keep it restricted while avoiding checks that lose material.
notes.teaches: When trying to trap a queen, use checks to force the king to a worse square, and use your pieces to control the queen's escape squares. Be wary of counter-checks that could lose material.
notes.plans: Start with a check to limit black's options, then continue with checks and threats to keep the queen restricted. Consider moves like knight g3 or knight d6 to control key squares.

notes.explains: In this endgame position, Black's queen and king are severely restricted. The white rook and knight coordinate to create threats that dominate the black queen, leaving Black with very few viable moves.
notes.teaches: Rook and knight can work together to create forking and double-attack patterns that restrict the opponent's pieces, often leading to zugzwang.
notes.plans: White should continue to use the rook and knight to maintain the net around the black king and queen, forcing Black into zugzwang and eventually winning material or the game.

notes.explains: A key move is rook to f5, which attacks the queen and restricts its squares. The queen cannot capture the knight because it is protected by a pawn, and moving to other squares allows checks that win the queen.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are protected, you can offer them as bait to force the opponent into a position where their queen has no safe squares.
notes.plans: After rook f5, if Black moves the king, White can deliver checks to win the queen or continue the domination.

notes.explains: Another strong move is rook g5, which hangs the rook but is safe because capturing it leads to a check that wins the queen. This move further restricts Black's options.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can leave a piece hanging if capturing it allows a decisive tactic, such as a fork or a check that wins more material.
notes.plans: After rook g5, Black's only reasonable move is king e6 to free a square for the queen, but White can continue with the same dominating pattern.

notes.explains: In king and pawn endgames, creating a passed pawn can be winning even if the opponent appears to have drawing chances. The key is precise calculation to ensure the pawn promotes or forces the opponent's king away.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn, don't fear it will draw; instead, calculate the race carefully. Often you can win by a tempo because the opponent cannot shoulder your king effectively.
notes.plans: Advance the passed pawn, use your king to support it, and if the opponent tries to block, use checks or pawn pushes to gain tempo.

notes.explains: In a rook versus pawn endgame, if the rook is attacked and has no safe square, you must find a forcing move like a check to gain time. The rook can then stop the pawn from promoting.
notes.teaches: When your rook is under attack and you need to stop a passed pawn, look for checks or other forcing moves to bring the rook to the right square in time.
notes.plans: Give a check to drive the king to a worse square, then bring the rook to the queening file to stop the pawn.

notes.explains: In a composed study, the defender may try to keep the rook from stopping the pawn by using the king. If the rook cannot reach the pawn in time, you must find a different idea, often involving sacrificing material for a mating attack.
notes.teaches: When a direct defense fails, look for tactical resources like mating threats. Sacrificing a rook can be correct if it leads to a forced mate or wins the queen.
notes.plans: Use the king's position to create mating threats, coordinate knight and rook for an Arabian mate, and force the opponent to give up material to avoid mate.

notes.explains: In the study, White sacrifices the rook to promote a pawn, but the real point is that the knight and queen create a mating net. Black's queen is overloaded, unable to stop both mate threats and the promotion.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn about to promote, don't cling to it if you see a stronger idea. Sometimes giving up the pawn (or the rook) leads to a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After the rook sacrifice, use the knight to control key squares, threaten mate, and if the opponent takes the rook, deliver check and win the queen.

notes.explains: In the final position, the pawn is promoting and the defender cannot stop it. If the defender captures the promoted piece, a check followed by a rook move to c6 wins the queen, leaving Black with no saving resource.
notes.teaches: Promotion tactics often involve a follow-up combination: if the promoted piece is taken, a discovered attack or skewer can win the queen. Always calculate the consequences of the opponent capturing the new queen.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to promotion, and if the opponent captures, execute the check and rook-to-c6 tactic to win the queen.

notes.explains: The studies presented illustrate the themes of domination and zugzwang, which are important in real games. Domination restricts the opponent's pieces, while zugzwang forces them to weaken their position when they must move.
notes.teaches: Domination and zugzwang are practical endgame motifs: aim to restrict the opponent's pieces and force them into a position where any move loses.
notes.plans: In endgames, look for ways to confine the opponent's king or pieces and create zugzwang positions where the opponent has no good moves.

notes.explains: In this endgame, the white king must first restrict the black king's movement. The correct first move is Kc4, which keeps the black king confined and forces it to make only legal moves that self-destruct.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, the first move often aims to restrict the opponent's king, not just to gain material. A forcing sequence can lead to mate even with few pieces.
notes.plans: After Kc4, black is forced to play d5, then white plays Kc5, black plays d4, and white returns to c4, repeating until black runs out of moves and is mated.

notes.explains: The same idea works even if white starts with Kc3 or Kc5, as long as the king eventually reaches c4. The key is to prevent the black king from escaping.
notes.teaches: In such positions, the precise first move is crucial; other moves may allow the black king to escape and turn the win into a draw.
notes.plans: If starting with Kc3, after black's forced moves, play Kc4 to reach the winning setup.

notes.explains: In a more complex composed position, black threatens to capture the rook and also to queen with check. White must find a creative forcing sequence, starting with a rook check that sacrifices the rook.
notes.teaches: When facing multiple threats, look for forcing moves that change the character of the position, even if they involve material sacrifice, to create a mating net.
notes.plans: After the rook sacrifice, white plays a surprising knight move, giving away the bishop, to set up a similar king-walk pattern that forces black's self-destruction.

notes.explains: In the final phase, the white king must choose the correct square to continue the confinement. Playing Kc4 would allow the black king to escape via b2, so the correct move is Kc2, maintaining the net.
notes.teaches: When driving the enemy king to the edge, always be aware of escape squares; choose king moves that keep the opponent's options minimal.
notes.plans: After Kc2, black is forced to play b3, then white plays Kc3, black plays b2, and white mates.

notes.explains: In this composed position, the black king is boxed in by its own pawns, and the white king must choose the correct route to deliver mate. Playing the king to c4 allows the black king to escape, so the precise king move is essential.
notes.teaches: When delivering mate with limited material, every king move must control the opponent's escape squares; a single inaccurate step can let the king slip out.
notes.plans: Use the king to shepherd the opponent's king toward the edge while keeping it confined; coordinate with the knight to cover all flight squares.

notes.explains: Normally king and knight cannot force mate, but in this exceptional position, if the opponent flags, the game may be awarded as a win because mate is demonstrably inevitable. This is a rare exception to the insufficient-mating-material rule.
notes.teaches: In tournament chess, if you can show a forced mate is coming even with minimal material, a win on time may be awarded; know the exceptions to the draw-by-insufficient-material rule.

notes.explains: In a practical rook endgame, white has a passed pawn on the seventh rank. The key is to promote while also threatening a rook check if the pawn is captured, exploiting the black king's poor placement.
notes.teaches: A pawn on the seventh rank is a powerful tactical weapon: combine the promotion threat with a rook check to win material or force promotion.
notes.plans: Push the pawn toward promotion; if the opponent's rook captures, deliver a check that wins the rook.

notes.explains: In a similar position, it is black to move and the correct defensive move is to place the king on g7, even though it moves away from the pawn. This prevents white's rook from delivering a decisive check or skewer.
notes.teaches: When defending against a passed pawn, sometimes the right king move is counterintuitive: prioritize preventing the opponent's tactical threats over approaching the pawn.
notes.plans: Keep the king on g7 to neutralize white's rook checks and skewers; if white's king approaches, use checks to drive it away.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame where white is up two pawns, the position is actually a draw if black can keep the king on e7 and prevent white's king from making progress. White's best try is to advance the h-pawn, but black can hold.
notes.teaches: Material advantage alone does not guarantee a win in rook endgames; the defending side can draw by maintaining a passive but solid king position and using checks to prevent the enemy king from advancing.
notes.plans: For black: keep the king on e7 and use rook checks to harass the white king if it tries to approach. For white: try to create a second weakness, but be aware that the draw is likely.

notes.explains: With a rook and pawn versus rook, if the defending king can stay on the queening square (e.g., e7 for an h-pawn), the position is a dead draw. The defender just keeps the king there and uses the rook to give checks or shuffle, preventing any progress.
notes.teaches: The defending king must occupy the queening square to draw. The attacker's only winning chances come from sacrificing the pawn to deflect the king, but if the defender simply ignores the pawn and keeps the king on the queening square, the draw is secure.
notes.plans: For the defender: keep the king on the queening square and use the rook to check or wait. For the attacker: try pushing the pawn to lure the king, but if the defender refuses, the game is drawn.

notes.explains: The same drawing method applies with a g-pawn: the defending king stays on g7, and the attacker's best try is to push the pawn to g6, hoping the defender takes. If the defender declines and keeps the king on g7, the position remains drawn.
notes.teaches: The principle is the same for edge pawns (h and g): the defender draws by keeping the king on the queening square and not capturing the pawn when it advances. The attacker cannot force progress without the defender's cooperation.
notes.plans: Defender: keep king on g7, ignore the pawn push, use rook to check. Attacker: push the pawn, but if ignored, accept the draw.

notes.explains: In a rook versus rook and pawn endgame, the placement of the defending king and rook is critical. Here, the black king on e6 and rook on a5 are poorly placed because they allow a skewer after a check, and the king is too far from the pawn to stop promotion.
notes.teaches: When defending against a passed pawn, keep the king close enough to block the pawn and avoid squares where checks can lead to skewers. The defender's rook should be active but not on squares that allow tactical tricks.
notes.plans: The winning side should look for checks that force the king to a rank where it is skewered or driven away from the pawn, then use the threat of promotion to win material.

notes.explains: In a complex rook endgame, black sacrifices a pawn with g4 to open lines and create threats against the white king and rook. This is a deep combination built on a simple tactical motif.
notes.teaches: Recognize fundamental tactical patterns (like skewers or back-rank mates) and look for ways to force the opponent into them, even at the cost of material. Sacrifices can be justified if they lead to a decisive tactical blow.
notes.plans: Black's plan is to open the second rank, deflect the white rook, and then use the passed pawn to win the rook, eventually converting to a win.

notes.explains: In a rook endgame where white has two rooks against black's two rooks and extra pawns, white can win by delivering mate threats. The black rooks are passive and unable to defend against the mating net.
notes.teaches: Active rooks can outweigh material deficits. Look for mating threats or checks that force the opponent's pieces to remain passive, and use the initiative to create a decisive attack.
notes.plans: White should aim to deliver mate with the rooks on the seventh or eighth rank, using the king's position to limit black's defensive options.

notes.explains: In this position, White has fewer pawns but more active rooks. The black rooks are passive and unable to defend against the mating threats on the eighth rank.
notes.teaches: Rook activity often outweighs material advantages. Place rooks on the opponent's seventh rank to cut off the king and create mating nets.
notes.plans: Deliver mate with a rook on the eighth rank, using the active rooks to exploit the black king's lack of escape squares.

notes.explains: White is down material but can force a draw by perpetual check. The key is to check with the correct rook, keeping the other rook stationary to maintain the checking pattern.
notes.teaches: When defending, use the right rook for checks to avoid allowing the king to escape. A stationary rook can control key squares and keep the perpetual check alive.
notes.plans: Keep one rook on the seventh rank and shuffle the other between checking squares, ensuring the king cannot escape the perpetual.

notes.explains: White has threats on the seventh rank, but Black also has counterplay with a rook on the first rank. White must act first and use the bishop on g2 as a key defender.
notes.teaches: In endgames, be aware of both your own threats and your opponent's. A distant piece like a bishop can support a mating net by covering critical squares.
notes.plans: Strike first with a rook check, using the bishop to cover escape squares and force mate.

notes.explains: White has a winning idea despite Black's threats. The first move must be precise: taking the pawn with the wrong rook allows Black's queen to return and stop the perpetual check.
notes.teaches: Choose the correct rook to take a pawn, preserving the ability to check the king and force it toward the center for mating threats.
notes.plans: Use the rook to take the pawn on g7, then drive the king toward the center and set up mating ideas.

notes.explains: The rook on g7 checks the king, forcing it toward the center and setting up mating threats. Taking the c7 pawn attacks both the rook on c8 and the rook on h8, creating a repetitive checking sequence that gradually wins pawns.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is boxed in, a series of checks can force it to shuffle while you pick off pawns, converting a static advantage into a decisive one.
notes.plans: Continue checking and capturing pawns (c7, b7, a7) until the queen is forced to give itself up to avoid mate, then win the resulting endgame.
