notes.explains: In this French structure, black has counterplay against the white queen and pieces. Taking with the queen leads to trouble, so white must be careful about piece captures.
notes.teaches: When a capture seems natural, check if it exposes your queen or other pieces to tactics. Sometimes declining the capture is better.
notes.plans: Consider alternative moves that maintain piece coordination and avoid creating weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black's idea of c4 challenges the bishop and forces white to respond. After bishop d2, the queen must move to b2, and the bishop can later occupy a strong diagonal.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, pawn breaks like c4 can create weaknesses and force opponent's pieces to awkward squares.
notes.plans: White should aim to activate the bishop on the long diagonal and pressure the black queen.

notes.explains: In this pawn structure, taking on c5 with the pawn is bad because it leaves two pawns isolated and gives up central control. Black's knight can come out, but white has options like castling or queen d2.
notes.teaches: In certain pawn structures, recapturing with a pawn can create permanent weaknesses. Sometimes it's better to maintain tension and develop.
notes.plans: White can choose a flexible move like queen d2, keeping options open and avoiding pawn weaknesses.

notes.explains: White's bishop on d3 is not very useful, so trading it for the knight on f5 is acceptable. White can also consider g5 to challenge the knight, but must be careful about counterplay.
notes.teaches: When a piece is poorly placed, exchanging it can be a good way to improve your position. Also, pawn pushes like g5 can be double-edged.
notes.plans: White might play g5 to force the knight to move, but must be ready for black's reactions.

notes.explains: White doesn't need to castle because the center is semi-closed and black cannot easily open it. The rook is more useful on the g-file for attacking.
notes.teaches: Castling is not always necessary; if the center is closed and the king is safe, you can keep the rook active for attack.
notes.plans: White can focus on a kingside attack with g5 and h5, using the rook on g1.

notes.explains: After black plays d4, white can exchange queens, which is fine. White has a better position due to the two bishops, black's bad bishop, and a semi-open file.
notes.teaches: Exchanging queens can be beneficial when you have a positional advantage, as it reduces black's counterplay.
notes.plans: White should continue to exploit the bishop pair and pressure black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this French Winawer position, White wants to launch a kingside pawn storm with g5 and h5, but Black can respond with g5 to create counterplay. White considered Rg1 to prepare h5, but it is slow and gives Black time for c4, which would undermine White's center and create new counterplay.
notes.teaches: When preparing a pawn storm, ensure your preparatory moves are not too slow, as they give the opponent time to strike in the center. Balance your own attacking plans with the need to prevent your opponent's counterplay.
notes.plans: White should look for a more active way to support the pawn advance, perhaps by improving piece activity before committing to the kingside push.

notes.explains: After Black played ...Rd7, White chose h5 instead of moving the king, because moving the king would concede to Black's threats. Pushing h5 maintains the initiative and creates immediate threats, even though Black can respond with g5.
notes.teaches: When faced with a choice between defending passively and advancing your own plan, often the active move is better, even if it allows some counterplay. Evaluate whether your threats are faster than your opponent's.
notes.plans: White should continue with the kingside attack, using the h-pawn as a lever, while being prepared to handle Black's central breaks.

notes.explains: After Black played g5, White chose Kc1 to avoid the pawn capture and prevent Black from gaining time. Black's development with tempo (like ...Be7) is a 'fake tempo' because it doesn't actually threaten the bishop yet, but White must still be careful.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent's developing moves are 'fake tempi' that don't create real threats. Still, be cautious about allowing such moves, as they can improve the opponent's position for free.
notes.plans: White should consolidate the king's safety and then continue with the plan, possibly by rerouting the rook or preparing a breakthrough.

notes.explains: In this position, White's bishop is more valuable than Black's knight, so Black would be happy to trade them. White must avoid moves like Be4 that allow Bxg2, and instead consider moves that maintain the pressure, such as Rd1 to attack the queen.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a piece that is more valuable than its counterpart, avoid trades that favor them. Look for active moves that create threats and force your opponent to defend.
notes.plans: White should continue to create threats, possibly by attacking the queen or other weaknesses, while keeping the bishop active.

notes.explains: A recurring idea in this game is placing a rook in front of a queen or king, even with pieces in between, to create new threats and unusual pressure.
notes.teaches: Rooks can be used in unconventional ways, such as in front of the queen or king, to create hidden threats and complicate the opponent's defense. This is a creative resource in many positions.

notes.explains: In this sharp position, the bishop on d3 is the best move because it attacks h7 and defends c2, addressing both offense and defense. The alternative king move leads to messy complications where the advantage is unclear.
notes.teaches: When a position is already complex, prefer moves that simplify and address immediate threats rather than inviting more chaos.
notes.plans: Play Bd3, then if the opponent captures on c2, recapture or move the king to g1 to maintain safety and prepare counterplay.

notes.explains: The opponent's move Rb5 looks innocent but is a mistake. The best response for Black was to push or capture to open the rook's path to the seventh rank, but time is short because c2 is falling.
notes.teaches: In chaotic positions, look for moves that activate your rooks to their maximum potential, even if they seem counterintuitive.
notes.plans: If possible, open the rook's file to invade the seventh rank, but be mindful of immediate threats like the fall of c2.

notes.explains: The move c3 is crucial because it prevents the knight from being kicked and keeps the rook defending the second rank. If the knight moves, a check follows, and the rook can join the attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet pawn move is the most important, as it maintains the coordination of your pieces and denies the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play c3 to solidify the knight's position, then use the rook to create threats, possibly leading to checkmate.

notes.explains: When the opponent tries to promote, capturing with the rook is a strong option, though not the only one. The rook on g4 is a good move because it maintains pressure and keeps the attack going.
notes.teaches: In endgame-like transitions, prioritize active pieces over material, and consider captures that keep your pieces on strong squares.
notes.plans: Continue the attack, using the rook to create threats and possibly force a decisive result.

notes.explains: In this position, the rook on g4 creates serious checkmating threats. The opponent's attempts to defend only allow more pressure to be brought on the position.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attacking setup, avoid unnecessary complications and keep the pressure on. Even if the opponent tries to defend, you can often increase the pressure rather than forcing the issue.
notes.plans: Continue building pressure with the rooks, aiming for checkmate or material gain. If the opponent takes, the rooks remain active and the threats persist.

notes.explains: After the opponent plays ...Nf3, the best move is to avoid giving the opponent any counterplay. Rook g4 is a strong choice, but taking is also possible. The key is to avoid chaotic positions that give the opponent chances.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, prefer moves that maintain control and avoid unnecessary risks. Even if a move is not the only good one, choosing the one that minimizes counterplay is often best.
notes.plans: If the opponent takes, the rooks remain active and the attack continues. If they don't, the pressure mounts.

notes.explains: In the French Defense, after ...Nbd7, the best move for White is often to play Qh4, piling up on the kingside. If Black plays ...h6, taking is possible but requires careful play.
notes.teaches: In the French, when Black plays ...Nbd7, White can often generate kingside pressure with Qh4. However, be cautious about capturing on h6, as it can lead to complications if not handled precisely.
notes.plans: Build up on the kingside with Qh4, and if Black plays ...h6, consider whether to take or maintain the pressure.

notes.explains: In a position where Black has just taken on e4, White's best move is Qg3, because with extra material, exchanging pieces is desirable. Even if the knight gets to e4, the bishop has already been exchanged, so it's fine.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for moves that facilitate exchanges and simplify the position. This reduces the opponent's counterplay and makes the win easier.
notes.plans: Play Qg3, aiming to exchange pieces and consolidate the material advantage. If the knight comes to e4, it's acceptable because the bishop is gone.

notes.explains: In a sharp position where the center is mobile, Black is threatening c2. White should avoid long castling because the king becomes exposed. Instead, moves like Qf2 or g2 are better, even if they allow the opponent to win a pawn.
notes.teaches: When the center is open and the opponent has threats, prioritize king safety over material. Long castling can leave the king vulnerable, so consider safer alternatives even if they cost a pawn.
notes.plans: Choose a safe square for the queen or play g2 to create an escape, rather than castling long into danger.

notes.explains: In a position where the opponent has just played ...Qe7, the best move for Black would have been ...d4 to cut off the queen, a move both players missed. This shows the importance of looking for such intermediate moves.
notes.teaches: Always look for moves that cut off the opponent's pieces or create tactical motifs. A move like ...d4 can disrupt the opponent's coordination and is easy to miss in the heat of battle.
notes.plans: If given the chance, play ...d4 to cut off the queen and gain a tempo. Otherwise, continue with the current plan.

notes.explains: In this line, Black's knight to c6 is a key move, preparing to challenge the center and create checkmate threats. The move order is crucial: first check to force a response, then develop the knight.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, precise move order matters; a check can force the opponent to respond, giving you time to develop and maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: After knight c6, aim to deliver a check, then develop the knight, keeping checkmate ideas in mind. Be wary of Black's c4 break, which may be delayed.

notes.explains: If Black plays c4, the response depends on the queen's position. If the queen is still on c7, taking with the knight may be problematic because the queen can recapture, trapping the knight. In some cases, you are forced to take with a pawn, after which queen g4 becomes interesting.
notes.teaches: When considering captures, always check if the opponent's queen can recapture and create tactical problems for your piece.
notes.plans: After c4, if forced to take with the pawn, follow up with queen g4, creating threats. Be aware of Black's possible b5, queen f7, or bishop d7 ideas.

notes.explains: In closed center positions, you don't need to castle; instead, you can focus on a kingside pawn storm. The choice of how to push pawns (h4, g4, f4) depends on where you want your queen and knight.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a pawn storm can be a winning plan, but you must coordinate piece placement with pawn pushes to avoid weaknesses.
notes.plans: Consider starting with knight g5 or h4, then later f4, moving the queen, and g4 to launch the attack. If the knight is attacked, it can retreat to h3.

notes.explains: In this position, the choice between a quick pawn storm and a slower piece-based attack depends on the opponent's setup. The rook on f5 and the delayed queen development change the evaluation of moves like h4 and h5.
notes.teaches: When preparing an attack, consider whether your pawns can advance quickly or if you need to switch to piece play. If the opponent's pieces are well placed to stop your pawns, it may be better to develop pieces and attack on the other side.
notes.plans: If the opponent has not committed their queen, consider moves like Qh3 to prepare a pawn storm, or Ng5 to create tactical threats. Be ready to retreat the knight if the opponent doesn't take it, and then switch to a piece-based attack.

notes.explains: The opponent's move h6 to stop Ng5 is actually a concession, as it weakens their kingside and gives White a target. The knight on g5 was a sacrifice offer, and if accepted, White gets the f-file and attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When you offer a piece sacrifice, if the opponent declines, you should be happy because they have weakened their position or lost time. Use that to continue your attack, possibly by switching to a different plan.
notes.plans: After h6, White can consider retreating the knight and then playing f4 to open lines, or use the g5 square for other pieces. The attack is not abandoned, just redirected.

notes.explains: The speaker emphasizes the importance of deep opening preparation, especially when you know your opponent. They mention a book by a grandmaster that covers the French, Caro-Kann, and Philidor, which helped them improve their score against these openings.
notes.teaches: Investing time in studying specific openings in depth, using quality resources, can significantly improve your results. Even strong players can benefit from well-written opening books that explain ideas rather than just moves.
notes.plans: If you face the French, Caro-Kann, or Philidor, consider studying a comprehensive book on these openings to build a solid repertoire and understand typical plans.

notes.explains: In this sharp attacking position, retreating the knight was considered, but the player preferred to keep the attack by switching from pawn pushes to piece play, bringing the knight out to join the attack.
notes.teaches: When your pawns have done their job in creating weaknesses, it's often right to stop pushing them and bring your pieces into the attack instead.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to a good square and start coordinating pieces against the opponent's king.

notes.explains: The opponent wisely avoided taking a pawn immediately because capturing would have been completely winning for White. Instead, they played a queen move to maintain tension.
notes.teaches: Before grabbing material, always check if the capture allows the opponent a decisive tactic or a strong initiative.

notes.explains: After the queen was attacked, the player chose a retreat square that kept the queen active and allowed future jumps into the attack, rather than a passive retreat.
notes.teaches: When retreating a piece, prefer squares that keep it active and maintain pressure, even if it means a slightly longer route back to the action.
notes.plans: Re-route the queen to a better attacking square, then continue the assault.

notes.explains: Black's position looked solid but was actually fragile because Black had to play very precisely, while White could afford a few inaccuracies and still keep a strong attack.
notes.teaches: Positions with a lead in development or an ongoing attack often allow more flexibility; the defender must be precise, while the attacker can be more forgiving.
notes.plans: Keep building the attack, bringing more pieces over, and be ready to sacrifice if the opportunity arises.

notes.explains: After a series of exchanges, White ended up with an extra pawn and a great attack. The player then brought pieces over to pile up on the king, ignoring the other side of the board.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, concentrate all your forces on the king; don't get distracted by play on the other wing.
notes.plans: Continue to bring pieces to the attack and look for a decisive sacrifice.

notes.explains: In the Winawer French, after certain moves, White can choose between taking on c7 or playing Bishop d3, which transposes into lines with Queen c7 that were covered previously. The player prefers Bishop d3 to avoid well-known theory and to surprise opponents.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's worth deviating from the most common move to reach a less familiar position, even if the main line is objectively fine.
notes.plans: Play Bishop d3 and aim for a comfortable middlegame with chances for an attack.

notes.explains: Against a knight on f5, the player doesn't love the position because it hinders their plans, but they are comfortable after castling. Black might try h5 to force the queen to move and then exchange queens, but that would weaken Black's pawn structure and reduce counterplay.
notes.teaches: When considering queen exchanges, weigh the loss of attacking chances against the safety of your own king and the weakness of your pawns.
notes.plans: Castle, keep the queen active, and use the weak pawn as a target if queens are exchanged.

notes.explains: In this game, Black's second move g6 in the French Defense is a mistake because it weakens the dark squares and fails to establish a central pawn presence, giving White a lasting advantage.
notes.teaches: In the French Defense, establishing a strong center with d5 is crucial; moves like g6 that don't support the center and leave pawns on light squares can create long-term weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit the dark-square weaknesses and maintain pressure, while Black should seek to catch up in development and eventually challenge the center.

notes.explains: White's move Bc4 (bishop to c4) is decent but not the most precise; the computer suggests bringing the knight out first because knights need more time to reach the center, while bishops can develop later.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize developing knights before bishops when possible, as knights are slower and need to be placed early, while bishops have more flexibility.
notes.plans: White should continue developing pieces rapidly, aiming to castle and create threats, while Black should try to establish the d5 pawn break to solidify the center.

notes.explains: Black's move c5, attacking the d4 pawn, is a good idea in principle but fails here because White can respond with a strong move that gives White a nearly winning advantage (evaluation jumps to +0.96).
notes.teaches: Attacking the center is often correct, but you must ensure the follow-up is sound; if the attack can be refuted, it may leave you worse. Sometimes the solid central move d5 is better than a tactical strike.
notes.plans: White should capitalize on the advantage by continuing to develop and create threats, while Black must find a way to stabilize the position and avoid further concessions.

notes.explains: In this French Defense position, black's early c5 attacking the d4 pawn is tempting but flawed because the c5 pawn is unprotected. Black hopes that if white takes on c5, the g7 bishop can recapture and win the rook for a bishop, but white can instead sacrifice the exchange for a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a pawn break like c5, consider whether the pawn is truly protected and whether the opponent can exploit the resulting weaknesses, especially on the color complex where your pawns are absent.
notes.plans: If black plays c5, white should consider taking the pawn and giving up the rook to open lines and attack the weakened dark squares on the kingside.

notes.explains: White's c3 is a reasonable but not best move, as it protects the d4 pawn but misses the stronger tactical idea of taking on c5. The evaluation drops from a near one-pawn advantage to about a third of a pawn.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a solid defensive move is good, but you should always look for more forcing continuations that exploit the opponent's weaknesses, even if they involve material sacrifices.
notes.plans: White should have taken the c5 pawn, and after black recaptures, develop the knight to a strong outpost on a dark square, aiming to wedge it into d6 with check.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, white's pawns on e5 and d4 are strong, with the d4 pawn protected by pieces and the e5 pawn supported by a pawn. Black's bishop on e7 is blocked by its own pawns, giving white a positional advantage.
notes.teaches: A pawn on the fifth rank that is well-supported can restrict the opponent's pieces and give you space to maneuver. Avoid trading pawns when it would open lines for your opponent's bad bishop.
notes.plans: White should advance the kingside pawns to attack, while black should aim to trade rooks on the f-file and use the bishop to defend the king, seeking to neutralize white's space advantage.

notes.explains: The computer evaluation of plus over minus indicates a big advantage for white, but not a winning one. A plus sign on the left and minus on the right means white is better; if it were winning, the plus would be on the left and minus on the right with a different notation.
notes.teaches: Understanding evaluation notation helps you gauge how serious an advantage is. A one and a half pawn advantage is usually enough for a strong player to convert, but it's not yet a forced win.

notes.explains: Black's move a6 is a waste of time because it does nothing to address the immediate threats. White is planning a kingside attack, so black needs to prepare defenses there, not make irrelevant pawn moves. The move also fails to activate black's pieces, leaving the rook on a8 blocked by the bishop.
notes.teaches: In positions where the opponent has a space advantage and attacking chances, avoid unnecessary pawn moves. Prioritize development and defensive preparation over slow maneuvers.
notes.plans: Black should instead trade rooks on the f-file, then bring the bishop to a good square and the queen out, preparing to contest the open file and counterattack.

notes.explains: Black's best plan is to trade rooks immediately with Rxf1+ (or similar), because white's rooks are not protecting each other. If white recaptures with the queen, black can later bring a rook to the file and attack the queen, gaining control of the open file.
notes.teaches: When an open file is contested, trading rooks can simplify to a favorable endgame or allow your remaining rook to dominate the file. Recapturing with the queen may leave it vulnerable to attack.
notes.plans: Black should trade rooks, then develop the bishop to a strong square (e.g., g4) to pin the knight and attack a weak square, followed by moving the queen to activate the rook.

notes.explains: After black's correct development, white's best is to move the queen up, but black can counterattack by targeting an undefended bishop. White must then decide whether to defend or retreat, but retreating costs time and blocks the rook's path.
notes.teaches: In tactical battles, look for moves that attack undefended pieces to gain tempo. Sometimes retreating a piece is better than losing it, but be aware of the cost in development and coordination.
notes.plans: Black should continue to create counterplay by attacking white's pieces and pawns, while white must carefully coordinate to maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: In this position, the bishop on c8 is blocked by its own pawns and the rook on a8, costing several tempi to develop. The knight on b4 is strong because it forces the bishop to move and the rook to be blocked, giving Black time to organize a counterattack.
notes.teaches: A well-placed knight can tie down multiple pieces and create lasting positional pressure. When your opponent's pieces are cramped, every move they spend untangling is a tempo you gain.
notes.plans: Black should continue to pressure the b2 pawn with the queen and knight, while White should aim to drive the knight back with a3 and then develop harmoniously.

notes.explains: Black's queen and knight are attacking the b2 pawn, which is defended by the knight and queen, but one defender must stay. When White plays a3, the knight retreats to a6, and the queen continues to attack the undefended b2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When defending, look for counterattacks rather than passive defense. A pawn that is attacked multiple times can become a liability if the defenders are tied down.
notes.plans: Black should maintain the pressure on b2 while also developing the bishop to a good diagonal, avoiding blocking it with pawns.

notes.explains: Black had a chance to simplify with rook takes rook, but instead made a wasteful move. This gave White an extra tempo, which is a significant advantage in a sharp position.
notes.teaches: Don't waste moves. Every move is a tempo, and wasting one gives your opponent a free move. In critical positions, a single tempo can decide the game.
notes.plans: White should use the extra tempo to improve piece activity and create threats, while Black must try to catch up in development.

notes.explains: White's queen moves to the kingside, attacking pawns and preventing Black's bishop from moving due to the threat of queen takes pawn check. This also unpins the knight, allowing it to go to g3, a strong square protected by two pawns.
notes.teaches: A queen can be used to restrict the opponent's pieces while also unpinning your own. Moving a piece to a protected outpost like g3 can be very strong, especially if it can trade off a key defender.
notes.plans: White should aim to trade off Black's best piece, the knight, and then use the open files to invade with rooks.

notes.explains: Black's knight moves to f5, but this is a mistake. The computer evaluates the position as 1.11 pawns in White's favor, whereas retreating the bishop to f8 would have kept the advantage to only half a pawn. However, f8 leaves the f6 square weak.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are under pressure, it's often better to retreat and defend than to lunge forward. A move that seems active can be tactically flawed if it leaves other weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should take the knight with the pawn, eliminating Black's best piece, and then proceed with a rook lift to the third rank to attack the king.

notes.explains: White has a slight advantage, about half a pawn, but after trading off Black's best piece, the advantage grows to over a pawn. The white knight is blocked by its own pawns and has no useful squares, so its only value is to be traded for Black's active knight.
notes.teaches: When a piece is poorly placed and cannot improve, trading it for an opponent's active piece is a good way to realize its value and reduce the opponent's counterplay.
notes.plans: White should proceed with the rook lift to the third rank, bringing the rook in front of the pawn to support an attack.

notes.explains: Black makes a blunder that allows White's advantage to jump to over three pawns. White's pieces converge on Black's bishop, which is pinned to the king, and Black's own bishop on the queenside is useless because it cannot return to defend.
notes.teaches: A pinned piece is a major weakness; attacking it with multiple pieces can force decisive material gains. Also, developing a piece to a square where it cannot participate in defense is effectively a wasted move.
notes.plans: White should continue to pile up on the pinned bishop, using the rook, queen, and bishop to increase pressure.

notes.explains: After winning the bishop, White has a decisive material advantage. Black's queenside pawns are doubled and weak, and White can trade off pieces and march the king to capture them. The extra pawn on the kingside is also a decisive factor.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, a passed pawn on the flank can be a decisive advantage, especially if the opponent has weak pawns that can be attacked by the king.
notes.plans: White should liquidate pieces, bring the king to the queenside, capture the weak pawns, and then promote the passed pawn.

notes.explains: White uses pawns to create a barrier that restricts the black king's movement, while also creating a passed pawn on the kingside. The black king cannot stop both a kingside and a queenside passed pawn simultaneously.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, creating a passed pawn on the opposite side of the board from the main action can distract the enemy king and win the game. Pawn walls can also restrict the enemy king's access to key squares.
notes.plans: White should advance the pawns to create a passed pawn and then use the king to support it, while the black king is tied down.

notes.explains: The excerpt recounts the historical context of Morphy and Anderssen, focusing on Morphy's tragic end and Anderssen's continued career. It highlights that Morphy, despite his brilliance, quit chess due to depression and blamed the game, while Anderssen remained active and successful.
notes.teaches: Chess history shows that even the greatest players face personal struggles; the game itself is not to blame for life's difficulties. A player's legacy is shaped by both their play and their character.

notes.explains: In the French Defense, the Winawer Variation arises after e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Bb4. The bishop move violates the principle of developing knights before bishops, but it is a modern and complex variation that leads to sharp play, rarely drawing.
notes.teaches: Opening principles are guidelines, not absolute rules; some variations intentionally break them for dynamic compensation. The Winawer is a theoretically sound but double-edged choice.

notes.explains: In the Winawer, White often should block the pawn chain with c3 to restrict Black's light-squared bishop, but Anderssen instead developed a piece and protected the center. Black counterattacked against the center pawns, and after White took, Black could have achieved equality with Qxd4, but chose a different move.
notes.teaches: In the French, the light-squared bishop is often a problem piece; White should consider moves that restrict it. When a pawn is attacked, recapturing with the queen can be a way to avoid structural weaknesses.

notes.explains: White missed a chance for an advantage by not playing dxc5, which would have opened the position. If Black recaptures the knight, White can recapture with the pawn, and after the bishop takes, White gets the two bishops and pressure on Black's weakened dark squares.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn capture that seems to lose a piece is actually strong because of tactical resources. The two bishops can be a long-term advantage, especially when the opponent's dark-squared bishop is gone.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit the open position and the bishop pair to attack Black's king side.

notes.explains: Black's best response was to develop the knight to f6, placing it in front of the king to block the rook's pressure on the f-file. This move also protects the pawn and prepares to castle.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's rook is aiming at your king, a well-placed knight can serve as a shield. Development should also address immediate threats.
notes.plans: Black should castle quickly and complete development, while White continues to build pressure.

notes.explains: In this French Defense structure, Black's early pawn move a6 is a mistake because it wastes time. The correct plan is to develop the knight to f6, which protects the pawn and blocks the rook's pressure on the king. White's setup with the knight on e2 supports the d4 pawn, avoiding doubled pawns if the bishop is taken.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves in the opening should have a clear purpose; developing pieces and castling are usually more important. Avoid wasting tempi on pawn moves that don't contribute to development or control key squares.
notes.plans: Black should castle quickly and aim for equality by completing development. White can use the extra tempo to build pressure, possibly targeting the weak d5 pawn.

notes.explains: White has a weak pawn on d5, and Black can exploit it by attacking it with pieces. The sequence of exchanges leads to Black winning a pawn, but the key is that Black must avoid allowing White to get counterplay. The bishop pin on the knight is strong because the knight cannot be defended by the bishop due to the knight on e6 controlling the square.
notes.teaches: Weak pawns are targets; use pieces to attack them. Pins can be decisive when the defender cannot break them, especially if the pinned piece is valuable.
notes.plans: Black should maintain the pin and convert the extra pawn in the endgame. White must find active counterplay to compensate for the material deficit.

notes.explains: Black again wastes time with a pawn move (a6) when castling was available. By castling, Black would have avoided the pin on the knight and achieved equality. White's subsequent capture of the bishop is not a loss of tempo because Black must recapture with a pawn, so White gains a move.
notes.teaches: Castling is often a critical developing move that also safeguards the king. When you capture a piece, you don't lose time if your opponent has to recapture with a pawn, as that uses their move.
notes.plans: Black should castle and aim for a solid position. White can use the extra tempo to continue development or create threats.

notes.explains: In a position where White's bishop is attacking a pawn, White should consider a pawn move that attacks the bishop, forcing it to retreat or be captured. If the bishop retreats, White wins a pawn; if it captures, White recaptures with the knight, and the bishop pair is slightly better than knight and bishop, giving White a small advantage.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pawn move is justified if it attacks a piece and gains time. Trading a bishop for a knight can be good if it improves your pawn structure or gives you the bishop pair.
notes.plans: White should proceed with the plan to win a pawn or improve the position. Black should try to minimize the damage and castle.

notes.explains: White's bishop move to a poor square allows Black to capture it, leaving White's rook on a bad square, blocked by its own pieces and undefended. This costs White time to reposition the rook. The rook is misplaced and will need to move back to a better file.
notes.teaches: Avoid placing pieces on squares where they are blocked or undefended. A misplaced piece can cost tempi and allow the opponent to seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Black should continue to exploit White's awkward piece placement. White must spend moves to improve the rook and coordinate pieces.

notes.explains: In this position, a rook is placed behind a pawn and is attacked by a knight. The rook is undefended and blocked by its own pieces, making it a poor square. The player who put the bishop there allowed the opponent to trade, forcing the rook to move again and costing a tempo.
notes.teaches: Do not trade pieces automatically, especially if it helps the opponent. Sometimes it is better to retreat a piece to a better square rather than trade, and avoid placing pieces on squares where they become vulnerable and require wasted moves.
notes.plans: Move the rook to a safer square where it can become active, and continue development.

notes.explains: A knight is on a square where it is protected by a pawn and attacks a backward pawn. The opponent's rook must stay to defend that pawn, tying it down. The knight is well placed, but it is only a way station; it wants to move to a better square where it attacks the queen.
notes.teaches: A knight on a strong outpost can be a temporary asset. Look for ways to improve its position further, and use pawns to control key squares and provide escape squares for the king.
notes.plans: Advance a pawn to block the knight's intended squares and give the king an escape square. Then consider moving the knight to a more active square.

notes.explains: When the knight is on g3, black can attack it with h5, threatening to win it. The knight is not well placed there and must retreat. White's best response is to bring the queen up to protect the knight, but that allows black to advance the pawn, which opens lines for the rook.
notes.teaches: Attack a poorly placed piece with a pawn to force it to move. If the opponent defends, you may gain space or open lines for your own pieces.
notes.plans: Black should play h5 to attack the knight. If white defends with the queen, black can push the pawn further, opening the rook's path to the kingside.

notes.explains: White misses a strong tactical opportunity: a rook sacrifice on a pawn. The sequence involves giving up a rook for a pawn and a bishop, but then a knight hops in, attacking the queen and rook, and after a check, white wins back the rook and ends up a pawn up with a nearly winning advantage.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical shots, even those that involve sacrificing material. Sometimes a temporary sacrifice leads to a decisive gain. Also, be aware of undefended pieces and the potential for forks.
notes.plans: If the opportunity arises, consider the rook sacrifice to win a pawn and gain a strong initiative.

notes.explains: Black again has the chance to attack the knight with h5. White must respond by moving the queen to guard a key square, preventing black's queen from infiltrating. The knight is forced to retreat, and black ends up slightly better.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a weak piece, use pawns to harass it. Also, be aware of the opponent's threats and keep your queen on squares that control critical entry points.
notes.plans: Black should play h5 to drive the knight away. White must keep the queen on a square that prevents black's queen from entering the position.

notes.explains: In this position, the black queen must be kept out of a key square, so White plays a knight to h7, forcing the queen to h4. The queen cannot capture the pawn because it must guard that critical square. The evaluation is slightly better for Black, about a quarter of a pawn.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a piece must be used to restrict the enemy queen's activity, even if it means giving up material. The queen's defensive duties can outweigh its attacking potential.
notes.plans: White continues to develop and coordinate pieces, aiming to exploit the queen's awkward placement.

notes.explains: White's attack proceeds with two rooks and the queen converging on the king, with no enemy pieces around to defend. The only check is covered by the queen. Black threatens to take the knight, but it's too late. White breaks down the pawn barrier with a rook check, and the king is driven into a mating net.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and your heavy pieces are coordinated, you can often force mate by breaking down the pawn shield and driving the king into the open.
notes.plans: White continues the mating attack, forcing resignation as mate is inevitable in a few moves.

notes.explains: The romantic era of chess featured aggressive, attacking play, and the old masters were very strong despite lacking computer assistance. Modern grandmasters are stronger because they have learned from accumulated knowledge and engines.
notes.teaches: Chess understanding evolves over time; studying historical games can inspire attacking ideas, but modern players benefit from deeper theoretical and computer-aided insights.

notes.explains: In chess, players often default to forward moves because the goal is to attack the enemy king, but backward moves can be just as strong, especially when they improve a piece's position or defend key squares.
notes.teaches: Always consider retreating moves, especially with knights, as they can be powerful and are often overlooked by opponents.

notes.explains: White has a three-on-two pawn majority on the queenside and is up a pawn, giving a clear advantage. The main plan is to create a passed pawn by pushing the c-pawn, but the black king may be able to stop it if it gets back in time.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn majority, your plan should be to create a passed pawn, but you must consider whether the opponent's king can stop it.
notes.plans: Push the c-pawn (or sometimes the a-pawn) to create a passer, while also improving the king's position to support the pawns.

notes.explains: White played Kf2, which prevents the black bishop from entering the game, effectively sealing it out. This is a key move because it neutralizes a piece that could otherwise defend the queenside pawns.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a king move can be used to restrict the opponent's pieces, especially in endgames where piece activity is crucial.
notes.plans: After Kf2, White can proceed with the pawn push, while Black's bishop is out of play.

notes.explains: In the game, Black took a pawn, but that was not best. Black should have played Kf4 to improve the king, staying close enough to stop the pawns. Instead, Black played Kd4, which allowed White to push c5, winning on the spot because the black king is no longer in time to stop the passed pawn.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, king activity is paramount. Always improve your king's position, especially when facing a passed pawn, and avoid moves that take the king out of the action.
notes.plans: For Black: keep the king near the pawns to prevent promotion. For White: push the c-pawn to create a decisive passer.

notes.explains: The winning move is a knight retreat to g2, which is counterintuitive because it appears to hang the knight. This retreat likely was missed because it is a backward move that also leaves a piece en prise, but it sets up a decisive tactic.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves can be powerful even when they seem to hang material, because they may create threats or improve the piece's position. Always calculate retreats, especially with knights, as they can be the key to winning.
notes.plans: After the knight retreat, White will have a winning continuation, likely involving the passed pawn or a tactical blow.

notes.explains: In this king-and-pawn versus knight endgame, white has a large advantage but must choose the right move. The tempting knight retreats allow black's king to collect white's pawns, forcing white to fight for a draw despite the earlier advantage. The winning idea is a king retreat, which keeps the advantage and leads to a clean win.
notes.teaches: When ahead, prefer moves that maintain the initiative and avoid allowing counterplay. A retreating king move can be stronger than a natural-looking piece move if it preserves winning chances.
notes.plans: After the king retreat, white advances the c-pawn, promoting with check if possible, and uses the king to support the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: In the game between Navara and Giri, black faces a decision after white's rook attacks a bishop. Taking the b2 pawn is tempting, but white has a tactical idea: rook to b1, attacking the bishop and then capturing on b7. Black instead finds a strong centralizing move with the knight to d5, which avoids the tactic and improves the piece.
notes.teaches: Before grabbing a pawn, check if the opponent has a tactical refutation. Sometimes a quiet, centralizing move is better than winning material if it keeps your position sound.
notes.plans: Black's knight on d5 eyes key squares and supports the attack, while avoiding the rook's tactical threats. Black can continue to pressure white's position.

notes.explains: Taking the b2 pawn with the bishop looks natural, but White has a tactical resource: Rook b1, attacking the bishop, and if the bishop moves, the rook can capture on b7. This shows that grabbing a pawn can walk into a pin or a discovered attack.
notes.teaches: Before taking a pawn, check if the opponent has a way to exploit the piece's position, such as attacking it with a rook while also creating threats on other targets.
notes.plans: If the pawn is taken, White will play Rook b1 and then Rook x b7, winning a pawn and activating the rook. Black should consider alternative moves that avoid this.

notes.explains: Black's idea of Knight e7 to d5 is a strong centralizing move that attacks the rook on c7 and prepares to kick it away. It forces White to react and gives Black time to improve their position.
notes.teaches: Centralizing a knight to a strong outpost can be more valuable than winning a pawn, as it creates threats and restricts the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Black will use the knight on d5 to harass the rook and eventually win material or gain a positional advantage.

notes.explains: Black's bishop takes b2 is actually a sound move because even though White can play Rook b1, Black has a follow-up: after the bishop retreats, Black can trap the rook with Bishop b6, attacking it and eventually winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can allow a tactical trick if you have a deeper resource that turns the tables. Look for ways to trap the opponent's piece after they commit to an attack.
notes.plans: Black will play Bishop b6, trapping the rook on b1. White may try to escape with e6 or other moves, but Black can maintain the pressure and win material.

notes.explains: White's rook is in danger of being trapped. Black uses a series of forcing moves, including Knight a5 and King f8, to restrict the rook's escape squares. The key is to coordinate pieces to cut off all retreat paths.
notes.teaches: To trap a piece, you must control all its escape squares. Use your pieces to cover the key squares and force the opponent into a losing position.
notes.plans: Black will continue to harass the rook, eventually winning it or gaining a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: The retreating move Knight d8 is excellent because it simultaneously attacks the rook and defends the pawn on b7. This dual-purpose move ensures that the rook has no safe squares and will be trapped.
notes.teaches: Backward moves can be powerful when they serve multiple purposes, such as attacking and defending at the same time. Always consider retreats as viable options.
notes.plans: After Knight d8, the rook is trapped, and Black will win the exchange and convert the extra material.

notes.explains: Backward knight moves are often overlooked because they go against the natural instinct to advance, yet they can be crucial for rerouting the piece to a better square or opening lines.
notes.teaches: When considering candidate moves, deliberately include retreats and backward moves, especially for knights, as they can be the key to improving your position.

notes.explains: In a position with no immediate threats and a relatively closed center, there is time for maneuvering. White has an open file, a good bishop, and a well-placed queen, while black has potential knight outposts. White is slightly better.
notes.teaches: Assess the position using standard criteria: piece activity, pawn structure, king safety, and open files. Identify which pieces are good and which are poorly placed.
notes.plans: Improve the worst-placed piece by finding its ideal square and maneuvering it there.

notes.explains: When the opponent has no immediate threats, you can focus on long-term improvement rather than concrete calculation.
notes.teaches: A practical method for planning: identify your worst-placed piece, imagine its dream square, and then find a route to get it there.

notes.explains: When looking for a plan, identify your worst-placed piece and imagine teleporting it to its ideal square. This clarifies the target and the route.
notes.teaches: Ask 'what is my worst piece and where would I put it if I could?' to generate concrete plans.

notes.explains: A knight on g3 is often awkward and offside, lacking a clear future. The dream squares for such a knight are central outposts like d5, e5, or f5, or a strong outpost like g5.
notes.teaches: Knights belong on outposts where they are safe and influential; identify those squares and maneuver the knight there, even if it requires backward moves.
notes.plans: Look for a path to a good outpost, possibly via h1-f2-h3-g5, and consider preparatory moves like exchanging bishops to weaken control of key squares.

notes.explains: A bishop that cuts off the king is a very strong piece. Trading it for a less active piece, like an undeveloped bishop, is usually a mistake.
notes.teaches: Do not trade your best pieces for opponent's pieces that are not yet active. Keep strong pieces and improve your bad ones.
notes.plans: Avoid bishop exchanges that give away your best piece; instead, improve the knight via a retreating maneuver.

notes.explains: Retreating a knight to the back rank can be a powerful maneuvering move, redeploying it to a better square while keeping the position flexible.
notes.teaches: Don't shy away from backward moves; they can be the best way to improve a poorly placed piece.
notes.plans: Look for squares where the knight can be more active, even if it means moving backward first.

notes.explains: Trading your good pieces for your opponent's bad ones is a mistake; instead, improve your bad pieces and trade them for their good ones.
notes.teaches: Piece exchanges should be evaluated by the relative quality of the pieces, not just material.
notes.plans: Identify your worst piece and find a plan to improve it or trade it for a better opponent piece.

notes.explains: When your opponent has pressure, trading pieces can relieve it, but sometimes the resulting position is even better for the attacker.
notes.teaches: Before trading, calculate the resulting positions carefully; a 'natural' trade may open lines for the opponent.
notes.plans: If you are under pressure, look for trades that genuinely simplify, not ones that give the opponent more activity.

notes.explains: A queen move can create threats that prevent the opponent from challenging your control of a file.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can use tactics to maintain control of a key line, rather than just trading pieces.
notes.plans: Look for moves that create threats while maintaining your positional advantages.

notes.explains: When your opponent plays a weakening move like g6, you should aim to exploit the weakened diagonal, perhaps by rerouting a bishop to it.
notes.teaches: Identify weaknesses created by pawn moves and plan to target them with your pieces.
notes.plans: Consider how to get a bishop onto the weakened diagonal, possibly by trading off the defender.

notes.explains: When your intended move is met by a strong response, you need to be flexible and find an even stronger alternative.
notes.teaches: Always consider your opponent's possible replies and be ready to change your plan if they refute your first idea.
notes.plans: If a move like Ng5 is met by h6, look for other moves that maintain pressure or create new threats.

notes.explains: A surprising queen retreat can be very powerful, hitting multiple targets and forcing the opponent to react.
notes.teaches: Retreats are not just defensive; they can be offensive, repositioning a piece to a more active square.
notes.plans: Look for retreats that create threats or improve your piece's scope, even if they seem counterintuitive.

notes.explains: A retreating queen move can be powerful when it both attacks a weakness and forces the opponent to commit a piece to passive defense. Here, the queen retreats to f2, pressuring the d-pawn and inducing the bishop to defend it, which takes the bishop out of play.
notes.teaches: Retreats are not always concessions; they can be the most effective way to improve a piece's activity and create threats. Look for backward moves that simultaneously attack and restrict the opponent.
notes.plans: After the bishop is forced to defend, continue improving your position and prepare to challenge the opponent's setup, aiming to exploit the bishop's passivity.

notes.explains: The opponent's bishop is on a good diagonal, so a pawn push (b4) is used to drive it away, permanently removing it from that active diagonal. This is a methodical way to worsen the opponent's position.
notes.teaches: Use pawn advances to chase enemy pieces off their best squares, especially when they are well-placed. This is a standard technique to reduce the opponent's activity.
notes.plans: After the bishop is driven away, continue improving your pieces and look for ways to exploit the weakened squares or the opponent's lack of coordination.

notes.explains: In a winning position, it's crucial to find the most precise move. Here, a queen move to e1 is stronger than the natural queen to h4 because it prevents the opponent's best defensive resource (rook e8). The queen can later return to h4 if needed.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attack, consider the opponent's best defenses and look for moves that cut them off. Sometimes a quieter, less obvious move is more effective than the flashy one.
notes.plans: After queen e1, the threat of rook e7 is decisive, and the opponent has no adequate defense. If they try to defend, you can capture and win material or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: In this position, White has a winning advantage and should switch from general strategic maneuvering to concrete calculation. The tactical sequence starting with a check and queen sortie leads to a forced mate or material gain, and the bishop is used in a crisscross pattern.
notes.teaches: When you have a clear advantage, stop playing 'strategy mode' and calculate concrete variations to convert. Look for forcing moves like checks and captures that exploit the opponent's weaknesses.
notes.plans: Execute the tactical sequence that wins material or delivers mate, using the bishop and queen in coordination.

notes.explains: White declines to capture a rook because it is poisoned—taking it would open a diagonal that exposes the king to danger. The priority is to keep the king safe and maintain the initiative.
notes.teaches: Not every material gain is sound; sometimes a piece is 'poisoned' because capturing it allows a devastating counterplay. Evaluate the resulting position before grabbing material.
notes.plans: Continue with moves that improve your position and maintain pressure, avoiding the poisoned rook.

notes.explains: White gives up the 'great bishop' by trading it for a knight on f7, but this is justified by a concrete tactical follow-up: the knight goes to g5, creating multiple threats. The strategic value of the bishop is outweighed by the immediate tactical gains.
notes.teaches: Piece quality is relative; a strategically good piece can be exchanged if the resulting tactics give you a decisive attack. Always weigh the concrete consequences against general principles.
notes.plans: Play the tactical sequence that follows the bishop trade, using the knight to generate threats and win material.

notes.explains: White identifies the worst-placed piece as the bishop, which is stuck on a poor diagonal. The plan is to reroute it to a better square, such as b2, where it will have a strong diagonal. This is a strategic improvement before launching the final attack.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions, find your worst-placed piece and improve it. Rerouting a piece to a better square can be more valuable than making immediate threats.
notes.plans: Play the improving move that brings the bishop to b2, then continue with the attack.

notes.explains: White plays b5 to open a route for the bishop, creating a decisive attack. The opponent, facing overwhelming threats, gives up a piece to avoid worse, and White converts the material advantage.
notes.teaches: A pawn break like b5 can open lines for your pieces and create a decisive attack. When you have a winning position, keep pressing with concrete threats and convert once you are ahead in material.
notes.plans: After the opponent declines the pawn, continue the attack and convert the material advantage to a win.

notes.explains: In this 1851 game, the opening was not theoretically sound by modern standards, but the point is the original ideas and the tactical nature of play. Black's early queen sortie to b6 attacks both d4 and b2, but it exposes the queen and invites White to develop with tempo.
notes.teaches: When your opponent goes pawn-hunting early, they often fall behind in development. You should be willing to sacrifice a pawn for rapid piece activity and attacking chances.
notes.plans: White aims to complete development quickly, using the exposed black queen to gain tempi, and then to open lines against the uncastled black king.

notes.explains: After Black grabs the b2 pawn, White has all pieces developed for the cost of a pawn. The position offers White many attractive options, and it's easy to become overwhelmed by the abundance of possibilities. The key is to keep the initiative and not allow Black to consolidate.
notes.teaches: When you have compensation for a pawn, you must act energetically. Choose moves that maintain the initiative, develop with threats, and prevent the opponent from catching up in development.
notes.plans: White should continue to develop while creating threats, possibly targeting the c-file or preparing a central break like d5, to exploit Black's lagging development.

notes.explains: Black's defensive moves like ...Na6 and ...Bf8 are passive and overprotective, failing to address the main issue: the king is stuck in the center and development is incomplete. White's pieces are active and coordinated, ready to strike.
notes.teaches: When you are behind in development and your king is unsafe, you should prioritize castling and simplifying, even if it means returning material. Passive, defensive moves that don't address the king's safety often lead to a quick collapse.
notes.plans: White should continue to increase the pressure, looking for tactical blows that exploit Black's uncastled king and the poor placement of Black's pieces.

notes.explains: When you have a large lead in development and all the space, it's easy to become complacent and imprecise because there are so many tempting options.
notes.teaches: Maintain focus and choose the most direct, principled continuation even when you feel you are winning; don't let abundance of choice lead to sloppy play.

notes.explains: White has a big lead in development and black is still uncastled. White plays d5 to open the position, which is correct when ahead in development.
notes.teaches: When you are ahead in development, open the position to create tactical opportunities and expose the opponent's king.
notes.plans: Continue with active moves like f4 or queen d2 to maintain pressure and prevent black from consolidating.

notes.explains: White couldn't find a direct win and played bishop d4, but a move like queen b3 would regain the pawn and keep pressure, as black can't defend a7.
notes.teaches: When no immediate tactical blow exists, prefer simple moves that maintain the initiative and recover material, rather than forcing unclear complications.
notes.plans: If possible, play queen b3 to win back the pawn and keep the pressure on black's weak points.

notes.explains: Black plays e5 to close the position, which is principled when behind in development because it limits white's attacking chances and buys time to develop.
notes.teaches: When you are behind in development, close the position to reduce the opponent's activity and gain time to catch up.
notes.plans: White should continue with f4 to try to open lines and use the lead in development, even though the position is closed.

notes.explains: The position is closed, so White cannot break open the center with e6. White has a lead in development and needs to find a way to use it despite the closed nature.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a development lead must be converted through pawn breaks or piece maneuvering, not direct confrontation.
notes.plans: White plays f4 to challenge the center and open lines, maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: Black responds with f6, avoiding taking on f4. White then plays fxe5, and Black recaptures with fxe5, keeping the pawn on f6 to maintain a solid structure and hope to castle.
notes.teaches: When facing an attacking player, keeping a solid pawn structure can be a defensive resource, even if it means conceding some space.
notes.plans: White considers moves like d6 to open the position and exploit Black's undeveloped pieces.

notes.explains: White plays Qa4, developing with tempo and threatening Nc7+ or Nxd6. Black is forced to play Bb7 to defend, as other moves allow tactics.
notes.teaches: Developing with tempo is a key way to maintain initiative and create threats while improving your position.
notes.plans: White aims to exploit the weak d6 square and keep Black's pieces tied down.

notes.explains: White plays Bb4, but this is criticized as the bishop is loose there. A better idea was Qa3, which would set up tactics against Black's weakened position.
notes.teaches: Pieces should be placed on squares where they are not vulnerable to tactics. Look for ways to combine threats with concrete tactics.
notes.plans: White could have played Qa3, threatening Qb6+ and then Rxf8+ with a winning attack.

notes.explains: The position offers White a forcing tactical sequence starting with a queen check, where Black's king is exposed and the rook on f8 is vulnerable. The key is that White can regain all material with interest because Black's king remains in the center and cannot find shelter.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, look for forcing checks that win material or expose the king further. A queen sacrifice can be sound if it leads to a decisive attack or regains the material with tempo.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack by bringing pieces to active squares, keeping the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal to support mating threats.

notes.explains: Black's king remains uncastled and pieces are undeveloped, so White can exploit this by opening lines and creating threats. The dark-squared bishop is valuable for controlling key diagonals, so keeping it can be more important than winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: In positions with a lead in development, prioritize maintaining pressure over grabbing material. A bishop that controls important diagonals can be worth more than a pawn, especially when the opponent's king is vulnerable.
notes.plans: White should aim to open the f-file and use the rook to create threats against the king, while keeping the bishop active to support the attack.

notes.explains: After Black finally starts developing with ...Nh6, White has a strong continuation involving a rook sacrifice on f8 followed by a knight check on d6. This wins material and leaves Black's king exposed, effectively ending the game.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is behind in development, a rook sacrifice can be a practical way to break through, even if it is not the only winning move. The resulting attack is often overwhelming because the opponent's pieces are not coordinated.
notes.plans: White should execute the rook sacrifice and then use the knight and bishop to continue the attack, forcing the king into a mating net or winning more material.

notes.explains: Both players take a pause to improve their positions: Black develops the knight to f7 and White moves the king to safety. This is a natural moment to consolidate before continuing the attack.
notes.teaches: Even when you have a strong attack, it is important to take time to improve your own king's safety and complete development. This prevents counterplay and ensures your attack is not compromised.
notes.plans: White should finish development and then resume the attack, using the extra piece activity to create new threats.

notes.explains: In this position, black has lagged in development, with pieces still on the back rank, while white has been building an attack. Black's priority is to complete development and get the king safe, even if it means returning material.
notes.teaches: When under attack, it is often worth giving back material to catch up in development and castle. A safe king and active pieces matter more than a pawn.
notes.plans: Black should look for ways to trade pieces and get the king castled, even at the cost of a pawn, to neutralize white's initiative.

notes.explains: Black missed a chance to trade queens and simplify, which would have reduced white's tactical threats. Instead, black played a move that allowed white to keep the queens on and maintain pressure.
notes.teaches: When defending, trading queens can be a key defensive resource, as the queen often enables many attacking tactics. Look for opportunities to exchange pieces to ease the defense.
notes.plans: Black should have played a move like bishop e7, giving back material to facilitate castling and piece trades, leading to a more manageable position.

notes.explains: White missed a strong tactical continuation, likely involving a knight check or a bishop move to hit f7 and d6, which would have maintained the attack. Instead, white played a quieter move, allowing black to consolidate.
notes.teaches: In positions with a lead in development and open lines, look for forcing tactics like checks and captures that exploit the opponent's uncastled king. If you see a win, play it; if not, keep the pressure.
notes.plans: White should have considered moves like knight c7 check or bishop c4, which would have created threats against f7 and d6, keeping the initiative.

notes.explains: After black traded pieces and equalized material, white's position was no longer objectively winning. White then played with renewed energy, as the position required practical play rather than a forced win.
notes.teaches: When a position is no longer objectively winning, you must switch to playing the best practical moves, often keeping pieces on the board to maintain pressure and create chances.
notes.plans: White should continue to play actively, using the lead in development and open lines to create threats, even if the material is equal.

notes.explains: After a mistake in a winning position, the game is no longer objectively winning, but the player can still recover by refocusing and playing accurately from that point on.
notes.teaches: When you realize you've missed a win, don't dwell on the mistake; reset and play the best moves from the current position.

notes.explains: With a lead in development, keeping queens on the board maintains attacking chances. Trading queens would lead to an endgame where the opponent's queenside majority and blockaded passed pawn give them the better chances.
notes.teaches: When ahead in development, avoid unnecessary queen trades; keep pieces on to exploit the initiative.
notes.plans: Play Qc7 to keep queens on and attack b7, provoking ...Nd6.

notes.explains: The knight on d6 is an excellent blockader: it stops the passed pawn, protects b7, attacks e4, and is hard to dislodge because it sits on a dark square, away from the bishop on d3.
notes.teaches: A knight on a strong blockading square can neutralize an enemy passed pawn and restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Black should aim to complete development and trade pieces to reduce White's attacking potential.

notes.explains: White's queen on a5 keeps the black king in the center by preventing castling (the knight on d6 covers f7). Black's h5 is a mistake because it ignores the danger and wastes time.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is behind in development, they should seek to trade pieces and complete development, not make pawn moves on the side.
notes.plans: Black should have played ...Rf8 to manually castle and trade rooks, easing the pressure.

notes.explains: When attacking a king stuck in the center, trading rooks would relieve the pressure and let the defender consolidate. Keeping the heavy pieces on the board maintains the initiative and the king's discomfort.
notes.teaches: In an attack against an uncastled king, avoid unnecessary trades of major pieces. Keep the queens and rooks to sustain the attack.
notes.plans: Continue to bring more pieces to the attack, using the rook to control open files and the queen to support threats.

notes.explains: The knight on d6 is a powerful blockade, restricting black's pieces and controlling key squares. Black's last move a6 prepares to move the king to f7, but white finds a way to prevent that.
notes.teaches: A well-placed blockade piece can be worth more than material. Look for moves that improve your worst-placed piece while maintaining the blockade.
notes.plans: Play knight d4, bringing the last piece into the attack and preparing to jump to e6 or f5, further harassing the black king.

notes.explains: The move knight d4 is surprising because it seems to move away from the action, but it actually brings the knight into the attack with tempo, threatening e6 and c6. Black's predictable defenses are bypassed.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is one that your opponent hasn't considered because it goes against the obvious plan. Look for unconventional moves that improve your position and create new threats.
notes.plans: After knight d4, if black takes on d4, the pawn recaptures with e5, opening lines and cracking the position. Otherwise, the knight goes to e6, creating serious threats.

notes.explains: After the knight reaches e6, white has a choice: trade into an endgame or keep pieces on. Trading into an endgame would let black's blockade hold and black would be fine. Keeping pieces on maintains the attack.
notes.teaches: When you have an attack, avoid simplifying into an endgame unless you have a clear win. Keep the tension and use your active pieces to increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Play rook c7, keeping the rooks on and the attack rolling. The black king remains stuck in the center, and white can continue to improve piece placement.

notes.explains: White's queen goes to b6, pinning black's queen to the king and restricting black's pieces. Black is reduced to shuffling, with no active plan. White's pieces are all on their best squares, and black is paralyzed.
notes.teaches: In a dominant position, improve your pieces to their optimal squares and restrict your opponent's counterplay. Patience is key; you don't need a tactic if you can slowly increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Continue to improve piece placement and look for ways to break through, such as the idea of queen f6, which threatens bishop takes e6 and creates mating threats.

notes.explains: White has a strong position with a knight on d6, but there is no immediate tactical finish. The opponent's pieces are awkwardly placed, and black's king is exposed, but concrete forcing moves are lacking.
notes.teaches: When a promising attack does not yield a direct tactic, the game must be converted through positional means, maintaining pressure and improving piece placement.
notes.plans: Keep pieces on the board, avoid exchanges that relieve pressure, and look for ways to increase the initiative without forcing moves.

notes.explains: After a queen move to f6, there are tactical threats: the d6 knight cannot be taken because of a back-rank mate, and there is a threat to capture on e6. This move follows the principle of exploiting a development advantage by avoiding piece trades.
notes.teaches: When you have a development or activity advantage, avoid trading pieces, as that reduces your attacking potential and can flip the evaluation.
notes.plans: Continue to create threats that force the opponent to react, while keeping the queens on the board to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Black's pieces are poorly coordinated, and there is no way to defend the e5 pawn. The position is collapsing, and white can win material or force a decisive advantage.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied up, look for ways to win material by attacking multiple weaknesses, even without a direct mate.
notes.plans: Exploit the weaknesses by attacking the e5 pawn and other loose pieces, converting the positional advantage into a material one.

notes.explains: White started with a sharp attack, missed the best continuations, and then had to switch to a more positional approach to win the game again with fewer pieces.
notes.teaches: It is important to be flexible and willing to reset your approach when an attack does not break through; converting a winning position requires patience and accuracy.
notes.plans: After missing the initial win, calmly rebuild the advantage by improving piece placement and exploiting long-term weaknesses.

notes.explains: After missing the initial attacking win, White must restart the game with fewer pieces, which is more difficult. The position requires a shift from direct attack to precise positional play.
notes.teaches: When an attack fizzles, you must reset and find the best moves for the new position, not force the old plan.
notes.plans: Consolidate the position, keep material on the board, and target the opponent's king position.

notes.explains: The final sequence shows a quick collapse: a knight and bishop sacrifice on b5, followed by a queen check and rook checks, leading to mate. The game ended in a few moves after the sacrifice.
notes.teaches: When you have a development advantage or an attack, look for tactical blows that expose the king, even if it means sacrificing material.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with checks and threats, driving the king into a mating net.

notes.explains: White had to switch from a failed attack to winning the game again, a difficult psychological task. The game lasted 44 moves, with the final checkmate coming four moves after the shown position.
notes.teaches: Admitting you missed a win and starting over is a key skill; stay composed and play the best moves regardless of past mistakes.

notes.explains: In top-level matches, early draws are common as players probe each other; a single decisive game can shift the narrative and momentum.
notes.teaches: Do not judge a match by the scoreline alone—long stretches of draws often precede a critical breakthrough.

notes.explains: In the Scheveningen Sicilian, White often plays Be2, castling, and then f4 to build a central pawn roller, while Black develops harmoniously with ...e6, ...Be7, ...Nc6, and ...Qc7, ready to meet central tension.
notes.teaches: The Scheveningen is a flexible setup for Black: develop pieces to natural squares and keep the center fluid, while White aims for a kingside pawn storm.
notes.plans: Black prepares ...Re8 and possibly ...d5 or ...e5 breaks; White will continue with Kh1, Qe1, and f4, looking for attacking chances on the kingside.

notes.explains: White's Kh1 is a prophylactic move to avoid pins along the a7-g1 diagonal, especially after ...e5 and potential ...Bc5 pins. If White plays Qe1 too early, Black can equalize with ...Bc5, pinning the bishop and neutralizing the attack.
notes.teaches: King safety and prophylaxis are crucial: moving the king to the corner before committing the queen can prevent tactical shots and preserve attacking chances.
notes.plans: White will continue with Qe1, Rg1, and f4, aiming for a kingside attack; Black will play ...Re8 and ...Bf8, preparing counterplay in the center.

notes.explains: The move order in the Scheveningen is flexible; Black can choose between ...Nc6 and ...Nd7, and White must decide whether to allow ...b5 or prevent it with a4.
notes.teaches: Understanding move-order nuances helps you steer the game into positions you know well and avoid your opponent's preparation.
notes.plans: Both sides will continue developing according to the chosen setup, with Black aiming for ...b5 or ...d5 breaks and White for f4 and kingside play.

notes.explains: In this line, the bishop on c5 pins the knight on f6, and the king on the long diagonal is vulnerable. The move e5 is no longer attacked, which helps Black secure equality.
notes.teaches: Pins can neutralize attacks on key pawns; understanding when a pawn is truly defended is crucial in the opening.
notes.plans: Black aims to complete development and challenge the center with moves like d5, while White seeks to maintain pressure and prevent Black's freeing moves.

notes.explains: White moves the king to h1 to step off the long diagonal, a prophylactic move that also prepares rare ideas like Bg1. The main point is to avoid future checks or pins along that diagonal.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic king moves can be essential in the opening to avoid tactical motifs and prepare for middlegame plans.
notes.plans: White continues to increase pressure with Bf3, eyeing the center and the long diagonal, while Black develops with Bd7.

notes.explains: Black's idea with Bd7 is to play Nxd4, then Bc6, completing development and pressuring the e4 pawn. The rook on d8 and the pawn break d5 are key plans to free Black's position.
notes.teaches: In the opening, completing development and creating pawn breaks in the center are primary goals; every move should serve those aims.
notes.plans: Black hopes to achieve d5, but White prevents it with Nb3, avoiding exchanges and making the bishop on d7 look misplaced.

notes.explains: White plays Nb3 to avoid exchanges and make Black's bishop on d7 awkward. White also threatens a5, which would bind Black's queenside. Black responds with Na5 to stop a5 and eye c4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a slight loss of tempo is worth it to maintain a favorable piece configuration and prevent the opponent's freeing moves.
notes.plans: White trades off the knight with Qxa5 and then plays Qd3, connecting rooks and adding pressure against d5. Black plays Rd8, preparing central action.

notes.explains: White plays Rd1, an idea attributed to John van der Wiel, to further restrain the d5 break. With e5 and f5, White restricts Black's central pawns.
notes.teaches: Rooks on open or semi-open files can be used to restrain pawn breaks; prophylactic moves that limit the opponent's plans are often strong.
notes.plans: White continues to restrict Black's d5 advance, while Black seeks counterplay on the queenside and in the center.

notes.explains: The rook on d1 supports a later b4 push, which gains tempo on the queen and restricts Black's pawn on e5. The idea is to create pressure rather than launch a direct attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a rook move to d1 is not about the d-file but about supporting a pawn break like b4. Pressure and restriction can be more valuable than immediate attacking chances.
notes.plans: After b4, the bishop on c6 will be attacked, forcing it to move with tempo, and White can continue to build pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: White avoids an automatic capture on b5 because it would open the a4 square for the knight. Instead, White plays a move that keeps the pawn on b5, allowing the knight to go to a4 and then b6, creating strong pressure.
notes.teaches: Before capturing, consider whether the capture helps your opponent. Sometimes keeping the tension and using a piece to improve its position is stronger.
notes.plans: The knight will go to a4, eyeing b6, which is a very unpleasant square for Black to allow.

notes.explains: White has a threat of Ba6 and then Bb6, skewering the queen and rook. Black must address this, and White's pieces are coordinating well on the queenside.
