notes.explains: Black faces a critical decision: whether to play c5-c4. If black leaves the pawn on c5, it's unclear how to get active play; white will eventually play e4 and open the position. Playing c4 allows black to start queenside counterplay with a5 and b4, using the open a-file. However, c4 gives up pressure on d4, conceding e4 to white.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, black's c5-c4 is a double-edged move: it creates queenside counterplay but releases pressure on the center, allowing white to advance e4. The player must weigh the urgency of flank play against central control.
notes.plans: If black plays c4, white should focus on the center with e4, as central breaks are typically more powerful than flank attacks.

notes.explains: If black avoids c4 and plays a move like Rc8, white can often play e4 directly if no pawn is hanging. In the line after e4, black captures twice, and white has a tactic with Nd5 exploiting the pin on the bishop. After Qe2 and Nxc4, white is significantly better, with central control and a plus-one advantage.
notes.teaches: When you can play a central break like e4 without losing material, it's usually good. Preparing it further with moves like Rae1 is often unnecessary if the break is already safe.
notes.plans: White should continue with central expansion, e.g., e5, f4, and take over the center.

notes.explains: If black tries Na5 to prevent e4, white can still play e4 because the knight on a5 no longer pressures d4. After Nc4, white can retreat the bishop to c1, and black cannot win the d4 pawn. White then pushes e5 and f4, achieving a nearly winning position.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, black's attempts to restrain e4 often fail because white can recapture or reposition pieces. Central breaks are powerful and should be played when safe.
notes.plans: White continues with e5, f4, and central domination.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian line, Black's c5 is often criticized, but here it is a viable try because White already defends d4 adequately and can play e4 without hanging a pawn. The pressure on d4 is meaningless if White can just advance e4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a move that looks suspect is actually the best practical chance when it creates active counterplay, even if it doesn't directly attack the center.
notes.plans: Black should aim for queenside counterplay with moves like b5 or a5, while White will focus on central expansion with e4 and f4.

notes.explains: After White plays Qe2, Black's h5 is a useful idea. The threat of h4 harasses the knight on f3, which has few good squares; g3 is its best square, and h4 would force it to move again.
notes.teaches: When an enemy piece has limited squares, a pawn advance can be a strong way to gain time and disrupt the opponent's setup.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with h4 to drive the knight away, while White should consider repositioning the queen to f2 to support the center and avoid pins.

notes.explains: Black's h4 is an attempt to delay White's e4 push, but White is fully prepared. White's central play with e4, f4, and f5 is more powerful than Black's queenside counterplay, often leading to a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed or fluid, a strong central pawn roller can overwhelm the opponent's flank play if they are too slow.
notes.plans: White should continue with e4, f4, and f5, using the f-pawn to open lines against the black king. Black must find active counterplay quickly or risk being overrun.

notes.explains: White's idea of Qf2 and Nf5 directly attacks the h4 pawn, which is hard to defend. Alternatively, if White had played Qd2, a knight maneuver Nh1-f2 could be used to defend the kingside.
notes.teaches: When an enemy pawn becomes weak, use pieces to target it from multiple angles, and be flexible in rerouting pieces to improve their defensive and offensive roles.
notes.plans: White will continue to pressure the h4 pawn and then switch to a central break with e4, while Black must decide whether to hold the pawn or seek counterplay.

notes.explains: In this f3 Nimzo-Indian line, white's central break with e4 is the key thematic move, often arriving with authority and giving white a lasting advantage even if black has handled the opening well.
notes.teaches: The e4 break is a central idea in the f3 Nimzo; it should be played decisively when available, as it opens lines and creates attacking chances.
notes.plans: After e4, white typically maintains pressure on the kingside, using the queen and bishop to target the black king.

notes.explains: When black plays on the queenside with ideas like ...Qa5 or ...Na5, white's rook to b1 is a useful prophylactic move, preventing tactics like ...Nb3 and adding pressure on the b7 pawn.
notes.teaches: Rook to b1 is a standard resource against early queenside piece play, as it both defends against tactical tricks and prepares to pressure the b-file.
notes.plans: White can follow up with central play (e4) or reroute the rook to e2 if black is slow.

notes.explains: Black has an alternative plan involving ...Bd7 and ...Na5-c4, aiming to gain tempo on the queenside instead of trading off the light-squared bishop. This can be a try for counterplay, though it is not fully trusted.
notes.teaches: When the light-squared bishop is passive, moving it to d7 to allow ...Na5-c4 can be a way to generate queenside pressure, but it often leaves black vulnerable to white's central break.
notes.plans: Black should be ready to meet e4 with accurate defense, while white should focus on the center.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian position, black is playing actively on the queenside with moves like ...Na5, while white's central break e4 is the key. The rook on b1 is useful to counter black's queenside play, whereas a2-e2 would be too slow if black is not passive.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is active on one side, your pieces should be placed to counter that activity, not to prepare slow central ideas. The rook to b1 is a flexible move that supports the b-pawn and can later join the center if needed.
notes.plans: White should aim to play e4 as soon as possible, opening the center and shifting the focus to the kingside. If black delays, the rook can come to e2 to reinforce e4.

notes.explains: After white plays e4 and black captures, white has tactical resources like Rxb4 or Qg5 that create multiple threats. The position shows that white's central play can lead to a decisive attack, while black's queenside efforts are too slow.
notes.teaches: When you open the center, the opponent's queenside play often becomes irrelevant because the game is decided by the attack on the king. Look for moves that create multiple threats, such as queen checks or rook captures that also attack.
notes.plans: White should continue to press the attack, using tactics to win material or force checkmate. Black's best defense is to find counterplay, but the position is already very good for white.

notes.explains: In the variation with ...c5 early, black aims to prevent white's bishop from developing to the b1-h7 diagonal, making e4 easier to achieve. This is a distinct idea that white must be prepared for, as it differs from the main lines where black plays ...b6.
notes.teaches: Early pawn moves like ...c4 can have a specific prophylactic purpose, even if they seem to allow central breaks. Recognize when a move is designed to restrict a piece's development rather than just to gain space.
notes.plans: White should find a way to handle the early ...c4, possibly by developing the bishop differently or by playing e4 anyway. The game between Vidit and Kramnik shows a handling that diverges from the world championship game.

notes.explains: Black's early c4 closes the center, preventing White from developing the bishop to the b1-h7 diagonal. This move is a deliberate strategy to limit White's piece activity and prepare queenside expansion.
notes.teaches: When the opponent closes the center early, White can consider aggressive kingside pawn moves because Black's counterplay is limited to the queenside.
notes.plans: White should aim to develop the bishop to g2 and prepare e4 to challenge the center, while being mindful of Black's queenside pawn pushes.

notes.explains: White's g4 is a strong response to c4 because Black has closed the center, so White's king is relatively safe on the kingside even after advancing pawns. The bishop can go to g2, and White gains space.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, pawn advances on the side where you have space can be made without immediate fear, as the opponent's counterplay is restricted.
notes.plans: White should continue with Bg2, Nb3, and prepare e4, while using the g-pawn to gain space and potentially open lines.

notes.explains: Black's Na5 targets the b3 square, aiming to control it and prepare queenside expansion with a5, b5, and b4. White's rook on b1 is better than on a2 because it controls b5 and b4, slowing Black's counterplay.
notes.teaches: Rook placement should be chosen based on the opponent's most likely plan. Here, preventing queenside pawn advances is more important than having the rook on the second rank for central support.
notes.plans: White should play Rb1 to restrain Black's queenside, then continue with e4 to challenge the center.

notes.explains: After Black plays b5, White must act urgently. The move e4 is critical to challenge the center immediately, as slower moves like Ng3 allow Black to gain queenside counterplay.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is generating counterplay on one side, you must often strike in the center to maintain the initiative and not fall behind in activity.
notes.plans: White should play e4, opening the center and creating chances against Black's king, while Black's queenside play is still developing.

notes.explains: After White has played g4, Bg2, and possibly Rb1, the move e4 is the key central break. The g4 pawn is intentionally sacrificed to gain a powerful central pawn duo on d4 and e4. Black must take on c1 with the knight to prevent the bishop from living, and then White's g4 pawn is hanging, but the central control is worth more than the pawn.
notes.teaches: In this variation, White should not hesitate to play e4, sacrificing the g4 pawn. The central pawn duo and the resulting space advantage are worth more than the pawn. The rook on b1 is well placed to support the b-pawn and put pressure on the b-file, which becomes important if Black tries to defend the b-pawn.
notes.plans: After e4, White will continue to develop and activate pieces, aiming to push d5 and e5 to cramp Black's position. The central pawns will be used to take away squares from Black's pieces and create a kingside attack or a direct central breakthrough.

notes.explains: In the game, White played Nf4 (instead of Ng3) because e4 is already played, so the knight no longer needs to support it. Black played Rb8, losing a tempo, and White forced the bishop back with h3, then played e5, trapping the knight on e8. White's central pawns dominate the board, and Black's pieces are uncoordinated.
notes.teaches: When you have a central pawn duo, you should push them forward to restrict the opponent's pieces. The knight on f4 is well placed to support the e5 push and later jump to d5. The rook on b1 is useful to pressure the b-file, and Black's rook on b8 is a sign of passivity.
notes.plans: White will continue to activate pieces, perhaps with Qa3, and then push d5 to further cramp Black. The central pawns will be used to create a winning attack, either on the kingside or by simply rolling forward and taking away all of Black's squares.

notes.explains: White's winning plan here is different from typical kingside attacks: White simply rolls forward with the central pawns, using them to take away every square in Black's camp. Black's natural move Nc7 is actually the losing move, as White responds with d6, then Ne6, Nxd5 hitting the rook, and Rf5 preparing to double on the f-file. The attack is overwhelming, and Black's queenside counterplay is irrelevant.
notes.teaches: A central pawn majority can be used as a battering ram to crush the opponent's position. Even if the opponent grabs a pawn on the queenside, if your attack is fast enough, it doesn't matter. The key is to keep pushing the central pawns and activate your pieces to support them.
notes.plans: White will continue to push the central pawns and bring the heavy pieces to the f-file. The threat of Nf6+ or Rf8 mate is decisive. Black's attempt to activate the knight is too slow, and the attack crashes through.

notes.explains: The general idea for White in this variation is to play g4, Bg2, and if the rook is attacked, Rb1; if not, castle. Then, against any move, White should play e4, sacrificing the g4 pawn. This is the standard plan, and it is not necessary to memorize all the direct theory.
notes.teaches: The g4 pawn is meaningless; the central break with e4 is the key. After e4, White should activate pieces and roll forward in the center. This plan is effective against any Black setup in this variation.
notes.plans: White will play e4, then continue with Nf4, h3, e5, and so on, aiming to dominate the center and launch a decisive attack. The rook on b1 is useful to support the b-pawn and put pressure on the b-file.

notes.explains: After the moves d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 O-O, White's setup is to develop the bishop to g2, the knight to e2, and castle. Then, against any black move, White should immediately play e4, sacrificing the g-pawn if necessary.
notes.teaches: The central break e4 is the key idea for White; the g-pawn is not important. Do not waste time on side moves like g5; roll forward in the center and activate pieces.
notes.plans: Play e4, and if black takes on g4, continue with development and central pressure.

notes.explains: If black plays Bxg4, White is not checkmated. White can respond with Bg2 or Ng3, and having an extra piece is decisive.
notes.teaches: A piece is a piece; don't fear tactics when you are up material. Solid development and material advantage lead to a win.
notes.plans: After Bxg4, simply develop and consolidate the extra piece.

notes.explains: In a final position, the queen is placed on f4 specifically to defend the e5 pawn. If the queen were on f2 or f3, Qxe5 would come with check.
notes.teaches: When placing pieces, consider tactical details like defending key pawns and avoiding checks. The best square is often the one that prevents opponent's resources.
notes.plans: Keep the queen on f4 to maintain the pawn structure and avoid tactical tricks.

notes.explains: Black's move Nc1 (likely a typo for Nc6? but as given) is important to trade off White's dark-squared bishop. If White keeps the bishop, it becomes a monster on an open board, especially because Black's play with b4 weakens the dark squares.
notes.teaches: The dark-squared bishop is crucial for White; Black should trade it off to reduce White's attacking potential and cover the weakened dark squares.
notes.plans: White should preserve the bishop, while Black should aim to exchange it.

notes.explains: The move Qc7 is a tricky and counterintuitive idea for Black in this opening. It is rare but can be dangerous if White is unprepared.
notes.teaches: Be aware of uncommon but tricky moves in the opening; they can pose practical problems. Understanding the ideas behind them is important.
notes.plans: Study the Qc7 lines to find the best response for White.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 O-O, Black's most interesting idea is …Qc7, a rare but tricky move. It prevents White's natural setup with Bd3, because if White plays Bd3, Black can play cxd4, cxd4, and Qc3+ forking the bishop on d2 and the rook on a1.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet-looking queen move can be a powerful prophylactic idea, preventing the opponent's most natural development while keeping central tension.
notes.plans: Black keeps the option to open the center later, unlike the ...c4 line which closes it. White should consider g4 to develop the bishop to g2 and avoid the tactics.

notes.explains: In the ...Qc7 line, if Black castles and White plays g4, Black can play ...Re8, putting pressure on the e-file. White's best response is Kf2, a shocking but safe move that steps off the e-file and avoids the Qc3 tactic, allowing the bishop to later go to d3.
notes.teaches: Sometimes moving the king in the opening can be the most accurate way to avoid tactics and prepare a better piece placement, even if it looks unnatural.
notes.plans: After Kf2, if Black plays ...Nc6, White can play Nf4, and then the bishop will develop to d3, its best square.

notes.explains: After Kf2 and ...Nc6, White plays Nf4, making a strong threat. Black's best response is ...Ne7, because ...Na5 would allow Ng5, winning the d5 pawn. Then White can start a kingside attack with h4.
notes.teaches: When a knight jumps to a powerful outpost, the opponent must often respond precisely to avoid material loss, and the attacker can then use the initiative to start a pawn storm.
notes.plans: White continues with h4, launching a kingside attack, while Black must defend carefully.

notes.explains: Black's best response to Nf4 is ...Ng6, challenging the knight, because otherwise White will develop naturally with Bd3 and continue pushing on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's piece is too powerful, it's often worth spending time to trade it off, even at the cost of some development.
notes.plans: After ...Ng6, the position remains complex, with White having a slight edge due to the better bishop placement.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 O-O, if White plays Bd3, Black's ...d5 is a key central pawn break, and if White captures on d5, Black's knight on f6 is attacked, forcing ...Ne7 to defend. This allows White to start a kingside attack with h4.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, Black's ...d5 break is often critical to challenge White's center, but it can expose the f6-knight to tactics. White should be alert to such central captures that create attacking chances.
notes.plans: White aims to develop naturally with Bd3 and push h4-h5 to attack Black's kingside, while Black should consider ...Ng6 to challenge the f4-square.

notes.explains: In the line after ...d5 exd5, Black's best is ...Ne7, and White can play h4. Black's ...Ng6 is necessary to prevent White's knight from landing on f4, which would be very strong. White can then play h5 and recapture with the e-pawn, creating a structure where Black's queen on a5 puts pressure.
notes.teaches: When a knight can occupy a strong outpost like f4, the opponent must often spend a tempo to challenge it. Creating pawn tension on the kingside can lead to favorable structures for the attacker.
notes.plans: White continues with h5 and exd5, aiming for a kingside initiative, while Black's queen on a5 pressures the queenside.

notes.explains: In a critical position, White's best move is the surprising a4!? (or similar), which prepares Rook a3 to defend laterally along the third rank. This is a refined version of the Rook a2 idea, and it proves vital if Black captures on c3. If Black goes pawn hunting, White's two bishops dominate the open position.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best moves are non-obvious prophylactic or preparatory moves that activate pieces in unusual ways. A rook on the third rank can defend key pawns and support an attack.
notes.plans: White aims to maintain the bishop pair and use the rook on a3 to defend the c3-pawn, while preparing to exploit Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: The f3 Nimzo-Indian is a practical opening choice because it leads to positions where the ideas are clear and the play is forcing, reducing the need for deep calculation.
notes.teaches: Choose openings that suit your style and give you comfortable, familiar positions where you can play confidently.

notes.explains: The f3 Nimzo-Indian often results in positions where the opponent's play is restricted and you can develop a lasting initiative with natural moves.
notes.teaches: Look for openings that create long-term pressure and give you winning chances without requiring excessive memorization.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian position, the light-squared bishop is a valuable piece for Black. Giving it up early is not advisable unless there is a concrete benefit, as it controls important light squares and can be used to pressure White's center.
notes.teaches: Do not part with a bishop without a clear reason; consider the long-term value of each piece, especially in closed or semi-open positions.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to d7 and aim to place it on c5, where it pressures White's queenside. Keep the light-squared bishop flexible, possibly fianchettoing or playing it to f5 later.

notes.explains: White's h3 is not a pressing move because the pin on the knight is not a real threat; Black can simply avoid trading the light-squared bishop. White's space advantage and two bishops are the main trumps, but Black's position is solid.
notes.teaches: Do not overreact to potential pins; evaluate whether the pin actually causes problems before spending a tempo to prevent it.
notes.plans: Black can continue development, perhaps with b6 and Bb7, or prepare to trade light-squared bishops if desired. White will look to exploit the bishop pair and space.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on c8 is not yet committed; it may go to f5 or b7. Since the knight's destination is clear (c5), it makes sense to develop that piece first, keeping the bishop flexible.
notes.teaches: When a piece has a clear ideal square, develop it first; keep other pieces flexible until their best squares become apparent.
notes.plans: Play Nbd7, then Nc5, and decide on the bishop's placement later, possibly trading it to open lines or to weaken White's light squares.

notes.explains: Black's plan with a6 and b5 is a typical queenside expansion in the Nimzo-Indian, undermining White's pawn structure. This can be played immediately or after preparation; it creates pressure and potential open files.
notes.teaches: In many black openings, especially the Nimzo-Indian, undermining the opponent's queenside with b5 is a standard idea. It can be a surprise weapon even early in the game.
notes.plans: Play b5, and if White captures, recapture and use the open a-file to target White's queenside weaknesses. If White doesn't capture, the pawn advances to gain space and further pressure.

notes.explains: White's bishop on d3 is well placed, but Black's plan of trading light-squared bishops can leave White with weaknesses on those squares. Black's knights are annoying and well-placed, giving good counterplay.
notes.teaches: Trading a bishop to exploit weak color complexes can be a strategic goal; also, active knights can compensate for a space disadvantage.
notes.plans: Black continues with moves like Re8, preparing to challenge the center, and looks to trade bishops to highlight White's light-square weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian setup, Black has played Bb4 and castled. White has not played e4, so the bishop on b4 is well placed on the long diagonal, pressuring e4 and the center.
notes.teaches: If White avoids e4, the bishop on b4 is a key piece on the a5-e1 diagonal, controlling central squares and pinning the knight.
notes.plans: Black can aim to play a6 and b5 to gain space on the queenside and open the a-file for the rook.

notes.explains: Black has a strong knight on f6, which is well placed to block the bishop's diagonal. White's queen on d4 is awkward, possibly aiming for e4, but it can be challenged.
notes.teaches: A knight on f6 can be a solid defensive piece when the opponent has a bishop on the long diagonal, as it blocks the diagonal and controls key squares.
notes.plans: Black can consider moves like Re8 to prepare against e4, or look to exploit the queen's placement by attacking it.

notes.explains: Black is up a pawn and has a strong bishop. White is trying to create complications to muddy the waters, as otherwise Black's extra pawn and control over e4 will be decisive.
notes.teaches: When behind in material, the defender should seek to complicate the position and create weaknesses for the opponent, rather than allowing a quiet game.
notes.plans: White might consider taking the knight to create isolated pawns for Black, giving White targets to play against.

notes.explains: Black has a choice of which knight to use to recapture on e4. Taking with the knight from c5 (if applicable) might be better because it keeps the f6 knight to block the bishop's diagonal and also allows a rook to come to the open file to pressure White's pieces.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece to use based on future plans: keeping a knight on f6 can be valuable for defense, and using the other knight can allow for tactical ideas like trapping pieces.
notes.plans: Black can aim to play a rook to the open file and use the knight on f6 to support tactics, possibly winning a piece.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian structure, Black's knight on f6 is a key defender. If White can provoke or force it away, Black's kingside becomes vulnerable and the bishop on b4 may lack good squares.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece is well placed, consider moves that challenge it or force it to move, even if it costs a tempo. A knight on f6 often protects the king and controls key central squares.
notes.plans: Black should consider exchanging knights or repositioning to avoid being kicked, while White should look to exploit the absence of the knight by targeting weak squares.

notes.explains: After the bishop on b4 is left stranded, Black's bishop has limited squares. White can potentially keep it 'marooned' and later attack it, while also pressuring Black's weak pawns.
notes.teaches: A bishop that is out of play can be a long-term liability. If you can restrict your opponent's piece to a bad square, you can often win material or gain time to improve your own position.
notes.plans: White should aim to keep the bishop passive and target the weak pawns, especially in potential rook endgames. Black should try to activate the bishop or trade it off.

notes.explains: In rook endgames, identifying weaknesses is crucial. Here, White can attack Black's weak pawns, while Black should counterattack White's. The side that attacks the opponent's weakness first often gains an advantage.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, look for the weakest pawns and attack them with your rooks. Also, use your king and pawns to support your own weaknesses and create counterplay.
notes.plans: White should focus on the weak pawns, possibly doubling rooks. Black should try to create counterplay by attacking White's weaknesses or pushing his own passed pawns.

notes.explains: A knight can become trapped if it ventures too far into enemy territory without support. Here, the knight on c3 is attacked and has few escape squares, so White must be careful not to lose it.
notes.teaches: Before moving a knight deep into enemy territory, ensure it has a retreat or can be defended. A trapped knight can cost the game, so always check for tactical refutations.
notes.plans: White should either find a way to rescue the knight or use it to create threats that distract the opponent. Black should try to maintain the trap and win the knight.

notes.explains: With a passed pawn, pushing it is often correct, but you must ensure it has enough support. Here, Black's passed pawn could be pushed, but timing is critical—pushing too early can allow the opponent to blockade or counterattack.
notes.teaches: Passed pawns must be pushed with support. Before advancing, make sure your pieces can defend the pawn and that the opponent cannot easily stop it. Sometimes it's better to improve your pieces first.
notes.plans: Black should consider pushing the passed pawn with the support of the king and rooks, while White should try to blockade it and attack Black's other weaknesses.

notes.explains: In this position, the knight on the edge is not immediately trapped because capturing it would allow a queen check. The immediate push of the pawn is a useful way to give the knight an escape square and create luft, avoiding back-rank issues.
notes.teaches: When a piece seems stranded, look for a pawn move that both gives it an escape route and addresses potential back-rank mates. Prophylactic pawn moves can be more valuable than they first appear.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to give the knight an escape, then bring the rook into play to support the knight's repositioning.

notes.explains: After the bishop retreats to f2, black gains control over d4 and places a rook on d8, preventing the knight from being trapped. The rook on d3 then becomes active, and the bishop retreats to c1, setting up a mating net.
notes.teaches: Rooks belong on open or semi-open files, and a rook can be used aggressively to restrict the opponent's pieces. Coordination between rook and bishop can create hidden mating threats.
notes.plans: Black continues to build pressure on the d-file and prepares a decisive checkmating combination involving the knight.

notes.explains: The move that leads to checkmate is a knight check on g3, which is a tricky move to find because it involves a sacrifice and a forced sequence. The opponent's mistake was blocking a check with a piece, allowing the knight to jump in with check.
notes.teaches: When defending against checks, consider all legal responses, including moving the king, and be wary of knight forks and checks that can lead to mate. A knight check on a square like g3 can be devastating if the king has limited escape squares.
notes.plans: Black executes the mating sequence starting with the knight check on g3, forcing the king to move and then capturing the rook, leading to checkmate.

notes.explains: In the opening, both players made strategically questionable moves, but black showed a good understanding by playing a6 and b5 to break down the queenside, eventually winning a pawn. This demonstrates the importance of pawn breaks to create weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Pawn breaks like b5 are essential in the middlegame to challenge the opponent's structure and create weaknesses. A well-timed pawn storm can lead to a material advantage.
notes.plans: Black continues to exploit the queenside weaknesses and convert the extra pawn into a win.

notes.explains: The player with white chose to play d4 in this game, showing a willingness to branch out from e4. This is a positive sign because playing a variety of openings improves overall chess understanding.
notes.teaches: To improve at chess, it's important to play a wide range of openings, even if you are less familiar with them. You can borrow ideas from other openings to handle unfamiliar positions.
notes.plans: White continues with the fianchetto setup, while black considers a kingside fianchetto or a Grünfeld-style setup.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian structure, White has avoided early exchanges on d5, so Black can support the center with a pawn rather than allowing a Grunfeld-style setup. White's position is solid, and the immediate central push e4 looks strong, preparing e5 to gain space and cramp Black.
notes.teaches: When your opponent avoids early central exchanges, you should often strike in the center yourself with a pawn push like e4, challenging their setup before they can consolidate.
notes.plans: White should play e4, then develop the knight and castle, aiming for a central pawn majority and a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Black's early queenside expansion with b5 is premature and gives White a target. White's a3 was unnecessary because if Black's knight goes to b4, White can simply kick it back with a3 later. White should focus on the center rather than reacting to minor threats.
notes.teaches: Don't waste tempi preventing moves that aren't real threats. If a piece can be kicked back later, it's often better to spend your move on more important central or developmental ideas.
notes.plans: White should continue with central development and prepare to exploit Black's overextended queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black's knight maneuver to e6 and then g5 is unorthodox and not a typical textbook route. White should not trade knights with such a misplaced piece, because Black doesn't know how to use it effectively. Trading would solve Black's problems and give him a better position.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a poorly placed piece, avoid trading it off. Keep the pressure and force them to waste more time trying to improve it.
notes.plans: White can consider moves like h4 to kick the knight away, or simply continue developing and preparing a central break, refusing to allow the trade.

notes.explains: Black's h6 attacks the knight on g5. White has the option to take on h6, opening the h-file for an attack, but this weakens White's own pawn structure. The position is not as one-sided as it could be, so White must weigh the attacking chances against the structural damage.
notes.teaches: When considering a pawn sacrifice to open a file, evaluate whether the resulting attack is worth the permanent pawn weaknesses. Sometimes it's better to maintain a solid structure and keep the pressure.
notes.plans: White could take on h6 to open the h-file, but must be ready for Black's counterplay. Alternatively, White can retreat the knight and maintain a healthy pawn structure.

notes.explains: After Black plays h6 to kick the knight, White has the option to capture the knight on g5, opening the h-file for Black but winning a pawn. The position is not one-sided, but White can also decline the trade and continue developing.
notes.teaches: When your knight is attacked by a pawn, you must weigh the benefit of capturing versus retreating; opening a file for the opponent can be a real concession.
notes.plans: If White captures on g5, Black gets the h-file but White has an extra pawn. If White declines, the knight can retreat and play h4 to kick the black bishop.

notes.explains: White plays f4, and Black responds with e6, a surprising move. White's next move is strong, placing a piece on e4 instead of a pawn, which is common in d4 openings where the e4 square is often used by pieces.
notes.teaches: In d4 openings, the e4 square is often a great outpost for a piece, not just a pawn. Use your pieces to occupy central squares when pawns are not available.
notes.plans: White's piece on e4 creates two threats: a check and capturing a pawn. Black must respond to both.

notes.explains: Black chooses d5 to counter the threats, and White captures the pawn. Black's position is difficult, and a move like f6 is not acceptable in this class because it weakens the position.
notes.teaches: When facing two threats, you must find a move that addresses both or creates a counter-threat. Avoid weakening pawn moves like f6 unless they are part of a concrete plan.
notes.plans: White has won a pawn and has a strong initiative. Black must try to develop and find counterplay, but the position is tough.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices a piece on d5, and White considers capturing it. The sacrifice aims to open lines and create attacking chances, but White can also decline and maintain the extra material.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be dangerous, but you must calculate whether the compensation is real. Sometimes the best response is to accept the material and defend accurately.
notes.plans: White can take the bishop and then try to consolidate, or decline and keep the extra pawn. The computer suggests a queen move, indicating that accepting the sacrifice may not be best.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian structure, White has sacrificed a piece for two pawns and is opening the position. Black's pieces are cramped and undeveloped, so White's active pieces and open lines give strong compensation.
notes.teaches: When you have material compensation, prioritize piece activity and opening lines over regaining material. Active pieces can be worth more than a pawn or two.
notes.plans: White should continue to develop and create threats, targeting Black's weak pawns and keeping the initiative.

notes.explains: Black voluntarily opens the position, which is suspicious because White's pieces are better placed for open lines. Trading rooks on the f-file is fine for White, but if White initiates the trade, the queen can come out with threats.
notes.teaches: Don't open the position when your opponent's pieces are more active. Let the opponent make the opening moves that favor them.
notes.plans: White should aim to keep pieces on the board and exploit Black's development lag.

notes.explains: White chooses D3 over C2 for the queen. On C2, the queen would be pinned after ...Bf5, and also White wants to prevent Black from playing ...Bf5. D3 is a good square, supporting the attack.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a piece, consider potential pins and whether the piece can be harassed. Also, prevent your opponent's freeing moves.
notes.plans: White continues to target the g6 pawn and maintain pressure.

notes.explains: White has identified a weakness (the g6 pawn) and repeatedly attacks it. Black is forced to defend, and White's pieces become more active. The attack is sound, and White has strong threats.
notes.teaches: Identify a weakness in the opponent's camp and target it with multiple pieces. This creates pressure and can lead to a winning attack.
notes.plans: White should continue to increase pressure, possibly with moves like Qc2 to enable Bxc6, and look for tactical blows.

notes.explains: In the game, White liquidated many pieces and ended up with two rooks vs a queen, but lost the attacking pressure. The preferred continuation keeps more pieces on the board, maintaining the initiative and pressure on Black.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attack, avoid unnecessary trades that reduce your attacking potential. Keeping active pieces is often more important than winning a little material.
notes.plans: White should seek to keep pieces and continue the attack, rather than simplifying to a material advantage.

notes.explains: In this Nimzo-Indian position, Black has developed the bishop to b4 pinning the knight on c3, and has castled. White's setup with e3 is solid, preparing to develop the bishop and challenge the center.
notes.teaches: The Nimzo-Indian is a hypermodern opening where Black lets White occupy the center with pawns, then attacks it with pieces, especially the bishop on b4 pinning the knight.
notes.plans: White should aim to complete development, possibly with Bd3, Nf3, and O-O, and then decide on a central break with e4 or d5. Black will try to maintain the pin and create pressure on the c-file or the center.

notes.explains: The queen on c5 is a good square, pressuring c3 and eyeing the kingside. The bishop on b4 remains well placed, pinning the knight and causing problems for White. Black's king is safe, but making inroads to attack White's king is difficult because White's position is solid.
notes.teaches: In such positions, the side with the bishop pair or better piece activity should seek to keep pieces on the board and avoid unnecessary trades, as trading pieces can reduce attacking chances.
notes.plans: Black might consider moves like Qa7 to keep pressure, or prepare to double rooks on the c-file. White should aim to neutralize the pin and possibly trade off the bishop to relieve pressure.

notes.explains: White played a sacrifice (likely a piece sacrifice) that is the move of the game, creating serious trouble for Black. Black responded with b5, but White continued well. The position became critical with threats of mate.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be powerful when they expose the enemy king and create mating threats. Recognizing when a sacrifice is sound is a key skill in attacking play.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, White should continue to bring pieces to the attack, while Black must find accurate defensive moves to avoid mate.

notes.explains: Black played Qb6, threatening mate, but White's opponent did not address it properly. A typical mating pattern emerged, and White had a forced mate, though there was also a perpetual check available.
notes.teaches: When you have a mating threat, you must either deliver mate or force a favorable outcome like perpetual check. Recognizing common mating patterns is crucial for converting an attack.
notes.plans: White should execute the mating pattern, for example with Bc6 or Ba6, leading to checkmate. If mate is not possible, a perpetual check can save the game.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black had a large advantage but made a mistake by trading off all the pieces, making the win tougher. Still, Black remained better and eventually won.
notes.teaches: In endgames, it's important to preserve winning chances by not trading pieces unnecessarily, especially if you have a material or positional advantage. Converting a big advantage requires technique and patience.
notes.plans: Black should use the extra material or better pawn structure to create passed pawns and win the endgame.

notes.explains: In this Rossolimo position, if White recaptures with the d-pawn after ...cxd4, they lose the chance to play d5 later, so simple development is better. Black is not actively contesting the center, so White can develop naturally.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is not fighting for the center, avoid pawn recaptures that compromise your central pawn structure; prefer simple development.
notes.plans: White can castle and follow with d3, c3, Be3, and Nd2, building a solid setup.

notes.explains: After ...bxa3, White can try the sideline b3, aiming to place the bishop on b2 and pressure the long diagonal. Black often responds with ...d6, but this traps the dark-squared bishop, so White can set a trap with e5.
notes.teaches: A bishop on b2 can exert long-range pressure, but be aware of potential traps when the opponent tries to open the center.
notes.plans: White plays e5, and if Black captures, White can recapture and then use tactics to exploit the exposed queen.

notes.explains: In the trap, after ...Qxb2, White plays Nc3, trapping the queen. The queen's only escape is a3, but then Qf3 threatens mate on f7 and also forks c6, winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing material, calculate forcing sequences; a trapped queen can be more valuable than a bishop.
notes.plans: White plays Qf3, threatening Qxf7 and Qxc6, gaining a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: The main line after ...bxa3 is for White to castle. Black typically plays ...d5, but White can defend the center. If Black captures, White recaptures and after queen trade White is fine with space and development.
notes.teaches: In the Rossolimo, castling is a solid main line, and central pawn tension can be resolved favorably for White.
notes.plans: White can meet ...d5 by defending the e4 pawn, and if Black takes, recapture and maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: In this Rossolimo setup, after White castles, Black can immediately play d5, challenging the center. If Black captures on e4, White recaptures and after queen trades, White has a comfortable position with space on the kingside and development.
notes.teaches: When facing a fianchetto setup, striking in the center with d5 is a standard way to fight for equality. Don't rush to capture if it leads to a favorable trade for the opponent.
notes.plans: Black should develop with Nf6, and if White plays e5, retreat the knight to d7, pressuring the pawn. White can overprotect, then Black develops and castles short.

notes.explains: Black's alternative plan is to play Ne7, aiming to control the center and support d5. However, this blocks the dark-squared bishop, delaying castling. Black will typically follow with Ng6, Be7, and castle short.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays e6, be alert to the possibility of Ne7, which reinforces the center but can hinder development. Consider the cost of blocking your bishop.
notes.plans: Black should avoid castling queenside due to the missing b-pawn creating a hole. White can play b3 to fianchetto the queenside bishop, putting pressure on the g7 pawn.

notes.explains: If Black tries to develop the bishop to e7 after White's bishop reaches b2, White can simply capture on g7, winning a pawn. Black should instead play d5 to fight for the center, even if it allows f6, which limits the bishop's scope but prepares to castle by hand.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's bishop is aimed at your king's fianchetto, be careful about developing the bishop prematurely. Sometimes playing f6 is acceptable to prevent a capture and enable castling, despite the general rule against early f-pawn moves.
notes.plans: After d5, White defends the e-pawn, Black plays f6, then Be7 and castles short. White may try e5 to break up the pawns, but Black can maintain a solid center.

notes.explains: If Black plays f6 immediately, White can respond with e5 to break up the pawns and give the bishop more scope. White gets simple development with Nd2, keeping the bishop on the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: An early f6 can be met by a central pawn advance to challenge the pawn chain and open lines for the bishops.
notes.plans: White develops naturally, Black plays Qc7, and the game continues with balanced chances.

notes.explains: In the main line where White castles, Black again plays Ne7 with the idea of d5. White can choose c3, leading to a structure reminiscent of the Ruy Lopez: after a6, Ba4, b5, Bc2, and Bb7.
notes.teaches: Recognize transpositions to familiar structures from other openings. The bishop retreat to c2 is a common maneuver to maintain pressure on the center.
notes.plans: Both sides continue developing, with Black aiming for d5 and White preparing to support the center.

notes.explains: Black's e6 is played with the specific idea of rerouting the knight to e7 and preparing d5, challenging White's center. White can respond with c3, a major setup that resembles the Ruy Lopez, where the bishop goes to a4 and retreats to c2 after b5.
notes.teaches: Recognize the opponent's plan behind a move like e6: it often prepares a knight maneuver and a central pawn break. When your bishop is attacked by a pawn, retreating it to a safe square while maintaining pressure is a common and sound idea.
notes.plans: White should aim to clamp down on the center with e5, activate the light-squared bishop on e4, and develop the queenside pieces later, similar to a Ruy Lopez or Gioco Piano structure.

notes.explains: In the c3 variation, after a6, Bg4, b5, Bc2, Bb7, White can try to expand with e5, while Black attempts to break through. The light-squared bishop becomes active on e4, and both sides develop with a purpose. The resulting endgame often features an isolated queen's pawn for Black, giving White a slight edge.
notes.teaches: In closed openings, piece activity and central control are paramount. Even if both sides have bishop pairs, a structural weakness like an isolated pawn can be a long-term target.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the central clamp and eventually target the isolated pawn, while Black must seek active piece play to compensate.

notes.explains: An alternative to c3 is Nc3, where the knight on e7 and bishop on b5 change the dynamics. After Nd4, Black can capture on d4 and then Ne2, pressuring the a6 pawn and gaining tempo. Black should avoid b5 and instead play Nc6, leaving the capture on d4 open, which can help Black bring a pawn to the center.
notes.teaches: When a knight is on e7, a central knight jump like Nd4 can be effective because the knight is not pinned. Tempo-gaining moves like Ne2 can disrupt the opponent's development. Sometimes leaving a capture available is better than taking immediately, as it can be used to improve your structure.
notes.plans: Black should aim to break in the center with d5, while White should try to maintain the bishop pair and develop harmoniously.

notes.explains: The main line is Re1, reinforcing the e4 pawn and preparing e5. If Black plays d5, White can capture with the knight, opening the file for the rook. Capturing with the pawn is problematic because it leaves the knight on c6 undefended and allows annoying pins, so the knight should take. Black should instead play a6, hitting the bishop, and if possible, White should retreat to f1 to preserve the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Reinforcing a central pawn is a common prophylactic idea. When capturing in the center, prefer the piece that maintains structure and avoids pins. Preserving the bishop pair is often worth a tempo, especially if you can retreat to a good square.
notes.plans: White should aim to play e5, expanding in the center, while Black should challenge the bishop and seek counterplay.

notes.explains: In this Rossolimo position, after Black plays a6 attacking the bishop on g2, White has the option to retreat the bishop to f1, preserving the bishop pair. This is generally preferable if available, as it avoids the trade on c6 that can help Black's central break d5.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is attacked by a flank pawn, consider retreating to keep the bishop pair if the retreat square is viable; otherwise, trading is acceptable in most lines.
notes.plans: White should play Bf1, maintaining the bishop, and then meet Black's d5 with central play, aiming to keep the bishop active on the long diagonal or reposition it later.

notes.explains: Here, taking on c6 is an exception: after bxc6, Black can play d5 immediately, and if White captures, the c-pawn recaptures, giving Black a strong center. This shows that the trade is not always harmless.
notes.teaches: Before trading a bishop for a knight on c6, check if it accelerates Black's central pawn break; sometimes preserving the bishop is necessary to prevent that.
notes.plans: White should avoid Bxc6 in this specific position and instead play Bf1, as the trade would help Black's central expansion.

notes.explains: After Bf1 and d5, Black breaks open the center, gaining space. White should capture on d5 to open the f-file for the rook, and then Black recaptures with the knight. Black then plays d4 to challenge the center, and White should not concede it too early.
notes.teaches: In the Rossolimo, when Black plays d5, White should capture to open lines, and Black should recapture with the knight to maintain central influence. Both sides should fight for central space.
notes.plans: White captures on d5, opens the f-file, and then prepares to meet Black's d4 with appropriate central play, possibly supporting the d4 pawn or challenging it.

notes.explains: Black's knight retreat to f6 keeps an eye on the center squares, especially in case White pushes a pawn. It also allows the bishop to develop to d6, putting pressure on the e4 pawn. White defends with Be3, and Black develops the bishop to e7.
notes.teaches: When retreating a knight, consider its role in controlling central squares and supporting future piece development. Developing the bishop to a diagonal that pressures the opponent's pawns is a common plan.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing, aiming to pressure White's center, while White defends and prepares to expand with c4.

notes.explains: In this Rossolimo setup, the light-squared bishop on f1 is not as active as in the Italian or Ruy Lopez. It currently guards the c4 pawn, which black may target after ...Bd7 and ...Rc8, and it also prevents ...b5 expansion. The bishop will not see much play soon, but later, after some minor pieces and rooks are traded, it can be developed to g2 to control the center.
notes.teaches: The light-squared bishop in the Rossolimo has a different role than in other open games; it is a defensive and prophylactic piece early on, but can become a powerful center-controlling piece later.
notes.plans: White should consider playing b3 to solidify the c4 pawn, but be aware of ...Bb4. Alternatively, Qb3 can target the queenside pawns. The bishop will later be developed to g2 after suitable trades.

notes.explains: Playing g3 immediately to develop the bishop to g2 can be premature because black can play ...Ng4, attacking the e3 pawn (or e4? unclear). This could create weaknesses on the kingside. It is better to delay this development until some minor pieces are traded.
notes.teaches: Rushing a fianchetto can allow tactical tricks; it is often better to wait until the position is simplified before committing to such a development.
notes.plans: Consider playing h3 to prevent ...Ng4, and later play g3 and Bg2 after trades.

notes.explains: In the e6 lines, black aims for ...d5 to fight for the center. White may want to trade off minor pieces, especially knights, to ease pressure and give the light-squared bishop more flexibility.
notes.teaches: Trading minor pieces can be a strategic way to improve the activity of a previously passive bishop.
notes.plans: Look for opportunities to trade knights and then develop the bishop to g2, where it will have a strong influence on the center.

notes.explains: When black plays ...e6, capturing on c6 with the bishop can be risky if it allows black to play ...bxc6 and then ...d5 quickly, challenging the center. In such lines, it is better to retreat the bishop to f1 instead of capturing.
notes.teaches: In the Rossolimo, the decision to take on c6 should be based on whether it gives black easy central play; sometimes preserving the bishop is more important.
notes.plans: If black plays ...e6 and later ...a6, consider Bf1 rather than Bxc6 to avoid giving black a quick ...d5.

notes.explains: In this Rossolimo setup, Black's early ...d5 is a central challenge. White prefers to develop the bishop to f1 (Bg2) before allowing ...dxc6, since after ...e6 Black can gain central space if White is careless.
notes.teaches: When facing a central pawn break, ensure your pieces are developed to support the center before allowing exchanges that open lines for the opponent.
notes.plans: Continue developing harmoniously, keeping the center stable, and avoid premature pawn advances that weaken your control.

notes.explains: The move f4 to attack the knight on e5 is too aggressive. Black can respond with ...Ng4, threatening to trade off White's dark-squared bishop, which is often the best minor piece in this structure. If White retreats the bishop, Black can expand with ...e5 or use tactics like ...Bc5 to pin the knight.
notes.teaches: Avoid overextending with pawn pushes that create weaknesses or allow the opponent to trade off your active pieces. Patience is often better than forcing the issue.
notes.plans: Instead of f4, play h3 to prevent ...Ng4 and keep the position solid, allowing the knight on e5 to remain harmless.

notes.explains: Black's queen moves like ...Qc7 or ...Qb6 can transpose to a Taimanov-style Sicilian, but Black spends extra tempi, giving White a development advantage.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes unnecessary queen moves in the opening, use the time to develop quickly and seize the initiative.
notes.plans: Continue developing naturally, aiming to exploit the lead in development with active play.

notes.explains: The Marshall Attack is a heavily analyzed opening that can be dangerous for unprepared opponents, but below master level, players often deviate from the main lines.
notes.teaches: To handle sharp openings, study not only the main lines but also the sidelines and the reasons they fail, so you can handle practical play.
notes.plans: Prepare the Marshall Attack thoroughly, covering both main lines and common deviations.

notes.explains: In this setup, White has played g3, Bg2, and d3, aiming for a flexible kingside fianchetto against the Sicilian. The position is heavily analyzed, with main lines often leading to near-draws at high levels.
notes.teaches: When studying an opening, it's important to understand not just the main line but also the sidelines and why they are inferior, because opponents below master level will often deviate.
notes.plans: White should be prepared for various Black setups, including the Marshall Attack, and understand the typical plans and pitfalls in each.

notes.explains: In this Anti-Marshall position, Black's queenside pieces are somewhat passive and blocked in. White's knight can maneuver to e2, then f4 or g3, supporting a kingside attack with queen to f3 or h5.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, piece activity on one side can be built by rerouting knights to squares that support pawn pushes and piece invasions.
notes.plans: White should aim to bring the knight to f4 or g3 and then the queen to f3 or h5, while Black can prepare counterplay with ...Rb6 and ...Qd7.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5, the position is roughly equal. White can try to organize a kingside attack, while Black's bishops and queen point toward White's king.
notes.teaches: In balanced middlegame positions, both sides should seek to improve piece coordination and create threats on the side where their pieces are aimed.
notes.plans: White can maneuver to attack on the kingside; Black can centralize the knight to e6 or possibly b5 to pressure d4.

notes.explains: In the h3 Anti-Marshall, if Black plays …Bb7, the bishop can become misplaced because White can play d3, and later Black may have to retreat it to c8 to trade it off for the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When your opponent develops a bishop to a square that can be blocked by pawns, consider whether it will become passive and need to lose time to reroute.
notes.plans: White can play d3 to restrict the bishop on b7, and later possibly play d6 to force the bishop back.

notes.explains: A common tactical question in the Marshall is whether Black can sacrifice with ...Bxh3 after White plays Nc3. In this Anti-Marshall, the knight on c3 supports the rook to e4, attacking the queen, so the sacrifice fails because Black's queen must leave the attack, and White can capture the bishop safely.
notes.teaches: Before accepting a sacrifice, check if your pieces can create counter-threats that force the opponent's queen to retreat, neutralizing the attack.
notes.plans: If Black tries ...Bxh3, White can play Re4, attacking the queen, and after the queen moves, capture the bishop on h3.

notes.explains: After c3, Black's most common reply is …d5, entering a sharp line. White must be wary of a trap: if White takes the d5 pawn, Black can play ...Nxe5, ...Rxe5, and ...Nf4, attacking g2 with decisive effect. Taking the pawn is losing.
notes.teaches: In the Marshall Attack, the d5 pawn is often poisoned; grabbing it can allow a devastating attack on the kingside. Recognize when a central pawn is a trap rather than a gift.
notes.plans: White should avoid taking on d5 and instead play d3, keeping the position solid and preparing to develop pieces harmoniously.

notes.explains: After c3 d5, if White plays d3, Black often responds with ...Qd7. White can then gain a tempo with Re5, and after ...Bf6, the rook returns to e1. White should not trade rooks on the e-file, as that would give Black the open file for free.
notes.teaches: In open positions, keeping rooks on the board can be important to control key files. Developing pieces with tempo (like Re5 hitting the queen) can be a useful resource.
notes.plans: White develops the knight to c3, maintaining pressure and keeping the rook on e1 to contest the e-file.

notes.explains: Black may sacrifice a knight with ...Nxc3, gaining three pawns for it. White should trade rooks to avoid Black's rook penetrating, and then play Bc2. Black's queen can become active with ...Qd5, generating counterplay.
notes.teaches: Material imbalances can be tricky; when the opponent sacrifices a piece for pawns, you must assess the activity and coordination of their pieces. Trading rooks can reduce their attacking potential.
notes.plans: White should aim to consolidate, using the extra piece to create threats while neutralizing Black's pawn mass.

notes.explains: The move c3 in this line is dubious; after Black plays ...h3, White's position is not great. The rook on e1 is not doing much, and the bishop on b3 may become passive. Most players prefer d3 instead.
notes.teaches: Not every natural-looking move is best; c3 can be a waste of time if it doesn't support a concrete plan. In the Ruy Lopez, d3 is often more flexible, especially when Black's bishop is on b7.
notes.plans: White should prefer d3, which prepares to develop the bishop and knight harmoniously, and avoids the weaknesses of c3.

notes.explains: In the line with d3, Black often plays ...d5 to open the position. After trades, Black may play ...Nxe5 or ...Nd4. If ...Nd4, White should not try to save the light-squared bishop at all costs; instead, continue development with Nc3, even if it means trading the bishop.
notes.teaches: In open positions, piece activity and development matter more than preserving a 'good' bishop. Sometimes you must trade a strong piece to keep up the initiative.
notes.plans: White should continue with natural development, aiming to castle and connect rooks, while being mindful of tactical threats like pins and mate patterns.

notes.explains: In this Marshall-style position, black's queen and bishop line up on the a8-h1 diagonal, creating a constant mating threat against g2. White's knight on f3 is essential because it both defends the knight and blocks that diagonal, addressing two threats at once.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a battery aimed at your king, a single defensive move that simultaneously protects a piece and blocks the line is often the most efficient resource.
notes.plans: Keep the knight on f3 to maintain the blockade, and avoid moving it unless you can replace the defense of the diagonal. If black pushes f5, reposition the knight to g3 to keep the diagonal closed.

notes.explains: Black's rook to e8 is a standard Marshall move, and white responds with Nd2 to prepare c3-c4, gaining space and potentially creating weaknesses on the queenside. Black's knight to e4 hits the queen, forcing it to move, and then black's queen and bishop coordinate on the same diagonal, again targeting g2.
notes.teaches: In open positions, piece coordination along key diagonals can create recurring tactical threats; the defender must remain alert to these patterns even after the immediate attack is parried.
notes.plans: White can consider the awkward-looking c4 push to encourage trades and create a weakness on a6, but must be wary of black's bishop to a4 skewer if the knight moves. Black should look to maintain pressure on the g2 square.

notes.explains: In the anti-Marshall main line, white's a4 is a key move. It challenges black's b5 pawn, and if black responds with b4, white can later play Ba2, giving the bishop a safe square and preparing to undermine the pawn chain. The move also has the potential to activate the rook if black allows axb5.
notes.teaches: A flank pawn move in the opening can serve multiple purposes: it can create weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure, provide a retreat square for a piece, and open files for rooks. Center control is not the only consideration; sometimes the edge of the board is where the action is.
notes.plans: After a4 b4, white can continue with Ba2, keeping the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal and preparing to break with c3 or d4. If black doesn't play b4, white may capture on b5 and use the a-file.

notes.explains: White's a4 in this Anti-Marshall position forces Black to commit: capture on a4, push b4, or develop the bishop to b7. Each option has a concrete consequence, so the move creates immediate tension rather than allowing Black to dictate the pace.
notes.teaches: A pawn thrust like a4 can be used to force the opponent to make a decision, even if the immediate threat (taking on b5) is not the main point. The value lies in restricting Black's options and creating potential weaknesses.
notes.plans: If Black plays b4, White can follow with a5, targeting the a6 pawn. If Black plays Bb7, White should avoid capturing on b5 and instead play d3 to slow the pace and block the bishop's influence.

notes.explains: The b4 pawn is not weak because it is protected by the knight on c6 and the bishop on e7. If White tries to attack it with d3, Black can respond with a5, and the pawn remains safe while Black gains space.
notes.teaches: Do not assume a pawn is weak just because it is advanced. Always check its defenders and the possibility of counterplay before targeting it.
notes.plans: If White plays d3, Black can play a5, and the b4 pawn is secure. White should instead focus on other plans like rerouting the bishop or preparing central breaks.

notes.explains: After Black plays Bb7, White should not capture on b5 because Black can recapture and White's e4 pawn becomes vulnerable. Instead, d3 is a good move, blocking the bishop's control of the center and preparing a slow buildup.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is better to avoid winning a pawn if it allows the opponent to activate their pieces or create counterplay. A solid developing move can be more valuable.
notes.plans: White plays d3, then develops the knight to d2, keeping the light-squared bishop flexible. Black may play d6 and later reroute the bishop to c8-e6 to challenge White's bishop.

notes.explains: After d6, White should not break the pawn tension by capturing on e5. Instead, developing the knight to d2 is flexible because the dark-squared bishop's best square is unclear (c1, e3, g5, or d2).
notes.teaches: When you are unsure where a piece belongs, delay its development and play a move that keeps multiple options open. Avoid committing to a plan until the position clarifies.
notes.plans: White continues with natural development, while Black may try d5, which White can capture. The game remains balanced with chances for both sides.

notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez, White's c1-bishop has several possible squares (c1, e3, g5, d2), and it's unclear which is best. Playing Nd2 keeps options open rather than committing the bishop prematurely.
notes.teaches: When a piece has multiple good squares, delay its placement and develop other pieces flexibly first.
notes.plans: White can follow up with Nf1-g3 or Nf1-e3, keeping the bishop's options open.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5, Black's d5 is playable but not stellar. White can capture on d5, and after Nxd5, White can take on b5. If White recaptures on a8 with the bishop, it loses some control of the a2-g8 diagonal compared to playing d5 earlier.
notes.teaches: In the Ruy Lopez, Black's early d5 can be met by capturing, but be aware of the diagonal control implications of recapture choices.
notes.plans: White can take on d5 and then on b5, accepting doubled pawns but maintaining piece activity.

notes.explains: In the Ruy Lopez and Italian, White often aims for c3 and d4 to build a pawn center. Nc3 is playable but allows Black to play Na5, hitting the bishop, and after Ba2, b4 kicks the knight to e2. The knight on e2 can only go to g3, whereas Nd2 allows Nf1-g3 or Nf1-e3, offering more flexibility.
notes.teaches: When choosing between knight moves, consider the future squares available to the knight and the opponent's potential to kick it.
notes.plans: White can play Nd2, then Nf1, and later Nf1-g3 or Nf1-e3, keeping the knight flexible.

notes.explains: After Black plays Na5 and Ba2, Black often plays c5 to gain queenside space, but this leaves d5 as a fantastic outpost for a white knight. White aims to occupy d5 with a knight via Nf1-e3-d5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent gains space on one side, look for outposts in the center or on the other side to plant a knight.
notes.plans: White plays Nf1, then Ne3, and if possible Nd5, establishing a strong knight.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, Black's bishops on e7 and c8 are poorly placed. The c8-bishop can go to d7 but not to f5 or g4 effectively. Black's pieces struggle to find good squares, and a trade of queens leads to a slightly better endgame for White due to better piece activity.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions, piece activity and coordination often decide the evaluation; look for opponent's poorly placed pieces.
notes.plans: White can aim to trade queens and exploit Black's passive bishops, while Black should seek to activate the c8-bishop via d7 or other squares.

notes.explains: In this position, black's knight on a5 is not ideally placed; it cannot go to f5 or g4 easily, and after a trade on c5, black may be left with isolated pawns. Black's challenge is to find good squares for the pieces and coordinate them.
notes.teaches: When a piece has no clear good square, consider whether it is worth moving at all; sometimes it is better to keep flexibility and improve other pieces first.
notes.plans: Black should look for ways to improve piece coordination, possibly by preparing ...b4 to cramp white and prevent Nc3, or by playing ...a5 to secure the b4 pawn.

notes.explains: After white plays a4, black can respond with ...b4, which cramps white's position and prevents the knight from developing to c3. This is a key idea in the Anti-Marshall, as it limits white's options and gives black a space advantage on the queenside.
notes.teaches: A pawn advance like ...b4 can be a powerful tool to restrict the opponent's piece development and create a spatial bind.
notes.plans: Black should aim to maintain the b4 pawn, possibly with ...a5 to support it, and then develop the bishop to b7, putting pressure on white's center.

notes.explains: White's attempt to strike in the center with d4 is met by ...d6, and after exd6, black can recapture with either piece, leaving a fine position. The tactical trick with ...Nxd4 is refuted by Bxf7+, Rxf7, Ne5, hitting the rook, and after Rf8, Qxd4 gives white a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: When considering a central break, always check the tactical consequences, especially if the opponent can capture with a piece that exposes your king or rook.
notes.plans: White can play d4, but must be aware that black will respond with ...d6, leading to a balanced middlegame. White should then develop pieces harmoniously, perhaps with Bg5 and Qe2.

notes.explains: White's alternative c3 aims to support a future d4, but black can simply ignore it and play ...d5, leading to a gambit-like position where black gets active piece play. This is similar to the Marshall Attack, which white wants to avoid in an Anti-Marshall setup.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a slow preparatory move, you can often seize the initiative by striking in the center, even at the cost of a pawn.
notes.plans: Black should consider ...d5 to open the position and develop rapidly, while white must be careful not to fall into a passive setup.

notes.explains: The move a5 is recommended as a practical solution: it secures the b4 pawn and prevents white from playing a4 to challenge it. This is a direct way to maintain the cramping effect on white's position.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is a simple pawn move that solidifies your gains and prevents the opponent from undermining your structure.
notes.plans: After a5, black can continue with ...Bb7, putting pressure on the e4 pawn, and then develop the queen's rook to a6 or b8, with a solid queenside bind.

notes.explains: In the Anti-Marshall, White can choose between d3 and c3, but the recommended move is a5, which fixes Black's a6 pawn and makes it a long-term weakness.
notes.teaches: A move like a5 can be strong even if it looks loosening, because it creates a permanent weakness in the opponent's camp.
notes.plans: After a5, White aims to pressure the a6 pawn, possibly with c3 and Bc4, while Black will try to counter in the center with d5.

notes.explains: After a5, Black often plays Rb8 to defend the b-pawn, and White can play Bc4 to hit a6. If Black plays d5, White should capture on d5 rather than on e5, to avoid giving Black active piece play.
notes.teaches: When recapturing in the center, prefer the capture that maintains your pawn structure and avoids opening lines for the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: White should continue developing, aiming for d4 to challenge the center, while keeping an eye on the a6 weakness.

notes.explains: In the line with c3, after Black plays Rb8, White can try to win the a6 pawn, but Black gets counterplay. The resulting endgames are often drawn, so c3 is not the most practical try.
notes.teaches: When a line leads to a drawn endgame against best play, it may be less practical than a more complex alternative, especially against a well-prepared opponent.
notes.plans: If White wants to avoid the drawn endgames, they should look for other moves that keep more pieces on the board and create more winning chances.

notes.explains: If Black trades on c3, White should recapture with the d-pawn to keep the c-pawn for support of d4 and to allow the bishop to develop to g5 or e3.
notes.teaches: When recapturing with a pawn, choose the pawn that maintains your central pawn structure and keeps your pieces flexible.
notes.plans: After recapturing with the d-pawn, White can develop the bishop actively and aim for central play with d4.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5, Black has played the Marshall Gambit. White can accept the pawn with exd5, but Black gets active play and a rook on b8 already, making it difficult for White to hold the extra pawn against a well-prepared opponent.
notes.teaches: In the Marshall Gambit, accepting the pawn can lead to long-term pressure and requires precise defense. If you are not comfortable defending, consider declining the gambit with moves like d3, which avoids the sharpest lines and leads to a more positional game.
notes.plans: If White plays exd5, they must be ready to return the pawn and defend accurately. If White plays d3, they aim for a slow buildup with c3 and d4 later, avoiding the immediate tactical battle.

notes.explains: If Black plays …dxe4 immediately, White can recapture with either the b-pawn or the d-pawn. Taking with the d-pawn (dxe4) is recommended because it keeps the b-pawn on b2 to support a future b4 advance, and it leaves the c1-bishop's diagonal open for development to g5 or e3.
notes.teaches: When recapturing in the center, consider which pawn recapture supports your long-term plans. Taking with the d-pawn can preserve flexibility for piece development and pawn advances.
notes.plans: After dxe4, White can develop the bishop to g5 or e3, and later play b4 to support the a-pawn and prevent it from becoming weak.

notes.explains: In the line after …dxe4 dxe4, Black can play ...Bd7, ...Nb8-d2, ...Qc8, ...Nf1, ...g6, ...Kg7, and White has two main plans: either play b4 and then Rook b1 to defend the b-pawn, or develop the bishop to e3. The b4 plan gives White a spatial plus, while bishop e3 can lead to awkward positions where Black's knights harass White's pieces.
notes.teaches: When facing a flexible setup, choose a plan that gives you a clear advantage. Here, the b4 plan secures the queenside and gives space, whereas developing the bishop to e3 may allow Black to bounce White's pieces around.
notes.plans: If White plays b4, after ...c5, Rook b1 defends the b-pawn, and after captures, White develops the dark-squared bishop to e3 or d2 and enjoys a spatial plus. If White plays bishop e3, they must be ready to handle ...Ng4 and subsequent harassment.

notes.explains: In the line with bishop e3, Black can play ...Ng4 hitting the bishop. White should not trade the bishop for the knight because the bishop is a good piece for White. Instead, White retreats to d2, but then Black's knights continue to hit White's pieces, forcing them to move around.
notes.teaches: Avoid trading a good piece for a less active one. When your opponent's knights are harassing your pieces, it may be a sign that your piece placement is awkward; consider alternative plans that avoid such harassment.
notes.plans: If White retreats the bishop to d2, they must be prepared for ...Nc5 hitting the queen and further pressure. This line can be uncomfortable, so the b4 plan is often preferable.

notes.explains: Instead of c3, White can play d3, which is a slower, more positional approach. It avoids the Marshall Gambit's sharp tactics and aims for a slow buildup with c3 and d4 later. Black's bishop is not on b7, so White doesn't get the full 'shutting out the bishop' idea, but White gets a nice pawn chain.
notes.teaches: The move d3 in the Ruy Lopez is a flexible way to avoid sharp lines and play a slow, maneuvering game. It allows White to develop normally and expand in the center later.
notes.plans: After d3, White can meet ...Be6 by trading bishops, and then continue developing. Later, White can play c3 and d4 to break in the center.

notes.explains: After d3, Black can play ...Be6 challenging the bishop. White can simply trade bishops, giving Black a pawn controlling the center and a half-open file, but White continues developing normally and should be fine. Black may also play ...Rb8 or ...Qe8, with ...Qe8 aiming for play on the light squares.
notes.teaches: Trading bishops can be a good way to simplify when the opponent's bishop is well-placed. It may give the opponent some small advantages, but if you can develop harmoniously, the position can be equal.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...Qe8, White can play c3 and develop normally, then break with d4. If Black plays ...Rb8, White can continue with standard development.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Qe8, White plays c3 and then d4, breaking in the center. Black may play ...Rb5 to pressure the a5 pawn, but White can use the open d-file with a rook to d1. The position is fine for White, with e5 and a5 being weak for Black, but White has the open file.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates weaknesses, use open files and central breaks to exploit them. Here, White's d4 break opens the d-file for a rook, giving White active play.
notes.plans: White should aim to place a rook on d1 and put pressure on Black's weak pawns, while maintaining the central pawn chain.

notes.explains: After d3, if Black plays ...Rb8, White can play c3 and then d4. Black may play ...Rb5 to pressure the a5 pawn, but White can respond with c4, and if Black takes on a5, White should not trade rooks but play Rb1, trapping the rook after ...Nb3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's rook becomes overextended, you can trap it by not trading and using your pieces to restrict its movement. This can win material or gain time.
notes.plans: White plays Rb1 to attack the rook, and after ...Rb8, White plays Nb3 to control d4 and prepare d4. This leads to a favorable middlegame.

notes.explains: In this Ruy Lopez position, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 O-O Be7 Re1 b5 Bb3 O-O c3 d5, the game has transposed into a typical middlegame structure. White has a slight edge due to the bishop on b3 and the central pawn mass, but black has equalized with natural development.
notes.teaches: The move d3 instead of castling is a viable but passive option; it leads to a Berlin-like structure where black has not made concessions on the queenside, so white gives up chances for an edge.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the tension in the center, develop the knight to d2 and then to f1-g3, and keep the bishop on c1 flexible, deciding its best square later.

notes.explains: The position can become locked up after moves like a5, which reduces the urgency of time pressure compared to open positions like the Marshall Attack. This allows white to take time for slow maneuvering without immediate tactical threats.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, you can afford to spend tempi on regrouping pieces, whereas in open positions, one tempo can be critical.
