notes.explains: The other try for Black after the bishop retreats to f1 is ...Ng4, threatening ...Nxf3 and then Qxf3#. White must address this threat, often with g3. Then ...Nf3+ is met by Qxf3, and ...Ne5 hits the queen. White plays Qe2, and Black plays ...e6, trying to get in ...d5 or open a square for the bishop. White again plays b3, preparing Bb2.
notes.teaches: When your opponent creates a direct mating threat, you must respond immediately, even if it means weakening your kingside pawn structure. After the threat is neutralized, you can continue with your own plans.
notes.plans: White plays g3 to stop the mate, then after ...Nf3+ and Qxf3, ...Ne5, Qe2, ...e6, White plays b3, aiming for Bb2, while Black tries to advance in the center.

notes.explains: In the Rossolimo, black's queen on b6 pressures b2 and d4, so white's setup aims to control d5 and neutralize black's counterplay. Black's knight to g4 creates an immediate threat against f3, which white must address before continuing development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates a concrete threat like a knight fork or attack on a key defender, address it first with a solid move such as g3, rather than continuing your own plans.
notes.plans: After g3, if black takes on f3, recapture with the queen, then use the e5 square to harass the queen and gain time.

notes.explains: Black's d6 is a flexible move that avoids immediate d5 because white's pieces on e5 and c6 would punish it. White develops the bishop to b2, reinforcing the center and preparing a future d4 break.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must delay a central pawn break if it loses material; instead, improve your pieces and wait for the right moment to push.
notes.plans: White aims to complete development with Bg2, Nc6, and then consider d4 to gain space, while black looks to play d5 once it's safe.

notes.explains: After black plays e6 and Bc6, white's queen to f3 targets f6 and c6, creating threats. If black tries e5 to stop white's e5 ideas, white can play Qc3, hitting the c6 pawn and forcing passive defense.
notes.teaches: Look for double attacks that hit multiple weaknesses; a queen can often create strong pressure by targeting two pawns or pieces simultaneously.
notes.plans: White should aim to double on f6 or use the queen on c3 to tie black down, then build up pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: If black avoids the tricks and plays Nf6, white can adopt a setup with c3 and d4, similar to Italian and Ruy Lopez structures. If black hasn't committed to g7 or the center, white can drop the bishop back to f1 and expand with d4.
notes.teaches: In these structures, the c3-d4 pawn duo supports a central space advantage; be ready to retreat the bishop to f1 if needed to maintain flexibility.
notes.plans: White should play c3, then d4, and if black plays Bg4, capture on f3 with the pawn, then use the g-file and king safety moves like Kh1 to generate attacking chances.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian Rossolimo position, Black has not committed the bishop to g7 or the center, so after Nf3 and a potential bishop attack, White can simply drop the bishop back to f1. Black's pin with Bg4 is not dangerous yet because White can expand with d4 and trade in the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent hasn't committed their pieces, retreating the bishop to f1 is a safe way to avoid complications. Don't fear pins if you can neutralize them by central expansion.
notes.plans: If Black captures on f3, recapture with the pawn, then plan Kh1, move the bishop, and possibly play Rg1 to use the open file. The bishop can also block on g2 if needed.

notes.explains: If Black plays d5, White should lock up the center by pushing e5, not trade. This gains space and restricts Black's pieces. After Black plays Nd7, White can play h3 to hit the bishop, and if it goes to h5, g4 can follow, gaining more space.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, avoid unnecessary trades and push forward to cramp the opponent. Use pawns to gain space and drive back pieces.
notes.plans: Continue with h3 and g4 if the bishop retreats to h5, then develop the rest of the pieces while maintaining the central space advantage.

notes.explains: If Black takes on f3 with the bishop, recapturing with the queen is logical, but after Nxd4, White must move the queen to d1, hitting the knight and the pawn behind it. This is not losing because White can regain the pawn. However, the recommended plan is to play e6, opening the f-file and later taking with the rook on e6, which can make Black's development difficult, especially the dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece to use based on future plans. Sometimes a quiet move like e6 can create long-term pressure on the opponent's development.
notes.plans: After e6 and fxe6, develop normally and aim to play Rxe6 later, putting pressure on Black's position and hindering the bishop's development.

notes.explains: In the line with Rxf6, exf6 opens the diagonal for the bishop, and then Nd5 wins the center pawn. Black may try b5 to counter, but White has tactics like Bg6+ forcing the king to take or losing the queen. This exchange sacrifice is justified because White gets the center pawn and easy development, gaining initiative.
notes.teaches: Exchange sacrifices can be worth it if you gain a central pawn and initiative. Always look for tactical resources like discovered attacks or checks to make such sacrifices work.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn, continue with natural development (e.g., Bf4, Rc1) and use the initiative to pressure Black's position.

notes.explains: In the Rossolimo, after e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Qb6, White has a slight edge due to the initiative: White captured first and Black recaptured, giving White a free developing move. Black's queen on b6 can be a target.
notes.teaches: In open Sicilians, the side that captures first gains a tempo; the queen on b6 can be vulnerable to attacks, so White should seek to exploit the initiative with natural development.
notes.plans: White aims to develop harmoniously, possibly castling kingside, and use the queen's position to gain time.

notes.explains: Black's ...b5 is a typical idea to gain space and prevent White's pieces from using b5, but it can backfire if White attacks the backward c-pawn with moves like Rc1 and Qb3. Tactical motifs like discovered attacks can punish premature pawn advances.
notes.teaches: Be cautious with pawn advances like ...b5 when they create weaknesses; the opponent can target backward pawns and use tactics to exploit the loosened structure.
notes.plans: White should consider moves like Rc1 and Qb3 to pressure the c-pawn, while Black must be ready to defend accurately.

notes.explains: In the mainline Rossolimo after …g6, White has two main options: castle or take on c6. Taking on c6 is attractive because Black's ...g6 loosens the dark squares and the bishop will take time to develop to g7, leaving holes that White can exploit if d4 is played quickly.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their pawn structure with moves like ...g6, exchanging on c6 can leave them with permanent dark-square weaknesses and a slow development of the bishop.
notes.plans: White should aim to play d4 quickly to exploit the dark-square holes, while Black must develop harmoniously to maintain equality.

notes.explains: After ...cxd4, Black should recapture with the d-pawn rather than the b-pawn because it opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop and avoids the awkward placement of the bishop on a6 after d3. This saves time and keeps the structure solid.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, recapturing with the d-pawn is often preferable because it aids piece development and avoids creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will play ...d6, ...Bg7, ...Nf6, and castle, while White will build a pawn chain with d3 and develop the bishop.

notes.explains: In the position after ...Bg7, White should play h3 to prevent ...Bg4, which can be annoying and pin the knight. If White allows ...Bg4, it can disrupt White's development and create pressure on the d-pawn.
notes.teaches: Preventing annoying pins with a timely h3 is a useful prophylactic move in the opening, especially when the opponent's bishop can become active.
notes.plans: White plays h3, then continues with Nf3, Nc3, Be3, Qd2, and castles, while Black castles and prepares ...b6 and ...e5.

notes.explains: Black's ...e5 appears to hang a pawn, but it is tactically sound because if White takes on e5, Black plays ...Nxe4, and if White recaptures, ...Bxe5 equalizes immediately. This is a common tactical resource in the Sicilian.
notes.teaches: Be alert to tactical resources like ...Nxe4 when a pawn seems hanging; the opponent may be offering a pawn to gain activity or equalize.
notes.plans: White should avoid taking on e5 and instead find a more challenging continuation, while Black uses the tactic to maintain balance.

notes.explains: In this Rossolimo position, Black's queen on b6 attacks b2 and d4, but taking the e5 pawn is dangerous because of the tactical resource Nxe4, which exploits the pin on the e-file and the loose bishop on b5.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is offered, check for tactical refutations like a central fork or a counterattack that wins material or equalizes.
notes.plans: If White avoids the pawn grab, they should develop solidly and aim to trade the dark-squared bishops to reduce Black's defensive resources.

notes.explains: After Black fianchettoes the bishop on g7, White can try Bxh6 to trade off the dark-squared bishops, which are key defenders of the fianchetto structure. Black should not recapture immediately but instead play Qd6, defending the e5 pawn and keeping the position solid.
notes.teaches: When the opponent offers a bishop trade, consider declining if recapturing would allow the opponent's queen to become active or if the bishop is a key defender. Defend the weak points and continue development.
notes.plans: Black will develop the light-squared bishop, connect rooks, and place a rook on e8 to support the e5 pawn, while White may expand on the queenside.

notes.explains: In the line where White castles instead of taking on c6, Black can develop with Bg7. If Black plays an early a6, White should just take on c6 because it's a move Black doesn't need to play, and it helps White achieve their goal of removing the knight from the center.
notes.teaches: Don't play provocative moves that force the opponent to do something they already want to do. Instead, develop actively and make useful moves.
notes.plans: White can proceed with normal development, and if Black ever plays a6, White takes on c6 to simplify and reduce Black's central control.

notes.explains: Trading off the dark-squared bishop on g7 is a good idea for White because it creates dark-square weaknesses in Black's camp, which the queen and knight can exploit. Rushing the h-pawn to hit g6 is also a plan, as seen in the Yugoslav Dragon.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a fianchettoed bishop, trading it off can weaken their king's defenses and create targets for your pieces. Use pawn storms to open lines against the castled king.
notes.plans: After trading bishops, White can aim to place pieces on the dark squares and potentially push the h-pawn to undermine Black's pawn shield.

notes.explains: In the fianchetto structure, the bishop on g7 is a key defender of the dark squares around the king. Trading it off creates lasting dark-square weaknesses that the opponent's queen and knight can exploit.
notes.teaches: When facing a fianchettoed bishop, consider exchanging it to create weaknesses, then target those squares with your minor pieces and queen.
notes.plans: If the bishop is traded, aim to place your knight and queen on the weakened dark squares, and consider advancing the h-pawn to further weaken the pawn structure.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian line, Black's early ...a6 is less useful than developing the bishop to g7, which is more active and contributes to the center and kingside.
notes.teaches: Prioritize active development over prophylactic moves that don't address immediate needs.
notes.plans: Black should develop the bishop to g7 and continue with natural moves like ...Nf6 and ...O-O.

notes.explains: After White plays c3 to reinforce d4, Black can play ...Nf6. If White tries e5, Black can respond with ...Nd5, and White must create central space with d4 to compensate for lagging development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent gains space, counter by occupying strong central outposts and aim to complete development before launching attacks.
notes.plans: Black should aim to complete development and possibly challenge White's center with moves like ...d6 or ...e5.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Nf6 and ...Nd5, White may try to trade pieces to reduce tension, but Black should maintain tension and keep pieces on the board to pressure the bishop on b5.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary trades when your opponent is underdeveloped; keep pieces to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Black can play ...Nxc3, ...d6, and later ...exd6, aiming to create an isolated queen's pawn for White that may become a target.

notes.explains: After c3 and ...Nf6, White has the alternative Re1, protecting the e-pawn. Black castles, and White plays h3 to prevent ...Bg4, then prepares e5. Black often plays ...e5 to stop White's pawn advance, but White can still push d4 because of the support on d4.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like h3 can prevent annoying pins, and central pawn advances should be supported by pieces.
notes.plans: Black should consider ...e5 to block White's pawn, but be ready for piece exchanges and a balanced middlegame.

notes.explains: In the line with ...e5, Black should capture with the knight on c6 first to gain a tempo on the bishop, rather than capturing with the pawn, which allows Bxc6.
notes.teaches: When capturing in the center, consider the order of captures to gain tempi and avoid unfavorable trades.
notes.plans: After ...Nxc6, ...exd5, ...Nxe5, and ...Qc7, the position is roughly equal.

notes.explains: Instead of c3, White can play Re1 directly. If Black tries ...e5 early, White can play Bxc6, then d3, and develop the knight to d2 heading to c4 to pressure e5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a knight goes to d2 to reroute to a better square like c4, where it attacks the center and is hard to kick away.
notes.plans: White will aim to pressure the e5 pawn and maintain a solid center.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Qb6, Black's queen move pressures b2 and d4. If Black tries an early ...e5, White can respond with Bxc6, doubling Black's pawns and later placing a knight on c4 to pressure the e5 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent plays an early pawn break, consider exchanging to create weaknesses and then use a knight to target the resulting weak pawn.
notes.plans: White can play Bxc6, then d3, Qe7, Nd2-c4, pressuring e5. Black can defend with ...Nf6 and ...Nd7, leading to roughly equal play.

notes.explains: In the Rossolimo, White's most aggressive try against ...e5 is to play Nxd5, forcing the knight to c7 and then recapturing with the d-pawn to open the a1-h8 diagonal, making the bishop on g7 less effective.
notes.teaches: When a knight can jump to a central outpost and force a favorable recapture, it can open lines and create attacking chances.
notes.plans: White can play Nxd5, Nc7, then dxc6, and if Black recaptures, White's knight on e4 can be used for a temporary sacrifice on f6 to expose the king and win the bishop on g7.

notes.explains: If Black avoids the knight fork by playing ...Ne6, White can continue with standard development (d3, Be3, Qd2) and after a trade of knights, White gets a small but solid advantage, typical of the Rossolimo.
notes.teaches: In solid openings, you don't need to create immediate threats; a small structural or developmental edge can be enough.
notes.plans: White can play d3, Be3, Qd2, and after ...Nxd4, recapture with the bishop, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: After …Nc6 (the main line), White can play c3 and h3, and if Black plays ...Qb6, the position can resemble a King's Indian Defense, with Black planning ...Ne8 and ...f5. However, this line is slightly dubious for Black because White gets a good plus.
notes.teaches: Recognize transpositions to other openings and adjust plans accordingly; a setup that is good in one opening may be worse in another due to move order.
notes.plans: White can develop with Bd3, Be3, and prepare central expansion, while Black tries to generate queenside play and a kingside attack with ...f5.

notes.explains: In this Rossolimo position, Black's queen to b6 is a bit dubious because White can get a good plus, though transpositions to the King's Indian are possible but slightly better for White.
notes.teaches: Avoid dubious queen moves early if they allow the opponent to gain a comfortable edge; be aware of transpositions to other openings.
notes.plans: White should consider developing and preparing central break with d4 rather than grabbing the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: White should not capture on c6 to win the e5 pawn because after rook to e8 and knight to f3, the e-pawn is hanging, so the pawn can be poison.
notes.teaches: Be cautious about capturing central pawns if the opponent has tactical resources to regain material or get counterplay; always double-check calculations.
notes.plans: Instead, play d4 to break in the center and develop pieces.

notes.explains: In the Carlsbad structure, white often prepares d4-d5 to open the center and create attacking chances. Black's most common response is Rc8, but other plans exist, including a pawn sacrifice to break open the position.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and a central pawn majority, breaking open the center can be a powerful attacking resource, even at the cost of a pawn.
notes.plans: White should aim to open the center with d5 and bring rooks to central files to support the attack.

notes.explains: After the center opens, white can launch a Greek gift sacrifice (Bxh7+) if black's king is vulnerable. This leads to a strong attack with the queen and knight joining in.
notes.teaches: The Greek gift sacrifice is a classic attacking motif when the bishop can take on h7 and the knight can jump to g5, forcing the king into the open.
notes.plans: If black accepts the sacrifice, white should bring the queen and knight to the kingside to continue the attack.

notes.explains: In the Carlsbad structure, white often delays Nf3 to keep the option of playing Ne2, preparing f3 and e4 to break in the center. This flexible move order is important.
notes.teaches: Sometimes delaying a natural developing move like Nf3 can preserve flexibility for a central pawn break.
notes.plans: White will play Ne2, then f3 and e4 to challenge black's center and create a pawn majority.

notes.explains: If black neglects to play c6, white can exploit the position with the tactical move b4. If the bishop takes, Bxf6 wins a pawn due to the pin on the queen; if the bishop retreats, Nxd5 and Qa4 create a double attack.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical pawn pushes like b4 that exploit the opponent's lack of a defensive pawn move (c6), leading to pins and double attacks.
notes.plans: White should play b4 to provoke weaknesses and then use tactics to win material or ruin black's pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black's move c6 is a useful prophylactic move that prevents white's tactical b4 ideas and also prepares ...d5. White often plays Qc2 to prevent black's bishop from developing to f5, which would pressure the queen.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like c6 can prevent tactical motifs and prepare central advances. Move order matters: Qc2 before e3 stops ...Bf5.
notes.plans: White will continue developing, aiming for a central break with e4, while black will try to complete development and challenge the center.

notes.explains: In this Queen's Gambit Declined Exchange variation, White's queen on c2 prevents Black's plan of developing the bishop to f5 and then doubling White's pawns after Qf3 and Bg5. Black's compensation would include the two bishops, the g-file, and a knight heading to d6 to pressure light squares.
notes.teaches: Understanding why prophylactic moves like Qc2 are played: they stop specific Black counterplay before it starts. Recognizing Black's compensation in the bishop-pair and active pieces is key to evaluating such positions.
notes.plans: White will develop the bishop to d3 and knight to e2, preparing to play f3 and e4 to establish a central pawn wedge.

notes.explains: White's knight on e2 prepares to support the f3-e4 pawn advance, which will create a strong center and potentially a knight outpost on e4. Black has a maneuver to challenge White's light-squared bishop: a knight to g7 and then Bf5, aiming to trade off an active piece.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, slow maneuvers like Nf8-g6-e7-g7 are viable because there is time. Recognizing the importance of neutralizing an opponent's actively placed piece is a key strategic idea.
notes.plans: White will play f3 and e4, possibly with b4-b5 to create queenside weaknesses. Black will counterattack on the kingside, and if the attack fails, White's long-term queenside pressure should win.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on g4 is misplaced because White can play f3 and e4, with the threat of e5 forking the bishop and knight. Black's only trick is Bxh2+ followed by Ng4+ to win the bishop on g4, but White can avoid this by moving the king to h1, protecting the h2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When a piece is placed on a square that invites a pawn fork, it is often a mistake unless there is a tactical trick. Recognizing cheapos and finding prophylactic king moves to neutralize them is a valuable skill.
notes.plans: White will continue with the f3-e4 plan, having safely avoided Black's trap. Black must find another way to generate counterplay.

notes.explains: In this Queen's Gambit Declined Exchange position, White's bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6, and Black's h6 is a typical try to harass it. However, White has just played Qc2, and the position is sharp: Black's ...Bxh2 trick is a common tactical idea, but White can avoid it by moving the king to h1, so that Bxh2 is not check and White can insert a zwischenzug.
notes.teaches: When a bishop attacks h2, moving the king to h1 can neutralize the check and allow a zwischenzug to win material. This is a standard prophylactic idea against back-rank or h-file tricks.
notes.plans: White aims to prepare e4, centralizing rooks and building a big center. Black should consider h6 to kick the bishop, but must be aware of tactical tricks and the possibility of White's strong initiative.

notes.explains: White has not played b4 but instead focuses on the center, threatening e4-e5 to create pins and forks. Black's bishop on g4 is misplaced, and Black feels compelled to retreat it to e7, admitting a mistake. White then prepares e4 with moves like bringing rooks to the center, ensuring all pieces are ready before the central break.
notes.teaches: Before making a central pawn break like e4, it's important to prepare by improving piece activity and ensuring the king is safe. This is a typical grandmaster approach: slow preparation rather than immediate action.
notes.plans: White will play e4, gaining space and creating threats. Black must find a way to develop and counter White's center, possibly by trading dark-squared bishops and attacking the e-pawn.

notes.explains: Black's h6 is a typical move to kick the bishop, but it has problems: the g-pawn may become weak, and White can sometimes sacrifice a piece for three pawns and a strong attack. Black must be cautious about such sacrifices, as White's pieces are well-placed for an assault on the king.
notes.teaches: When considering a move like h6, be aware of potential piece sacrifices on the kingside. Even if the sacrifice is not objectively best, it can give a dangerous initiative that Black must handle precisely.
notes.plans: If Black plays h6, White may consider a piece sacrifice to open lines against the king. Black should aim to consolidate and avoid falling into a lasting attack.

notes.explains: After Black retreats the bishop to e7, White can trade dark-squared bishops, and Black has the choice of recapturing with queen or rook. Taking with the rook is common, as the queen may be better placed on c7 to pressure the c-file or support the center. White then must address the d-pawn's safety before playing e4.
notes.teaches: When recapturing with a piece, consider which piece is better for the resulting structure. Here, the rook on e7 supports the e-file, while the queen can go to c7 for pressure on the c-file.
notes.plans: White will play e4, supported by the knight, and Black will try to develop and challenge the center. The d-pawn may become a target, so White must ensure it is defended.

notes.explains: In this Carlsbad structure position, White's queen on c2 defends the d-pawn, allowing the e4 break. Black's knight on f6 is awkwardly placed, and White's knight on f3 supports e4. The immediate e4 is not yet possible because the d-pawn would be loose, so White first ensures its defense.
notes.teaches: Before playing a central pawn break like e4, make sure the pawn you leave behind is defended. Here, the queen on c2 covers d4, enabling the break.
notes.plans: White aims to play e4, opening the center and creating a strong pawn chain. Black must develop pieces and find counterplay, often by pressuring the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's knight on f5 is very strong, dominating the position. Black faces a choice: allow it to remain or trade a bishop for it. If Black avoids the trade, White can play g4, trapping the knight, and if Black ever takes, White recaptures with the g-pawn, opening the g-file for the rook.
notes.teaches: A well-supported outpost knight can be worth more than a bishop. Use pawns to maintain the outpost and open lines for your rooks.
notes.plans: White will keep the knight on f5, support it with g4, and prepare to open the g-file. Black must decide whether to trade or suffer a long-term positional disadvantage.

notes.explains: White plays e4, a critical moment. If Black captures, the f-file opens for White's rook, which is good for the attack. If Black declines, White plays e5, followed by f4, rolling the pawns forward. Black's only counterplay is pressure on the d4 pawn.
notes.teaches: In the Carlsbad, the e4 break is a key lever. When the center opens, the side with better piece activity and attacking chances benefits. If the opponent declines the capture, the pawn roller can be decisive.
notes.plans: White will continue with e5 if Black doesn't take, then f4, pushing the kingside pawns. Black must generate counterplay against d4 to survive.

notes.explains: After the e4 break, White's knight can jump to e4, and later to d6, putting pressure on f7. Black is forced to defend f7 repeatedly. White's bishop on e4 creates threats, and the knight can return to f5 to support a mating attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and a strong knight, use it to target weaknesses like f7. Force the opponent to defend passively, and then switch to a mating attack.
notes.plans: White will continue to increase pressure on f7, possibly with rook lifts to f3 or h3, and look for a decisive breakthrough.

notes.explains: White plays a tactical sequence: knight to f5, threatening mate on g7. If Black captures, rook to g3 leads to unstoppable mate. White also forces the black queen to a passive square (d6) before launching the rook lift, preventing counterplay.
notes.teaches: Before starting a direct attack, drive the opponent's key defender (like the queen) to a worse square. This prevents counterplay and makes the mating net tighter.
notes.plans: White will bring the rook to g3 or h3, and with the queen on f6, mate on g7 is unstoppable. Black must find a way to defend, but the threats are overwhelming.

notes.explains: In this attacking position, White has massed pieces against the black king, and the immediate threat is a checkmate on g7 or f7. Black is forced to defend with the knight, but White's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive attack, keep creating threats and force the defender to respond. Use all your pieces to join the attack, and look for tactics like pins and discoveries.
notes.plans: Continue the attack by taking on f7 and then exploiting the discovered threats. If the queen is attacked, move it to safety while maintaining the pressure.

notes.explains: The final tactic is g4, attacking a pinned knight. The knight cannot move because it would expose the king to check, so Black loses material.
notes.teaches: Always look for ways to attack a pinned piece. A pinned piece is a target because it cannot move without exposing the king or a more valuable piece.
notes.plans: After winning material, convert by simplifying or continuing the attack.

notes.explains: In the Queen's Gambit Declined Exchange variation, Black deviates with Nh5, forcing the trade of dark-squared bishops. This makes it harder for White to play f3 and start a kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to deviate from the main plan, consider whether trading pieces helps or hurts your position. Here, trading the dark-squared bishops weakens White's dark squares and slows down the f3 plan.
notes.plans: White should accept the trade and then look for alternative plans, such as a minority attack on the queenside with b4-b5.

notes.explains: Black's setup involves putting the knight on g7, then bringing the other knight to f6, and the bishop to f5, aiming to trade the light-squared bishop. White responds with Nf3 and often castles kingside, as played by Korobov.
notes.teaches: In the Carlsbad structure, piece placement is key. Black tries to trade off White's strong bishop, while White should consider castling kingside and preparing a minority attack with b4-b5.
notes.plans: White plays Rb1 to prepare b4, while Black plays a6 to slow down b5. White can respond with a4 to maintain the possibility of b5 later.

notes.explains: After the early trade of dark-squared bishops, Black's dark squares are weak. Black plans to put a knight on c5 to pressure the b-pawn, and first plays Qc5 to trade queens and remove a defender of the dark squares.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has weak squares, try to occupy them with a knight and eliminate the pieces that defend those squares. Trading queens can also reduce your opponent's defensive resources.
notes.plans: Black will play Na4 and then Nc5, putting pressure on the b-pawn and exploiting the dark-square weaknesses.

notes.explains: White's knight maneuver to g3 supports the e4 break, and after h4 to prevent the knight being kicked, White prepares f3 and e4. The knight later goes to d6 to control light squares, and after trading bishops, White's knight reaches c5, attacking the b-pawn.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, piece maneuvers that support central pawn breaks are crucial. Use pawn moves like h4 to secure a knight's post and prevent harassment.
notes.plans: White continues with f3, then e4 to open the position, while the knight on c5 maintains pressure on the b-pawn.

notes.explains: White's rook improves by going to e2, then to e1, supporting the e4 break. This is a slow improvement of the worst-placed piece, a common theme in the Carlsbad structure.
notes.teaches: When there is no immediate tactic, improve your worst-placed piece. Rooks often belong on open or semi-open files or behind advancing pawns.
notes.plans: White plays e4, and after the exchange, recaptures with the knight to keep the e-file open, then repositions the knight to g3.

notes.explains: After e4 and the exchange, White's knight recaptures on e4 and then jumps back to g3, keeping the e-file open and maintaining pressure. Black's king comes over, but White is winning.
notes.teaches: In the Carlsbad structure, the e4 break is a key plan. Recapturing with the knight keeps the e-file open for the rook and maintains central control.
notes.plans: White continues to exploit the weak dark squares and the pressure on the b-pawn, while Black struggles to coordinate.

notes.explains: In this position, after the exchange on d5, Black's c6-pawn is potentially weak, but Black is far from being able to attack it. White has just played Qc2, preparing to take on e4 with the knight, which would keep the e-file open and allow the knight to retreat to g3.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is weak, consider whether the opponent can realistically attack it; if not, it may not be a pressing concern. Keeping the e-file open can be important for piece activity and future tactics.
notes.plans: White aims to play Nxe4, keeping the e-file open, then retreat the knight to g3, maintaining pressure and central control.

notes.explains: White has the option to trade all pieces and enter a king-and-pawn endgame. This is a critical decision: if the resulting endgame is winning, it is the simplest path to victory, so it must be calculated precisely.
notes.teaches: When you have the opportunity to simplify into a winning endgame, calculate it thoroughly and take it if it is clearly winning. Trading down is often the most reliable way to convert an advantage.
notes.plans: White should take the knight, then the bishop, and trade rooks to reach a winning king-and-pawn endgame.

notes.explains: In the resulting endgame, the most important factor is king activity. White will try to create a passed pawn on the queenside, using the king to support it. The king can come to f4, possibly attack Black's kingside pawns, or play g4 to create a passer.
notes.teaches: In king-and-pawn endgames, king activity is paramount. Aim to create a passed pawn on the side where you have a majority or where the opponent's pawns are weak.
notes.plans: White will bring the king to f4, then play g4 to create a passed pawn on the kingside, or attack Black's queenside pawns if possible.

notes.explains: White can force zugzwang by playing g3, leaving Black with no good moves. Black's pawns are all blocked, and any king move allows White to make progress. Eventually, White's g4 break forces trades and wins the pawn race.
notes.teaches: Zugzwang is a powerful tool in endgames: if your opponent has no useful moves, any move they make worsens their position. Use waiting moves like g3 to put the burden on them.
notes.plans: White plays g3 to put Black in zugzwang, then follows with g4, forcing favorable trades and promoting a pawn.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian position, after e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6, White's setup with Bc4 or Bd3 can allow Black to equalize easily with ...d5. The move Nd2 is also suspect because it blocks the queen and bishop, giving Black comfortable development in a Scheveningen-style setup.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, White should avoid moves that hinder natural development or allow Black easy central breaks like ...d5. Develop pieces to active squares while maintaining pressure.
notes.plans: White should prefer Nc3, which is the natural developing move and invites ...Bb4, leading to typical Sicilian pressure on the e4 pawn.

notes.explains: After Nc3, Black plays ...Bb4, pinning the knight and attacking the e4 pawn. White has several ways to handle the pressure: Nb5, Bd3, or the aggressive e5 push. Nb5 allows Black to play ...d5, breaking in the center, while Bd3 allows ...Nc6, pressuring the knight. The critical move is e5, which kicks the knight and creates immediate tension.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is attacked and difficult to defend, consider advancing it to create counterplay. In the Sicilian, the e4-e5 push is a common resource to disrupt Black's setup.
notes.plans: After e5, if Black plays ...Nfd7 or ...Nfd5, White can follow up with Qg4, attacking g7 and the b4 bishop, or continue developing with Be2 and castling.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Qa5, Black ignores the threat to the f6 knight and adds pressure on c3. White can simply capture the knight with exf6, and after ...Bxc3, bxc3, Black's queen is misplaced and White has a sound pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When an opponent ignores a threat, punish it by capturing. Also, be wary of queen sorties that can leave the queen exposed or allow structural damage.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and use the open files and central pawn majority to build an initiative.

notes.explains: In the Pin Variation of the Sicilian, after e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Bb4, Black's move e5 attacks the knight on d4 and invites it to d5 or e4. A third option, Qa5, tries to pile up on c3 while ignoring the threat to the f6 knight, but it is losing.
notes.teaches: When your opponent ignores a threat to create counterplay, you should often proceed with the threat if it wins material or gains time. Here, White takes the knight on f6, forcing Black to recapture, and then White can set a trap.
notes.plans: After exf6 Bxc3 bxc3 Qxc3+, White should play Qd2, sacrificing the rook, and after Qxa1, play fxg7, trapping the black rook and queen.

notes.explains: After exf6 Bxc3 bxc3 Qxc3+, the natural Bd2 is inferior because Black can take on d4 and later develop easily, leaving White with a misplaced bishop. Instead, Qd2 is strong: if Black takes the rook, White plays fxg7, forcing Rg8, and then c3 traps the black queen.
notes.teaches: When your queen is attacked, look for a move that not only saves the queen but also creates a bigger threat. Here, Qd2 defends the queen while setting up a pawn fork and a queen trap.
notes.plans: After Qd2 Qxa1 fxg7 Rg8 c3, the black queen has no good squares: b2, c3, and a2 are all covered by the white queen. The only move is Qb1, but then White develops with Bd3 and castles, with a winning position.

notes.explains: In the trapped queen line, Black may try Qb1, but White plays Bd3, and after Qb6, White's development advantage is decisive. Black's queenside pieces are undeveloped, and White can castle next. If Black tries to break the pin with Ba3, White can meet it with Qh6, attacking the rook, and the rook remains trapped.
notes.teaches: A lead in development can be more valuable than material. Even if the opponent wriggles out of a trap, the resulting position is often winning because of the activity of your pieces.
notes.plans: White should continue developing, castle, and then use the initiative to attack Black's uncoordinated pieces. The pawn on g7 is a constant threat, and Black's rook is tied down.

notes.explains: In the Qa5 line, after exf6 Bxc3 bxc3 Qxc3+ Qd2 Qxa1 fxg7 Rg8 c3, Black's queen is trapped. The only move is Qb1, but White can play Bd3 and then castle, with a winning position. If Black tries to take on g7 immediately, White has Qh6, attacking the rook, and the rook is trapped.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's queen is trapped, you should not rush to take material; instead, consolidate your position and maintain the pressure. The threat of promotion on g7 is a powerful long-term asset.
notes.plans: White should aim to develop the bishop to d3, castle, and then use the passed pawn on g7 to tie down Black's pieces. If Black tries to free the rook, White can use the queen to harass it.

notes.explains: In the line with Qh6, Black may try Qc5, but White castles, and after Qe5, White plays Nb5, threatening to fork on c7 or d6. Black must play Na6 to prevent the fork, but then White plays Bg5, and after Qxg7, Nd6+ Kf8, Qh5 keeps the pressure, threatening Bh6 and mate.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's queen is active, you can use tactical threats like forks and pins to drive it away. Here, the knight on b5 creates a fork threat, and the bishop on g5 pins the queen to the king.
notes.plans: White should continue to harass the black queen and king, using the threat of Bh6 to force a favorable endgame or win material. The passed pawn on g7 remains a constant threat.

notes.explains: In the alternative Qg5 line, Black may play Qd8 to trade queens, but White has Bg5+ and after the king moves, Bf6 holds the g7 pawn forever. This leaves White with a protected passed pawn that is always one move from promotion, making it very hard for Black to draw.
notes.teaches: A protected passed pawn on the seventh rank is a decisive advantage. Even if queens are traded, the pawn can win the endgame by tying down the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: White should aim to trade queens and then use the passed pawn to win material or force promotion. The bishop on f6 protects the pawn and cannot be easily dislodged.

notes.explains: After …Nxe4, White can play Qg4, attacking the knight on e4 and the pawn on g7. This is a strong move because it creates a double attack and forces Black to respond. Black's best is probably Qa5, but then White can take on g7, threatening the rook.
notes.teaches: In the opening, look for moves that create multiple threats. Qg4 attacks two pieces at once, gaining time and forcing Black to defend.
notes.plans: After Qg4, if Black plays Qa5, White can take on g7, and if Black plays Rf8, White can play Bh6, threatening to take on f8. White should continue to develop and maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: In the Nxe4 line, after Qg4 Qa5 Qxg7 Rf8 Bh6, Black may try Nxc3, but White has the resource a3, attacking the knight and preparing to recapture with the bishop if needed. This keeps the pressure on Black's position.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to counterattack, look for quiet moves that maintain your advantage. Here, a3 is a useful move that kicks the knight and prepares to develop the bishop.
notes.plans: White should continue to develop and use the threats against the black king and rook to maintain the initiative. The bishop on h6 is well placed, and the pawn on g7 is a constant threat.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian Pin Variation, Black's bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3 to the king. If Black plays …Nxe4, White's queen can go to g4, attacking the knight on e4 and the pawn on g7, creating strong pressure.
notes.teaches: When your opponent grabs a pawn with a knight that is pinned, look for aggressive queen moves that create multiple threats, such as attacking the knight and a weak pawn.
notes.plans: White should follow up with Qxg7, attacking the rook on h8, and then use the bishop to h6 to increase pressure on the f8 rook.

notes.explains: If Black responds to Qg4 with …Qa5, piling on the c3 knight, White can simply take on g7, threatening the rook. Black's best defense is …Rf8, but then White plays Bh6, threatening to win the exchange. If Black tries …Nxc3, White has the resource a3, hitting the bishop on b4. After the knight moves, White recaptures on b4, removing the checking piece.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are under attack, look for counter-threats that are bigger than the immediate threat. Also, when a bishop is checking your king, you can often drive it away with a pawn move if it is not defended.
notes.plans: White should continue developing, perhaps with Nc6 or Nb3, and aim to win the exchange with Bh6.

notes.explains: If Black tries to give check with …Bxc3+ before moving the rook, White should recapture with the b-pawn, and then play Ke2! This is crucial because Kd1 would allow Black to win material with ...Nf2+ and ...Nxd1. With the king on e2, if Black takes the knight on c3, White can take on h8 with check, because the king is not in the way.
notes.teaches: When your king is in check, choose the escape square that avoids allowing your opponent to win material. Sometimes moving the king forward is safer than moving it backward.
notes.plans: After Ke2, White is ready to take on h8 with check if Black captures the knight, or to continue developing with a winning position.

notes.explains: In the main line, Black plays …Rf8, and White plays Bh6. If Black plays …Qc5, protecting the rook, White can play Nb3, hitting the queen. This allows Black to play …Qf2+, but White can calmly play Kd1, because the bishop on h6 and knight on b3 control the mating squares. Black has no real threats, and the rook on f8 is still under attack.
notes.teaches: Scary-looking checks are not dangerous if the opponent has no follow-up. Always ask what threats the opponent actually has. If they have none, you can ignore the check and continue your own plan.
notes.plans: White should continue with moves like Bd3 and Rf1, preparing to win the exchange and then the f7 pawn.

notes.explains: If Black plays …Nxc3 instead of …Nxe4, White cannot recapture on c3 because of …Bxc3+, forking the king and rook. Instead, White should play Qxg7, attacking the rook on h8. If the knight moves back to d5, White can play c3, blocking the check and also attacking the bishop on b4. The queen on g7 also hits h8, so Black cannot defend both.
notes.teaches: When you cannot recapture a piece because of a tactic, look for a bigger threat that forces your opponent to deal with it. Also, pawn moves can block checks and attack pieces simultaneously.
notes.plans: White should continue to pressure the rook on h8, possibly with Bh6, and emerge with a material advantage.

notes.explains: In the Pin Variation of the Sicilian, black's bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3 to the king, creating pressure on c3. White can respond with a3, forcing the bishop to declare its intentions; if it retreats, white can take on b4 and then use tactics like Bg5 and Bh6 to create threats.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, you can often use tactical motifs like discovered attacks or pins to exploit the pinned piece's immobility. Here, white uses the pin on the knight to generate a strong attack, even sacrificing material for initiative.
notes.plans: White aims to develop rapidly, use the bishop pair, and create threats against black's king, while black tries to maintain the pin and pressure on c3.

notes.explains: After the main line with Nd5, white has several options. Nb5 is a candidate, aiming for d6, but it allows black to double white's b-pawns, creating long-term weaknesses. Qg4 is another strong move, directly attacking the g7 pawn and threatening Bh6 with mate threats.
notes.teaches: When choosing between moves, consider not only immediate tactics but also long-term structural consequences. Doubled pawns can be a permanent weakness, so avoid them if possible, even if the immediate position seems fine.
notes.plans: White should prefer Qg4 to keep the pawn structure intact and maintain the initiative, while Nb5 leads to a more equal game with potential weaknesses.

notes.explains: After Qg4, black has two main defenses: castling or Kf8. If black castles, white can play Bh6, threatening mate, forcing g6, and winning the exchange on f8. However, the pin on c3 remains annoying, so white must address it with Qg3 or Ne2.
notes.teaches: When you have a material-winning tactic, you must also consider the resulting position. Here, winning the exchange is good, but the pin on c3 gives black counterplay, so white must consolidate by defending the pinned knight.
notes.plans: White should play Qg3 to defend c3 and maintain the extra exchange, while black will try to increase pressure on c3 with moves like Qc5.

notes.explains: In the line with Kf8, black avoids the Bh6 tactic because the king can simply capture the bishop. White then plays Bd2 to break the pin, and after d6, there is a tactical sequence where black takes on c3, giving white the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to avoid castling if it allows a tactical refutation. Here, Kf8 is a safe haven that prevents the mate threat, and black can still fight for equality by opening the position and forcing favorable trades.
notes.plans: White should capture with the pawn on c3 to maintain the bishop pair, while black hopes to use the central pawns and activity to compensate.

notes.explains: In the Sicilian Pin Variation after e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Bb4, White's bishop is pinned. Black threatens ...Bh6, attacking the queen and threatening mate on g2 if White takes the bishop. White must address the pin, typically with Bd2.
notes.teaches: When your piece is pinned and the pin is uncomfortable, break it with a developing move that also prepares castling, rather than allowing the pin to worsen.
notes.plans: White plays Bd2, unpinning the knight, and prepares to castle. Black will likely play d6, opening the center.

notes.explains: After Black plays d6 and White captures on d6, Black should consider taking on c3 before recapturing on d6. This gives White doubled pawns but also gives White the bishop pair. White should recapture with the pawn to keep the bishop pair and maintain more pieces for attacking chances.
notes.teaches: When you can give your opponent doubled pawns, weigh the cost: if you also give them the bishop pair, it may not be worth it. Keeping pieces on the board can be advantageous when you have the bishop pair.
notes.plans: White keeps the bishop pair and aims to use the open files and extra pieces to create pressure.

notes.explains: After Bd2, Black's natural developing move Nc6 is actually a serious mistake. The idea is that White can play Nxd5, and after Bxd2 Qxd2, White plays e5, forcing the knight away and gaining access to the d6 outpost. The knight will land on d6, a permanent outpost because no enemy pawns can attack it (the c- and e-pawns are gone). This knight dominates the position and blocks Black's development, especially the c8 bishop.
notes.teaches: A permanent outpost for a knight on a central square like d6 can be positionally winning. Look for tactics that force the opponent's pieces to give up control of key squares.
notes.plans: White plays Nxd5, then after Bxd2 Qxd2, plays e5, followed by Nb5 or Nf5, and then Nd6, establishing a powerful knight outpost.

notes.explains: If White instead captures on c6 with the knight, Black recaptures with the d-pawn, gaining a strong pawn center and freeing the c8 bishop. Black's position improves dramatically, so White should avoid this capture.
notes.teaches: Do not trade a powerful outpost knight for a pawn that helps your opponent's development. Maintain your positional advantages.
notes.plans: White should keep the knight and aim for the d6 outpost, not trade it off.

notes.explains: If White delays the knight maneuver and castles first, Black can also castle. Then Black might try Nxd4 to eliminate the knight, but after Qxd4, Black cannot protect d5, so White wins a central pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have a powerful knight outpost idea, be aware of moves that eliminate it, but also see if the elimination allows you to win material.
notes.plans: White can castle first, and if Black tries Nxd4, White recaptures and wins the d5 pawn.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian Pin Variation, after e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Bb4, Black is ready to castle and the queen can develop. The position is already better for Black than a move ago, so White must act precisely.
notes.teaches: Do not take on c6 with the knight, as it relieves pressure and allows Black to consolidate. The idea of Nb5-d6 remains a strong plan for White, aiming to plant a knight on d6 and attack the center.
notes.plans: White should consider castling first, then Nb5, heading to d6. If Black plays Nc6, White can still proceed with Nb5, and if Black takes on e5, White's knight reaches d6 and the d5 pawn becomes vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black's natural move Nc6 looks active, hitting the hanging bishop, but it is positionally losing because it allows White's knight to reach d6 with great effect.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a natural developing move that attacks a piece can be inferior if it allows the opponent to achieve a powerful outpost. Evaluate the resulting position, not just the immediate threat.
notes.plans: White should continue with Nb5, and if Black takes on e5, White plays Nd6, after which the d5 pawn will fall.

notes.explains: Black has the option to take on c3 with the bishop. After bxc3, Black plays Qc7, forking the c3 and e4 pawns. This is a critical moment: White must not take with the bishop, as that would allow the fork.
notes.teaches: When recapturing on c3, prefer the pawn over the bishop to avoid leaving both pawns vulnerable. The queen on d1 cannot defend both pawns, so the pawn recapture is essential.
notes.plans: White should play f4, keeping lines open and preparing to use the f-pawn to break into Black's position. If Black plays Nxc3, White can respond with Qf3, hitting the knight, and after Nd5, Nb5 again heads to d6.

notes.explains: If Black castles instead of taking on c3, White can develop naturally with Bd3. If Black then plays Nxc3, White has Qh5, threatening mate on h7. Black must play g6, and White continues with Qh6, preparing h4-h5 to open the h-file.
notes.teaches: When the opponent leaves the king in the center or castles late, a quick queen sortie can create a mating net. The h-pawn can be used as a battering ram to open lines against the castled king.
notes.plans: White's plan is to play h4-h5, ripping open the h-file, and possibly f5 and Bg5-f6 to continue the attack. Black gets some counterplay with d6, but White's attack is strong.

notes.explains: After White plays Qg4, the immediate threat is against the weak g7 pawn, especially if Black has not castled. Castling is the natural defensive move, as alternatives like Kf8 allow White to push h4 and attack the kingside pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When the queen comes to g4 in similar positions, it targets the g7 pawn and creates kingside pressure. Castling is often the best way to neutralize this threat.
notes.plans: Black should castle to protect the king and prepare to develop the kingside pieces.

notes.explains: After White plays Nf3, the combination of bishops on d3 and d2, queen on g4, and knight on f3 sets up a potential Greek gift sacrifice on h7. If Black takes on f3, White can play Bxh7+ and follow with Ng5, leading to a strong attack.
notes.teaches: The Greek gift sacrifice (Bxh7+) is a classic attacking motif when the bishop on d3 and knight on f3 are in place. Recognizing the warning signs helps Black avoid falling into it.
notes.plans: Black should prevent the Greek gift by playing g6, creating a fianchetto setup, and then be ready to meet h4 with f5.

notes.explains: After Black plays g6, White pushes h5 to attack the kingside. Black's best response is f5, hitting the queen, but White can sacrifice the bishop on f5. If Black recaptures with the e-pawn, Qc4+ creates serious threats, and the h-pawn can open the h-file.
notes.teaches: When facing a fianchetto setup, advancing the h-pawn is a standard way to open lines. A bishop sacrifice can be justified if it exposes the king and opens attacking files.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack by opening the h-file and bringing the knight to g5, while Black must be careful about king safety.

notes.explains: In the main line with Black playing Be7, White again plays Qg4, targeting g7. Black has several defensive options, including Kf8 and g6. Kf8 is slow, allowing White to develop with Bd3 and then h4 to freeze the h-pawn, while g6 leads to a more complex fight.
notes.teaches: When the queen attacks g7, Black must choose a defensive plan that addresses the threat while maintaining development. Moving the king to f8 can be too passive, allowing White to build a lasting attack.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and preparing kingside breaks, while Black should look for active counterplay to avoid being overrun.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian Pin Variation, Black's bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3 to the king. White's e5 pawn is a key asset, restricting Black's d-pawn and making the d6 square a permanent outpost for a white knight.
notes.teaches: When you have a central pawn on the fifth rank, look for outposts like d6 for your knights, and use pawn pushes like h4 to start an attack before Black can consolidate.
notes.plans: White should aim for Nb5, targeting d6, and follow up with h4 to attack Black's kingside, especially if Black castles.

notes.explains: Black's move ...g6 weakens the kingside but prepares to fianchetto the bishop. White's immediate h4 is strong, preventing ...Bg7 and starting an attack. If Black tries ...Bh6, they must be willing to give up the exchange to reach equality.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens the kingside with ...g6, a quick h4 can be a powerful attacking resource, and you should be alert to exchange sacrifices to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: White should continue with h4, and if Black plays ...Bh6, consider taking on f8 to open the h-file and keep the attack rolling.

notes.explains: After ...Nc6 attacks the e5 pawn, White should protect it with Qg3. If Black plays ...a6, White can proceed with Nd6, and after ...Bxd6, exd6, Black's queen sortie with ...Qa5 is met by h5, exploiting the pin on the g6 pawn and the rook on h8.
notes.teaches: Protect important central pawns, and when the opponent creates a weakness like ...g6, use pawn pushes like h5 to open lines and exploit pins.
notes.plans: White should continue with h5, and if Black plays ...Qe5+, trade queens and then capture on g6, leaving Black with a passive bishop on c8.

notes.explains: Black's best defensive try is ...f6, breaking the center. After exf6, Bxf6, Black must be willing to give up the exchange to survive. If Black tries to save the rook with ...Rf7, h5 wins the g6 pawn, and ...g5 is met by Nd6, hitting the bishop and rook.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must sacrifice material to activate your pieces and relieve pressure. Recognize when a pawn break like ...f6 is necessary to counter a bind.
notes.plans: White should continue with h5, and if ...g5, play Nd6, then develop the bishop to b5 and castle, reaching a position with a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, White has a huge advantage, and Black is in a near-zugzwang. Black's pieces are tied up, and any move seems to lose material. White's pieces are optimally placed, and Black's bishop on c8 is still undeveloped.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and the opponent is cramped, look for ways to improve your pieces and avoid trades that give them air. Recognize when the opponent has no good moves.
notes.plans: White should aim to trade pieces on favorable terms, such as Bxf8, and then use the knight to dominate the board, while Black struggles to find a constructive move.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian Pin Variation, after Black plays Bb4 pinning the knight, White can sacrifice the exchange on f8. Black must be willing to give up the exchange and should play a6 to create luft and avoid further tactics. White's best is Bxf8, after which Black recaptures with the queen or king, and White's knight can retreat to d4 or the bishop can go to h6, depending on Black's choice.
notes.teaches: When facing a pin, sometimes giving up the exchange is the best defense to relieve pressure and activate pieces. Recognize when a sacrifice is necessary to avoid worse outcomes.
notes.plans: Black should play a6 to give the king an escape square and prepare to recapture on f8. White should proceed with Bxf8, then reposition the knight or bishop to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Black can try Qa5 to hit the pawn on e4, but White can defend with Bd2, and if Black plays b4 to add pressure, White has the resource Rh3 to bring another defender to the kingside. After Black plays d5 to give the bishop squares, White can respond with h5, maintaining a healthy advantage.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, look for defensive resources that also improve your piece placement, such as Rh3 to defend and prepare an attack. Always consider all your pieces, including the rook, in defense and offense.
notes.plans: White should continue with h5 to open the kingside, while Black must find ways to develop and create counterplay.

notes.explains: In the main line where Black castles, White's key move is Bh6, threatening mate on g7. Black must respond with g6, after which White can win the exchange by taking the rook, but White has even better: continue the attack with h4-h5 to rip open the kingside. Black's bishop on e7 is a liability compared to a dragon setup with Bg7.
notes.teaches: When attacking the king, prioritize opening lines and creating threats over winning material. A bishop on e7 can be a target, whereas a fianchettoed bishop on g7 would defend better.
notes.plans: White should play h4-h5 to open the g-file and continue the onslaught. Black must develop the queenside quickly to generate counterplay.

notes.explains: Black often tries Qa5 to fork pawns, but White can respond with Qg3, protecting both pawns. Black then plays d6 to create squares for development, but White can play Nb5, overprotecting c3 and threatening to capture on d6 and then c7 to trap the rook. Black finally develops a knight to d7, but White continues with h5, maintaining the initiative.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, use your pieces to defend multiple points simultaneously (Qg3) and create tactical threats (Nb5) that also improve your position. Black must prioritize development even while defending.
notes.plans: White should continue the attack with h5, while Black must find a way to develop the queenside and relieve pressure.

notes.explains: After Black plays Nxe5, White has a choice. Playing f4 gives Black chances with a6, hitting both knights, and after trades, White is only slightly better. The stronger move is to take on g6 with the h-pawn, opening the h-file and then taking the rook on f8, because the rook is now active on the open file. This brute-force attack is more effective than the slower f4.
notes.teaches: When attacking, prefer moves that open lines and increase the activity of your pieces over slower consolidating moves. An open file for the rook makes it a powerful attacker.
notes.plans: White should play hxg6, opening the h-file, and then take the rook on f8, maintaining the attack. Black must try to generate counterplay with the pieces.

notes.explains: In this Sicilian Pin Variation, after the early moves, White has a choice between f4 and taking on g6. The transcript suggests that taking on g6 with the h-pawn is more effective, opening the h-file for the rook and maintaining the attack.
notes.teaches: When attacking, prioritize opening lines for your rooks over slower positional moves. A rook on an open file is a powerful attacking asset.
notes.plans: White should play hxg6, opening the h-file, and then consider capturing the rook on f8 once it becomes active.

notes.explains: After the rook on f8 is captured, White plays Rd1 to add pressure on the center, while Black's queen goes to b6 to defend d6. White then plays Qh3, hitting h7, and after Black's h6 fails due to Nxd6, Black must play h5, leaving a backward pawn.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for tactics that overload the defender. Here, the bishop on d6 is overloaded, allowing a knight fork or capture.
notes.plans: White continues with Be2 to complete development, then prepares a sacrifice on h5 to break through.

notes.explains: White's best move is Bxh5, sacrificing the bishop to open the h-file. After gxh5, Qxh5 threatens mate on h7, forcing Black to play Bg7, which removes a defender of d6, allowing Nxd6.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be justified if they lead to a decisive attack. Removing defenders and creating mate threats are key tactical motifs.
notes.plans: White plays Bxh5, and after the forced sequence, captures on d6 with a winning advantage.

notes.explains: Black has an alternative early move, Bf8, which resets the pieces and gives Black chances to develop. However, White can maintain a healthy advantage with Bd3, simply being ahead in development.
notes.teaches: When your opponent retreats a piece to an original square, they lose time. Use that lead in development to create pressure and let targets appear naturally.
notes.plans: White plays Bd3, keeping the development advantage and looking for natural attacking chances.

notes.explains: In the Sicilian Pin Variation, Black has played ...Bb4 to pin the knight on c3 to the king, creating immediate pressure on White's center and development.
notes.teaches: Pins in the opening can disrupt the opponent's natural development and challenge their control of key central squares.
notes.plans: White should consider moves like Bd3 or Qd3 to break the pin, or a3 to ask the bishop to declare its intentions, while Black aims to maintain the pin and develop harmoniously.

notes.explains: White's queen to c2 is a precise move-order device in this Queen's Gambit Declined line. It prevents Black from playing Bf5, which would be a comfortable developing move that could lead to queen trades and an equal game despite Black's pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In the opening, small move-order subtleties can cut out entire defensive lines for the opponent. A queen move like Qc2 can be prophylactic, stopping a key developing resource before it becomes available.
notes.plans: White continues development with e3, Be2, and O-O, while Black develops normally with Be7 and Nbd7.

notes.explains: White deliberately avoids putting the knight on f3, instead planning to place it on e2. This is because the knight on e2 supports a different central plan: playing f3 and building a big pawn center with e4, rather than the standard Carlsbad minority attack on the queenside.
notes.teaches: The choice of piece placement (knight on e2 vs f3) determines the entire middlegame plan. Here, the knight on e2 keeps the f-pawn free to advance, supporting a central expansion with e4.
notes.plans: White will play f3, then e4, aiming for a space advantage in the center. Black will try to free their cramped position, possibly with the Lasker freeing maneuver.

notes.explains: Black's rook to e8 is a common freeing idea in cramped positions, giving the bishop access to f8 to reroute. Additionally, Black has the Lasker freeing maneuver in mind, which involves trading pieces and occupying the center, especially if White's knight were on f3.
notes.teaches: When cramped, look for freeing maneuvers that trade pieces and open lines. Rook moves like Re8 can prepare bishop rerouting and create counterplay.
notes.plans: Black will aim to free their position, potentially with ...Ne4 or ...Bf8, while White continues with f3 and e4.

notes.explains: In this Queen's Gambit Declined position, Black's pieces are cramped and he seeks a freeing maneuver. The Lasker freeing idea is ...Nf6-e4, aiming to trade pieces and gain central space, but here it is flawed because the bishop on g5 is attacked and the knight on e4 is insufficiently defended.
notes.teaches: The Lasker freeing maneuver (...Ne4) is a typical resource in these structures, but its viability depends on tactical details like the defense of the knight and the activity of the opposing bishop.
notes.plans: Black should look for alternative freeing moves, such as preparing ...Ne4 with ...Nf8, which also defends h7.

notes.explains: White can refute the premature ...Ne4 with a tactic: after ...Nxc3, White has Bxh7+ winning a pawn, and if Black retreats the knight to f6, White has Nb5, which traps the queen on c7 after ...Qxb5 Bxc7, or if Black avoids the capture, Nc7 and Ne6 create double attacks.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are clustered and uncoordinated, look for tactical blows that exploit the lack of escape squares for the queen or other pieces.
notes.plans: White should continue with Nb5, threatening to trap the queen and win material, or if Black gives the queen an escape, follow up with Nc7 and Ne6.

notes.explains: Black's best try is to prepare ...Ne4 with ...Nf8, which defends h7 and gives the queen more space, making the freeing maneuver more viable.
notes.teaches: When a freeing move is tactically unsound, look for preparatory moves that address the specific tactical weaknesses (e.g., defending a pawn, giving the queen a square).
notes.plans: Black should play ...Nf8, intending ...Ne4 next, while White should seek ways to maintain pressure and prevent Black's freeing plan.

notes.explains: In this Queen's Gambit Declined position, Black's freeing move ...e4 is not good because it allows tactics involving the bishop on g5 and the knight on e5. Black prepares it with ...Nf8, defending h7 and avoiding the immediate tactical refutations.
notes.teaches: When a freeing move is tactically unsound, the opponent may prepare it with a quiet move that addresses the tactical issues. Recognize when a move like ...Ne4 is only good after preparatory moves.
notes.plans: White should prevent ...Ne4 with f3, stopping Black's freeing maneuver and maintaining the bind.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...Be6, overprotecting d5, Black signals the intention to play ...c5 to break in the center and gain activity. White needs a move that discourages ...c5 while continuing to prepare e4.
notes.teaches: Overprotection of a central pawn often indicates a planned pawn break. The opponent should look for moves that either prevent the break or make it costly.
notes.plans: White should choose a developing move that supports the center, such as Rook to d1, which indirectly discourages ...c5 by keeping the d-file open for tactics.

notes.explains: White considers moves like a3 to prepare b4, but this is too slow and allows Black to counter with ...a5, making b4 difficult. The knight on e5 changes the character of the position, making a queenside expansion less relevant than central play.
notes.teaches: In positions with a knight on e5, focus on central breaks (e4) rather than flank expansions. Wasting time on slow plans can allow the opponent to free themselves.
notes.plans: White should prioritize central development, such as Rook d1, to prepare e4 and keep the initiative.

notes.explains: With the rook on d1, White has tactical threats against h7 if Black plays ...c5, because the bishop on b3 (or similar) can take on h7 with the rook supporting. This makes ...c5 risky for Black.
notes.teaches: A rook on an open file can support tactical blows on the king side, making central pawn breaks by the opponent more dangerous. Use such indirect pressure to restrain the opponent's freeing moves.
notes.plans: White will continue preparing e4, while keeping the rook on d1 to punish any ...c5 attempt.

notes.explains: In this Queen's Gambit Declined position, White's d4-pawn is only defended once, making it a target. Black's natural plan is to play ...c5, attacking the center, and White must anticipate this.
notes.teaches: When choosing a move, consider your opponent's most natural plan and place your pieces to discourage it. Here, Rook to d1 both defends the d4-pawn and prepares to occupy the open d-file after ...cxd4.
notes.plans: White can play Rfd1 to double rooks on the d-file, or play Kh1 to avoid tactics on the a7-g1 diagonal, then prepare to advance in the center.

notes.explains: White might be tempted to play e4 to build a strong center, but this is premature. Black can respond ...dxe4, opening the d-file and putting pressure on the d4-pawn. If White recaptures with the f-pawn, the e4-square becomes weak, allowing ...Ng4, forking and creating threats on the kingside.
notes.teaches: Before breaking in the center, ensure your pawns are adequately defended and that recapturing won't weaken key squares. Central breaks can backfire if they create tactical opportunities for the opponent.
notes.plans: White should avoid e4 until the d4-pawn is solidly defended and the king is safe, perhaps after Kh1 and Rfe1.

notes.explains: Kasparov's preparatory moves like Re1 and Kh1 are designed to avoid the tactical pitfalls of an early e4. Kh1 anticipates the weakening of the dark squares and the possibility of ...Ng4, which would target the h2-pawn.
notes.teaches: Long-term preparation involves foreseeing your opponent's counterplay and making small prophylactic moves that neutralize it before committing to a central advance.
notes.plans: White continues with Re1, Kh1, and then prepares to advance in the center once the king is safe and the d4-pawn is secure.

notes.explains: White has a comfortable grip on the position: Black's only active idea is c5, which is not good enough, and Black lacks freeing moves like Ne4. White's pieces are well-placed and Black's pieces are somewhat cramped.
notes.teaches: When you have more space and a solid grip, you can afford to spend time on preparatory moves that improve your position, because your opponent has no active counterplay.
notes.plans: White should continue improving pieces and preparing the central break e4, while keeping an eye on the d4 pawn and potential dark-square weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black is cramped and lacks freeing moves like c5 or Ne4. In such positions, trading pieces is a common strategy to reduce congestion and gain more freedom.
notes.teaches: When you have less space, trading pieces can relieve cramping and make your position easier to play, as fewer pieces get in each other's way.
notes.plans: Black should look for trades, but must be careful about the pressure on the diagonal and the weakness of the d5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's attempt to trade with Nd7 is a retreat that gives up control of central squares, allowing White to maneuver even more freely. White can then take on e7 with the rook, maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves that concede central control can be costly, even if they facilitate trades, because they allow the opponent to improve their piece activity.
notes.plans: After Black's Nd7, White can capture on e7 and then prepare e4, but must still be wary of c5 and c4 tactics.

notes.explains: White has been preparing e4, but must first address the defense of the d4 pawn and potential c5/c4 tactics. Moves like Qf2 and Nf4 help solidify the position before the break.
notes.teaches: Before executing a central pawn break, ensure that all your key pawns are defended and that you have addressed tactical threats, so the break is sound.
notes.plans: White should finish preparation (e.g., Qf2, Nf4) and then play e4 when the time is right, after dealing with c5 and c4 ideas.

notes.explains: The d4 pawn is under-defended; the e4 square is well covered, but the dark squares around d4 need reinforcement. Qf2 is a useful move that adds a defender to d4 and prepares the e4 break.
notes.teaches: Before playing a central pawn break, ensure your key central pawns are adequately defended, especially if the opponent has pressure on them.
notes.plans: After Qf2, prepare e4 once the c5-c4 and Ng4 tactical ideas are neutralized.

notes.explains: The e4 break is only safe after dealing with two specific tactical threats: c5-c4 (attacking the bishop) and Ng4 (harassing the queen). Once those are handled, e4 can be played.
notes.teaches: When considering a central break, identify and neutralize the opponent's typical counter-tactics first.
notes.plans: Play e4 after ensuring the bishop has flight squares and the queen can meet Ng4 effectively.

notes.explains: After e4 exf4, recapturing with the f-pawn opens lines and gives White a powerful pawn roller. If Black declines the capture, White pushes e5 and then advances the f-pawn, creating a dangerous attack.
notes.teaches: A central pawn break that opens lines for your pieces and creates a pawn majority can be decisive if the opponent doesn't accept the challenge.
notes.plans: If Black captures, recapture with the f-pawn and continue with d5 to open the diagonal. If Black declines, push e5 and then f4-f5.

notes.explains: After the e4 break, White's grip loosens as files open and Black's pieces become active. White must strike quickly with concrete moves like d5, opening the diagonal and targeting the a7 pawn.
notes.teaches: After a successful break, maintain the initiative with forcing moves; don't allow the opponent to consolidate.
notes.plans: Play d5 to open the bishop's diagonal and create threats, possibly winning the a7 pawn.

notes.explains: In the tactical sequence, White can use pins to exploit Black's misplaced pieces. Rook to d1 pins the knight, and Black cannot defend everything.
notes.teaches: Look for pins to win material or gain a decisive advantage when the opponent's pieces are awkwardly placed.
notes.plans: After cxd5, play Bb5 and then Rd1 to pin the knight, winning material.

notes.explains: In this position, black's pieces are awkwardly placed, and white can exploit this by pinning the knight on d5 with Rc1-d1. The pin is decisive because black cannot easily unpin without losing material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated, look for pins that tie them down and prevent them from improving.
notes.plans: Play Rc1-d1 to pin the knight, then increase pressure and capture the pinned piece if black cannot defend adequately.

notes.explains: White has a passed pawn on d5, which is strong because it harasses the black knight on e6 and controls key squares. Advancing to d6 would be a mistake because black can simply take on e1, removing the rook and saving the piece.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn is often more valuable when it stays on a square that restricts the opponent's pieces, rather than advancing prematurely and allowing tactical simplifications.
notes.plans: Keep the pawn on d5, retreat the bishop to maintain the bind, and continue to pressure black's position.

notes.explains: Black's plan of h6 and g5 to break the pin is an overextension on the kingside. White can respond by placing the bishop on f2, which covers key squares and leaves black with weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside with pawn moves, you don't need to change your plan drastically; your pieces can often exploit the new weaknesses.
notes.plans: Continue with the normal plan of central play (e4 break), while using the bishop on f2 to control light squares and target the weakened kingside.

notes.explains: In this position, White's light-squared bishop on d3 and the knight on e5 give strong control over light squares, especially f5. Black's attempt to weaken with c4 only creates weaknesses that White can exploit.
notes.teaches: When your opponent weakens squares, occupy them with your pieces. Here, the bishop can go to f5 to dominate the weakened light squares.
notes.plans: Continue with the normal plan: develop, castle, and use the light-square control to increase pressure.

notes.explains: Black's early h6 and knight e8 to trade dark-squared bishops costs time, as the knight retreats and the rook is blocked. This gives White time to develop and maintain the initiative.
notes.teaches: Trading pieces to relieve pressure is fine, but if it costs too much time, it can backfire. Use the extra time to improve your position and start your own plan.
notes.plans: White can castle, play rook e1, and prepare e4 to open the center, following the standard plan.

notes.explains: When Black plays knight h5 to force the trade of the dark-squared bishops, White must decide where to recapture. If White recaptures with the queen, the e5 square becomes weaker, but White can still choose the right knight placement.
notes.teaches: After a bishop trade, reassess the resulting pawn structure and piece placement. Sometimes it's better to recapture with a piece that keeps control of key squares.
notes.plans: White can play knight e2 to maintain control of f4 and keep the position solid, avoiding time-wasting moves.

notes.explains: The idea of attacking with h4 and castling queenside becomes more relevant when the opponent has a pawn on g5 that can be used as a hook to open lines against the king.
